title: Critical Indigenous Studies
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the Global Indigenous Studies degree, its rationale, central concepts and key skills. This is an interdisciplinary course that studies the history and core learning principles of the discipline of Indigenous studies, also exploring how critical and creative thinking occurs within Indigenous studies globally today. Students will engage with informed, present-day debates relating to Indigenous ways of knowing, being and doing including exploring major concepts and projects underpinning the discipline such as decolonisation, cultural resurgence and revitalisation, and identity and representation. At the conclusion of the course, students will have developed level-appropriate research and communication skills that are vital for both success in the Bachelor of Global Indigenous Studies and an increasing range of potential career paths. They will also be able to demonstrate a foundational understanding of the importance of centralising Indigenous studies' role in broader knowledge creation and ethically aware problem solving. All ABOR courses are developed in alignment with the Wollotuka Institute’s Cultural Standards Framework, ensuring respect for cultural principles and practices.
learning_outcomes: Examine historical and political influences on Global Indigenous peoples and communities.
Outline the complexity of debates within the discipline including the historical importance of issues such as Indigenous identity, culture and knowledges.
Apply introductory knowledge of the discipline of Global Indigenous Studies to critically engage with key movements relating to Indigenous peoples and current global issues.

title: Blak Australia
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Blak Australia introduces students to Aboriginal ways of knowing, being and doing as living knowledge systems. Students will confront the weight of history, including colonial policies, representations and practices, and their ongoing impacts on Aboriginal lives. They will also engage with stories of resistance, resurgence and leadership that have reshaped communities and the nation. The course builds the tools to understand how power, policy and history intersect and to recognise the strength of Blak perspectives in driving justice, culture and change. All ABOR courses are developed in alignment with the Wollotuka Institute’s Cultural Standards Framework, ensuring respect for cultural principles and practices.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate understanding of Aboriginal ways of knowing, being and doing, and their significance in contemporary contexts.
Identify and evaluate contemporary challenges facing Aboriginal, including education, health, housing, employment and other domains where movements are challenging settler colonialism.
Analyse the ongoing impacts of colonial policies and practices, and evaluate Aboriginal experiences, perspectives and resistance.
Respectfully engage in dialogue informed by Aboriginal ways of communicating, including storytelling, collaboration, listening and knowledge sharing.
Explain how Connection to Country and cultural practices are central to Aboriginal identity, wellbeing and healing.

title: Community Engagement: Respect and Reciprocity
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Students in this course will explore how Aboriginal communities live, work and thrive in contemporary Australia. They will gain insight into the structures, relationships and dynamics that shape community life, and how these have been impacted by colonisation. A holistic approach highlights the political, social, cultural and economic forces influencing communities today, while also recognising the resilience, strength and reciprocity that underpin Aboriginal ways of working together. By the end, students will be equipped with the understanding and respect needed to engage ethically and effectively with Aboriginal people in professional and community contexts. All ABOR courses are developed in alignment with the Wollotuka Institute’s Cultural Standards Framework, ensuring respect for cultural principles and practices.
learning_outcomes: Describe and evaluate decision-making processes, leadership, and the principles of respect and reciprocity in Aboriginal communities.
Analyse the historical and political influences that have shaped Aboriginal community structures.
Explain cultural differences between Aboriginal and European communities and the role of oral traditions in sustaining knowledge.
Demonstrate understanding of how Aboriginal communities operate and the processes that shape relationships within them.

title: Blak Rights and the Fight for Justice
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Justice? Or Just Us? This course asks what human rights really mean in theory and in practice, and how they have been applied or denied, to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples in Australia. Students will examine international mechanisms such as the United Nations and Australia’s responsibilities as a nation state, while also engaging with Aboriginal responses that assert self-determination and demand justice. Along the way, they will learn from the long history of Aboriginal activism and community action and consider how rights frameworks continue to be reshaped by Blak voices and movements today. All ABOR courses are developed in alignment with the Wollotuka Institute’s Cultural Standards Framework, ensuring respect for cultural principles and practices.
learning_outcomes: Describe and critique concepts of human rights and social justice through Aboriginal perspectives, past and present.
Critically analyse contemporary justice issues including health, incarceration, leadership, and advocacy.
Evaluate the institutions and mechanisms that aim to protect human rights in Australia, considering their accessibility, effectiveness, and limitations for Aboriginal peoples.
Examine Aboriginal resistance, governance, and truth-telling as pathways to justice beyond colonial rights frameworks.

title: Yarning, Media and Futures
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Storytelling is the heart of this course. Through yarning, interactive learning and practical application, students examine how Aboriginal knowledge and perspectives have been expressed, silenced, resisted and reimagined across journalism, mass media and digital platforms, and how emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence are reshaping the landscape. Along the way, they will sharpen critical thinking, test notions of truth in complex media systems, and build the skills to communicate as informed, future-ready professionals. All ABOR courses are developed in alignment with the Wollotuka Institute’s Cultural Standards Framework, ensuring respect for cultural principles and practices.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate culturally informed media literacy by testing truth, verifying information, and communicating effectively in complex information environments.
Evaluate the influence of power structures, algorithms, and artificial intelligence on media and communication systems, and their implications for Aboriginal representation and digital sovereignty.
Critically analyse how Aboriginal knowledge and perspectives have been represented, silenced, resisted, and reclaimed across historical and contemporary media systems.
Apply yarning as a methodology for respectful dialogue, storytelling, and collaborative knowledge-building.

title: Global Indigenous Comparative Studies
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course provides the opportunity for students to explore Indigenous cultures outside Australia. Through comparative analysis, students will examine distinctions and similarities between Indigenous peoples and communities throughout the world, developing a greater understanding of other Indigenous peoples in contemporary settings. The course aims to amplify the voices and experiences of Indigenous groups and communities through the promotion of strength-based approaches to the ongoing challenges of settler-colonialism and in identifying transnational networks that demonstrate growing solidarities across the globe. Engaging with online platforms and digital information sources, this course encourages students to recognise the many connecting features of Indigenous cultures, politics and societies and experience these movements through current case studies. All ABOR courses are developed in alignment with the Wollotuka Institute’s Cultural Standards Framework, ensuring respect for cultural principles and practices.
learning_outcomes: Examine comparative cultures, analysing similarities and differences in colonisation processes and impacts on Indigenous peoples.
Use online technology to research Indigenous cultures, transnational networks and relationships.
Assess strategies of contemporary Indigenous groups and the various approaches to political resistance, cultural resurgence and struggles for self-determination and sovereignty.
Explain key aspects of various Indigenous cultures around the world.

title: Aboriginal Cultural Practices
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course provides an immersive cultural experience where students are welcomed into Aboriginal spaces to engage with cultural knowledge on our terms. Through direct participation in a range of practices, students will gain a deeper understanding of Aboriginal ways of knowing and being. This applied program emphasises learning through engagement with Aboriginal practitioners from local communities, ensuring the experience is grounded in respect for Aboriginal sovereignty and perspectives. All ABOR courses are developed in alignment with the Wollotuka Institute’s Cultural Standards Framework, ensuring respect for cultural principles and practices.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate cultural awareness and respect for Aboriginal ways of knowing, being, and doing.
Communicate a clear and informed understanding of the significance of cultural expression, identity, belonging, and community within Aboriginal contexts.
Apply practical skills learned from Aboriginal cultural practices in a way that reflects cultural understanding and respect for tradition.
Actively participate in selected Aboriginal cultural practices.

title: Aboriginal Education, Relationships and Responsibilities
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course explores the ongoing impacts of colonial and current policies on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students, families, and communities when accessing the schooling system in New South Wales. Students will critically reflect on their own positionality, and the ways their identities and experiences shape their teaching practice. Students will also learn approaches to nurture Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students’ sense of belonging at school, and become aware of their responsibilities to design teaching and learning experiences that authentically represent Aboriginal pedagogies, histories, cultures, knowledges, and lived experiences. This course prioritises relationship building and collaboration between course tutors, initial teacher education students, and community through Aboriginal ways of knowing, doing, being, and relating. All ABOR courses are developed in alignment with the Wollotuka Institute’s Cultural Standards Framework, ensuring respect for cultural principles and practices.
learning_outcomes: Design curriculum that respectfully and authentically represents Aboriginal histories, cultures, knowledges, and lived experiences.
Apply Aboriginal pedagogy appropriately in teaching and learning.
Demonstrate Aboriginal ways of knowing, doing, and being informed by Aboriginal epistemologies.

Evaluate best practice approaches to Aboriginal Education that support and affirm Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultural identities and contribute to student wellbeing and educational outcomes in culturally safe schooling environments.
Identify colonial and current policies and evaluate their ongoing impacts on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities, including implications for education.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Positionality and Relationality to Aboriginal Education

title: Indigenous People and Sustainable Environments
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: As the custodians of the oldest continuing cultures on Earth, Indigenous Peoples across the globe demonstrate an extraordinary capacity to withstand the most drastic processes of change, as well as holding acute understandings of our environments. These vital capabilities to adapt to environmental and other external factors provide an invaluable lens through which we can explore climate change and sustainable environments from Indigenous viewpoints. From historical adaptation to current issues faced by Indigenous peoples on the frontlines, this course considers both the vulnerability and resilience of Indigenous peoples in policy and practice across the world. Focusing on a range of different global locations and the Indigenous peoples of those places, we explore the ongoing challenges of colonialism in all its forms with an emphasis on the resistance and ingenuity of Indigenous peoples in leadership, innovation, adaptation and survival today and into the future. All ABOR courses are developed in alignment with the Wollotuka Institute’s Cultural Standards Framework, ensuring respect for cultural principles and practices.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the diversity of environmental experiences of global Indigenous peoples including adaptation and resilience.
Identify Indigenous philosophies relating to the environment and their broader relevance.
Examine the fundamental impacts of colonisation on the environment and its peoples, historically and today.
Explore the ongoing challenges Indigenous peoples face protecting their territories.

title: Aboriginal Knowledge Systems
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Explores Aboriginal knowledges from pre-colonial history to contemporary Australia, through such areas as Country, kinship, law, lore, governance, water, land and food. All ABOR courses are developed in alignment with the Wollotuka Institute’s Cultural Standards Framework, ensuring respect for cultural principles and practices.
learning_outcomes: Apply an informed and reflexive understanding of Aboriginal cultural knowledge and practices
Provide an understanding of the diversity of Aboriginal cultures and people.
Challenge Terra Nullius and provide critical analysis of the ongoing issues stemming from the disruption of traditional knowledges and practices.
Provide an insight into traditional Aboriginal Australia before European arrival and invasion.

title: Blak Advocacy: Empowerment and Solidarity
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course is designed for students to develop an understanding of community development and advocacy in Aboriginal contexts while building awareness of social justice praxis. It provides students with the opportunity to develop a high-level understanding of Aboriginal peoples’ capacity for community development and need for advocacy skills. Students are exposed to the theoretical underpinnings of empowerment and are encouraged to develop skills in effectively meeting demands for more equitable outcomes for Aboriginal peoples in an Australian context. All ABOR courses are developed in alignment with the Wollotuka Institute’s Cultural Standards Framework, ensuring respect for cultural principles and practices.
learning_outcomes: Examine the impact of socio-economic and political policies for Aboriginal peoples with an emphasis on empowerment principles.
Analyse the needs of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities and demonstrate the capacity to respond effectively.
Design effective advocacy strategies to promote social justice for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.

title: Business Innovation and Entrepreneurship
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to key workplace skills and competencies required when working with Indigenous business or Indigenous employees. This course provides students with the opportunity to build skills and knowledges within the particular lens of Indigenous work and enterprise, community building and cultural affirming practices. At the conclusion of the course, students will have developed level-appropriate research, communication and work focused skills that are vital for success in the Bachelor of Global Indigenous Studies and a range of potential career paths. Upon successful completion, students will also be able to demonstrate and apply a concrete understanding of the importance of centralising Indigenous studies' role in Indigenous knowledge creation, ethically conscious problem solving, and policy analysis.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate effective research and communication skills in written, verbal and online literacies
Develop professional written pieces for application to Indigenous work and enterprise
Demonstrate knowledge of the complexity of workplaces, including entrepreneurial and professional behaviours
Examine and define the nature of diversity and cross-cultural knowledges and skills and apply this to the context of Indigenous work and enterprise

title: Indigenous Research
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This introductory research course explores culturally capable and responsive approaches to Indigenous research. The program critically examines the historical and ongoing impact of Western research on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Country and communities. An exploration of Indigenous ways of knowing, being, and doing that inform Indigenous research principles and methodologies is incorporated. The course fosters the development of ethical research projects, processes, and engagement, and explores how research leadership, results, and benefits can be returned to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities. All ABOR courses are developed in alignment with the Wollotuka Institute’s Cultural Standards Framework, ensuring respect for cultural principles and practices.
learning_outcomes: Communicate an awareness of Indigenous research methodologies, knowledge, and perspectives.
Demonstrate knowledge of ethical principles and practices that respect Indigenous cultures in research contexts.
Identify methods to protect and honor Indigenous knowledge in research.
Demonstrate cultural awareness and capability in planning and proposing research.
Evidence critical evaluation of Western research histories and approaches.

title: Global Indigenous Human Rights
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course engages with Indigenous responses to and use of international human rights instruments including treaty bodies and agencies and other relevant international law mechanisms. It offers insight into the role of such bodies in the effective delivery of social justice for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples in Australia and Indigenous peoples globally. By examining some of the key issues identified by Indigenous peoples, the course provides critical development in understanding the significant socio-political and economic factors impacting on the delivery of human rights and social justice more broadly. All ABOR courses are developed in alignment with the Wollotuka Institute’s Cultural Standards Framework, ensuring respect for cultural principles and practices.
learning_outcomes: Examine the significance of rights to environmental and biodiversity protection and Indigenous land management practices.
Critically evaluate the effectiveness of international treaty bodies and agencies, such as the United Nations, in promoting social justice for Indigenous peoples globally.
Identify key debates relating to racism, self-determination and settler-colonialism.
Analyse Indigenous responses to challenges to human rights, providing evidence-based insights into their strategies and impacts.
Justify the inclusion of Indigenous peoples' voices and experiences in discussions on social justice.

title: Aboriginal Studies: Knowledge and Blak Perspectives
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Explores Aboriginal knowledges and practices of from pre-colonial history to contemporary Australia and how Aboriginal communities have survived and continue to live today. All ABOR courses are developed in alignment with the Wollotuka Institute’s Cultural Standards Framework, ensuring respect for cultural principles and practice.
learning_outcomes: Challenge Terra Nullius and provide critical analysis of the ongoing issues stemming from the disruption of traditional knowledges and practices
Provide an insight into traditional Aboriginal Australia before European arrival and invasion
Provide the foundation for future knowledge relating to contemporary Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander issues
Provide an understanding of the diversity of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultures/people

title: Aboriginal Professional Experience
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course is a core component of the Bachelor of Global Indigenous Studies program which provides students with a professional placement in an associated workforce related to the student's major studies. The placement is the equivalent of 210 hours and is designed to maximise Aboriginal-related experiences in a cross-cultural work environment. Placements are flexible and can be paid, unpaid, completed in voluntary roles or community organisations/workplaces, including both the government or private sectors, and will enhance student’s capabilities related to the program’s objectives. Students will also have the opportunity to attend field trips to peak Aboriginal organisations, such as local Aboriginal Land Councils and Regional Alliances, facilitating networking and relationship-building with key external stakeholders. All ABOR courses are developed in alignment with the Wollotuka Institute’s Cultural Standards Framework, ensuring respect for cultural principles and practices.
learning_outcomes: Experience real exposure to the professional chosen fields of students in their major subject area of choice.
Acquire a cross-cultural understanding of the political, social and economic world of work.
Explore relevant knowledge and experience in genuine work-related practices in the work environment.
Outline the theoretical and knowledge bases of the program and adapt these to practical workplace situations.
Examine skills required for the workplace, including communication and teamwork.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Students must demonstrate competency in all listed assessments (individual)

title: Professional Practice and Entrepreneurship
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course will prepare students for their capstone project/placement whilst embedding many critical skills for successful work life. Students will examine embodying Indigenous interests in communication, career development and professional and entrepreneurial identities. Students who successfully complete this course will develop strategies for respectful and culturally appropriate communication via the multiple methods including social media and utilise opportunities to apply them. They will be encouraged to develop strategies for resilience to aid their response to new experiences like learning new software, new work and employer expectations.
learning_outcomes: Develop professional written pieces for application to the career and workplace context
Apply extensive research and communication skills in written, verbal and online literacies
Apply knowledge of the complexity of workplace cultures to individual and group entrepreneurial and professional behaviours and tasks
Demonstrate comprehensive knowledge of organisational structures, technologies and how to negotiate them

title: Contemporary Aboriginal Studies
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: ""The idea of contested stories and multiple discourses about the past, by different communities, is closely linked to the politics of everyday contemporary indigenous life. It is very much the fabric of communities that value oral ways of knowing. These contested accounts are stored within genealogies, within the landscape, within weavings and carvings, even within the personal names that people carried. The means by which these histories were stored was through their systems of knowledge."" (Tuhiwai Smith, L. 1999, p.33). This course has been designed to provide the foundation to knowledge within the course work masters. The issues are relevant to the current debates within the contemporary Aboriginal and non Aboriginal communities. The final weeks of the course will entail students looking at their local Aboriginal communities, in particular their response to government policies, media coverage and successful community projects.
learning_outcomes: Develop an understanding on the processes used by Aboriginal people to negotiate appropriate futures.
Develop an understanding of Aboriginal perspectives within current social debates
Critically analyse policies that have impacted on Aboriginal cultural heritage
Develop an understanding on the importance of the Aboriginal voice within the academic context
Develop an understanding of Aboriginal knowledges/world views in particular those knowledges of the local area

title: Sovereignty and Reconciliation
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with a critical understanding of contemporary race relations in Australia. Key topics include Indigenous sovereignty, European Imperialism, and Indigenous and non-Indigenous activism to address ongoing colonisation. The course critically analyses public policy and discourse for the purpose of generating an equitable future for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples in 21st Century Australia. The course will examine diverse perspectives on reconciliation, Australian Citizenship and the legacies of European Imperialism, and Indigenous sovereignty, while engaging with healing frameworks and Indigenous-led initiatives towards self-determination. All ABOR courses are developed in alignment with the Wollotuka Institute’s Cultural Standards Framework, ensuring respect for cultural principles and practices.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a critical understanding of race relations that impact on Indigenous people in Australia.
Analyse the historical and ongoing legacies of Dispossession and Assimilation with a focus on social justice.
Reflect on Aboriginal experiences and resistance, exploring their role in shaping justice and Sovereignty efforts.
Apply insights into European Imperialism advocating for Indigenous Sovereignty.
Evaluate perspectives on reconciliation, race relations and the legacies of ongoing colonisation.

title: Fundamentals of Accounting
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Financial accounting and management accounting concepts provide the very foundation for business decision making. This course provides an introduction to financial accounting by analysing the accounting function and the preparation of conventional financial statements. Students will develop the initial skills of financial management while beginning to engage in appropriate ethical practices.
learning_outcomes: Prepare and interpret financial statements according to conventional methods of accounting.
Apply ethical decision making within the accounting environment.
Calculate and analyse financial information relevant to decision making.
Evaluate Indigenous perspectives on Corporate Social Responsibility.
Identify, analyse and evaluate financial information relevant to the operating, investing and financing decisions of a business entity.
Discuss and explain the nature and purpose of accounting.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Mid Semester Test in Week 6 (covering topics week 1 to 4)

title: Aboriginal Communities: Advocacy, Development and Partnerships
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course develops an advanced understanding of how Aboriginal communities operate in contemporary Australia, with a focus on communication, advocacy, development, and partnerships. Students will gain insight into the structures and diversity of Aboriginal communities, and how political, social, economic, and cultural factors shaped by colonisation continue to influence community life. The course highlights the resilience of Aboriginal communities and the ways they have adapted and advocated in response to ongoing challenges. Emphasis is placed on communication, cultural protocols, and respectful engagement as the basis for effective community relationships. Students will examine historical and contemporary forms of advocacy, including politics, the arts, and social media, and consider the role of allyship in supporting Aboriginal voices. Through case studies and applied learning activities, students will develop skills in community planning, evaluation, and partnership-building grounded in Aboriginal self-determination All ABOR courses are developed in alignment with the Wollotuka Institute’s Cultural Standards Framework, ensuring respect for cultural principles and practices.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the different communication processes in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities.
Describe the historical development of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities and evaluate the impact of political factors on contemporary Indigenous society.
Create frameworks for development relating to funding, community cohesion, and sovereignty of communities.
Explain the cultural diversity across Aboriginal communities and how this informs decision-making processes.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Live Oral Presentation and Community Plan

title: Aboriginal Education
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course centres Aboriginal Education as a relational and collaborative practice between course tutors, initial teacher education students, and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities. Students explore the ongoing impacts of colonial and current policies on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples’ access to education, with a particular focus on the New South Wales schooling system. Through critical reflection on their own positionality, students examine how their identities and experiences shape their approach to teaching. Students will also learn approaches to being culturally responsive, and become aware of their responsibilities to design teaching and learning that authentically represent Aboriginal pedagogies, histories, cultures, knowledges, and lived experiences. All ABOR courses are developed in alignment with the Wollotuka Institute’s Cultural Standards Framework, ensuring respect for cultural principles and practices.
learning_outcomes: Apply Aboriginal pedagogy appropriately in teaching and learning.
Design strategies that support the safety and belonging of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in educational settings.

Apply effective practices and principles to build meaningful relationships, partnerships, and processes for consultation with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students, families, communities, and key stakeholders.
Demonstrate Aboriginal ways of knowing, doing, and being informed by Aboriginal epistemologies
Design curriculum that respectfully and authentically represents Aboriginal histories, cultures, knowledges, and lived experiences.
Identify and evaluate the ongoing impacts of colonial and current policies on Aboriginal communities.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Exploring best practice approaches to Aboriginal Education

title: Aboriginal People and Law
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course explores the impacts of the legal histories and contemporary issues faced by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples in an Australian legal context. Students will gain an understanding of British colonial law as a tool of colonisation and invasion. The course examines several legal cases, the doctrine of terra nullius, criminalisation, and Black deaths in custody. The course also examines contemporary social and economic issues stemming from broader colonial legal systems including the over- representation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples in the criminal justice system, child protection, youth justice, land rights and Native Title. In considering remedies, the course highlights the importance of self-determination in solutions such as circle sentencing, justice reinvestment and other community-based approaches. All ABOR courses are developed in alignment with the Wollotuka Institute’s Cultural Standards Framework, ensuring respect for cultural principles and practices.
learning_outcomes: Examine key foundational concepts and legal instruments relating to colonial policies and legislations such as the Aborigines Protection Act 1909 (NSW) and assimilation policies.
Explore culturally responsive understandings of key legal issues affecting Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples in Australia.
Explain the foundations of legal inequity as it relates to social justice.
Examine the historical impacts of Western legal instruments and their role in colonialism

title: Decolonisation: An Australian Context
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: "The heritage of an indigenous people is not merely a collection of objects, stories and ceremonies, but a complete knowledge system with its own concepts of epistemology, philosophy, and scientific and logical validity." (Battiste, M. 2000 p.19) This subject has been designed to explore the process and framework by which indigenous peoples currently find ourselves addressing issues, within a framework that embodies the concept of decolonisation. This subject will analyze the process and impact of colonization and imperialism on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Australians, specifically, Euro-centrism and the resulting representation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Australians. It will explore the confluence of differing world views; indigenous and non-indigenous.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse knowledge that exists about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Australians and has 'defined' Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Australians; specifically explore the impact of colonisation and euro centrism on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Australians
Develop an understanding of Australian Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander knowledges/world views
Explore Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Australian experiences and challenges of decolonisation
Develop an understanding of different world views and their confluence; specifically Australian Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander and Western/European world views
Listen to and centralise the voices of Australian Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
Develop an understanding of the concept and framework of decolonisation.

title: Financial Accounting and Reporting
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Financial Accounting and Reporting develops two main themes for students. Firstly, it introduces various accounting standards and accounting policy choices. Secondly, it investigates applied issues in financial accounting. Students develop extended accounting knowledge and skills to generate external financial reports in accordance with International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRSs).
learning_outcomes: Apply relevant accounting standards in the preparation of financial statements for reporting entities.
Analyse and evaluate accounting practice, choices, and decisions.
Explain and analyse contemporary accounting issues within the profession.
Apply International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRSs) and other relevant standards to accounting transactions and events.

title: Taxation
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Australian income tax laws are complex and varied. This course introduces students to Australian income tax laws with specific emphasis on how to access provisions of the Income Tax Assessment Act and related legislation. In addition, students will be made aware of tax planning issues that exist in relevant personal and business environments and learn how to communicate technical tax information to client taxpayers. The graduate qualities of problem solving, decision making and communication are enhanced throughout.
learning_outcomes: Communicate technical tax information to client taxpayers.
Analyse, evaluate and synthesise information to solve tax problems.
Identify and apply relevant provisions of Australian Taxation Law and related case law.
Recognise and interpret tax planning, tax avoidance and tax evasion issues in particular situations.

title: Accounting for Corporate Entities
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Company financial statements are a crucial source of information used by stakeholders when assessing companies. Company accounting and reporting focuses on the mechanisms that underpin the preparation of financial records for corporations including consolidated accounts. This course introduces the regulatory environments, disclosure requirements and concepts behind corporate reporting that are crucial to financial accounting practices. The analysis, evaluation and communication of both financial and non-financial information is also emphasised as an essential professional attribute in the accounting profession.
learning_outcomes: Identify and interpret the underlying theories and concepts in corporate accounting and reporting for both financial and non-financial information.
Apply verbal and written communication skills in effectively presenting accounting information, analysis, and evaluation.
Contribute collaboratively and ethically in groups to prepare and communicate corporate accounting information to stakeholders.
Describe and apply the Australian Accounting Standards, relevant statutory requirements and accounting.
Critically analyse and evaluate disclosure issues around current financial reporting practices.

title: Accounting Practice and Reporting
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Accounting Practice and Reporting extends both the knowledge and skills developed in Fundamentals of Accounting (ACCT1001). This course aims to give students an understanding of the fundamental principles underpinning accrual accounting and financial reporting and develops their technical skills of accounting, including the analysis, recording, preparation and interpretation of accounting information. This course also develops professional skills that are necessary for accounting profession.
learning_outcomes: Identify business transactions and apply the double-entry system of accounting to explain and record them.
Prepare, analyse, and interpret financial reports (Income Statement, Balance Sheet, and Cash Flow Statement) to inform business decision making.
Communicate financial information clearly and concisely to a range of stakeholders.
Apply and evaluate accounting policies used to record and prepare financial accounting information.

title: Business Analysis and Valuation
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course introduces essential theories related to business analysis and equity valuation. Students will work with the financial statements and conduct a business analysis of a publicly listed company. Through this process, they will acquire the knowledge and skills needed to develop and apply various methods for estimating the company's equity value.
learning_outcomes: Conduct accounting analysis, financial analysis and forecasting.
Prepare an analyst report based on the evaluation of financial statements.
Identify and explain accounting information required for financial statement analysis.
Describe and apply valuation theories for security valuation.

title: Management Accounting
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course aims to introduce students to the role of management accounting information in managing and measuring business performance to design, implement and monitor business level strategy using management accounting controls. The first part of the course introduces students to strategic planning processes, including an analysis of an organisation’s external, competitive and internal environments required to design business strategy. Concepts include PESTEL and SWOT analyses, Porter’s 5 Forces, Value Chain analysis and the Risk Calculator. The second part of the course equips students with practical skills and tools for the implementation and monitoring of business strategy with a focus on cost management and profit. Concepts include the Balanced Scorecard, Customer Profitability Analysis, Standard versus Flexible Budgets, Variance Analysis, and Managing Working Capital. At the conclusion of the course, students will have developed practical skills to manage and control business performance in a strategic context.
learning_outcomes: Explain the strategic planning process from the perspective of the CFO and formulate business strategy based on analysis of an organisation's external, competitive and internal environments.
Explain the role and use of management accounting information in an organisational context and for business decision making.
Solve business problems ethically using management accounting concepts and techniques.
Apply key management accounting techniques to implement business strategy and monitor business performance, cost and profitability.
Prepare quantitative analyses (including costs, profitability and cash flow analyses) as well as budgets and forecasts to inform short and long term management decision making.

title: Accounting Information Systems
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course is designed to equip students with a solid foundation in understanding the principles, concepts, and applications of accounting information systems. It covers the key accounting systems and processes that support an organisation's business and produce valuable information for decision-making. Throughout this course, students will learn how accounting information systems are designed, implemented, and utilised in organisations to capture, store, process, and report financial information. Additionally, students will develop technical competence in using various productivity tools and accounting software.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the adequacy/risk of an organisation’s accounting information systems and controls.
Apply the principles of accounting information systems to produce useful information for decision making.
Utilise data analytics in accounting information systems.
Explain the principles and concepts of accounting information systems.

title: Advanced Management Accounting
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: The management accounting function has both an informational and motivational role in organisational decision making. Analysis of information is considered within the context of activity-focused-costing systems and the assessment of non-financial performance measures. The motivational effects of budgets, control processes and performance measures are considered. Issues in human information processing are introduced. Students engage in problem based learning applying strategies to conceptualise problems and formulate optimal solutions.
learning_outcomes: Identify and comprehend the issues arising as a result of these current developments.
Work independently and collaboratively in accounting environments to critically analyse problem scenarios and employ conceptual accounting models to formulate solutions.
Demonstrate an integrative understanding of the theoretical concepts supporting the accounting processes covered.
Demonstrate current knowledge of developments in management accounting.
Identify, analyse, evaluate and communicate information reflective of management accounting approaches and contexts.
Display the ability to soundly apply these accounting processes.

title: Auditing and Assurance
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In the absence of an independent audit, the users of financial statements are constrained by the amount of reliance they can place on the financial statements. Consequently, the provision of an independent and professional audit opinion improves the quality and reliability of financial information presented to decision makers. In this course the major conceptual and technical aspects of auditing are introduced, with an emphasis on financial statement audits conducted under the Corporations Act 2001. Students will also be exposed to other types of audit and assurance activities while examining the legal, ethical and societal role and responsibilities of the auditor.
learning_outcomes: Analyse, evaluate and synthesise both quantitative and qualitative information to inform auditing theory and practice.
Describe and apply the conceptual underlying theory of auditing.
Explain and apply professional auditing techniques.
Effectively communicate auditing issues and practice in oral and written contexts.
Recognise and appraise contemporary auditing issues.
Appraise the legal, ethical and societal role and responsibilities of the auditor.

title: Accounting for Decision Makers
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Financial accounting and management accounting concepts provide the very foundation for business decision making. This course provides an introduction to financial accounting by analysing the accounting function and the preparation of conventional financial statements. Students will develop the initial skills of financial management while beginning to engage in appropriate ethical practices.
learning_outcomes: Organise, calculate and analyse information relevant to decision making;
Discuss and explain the nature and purpose of accounting;
Prepare and interpret financial statements according to conventional methods of accounting;
Identify, analyse and evaluate financial information relevant to the operating, investing and financing decisions of a business entity;
Demonstrate a growing awareness of ethics within the accounting environment.

title: Introduction to Finance
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Financial institutions, assets and markets are the cornerstones of the modern financial system. This course provides students with an introduction to the Australian financial markets and an evaluation of the institutions, assets and participants involved in the industry. It develops knowledge of relevant finance theory and financial techniques to explain the functioning of the financial system and evaluate investment, financing and payout decisions. Upon completing this course, students will have the analytical and problem-solving skills necessary to critically evaluate introductory financial problems reflective of contemporary professional practice in financial management.
learning_outcomes: Identify and explain the basic instruments of corporate funding and the corporate decision to pay dividends
Analyse financial instruments and apply valuation techniques to financial instruments
Apply basic financial mathematics to financial problem solving
Describe and communicate the components of the Australian financial system
Analyse the participants, operations and characteristics of the equity and bonds markets.

title: Business Finance
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: The key intent of business finance is to maximise firm value while reducing firm risk. Focused particularly in the context of the business entity, Business Finance introduces the theory and practice of securities markets, valuation, and execution of optimal investment decisions. Investment goals, investment evaluation techniques, security characteristics, financial mathematics, modern portfolio theory, the capital asset pricing model, and security valuation techniques are included within the array of topics.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a basic understanding of the theory of finance to facilitate the evaluation of investment and financing the firm.
Comprehend the fundamentals of capital budgeting as applied to the investment decision of a business.
Comprehend the effect of dividend decision and identify the relevant factors that may affect this decision.
Demonstrate a descriptive understanding of the pricing of risky assets.
Demonstrate the ability to calculate firms weighted average cost of capital and the effect of imputation tax.

title: Corporate Finance
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: All firms face decisions amongst alternatives when determining both how the firm will be financed and which projects offer the greatest return on investment. ACFI2080 expands across the financing decisions of firms, considers the implications of competitive markets for management, sources of long-term financing, alternative methods of raising capital, and the impact of mergers and acquisitions. Students engage in problem solving and decision making techniques reflective of current professional practice.
learning_outcomes: Apply the theory of mergers and acquisitions and evaluate the evidence and its' implications for management.
Analyse, synthesis and evaluate the outcomes of financial problems.
Apply and analyse capital structure theories to the financing decision of firms.
Critically appraise the efficient market hypothesis including the impact of behavioural finance of efficient markets.
Examine the characteristics of firms in distress and its associated implications.
Identify and explain the sources of long-term financing that affect a firm's financing decision.

title: Personal Financial Planning
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Within Australia, Personal Financial Planning is now a highly regulated industry. The course aims to provide you with a broad overview of the nature and scope of personal financial planning within the national context. Specific coverage of each of the major components necessary for the development of Personal financial advice is given, and the regulatory environment in which practicing financial planners operate is examined. Emphasis is market orientated and thus quantitative, supported by conceptual theory.
learning_outcomes: Engage in collaborative planning, work in consultation, and evaluate the process.
Utilise appropriate investigative methods to collect financial and business information in order to inform well supported decision-making
Examine the changing financial planning environment and identify key issues facing the financial planning sector.

Comprehend and interrelate the key conceptual, methodological and regulatory considerations involving investment, superannuation, retirement planning, risk management and estate planning needs of individuals.
Compare and contrast strategies.
Analyse taxation implications of alternative investments and strategies

title: Financial Analysis and Valuation
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course introduces key valuation theories for financial statement analysis. The primary emphasis is on fundamental valuation, with a focus on developing and applying methods for valuing equity. Topics include the residual earnings model and the abnormal earnings growth model.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse and evaluate information contained within financial statements to conduct business analysis.
Demonstrate critical thinking, analytical and problem solving skills in the context of financial statement analysis.
Conduct accounting analysis, financial analysis and forecasting.
Describe and apply various valuation theories for security valuation.

title: Portfolio Management
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course begins with an overview of investment environment and products, and then provides students with a solid foundation in modern portfolio theory and demonstrates its applications to portfolio management. Alternative asset allocation models are introduced to equip students in developing and implementing investment strategies, assessing and controlling portfolio risk, and evaluating portfolio performance. The course takes students beyond investment theories and trains them to use widely available technology to perform quantitative modelling using real world data. The course covers ASIC RG146 specialised knowledge requirements in the areas of funds management and managed investments.
learning_outcomes: Understand the investment environment, institutional investment and empirical evidence on security performance.
Demonstrate communication, planning, problem-solving and presentation skills individually and as part of a team.
Demonstrate critical thinking, analytical and problem solving skills in the context of portfolio construction and management.
Evaluate the performance of a portfolio and evaluate risk exposures.
Develop mean-variance efficient portfolios using appropriate technology.
Critically evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of international diversification.

title: Derivative Securities
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Investment concerns financial decision-making about where to place wealth to provide for future returns. Students develop an understanding of binomial option pricing, the Black-Scholes option-pricing model, put-call parity for equity options and are introduced to currency options. The use of futures and options, payoff structures for options and arbitrage bounds will also be examined. Focus is given to options on futures. Students engage in independent or collaborative work processes developing communication experience reflective of professional practice.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate what a futures contract is, how futures markets are organised and the determinants of futures prices.
Evaluate different financial paradigms and outcomes to inform and direct personal and professional learning.
Interrelate the system of deposits, margins and marking-to-market used by futures exchanges.
Interpret and explain speculation and hedging strategies using futures contracts, inclusive of reasons for imperfection.
Comprehend the nature and pricing of options contracts together with their uses in portfolio management and risk reduction strategies.
Explain the characteristics and uses of foreign currency options.
Work individually or in teams to analyse and communicate investment information leading to independent investment decision making.
Examine the Black-Scholes and binomial option pricing models and how they are used to calculate option prices.
Identify the major types and characteristics of options, distinguish between options and futures, and expound the factors that affect option prices.
Explain the uses of forward-rate agreements.
Apply basic option pricing theorems, including put-call parity.
Define the features of the major financial contracts traded on the Sydney Futures Exchange and analyse the speculation and hedging strategies using their futures contracts.

title: Funds Management
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: As the value of assets under management reach unprecedented levels across the world, demand in this rapidly growing area of the financial services industry is only set to continue. Funds Management provides students with an advanced understanding of portfolio management through experiential learning by assuming responsibility for development, monitoring and management of the University of Newcastle's Student Managed Investment Fund. All foundational material in portfolio theory and investments is covered. Students gain knowledge of alternative asset allocation models, research techniques, risk management principles, and methods of portfolio performance evaluation, which will assist them in devising an optimal investment strategy. Note: The course is available to select students based on academic merit (see assumed knowledge). An application is required for enrolment in this course and is available at the ACFI3019 application link below: https://www.newcastle.edu.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0005/540635/PCAC-5-13-June-2019-Item-11.1-Doc-PCAC19063-Application-to-Enrol-in-ACFI3019-Funds-Management.PDF
learning_outcomes: Communicate in writing their understanding of the investment environment, institutional investment, and empirical evidence on security performance;
Demonstrate critical thinking, analytical problem solving skills in the context of portfolio management to identify suitable investments for UoN Student Managed Investment Fund;
Evaluate the performance and risk exposure of a portfolio by analysing actual performance of UoN Student Managed Investment Fund (or a suitable alternative if sufficient data is unavailable);

Communicate effectively and collaborate in teams by presenting investment recommendations for inclusion in the UoN Student Managed Investment Fund to the UoN Student Managed Investment Fund Investment Committee.
Experience of managing actual money by researching, proposing, and implementing investment allocations of UoN Student Managed Investment Fund;

title: Business Acumen Fundamentals
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Welcome to ACCT1002, a course designed for students with no prior knowledge of accounting and finance. In today’s interconnected world, having a good understanding of the nature and purpose of accounting and the role and importance of financial management is essential. The course delivers the knowledge of preparing and interpreting financial statements. It also delivers basic financial techniques to evaluate financial decisions. Whether you are starting your own business, working in a corporate environment, or pursuing a career in the public sector, knowledge of accounting and finance helps you achieve long-term growth and navigate the modern financial landscape.
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge of basic financial techniques to inform business decision making.
Explain the role and importance of financial management to create value for business.
Prepare and interpret financial statements according to conventional methods of accounting.
Discuss and explain the nature and purpose of accounting.

title: International Finance
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In an increasingly global business world, awareness of the most important dimensions of international finance is vital. This course exposes you to the advanced aspects of corporate financial management in an international setting such as currency loans hedged with options and real exchange rates. International Finance equips you with both the knowledge and the technical skills required to understand and analyse a range of relevant financial issues within the global environment.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the capacity to work independently and respond to change in a flexible adaptive manner.
Demonstrate an integrative understanding of the foreign exchange market and the relationships between interest rates, spot and forward rates and expected inflation rates.
Review the problems of dealing in foreign currency and the advantages and disadvantages of overseas funding.
Identify market conventions on exchange rate quotation and correctly calculate those quotations.
Apply appropriate formats and technologies to financial communication.
Explain the use of futures and option contracts in hedging foreign exchange exposure.
Comprehend the range of hedging strategies including forward rate hedging and contingent hedging.
Analyse, evaluate and synthesise both quantitative and qualitative financial information to influence problem solving and decision making.
Recognise and calculate forward exchange rates given spot rates.

title: Aircraft Performance and Operations
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to critical factors that affect the performance, operation and design of aircraft. The course has a strong emphasis on the physical understanding of aircraft performance including take-off speeds, climb rates, turns, cruise, and descent and landing performance. The course covers operational issues including the regulatory environment for aircraft, and addresses economic considerations.
learning_outcomes: Apply the concepts of aircraft longitudinal static stability, control, and weight and balance to aircraft operations.
Accurately calculate speed, climb, descent, range and endurance characteristics of aircraft.
Confidently discuss the regulatory environment for aircraft operations.
Correctly identify the relative advantages and disadvantages of various aircraft propulsion systems.

title: Flight Dynamics
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Students learn how to represent and evaluate aircraft stability, controllability and handling qualities. Commencing with the characterisation of aerodynamic properties, the course develops the mathematical representations and tools used to model the dynamics and stability of an aircraft, and its response to control. Students will obtain practical numerical skills in mathematical representation through flight simulation.
learning_outcomes: Analyse flight control mechanisms and critique their effectiveness.
Evaluate flight stability and interpret its impact on aircraft operations and pilot workload.
Appraise the handling qualities of an aircraft.
Model aircraft flight behaviours using computational techniques.
Analyse aircraft equilibrium and trim conditions.
Participate as an effective group member in a group project.
Estimate aerodynamic and control derivatives and their effects on equilibrium.
Mathematically represent the motion of an aircraft.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Aircraft Motion Modelling and Coordinate Transformation

title: Financial Institutions Risk Management
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Effective firm wide risk management sustains financial institutions. This course provides an overview of financial markets and the role of financial institutions, liquidity management, the use of financial derivatives in the management of interest rate risk, financial institutions liability management, management of the securities portfolio, credit analysis, management of the loan portfolio, management of bank capital, an overview of financial institutions regulations and issues in international banking. International perspectives to risk management and building skill in problem solving and decision making will be developed.
learning_outcomes: Provide an overview of the regulatory constraints under which Australian banks, foreign banks, building societies and credit unions operate.

Construct asset-liability portfolios for financial institutions, together with portfolios of financial derivative instruments, that effectively minimise the potentially damaging effects of interest rate volatility on bank (and corporate) profitability.
Identify in the financial statements of institutions the indicators of impending crisis.
Provide an overview of basic risk management procedures of banks.
Analyse, evaluate and synthesise quantitative and qualitative information accessed to manage risk.
Apply appropriate procedures for appraising the credit risks inherent in bank loans, and for the pricing of loan agreements.
Define sources of international finance, and analyse how the current banking system provides access to such funds.
Recognise and employ the processes and strategies which assist independent learning.
Define and distinguish the various sources of commercial and retail debt financing available through Australian financial institutions.

title: Aerospace Propulsion Systems
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Students will learn to analyse and control thrust generation mechanisms common in modern aerospace systems. For Piston-prop, turboprop, turbojet, turbofan and rocket engines, the thermodynamics, aerodynamics, thrust and torque characteristics will be developed analytically via modelling and simulation. There will be a strong emphasis on testing and control of engines and developing an understanding of engine response to control and integration with other relevant aircraft systems.
learning_outcomes: Discuss engine noise and pollution issues.
Assess engine interaction and integration issues with other aircraft systems.
Quantify the response characteristics of aeronautical propulsion systems.
Analyse and estimate the performance characteristics of various aeronautical propulsion systems.
Explain engine health monitoring concepts and strategies.
Undertake experimental testing of engines and communicate engine performance characteristics in a written report.
Evaluate engine suitability relative to aircraft performance requirements.
Devise appropriate control strategies for aerospace propulsion systems.

title: Embedded Control Systems
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to embedded control systems design. This encompasses modelling the embedded system, design and implementation trade-offs, and verification and validation. A focus of this course is to provide a unified framework that enables the synthesis of real-time control solutions that accommodate interlocking design trade-offs and conflicting requirements.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the impact of sampling and sampling rate on state-space system models
Evaluate the impact of control system limitations and finite computing capabilities of embedded systems and the design trade-offs between performance, robustness and certifiability
Implement state inference on an embedded system
Design and implement a basic control solution on an embedded system
Demonstrate the design of embedded control systems as a holistic and synergetic integration of cyber-physical systems
Model and accommodate state and actuator constraints into a control solution

title: Airframe Systems
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course gives a thorough grounding in the essential methods and processes involved in the design, test and dynamic response of aircraft structures. It builds upon background in mechanical design and mechanics of solids and considers how these and more elaborate concepts and methods are applied to the analysis of aircraft structural strength and the design of aircraft structural components. This course will encompass structural design regulations, flight loads analysis, structural design methods, static and dynamic structural analysis, aeroelasticity and aeroelastic stability and response. It further investigates the links between other aircraft systems like propulsion, sensing and control actuation systems, the structural loads they create, and the static and dynamic responses of the structure to them. Aircraft construction techniques are considered as part of the process, as are testing, validation and verification of structural integrity relative to certification requirements. Case studies of incidents and accidents will be used to elucidate important historical lessons regarding aircraft structural dynamics and failure, reparations and redesign. Students will gain experience from group activities involving analysis and design of aircraft structural components and testing of their performance.
learning_outcomes: Apply the principles of structural analysis and strength estimation to the design of aircraft structural components and validate them against regulations.
Analyse the interactions between the dynamic structure and the sensing and control systems of an aircraft, and the cross-implications on the design/redesign of each.
Evaluate suitability of construction approaches to the fabrication of structural components for test and evaluation.
Analyse the stiffness, compliance and modal dynamic behaviour of an aircraft structure.
Interpret aircraft design and certification regulations regarding aircraft structural integrity.
Estimate flight loads and determine their interaction with an aircraft structure.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Fabrication and Testing of Airframe Structures

title: Aircraft Systems and Avionics
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course develops a detailed understanding of the range of systems typical on complex modern aircraft, including sensors and actuators, flight control, navigation, flight management, engine management, power, communication, display, data bus and other avionics technologies. It takes a systems engineering perspective and addresses the complex interplay, and the design and integration issues between the many subsystems of an aircraft. The course will cover important aspects of reliability, robustness, redundancy, validation and verification in the systems engineering process. The syllabus will contain substantial case studies to reaffirm these lessons with examples from incidents and accidents in aeronautical history. Students will gain experience from group activities involving systems engineering practice.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and appraise system performance and interoperability.
Describe typical aircraft systems and their functions.
Critically assess complex aerospace systems using a 'systems of systems' approach.
Communicate engineering information effectively both orally and in writing.
Exercise systems engineering principles and procedures in complex system specification, design and evaluation processes.
Participate effectively in systems engineering practices in groups.

title: Automatic Flight Control Systems
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course builds upon the flight dynamics modelling in 'AERO3000 Flight Dynamics' and considers dynamics, stability, response and hardware integration aspects of flight control system development. It treats the representation of aircraft response to deterministic control inputs in the frequency domain. Following this, the response of an aircraft to stochastic inputs (wind gusts) is investigated after developing the necessary probabilistic tools to represent wind gusts. A detailed revision of classical control theory and design methods is given in the context of control design for full multi-modal longitudinal and lateral-directional cross-coupled flight control problems. The course culminates with a full six-degree-of-freedom aircraft flight control design exercise, including implementation and testing in a flight simulation framework. Students will gain experience from group activities involving flight control loop analysis, design, implementation and testing in a flight simulation environment.
learning_outcomes: Analyse an aircraft's response to disturbances (wind gust inputs) by combining Transfer Function representations with gust PSD's.
Analyse an aircraft's response to control inputs in the frequency domain using Laplace Transforms and Transfer Function representations.
Design and implement multi-loop control design solutions in the time domain and evaluate their effectiveness.

Apply classical frequency domain loop analysis to understand closed loop system stability and response, and design PID, Lead, Lag and Lead-Lag compensators using Bode and Root-locus design techniques.
Articulate the principles of stability augmentation systems and autopilot control systems in aircraft operation, their functions and purposes.

title: Aerospace System Design
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course is intended to introduce students to the process, techniques and regulations of aerospace system design. The course considers the configuration design of a complete aerospace vehicle system at the conceptual stage to meet a pre-defined set of requirements. The course covers aerospace design regulations, design requirements, design cycles and the approvals process. It will draw together the background covered in aircraft performance, dynamics and propulsion courses to optimise the design of the aerospace vehicle to meet a set of requirements. The course will consider the integration of other subsystems, the implied requirements on those systems and the effects of subsystem requirements on the aerospace vehicle configuration. The course will provide students with opportunities to apply all of their aeronautical knowledge, to perform effectively in group activities and develop their team participation and management skills through a systems engineering process.
learning_outcomes: Assess the requirements of ancillary aerospace vehicle systems and their effects on primary systems design considerations.
Apply the principles of system engineering to an aerospace vehicle system design at the concept stage.
Engage effectively in design teams and inter-disciplinary negotiations.
Apply the physical principles of aircraft performance, stability and controllability, and propulsion to the aerospace vehicle design process.
Design an aerospace vehicle concept and articulate its benefits in written and verbal forms.

title: Ancient Greece
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: AHIS1000 traces the history of Greece from the Bronze Age to the aftermath of the Peloponnesian Wars in the 4th Century BCE. The course content is examined through written and archaeological evidence. This introductory course prepares students for the courses at 2000 and 3000 levels as well as providing an introduction to other courses in Ancient History, including other courses at 1000 level.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate differing versions of major authorities, ancient and modern, on major historical issues relating to Ancient Greece.
Analyse and construct arguments about a major issue related to Ancient Greece.
Contribute to group discussions related to major issues in Ancient Greek history.
Apply and interpret information collected through research tasks on Ancient Greek history.

title: Rome to Julius Caesar
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course covers the rise of Rome from its mythical foundation in the 8th Century BCE to its prominent role in the Mediterranean by the middle of the 2nd Century BCE. The focus is on the geography and topography of Italy and Rome; a study of Roman political and social structures; military organisation; and the evolution of the Roman empire. Attention is also on the Roman self-image, as evidenced in the value system, foundation mythology, and propaganda. Students study the major evidence for Rome – both written and archaeological – in order to develop the skills of the ancient historian, and are introduced to the applications of Digital Humanities in the study of Ancient History.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a broad knowledge and understanding of the development of Rome between the legendary period and the mid-2nd Century BCE
Evaluate major types of primary evidence, from written works to various forms of material culture
Construct arguments that evince criticisms succinctly and accurately
Develop introductory skills in translating information on ancient Rome to a digital format

title: The Byzantine Empire: From Constantine to Iconoclasm (306-726)
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Students will study the primary literary and material sources of the Eastern Roman empire, better known as the Byzantine empire. Byzantium was the cultural and historical successor to the Greeks and Romans and adopted and transformed this inheritance in unique ways. We will explore the religious, political and military history of this important but neglected global empire from the rise of the Emperor Constantine to the Iconoclast controversy. We will consider the interactions between church and state, the continuities and changes with the earlier Roman Empire and role of Roman identity in the Christian east, especially in light of the rise of Islam. We will also discuss responses to invasion and plague, gender roles, and education. Students will learn how to analyse primary sources and how to use new technologies in research communication.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the historical development of the Byzantine Empire.
Analyse major types of primary historical evidence, from written works to various forms of material culture.
Construct arguments about the history of the Byzantine Empire that evince criticisms succinctly and accurately in written assessments.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Write a report on a Byzantine Artefact with a presentation
Create an argumentative essay using primary and secondary evidence

title: The Augustan Age: Politics, Society and Literature
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The course covers military and social history from the death of Caesar to the death of Augustus; the main focus is on political and social change, and the quality of the main sources on the period.
learning_outcomes: Identify the development of broad trends in the Augustan period.
Evaluate differing versions of major events in a historical period.
Analyse major developments in the Augustan period.
Critique contradictory versions in ancient sources.

title: Sparta
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course focuses on Spartan history from the ancient origins down to the 4th Century BCE and key aspects of the political and social organisation and practice. Emphasis is placed on the use of ancient source material in translation (incorporating Greek and Roman value terms) in conjunction with modern scholarly opinion. Attention is also given to archaeological evidence. In addition to political and military histories, the course covers Spartan cultural history, such as the importance of religion, ritual and cult worship, as well as the role of children, education and gender. Through an online assessment, students also develop digital competence to facilitate transferable workplace skills.
learning_outcomes: Develop and demonstrate skills in presenting historical information on Sparta in a digital context.
Analyse the history, culture, and traditions of Sparta in antiquity;
Evaluate primary and secondary sources of evidence relevant to the history of Sparta;
Explain oral and written arguments in a clear, concise and analytical manner;

title: Egypt: The New Kingdom
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course examines the New Kingdom of Egypt. It covers the historical background of the age, geography and landscape, and features study of significant sites.
