faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Architecture and Built Environment
syllabus_overview: This course examines the process of building measurement and bills of quantity through the development and demonstration of 'essential skills'. Elements of measurement and bills of quantities in accordance with the Australian and New Zealand Standard Method of Measurement of Building Works (ANZSMM) will be applied.
learning_outcomes: Investigate the process of building measurement
Prepare building measurement and bills of quantities for four major trades and preliminaries according to the ANZSMM: preliminaries, groundworks, concrete/formwork/ reinforcement
Apply the rules for bills of quantities and Australian and New Zealand Standard Method of Measurement (ANZSMM)

assessment_tasks.task_name: Measurement of concrete, formwork and reinforcement

Master of Architecture studios help students to act in the world in a conscientious manner, to work with others, and to communicate (through verbal and visual means) with clarity and maturity. Architecture Studio 10 projects substantiate students’ research and design exploration, culminating in an explicable, defensible, robust and well-resolved architectural scheme. Studio 10 is about engaging in architectural discourse: students are encouraged to reflect on, and contribute to, avenues of study through their projects
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on a brief or project framework toward the refinement of a design research strategy.
Develop a cogent articulation of your scheme through clear and compelling communication methods.
Exercise discerning use of design methods, processes, and media, in a process of ongoing conceptual/formal experimentation.
Test and refine design possibilities that synthesise project contexts and constraints including physical, ecological, environmental, social, cultural, ethical dimensions.
Demonstrate a capacity for self-direction and critical reflection through verbal and textual means.
Demonstrate knowledge of construction elements, building components and methods, and building services and systems, in a cohesive architectural scheme.

Apply the legislative and statutory terminology/requirements of a construction contract.
Apply contract forms appropriate for large construction and infrastructure projects.

learning_outcomes: Prepare building measurement and bills of quantities for major trades utilising on-screen and 3D software: groundworks, masonry, roofing, finishes.

title: Advanced Construction Procurement and Tendering
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Architecture and Built Environment
syllabus_overview: This course examines the tender process and how construction projects are procured. Tendering principles and the process of procurement selection will be investigated by analysing the various strategies within both the public and private sectors using case study building and infrastructure projects.
learning_outcomes: Investigate the tender process and supporting documentation
Develop an appropriate risk management strategy
Analyse and select an appropriate procurement method and standard form of contract to meet stakeholder requirements
Investigate the inception, development and implementation stages of the procurement process
Investigate the processes of procuring and tendering for infrastructure projects

title: Project Scoping and Integration
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Architecture and Built Environment
syllabus_overview: Examines the core concepts, principles and techniques underlying project scoping and integration.
learning_outcomes: Organisational processes leading to project authorisation, start-up and designation of project manager
Internal and external environment factors that may affect the project
A range of suitable methodologies, techniques and tools available to project managers
Methods to define products and activities, e.g. work, organisation and product breakdown structures
The project process, the project life-cycle and the relationship between project phases
The components of a scope statement
The need for scope definition during project start-up and ongoing during the project life cycle
The place of scope management and scope control in the context of the project life cycle
Planning and control procedures, resource management and risk management
The practice of change control

title: Project Scheduling, Resource Management and Leadership
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Architecture and Built Environment
syllabus_overview: Explores the management of project time, through the management of planning and scheduling activities. Examines the process of Human Resource Management (HRM), including the development and leadership of individuals into a cohesive project team with the common purpose of meeting project objectives.
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of human resource development practices such as mentoring, coaching, etc, and identify the policies, standards and methods required to achieve HRM outcomes
Explain the place of time management in the context of the project life cycle and other project management functions
Apply leadership and management skills within a project environment
Outline the importance of HRM in the project management environment
Link time and resources to the project schedule
Apply a project management schedule as a control mechanism
Discuss the conflict and stress issues associated with individuals tasked with project management, especially within a human resource matrix management environment
Apply established HRM selection, assignment, training, performance evaluation and motivation tools
Match appropriate time management methodologies to particular projects, by identifying their capabilities, limitations, application and outcomes
Assess HRM outcomes, using success and failure criteria and HRM performance measures
Assess interpersonal strengths and weaknesses

title: Negotiation and Conflict Resolution
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Architecture and Built Environment
syllabus_overview: Describes the principles and application of negotiation and conflict resolution skills throughout the project life cycle.
learning_outcomes: Identify the potential points of conflict during the project life cycle.
Explain and compare the principles of a variety of negotiation and conflict resolution techniques
Apply a variety of negotiation and conflict resolution techniques

title: Project Closure
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Architecture and Built Environment
syllabus_overview: Examines the process of project closure including project handover, evaluation and sustainability.
learning_outcomes: The components of successful project closure
Evaluating, sharing and celebrating project outcomes
The finalisation of contracts and project infrastructure
The key techniques of ensuring the sustainability of project outcomes

title: Program Management
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Architecture and Built Environment
syllabus_overview: Examines the core concepts, principles and techniques of Program Management as opposed to Project Management.
learning_outcomes: Critically articulate the goals and objectives of program
critically understand the difference between project and program management
critically evaluate the key techniques of program management

title: Community-led Resilience and Leadership
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Architecture and Built Environment
syllabus_overview: The course provides students with an overview of professional practice for disaster professionals. Effective disaster management involves building community resilience through adequate preparation and inclusion of all stakeholders, but especially community members. Students will develop an understanding of the challenging dynamics of hazards (including climate change), risks, policies, capacities. They will be able to apply leadership principles to reduce the risks and impacts of disasters.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate and apply methods to empower community stakeholders within decision-making processes for disaster mitigation and reconstruction activities.

Critically analyse the concept of adaptive resilience for individuals and organisations. Assess the capacity of an organisation to respond, able to learn and adapt to different disasters and become more agile.
Assess targeted and integrated leadership approaches to DRR/CCA, and how these approaches have been implemented in different risk contexts.

Identify and compare a range of stakeholders who may receive damage or benefit from disaster mitigation and reconstruction activities, and judiciously assess the needs of different stakeholder groups in the event of a disaster.
Appraise different mitigation approaches for Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) and Climate change adaptations (CCA) and their underlying concepts, methodologies, tools and applications.

title: Project Management Principles
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Architecture and Built Environment
syllabus_overview: This course covers the foundational elements of managing projects from initial planning to project closure. It also emphasises the skills related to managing project timelines, budgets, risk, and procurement. Students will also explore common obstacles within project management and develop a problem-solving attitude pertaining to project management.
learning_outcomes: Outline a detailed project plan using an industry ready software tool.
Develop a project management schedule as a control mechanisms.
Identify the place of time management in the context of the project life cycle and other project management functions.
Demonstrate the need to link time, cost and resources to the project framework.
Apply skills in risk management planning and quality planning.

title: Disaster Risk and Resilience Principles
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Architecture and Built Environment
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with an overview of the core theories and principles of disaster risk reduction and resilience. It examines the social, political, economic and environmental impacts of disasters and conflicts. Students learn the theory, practice, ethics and social responsibility of disaster management in the context of community involvement. This is achieved through investigating the levels of resilience (individual, community, national). Attention is given to examining the level of participation of Indigenous peoples and how Indigenous-led initiatives can contribute to future disaster practice.
learning_outcomes: Develop and apply strategies including indigenous knowledge and practices to reduce risk and mitigate against the effects of a disaster or conflict and align to a relevant International Framework(s)
Collaborate to problem solve and execute solutions in different disaster contexts.
Analyse the impact of disasters and conflicts on physical, social infrastructure and communities
Identify and assess factors that make communities vulnerable to natural hazards and disaster situations
Critically evaluate the concept of disasters in the context of the United Nations Frameworks including the UN Declaration of Rights of Indigenous Peoples.

title: Disaster Resilience Economics and Business Resilience
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Architecture and Built Environment
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with a systematic approach to disaster risk reduction and explores the role and function of private businesses in reducing disaster risk. Students gain an appreciation of the role economic plays in business decisions in a disaster risk and resilience context.
learning_outcomes: Explain how economics can inform disaster risk and resilience
Identify organisational systems, policies, and procedures, as well as environmental and social factors, that influence hazard exposure and disaster risk in private sector organisations.
Apply economic concepts to deliver the objectives of private businesses in a disaster context
Develop an effective disaster risk reduction plan for a given business context based on identified risk and hazards

title: Project Procurement, Cost, Quality and Risk Management
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Architecture and Built Environment
syllabus_overview: Examines the core concepts, principles and techniques of Project Procurement, Cost, Quality & Risk Management.
learning_outcomes: the principles of procurement management and their application;
the need to link time, cost and resources to the project framework;
Appropriate risk management methodologies, their capabilities, limitations, applicability and outcomes
Risk management planning, risk identification, qualitative risk analysis, quantitative risk analysis, risk response planning, risk monitoring and control
Use of the budgets and expenditure forecasts as control mechanisms
procurement management processes and procedures;
Appropriate cost management methodologies, their capabilities, limitations, application and outcomes
Development of project budgets and expenditure forecasts
Quality processes, quality planning, perform quality assurance, perform quality control
Quality management systems, methodologies and tools
The principles of quality management and their application

title: Disaster Governance and International Frameworks
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Architecture and Built Environment
syllabus_overview: The course provides a systematic approach to disaster risk reduction (DRR) and how it interacts with various governance structures. Students will study current UN International Frameworks from the perspective of governments in all their various forms, differentiating between national/federal, state/province/territory, and local/city levels. Students will apply several DRR assessment tools in a governance context. Students will also gain insight into the potential limitations of the UN and National frameworks for Indigenous peoples and cultures.
learning_outcomes: Recognise the impacts of the UN and National frameworks for Indigenous peoples and cultures in a governance context
Explain the development of the current UN Frameworks and their function in guiding development activities
Develop an effective disaster risk reduction plan for a given governance context based on identified risk and hazards
Identify the societal systems, policies and procedures used to govern a given geographical location in relation to potential hazards and risk reduction
Analyse and explain the relationship between goals, targets and indicators within the UN DRR frameworks

title: Methods for Evidence-Based Decisions in Disasters
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Architecture and Built Environment
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with a sound grounding in a range of evidence-based methods relevant to the wider context of Disaster Risk Reduction and Resilience. It also provides an awareness of some of the relevant debates in the area of methodology. Both quantitative and qualitative research methods will be covered. The course is student-centred and problem-oriented.
learning_outcomes: Develop context specific research strategy and research methods to develop ethical evidence-based decisions for building disaster resilience
Assess existing, emerging, and innovative systems and technologies for building disaster resilience
Apply multidisciplinary concepts to frame evidence-based decision making for building disaster resilience
Explain the defining features of sound evidence-based decision-making approaches for building disaster resilience
Apply research methods/tools to analyse data, interpret and communicate the results leading to evidence based decisions

assessment_tasks.task_name: Framing a problem for evidence-based solution: Case Study

title: Building Design Management
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Architecture and Built Environment
syllabus_overview: Design Management has developed an increasingly important role within the construction industry since the development of new project acquisition methods from the 1990s onwards. These recognise the importance of the integration of the design and construction processes, the emergence of the project management profession as well as the more specialised role of architects and engineers. This course will investigate these roles and responsibilities within the different organisational environments and throughout the project’s lifecycle. In addition, the unique stakeholder relationships and expectations of the design manager acting on behalf of the client, consultant or contractor will be explored and a design management plan developed for a contemporary commercial building project.
learning_outcomes: Differentiate the role of Building Design Management within Architectural, Engineering and Construction environments.
Analyse stakeholder relationships, communication practices, and leadership capabilities to manage collaborative design processes effectively .
Apply design management principles to develop a Design Management Plan for a commercial building project.
Compare the expectations and responsibilities of the Building Design Manager in different organisational, contractual and project environments.

assessment_tasks.task_name: A presentation of the opening of a stakeholder meeting

title: Disaster Risk and Resilience Capstone Project
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Architecture and Built Environment
syllabus_overview: Students undertake a supervised individual research project, culminating in the production of a final research report. This course allows students to target their capstone research project to their individual learning goals. This project will be undertaken through supervision with either an academic or practitioner, depending on the goal of the student.
learning_outcomes: Document the research report using appropriate methods and techniques to ensure it is well-supported and coherent.
Analyse the evidence gathered for the research report and use it to support the argument presented.
Develop and organise a research report that presents a coherent argument supported by evidence.
Select and apply research strategies and methodologies appropriate to the discipline area generally and the topic area selected for study.

title: Major Project in Construction Management
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Architecture and Built Environment
syllabus_overview: In this course, students will conduct an independent research study in the form of a literature review, an experimental or theoretical investigation into a construction industry problem associated with issues covered in the program. Results will be communicated in the form of a seminar, final report and poster.
learning_outcomes: Communicate the project findings using appropriate methods and techniques as per industry expectations.
Develop and organise a research report on the selected project that communicates a coherent argument supported by evidence.
Analyse the evidence gathered for the project report and use it to support the argument presented.
Select, apply, and present research strategies and methodologies appropriate to construction management generally and the project topic area selected for study.

title: Volumetric and Modular Construction
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Architecture and Built Environment
syllabus_overview: During the 21st century off-site manufacturing, volumetric and modular construction has developed an increasingly significant role within the construction industry even though its roots can be traced back to the earliest periods in history. This course recognises the importance of integrating and mainstreaming off-site manufacturing, volumetric and modular construction processes into general construction practices. This course will investigate the theory, processes and integration of these practices in the context of modern construction management, procurement and contractual arrangements.
learning_outcomes: Develop a project plan for the inclusion of off-site manufacturing and volumetric construction for a commercial project.
Analyse the historical developments of off-site manufacturing, automation, volumetric and modular construction that has led to the present situation.
Evaluate the inclusion of off-site manufacturing, automation, volumetric and modular construction technologies in the construction process
Justify the benefits of off-site manufacturing, volumetric, automation and modular construction in the context of sustainable development

title: Decolonisation and Indigenous Ways of Knowing
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Architecture and Built Environment
syllabus_overview: This micro credential introduces students to decolonised practices and Indigenous knowledge systems in their professional practice. Participants will learn how to critically engage with Indigenous ways of knowing, doing and being, and apply creative research methodologies that centre Country and community. The course blends theoretical frameworks with practical application through a live project case study and reflective research design.
learning_outcomes: Identify the key concepts and theory of decolonisation
Propose methods for decolonisation of professional practice.
Outline basic principles of Indigenous research methods and their relevance to community consultation
Engage with Indigenous Knowledges ethically

title: Indigenous Cultural Heritage: Spatial dimensions within cultural place and spiritual space
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Architecture and Built Environment
syllabus_overview: This postgraduate course is designed to provide students with a comprehensive understanding of the cultural heritage of Australian Aboriginal communities and its intersection with the built environment. By examining the rich history and cultural heritage of Aboriginal communities, students will learn to understand how Aboriginal Cultural Heritage can inform contemporary projects in the built environment. Through a combination of lectures, workshops, site visits, and practical projects, participants will gain the knowledge and skills required to engage in culturally sensitive design and planning in collaboration with Aboriginal communities.
learning_outcomes: Interpret relevant legislation and policies relating to the protection and preservation of Aboriginal Cultural Heritage in the built environment.
Analyse the features, histories and spiritual practices giving rise to the cultural significance of an Aboriginal site/place.
Respectfully engage with Aboriginal communities to learn and understand their perspectives in the planning, design and management of Aboriginal Cultural Heritage in the built environment.
Summarise the history, culture and heritage of Aboriginal communities.

title: Indigenous Creative Methodologies in Country Guided Research Design
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Architecture and Built Environment
syllabus_overview: Indigenous creative research methodologies are innovative approaches that are deep-rooted in the connection between Indigenous peoples and place (Country). These methodologies recognise the intrinsic value of Indigenous knowledge systems, cultural practices, and artistic expressions in research. Students can incorporate these methodologies into their practice by engaging in respectful, collaborative partnerships with Indigenous communities. By focusing on Country, these methodologies allow students to delve into the intricate relationships between Indigenous communities and their environments, understanding not only the physical aspects of the land but also its spiritual and cultural significance. This approach plays a critical role in fostering genuine understanding, decolonising research practices, and promoting the preservation of Indigenous heritage. This course examines Indigenous expressive and aesthetic ways of knowing and being within a research framework that decolonises and transforms ideas. Students will examine the differences between traditional western academic approaches to research and Indigenous epistemologies (ways of knowing) and methodologies (ways of doing) in place-based modalities within an ethical framework. Students will explore and apply a choice of creative-based research mediums such as photography, video production, multimedia arts, drawing/painting/building to articulate and mobilise concepts of Country. Through this course students will undertake a Country led Country-guided design research project of their choice by engaging with Indigenous communities/individuals in knowledge production that is relevant, respectful, and collaborative.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the relationship between Indigenous design, environmental (ecological and sociocultural) systems, and impacts on Country through culturally responsive project planning to support the health and wellbeing outcomes for Country.
Demonstrate the use of different research methods within an Indigenous research methodological framework.
Design and produce a creative artefact to communicate ideas, analysis, findings from an inquiry-led project.
Compare and contrast the key differences between western and Indigenous research methodologies.

title: Decolonised Country Guided Practice
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Architecture and Built Environment
syllabus_overview: This practice based course is designed for students who are passionate about exploring Indigenous knowledge and its profound impact on reshaping the way we interact with the built environment. In this course, we will delve into the concept of 'decolonised Country-guided practices' and initiate critical dialogues to transform our current approaches within the built environment through interactive, self-guided and practical applications. Understanding Decolonised Practices: We will embark on a journey to grasp the essence of decolonised practice - what it truly means to work on projects that occupy unceded land. Our aim is to equip students with the knowledge, ethics, and sensitivity to act with custodianship and care, acknowledging the historical injustices and fostering reconciliation. Bridging the Knowledge Gap: Our program addresses the critical knowledge on the subject of colonisation and its ongoing impacts on Indigenous peoples. Students will gain a deep understanding of the richness and diversity of Indigenous perspectives, practices, and knowledge systems. Real-World Application: Practicality is at the core of our approach. Students will have the opportunity to select a live project of their choice, allowing them to identify colonial practices at play and propose decolonised approaches that draw on Indigenous ways of knowing, doing, and being. Through this, students will evaluate the tangible outcomes of their newfound knowledge and skills
learning_outcomes: Define the history and theory of Indigenous decolonisation and critically analysis and synthesise methodologies.
Employ a range of skills using computer programs and other digital literacies to source, analyse, generate and disseminate critical solutions.
Use critical analysis to effectively communicate a deep engagement with Indigenous knowledge literature and lived experience.
Transmit ideas, analysis, findings and strategies through advanced written, oral and/or creative expressive presentation.
Critically apply Indigenous decolonisation practices to a live project.

title: First Nations Community Engagement and Indigenous Cultural Heritage
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Architecture and Built Environment
syllabus_overview: This micro credential focuses on respectful collaboration and engagement with Indigenous communities to support the protection of cultural heritage and uphold cultural protocols. It is designed for professionals working in government and industry who seek to build meaningful relationships and practice cultural accountability in their work with First Nations peoples and places.
learning_outcomes: Plan for ethical and respectful engagement with Indigenous communities.
Apply Indigenous research approaches in a project based setting.
Identify basic policies and laws related to Indigenous heritage protection.
Recognise the value of Indigenous Cultural Heritage to First Nations Communities.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Indigenous Knowledge Systems and Ethical Engagement

title: Creative Collaborations
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Being able to collaborate effectively in a range of contexts is a vital life skill. It is fundamental to how you learn, how you work and live with others and how you can express your views when it comes to creative projects that matter to you. In this course, you will learn the fundamentals of collaborative creative research and enquiry, and how to identify a purposeful group project opportunity. You will participate in constructive co-design processes and present your ideas to peers. Through journaling and reflecting on your experiences in a collaborative framework, you will develop an understanding of creativity in action and the challenges and opportunities of working together. You will also begin to contextualise your own creative values, goals and agency within creative practice.
learning_outcomes: Analyse group dynamics and collaborative processes.
Show evidence of creative research and outcomes in a range of formats.
Describe a range of different interpretations of creativity and how they impact on collaboration.
Employ strategies for effective, ethical and productive collaborations.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Reflection on Creative Practice and Collaboration

title: Indigenous Collaboration
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Architecture and Built Environment
syllabus_overview: Addressing the complex challenges of the twenty-first century calls for heterogeneous perspectives and multi-disciplinary collaboration. Indigenous ways of knowing and relating with Country are increasingly sought after in these efforts. However, achieving mutual understanding in such collaborations is particularly challenging within a colonial context. This course aims to equip students with the skills and understanding necessary for effective and respectful engagement with First Nation communities. It offers a framework for critically evaluating real-world instances of such engagement, identifying what works, what doesn't, and avenues for improvement. The course introduces key concepts from communication theory, shedding light on the various factors that influence the communication process. Special attention is given to the role of diverse perspectives in addressing problems that emerge from complex systems.
learning_outcomes: Describe the conditions required for successful collaborations with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities.
Critically examine their own disciplinary, vocational, or personal stance and articulate how these may influence communication in specific settings.
Explain why diverse ways of knowing, or “epistemic diversity” are essential to solving problems that arise from complex systems.
Identify and compare different models of communication , providing justification for their applicability in enhancing collaboration and mutual understanding between First Nations peoples and others.
Appraise instances of engagement involving First Nation and Western stakeholders, identifying strengths, weaknesses, and opportunities for improved mutual understanding.

title: Professional Career Ready Studio
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: In this course you will apply your learning to complete a real-world brief for a client (140 hours of studio work placement). You will work either individually or as part of a multi-disciplinary team and you will take responsibility for all aspects of project delivery. In doing so you will reflect on the skills and knowledge you have developed during your studies and identify areas for further professional development. You will work with a Studio Supervisor and reflect on your experience of working in a studio with a disciplinary mentor. This is a professional course in which you will take responsibility for your own career development, building a personalised plan for the next phase in your career journey.
learning_outcomes: Explain how their learning and experience connect with skills required for work in relevant fields.
Apply knowledge and skills to successfully complete a significant project to a client brief.
Reflect on their experience of working in a studio environment to identify areas of strength and priorities for further development.
Explain how the experience of working in a studio environment has enhanced their understanding of their field.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Complete Project to a Client Brief and Respond to Client Feedback

title: Molecules, Cells and Organisms
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Introduces the basic principles and concepts of cell and molecular biology to explore the nature of life's molecular building blocks and systems and how these interact to form functional cells and ultimately organisms. Students will discover some of the principles behind how cells work and explore ideas about how biological complexity and life itself may have originated. This knowledge underpins our ability to combat disease, to harness solar energy to feed the world, to sustainably power human industry and to recycle our waste efficiently using microbial systems. The production of new cells is vital to the survival of species and there will be an introduction to basic genetic concepts to explain how organisms can pass on their traits which convey selective advantages for survival in a fiercely competitive world. Cells must also communicate with other cells and be able to detect and respond to external stimuli from its environment. Students that have completed this course will be well placed to further their studies in cell and molecular biology, biochemistry, microbial biology, molecular genetics and animal & plant physiology courses at 2000 and 3000 level.
learning_outcomes: Explain the processes which regulate and integrate cell function
Apply critical thinking and the scientific approach
Retrieve, collect and interpret biological information
Define the hierarchy of structure within cells
Summarise the mechanisms and characteristics of reproduction and inheritance
Demonstrate understanding of biological terminology and concepts in relation to molecules and cells
Interpret the origin and evolution of biological complexity at the cellular level

title: Professional Skills for Biological Sciences 1
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students are introduced to the principles of scientific investigation and initiate the development of analytical and practical skills necessary for an active career in the diverse fields of modern biology. This equips the student for further studies in both lab-based biotechnology and field based environmental biology subjects. Students will be taught practical laboratory and field skills together with experimental design, data evaluation and technical report writing within the context of a number of exciting hands on biological investigations.
learning_outcomes: Maintain an accurate and organised lab book, communicate experimental outcomes through structured reports, and collaborate effectively within laboratory teams.

Ethically utilise artificial intelligence tools to support scientific report writing process, evaluating the accuracy, relevance, and limitations of AI-generated biological content, and applying appropriate revisions to ensure scientific integrity.
Recognise hazards and minimise risks when using basic experimental apparatus, and demonstrate ethical conduct in learning.
Demonstrate an understanding of biological terminology and foundational concepts in experimental contexts.
Implement the scientific method and experimental design.

title: Molecular Laboratory Skills for Biological Sciences
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course is designed to provide extensive training in the laboratory practices associated with biological research. Module 1 will focus on enzymes and biochemical reactions; Module 2 will focus on the chemistry of DNA; and Module 3 will focus on Immunochemistry and its application to biological research.
learning_outcomes: Maintain an accurate and organised lab book, communicate experimental outcomes through structured reports, and collaborate effectively within laboratory teams.
Recognise and apply biological terminology and concepts in experimental contexts.
Use fundamental skills in the collection, processing and interpretation of biological information.
Practice safe use of experimental apparatus with hazard minimisation, and begin applying ethical thinking in biological investigations.

Ethically utilise artificial intelligence tools to support scientific report writing process, evaluating the accuracy, relevance, and limitations of AI-generated biological content, and applying appropriate revisions to ensure scientific integrity.

title: Organisms to Ecosystems
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course introduces the taxonomic and functional diversity of organisms together with their interactions with each other and the physical world. Students will gain an understanding of the immense scale of biological diversity, how that diversity arose and what are the essential elements required to maintain that diversity. This course is also the gateway to real understanding of how organisms work including the development and function of multicellular organisms. This understanding of the organism will then be expanded to interactions between organisms as populations, communities and ecosystems. Understanding how organisms and ecosystems function enables us to move towards living systems that are aligned with natural processes and are essential ingredients to sustainability. Students who have completed this course are well placed to study further studies in: animal and plant development and function; microbiology; ecology, biodiversity and environmental biology courses at 2000 and 3000 level.
learning_outcomes: Explain concepts of evolutionary processes and population and community ecology;
Define biological terminology in relation to tissues, organisms, ecology and ecosystems;
Recognise the diversity of the form, development and function of multicellular organisms, particularly plants and animals;
Explain biodiversity and its evolutionary history;
Apply critical thinking and the scientific approach to interpret biological information in the form of diagrams, graphs, tables and text.
Explain the concepts of micro and macro evolution and speciation and describe mechanisms underpinning taxonomic and functional diversity;

title: Biochemistry
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: Living systems are made up of molecules and this course introduces the diversity of important biological molecules and shows how their structures relate to their function. The smaller biomolecules such as amino acids, nucleotides and sugars have important biological functions of their own, and are also utilised as building blocks for biopolymers such as proteins, nucleic acids and polysaccharides. The metabolic processes that occur in cells to synthesise and degrade these biomolecules and to provide energy for the cell will be presented with a view to showing how biochemical reactions and pathways are connected and controlled.
learning_outcomes: Identify the sources of energy for cells, and explain how cells utilise this chemical energy for growth and maintenance;
Apply scientific philosophy of research in biochemistry;
Outline the diversity of biomolecules, and distinguish their metabolic and structural roles in cellular function;
Describe how chemical reactions are mediated, integrated and regulated in the cell.

title: Fundamentals of Biology and Biochemistry
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: The diversity of important biological molecules and how their structures relate to their function in relation to living systems is demonstrated. Smaller biomolecules such as amino acids, nucleotides and sugars that were studied in first year chemistry (CHEM1120) are known to have important biological functions of their own, and are also utilised as building blocks for biopolymers such as proteins, nucleic acids and polysaccharides. The metabolic processes that occur in cells to synthesise and degrade these biomolecules and to provide energy for the cell will be presented with a view to showing how biological structures, biochemical reactions and pathways are connected and controlled in living systems. Students will gain competency in laboratory skills.
learning_outcomes: Competently operate laboratory equipment, follow protocols and solve practical problems relevant to biochemistry experiments;
Define how chemical reactions are mediated, integrated and regulated in the cell;
Correlate practical activities conducted in the laboratory to key biochemistry concepts;
Delineate the sources of energy for cells, and describe how cells utilise this chemical energy for growth and maintenance;
Communicate the results of both theoretical and experimental work in written, oral and report formats.
Characterise the diversity of biomolecules, and describe their metabolic and structural roles in cellular function;
Explain and describe the cellular structure and function of animal and plant cells;

title: Plant Adaptation to Climate Change
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: Plants are multicellular, sessile organisms composed of many different cell types originated from restricted regions of plant tissues called meristems. The coordinated development of different plant cell types requires cell division, expansion and differentiation and their organisation into specific tissues and organs to produce a functional plant. Much of this highly ordered cell development is driven by gene expression in response to the surrounding environment. Building on this knowledge, this course explores the adaptive response of plant vegetative and reproductive development to a changing environment. Understanding this complex interaction between plants and their environment is of high importance as it can be exploited to sustain and improve plant fitness and productivity to benefit ecosystem health and/or agriculture. The course provides opportunities to (i) achieve a systematic understanding of plant development and function, and (ii) hone skills in developing logical arguments via the analysis and interpretation of scientific data.
learning_outcomes: Define the unique processes specific to plant vegetative and reproductive development;
Identify and investigate biological problems.
Describe specific plant cell structures and explain their functional significance;
Explain how plant cells perceive and interpret environmental signals;
Interpret scientific data and literature;
Define the core concepts of plant cell development and describe their interaction with the surrounding environment;

title: Molecular Genetics
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Molecular genetics is at the centre of contemporary biology with DNA technology of ever increasing social relevance. This course will provide the core information required to understand molecular genetics and will examine the central roles of nucleic acids and proteins in the storage and flow of genetic information. The central dogma of molecular genetics will be examined in detail as well as outlining the mechanisms of transferring genetic information from one generation to the next. The replication, reading and the expression of genetic information will also be discussed in detail in this course. Questions to be addressed include: What is a gene? What are genes made of and where are genes located? How does a gene exert its effect? How is a gene mutated? How is a gene inherited? How are different genes maintained within a population?
learning_outcomes: Identify, gather, retrieve and analyse appropriate molecular genetics information via the internet;
Describe the structure of nucleic acids: from single nucleotides through to whole genomes;
Explain how gene expression is regulated at multiple levels;
Describe the role that mutation plays both in cancer genetics and in evolution;
Use online resources to interpret molecular genetics data.
Compare and contrast the principles of Mendelian and population genetics;
Explain the differences between the core molecular processes of replication, transcription and translation;
Critically review scientific papers and general media presentations on issues related to molecular genetics;

title: Microbial Biology
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: Microbiology is the fundamental biological science that studies microscopic single-celled organisms including bacteria, archaea, protists, fungi, and viruses. An understanding of the structure, life-cycle, metabolism and growth of microbes is essential for further study in a variety of biological sciences including genetics, ecology, evolution, health and biotechnology. Knowledge of microbes also has important applications in environmental sciences, agriculture, food production and safety. This course provides students with a foundation in microbial biology, sufficient for further study in a range of disciplines and necessary for continued studies in microbiology and biotechnology.
learning_outcomes: Describe the diversity and characteristics of microorganisms;
Link principles and theory of microbial genetics to applications in biotechnology;
Characterise beneficial and pathological interactions of microorganisms with the human body;
Apply knowledge of the physio-chemical factors to the growth of microorganisms;
Communicate scientific concepts in written form using appropriate terminology;
Explain how food production, spoilage and disease transmission is orchestrated by microorganisms;

title: Advanced Laboratory Skills in Biological Sciences
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course is designed to provide extensive and advanced training in the laboratory practices associated with biological research. Students will undertake scientific experiments in molecular biology, microbiology, plant and animal biology. Students will consolidate their appreciation of the scientific method and philosophy of science; experimental design, hypothesis testing and problem solving; health and safety in the laboratory; the use of lab books to organise and document experimental details and results; data analysis, interpretation and presentation; report writing demonstrating effective use of the introduction, methods, results, and discussion format; referencing; ethics, academic and personal/professional integrity.
learning_outcomes: Ethically utilise artificial intelligence tools to support scientific report writing process, evaluating the accuracy, relevance, and limitations of AI-generated biological content, and applying appropriate revisions to ensure scientific integrity.
Maintain an accurate and organised lab book, communicate experimental outcomes through structured reports and oral presentations, and collaborate effectively within laboratory teams.
Apply biological terminology and advanced concepts to conduct and interpret experimental investigations.
Apply ethical conduct in research and demonstrate advanced hazard recognition and safe use of complex experimental apparatus in biological investigations.
Apply scientific philosophy and methodology in the design, analysis, and interpretation of advanced experimental investigations, including complex quantitative calculations.

title: Laboratory Skills in Biological Systems
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course is designed to provide students with extensive training in the laboratory practices associated with biological research. The course is divided into three modules, the focus areas include microbial systems, plant biology systems and animal biology systems. Students completing this course will be able to demonstrate intermediate-level training in experimental design and development which will enable progression to advanced training in these skill sets in 3000-level courses.
learning_outcomes: Ethically utilise artificial intelligence tools to support scientific report writing process, evaluating the accuracy, relevance, and limitations of AI-generated biological content, and applying appropriate revisions to ensure scientific integrity.
Explain experimental design and show the skills required to collect, process and interpret biological information.
Use biological terminology to explain experimental approaches and demonstrate a working knowledge of the scientific method.
Demonstrate ethical conduct in learning and research, with responsible use of experimental apparatus in biological investigations.
Maintain an accurate and organised lab book, communicate experimental outcomes through structured reports, and collaborate effectively within laboratory teams.

title: Animal Physiology, Reproduction and Development
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: The process of sexual reproduction is a critical driver of population genetics, facilitating trait variations that shape our biosphere. This course will establish knowledge of animal physiology and reproduction by examining the tissues, organs and cells that govern the life cycle. The course will uncover the biological processes that drive the formation of the female and male gametes, how these cells form a new body and factors that may disrupt these critical processes. Indeed, the programing, founded in the gametes, provides the trajectory for embryo development and the establishment of a new individual. This course will also focus on the development and physiology of some key organs including the circulatory and nervous systems, as well as the organs that provides reproductive capacity, completing the reproductive life cycle. Animal Physiology, Reproduction and Development focuses on mammalian systems but also uses other animal systems as models to advance our understanding. During the course, we will also discuss the technologies currently used and the latest scientific inroads into assisted reproduction or ‘IVF’ for mammals, including livestock.
learning_outcomes: Integrate and explain the basic operations of the nervous and circulatory systems as well as the nutritional requirements of animals;
Summarise the processes of spermatogenesis and oogenesis and justify the importance of sperm post-testicular maturation events required for fertilisation;
Interpret experimental data, assimilate research articles, prepare figures and tables and communicate an understanding of animal reproduction and physiology via the production of scientific reports.
Link the molecular mechanisms of early embryo development and explain the mechanisms involved in embryo development, sexual differentiation and organogenesis;
Outline the basic structure and control processes of the nervous systems and explain the molecular processes of how muscle movement is achieved;
Differentiate the reproductive hormones and describe how reproductive processes are regulated by the endocrine system;

title: Molecular Biology
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course is designed to encompass the major process of molecular biology. These are examined in both eukaryotes and non-eukaryotes. A particular focus will be given to transcriptional regulation in both these systems. An additional section will encompass systems biology.
learning_outcomes: Interpret and review research in molecular biology;
Illustrate the complexities of the regulation of gene expression;
Develop and communicate scientific theories;
Apply skills in information retrieval, interpretation and presentation.
Explain the ways in which knowledge of the basic biology of an organism can inform applied research;

title: Microbiology
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: Microorganisms are by far the most abundant and diverse life-forms. BIOL3100 will explore the range of microorganisms that exist and how they have adapted to live in almost every environment on the planet. It will also examine the involvement of pathogens in human disease, how the immune system fights infection and how epidemiology can be used to monitor, track and prevent further spread of infectious disease. Microbes are also of great use to us; the modern biotechnology applications of microbes will be examined showing how microorganisms have been used by industry to produce a range of products essential to modern society, including the development of novel antibiotics to combat the growing threat of antimicrobial drug resistance.
learning_outcomes: Describe the application of microbiology to industrial processes and environmental management in the modern world.
Explain the problems involved in antimicrobial therapy and the need for development of new chemicals for the control of microorganisms;
Describe the biotechnology processes for which microorganisms can be used and manipulated;
Contrast the protective role of the human immune system with strategies of pathogenic microorganisms to evade the immune system and cause disease;
Outline the dynamic nature of symbiotic interactions and apply this knowledge to the changing environment;

title: Clinical Trial Design
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview: Introduces randomised controlled trials and the reasons why they are considered the gold standard in modern medical research. Important statistical issues such as randomisation, the intention to treat principle and sample size are covered in detail.
learning_outcomes: Explain the importance of randomisation in the context of clinical trials
Choose an appropriate trial design and provide a justification for that choice in clinical context
Demonstrate knowledge of the advantages and disadvantages of different clinical trial designs
Describe the difference between the per protocol, as treated and intention to treat analyses
Propose and implement an appropriate randomisation scheme for a range of clinical trial designs
Calculate the power and/or required sample size for a variety of clinical trial designs and comparisons
Explain the difference between superiority, non-inferiority and equivalence comparisons
Assess the implications to sample size and analysis of going from an individually randomised design to a cluster randomised design

title: Linear Regression Modelling
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview: Introduces the core theoretical concepts and practical application issues relating to a widely used analysis technique in contemporary health related research: linear regression modelling.
learning_outcomes: Recognise situations in which an analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) model should be applied, and implement this regression model using statistical software.
Express linear regression models mathematically and construct mathematical arguments about regression concepts;
Use appropriate diagnostic tools to evaluate the reliability of fitted regression models;
Apply model building strategies which take into account interactions and confounders where applicable;
Use statistical software (such as SAS or Stata) to fit appropriate linear regression models answering specific questions;
Interpret and describe the results of regression models using non-technical language that clinicians or other clients can understand;
List and describe the assumptions of linear regression;

title: Applied Longitudinal Analysis
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview: The course aims to provide students with the understanding and skills to undertake statistical analysis of longitudinal data.
learning_outcomes: Specify and fit generalised linear mixed models for longitudinal data with a categorical or count response variable
Interpret interaction parameters in linear regression models and explain the relevance of interaction to longitudinal analysis
Explore longitudinal data by graphing and describing response trajectories
Specify and fit marginal models for longitudinal data with a categorical or count response variable using generalised estimating equations

For a specified research question and sample of longitudinal data, select an appropriate regression model, assess the validity of alternate fitted models and interpret model parameters for a non-statistical audience
Identify and describe longitudinal data and convert between wide and long data forms
Specify and fit linear regression models with specified covariance structures or random effects (linear mixed model) for longitudinal data with a continuous response variable

title: Biostatistics A
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview: The aim is to provide students with an understanding of statistical reasoning and its application to epidemiological studies and the ability to read and critically evaluate the statistical section of journal articles. The course introduces basic statistical concepts of data presentation, probability distributions, confidence intervals hypothesis testing, sample size and power.
learning_outcomes: Describe the importance of considering power and the Type II error rate during study design.
Apply exploratory data analysis methods to describe/summarise a distribution and assess whether data are normally distributed.
Interpret results of commonly used statistical methods as they are presented in published literature.
Perform sample size calculations relating to means and proportions for common study designs.
Conduct hypothesis tests relating to means and proportions and explain the role of the test statistic, p-value, and significance/Type I error rate.
Use properties of the probability distribution function to calculate Normal probabilities and Z-scores.
Calculate and interpret Confidence Intervals for means and proportions and state the assumptions on which they are based.
Discuss the difference between statistical significance and clinical significance.

title: Generalised Linear Models
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview: This course presents methods for analyses of categorical data, with a key focus on generalised linear models (GLMs). Students will study contingency tables and gain experience with a range of generalised linear models appropriate to binary, count, nominal, ordinal and time-to-event response variables. There will be an emphasis on understanding model equations, fitting statistical models using statistical software, using fitted model equations to identify estimates of interest, checking model assumptions and accurately interpreting results for reporting or publication.
learning_outcomes: Propose and fit appropriate GLMs for binary, ordinal and nominal data, and interpret results in relation to the original research question
Present results from GLMs in publication-ready tables and interpret results for a non-statistical audience
Construct GLMs for count data using Poisson or negative binomial regression and defend the choice of model
Recognise time-to-event response variables and correctly format and analyse these using Kaplan-Meier estimators and Cox regression
Identify and define the components of a generalised linear model (GLM)
Determine when contingency table analysis requires methods for stratified or matched data, and correctly apply and appraise the results of such methods
Construct and analyse contingency tables for a range of study designs, using both manual calculations and statistical software
For a given generalised linear model equation and sample from an exponential family distribution, estimate distributional parameters and interpret these in relation to a linear predictor

title: Biostatistics B
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview: The purpose of this course is to build on the knowledge and skills obtained in Biostatistics A, and to introduce more complex methods of analyses which are commonly used in epidemiologic research.
learning_outcomes: Conduct analysis of variance (ANOVA) or the non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis alternative as appropriate using statistical software and interpret output.
Analyse survival outcomes with the log-rank test and/or Cox 'proportional hazards' regression using statistical software and interpret output.
Calculate correlation coefficients using appropriate parametric and non-parametric methods.
Explain the problem of multiple comparisons and apply common adjustments to account for multiple testing.
Identify when the Mantel-Haenszel method is appropriate in order to adjust for stratification.

Analyse 2 x 2 contingency tables arising from a variety of study designs by choosing appropriate measures of association, calculating their confidence intervals, and selecting appropriate hypothesis tests.
Perform logistic regressions using statistical software, interpret output, and describe results about binary outcomes in terms of Odds Ratios.
Perform linear regressions using statistical software, interpret output, and identify violations of model assumptions.
Recognise situations when survival analysis methods are to be used and obtain Kaplan-Meier estimates of survival functions.
Select appropriate methods of analysis from those covered in Biostatistics courses A and B for a given situation.
Use the Chi-squared test or the alternative Fisher's exact test for testing hypotheses about categorical data expressed in an r x c contingency table.

title: Probability and Biostatistical Inference
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview: The first half of the course covers the foundations of probability theory including: probability laws, conditional probability, random variables, probability distributions, expectation and variance, independence, covariance and correlation. Commonly used families of probability distributions and their properties will be discussed. Large sample results such as the Central Limit Theorem will be used to approximate sampling distributions. The second half of the course introduces the basics of statistical inference including: likelihood, point and interval estimation, properties of estimators (such as bias), and hypothesis testing paradigms. Emphasis is placed on theoretical understanding combined with problem solving using basic simulation methods such as Inverse Transform Sampling and Monte Carlo. Practical exercises will include estimating probabilities theoretically and empirically, investigating the performance of basic statistical methods under different assumptions, and interpreting the use of probability and inference in medical statistics research.
learning_outcomes: Calculate statistics such as the mean and variance of common probability distributions.
Calculate probabilities by applying probability laws and theoretical results.
Explain the role of probability in hypothesis testing and describe issues related to interpreting statistical significance.
Apply results from large-sample theory and the Central Limit Theorem to approximate a sampling distribution.
Determine whether random variables are independent and find their covariance and correlation.
Calculate and interpret maximum likelihood estimates and their confidence intervals.
Explain the desirable properties of estimators.
Identify an appropriate probability distribution for a given discrete or continuous random variable and use its properties to calculate probabilities.
Calculate probabilities for joint distributions including marginal and conditional probabilities.
Implement basic simulation methods using statistical software to investigate sampling distributions.

title: Biomolecules
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course examines the analysis of biomolecules. The focus is on using molecular technologies to address current issues. In particular applications in the areas of plant biotechnology and biopharmaceuticals will be discussed. Questions to be addressed include: How are genes cloned? How is plant genetic engineering accomplished? What are the current applications of plant biotechnology? What are the current approaches to the development of drugs? What approaches can be taken to large scale screening of biological compounds for commercial applications?
learning_outcomes: Describe the key principles underpinning the production of transgenic plants for commercial applications.
Critically analyse molecular based data.
Effectively appraise the broad scope for agricultural, industrial, and pharmaceutical applications of molecular techniques.
Provide multiple examples of current day applications of molecular biology.

title: Introduction to the Biotechnology Sector
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Worldwide, the Biotechnology sector is the fastest growing of the scientific sectors. BTEC1000 introduces students to the Biotechnology sector, the range of industries and professions that make up this broad and diverse sector, as well as to present an overview of the key scientific, technological, social, environmental and economic drivers of the Biotechnology sector. There is also a strong focus on the emerging Biotechnologies that are transforming the Biotechnology sector, and society more broadly, through addressing key health, agricultural and environmental challenges. Knowledge of the structure and organisation of the Biotechnology sector will be developed through an emphasis on the role of innovation, technological and scientific advances, intellectual property protection, and the business models that exploit the commercial potential of Biotechnology and take new discoveries to the market place. Students will acquire basic knowledge of how patents work, clinical trials operate in drug discovery and development, and how individual companies operate in the Biotechnology space. Basic skills will be acquired in discovering, analysing and presenting information about the innovation, Research and Development, emerging technologies, intellectual property, businesses and commercialisation in the Biotechnology Sector. The course will set the scene for the development of these themes in more detail in later years of the Bachelor of Biotechnology Program.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a basic familiarisation with major areas of Biotechnology, including pharmaceuticals and disease therapies, plant, animal, reproductive, fermentation and environmental technologies, and the continually evolving area of innovation in the Biotechnology sector.

Demonstrate knowledge on the significance of Intellectual Property and the patents system to the Biotechnology sector, and display a practical working knowledge of accessing, searching and interpreting patent databases.

Demonstrate basic skills in acquiring and presenting information on the business model and technology of individual companies in the biotechnology sector, including summarising and presenting this information through written reports.

Demonstrate knowledge of the organisation and complexity of the Biotechnology Sector, including the role this sector plays in addressing problems and exploiting commercial opportunities in human health, agriculture and the environment.

Display basic knowledge of the critical steps involved in the commercialisation of Biotechnology, including; innovation, Research and Development, intellectual property protection, product testing, licencing and regulatory approval, raising and allocating capital.

title: Cellular Biotechnology
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Techniques that are frequently used in biotechnology research are the basis for this course. The way in which these techniques are integrated in the development of research strategies to solve biotechnology problems then constitute the problem-solving component of the course. Groups are assigned one of a series of biotechnology problems to use as the basis for formulating a position paper and research strategy. The examples that are used to illustrate this course come from the area of reproductive science. The course culminates in an oral presentation describing the background behind a particular biotechnology problem and the research strategy that would be followed in pursuit of a solution.
learning_outcomes: Explain the current molecular and cellular techniques that are used in biotechnology research;
Interpret the ethical consequences of modern reproductive technologies.
Develop a range of communication skills (report writing and audio-visual presentation) appropriate for the biotechnology profession;
Apply scientific thinking to collaboratively problem solve a current research question;
Apply theory and design experimental approaches using current technologies to achieve defined biotechnology objectives;

title: Biotechnology Placement
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course provides the opportunity to complete a 10 week placement in a practicing biotechnology environment in the Private, Public or University sector. This experience will provide a different perspective and context for academic learning, and allows theory to be put into practice. The course requires students to integrate real world skills and experience with theoretical concepts and knowledge obtained during their program. Students will undertake work-integrated placement to position themselves for a career upon graduation. This is achieved through integrating real world skills and experience with work-integrated, experiential learning. Students will be able to undertake their work integrated learning placement in a broad spectrum of work environments (within or outside the University). Students are provided with a range of placement opportunities by the course coordinator.
learning_outcomes: Display an array of Biotechnological skills and knowledge within the workplace environment.
Apply and extend learning from biotechnology theory and laboratory practice to the workplace environment.
Demonstrate and reflect on the application of skills and knowledge from their studies to an authentic workplace environment.
Employ observational, analytical, communication and reporting skills to work effectively within discipline-specific workplaces.
Evaluate the interactions between research and development and business in the Biotechnology sector.
Identify, synthesise, and reflect on key issues in a discipline-specific workplace, integrating theoretical knowledge with practical requirements of the workplace.

title: Introduction to Business Information Systems
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Business Information Systems are considered a key business resource as a platform to process and deliver information that can be used strategically by organisations to improve operational efficiency. This course introduces various types of information systems in an organisation, how information is processed in business information systems, and how huge volume of accounting, financial, marketing or human resource data can be transformed into actionable information. Students will make use of software and employ techniques to understand and learn how information is handled within a business. Ethical issues surrounding the use of information within business organisations will also be addressed in this course.
learning_outcomes: Understand the core principles and definitions of Business Information Systems.
Evaluate the role of Information Systems in supporting management decision-making in the areas of accounting, finance, and marketing.
Recognise how Business Information Systems collect and process information to support business decisions.
Describe the ethical procedure when handling personal information in Business Information Systems.

title: Big Data Analytics
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Big Data Analytics is regarded as one of the important emerging technologies in different fields of business including accounting, economics, finance, marketing, and management. Big data refers to data sets with large sizes that are beyond the ability of traditional data management software tools. While traditional data processing technologies are inadequate, practical knowledge addressing challenges of huge or complex data handling in terms of their analysis, transformation, visualisation and prediction is paramount in businesses. This course introduces students to various massive data sets that can be structured, semi-structured, or unstructured and sourced from multi-media, social media, cloud platforms, web, IoT and traditional economic and business databases. Students will apply data mining and natural language processing tools to these big data to gain business insights such as hidden patterns, untold facts, unknown correlations, market trends, and customer preferences. Big data from social media and financial statements now play a significant role in extracting information for making informed business decisions related to understanding customer behaviours and financial investments. Case studies on big data analytics will be utilised to design and communicate concepts and techniques used in business decision making.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate data sources, data sets, and inferences made from big data analytics.
Discuss the key concepts, benefits, and challenges of big data analytics.
Demonstrate skills in processing and utilising social media data and finance data.
Discuss and evaluate fundamental concepts and principles in big data analytics.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Data Cleansing and Processing in an area of business
Case study - Methods of Data Analytics in an area of business

title: Data Visualisation for Decision Makers in Business
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In order to develop solutions for real-world business problems, managers and senior decision makers require a range of visual graphs, tables, and meaningful descriptive information presented, utilising underlying statistical analyses of big data. This course focuses on the tools, techniques and approaches to effectively analyse and communicate business data to decision makers. The key deliverables are related to different forms of communication through data visualisation for managerial reporting in business, data dashboarding and the benefits and limitations of such forms in business operation. Both statistical software and data visualisation software will be used to demonstrate the process of transforming raw data into useful information that could provide actionable decision-making insights. Students will be taught effective communication skills for presenting complex data-based information to support decision-making.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the key techniques and theory used in visualisation.
Evaluate graphical presentation technique for different types of business data in the form of multivariate data, networks, text and cartography.
Demonstrate understanding of effective communication practices for supporting decision-making.
Use software to effectively visualise and communicate data.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Creating a Managerial Report Using Business Data

title: Business Analytics in Practice
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course is the capstone course for the Bachelor of Business Analytics. Students are required to apply and integrate domain specific knowledge and skills they have gained in the program in business areas including accounting, finance, human resource management, and marketing. Throughout the course, workshops utilising 'live' cases will demonstrate the benefits of business analytics to decision making in these functional domains. Guest lectures from business will be included and the course culminates in a project applying business analytics to a business problem.
learning_outcomes: Collaborate with others to produce a written report
Develop and communicate orally and in written form, a comprehensive proposal for improvements in the use of Business Analytics
Using business analytics processes and intelligence, evaluate a set of problems in the areas of business
Critically assess the usage of business analytics in the areas of business including accounting, finance, human resource management, and marketing
Demonstrate visually to stakeholders how business improvements might be achieved

assessment_tasks.task_name: Reflection on groupwork with plan for improved practice
Profile report on the use of Business Analytics in the context of live business cases

title: Business Process Modelling
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: A business process is a set of activities that jointly realise a business goal in an organisational and technical environment. This course looks at ways in which business processes can be analysed, redesigned, and improved. Managing business processes involves analysis of the focal organisation but can extend to other interacting organisations. The aim of implementing an optimal Business Process Model (BPM) is to ensure the technology is aligned with strategic objectives and cultural practices of the business organisation.
