Students taking this course will be able to analyse and innovate an existing business process to provide operational efficiencies within the business.
learning_outcomes: Explain and elaborate upon the role of the Business Process Modelling (BPM) in Business.
Discuss an existing business process and evaluate its alignment with organisational strategy.
Analyse and evaluate an existing set of Business Processes recommending areas for improvement. Create an optimal BPM Plan.
Discuss the principles of Business Process Design.

assessment_tasks.task_name: BPM implementation strategy and implementation plan

title: Cybersecurity for Business
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In this course, students will dive into the crucial world of protecting digital assets while mastering the skills needed to keep an organisation's information safe. As they explore contemporary cybersecurity principles and tackle real-world cyber threats, students will learn to craft and enact strong cybersecurity strategies that align with business goals. Our diverse modules will take students through the technical heart of cybersecurity, covering network and application security, and will also delve into the human aspect, exploring topics like social engineering. With a mix of engaging lectures, practical labs, and a hands-on capstone project, students will face actual cybersecurity challenges and develop robust solutions. This course is a gateway to understanding the indispensable role of cybersecurity in today’s business arena, preparing students for a rewarding career in either a managerial or technical pathway.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the core principles of cybersecurity in the context of business operations.
Employ and appraise emerging cybersecurity technologies.
Formulate effective responses to cybersecurity incidents to ensure business recovery and continuity.
Develop and implement comprehensive cybersecurity risk assessments to mitigate potential threats.
Formulate and implement robust cybersecurity strategies aligned with organisational objectives.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Business
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Businesses and governments have massive data available to them with which to make systematic strategic decisions. Artificial Intelligence (AI) and machine learning can process and provide fast turnover of these very large amounts of information. This course is designed to provide students with knowledge related to established and emerging developments of AI in organisations using real-world examples. Applications of AI in various areas including finance, fraud detection, customer relationship management, and human resources management will be discussed.
learning_outcomes: Discuss advantages and the risk of using Artificial Intelligence and machine learning techniques for strategic decision making.
Demonstrate understanding of how to operationalise Artificial Intelligence and machine learning.
Demonstrate an understanding of the main concepts of Artificial Intelligence and machine learning.
Identify key areas to apply Artificial Intelligence and machine learning techniques within a business organisation.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Case Study and Report on Artificial Intelligence (AI) in business

title: Data Governance Using Blockchain for Business
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Blockchain is considered a ledger system that assists in governing business data through time-stamped blocks that works mainly in a decentralised manner. For businesses, blockchain applications enable fundamental changes across different sectors, including fintech, government, health and supply chain, specifically for its potential benefits which include reduction in costs and complexity of transactions data between parties, enhanced security, improved transparency and regulation. This course aims to provide a conceptual understanding of the function of Blockchains as a data governance method and how the new applications that they enable for businesses. It covers the technological aspects of Blockchain operations as distributed data structures and decision-making systems with their functionality, data structure, and different platforms. Students will learn critical evaluations of Blockchain applications in different sectors, identifying data governance demands, opportunities, legal issues, risks and challenges.
learning_outcomes: Examine how Blockchain works for data governance and the elements and technologies of transactions, blocks, proof-of-work, and consensus building.
Explain the main concepts of Blockchain for business data governance.
Identify key issues of data governance and assess how Blockchain exists in the public domain in decentralised manner
Critically evaluate Blockchain applications in different sectors

assessment_tasks.task_name: Case Study Analysis for Application Design

title: Business Intelligence and Data Management
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Business Intelligence (BI) aims to deliver straightforward snapshots of the current state of affairs to business managers. It uses a combination of software tools, databases and models to support business professionals in their understanding of business operations and performance. One of the goals of BI is that it should be easy for relatively non-technical end users to understand, and even to explore the data and create new reports.
learning_outcomes: Critically assess existing BI practices when using data such as product reports, sales reports, and financial reports.
Demonstrate understanding of how Business Intelligence (BI) supports managerial decision making and problem solving in the real-world.
Make use of BI tools and models which are available to assist in managerial decision making.
Apply knowledge about decision-making processes by interpreting business intelligence to identify a current business issue.

title: Digital Ecosystems and Transformation
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course offers a comprehensive insight into the world of digital ecosystems and their role in driving digital transformation. Students will explore the fundamentals of digital ecosystems, delve into transformation strategies, understand interconnected digital platforms like AI and blockchain, and design robust ecosystem strategies. The curriculum also addresses challenges, ethical considerations, and future trends, enriched with real-world case studies. This course is ideal for business leaders, IT professionals, entrepreneurs, and those keen on the digital landscape.
learning_outcomes: Develop and implement effective digital ecosystem strategies that align with organisational objectives and respond to market demands.
Define and differentiate between various components of digital ecosystems.
Identify and explain the core principles and methodologies behind successful digital transformation, including its impact on industries, businesses, and consumers.
Evaluate the role and interplay of key digital platforms, including cloud computing, IoT, AI, and blockchain, in creating and enhancing value within digital ecosystems.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Business Management
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Artificial Intelligence (AI) makes computer systems to mimic human problem solving and decision making abilities used in businesses. AI systems used in business are increasingly substituting human’s tasks, roles, responsibilities, and their decision making. Consequently, business management reshapes the business processes and core actions in management for better interaction with the AI system. While the ‘new normal’ disruptive technology AI opens up the door to design and implement smart practical applications transforming the new abundance of data to empower intelligent decisions, the essence of AI knowledge become more pervasive reality of automation for business management and its potential impact on human engagement in business operation is massive. This course is designed to provide students with knowledge related to established and emerging developments of AI systems in organisations using real-world examples. Applications of AI systems in various areas including management, finance, customer relationship management, and human resources management will be explored.
learning_outcomes: Justify AI application selection, AI systems assessment, planning and integration in order to safeguard appropriate automation and substitute processes that precisely contribute to meet management needs in contemporary organisations.
Appraise AI solutions implementation in contemporary organisations.
Conceptualise business problems to design and employ AI solutions for improving business management and relevant data-driven decision making.
Communicate appropriate and authenticate ethical AI systems and purposeful recommendations considering societal and moral boundaries/issues with reference.
Critically review the assortment and provisions of AI applications in business management focusing data processing approaches and smart solutions.

assessment_tasks.task_name: AI training video plus Peer review

title: Globalisation and International Management
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course is only available to students enrolled in the High Performing Students Program. This course will analyse the challenges and opportunities presented by the globalisation of markets and production for managers in both domestic and multinational companies (MNCs). The cultural, political, economic and technological drivers (and implications) of Globalisation will be presented providing an introduction to basic concepts in global economics and international business. This course will also analyze how globalisation impacts upon a variety of management functions e.g. human resource management, marketing and supply chain management. While a key purpose of the course will be to understand how managers design effective strategic business decisions cognizant of cultural, political and economic difference internationally, a critique of the basic paradigm of profit maximizing behaviour by MNCs will also be presented through discussion of strategizing with corporate social responsibility.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate critical thinking and conduct a basic analysis of business opportunities in an international context.
Think critically about underlying theories, concepts, assumptions and arguments in international business management.
Develop the essential international perspectives which inform professional standards and ethical practice in international management.
Identify the key business, political and social issues raised by Globalisation
Work independently and collaboratively to analyse international business opportunities and communicate the outcomes of a research project.

title: Business Communications
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Effective communication forms the cornerstone of organisational success, pivotal to today’s global landscape. This course immerses students in the fundamentals of professional communication, bridging the gap between theory and real-world application. Delving into contemporary management and organisational communication theories, students will gain insights into building and nurturing professional relationships in diverse business contexts. The curriculum emphasises the significance of clear business writing, the art of persuasive oral discourse, and the intricacies of non-verbal cues, all while understanding the dynamics of communication across varied teams and cultures. This course provides a steppingstone for those eager to navigate the multifaceted world of business communication with confidence.
learning_outcomes: Apply techniques to deliver clear and relevant oral presentations on introductory business topics.
Collaborate in teams to demonstrate effective business communication.
Deliver appropriate information on foundational business subjects using written and oral communications.
Explain key theories and principles underpinning effective business communication within a global context.

title: Analytics in Business
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course serves as an initiation into the imperative yet exciting problem world of business analytics. Today's organisations exist in a data-rich landscape, replete with intricate streams of information originating from diverse domains such as marketing, finance, and operations. This course aims to equip students with the core statistical knowledge behind business analytics skills required to navigate this complex terrain, enabling them to make informed managerial decisions. Beyond traditional statistical methods, the course focuses on a holistic and hands-on approach to inform data driven solutions to business problems. Students will not only learn to organise and analyse business data but will also acquire the skills to interpret this data within real-world contexts, ensuring that their insights can be communicated effectively to a non-technical audience. This course also aims to address the key dimensions of applied analytics, statistical rigour, visualisation, ethics, and practical relevance, aligning with an applied focus and the synthesis of multiple skill sets. It emphasises not only the 'what' but also the 'how' and 'why' of analytics in business.
learning_outcomes: Apply data analytics to real-world data to help inform business decision making.
Describe the role of the application of data analytics in business and outline the sources and use of data.
Create and analyse data visualisations to inform business decision making.
Clearly communicate data insights to a wide range of audiences within the business domain.

title: Ethical Principles for Responsible Business
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Contemporary business no longer operates behind closed doors. Corporate conduct is now subject to sustained scrutiny from an expanding range of stakeholders, investors, regulators, employees and civil society. Each of these stakeholders requires reassurance that the organisations serves more than shareholder interests alone. Managers are increasingly called upon to reconcile short-term performance with long-term commitments to economic, social and environmental sustainability often amid competing pressures. This course develops students’ capabilities to operate as ethical and sustainable business leaders in this environment. Students will engage with frameworks for ethical decision-making, examine innovative approaches to corporate, social and environmental responsibility, & develop sophisticated stakeholder engagement strategies. They will explore the evolving landscape of professional ethics standards and consider the role of leadership in the management of these complexities.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the role of global stakeholders, their relationships, interest and leadership in the creation of successful strategies for the resolution of ethical issues.
Explain the significance of ethics across a diverse range of real-world issues.
Propose ethical, evidence-based solutions to global business challenges and inequalities
Apply ethical principles and theories to global decision-making practices.

title: Project in Business
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Apply your knowledge in a real world organisational environment. Within this engaged learning course you will work on a project that is of value to your host organisation. This project may require problem resolution or may involve the development of something new for the organisation. You will work to generate an understanding of organisational context; gather and analyse data relevant to the project; apply what you have learnt in your Major, within that context; and deliver a report on the issue to your host organisation. Host organisations may be public sector, private sector, not for profit, or for-profit. They may be manufacturing, service industry, professional service or healthcare. You will scope and plan your project in collaboration with your host organisation. This Course enables you to engage a real world organisation with your skills, talents and prior learning while you continue to learn but in a very different way. Note: Students cannot complete a project with their current employer. Students undertaking this course will be allocated to a project provider, namely a local business. They will be required to attend the workplace in order to gather data relevant to their project.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the actual project outcomes and identify reasons for any deviations from the stated expected outcomes.
Demonstrate an integrative understanding of the diverse perspectives apparent within the work environment.

Analyse the needs of an organisational issue within the workplace and meet the organisation's requirements through the development and completion of a disciplined project, culminating in a written report.
Appreciate and apply professional behaviour and ethical practices.
Employ the inquiry and research process to contribute to organisational improvement.
Locate, analyse and evaluate contemporary research information relevant to the workplace project.
Engage in reflective practices throughout a project cycle to improve personal and business outcomes.

title: Industry Placement
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: The Industry Placement course supports Newcastle Business School undergraduate students to undertake a Career Ready Placement relevant to their area of study. Through a structured Work Integrated Learning experience, students apply the knowledge and skills they have developed throughout their degree in a professional setting, build professional networks, and enhance their career readiness. The course is delivered through a range of placement pathways. Students may indicate their preferred pathway; however, placement arrangements are subject to availability, suitability, and alignment with the student’s circumstances and area of study. Although activities vary across pathways, each provides a comparable professional development experience with an equivalent overall time commitment. All pathways are designed to develop the skills and career readiness required to achieve the course learning outcomes.
learning_outcomes: Develop a strategic career plan that draws on relevant experience within a professional business environment and utilise industry relevant language to present this plan.
Evaluate their ethical practices and behaviours in a professional business environment.
Assess their technical, discipline-specific, and professional skills within a professional business environment.
Apply technical, discipline-specific, and professional skills, and knowledge to strengthen their employability.
Reflect on relevant individual technical, discipline-specific, and personal skills and competencies.

title: Career-Ready Industry Led Project Lab
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: BUSN3004 provides students with an opportunity to develop professional skills and career readiness through experiential learning. Students will engage in one of three streams: WAIVER/Accelerator Discipline-Specific Industry Led Lab Project External Labs or Clinics Lab Projects Each stream offers tailored activities and experiences designed to enhance employability and professional growth. Students will complete a combination of workshops, projects, and reflective tasks aligned with the course learning outcomes.
learning_outcomes: Present a strategic career plan on relevant experience within the professional business environment.
Synthesise technical skills, competencies, and knowledge to improve their employability.
Assess their technical skills in a professional business environment.
Reflect on relevant individual skills and technical competencies.
Evaluate their ethical practices and behaviours in a professional business environment.

title: Theory in Commerce
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course provides a detailed analysis of historical and theoretical issues in commerce. Students may choose to focus on the discipline of finance, economics, or accounting.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of the methodological foundations of commerce.
Apply key theoretical concepts to qualitative and empirical data.
Demonstrate an understanding of key theoretical concepts in commerce.
Use advanced communication skills to disseminate findings in a professionally acceptable manner.

title: International Work Placement in Business
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: The International Work Placement in Business course provides an opportunity for students enrolled in Newcastle Business School undergraduate programs to undertake a Career Ready International Placement or similar community learning relevant to their study. Students complete supervised international placement, whereby they apply knowledge developed throughout their studies and acquire new knowledge and professional networks to support their work readiness. Students observe and engage in a range of work practices with the host organisation during their placement.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on relevant individual technical, discipline-specific, and personal skills and competencies.
Assess their technical, discipline-specific, and personal skills within a professional business environment.
Develop a strategic career plan that draws on relevant experience within a professional business environment and clearly articulate it in an oral presentation.
Evaluate their ethical practices and behaviours in a professional business environment.
Apply technical, discipline-specific, and personal skills, and knowledge to strengthen their employability.

title: Theory in Business
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course provides both theoretical and applied perspectives on business theory and concepts. Students may choose to focus on the discipline of International business, Human Resource Management, Marketing, Leadership and Management, or Tourism, Sport and Event Management.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate polished oral communication skills to disseminate research findings and insights.
Use relevant secondary data for business.
Critically evaluate business related literature in discussion.
Apply theories, models and concepts to contemporary business issues.
Defend theories, applications, debates, and recent developments in business.

title: Business Research Methods
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Business Research Methods equips students with the skills to develop and undertake a research dissertation. It provides the theoretical and practical preparation for business research The course covers the necessary skills and requirements for a literature review, qualitative and quantitative methods, and a research proposal in addition to the pragmatics of ethics and project management. Peer review, skill development workshops and practice exercises are the key learning strategies.
learning_outcomes: Present and defend research literature, methodology and proposal.
Develop a research proposal as the basis for a thesis.
Write a literature review that synthesises and evaluates literature in a specific topic area to justify a research questions.
Apply appropriate research design and methods to address a specific research question and acknowledge the ethical implications of the research.

title: Research Thesis 1
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Commencing a research thesis of approximately 20,000 words.
learning_outcomes: Select and execute an appropriate research design.
Develop and articulate a research problem.
Link the research problem to an appropriate body of literature, identifying specific question(s) to be addressed.
Prepare draft thesis chapters corresponding to outcomes 1, 2 and 3.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Draft thesis chapters in collaboration with supervisor

title: Research Thesis 2
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Completion of a research thesis of approximately 20,000 words under the guidance of an individual supervisor.
learning_outcomes: Interpret findings and place them in the board context of relevant theory.
Collect and analyse data relevant to a pre-determined research question and design.
Conclude and report the project consistent with discipline conventions.

title: Acting and Performance 1
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course offers a basic introduction to the craft of the actor and performer with particular emphasis upon the creation of performance from text-based sources. The course addresses the physical, vocal, character development and presentation skills necessary for creating engaging live performances for contemporary theatre, performance and public live appearances.
learning_outcomes: Perform physical communication methods accurately to convey character and emotion in live performances.
Apply basic acting techniques from Stanislavski and associated practices in a live performance setting.
Analyse a play script and executeperformance objectives based on a detailed textual analysis.
Utilise vocal techniques effectively during live performances to enhance clarity and expression.
Demonstrate relaxation techniques through specific exercises to achieve performer readiness.

title: Creative and Performing Arts 1
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course is a core foundational course providing students with theoretical and practical resources for creating Contemporary Creative and Performing Arts, including Theatre, Performance and Drama. The course introduces an overview of 20th and 21st century practice in live and mediated performance-making. Exploring theories and key exemplars, students engage in practical inquiry from a range of sources and stimuli in a variety of devising contexts to develop critical thinking and creative problem-solving skills. As part of cohesive creative teams students develop collaborative group performances. With this development base of knowledge students will advance their skills in the study and creation of performance in the Bachelor of Music and Performing Arts.
learning_outcomes: Identify and apply the stages and benchmarks of devising in live performance-making;
Analyse contemporary performance practices;
Apply an approach to the craft of acting that emphasises the physicality of the actor.
Collaboratively create new, devised performance works;

title: Stagecraft
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Stagecraft is crucial to successful public events, live performances, festivals and musical productions. This course introduces students to the fundamental skills of stage management. Students will learn about the safe and efficient installation, operation and design of lighting, sound, actors/performers and projections. They will learn the basics of the role of the stage managers, lighting and sound designers and engineers. Students will engage in practical and technical skill-based learning, develop strategies for time management and practice collaborative teamwork during staged events.
learning_outcomes: Employ appropriate tools, technologies and electrics safely in the context of a performance;
Evaluate the stage manager’s roles and responsibilities and the different roles of stage production teams in light of the course's theoretical underpinnings;
Apply basic construction and programming techniques in light, sound and set design;
Facilitate collaborative workflows from concept design to building, running and tearing down after a production close.

title: Creative and Performing Arts 2
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course introduces areas that are fundamental to the Creative and Performing Arts, including Theatre, Performance and Drama in a variety of contemporary cultural contexts. It develops approaches to collaboration and devising introduced in CAPA1001. It explores a range of creative and analytical approaches to applied theatre addressing contemporary social issues and themes in contemporary cultural contexts. The course introduces practical and analytical approaches needed for the understanding of socially-engaged arts practice in a contemporary setting.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate written / oral communication skills using language appropriate to the field of contemporary performance;
Analyse and critically appraise theoretical and practical approaches to creative works, events and performance making in a range of cultural contexts.
Design a socially-engaged arts project;
Apply and develop skills in applied theatre praxis.

title: Directing Workshop
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The director's creative process can make or break the audience's experience of live performances. Students in this course will build their performing arts skills in theatre, live art, drama and sound in a variety of forms and cultural contexts. Collaborative methodologies will be applied to the director's role through group dynamics of performance. Analytical, theoretical and practical approaches are considered in relation to gesture, movement, text and sound. Formal elements, including language and text, representation, symbolism, abstraction, hybridity, texture, scale and narrative, are applied to distinct theatrical forms in a variety of settings.
learning_outcomes: Implement written and oral communication skills and language relevant to the field of contemporary performance.
Generate directions that enhance a rehearsal of a set text
Apply collaborative skills in the creation of live performance works.
Examine a creative event that makes use of gesture, image, movement, space, text and/or sound.
Critically appraise theoretical and practical approaches to creative works, events and performance in a range of cultural contexts.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Presentation in class with short written text

title: Process Engineering Principles
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course will introduce you to a number of principles and concepts that are fundamental to process engineering. The course gives real-life examples of process industries to provide you with the context of engineering in practice. As part of this course you will also be given training in producing technical drawings such as piping and instrumentation diagrams (P&IDs), and provided with an introduction to safe workshop practice.
learning_outcomes: Produce piping and instrumentation diagrams (PandID) and other technical drawings to an acceptable standard using AutoCAD PandID, Visio and/or similar packages.
Develop problem solving skills and encourage decision making.
Introduce first year students to fundamental chemical engineering concepts and principles.
Develop safe workshop procedures and skills, and demonstrate the correct use of basic hand tools.

title: Australian Theatre and Performance
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course will explore various ways in which theatre and performance making in Australia is shaped by specific cultural identities. A diverse range of approaches to theatre and performance making will be examined, such as the role of Indigenous, queer, feminist, disabled and culturally diverse artists. This particular focus on the construction of cultural identities will inform students in creating their own scene-based performances.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate awareness of a diverse range of approaches to expressing cultural identities via the medium of theatre and performance.
Develop a portfolio of Performance Resources for a contemporary theatre event.
Demonstrate foundational skills in researching, analysing, structuring and creating a feasible performance proposal that explores cultural diversity.

title: Writing for Performance
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course explores the key principles of dramatic writing for a range of contemporary performance modes. Students are given opportunities to develop their own creative potential through original script writing.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate understanding of the role and craft of the writer in contemporary theatre and performance.
Demonstrate understanding of the differences between dramatic and other forms of creative writing.
Practically demonstrate awareness of the skills required to translate an idea into a performable script.

title: Energy Transfer and Technologies
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course comprises two components; heat transfer and energy technologies. The first component of the course presents an elementary treatment of the principle of heat transfer, in which students are introduced to the fundamentals of conduction, convection and radiation. The second component of the course provides an overview of the fuels, power generation, and environmental implications of energy technologies. This component also covers design aspects of energy technologies from an energy transfer point of view.
learning_outcomes: Identify and define, at an introductory level, fuel types, power generation, and environmental implications of energy technologies.
Work as part of a team on the development of an engineering idea from the conceptual stage through to build and operation.
Apply heat transfer principles and mechanisms, and knowledge of existing commercial energy systems, in practical engineering design.
Describe and identify the main physical processes and mechanisms by which heat transfer occurs in different real-world and engineering systems.
Explain energy systems and energy transformations in the context of modern energy sources and use.
Apply the mathematical concepts of one dimensional, multi-dimensional and transient heat transfer to predict numerical outcomes of example systems.

title: Creative and Performing Arts 3
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course focuses on visual media technologies in contemporary Creative and Performing Arts, including Theatre, Performance, Drama and Sound. The course synthesises key ideas already developed in CAPA1001 and CAPA2001. It explores both mediatised and mediated live performance through screen and projection technologies and its impact on the live performer. Using various practical and technological resources, students will engage collaboratively in practical workshops and processes of group reflection, analysis, and aesthetic judgment towards the production of events and performances.
learning_outcomes: Apply collaborative processes, critical analyses, aesthetic judgments and creative production skills to realise a performance event.
Employ physical theatre skills and technologies for several small dramatic presentations;
Analyse critical approaches to the contemporary creative and performing arts;

title: Thermodynamics of Chemical Processes
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course builds upon the first and second laws of thermodynamics, with a focus on flow processes as used in the chemical and power generation industries. A number of cycles are studied in detail, commencing with ideal gas and vapour power and refrigeration cycles. The course is complemented by lectures on how to calculate the fundamental thermodynamic properties of fluids as used in flow processes, together with the thermodynamics of vapour-liquid equilibria. The thermodynamics of chemical reactions is also covered in this course.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate problem solving skills through the application of thermodynamics
Explain and apply thermodynamics as it applies to real cycles, and process engineering

title: Chemical and Renewables Engineering Laboratory
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Comprises experiments related to various aspects of heat, mass and momentum transfer. After successfully conducting an experiment, the students need to write a well formatted technical report. In addition, the course will introduce students to numerical methods, including spreadsheets, for solving typical chemical and renewable energy engineering design and process problems. The computational section also covers key statistical concepts and practice relating mainly to the following: normal distribution, 1 and 2 sample tests and confidence intervals, and the design of experiments.
learning_outcomes: Apply principles learnt in other chemical engineering and renewable energy engineering courses to practical situations
Write technical reports
Demonstrate skills with numerical methods and computing applications
Identify and analyse the fundamental physical parameters of an experimental system
Perform statistical analysis on data and conduct statistically designed experiments
Demonstrate laboratory and analytical skills, safety awareness and organisational skills

title: Particle and Resources Engineering
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course teaches you the fundamentals of particle processing technology and characterisation, including measurement of particle characteristics, particle packing, segregation and sampling, storage and transporting of particles. You will also be exposed to some more advanced topics in particle engineering such as colloidal suspension stability and rheology. You will also learn the unit operations associated with resources engineering which include comminution and grinding, flocculation, agglomeration and granulation and particle separations.
learning_outcomes: Apply a proficient use of mathematics and science skills in solving chemical engineering problems associated with particulate and resources processes
Demonstrate an awareness of unit operations involving particulate processing
Show familiarity with advanced particle processing topics
Demonstrate an understanding of unit operations and processes relating to the utilisation of resources

Apply the fundamental particle processing concepts and unit operations to a range of industrially important processes in the fields of mineral processing, ceramics, paints, food processing, and pharmaceuticals
Apply mathematics and science basic principles in the solution of problems associated with mineral processing, ceramics, paints, food processing and pharmaceuticals
Demonstrate an understanding of the fundamentals of particle technology

title: Resource and Energy Optimisation
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course introduces you to the concepts of sustainability and cleaner production as applied in an industrial context. The course explores the potential role of engineers in the development of sustainable technologies, with a focus on energy and resources. Process impacts including atmospheric pollution and water use are also considered in addition to greenhouse gas emissions from a variety of energy technology types. Quantitative tools to optimise chemical processes are outlined to increase resource use efficiency.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a thorough understanding of the concepts of sustainability and cleaner production, and the challenges that engineers face in applying these concepts in an industrial and societal context
Present clear arguments to support the findings of analysis undertaken as part of an open-ended Case Study
Exhibit an understanding of basic principles of green engineering applied to product design and manufacturing processes
Show familiarity with the concept of cleaner production and how to apply it to real life applications
Critically analyse environmental emissions and develop simple methodologies to reduce these emissions
Quantify environment flows using appropriate mass and energy analysis
Optimise industrial heat exchanger systems in order to reduce overall energy consumption
Assess different energy sources in their ability to deliver clean and reliable electricity and heating/cooling utilities

title: Chemical Reactor Design
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the application of kinetics and reaction engineering in chemical engineering processes. The course will not only serve as an introduction to the fundamental principles of kinetics and reaction engineering, but also to the practical application of the technology in industry. Calculations involving a number of chemical reactions and reactor designs will be undertaken using computer software packages. Concepts such as standard states, chemical reaction rates, reaction mechanism mass balances and design equations for ideal reactors including plug flow, packed-bed, batch and continuously stirred tank reactors will be covered. Design equations will initially be formulated for reactors described by a single chemical reaction, then generalised to multiple reactions. Both isothermal and non-isothermal reactor design will be dealt with. The course will also include advanced topics on practical reactor design involving biochemical reactions and catalytic reactions.
learning_outcomes: Exhibit expertise relevant to the practice of kinetics and reaction engineering
Show an awareness of issues related to the practical application of reaction engineering
Demonstrate an understanding of the fundamental principles underlying kinetics and reaction engineering

title: Environ. Process Technology
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Environmental Process Technology course is designed to provide you with an understanding of the principles, processes and regulations involved in the treatment and sustainable management of potable water and municipal wastewater cycle. The course covers the role of various unit operations and the design approach involved in the water treatment processes. The key objective of the course is to ensure you are able to take an integrated approach to design of water infrastructure for managing our urban water cycle and understand the water-energy nexus. The course will involve multiple visits to water and wastewater treatment plants to gain practical exposure to the operational aspects. The course will also include a comprehensive case study on designing a wastewater treatment facility with a particular focus on energy recovery.
learning_outcomes: Apply the basic principles that underpin physical, chemical and biological treatment of both potable and wastewater streams to simple problems.
Create an appropriate unit operations process that meets the required water quality standard.
Quantify the energy requirements associated with biological wastewater treatment plants.
Analyse the available information on influent and effluent water conditions, and set the design parameters for treatment processes necessary to meet water quality requirements.
Identify the key issues associated with effective management of water resources for urban communities.

title: Chemical Process Safety
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course will introduce students to advanced topics in the application of safety and risk management in chemical engineering processes. The course will not only serve as an introduction to the fundamental principles of safety and risk management, but also extend this knowledge to the practical application of the technology in industry using real-world experiential learning via a site visit and safety report.
learning_outcomes: Establish expertise relevant to the practice of safety and risk management.
Implement safety and risk management in a practical context.
Demonstrate management skills related to planning, developing and report writing activities.
Apply the fundamental principles underlying safety and risk management.
Interpret and apply the professional obligations related to the discipline of safety and risk management.

title: Process Modelling and Separation Processes
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: In this course, students will gain the skill necessary to develop simple models, transfer functions, block diagram representation and analysis, and simple control systems. Most of the model development is based on simple unit operations and separation processes. Students will also learn the fundamentals necessary to design or evaluate a broad range of separation processes.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of the fundamentals of process modelling
Determine the type of equipment required
Suggest a separation method for a particular process requirement
Work with commercial modelling packages
Make suggestions regarding the size, operating parameters, etc. based on design considerations such as throughput

title: Mass Transfer Processes
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with the fundamentals governing mass transfer and the principles governing a range of processes such as absorption, distillation, humidification, leaching and liquid extraction. Students will apply their theoretical knowledge to the design and evaluation of these processes.
learning_outcomes: Combine principles of operating lines and equilibrium descriptions to analyse or design processes involving mass transfer
Interpret problems by presenting a sketch of the system containing information in the problem
Perform material and/or energy balances around separation processes
Utilise thermodynamic equilibrium data to support the description of the separation process
Undertake problem solving concerning the analysis and/or design of transfer processes

title: Project Management and Innovation in Process Industries
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Complements the earlier work on chemical engineering process design and operation, and includes specific material on planning, selection, estimation and control of chemical engineering processes. Previous material given in the course, involving chemical engineering unit operation design, is related to process flowsheets, process economics and cost estimation. The course will include a general overview of management, company structures, taxation, legal frameworks (especially related to environmental legislation), intellectual property and patents, business plans and proposals, markets, competition, and Strength, Weakness, Opportunity, Threat analysis as related specifically to chemical engineering industries.
learning_outcomes: Apply project planning skills.
Demonstrate an awareness of intellectual property.
Write a project proposal.
Apply management computing applications skills.
Demonstrate an awareness of legal frameworks (esp. environmental legislation).
Describe the chemical engineering business environment and economics.
Demonstrate professional communication and organisational skills both individually and within a team.

title: Chemical Engineering Laboratory 2
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course advances your learning and experience in experimental aspects of a number of areas of chemical engineering. Both fundamental aspects, such as kinetics and reaction engineering, process control, heat and mass transfer and fluid flow as well as more applied topics will be covered. The course will not only serve to reinforce fundamental principles of chemical engineering, but also to the application of the technology. The course emphasises and reinforces topics and principles introduced in lectures through experiential learning in the laboratory and with practical work in general. In successfully completing the course you will develop report-writing skills and the ability to critique experimental data and techniques.
learning_outcomes: Show management skills related to planning, developing and report writing activities
Demonstrate an understanding of the fundamental principles underlying chemical engineering through practical experimentation
Exhibit expertise relevant to the practice of engineering

Demonstrate some understanding of the professional obligations related to the discipline of engineering, with a special emphasis of the development of safe working practices during laboratory exercises
Show an understanding of the issues related to experimental aspects of chemical engineering

title: Dynamic Process Simulations and Control
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Chemical Engineers are often deeply involved in the control of processes throughout a wide range of industries. Through this course senior chemical engineering students are provided a grounding in the application of control theory. Students will develop models for physical systems, translate these to transfer functions, block diagrams, leading to their analysis, particularly concerning stability and response. Both steady state and dynamic processes will be examined with students building and analysing these in the provided numerical simulation package.
learning_outcomes: Identify the causes of different dynamic characteristics
Show how block diagrams may be used and manipulated to represent relatively complex systems
Discern the difference between steady state and non-steady state behaviour
Evaluate models and develop an appreciation of their use in chemical engineering
Analyse the behaviour of linear dynamic systems
Create mathematical models for processes governed by equilibrium, conservation (eg mass, momentum and energy), transport and kinetic
Develop models of representative chemical and/or physical processes from the first principle
Demonstrate an appreciation of the importance of dynamics in process design and operation
Use simulation software packages to solve practical problems

title: Design Project A
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course is part of a multi-term sequence. Both Part A and Part B must be completed to meet the requirements of the sequence. Students prepare a design for a process which includes aspects related to equipment, location costs and regulatory issues. The design report resulting is equivalent to a feasibility study. Students work in groups, with the objective of establishing communication skills and will need to make deadlines, 'engineering' decisions, perhaps for the first time, and yet must recognise the effect of uncertainties in their decisions on the viability of the design.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate effective professional interaction with other disciplines, professions, other people and within a team.
Apply chemical engineering knowledge and project management skills in real situations.
Design a chemical process.
Demonstrate in their written report an appreciation of aspects related to equipment, location costs and regulatory issues.
Present a design for a chemical engineering process as an item of professional communication (written or oral).
Produce a design report equivalent to a feasibility study.

title: Design Project B
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course is Part B of a multi-sequence. Part A must be successfully completed before undertaking Part B. Students prepare a design for an engineering process which includes aspects related to equipment, location, economics and regulatory issues. The design report resulting is equivalent to a feasibility study. Students work in groups, with the objective of establishing communication skills and will need to meet deadlines, make 'engineering' decisions, and must recognise the effect of uncertainties in their decisions on the viability of the design.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an appreciation of aspects related to equipment, location, economics and regulatory issues.
Demonstrate effective professional interaction with other people and within a team.
Produce a design report equivalent to a feasibility study.
Design a chemical and/or renewable energy engineering process.
Apply chemical and/or renewable energy engineering knowledge and project management skills in real situations.
Present a design for a chemical and/or renewable energy engineering process as an item of professional communication (both written and oral).

title: Chemical Engineering Research A
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course is Part A of a multi-term sequence. Part B must also be completed to meet the requirements of the sequence. Develops research techniques and ability to work individually on a problem. The student and academic supervisor (frequently an industrial sponsor is involved) establish the objectives and expected outcomes of the research project, which is then pursued by the student under the guidance of the supervisor(s).
learning_outcomes: Develop research techniques such as literature reviews, evaluations of previous work in the area.
Demonstrate the ability to independently perform primary research activities (experiments, numerical modelling, etc.)
Present a major piece of research as an item of professional communication (written or oral).
Carry out a major research project in the field of process technology.
Produce a major written report for their project, including bibliographic referencing.

title: Chemical Engineering Research B
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Develops research techniques and ability to work individually on a problem. The student and academic supervisor (frequently an industrial sponsor is involved) establish the objectives and expected outcomes of the research project, which is then pursued by the student under the guidance of the supervisor(s).
learning_outcomes: Produce a major written report for their project, including bibliographic referencing.
Carry out a major research project in the field of process technology.
Develop research techniques such as literature reviews, evaluations of previous work in the area.
Present a major piece of research as an item of professional communication (written or oral).
Demonstrate the ability to independently perform primary research activities (experiments, numerical modelling, etc.)

title: Safety and Risk Management
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the application of safety and risk management in chemical engineering processes. The course will not only serve as an introduction to the fundamental principles of the safety and risk management, but also to the practical application of the technology in industry.
learning_outcomes: Interpret and apply the professional obligations related to the discipline of safety and risk management.
Implement safety and risk management in a practical context.
Apply the fundamental principles underlying safety and risk management.
Demonstrate management skills related to planning, developing and report writing activities.
Demonstrate awareness of company approach to Process Safety and Risk Management within the Chemical Engineering sector.
Establish expertise relevant to the practice of safety and risk management.

title: Project Management and Innovation in Process Industries
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Complements the earlier work on chemical engineering process design and operation, and includes specific material on planning, selection, estimation and control of chemical engineering processes. Previous material given in the course, involving chemical engineering unit operation design, is related to process flowsheets, process economics and cost estimation. The course will include a general overview of management, company structures, taxation, legal frameworks (especially related to environmental legislation), ethical perspectives, intellectual property and patents, a critical perspectives on business plans and proposals, markets, competition, and Strength, Weakness, Opportunity, Threat analysis as related specifically to chemical engineering industries.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate awareness of Company Structure within an environmental sector
Apply management computing application skills
Demonstrate professional communication and organisational skills both individually and within a team
Demonstrate an awareness of legal frameworks (esp. environmental legislation)
Describe the chemical engineering business environment and economics
Apply critical perspectives and demonstrate insights into project planning methodology
Write a project proposal
Demonstrate an awareness of intellectual property and deeper critical ethical perspectives

title: Advanced Particle Processing
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course is concerned with advanced topics in particle processing, especially in relation to the coal and minerals industries. Following a general introduction to mineral processing, particle characterisation and particle-fluid interactions, the course provides a flux curve treatment of gravity separation, flotation and thickening circuits. Students gain a unique and fundamental appreciation of the governing principles.
learning_outcomes: Apply a proficient use of mathematics and science skills in solving chemical engineering problems associated with particulate and resources processes
Apply advanced particle processing principles
Apply unit operations and processes to the utilisation of resources
Apply mathematics and science basic principles in the solution of problems associated with mineral processing, ceramics, paints, food processing and pharmaceuticals
Apply fundamental principles and important unit operations in particle technology

Apply the fundamental particle processing concepts and unit operations to a range of industrially important processes in the fields of mineral processing, ceramics, paints, food processing, and pharmaceuticals

title: Resource and Energy Optimisation
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course introduces you to the concepts of sustainability and cleaner production as applied in an industrial context. The course explores the potential role of engineers in the development of sustainable technologies, with a focus on energy and resources. Process impacts including atmospheric pollution and water use are also considered in addition to greenhouse gas emissions from a variety of energy technology types. Quantitative tools to optimise chemical processes are outlined to increase resource use efficiency.
learning_outcomes: Apply advanced technical knowledge of resource and energy optimization principles, methodologies, tools and life cycle assessment techniques for assessing the environmental impact of clean energy projects.

Communicate technical findings, optimisation strategies, and recommendations related to clean energy resource and energy optimisation, to facilitate informed decision-making and support the successful implementation of clean energy projects.

Design and implement effective resource and energy optimisation strategies within the clean energy sector, integrating renewable energy sources such as solar photovoltaics, wind turbines, and hydroelectric power with energy storage technologies and demand-side management practices to maximise efficiency, reliability, and sustainability of clean energy systems.

Evaluate the economic and technical feasibility of clean energy optimisation projects, conducting cost-benefit analyses, assessing return on investment (ROI), and identifying opportunities for optimisation within the constraints of clean energy project budgets and regulatory frameworks.

Analyse complex systems and processes within the clean energy sector to identify opportunities for resource and energy optimisation, utilising quantitative and qualitative techniques to assess the performance of renewable energy technologies, grid integration strategies, and energy storage solutions.

title: Introductory Chemistry I
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Often referred to as a 'Central Science', Chemistry is the study of chemicals and chemical processes that underpin physical and biological phenomena. Chemistry impacts and interacts with our lives on a daily basis, including the food we eat, the medicine we take, and the energy we use. CHEM1010 is the first of two foundation subjects in the key central scientific discipline of chemistry, providing core knowledge and skills, useful in science, engineering and life sciences. In CHEM1010, students will explore the primary concepts of chemistry, including basic atomic and molecular structure, the chemistry of carbon compounds, and principal physical concepts of the discipline.
learning_outcomes: recognise and identify isomers and organic functional groups, particularly hydrocarbons and their characteristic reactions;
participate in and contribute to group problem solving.
recognise and use chemical language, representations, structures and symbolism;
describe and apply basic chemistry concepts and extend to their chosen fields of study or programs.
Work safely and competently in a laboratory setting.
apply the scientific method in the conduct and reporting of experiment results.

title: Introductory Chemistry II
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Often referred to as a 'Central Science', Chemistry is the study of chemicals and chemical processes that underpin physical and biological phenomena. Chemistry impacts and interacts with our lives on a daily basis, including the food we eat, the medicine we take, and the energy we use. CHEM1020 is the second of two foundation subjects in the key central scientific discipline of chemistry, providing core knowledge and skills, useful in science, engineering and life sciences. In CHEM1020, students will continue to explore the primary concepts of chemistry, including atomic and molecular structure, the chemistry of carbon compounds, and principal physical concepts of the discipline.
learning_outcomes: apply the scientific method, namely, employ systematic observation, measurement and experimentation, and the formulation, testing and modification of hypotheses in the conduct and reporting of experiment results;
describe and apply foundational concepts in inorganic chemistry;
describe and apply foundational physical chemical principles as they apply to kinetics, energy, acidity and electrochemistry;

implement safe laboratory practice, including wearing of appropriate personal protective equipment, safe handling of chemicals and laboratory equipment and safe disposal of chemicals according to the relevant safety data sheets (SDS).
recognise, identify, name and cite examples of bio-organic compounds, their functional groups, their reactions and spectrometric characteristics;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Written exam covering foundation concepts of chemistry

title: Materials Chemistry
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: There are some ninety-two naturally occurring elements in the periodic table. When in combination, these elements form the materials that underpin our everyday lives. This course provides a foundation for understanding the structure, synthesis and chemistry of these materials and nanomaterials. The course includes the descriptive chemistry within four principal classes of materials, integrating key concepts such as symmetry, structure, bonding, synthesis and characterisation. Applications within these classes of materials will also be discussed, such as catalysis, clean energy technologies, and biosensing.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an awareness of the safety responsibilities involved in working with chemicals and hazardous substances.
Describe the synthesis and characterisation of inorganic, organic, carbon and composite materials;
Compare the chemistry, structure and application of inorganic, organic, carbon and composite materials;
Apply the scientific method in conducting and reporting experimental investigations;
Investigate the synthesis, structure, design and reactivity of materials using experimental and computational techniques;
Independently integrate key concepts regarding the synthesis, characterisation and chemistry of materials;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Reports for Wet and Computer Laboratories

title: Applied Analytical Chemistry
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: The aim of this course is to provide students with a broad understanding of the principles of analytical chemistry and their application in the areas of environmental and medicinal/pharmaceutical sciences and advanced materials. Depending on their program, students will have the opportunity to apply analytical chemical methods in any one of the following areas: 1. Environmental Sciences: Students apply analytical techniques to study the chemical processes that form the basis for the operation of the three spheres of the natural environment (atmosphere, geosphere, hydrosphere), and the changes brought about by human activities and broad environmental factors (e.g. climate). 2. Medicinal/Pharmaceutical Sciences: Students are introduced to the fundamental instrumental methods of chemical analysis commonly used in pharmaceutical laboratories. The laboratory introduces the students to practical skills on the separation, purification and quantitation of pharmaceutically relevant compounds. 3. Advanced Materials: Students are introduced to the fundamental analytical techniques that are useful for the purification and characterisation of advanced materials. Students will be given the opportunity to further apply these methodologies to more specific groups of advanced materials in other courses within the BSc Chemistry (Advanced Materials) program. This course will provide lectures for all students focusing on analytical methods and the underlying theoretical principles. Lectorials and laboratories will extend the lecture with emphasis on applications on any of the above-mentioned areas. Students will be streamed in lectorials and labs according to their program or major or interest (in the case of those taking the course as an elective).
learning_outcomes: Work safely and competently in an analytical laboratory setting.
Describe and compare a range of analytical chemistry methods and explain the underlying theoretical principles;
As part of a team or individually, conduct, analyse and interpret results of a chemical analysis and effectively communicate these in written reports and other formats;
Employ a variety of analytical methods to prepare, separate and characterise samples from various matrices;
Explain the broad role of analysts in quality control and assessment of experimental measurements from various application contexts;

title: Chemistry for the Life Sciences I
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: Often referred to as a 'Central Science', Chemistry is the study of chemicals and chemical processes that underpin physical and biological phenomena. Chemistry impacts and interacts with our lives on a daily basis, including the food we eat, the medicine we take, and the energy we use. This course focuses on the foundation concepts of chemistry and will explore the primary concepts of chemistry, including atomic and molecular structure, the chemistry of carbon compounds, and principal physical concepts of the discipline. This is the first of two foundation subjects in the key scientific discipline of chemistry, providing core knowledge in science, engineering, human nutrition and the life sciences.
learning_outcomes: Recognise, identify, name and cite examples of organic compounds, their functional groups, their reactions and spectrometric characteristics;
Describe and apply foundational concepts in chemistry;

Apply the scientific method, namely, employ systematic observation, measurement and experimentation, and the formulation, testing and modification of hypotheses in the conduct and reporting of experiment results;

Implement safe laboratory practice, including wearing of appropriate personal protective equipment, safe handling of chemicals and laboratory equipment and safe disposal of chemicals according to the relevant safety data sheets (SDS).

title: Organic Chemistry
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course deals with concepts in organic chemistry, the branch of chemistry that deals with compounds of carbon. The course covers the chemistry of functional groups, their chemical reactions and their spectroscopic identification and characterisation. The laboratory introduces the students to practical skills on the synthesis, separation, purification and identification of organic compounds employing exemplar reactions, methods and techniques. A good understanding of organic chemistry is important for students intending to become chemists and those involved in other STEMM disciplines. The spectroscopic (infrared, nuclear magnetic resonance) and mass spectrometric techniques for the characterisation of organic compounds are taught in the first 3 weeks of the semester.
learning_outcomes: Independently integrate key organic chemistry concepts that apply to the identification, characterisation and reactions of functional groups;
Acquire practical skills on the synthesis, separation, purification and identification of organic compounds employing exemplar reactions, methods and techniques;
Apply spectroscopic techniques in the identification of functional groups and elucidation of the structure of organic compounds;
Record and present data and write reports in a format suitable for organic chemistry.
Work safely and competently in an organic chemistry lab setting;
Identify characteristic organic reactions and illustrate reaction mechanisms;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Online quiz or in-class quiz or assignment

title: Physical Chemistry
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the core area of physical chemistry, based around the themes of systems, states and processes. Topics covered are quantum mechanics and structure, chemical thermodynamics, phase changes, and chemical kinetics. Throughout the course, the relationship between physical phenomena and the molecular structure and reactions underpinning advanced materials will be highlighted. This content is designed to complement other 2000 level Chemistry courses which have a synthetic focus. The laboratory component provides training in a range of theoretical and applied physical chemistry techniques which are relevant to both industrial and research settings. A good understanding of physical chemistry is important to students intending to complete a major or minor study in chemistry, and will also be valuable for students studying engineering.
learning_outcomes: Contribute to team and group work for scientific investigation and reporting;
Explain and apply concepts of physical chemistry;
Independently integrate qualitative and quantitative concepts of physical chemistry.
Apply the scientific process in the design, conduct, evaluation and reporting of experimental investigations;
Assess and mitigate risks when working with chemicals and hazardous substances;
Explain the broad role of the chemist and chemical engineer in physical chemical measurements and processes;
Demonstrate procedures and methods applied in analytical, computational and practical tasks of physical chemistry;
Solve problems in physical chemistry by using appropriate methodologies;

title: Instrumental Chemical Analysis
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: Chemical instrumentation is important in providing experimental data necessary for basic research and applications in analytical, environmental, organic, medicinal and advanced materials chemistry. Instrumentation fills only part of the need, as the challenges presented often require highly developed skills and judgement of the experimenter in order to obtain the most reliable results. This course provides the conceptual knowledge, experience and skills related to a variety of instrumental analytical and separation techniques suitable for materials in complex matrices and interfaces. Building on the foundations provided in CHEM2110, this course introduces students to advanced instrumentation and analytical skills.
learning_outcomes: Acquire practical analytical skills and employ a variety of instrumental techniques for the analysis of samples in various formats and from various matrices;
Analyse and present experimental results and draw sound conclusions based on experimental evidence;
Assess the appropriateness of the instrumental methods for the analysis of samples in various formats and from complex matrices;
Contribute to team and group work for scientific investigation and reporting;
Work safely and competently in an analytical laboratory setting;
Explain the theoretical principles underpinning the instrumental techniques and their applications;
Independently integrate concepts and techniques in instrumental analysis and correlate to relevant applications.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Workshop and Laboratory Exercises and Reports

title: Functional Materials
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: Over the last 20 years, polymers, nanostructured, and self assembled materials have revolutionised medicine, biomaterials, diagnostics, energy production and storage, and environmental remediation. This course will explore the chemistry that underpins how these materials are made and applied. The course will span both synthetic and electrochemistry, and expose students to advanced materials characterisation techniques like electron microscopy.
learning_outcomes: Independently integrate key concepts regarding the chemistry and application of nanostructured functional materials.
lnvestigate the synthesis, structure and reactivity of exemplar functional materials;
Describe the synthesis and characterisation of functional materials;
Demonstrate an awareness of the safety responsibilities involved in working with chemicals and hazardous substances;
Apply the scientific process in the conduct and reporting of experimental investigations;
Compare and correlate the chemistry, structure and application of functional materials;

title: Molecular Organic Synthesis
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: The development of modern synthetic materials, whether they be new drugs for the treatment of cancer or for the latest synthetic fabric, requires a knowledge of molecular organic synthesis. Students will develop pre-existing skills (from CHEM2310) to a higher level examining a range of synthetic transformations for functional group transformations, carbon-carbon bond formation and skeletal rearrangements, emphasising the chemo- and stereo-selectivity and mechanism of these reactions. A logical, applied approach backed up by laboratory work and state-of-the art computational approaches will be utilised to emphasise key concepts. Selected literature classics of chemical synthesis will also be included.
learning_outcomes: Identify chemical reactions required for functional group transformations;
Work safely and competently in an organic chemistry laboratory setting.
Illustrate mechanisms of organic chemical reactions;
Plan, conduct, critically evaluate and report organic synthesis experiments;
Design targeted organic synthesis by applying functional group transformations;
Independently integrate key concepts as applied to chemical reactions, functional group transformations and organic synthesis;
Use advanced practical lab skills in synthetic tasks and identification of organic compounds;

title: Medicinal and Biological Chemistry
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course examines the key features of the rational design of new medicinal agents and of the importance of close links between the biological and chemical sciences. The basic principles of synthetic and structural chemistry are applied to the evaluation of biologically active molecules from hit discovery through to delivery and clinical use. A range of key drug types are explored including aromatics, carbohydrates, metal-based drugs, natural products and biopharmaceuticals. The course is delivered in three 4-week modules (Weeks 1-4, 5-8 and 9-12) linked to a lab project and module assessment.
learning_outcomes: Identify and explain key features in drugs that make them appropriate therapeutics;
Apply organic chemistry techniques to synthesise, isolate and characterise drugs and drug-like molecules and report findings;
Demonstrate competency in the use of computational modelling for drug design;
Work safely and competently in an organic chemistry laboratory setting.
Critically evaluate the scientific literature as applied to pharmaceuticals;
Describe the key pathways by which naturally occurring therapeutics are synthesised by plants and animals;
Describe and assess strategies to improve drug delivery;
Describe the methods chemists use for identifying and screening drug leads;

title: Energy and Materials
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course explores the synthesis, characterisation and chemistry of materials and nanostructures relevant to energy conversion applications. Electrode dynamics, including the metal-solution interface and structure of the double layer, is examined, along with rates and mechanisms of charge transfer reactions, electrochemical techniques and corrosion. The synthesis, characterisation and electronic structure of nanomaterials is examined in the context of energy applications and catalysis. An introduction to modelling the electronic structure of solid state materials with computational chemistry is provided, and the fundamental nature and applications of semiconductor materials will also be discussed.
learning_outcomes: Describe the electronic structure, surface chemistry and morphology of nanomaterials, and apply this knowledge to synthesis, characterisation and energy-related applications;
Apply the scientific process in the design, conduct, evaluation and reporting of experimental investigations;
