Competently use instrumentation and methods employed in applied physical chemistry;
Relate electrode dynamics to the performance of electrochemical systems;
Assess and mitigate risks when working with chemicals and hazardous substances;
Apply concepts and solve problems of applied physical chemistry;
Competently use computational chemistry software to model the electronic structure of semiconductor materials and nanomaterials;
Contribute to team and group work for scientific investigation and reporting.

title: Chemistry Honours 412
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course is composed of readings in a selected area of current chemistry at an advanced level, a literature search and review on the selected area of project research, and an analysis and report of experimental methodology relevant to the project area.
learning_outcomes: Experienced and developed independence in the pursuit of an advanced experimental project
Developed skills in procedures and instrumental methods relevant to pursuit of an advanced experimental project
Developed an understanding of the tasks of the research chemist in project development and problem solving
Advanced knowledge relevant to the professional practice of chemistry at an advanced level
Developed a deeper understanding of the professional and safety responsibilities residing in experimental research and development projects
Developed high-level skills in information searching, selection, retrieval and interpretation
Developed an understanding of the application of chemistry to problems in industrial and research environments
Developed high-level skills in the scientific method of planning, developing, conducting, reviewing and reporting a major project

title: Colloids, Interfaces and Soft Matter
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to colloid and interface science. Key surface chemistry concepts are introduced, including the role of surface energy and adsorption of molecules at phase boundaries or interfaces. In introducing colloidal materials, emphasis is placed on the methods of their preparation and structure-property relationships. Dissolved polymers are ubiquitous in everyday formulations and thus the behaviour of polymers in solution is investigated. The self-assembly of amphiphiles into soft materials including micelles, liquid crystals and microemulsions is examined, and the relationship between these structures and formulations in which they are used is explained. The laboratory component provides training in techniques which are specific to the preparation, characterisation and simulation of dilute and concentrated surfactant and polymer solutions, and colloidal dispersions. Throughout the course, the relationship between the structure and properties of the materials and their performance in household, environmental and industrial applications will be highlighted.
learning_outcomes: Relate the structure and properties of surface active and polymer molecules, and colloidal materials to their performance and intended applications;
Demonstrate an awareness of the safety responsibilities involved in working with chemicals and hazardous substances.
Describe the different approaches to the classification and preparation of colloidal materials and soft matter;
Apply the scientific process in the conduct and reporting of experimental investigation;
Demonstrate competence in the use of various procedures and instruments for the synthesis and/or characterisation of surface-active molecules, soft matter and colloidal materials;
Describe the use of surface-active, soft matter and colloidal materials in household, industrial and environmental applications;

title: Chemistry Honours 411
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course is composed of five formal lecture series that cover broad areas of current chemistry at an advanced level. Topics involved are in the areas of advanced materials, advanced methods of characterisation, advanced synthetic methods, computers in chemistry, and health and safety and quality assurance.
learning_outcomes: To provide training which develops appreciation and understanding of both the methods and the processes of scientific investigation and their roles in the practice of chemistry in a social and commercial context
To provide advanced training in chemistry appropriate for registration and practice as a professional chemist and/or for pursing further research for a higher degree
To provide current and high-level practical and technical skills appropriate for the chemical practitioner in the modern workplace
To provide training consistent with aims of the School and University strategic plans
To produce a flexible and skilled honours graduate with the capacity to compete and work professionally in a range of fields relevant to their training in any state or nation

To develop in graduates well-developed and appropriate skills for scientific practice and problem solving, including logical thinking, critical appraisal, analytical skills, organization and planning, development and presentation of logical arguments, skills in research, and skills in report writing and presentation

title: Chinese Language and culture Beginners 1 (A0 to A1.1) for students with other language backgrounds
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course teaches Modern Standard Chinese (MSC) as a foreign language, designed for students with little or no previous knowledge of Chinese. It aims to help learners achieve a basic level of communicative competence in Modern Standard Chinese, as well as cross-cultural competence through intercultural learning and teaching.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate understanding of basic grammatical structures and the ability to express orally interrogative and affirmative sentences, and simple dialogues on various topics.
Demonstrate a clear understanding of modern Chinese society and culture associated with the topics covered in the course.
Demonstrate a firm pronunciation basis in MSC.
Demonstrate understanding of the basics of the written system including the ability to recognize radicals, formation of Chinese characters, and the general rules about stroke orders.
Identify approximately 100 high frequency Chinese characters and associated compounds in their simplified forms and to use these characters in writing simple phrases and sentences.

title: Chinese Language and Culture Beginners 2 (A1.1 to A1.2) for students with other language backgrounds
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course is designed for students with little or no previous knowledge of the language. It provides beginners with a basic level of communicative competence in Modern Standard Chinese (MSC - also known as Mandarin or Putonghua) and a further introduction to Chinese civilisation integrated into the language instruction. It builds on CHIN1110.
learning_outcomes: Recognise the radicals and formations of approximately 400 high frequency Chinese characters and associated compounds in their simplified forms and to use these characters in simple written sentences.
Demonstrate a firm pronunciation basis in MSC to express themselves confidently in spoken Chinese (Mandarin) with appropriate vocabularies and grammar structures.
Demonstrate abilities of analysing aspects of contemporary Chinese culture and modern society.
Use appropriate vocabularies and grammatical structures in simple conversations.

title: Chinese Language and Culture Elementary 1 (A1.2 to A2.1)
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Provides a comprehensive language course designed for students with a basic knowledge of Chinese.
learning_outcomes: Use an expanded vocabulary for topical conversations and practical writing in Chinese.
Demonstrate listening and speaking skills in Modern Standard Chinese.
Apply Chinese grammar at an intermediate level in oral and written communication.
Outline key features of Chinese culture and contemporary life.
Demonstrate reading and writing skills in Modern Standard Chinese.

assessment_tasks.task_name: 3 x In-class listening, reading and writing tests

title: Chinese Language and Culture Elementary 2 (A2.1 to A2.2)
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course is designed as a continuation of CHIN 2301 or for students with equivalent intermediate Chinese language proficiency.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate deeper awareness of intercultural communication.
Use an expanded vocabulary for topical conversations and practical writing in Chinese.
Demonstrate an expanded knowledge of grammatical features and structures.
Demonstrate intermediate level of listening, speaking, reading and writing skills in Modern Standard Chinese.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Two in-class Group presentations - oral presentation

title: Chinese-English Translation
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course is designed for students with a high level of proficiency in Chinese, including background and native speakers of Chinese. Students will learn basic translation theories and techniques. Through translation practice, students will also further develop their English language proficiency.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on collaborative learning through group assignments.
Apply knowledge acquired in the course to translate English and Chinese texts of moderate difficulty.
Demonstrate an understanding of the complex linguistic and cultural problems which form part of the translation process.
Acquire some basic knowledge of cultural and linguistic differences between English and Chinese.
Acquire some basic knowledge of translation theories and techniques.

title: Business English and Chinese
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course aims at developing a better grasp of English and Chinese business language and cultural knowledge.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a better grasp of the language related to economic and business contexts.
Use an expanded Chinese and English vocabulary for topical conversations and practical writings in business environments.
Demonstrate a better understanding of social, economic and business issues of the Australian and Chinese societies.
Exhibit an awareness of intercultural communication in business contexts.

title: Advanced Spoken Chinese I
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: A comprehensive language course designed for students who have achieved proficiency at an intermediate level. Particular emphasis is on developing students' ability to use the language competently in real life situations, including conducting conversations and writing practical compositions in Modern Standard Chinese.
learning_outcomes: Translate simple conversations from and into Chinese at advanced level.
Understand spoken Chinese at an advanced undergraduate level.
Converse in Chinese at an advanced undergraduate level.

title: Advanced Written Chinese
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Emphasis is on the development of reading and writing skills and cultural background knowledge (written expression, intensive and extensive reading) through reading and examination of a range of carefully selected texts at an advanced level, including newspaper articles, contemporary Chinese literary texts and films with particular reference to practical language use.
learning_outcomes: Analyse a range of Chinese texts including newspaper articles, broadcasts and films in Modern Standard Chinese.
Read and write 300 new words and associated compounds.
Use the 300 new characters and expressions in basic practical writings.
Identify advanced grammatical structures.

title: Advanced Spoken Chinese II
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: A comprehensive advanced language course, offered as a sequel to CHIN3101. Emphasis is on the further development of communication skills (oral expression, listening comprehension) in Modern Standard Chinese.
learning_outcomes: Translate simple conversations from and into Chinese.
Converse fluently in Chinese at an advanced undergraduate level.
Understand written Chinese within their vocabulary range.
Use 800 words in simple conversations in Chinese.

title: Advanced Chinese with Translation
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The course offers a sequel to CHIN3201. Emphasis is on the further development of writing skills in Modern Standard Chinese (MSG). It also equips students with the basic techniques of translation.
learning_outcomes: Use an expanded Chinese vocabulary.
Translate different forms of writing (short dialogues, letters, emails, resumes, compositions, etc.).
Identify basic techniques of translation between Chinese and English.
Produce short texts with appropriate vocabulary, punctuation and grammatical structures.

title: Entrepreneurship
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course focuses on frameworks for understanding different market sectors within the Creative Industries, and the opportunities and challenges for new and innovative initiatives in these sectors. Students will gain a deeper understanding of entrepreneurship as the basis for generating income from intellectual property. Students will work collaboratively to conceive and develop a business model for a possible project in the Creative Industries.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the relationship between service, product and market with a focus on innovation and ideation;
Undertake market analysis for different sectors within the Creative Industries;
Demonstrate an ability to work collaboratively on projects.
Identify audiences as key stakeholders in any creative project;
Identity and evaluate enterprise opportunities within a market sector;
Develop and communicate a business model for a project, service or event in the Creative Industries;

title: Directing Workshop
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course builds on student’s knowledge of performing arts including theatre, live art, drama and sound in a variety of forms and cultural contexts. Collaborative methodologies and the potential of group-dynamics are applied to creative processes. Analytical, theoretical and practical approaches are considered in relation to gesture, movement, text and sound, challenging the audience-performer experience of live performances. Formal elements including language and text, representation, symbolism, abstraction, hybridity, texture, scale and narrative are applied to distinct theatrical forms in a variety of settings.
learning_outcomes: Critically appraise theoretical and practical approaches to creative works, events and performance in a range of cultural contexts.
Embody collaborative skills in the creation of live performance works.
Propose a creative event that makes use of gesture, image, movement, space, text and/or sound.
Implement written and oral communication skills and language relevant to the field of contemporary performance.

title: Stagecraft
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the fundamental skills of stage management for live performances, festivals or musical productions. Students will learn about the safe and efficient installation, operation and design of lighting, sound, actors/performers and projections. They will learn the basics of stage management for a range of public events and venues, and the role of the stage manager, lighting and sound designers and engineers. Students will engage in practical and technical skill-based learning, learn strategies for time-management and practice collaboration and team-work during staged events.
learning_outcomes: Explain the stage manager's roles and responsibilities.
Work safely with appropriate tools, technologies and electrics;
Manage collaborative work-flows from concept design to build, run and strike;
Describe the different roles of stage production teams;
Apply basic construction and programming techniques in light, sound and set design;

title: Professional Placement
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Students will undertake a work placement in an organisation to apply the professional skills and practices acquired during their program of study. During the placement they will develop professional skills and practices appropriate to their chosen profession and experience the dynamics, discourses, practices and realities of working in a professional environment. Direction is provided onsite by a placement supervisor. Student projects may include, but are not limited to: theoretical explorations and reviews; speculative design practices; professionally oriented projects; work-integrated learning and research-integrated learning opportunities; group / collaborative projects; external stakeholder based projects Students undertaking CIND3500 – Professional Placement may be eligible to apply for a Scholarships with our industry partners. The Work-Integrated-Learning placement with the industry partner would contribute to their completion of CIND3500.
learning_outcomes: Apply, under supervision, their professional skills and knowledge acquired during the degree program to the workplace environment;
Develop critical and creative thinking skills by participating in the workplace of creative and cultural industry professionals;
Complete Risk Assessments and apply appropriate Work Health Safety competencies to the workplace environment.
Produce products and/or materials and participate in activities at a professional standard;
Analyse and evaluate their knowledge, skills and practices in the placement environment
Articulate an understanding of the social and professional contexts in which contemporary creative and cultural practice operates and of the role of the practitioner within these contexts;

title: Studio Q
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Students will undertake an authentic and genuine experience of work through a creative studio-based environment, responding to a professional brief that has been developed in partnership or collaboration with industry, business or community partners. In undertaking the experience, students will apply the professional skills and practices acquired during their program of study and will experience the dynamics, discourses, practices and realities of working in a professional environment to a brief, and under supervision. Student projects may include, but are not limited to: creative works, commercially orientated creative content, speculative design practices; group / collaborative projects; non-for profit stakeholder based projects
learning_outcomes: Apply, under supervision, the professional skills and knowledge acquired during the degree program in a creative Studio environment;
Produce products and/or materials and participate in activities at a professional standard;
Analyse and evaluate their knowledge, skills and practices in the professional Studio environment
Complete Risk Assessments and apply appropriate Work Health Safety competencies to the workplace environment.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Presentation of Final Deliverables to Client/Studio

title: Honours Project 1
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This is the first part of the thesis/project component of the Creative Industries Honours year, the other being CIND4004. The honours project gives students the opportunity to put the skills they have acquired over the course of their undergraduate studies into advanced practice in the form of a substantial research project. This project can be in one of three formats: 1) Academic, 2) Practice-based Practice-led or 3) Work-Integrated Learning Across its three options, the two project courses of the Honours year are intended to develop and strengthen professional skills, challenge students intellectually, and round off their undergraduate studies with higher-level independent studies designed to be useful in many fields of future endeavour. Student projects may include, but are not limited to: theoretical explorations and reviews; speculative design practices; professionally oriented projects; work-integrated learning and research-integrated learning opportunities; group / collaborative projects; external stakeholder based projects.
learning_outcomes: Interpret and critically analyse data or practice-based outcomes.
Demonstrate an understanding of the key issues and concepts relating to the chosen field of study.
Articulate research findings using appropriate discipline specific communication skills.
Present a well-designed written thesis, creative work with exegesis or WIL with exegesis to a research and professional standard.
Produce an extended piece of research designed to set up and defend the intellectual position taken by the researcher/creative practitioner.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Final Thesis/ Creative Work with Exegesis/ WIL with Exegesis

title: Honours Project 2
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This is the second part of the thesis/project component of the Creative Industries Honours year, the other being CIND4003. The honours project gives students the opportunity to put the skills they have acquired over the course of their undergraduate studies into advanced practice in the form of a substantial research project. This project can be in one of three formats: 1) Academic, 2) Practice-based Practice-led or 3) Work-Integrated Learning Across its three options, the two project courses of the Honours year are intended to develop and strengthen professional skills, challenge students intellectually, and round off their undergraduate studies with higher-level independent studies designed to be useful in many fields of future endeavour. Student projects may include, but are not limited to: theoretical explorations and reviews; speculative design practices; professionally oriented projects; work-integrated learning and research-integrated learning opportunities; group / collaborative projects; external stakeholder based projects.
learning_outcomes: Present a well-designed written exegesis or thesis to a research and professional standard.
Demonstrate an understanding of the key issues and concepts relating to the chosen field of study.
Produce an extended piece of research designed to set up and defend the intellectual position taken by the researcher/creative practitioner.
Articulate research findings using appropriate discipline specific communication skills.
Interpret and critically analyse data or practice-based outcomes.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Final Thesis/ Creative Work with Exegesis/ WIL with Exegesis

title: Fundamentals of Engineering Mechanics
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course introduces some basic principles of engineering mechanics in as simple a manner as possible. Emphasis is placed upon students gaining a real understanding of the laws and principles of mechanics. This course provides essential foundation knowledge for all disciplines of engineering and surveying and will be assumed knowledge in many of the courses taken in later years of undergraduate programs.
learning_outcomes: Formulate, analyse and solve simple problems in mechanics
Recognise the assumptions and limitations of the approaches used
Apply the laws and principles of mechanics to a basic level

title: Earth Systems
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to geomaterials and their origin. It describes the context in which geomaterials are formed, transformed and commonly occur. Particular attention is given to the occurrence of materials in the near surface environment and the conditions and processes which occur there. The physical principles which prevail in natural processes and systems are established and emphasised.
learning_outcomes: Recall the structure and composition of the Earth and explain the processes which shape continents, produce earthquakes and impart fabric and structure to rocks.
Differentiate, identify, describe and classify soils, sedimentary rocks, igneous rocks and metamorphic rocks.
Understand the basic spatial forms and relationships between rock interpret spatial relationships and extrapolate simple surface outcrop patterns.
Describe the geological processes responsible for making rocks from soil, and soil from rocks.
Describe the basic interactions between water and geomaterials in the near-surface geologic environment.
Explain the fundamental physical processes involving geomaterials and water with appropriate appreciation of the basic laws of physics and chemistry.
Relate geomaterial properties and geologic/hydrogeologic processes to practical engineering situations.

title: Numerical Methods
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the development and application of numerical methods to provide solutions to common problems formulated in engineering. Its purpose is to provide foundation material for later year courses in water, structural, and geotechnical engineering.
learning_outcomes: Interpret the physical significance of partial differential equations enabling application of appropriate finite difference method for their solution.
Select and implement an appropriate numerical method to solve a single nonlinear equation based on accuracy, efficiency, and convergence requirements.
Solve ordinary differential equations through selection and implementation of appropriate numerical methods, suited to the physical nature of specified ordinary differential equations.
Select and implement an appropriate numerical method to perform numerical differentiation and numerical integration.
Select and implement an appropriate numerical method to perform interpolation, curve fitting on field data sets.
Select and implement an appropriate numerical method to solve a system of linear equations based on accuracy, efficiency, and convergence requirements.

title: Structural Analysis 1
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: CIVL2130 introduces students to mechanics of structures under static loading conditions. The course forms the second of the sequence dealing with structural engineering and geotechnics for Civil and Environmental engineering students. Specifically, the course objective is to teach students the methods and techniques outlined in the syllabus such that they can solve the type of problems as outlined in the lectures, in the lecture notes and as discussed in tutorials.
learning_outcomes: Formulate complex problems from Theory of Structures into analytical forms
Apply appropriate solution techniques from Theory of Structures to mechanical problems
Formulate, analyse and calculate the mechanical behaviour of simple structures
Recognize and describe analytical limitations used in Theory of Structures

title: Civil Engineering Materials
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Introduces the important physical and chemical properties of materials that are commonly used in civil engineering.
learning_outcomes: Explain the fundamental (engineering related) issues surrounding the use of the following Civil Engineering Materials; concrete, structural steel (and other important structural metals), timber, masonry, ceramics and composites, and polymers.
Communicate their learned knowledge of these materials.
Describe and critically analyse the limitations of these materials under various loading circumstances.
Explain the production and/or manufacturing methods associated with these materials.
Explain, describe and characterise some of the variability and uncertainty associated with these materials.

title: Introduction to Geomechanics
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This is a first course in Geomechanics devoted to soil index properties, stress, seepage and deformation. It introduces the concepts of porous granular materials, total and effective stress, pore pressure and excess pore pressure, stress distributions in elastic materials, elastic deformation consolidation and time-dependent settlement.
learning_outcomes: Identify/estimate important soil properties and describe and classify soils according to AS1726.
Estimate the stress distribution in the ground due to a range of spatially-discrete surface loadings.
Recognise that soil strength contains two components (cohesion, friction).
Estimate steady-state seepage rates using flow net theory.
Calculate primary settlements and rates of settlement in coarse and fine grained soils using appropriate theories.
Recall and describe common laboratory tests in soil mechanics and analyse data from these tests to determine quantities of interest.
Explain which strength component applies to granular soils and cohesive soils for different loading and time scenarios.
Quantify important physical characteristics of partially saturated and saturated porous materials from basic measured data.
Determine the total stress, pore pressure and effective stress in the ground, under both hydrostatic and steady-state seepage conditions.

title: Reinforced Concrete Design
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course covers the structural design of reinforced concrete and prestressed concrete members. Topics include the structural design of reinforced concrete slabs (including two way slabs and flat plates), beams, columns and footings, and prestressed concrete beams.
learning_outcomes: Design and check for serviceability (crack and deflection) conditions and for ultimate limit state conditions in accordance with relevant reinforced concrete design and building standards.
Synthesise the design of reinforced concrete elements into a realistic structure.
Apply concepts for reinforced concrete and prestressed concrete design.
Synthesise and apply fundamental mechanics to the reinforced concrete design process.
Design, analyse and size simpler elements of reinforced and prestressed concrete elements.

title: Transportation Engineering and Design
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to methods and underlying principles for the design and control of the elements of road and railway infrastructure. Students also become familiar with transportation system terminology, flow analysis, driver, vehicle and road characteristics, and aspects of road geometrics, road construction, drainage, pavements and maintenance.
learning_outcomes: Present the concepts associated with the geometric and structural design of highway and railway engineering systems.
Apply and present the basic concepts of transportation in civil engineering practice.
Utilise the terminology of the highway and railway transportation industries.
Explain the basic service requirements of highway and detail the procedure to conduct level of service analysis.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Road Design and Level of Service

title: Structural Analysis 2
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will apply advanced methods of structural analysis and explore the fundamental theory and concepts behind existing computer software used for the analysis of complex structural systems. You will also apply a comprehensive knowledge of the theoretical framework underpinning linear-elastic analysis of various types of structures (e.g. statically indeterminate trusses, beams and frames) encountered in civil engineering design work. You will be introduced to the principles of plasticity and non-linear analysis. The skills and knowledge gained in this course are essential for the design of structures.
learning_outcomes: Analyse complex structures using structural analysis software.
Analyse complex structures using appropriate techniques.
Apply qualitative analysis skills to estimate the behaviour of structures.
Critically analyse and correctly interpret results obtained from structural analysis software.
Critically review and present results with respect to design, sustainability and community expectations.
Apply principles of structural analysis for linear-elastic and non-linear analysis.

title: Steel Design
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: The course covers the structural design of steel members and connections. Topics include design loads and the structural design of steel beams, columns, tension members and bolted and welded connections.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate wind loads as per the Australian Standards for steel framed structures
Optimise structural steel sizes in simple and complex structures

title: Geomechanics 2
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: The aim of this course is to introduce the principles of soil mechanics. Its purpose is to provide the foundation for geotechnical and geoenvironmental engineering design.
learning_outcomes: Apply basic concepts in critical state soil mechanics to describe soil behaviour.
Calculate and explain soil shear strength and strength parameters.
Apply strength failure criteria to the analysis of shallow foundations, retaining walls and slope stability.
Conduct basic laboratory experiments and derive soil shear strength and strength parameters from these experiments.
Interpret the Mohr-Coulomb failure criterion for geomaterials and apply it in geotechnical analysis and design.

title: Hydrology
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to basic and advanced hydrology and open channel hydraulics concepts and their application in a range of civil and environmental engineering contexts. It lays the foundation for subsequent environmental modelling and water resources courses studied in the following years.
learning_outcomes: Conduct open channel experiments in a laboratory setting
Demonstrate report writing skills commensurate with 3rd year engineering students
Identify hydrology and open channel related problems
Solve elementary hydrology and open channel problems encountered by engineers

title: Virtual Design and Construction
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course gives students an appreciation of the requirements for, and integration of, Building Information Modelling (BIM) within the context of Virtual Design and Construction (VDC). The course explores aspects of current VDC tools and services, to be tailored to the location of offer. Further information is given with respect to BIM and its appropriate management, implementation.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on technical issues encountered during site visits (WIL) and propose solutions in visit reports
Explain the concept, and applications, of VDC in civil engineering projects
Differentiate and categorise VDC implementation requirements
Critically analyse and categorise different types of VDC technologies
Retrieve select information from virtual building model database (BIM system)
Build and manipulate simple building information models
Demonstrate team work through creation and presentation of appropriate BIM models

title: Design For Manufacturing and Assembly
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course gives students an appreciation of design requirements for specific structural elements; in particular, those aspects of design associated with the manufacture (and assembly) of modular structural components, which are important features within Singapore’s structural engineering context. The course explores the different aspects of Design for Manufacturing and Assembly (DfMA) for Steel, Concrete and Timber modular-structures. The course also explores elements of Mechanical, Electrical and Piping (MEP) services within structural modules. Students will work individually, and report on industry best-practice (both within Singapore and Internationally).
learning_outcomes: Describe Mechanical, Electrical and Piping (MEP) services within structural modules.
Reflect on technical issues encountered during site visits (WIL) and propose solutions in visit reports
Appraise manufacturing and assembly methods, as currently used in the production of modular elements.
Differentiate and compare structural engineering materials, for use within modular-construction.
Describe the design, production and assembly methods for (simple) manufactured modular elements
Explain the concepts and applications of DfMA in civil engineering.

title: Hydrobiological Modelling
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Introduces the notions of mixing, diffusion and dispersion modelling. It extends the ideas of CIVL2310 Fluid Mechanics to include methods of modelling surface water flows. Modelling of surface water transport processes using convection-diffusion equations and particle tracking methods are used. Aquatic chemical and biological processes are described, their kinetics examined and a range of models are illustrated and used. Methods of estimation of parameters in water quality or ecosystem models are introduced and used.
learning_outcomes: Apply and optimise state-of-the-art entry level hydrobiological models in defined applications.
Formulate hydrodynamic, mixing and dispersion problems in aquatic environments.
Formulate chemical and biological problems in aquatic environments.
Estimate parameters in selected predictive models.

title: Land Surface Process and Management
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Students will gain a general understanding of environmental physics, acquisition and use of environmental data and numerical modelling of earth system processes. Students will gain experience with several numerical methods and management tools for addressing environmental degradation under changing climate.
learning_outcomes: Appraise environmental models of land surface processes and apply their knowledge through hands-on experience with hydrological models.
Illustrate the theoretical background of land surface transport processes.
Describe the Australian environment, with a particular emphasis on the atmospheric environment and soils.
Apply model-based tools for management of major environmental issues.
Employ adequate skills in environmental monitoring (including data collection, storage, retrieval and analysis).

title: Contaminant Hydrogeology
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: The theory of groundwater flow and the transport of pollutants in groundwater are covered in this course. Topics include the modelling of groundwater flow and contaminant transport, well hydraulics, flow nets, subsurface chemical and microbial processes, sea water intrusion, groundwater monitoring and remediation.
learning_outcomes: Generate technical reports that integrate key concepts and develop critical thinking skills.
Demonstrate key concepts by interpreting data from laboratory experiments.
Implement solution techniques to solve common problems in hydrogeology and contaminant transport.
Identify and explain the key concepts of hydrogeology and contaminant transport.

title: Advanced Analysis for Design
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the development and use of finite element analysis and modelling for structural, water and geotechnical engineering.
learning_outcomes: Describe sources nonlinearity and compare techniques for solving linear and nonlinear finite equations.
Apply interpolation and numerical integration to derive and evaluate finite element stiffness equations from first principles.
Modify an existing finite element program to implement alternative finite elements and/or finite element techniques.
Interpret results and evaluate the efficiency and accuracy of a finite element analysis.
Apply finite element techniques to solve simple engineering problems.
Use a commercial finite element package.

title: Advanced Structural Analysis
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course Introduces students to higher-level theory of structures. Topics include: elementary plastic theory of structures with application for slab analysis and design, dynamics of structures, stability of structural elements and structural systems. Where possible, topics are linked to the requirements of Australian Standards. The most common software used in the work force for advanced structural analysis is also investigated.
learning_outcomes: Apply Plastic Theory, Structural Dynamics Theory and Stability Theory to solve structure-related problems
Identify the terminology of higher level Theory of Structures at a professional level
Identify the major requirements of relevant Australian Standards
Describe features and limitations of common software used in professional practice for advanced structural analysis

title: Rock Mechanics and Rock Engineering
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course presents a comprehensive introduction to rock mechanics and its applications for civil and mining environments. The course is designed for future civil engineers who will work on projects in rock engineering. Major topics of the course include: introduction to rock structures, rock and rock mass properties, rock engineering for underground openings, and rock slope engineering.
learning_outcomes: Propose designs of excavation supports.
Define the characteristics and the mechanical properties (strength and failure criteria) of rock mass, rock matrix and discontinuities.
Use rock mass classification systems (RMR, Q, GSI).
Explain methods for in situ investigation and laboratory testing of rock matrix and discontinuities.
Analyse the stress distribution (isotropic, anisotropic) in situ and around an opening in rock (competent rock, jointed rock mass, blocky rock).
Conduct rock slope stability analyses.

title: Residential Footings/Masonry/Timber Design
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Covers the properties of masonry and timber and the design of structures containing these materials, together with the design of footings for low rise structures. For masonry and timber design, the engineering properties of each material are studied, followed by the design of structural elements such as masonry walls and piers, timber columns, beams, tension members and connections. The foundation design component deals with site characteristics including testing and calculation methods for reactive clays, various footing systems and their characteristics, design performance expectations, numerical models for soil-structure interaction and structural design.
learning_outcomes: Develop a structural concept design for a building structure and be able to describe the way in which the structure safely transfers gravity and lateral loads to the supporting foundation.
Design and detail unreinforced and reinforced masonry elements in accordance with AS3700 Masonry Structures taking into account the properties of masonry as a structural material.
Design footing systems for residential structures in accordance with AS2870 taking into account the behaviour of residential structures founded on reactive clay soils.
Design and detail basic timber members and connections in accordance with AS1720.1 taking into account the properties of timber as a structural material.

title: Geotechnical Engineering
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course draws on the students’ background knowledge from CIVL2282 (previously CIVL2280) and CIVL3280 and expands it by focusing on practical solutions for commonly experienced geotechnical issues. These include geotechnical site investigation, soil consolidation applications, foundation settlements, deep foundation analysis and design, and ground modification methods. These are explored using both analytical and numerical methods, as appropriate. Finally, this course provides students with a demonstrated capacity to complete the CIVL4571 Geotechnical Project.
learning_outcomes: Identify the conceptual, technical and practical issues in conducting geotechnical investigations, and develop a geotechnical model for subsurface engineering designs.
Reflect upon professional issues associated with geotechnical engineering practice.
Solve geotechnical analysis and design problems using analytical and numerical methods, and design simple foundation solutions.
Determine the collapse load of shallow and deep foundations.
Determine the immediate and consolidation settlement of shallow and deep foundations.
Recognise the roles and limitations of analytical and numerical methods used in geotechnical analysis and design.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Group Assignment 1 - Calculation of short and long-term settlement of geostructures
Group Assignment 2: Interpretation of site investigations and analysis of foundations

title: Geotechnical Site Characterisation
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: The aim of this course is to introduce to the in-situ techniques commonly employed in geotechnical practice as well as conventional and advanced laboratory testing procedures available for soil characterisation aimed at developing geotechnical models to be used in current practice.
learning_outcomes: Design a soil sampling campaign for geotechnical characterization in laboratory.
Estimate geotechnical parameters from index and mechanical laboratory tests to be used in geotechnical design.
Interpret and analyse common in situ tests using in geotechnical practice.
Design a laboratory program for soil characterization.
Estimate geotechnical parameters from in situ tests to be used in geotechnical design.
Interpret and analyse index and mechanical (non-conventional) laboratory tests.
Assess sample quality and select proper specimens for laboratory testing.

title: Structural Engineering Project
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course provides a practical introduction to design techniques in structural engineering. The emphasis is on realistic design problems, such as the structural design of a new residential, commercial or industrial building. Problems are set and supervised by practicing engineers in consultation with academic staff and test most aspects of structural design.
learning_outcomes: Identify and use the major Australian Standards for structural engineering design.
Critically analyse the features and limitations of the most common software used in professional practice at design stage.
Demonstrate knowledge of the basics of conceptual design.
Communicate design outcomes at a professional level.
Apply the research and design skills acquired in earlier courses for the solution of realistic practical problems as a part of the team.

title: Water Engineering
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to water engineering practice. It builds on prior learning in fluid mechanics, hydrology, and statistics, and demonstrates how concepts from these areas are applied in stormwater drainage design, Water Sensitive Urban Design (WSUD), and water resource systems. By examining a range of water engineering design problems, the course fosters holistic thinking and develops technical skills in water engineering design, analysis, and decision-making.
learning_outcomes: Explain the impacts of urbanisation on stormwater, stormwater systems, and receiving waters, and the principles of stormwater management.
Understand and apply hydrologic, hydraulic, and stormwater management principles to the analysis and design of stormwater drainage and WSUD systems.
Evaluate water engineering solutions using technical, environmental, economic, and social considerations.
Analyse water resource systems including water supply and reservoir operation.
Communicate water engineering analyses and design solutions professionally.

title: Water Engineering Project
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course provides a practical introduction to investigation and design techniques in water engineering. The emphasis is on a realistic problem requiring investigation of several options in a multi-objective context and conceptual design. The problem is set by a practicing engineer.
learning_outcomes: Work as part of a design team.
Communicate and interact at a professional level.
Apply research and design skills acquired in earlier courses to solve design problems.
Demonstrate basic investigation and conceptual design skills in a multi-objective, multi-option problem framework.

title: Geotechnical Engineering Project
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Provides a practical introduction to research and design techniques in geotechnical engineering. An open-ended, integrated, practical problem is considered. Emphasis is on a realistic design problem. Problems are set by practising engineers.
learning_outcomes: Integrate and extrapolate the theory presented in earlier courses to solve a broad range of real problems.
Apply research and design skills to model and understand complex geotechnical systems and to solve open-ended geotechnical problems.
Critically analyse and communicate outcomes at a professional level, both verbally and as a report.
Incorporate design tools such as standards and software in the formulation of solutions to real problems, and explore the limitations of these tools.
Work as part of a team in the solution of problems that are posed and directed by experienced practising engineers and academics.

title: Environmental Engineering Project 1
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Provides a problem-based introduction to design techniques in environmental engineering. Several applications are considered with an emphasis on real-world problems typically encountered by graduates. The problems are set by practicing engineers and cover most aspects of environmental engineering design.
learning_outcomes: Communicate design solutions.
Apply research and design skills acquired in earlier courses in environmental engineering and related disciplines to solve design problems and conduct investigations
Apply environmental engineering design philosophies to a multifaceted project.
Develop the ability to function effectively as a member of a design team.
Develop an appreciation of the social, economic and institutional factors affecting environmental engineering design and investigation.

title: Environmental Engineering Project 2
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course introduces problem-based learning in environmental engineering through a supervised team project. It emphasises the application of design thinking to real-world environmental challenges. Projects are set and guided by practising engineers and reflect the types of design tasks graduates are likely to encounter in professional practice.
learning_outcomes: Develop the ability to function effectively as a member of a design team.
Apply research and design skills acquired in earlier courses in environmental engineering and related disciplines to solve design problems and conduct investigations.
Apply environmental engineering design philosophies.
Apply mainstream environmental modelling tools for design analysis and evaluation.
Construct a professional report synthesizing design recommendations and analytical findings.
Demonstrate consideration of environmental, regulatory, and institutional factors affecting environmental engineering design and investigation.

title: Project S1
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Independent research study in the form of a literature review, an experimental or theoretical investigation, an engineering design problem etc. Results are communicated in the form of a seminar, poster and final report.
learning_outcomes: Critically assess the achievements, limitations and further requirements of their own work.
Use their initiative in an area of self-selected engineering interest.
Demonstrate initiative through the work performed.
Critically analyse the work performed previously by others.
Demonstrate, through oral and written presentations, the ability to communicate the objectives and outcomes of the work.
Demonstrate an appreciation of the state-of-the-art in the selected area.

title: Advanced Structural Analysis
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to higher-level Theory of Structures. Emphasis is placed upon students gaining a real understanding of elementary plastic theory of structures with application for slab analysis and design; dynamics of structures; stability of structural elements and structural systems. The topics are linked to requirements of Australian Standards. The course also revises the most common software used in the workforce for Advanced Structural Analysis.
learning_outcomes: Apply Plastic Theory, Structural Dynamics Theory, and Stability Theory to solve structure-related problems
Describe features and limitations of common software used in professional practice for advanced structural analysis
Identify the major requirements of relevant Australian Standards
Identify the terminology of higher-level Theory of Structures at a professional level

title: Project S2
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Independent research study in the form of a literature review, an experimental or theoretical investigation, an engineering design problem etc. Results are communicated in the form of a seminar, poster, and final report.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate initiative through the work performed.
Critically analyse the work performed previously by others.
Demonstrate, through oral and written presentations, the ability to communicate the objectives and outcomes of the work.
Demonstrate an appreciation of the state-of-the-art in the selected area.
Use their initiative in an area of self-selected engineering interest.
Critically assess the achievements, limitations and further requirements of their own work.

title: Reinforced Concrete Design
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the structural design of reinforced concrete and pre-stressed concrete members. Topics include the structural design of reinforced concrete slabs (including two way slabs and flat plates), beams, columns and footings; and pre-stressed concrete beams.
learning_outcomes: Design, analyse and size simpler elements of reinforced and prestressed concrete elements.
Apply concepts for reinforced concrete and prestressed concrete design.
Design and check for serviceability (crack and deflection) conditions and for ultimate limit state conditions in accordance with relevant reinforced concrete design and building standards.
Synthesise the design of reinforced concrete elements into a realistic structure.
Comparatively assess and critique ultimate and serviceability limit state design conditions between relevant national and international reinforced concrete design and building standards.
Synthesise and apply fundamental mechanics to the reinforced concrete design process.

title: Residential Footings, Masonry, Timber Design
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course revises the basic material properties of timber and masonry as they relate to structural design using these materials. It then introduces students to the structural design of timber and masonry structures as well as footings systems for low-rise residential structures. The course aims to enable students to develop competence in the use of the Australian Standards used for the design of such structures.
learning_outcomes: Have a commanding knowledge of the behaviour of residential structures founded on reactive clay soils and be able to design footing systems for residential structures in accordance with AS2870.
Have a commanding knowledge of the properties of timber as a structural material and be able to design and detail basic timber members and connections in accordance with AS1720.1 Timber Structures.

Have a commanding knowledge of the properties of masonry as a structural material and be able to design and detail unreinforced and reinforced masonry elements in accordance with AS3700 Masonry Structures.
Develop a structural concept design for a building structure and be able to describe the way in which the structure safely transfers gravity and lateral loads to the supporting foundation.

title: Geotechnical Engineering
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course draws the students’ background knowledge from CIVL2282 (previously CIVL2280) and CIVL3280 and expands it by focusing on practical solutions for commonly experienced geotechnical issues. These include geotechnical site investigation, soil consolidation applications, foundation settlements, deep foundation analysis and design, and ground modification methods. These are explored using both analytical and advanced numerical methods, as appropriate. Finally, this course provides students with a demonstrated capacity to complete the CIVL6571 Geotechnical Project.
learning_outcomes: Determine the collapse load of shallow and deep foundations.
Recognise the roles and limitations of analytical and advanced numerical methods used in geotechnical design.
Identify the conceptual, technical and practical issues in conducting geotechnical investigations, and develop a geotechnical model for subsurface engineering designs.
Determine the immediate and consolidation settlement of shallow and deep foundations.
Reflect upon professional issues associated with geotechnical engineering practice.
Solve advanced geotechnical and geoenvironmental design problems using analytical and numerical methods, and design simple foundation solutions.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Individual Assignment: Open-ended analysis of geostructures
Group Assignment 2: Interpretation of site invesigations and analysis of foundations
Group Assignment 1: Calculation of short and long-term settlement of geostructures

title: Steel Design
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course covers the structural design of steel members and connections. Topics include design loads and the structural design of steel beams, columns, tension members, and bolted and welded connections.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate wind loads as per the Australian Standards for steel framed structures
Demonstrate an advanced level of steel design skills
Optimise structural steel sizes in simple and complex structures

title: Rock Mechanics and Rock Engineering
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course presents a comprehensive introduction to rock mechanics and its applications for civil and mining environments. The course is designed for future Civil Engineers who will work on projects in rock engineering. Major topics of the course include: introduction to rock structures, rock and rock mass properties, rock engineering for underground openings, and rock slope engineering.
learning_outcomes: Explain methods for in situ investigation and laboratory testing of rock matrix and discontinuities.
Propose designs of excavation supports.
Define the characteristics and the mechanical properties (strength and failure criteria) of rock mass, rock matrix and discontinuities.
Conduct rock slope stability analyses.
Use rock mass classification systems (RMR, Q, GSI).
Analyse the stress distribution (isotropic, anisotropic) in situ and around an opening in rock (competent rock, jointed rock mass, blocky rock).

title: Geotechnical Site Characterisation
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: The aim of this course is to introduce the in-situ techniques commonly employed in geotechnical practice as well as conventional and advanced laboratory testing procedures available for soil characterization aimed at developing geotechnical models to be used in current practice.
learning_outcomes: Estimate geotechnical parameters from index and mechanical laboratory tests to be used in geotechnical design.
Design a laboratory program for soil characterization.
Interpret and analyse common in situ tests using in geotechnical practice.
Estimate geotechnical parameters from in situ tests to be used in geotechnical design.
Interpret and analyse index and mechanical (non-conventional) laboratory tests.
Propose a geotechnical model based on in situ and laboratory tests.
Design a soil sampling campaign for geotechnical characterization in laboratory.
Assess sample quality and select proper specimens for laboratory testing.

title: Hydrology
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to hydrology and the hydraulics of open channels. Topics include analysis of precipitation, evaporation, infiltration and runoff. Hydrology, frequency and routing of floods. Yield analysis, climate and hydrologic mass balance. Open channel hydraulics including mass, energy and momentum equations. Characterization of steady flow, controls and channel design. Unsteady flow in channels. Content of this course is similar to CIVL4330.
learning_outcomes: Conduct open channel experiments in a laboratory setting
Solve elementary hydrology and open channel problems encountered by engineers
Summarise and interpret the research literature and apply it to practical problems
Identify hydrology and open channel related problems
Demonstrate report writing skills commensurate with master's level engineering students

title: Geomechanics 2
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the principles of soil mechanics. The purpose of the course is to provide the foundation for geotechnical and geoenvironmental engineering design.
learning_outcomes: Calculate and explain soil shear strength and strength parameters
Use critical state soil mechanics to interpret undrained and drained shear strength of soils
Apply basic concepts in critical state soil mechanics to describe soil behaviour
Conduct basic laboratory experiments and derive soil shear strength and strength parameters from these experiments
Apply strength failure criteria to the analysis of shallow foundations, retaining walls and slope stability
Interpret the Mohr-Coulomb failure criterion for geomaterials and apply it in geotechnical analysis and design

title: MPE Thesis A
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course is Part A of a multi-term sequence. Over two 10 units courses, students will conduct an independent research study in the form of a literature review, an experimental or theoretical investigation, an engineering design problem etc. Results are communicated in the form of a seminar, and progress report.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate initiative through the work performed
Critically analyse the work performed previously by others
Demonstrate an appreciation of the state-of-the-art in the selected area
Demonstrate an advanced ability to communicate the objectives and outcomes of the work
Use their initiative in an area of self-selected engineering interest
Critically assess the achievements, limitations and further requirements of their own work

title: Water Engineering
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to water engineering practice. It builds on prior learning in fluid mechanics, hydrology, and statistics, and demonstrates how concepts from these areas are applied in stormwater drainage design, Water Sensitive Urban Design (WSUD), and water resource systems. By examining a range of water engineering design problems, the course fosters holistic thinking and develops technical skills in water engineering design, analysis, and decision-making.
learning_outcomes: Understand and apply hydrologic, hydraulic, and stormwater management principles to the analysis and design of stormwater drainage and WSUD systems.
Evaluate water engineering solutions using technical, environmental, economic, and social considerations.
Explain the impacts of urbanisation on stormwater, stormwater systems, and receiving waters, and the principles of stormwater management.
Analyse water resource systems including water supply and reservoir operation.
Communicate water engineering analyses and design solutions professionally.

title: MPE Thesis B
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course is Part B of a multi-term sequence. Students conduct an independent research study in the form of a literature review, an experimental or theoretical investigation, an engineering design problem etc. Results are communicated in the form of a seminar, and final report (conference paper).
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate initiative through the work performed
Critically assess the achievements, limitations and further requirements of their own work
Critically analyse the work performed previously by others
Use their initiative in an area of self-selected engineering interest
Demonstrate an appreciation of the state-of-the-art in the selected area
Demonstrate an advanced ability to communicate the objectives and outcomes of the work

title: Structural Engineering Project
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course provides a practical introduction to design techniques in structural engineering. The emphasis is on realistic design problems such as the structural design of a new residential, commercial or industrial building. Problems are set and supervised by practising engineers in consultation with academic staff and test most aspects of structural design. The course will also facilitate real-world experiential learning via a site visit.
learning_outcomes: Apply the research and design skills acquired in earlier courses to solve realistic practical problems as part of a design team
Know the major Australian Standards relating to structural engineering analysis and design
Develop the structural concept for a complete building system including the description of the load resisting system for the building
Understand the features and limitations of the most common software used in professional practice at the design stage
Communicate design outcomes at a professional level and demonstrate a sophistication and maturity in approach to the execution of a project

title: Contaminant Hydrogeology
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: The theory of groundwater flow and the transport of pollutants in groundwater are covered in this course. Topics include the modelling of groundwater flow and contaminant transport, well hydraulics, flow nets, subsurface chemical and microbial processes, sea water intrusion, groundwater monitoring and remediation.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate key concepts by interpreting data from laboratory experiments.
Implement solution techniques to solve common problems in hydrogeology and contaminant transport.
Identify and explain the key concepts of hydrogeology and contaminant transport.
Demonstrate capability to research the literature and apply it to practical problems.
Generate technical reports that integrate key concepts and develop critical thinking skills.

title: Water Engineering Project
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course provides a practical introduction to investigation and design techniques in water engineering. The emphasis is on a realistic problem requiring investigation of several options in a multi-objective context and conceptual design. The problem is set by a practising engineer.
learning_outcomes: Work as part of a design team
Demonstrate a sophistication and maturity in approach to and execution of project with evidence of professional level skills and attitudes
Communicate and interact at a professional level
Apply research and design skills to solve design problems
Develop investigation and conceptual design skills in a multi-objective, multi-option problem framework

title: Advanced Analysis for Design
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the development and use of finite element analysis and modelling for structural, water and geotechnical engineering.
learning_outcomes: Apply finite element techniques to solve simple engineering problems using a commercial finite element package
Interpret results and evaluate the efficiency and accuracy of a finite element analysis
Apply interpolation and numerical integration to derive and evaluate finite element stiffness equations from first principles
Perform a detailed finite element study to investigate and design a real world engineering problem
Describe sources nonlinearity and compare technique for solving linear and nonlinear finite equations
Modify an existing finite element program to implement alternative finite elements and/or finite element techniques

title: Geotechnical Engineering Project
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course provides a practical introduction to investigation and design techniques in geotechnical engineering. The emphasis is on a realistic problem requiring investigation of several options in a multi-objective context and conceptual design. The problem is set by a practising engineer.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a sophistication and maturity in approach to and execution of a project with evidence of professional level skills and attitudes.
Critically analyse and communicate outcomes at a professional level, both verbally and as a report.
Incorporate design tools such as standards and software in the formulation of solutions to real problems, and explore the limitations of these tools.
Integrate and extrapolate the theory presented in earlier courses to solve a broad range of real problems.
Work as part of a team in the solution of problems that are posed and directed by experienced practising engineers and academics.
Apply research and design skills to model and understand complex geotechnical systems and to solve open-ended geotechnical problems.

title: Evaluating, Assessing and Developing Clinical Competence
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview: This course covers the theory and practice of clinical teaching and assessment and staff appraisal in the workplace. It comprises components of Clinical Teaching on the Run and Workplace Based Assessment methods. Candidates' own continuing professional development strategies will be critically reviewed and clinical competence will be assessed using a variety of assessment tools as part of this course.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate competence as a clinical teacher
Evaluate learning outcomes
Improve teaching in the workplace by recognising opportunities in the clinical setting
Plan learning activities covering a clinical term
Identify and develop strategies to overcome learning difficulties.
Incorporate principles of teaching and learning into clinical activities
Develop and implement a personal continuing professional development program (CPDP)
Run group teaching sessions and group learning activities
Utilise the 4-Step approach to clinical skills teaching and apply it in the workplace
Plan and undertake workplace based assessment of junior staff using a variety of tools
Reflect on and assess one's own workplace performance

assessment_tasks.task_name: Assessing Performance Difficulties and Emerging Competency Areas - Reflective Tasks - Part A
Assessing clinical skills and small group learning - Reflective Tasks - Part B
Assessing clinical skills and small group learning - Reflective Tasks - Part A
Assessing Performance Difficulties and Emerging Competency Areas - Reflective Tasks - Part B

title: Foundations of Clinical Leadership and Management
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview: This course introduces candidates to the foundations of management and leadership theory within the clinical context. It comprises the definition and analysis of management theory, characteristics and styles of leadership and introduces individual, group and organisational structures. Foundations of Clinical Leadership and Management is designed to be largely theoretically based and self-directed.
learning_outcomes: Apply leadership and management skills to effectively manage clinical teams.
Understand theoretical aspects of leadership and management;
Apply leadership and management theory and practical skills to real life leadership or management problems; and

title: Application of Leadership and Management Skills
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview: This course provides candidates with the opportunity to build upon their theoretical knowledge of leadership and management and apply these in a clinical work context. Candidates will work individually and in small groups on case-based and problem-based scenarios and on a real life managerial issue identified by the student. Candidates are also scaffolded to analyse their own part in leadership, their personal leadership and management attributes and their preferred management styles. Application of Leadership and Management Skills requires candidates to work in a 'management team' to consider the theories in the context of every day leadership and management in familiar contexts. This requires synchronous and asynchronous contact with group members, course coordinators and tutors. It enables the consideration of leadership in action.
learning_outcomes: Show their managerial and organisational skills in arranging real time meetings with their peers, allocating roles within a problem-based context and striving towards a solution
Identify a management challenge in their own environment and apply their learning to design an appropriate management strategy.
Demonstrate their ability to manage their own learning and be insightful, reflective leaders in their online discussion forum contributions and submissions
Analyse their own Leadership attributes and preferred Leadership and Management styles
Demonstrate understanding of Leadership and Management theory by application to case and problem based scenarios and a real life situation

title: Communication Skills
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Being able to communicate effectively in a range of contexts is a vital life skill; it is fundamental to how you learn, how you work and live with others and how you can express your views when it comes to those things that matter to you. It’s also a set of skills that employers are often looking for in their staff. In this course you will develop your ability to speak and listen effectively in a range of public and interpersonal contexts. You will learn how to deliver effective presentations, express yourself in formal and informal settings, and use your voice and your body to communicate clearly. You will embark on a process of finding your voice, reflecting on the ways you do already talk about the things that matter to you and considering how you want to develop your voice to be an engaged citizen. This is a practical class that will involve speaking in a range of contexts. It is intended for students from all disciplinary backgrounds. It would be particularly valuable for students who would like additional support to participate in seminars and tutorials and who may feel unsure about giving presentations in the course of their studies and work.
learning_outcomes: Reflect critically on the cultural construction of notions of effective communication.
Critique their own and others’ communicative performances in a range of contexts.
Apply knowledge of the characteristics of effective communication to communicate in a range of contexts.

title: Media and Communication Concepts
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the major perspectives and debates in media and communication and how they influence communication processes and creative practices. Drawing on real-world examples in Australia and internationally, the course examines the practice of media and communication in different professional contexts. The course will include considerations of audiences and media representations, including intersecting narratives such as gender, race and class that occur in communication contexts. Students will develop an understanding of the social, economic and cultural contexts in which communication occurs and requires students to think critically and analytically about the impact of media and communication on society and social groups.
learning_outcomes: Interrogate key perspectives and debates that shape the role and influence of media and communication in society.
Apply relevant theories and concepts to reflect on the practice of media and communication in a defined professional context.
Analyse key perspectives and debates in media and communication in the context of current developments in the creative industries.
Present arguments and evidence on the impact of media and communication on society and social groups.

title: Media, Culture and Narrative
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the power of storytelling in Australian culture and media, with a focus on visual storytelling.
