Students will explore how stories are constructed, shared and consumed across a range of media formats for diverse audiences. How do professionals in media production, strategic communication and journalism shape stories for their target audiences? The course will cover a range of concepts, techniques and conventions related to storytelling across the media landscape, including in news, film and television, advertising and social media. Students will acquire understanding of the 'grammar' and structure of stories and the role of narrative in shaping media content, and will utilise content creation skills by developing their own creative story project.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the histories, conventions and structures of narratives across a range of media formats.
Employ effective oral and written communication skills.
Apply appropriate audiovisual production terminology to describe media narratives and techniques.
Develop a creative story project for a defined audience using narrative concepts and theories.

title: Introduction to Media Production
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Proficiency in recording and editing audio-visual content is essential in media and the creative industries. This course equips students with the technical and conceptual skills to produce high-quality media projects for various platforms. Students will use their own recording equipment—smartphones, DSLRs, or mirrorless cameras—while conducting editing and audio post-production on professional software. They will also create promotional materials to complement their final video project. Through hands-on learning, they will work together to plan, capture, and refine media content, developing proficiency in all stages of production. By the course’s conclusion, students will have gained practical expertise in media storytelling and professional production practices
learning_outcomes: Evaluate one's own work in the context of media production industry processes and best practice.
Apply media production skills to develop and produce a project that creatively combines audio, screen and graphic content.
Implement industry standards for media production deliverables.
Develop a collaborative strategy to promote a client through a targeted media production.

title: Introduction to Professional Writing
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to professional writing skills for a range of communication media forms and platforms. Workshops provide the opportunity for students to develop skills to meet new writing challenges, to critically examine examples of professional writing, to discuss their own work with their peers, and to consider the ethical and legal obligations of the professional writer. Students are set writing tasks which offer the potential for publication.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate professional writing and editing skills.
Produce written work at a publishable standard.
Apply scripting, interviewing and audio-visual recording skills.

title: Interactive Storytelling
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course provides an introduction to interactive storytelling and media production for distribution on the World Wide Web and social media platforms. It will attract students from diverse backgrounds who are interested in developing multidisciplinary skills from the domains of Design, Communication and Information Technology. This is a hands-on course that will develop in-demand creative production skills for those looking for a career in social media and traditional media production.
learning_outcomes: Exhibit skills in the development and promotion of media content for the web and social media
Critically appraise their own and the work of others
Display their ability to conceive, design and construct interactive and branded media

title: Digital Media Engagement
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Digital and social media have transformed our lives, and how individuals, professionals, and organisations engage with their audiences. Students will learn about the theoretical and cultural dynamics of digital communication. This course provides students with an opportunity to investigate a range of digital and social media forms and practices. It provides students with an opportunity to investigate social, political, economic, and cultural implications of digital media engagement from both Western and non-Western perspectives. Students will also create a professional profile that enables and equips students to connect with industry professionals and become work-ready.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse digital audience engagement strategies with a particular focus on legal and ethical issues.
Explain how a range of digital media tools and/or platforms can be used to foster audience engagement.
Develop a digital media engagement strategy to achieve a professional objective.
Communicate effectively orally and using digital media.

title: Interactive Art Practice and Production
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: In the last 50 years, interactions between software, machines and humans, have profoundly changed culture and society, producing new ways of making art and media. Interactive Arts is a collection of creative practices that leverage digital technologies to generate expressive, participatory and public real-time media environments for human-computer interaction. This course will establish a theoretical framework for understanding key critical debates and concepts in interactive media art, examining case studies of seminal artistic innovations, before proceeding to teach best practice techniques and methods for capturing, and visualising data using sensors, object-oriented software, scripting, video and other digital assets.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and critique contemporary examples of interactive art;
Integrate data capture with various interfaces and display mechanisms in an installation concept.
Demonstrate technical and aesthetic aspects of interactive arts production through developing a creative project;

title: Sound Production
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: In this course students will develop skills in sound production applicable to radio, video, multimedia and other related communication operations. The course examines the practices of sound producers, sound engineers and sound designers while developing skills in sound capture, editing, mixing and arrangement. It provides practical experience with microphones, portable audio recording equipment and software production while considering the importance of audio monitoring, signal processing, audio data storage and sound levels. The course applies this knowledge to produce stereo audio projects of an industry standard that demonstrate the creative use of sound technology.
learning_outcomes: Recognise media and communication concepts in sound production scenarios
Develop multi-layer sound production arrangements
Use sound production processes to create cohesive media content

title: Cinematography
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: In this course, students will develop skills and knowledge in cinematography through an exploration of the cinematographer's role in a film crew and an understanding of the technical and aesthetic parameters of professional practice in collaborative groups/teams. Building on fundamental techniques, this course will provide an understanding of creative visual storytelling in cinematic form and is informed and contextualised by an overview of the history of cinematography. Students will learn single camera recording skills, editing techniques, and the application of video codecs and export formats appropriate for screen delivery.
learning_outcomes: Display proficiency in acquiring moving images that tell a visual story and meet a pre-determined narrative.
Display safe operational procedures when shooting short video productions;
Apply digital cinematography practices and techniques in short video productions;
Demonstrate digital cinematography skills through selection of visual compositions using lens perspective, lighting contrasts, tone and visual montage techniques;

title: Principles of Public Relations
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the field of public relations and provides a foundational knowledge of public relations theory and practice. Students will begin to develop an understanding of professional practice, the ethical codes of conduct guiding public relations practice, and the role of communication strategies and tactics in building dialogic relationships among organisations, publics, and stakeholders. Students will learn how to carry out public relations planning, respond to client briefs, and formulate communication plans. They are also encouraged to explore how public relations can help organisations achieve their purpose, vision, and mission and start positioning themselves for a career in public relations.
learning_outcomes: Explain core public relations theories and concepts and how they apply to practice.
Describe public relations activities and tactics and illustrate their use in real-world contexts.
Interpret and apply ethical frameworks for public relations.
Design public relations strategies and tactics to solve real-world problems and fulfill organisational communication goals.

title: Screenwriting
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the concepts, skills and knowledge required for writing short scripts for the screen. The course will examine elements of dramatic, factual and documentary storytelling such as structure, theme, character and storyworlds, content and plot devices, as well as scene, action, dialogue and narration. Students will write concept documents, outlines, treatments and pitch decks to gain an understanding of the stages of script production as well as new and evolving forms and conventions of screenwriting.
learning_outcomes: Apply different styles and techniques to the screenplay form;
Analyse films and other audio-visual forms of media entertainment;
Write and edit imaginative and creative scripts;
Integrate constraints imposed by budgets and time schedules.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Assessment 1 - Script Proposal & Initial Proof of Concept
Assessment 3 - Final Draft & Final Proof of Concept

title: Activism and Social Change
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Social media and digital technologies have become indispensable communication and engagement tools for individuals, organisations, and governments. As they gain dominance in our communication eco-system, they are also shaping our understanding of the world and its people. This course examines how public interest communication contributes to activism, social change, and social movements. Students will develop a nuanced understanding of communication’s potential to facilitate social change by investigating its theoretical frameworks and practical implementation in the context of critical social and global challenges, which include humanitarian crises, international development, and disparities in society. This course will analyse the contributions of advocacy and activist groups, grassroots organisations, and NGOs in resource mobilisation and the communication of organisational objectives. It will also consider how public policies and international governance shape the communication of social and global issues in Australia.
learning_outcomes: Communicate effectively orally and using digital media.
Describe how legal, political, and ethical frameworks impact on public interest communication’s facilitation of activism and social change.
Critically examine current activism and social change communication practices using communication and social movement theories.
Analyse the role of NGO and advocacy group communication and evaluate their impact on individuals, organisations, governments, and society.

title: News Media
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Digital disruption has transformed news media and consequently change in the industry is constant. This course will introduce students to how news media operates and will develop analytical, research, interviewing, production, multimedia and writing skills relevant to multi-platform journalism in a dynamic media environment. Course content will contextualise and analyse news media through a lens that explores cultural, historical, political and economic perspectives.
learning_outcomes: Critique the skills and practices of professional journalism.
Analyse the role of news media in society;
Apply news reporting skills for text-based and multiplatform publications in practical presentations;
Identify key issues relating to journalism practice and news processes.

title: Global Media Industries
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course examines local and international developments in global media industries and the perspectives and practices guiding the creation of factual media, fictional media, and synthetic media. Through analysing the media texts created by local and global media industries, students will gain an understanding into how creative and communication practices are shaped by cultural, historic, economic, and technological factors. Students will also develop their understanding of global media practice and theory and gain skills to navigate and work in globalised media environments.
learning_outcomes: Examine the role and function of local and global media in Australia, including indigenous media.
Construct a comparative case study to explain the localisation and globalisation of media texts using global media theories and concepts.
Identify and evaluate the practical implications of global media industries on creative and media practices.
Analyse and discuss the cultural, historic, economic, and technological factors that influence the developments in global media industries.

title: Data Storytelling
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The ability to interpret and visualise data is a critical skill for communicating complex ideas and issues. With the rise of misinformation and disinformation across the world, data literacy and data storytelling are competencies that are in demand across multiple industries. Students will learn to interpret data through the creation of tables, charts, animations and infographics for various storytelling contexts, including journalism. Students will build on skills learnt in other Media and Communication courses to interpret and visualise data to represent complex ideas and issues. The legal, ethical implications of working with big data will be an integral part of the course as will an understanding of the social implications of visualising data.
learning_outcomes: Analyse data from publicly available sources.
Explain the social, legal and ethical implications of working with data.
Create visualisations of primary data using research and technical tools.
Employ data to create factual stories in a range of styles.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Plan for original data storytelling project

title: Organisational Communication
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course will provide students with an understanding of the fundamental communication and relational concepts and processes that underpin strategic communication and public relations strategy. The course focusses on organisational communication behaviour and strategic engagement with key publics, and the role of strategic communication within an organisation. Using a problem-based learning approach, students will work collaboratively to identify, analyse and address real-world communication issues. Students will develop strategic responses that are underpinned by relevant theoretical, ethical and legal frameworks.
learning_outcomes: Explain key concepts of strategic communication, stakeholders and publics in an organisational context;
Identify key issues and trends in strategic organisational communication practices and effectively communicate research outcomes;
Assess the strengths and weaknesses of key theories in underpinning and informing approaches to contemporary practice;
Develop strategic responses that conform with the ethical and legal dimensions of organisational communication.

title: Audience Participation and Interaction
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course will examine the way audiences are researched within academic practices, and understood and positioned by media organisations. Students study competing conceptions of ‘audience’ and how they are operationalised through different media industries.
learning_outcomes: Design and conduct audience research appropriate to an industry context.
Explain the differences between different forms of audience measurement.
Critique approaches to the understanding of audiences.
Explain the role and significance of audiences within the media and communication industries.

title: Feature Writing
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: In this course students will explore the theory and practice of features journalism in print and online formats. Students will develop their research, interviewing, and writing skills by producing a variety of feature articles for publication in text and online forms.
learning_outcomes: Apply professional writing and research skills to produce features journalism appropriate to print and online forms.
Critically reflect on their professional practice.
Identify the role of journalism in society.

title: Create Your Own Business
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course explores activities, structures, and opportunities of creating a new (small) business in the media and communication industry. Students will gain an understanding of the increasingly fragmented and digitized job market on a local, national, and international level, and the common practice of freelancing Ethical and legal frameworks for creating a new business will be considered and practical aspects such as incorporation & governance, finances, budgeting time and money, intellectual property and copyright, as well as marketing will be discussed. Students will have the opportunity to work towards creating their own business.
learning_outcomes: Develop a business plan to create a new business within the media and communication industries.
Recognise and discuss opportunities to establish independent businesses in the industry including legal and ethical frameworks;
Understand the employment landscape in the media and communication industries, locally, nationally, and internationally;
Demonstrate an understanding of business-related matters including but not limited to governance, finances, intellectual property, and marketing;

title: Documentary Filmmaking
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course explores documentary storytelling, and provides students with the knowledge, skills and technologies to devise documentaries for the screen. Students work in teams to develop, write and produce an original short documentary suitable for submission to a real-world media industry output such as a local, national or international video festival, broadcast, or online environment. The course examines international documentary concepts, practices and modes across 20th and 21st century screens, and their social, political and cultural implications. Students develop the ability to analyse and apply diverse forms of documentary storytelling techniques and approaches. During the course students develop a professional approach to their crew roles, participants and documentary practice. The ethical relationships and responsibilities between filmmakers, participants and viewers in global screen cultures are also considered, including protocols that apply when working with Indigenous participants and topics.
learning_outcomes: Synthesise practical, technical and conceptual skills through the research, development and collaborative realisation of a documentary screen production;
Evaluate one's own production works and identify creative, collaborative and technical issues in these works;
Collaborate and communicate effectively with fellow students and work to production deadlines;
Implement contemporary production processes, crew responsibilities, basic on-set protocols, and screen industry related safety procedures.
Apply knowledge of screen production terminology to critically analyse documentary screen works.

title: Podcasting
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: In this course, students will develop the skills to produce audio content suitable for distribution via broadcast or online podcasting platforms. The course will follow the production cycle of audio content from conceiving an original idea through production to post-production and distribution. Students will analyse audio storytelling genres, techniques, and formats, and create their own factual audio project. They will develop and apply audio production skills, including writing and presenting, interviewing talent, recording location sound, editing and mixing audio sources, and operating the podcasting studio.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the contexts and techniques of podcast production and reception
Create an audio story appropriate for specified audiences and suitable for dissemination via online podcasting platforms
Utilise effective oral and written communication
Employ appropriate audio storytelling skills informed by theory and industry best practice
Reflect on the relationship between media practice and theory

title: Transmedia Documentary
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course explores documentary production and provides students with the knowledge, skills and technologies to devise documentaries for the screen. Students work in teams to develop an original short documentary for submission to a real-world media industry output such as a local, national or international video festival, broadcast, web, mobile or transmedia environment. The course examines diverse modes, experimental movements and transmedia documentary practices across 20th and 21st century screens, and their social, political and cultural implications. Students develop the ability to analyse evolving forms of documentary storytelling. During the course students develop a professional approach to their crew roles, participants and documentary practice. The ethical relationships and responsibilities between filmmakers, participants and viewers in global screen cultures are also considered.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and apply elements of the documentary genre in a project pitch and in production
Apply professional practices of documentary development and production;
Develop knowledge of transmedia approaches and practices in documentary
Employ documentary storytelling, methods, modes and practices in the production of a short documentary video;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Development of a Documentary Proposal and Pitch

title: Communication and Creativity
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Students will analyse competing theoretical frameworks and study various individual and collective creative practices as well as discuss methods of enhancing creativity. They will examine and analyse the issues associated with creativity and cultural production such as originality and authenticity, the notion of individual genius, and possible limitations placed upon creative freedom by culture industries. Students will gain an understanding of creativity as it applies to professional careers in radio, film and television, journalism, audio and other spheres of cultural production. For students contemplating undertaking an Honours year by creative project and exegesis this course provides key theoretical understandings.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate research themes in practical careers in radio, film, journalism, photography, sound production, television and other spheres of cultural production.
Critically assess questions and issues related to creative practice in historical or contemporary contexts.
Develop an independent research project that integrates creative practice and theory.
Investigate diverse theories of creativity and cultural practice.

title: Global Trends in Media and Communication
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course examines global issues in communication and media industries. Students will deepen their understanding of international media practice and theory and develop skills to assist them in working in a global environment. They will learn the role of media professionals in society. The course examines variations in media systems around the world including how social, cultural, political, economic and historical contexts influence and impact media practice.
learning_outcomes: Construct a case to explain global media concepts and contexts.
Compare the role and function of the media in Australia with media systems in other countries.
Evaluate the practical implications of a globalised media and communication industry on media practice.
Analyse and discuss the cultural, historic, economic and political context of international media and communication.

title: Short Film Production
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Students will develop the skills, knowledge and ability to create a live-action short film. Working in groups students will take on the role of either a screen-writer, a director, a cinematographer, an art director, a sound recordist/composer or an editor. Emphasis in this course will be focused on original treatment of the story through crew collaboration and creative processes for location film production.
learning_outcomes: Apply appropriate technical, creative and organisational skills to plan, shoot, and edit a short film production.
Collaborate and communicate effectively with fellow students to produce a location-based short film.
Demonstrate an understanding of industry expectations in regard to WHS, risk assessments, budgeting, ethical and moral issues, and safe working practices.
Critically reflect on the creative process related to short film production practices;

title: Multiplatform Journalism
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The course blends practical experience with critical insights into news genres and careers. It will cover emerging trends in news, including strategies for dissemination of news via social media platforms. Students will develop advanced writing, researching, interviewing, and production skills suitable for multiplatform journalism. They will create fast turnaround, mobile news stories for television, online and social media audiences. Students will develop skills demonstrating ethical and legal obligations of news story creation.
learning_outcomes: Utilise effective oral and written communication skills relevant for contemporary journalism practice.
Produce engaging digital stories for online and social media audiences, employing theoretical knowledge of emerging trends in news media and technological changes.
Create news stories for television, online and social media platforms using journalism principles and practices.
Reflect on the relationship between media practice and theory

title: Data Visualisation in Journalism
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course will require students to interpret data through the creation of tables, charts, animations and infographics for journalism. Students will build on skills learnt in other Communication courses to visualise data in a journalistic context and learn how to represent complex ideas, issues and data using various forms of visualisation. The legal and ethical implications of working with big data will be an integral part of the course as will an understanding of the social implications of data journalism and visualisation.
learning_outcomes: Reproduce data and visualisation in a range of journalistic styles;
Create visualisations of primary data using research and technical tools;
Access, analyse and curate data from publicly available sources;
Explain the social, legal and ethical implications of data journalism

assessment_tasks.task_name: Data plan, story and visualisations plan

title: Public Relations Campaigns
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course focuses on researching and planning a real-world public relations campaign. Students will critically examine and evaluate a range of past campaigns considering strategic, theoretical, ethical and legal aspects of campaigning. The course simulates an agency scenario that offers students insights into professional agency processes and practices. Students will work independently to develop a comprehensive public relations campaign with a coherent storyline that addresses a client brief. Students will draw on strategic and practical skills developed throughout their degree to develop a campaign that could be practically adopted by a client organisation
learning_outcomes: Research, plan and creatively design an integrated public relations campaign that meets the client brief and is underpinned by academic and industry resources;
Present and defend the campaign concept in a pitch format supported by visual campaign examples
Effectively work in a group/team by contributing to the planning, research, analysis, and reporting components of a group project, and supporting and encouraging other group members.
Critically analyse and evaluate a range of public relations case studies drawing on relevant theoretical, ethical and legal frameworks;

title: Experimental Media
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Experimental media provides an opportunity to explore new tools and techniques to enhance your existing creative practice and explore new possibilities of creative expression. This is a hands on course that takes the form of a studio lab. It promotes collaboration with others across disciplines and also with a variety of new or repurposed technologies. In the last 50 years, interactions between technology and humans have profoundly changed culture and society, producing new ways of story telling. This has also inspired completely new mediums and environments for creative expression such as immersive caves, extended reality, drone light shows and interactive installations. This course will establish a theoretical framework for understanding key critical debates and concepts in experimental media making, examining case studies of seminal innovations, before proceeding to teach best practice techniques and processes to explore your own ideas. The sky is not the limit.
learning_outcomes: Self-reflection and evaluation of experimental process from idea to prototype
Analyse and critique contemporary examples of experimental media practice;
Demonstrate experimental media making through developing a creative outcome;

title: Political Communication
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The course explores the processes of communication as they relate to structures of government and to other socio-political and institutional forces. It examines responsibilities and relationships between different groups of actors in society and how political communication contributes to the shaping of public opinion, policy formation, and electoral campaigns. The course considers concepts related to power, influence, ideology and values, political involvement, and active citizenship. Through contemporary political issues and events, consideration is applied to the Australian system of government, and the role and influence of communication professionals in political communication processes.
learning_outcomes: Identify and explain how political communication contributes to the shaping of public opinion, policy formation, and electoral campaigns.
Identify and describe the role of local, regional and national systems of government and the key forces shaping the Australian political communication landscape.
Outline and explain the role and influence of communication professionals on political communication processes.
Analyse and interpret current political events and issues using political communication theories and analytical practices.

title: Computing Fundamentals
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the principles and techniques behind hardware and software systems. This includes the technical skills required to model and develop working software solutions and identify related ethical issues. This course also develops the career-long skills required to work and manage tasks in a team environment.
learning_outcomes: Explain ethical issues associated with the use of IT in business;
Describe the history of computing, its role in the ICT industry, and societal impact;
Describe the concepts and interdependencies of hardware and software systems;
Work and communicate as an effective member of a well-managed team utilising appropriate project management techniques and tools.
Apply different software development models;
Model and analyse the ways that organisations or other systems work;

title: Public Relations Project
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course is the capstone unit in the Public Relations and Strategic Communication Major. It provides students with the opportunity to draw on and assimilate the knowledge and skills they have developed throughout their major, while extending and refining these skills to provide strategic and tactical solutions for a real-world client-based campaign. Students will engage with and apply the theoretical, ethical and legal understandings that underpin public relations campaign practice. Working both independently and collaboratively, it will prepare students for professional practice through the delivery of well-researched and creative responses and materials, that practicably meet their client’s brief within allocated budgets and timeframes.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and apply public relations theories in creating engaging campaign content;
Implement planning processes, including researching content, identifying and working to a brief, and addressing target publics;
Explain aspects of public relations content production including implementation, monitoring and evaluation, budget, OHS insurance and legal matters, and public relations ethics
Design a collection of works in either print, video, sound, web-based, on-line or multimedia productions with a coherent campaign message;

title: Gamified Media
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course focuses on the development of interactive gamified interfaces. Students will use a range of technologies to develop interactive interfaces for entertainment, information and educational purposes incorporating serious games. The course will allow students to integrate their media and digital production skills with interactive production to develop material for a range of physical and online media forms.
learning_outcomes: Use relevant scripting languages and coding tools in the construction of an online interactive
Plan and produce an interactive physical media interface;
Evaluate their own and the work of others by examining production techniques used to create interactive media.
Integrate relevant technologies in the production of a game interface;

title: Contemporary Journalism
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The practice of journalism has evolved over the years. Contemporary journalism around the world is marked by the inclusion of digital and social media and the diversity of approaches to disseminating news and information. In this course, students will gain an understanding of the key theories and developments in contemporary journalism and various types of journalism such as public interest, constructive, and investigative journalism. They will use advanced research, interviewing, writing, and digital production skills to develop journalistic content targeted at audiences across a range of news media platforms. They will produce industry-standard journalistic content and reflect on their creative and journalism practices. Students will also explore topics, ethical issues, and approaches relevant to contemporary global journalism practice. The integration of theoretical and practical knowledge will prepare students for the transition to professional practice in journalism or for further study in media and communication studies.
learning_outcomes: Examine contemporary journalistic approaches and apply digital and mobile newsroom practices in their creation of journalistic content.
Communicate the history, development, and ethics of journalism and describe the factors influencing contemporary storytelling approaches in journalism.
Define their approach to contemporary journalism and digital storytelling and critically reflect on their own creative and journalism practices.
Apply news gathering and editing skills and use a range of technologies to create industry-standard journalistic content for publication.

title: Social Media Listening and Monitoring
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: As social media becomes ever more integrated into our lives, the lines blur between our private and public personas as our personal data becomes an increasingly valuable commodity. This course exposes students to the key theories, debates, approaches, and regulatory developments relating to the practice of social monitoring and listening. Using real-world examples, students will explore and learn about social monitoring and listening tools, as well as investigate the ethical issues and the impacts of social monitoring and listening for different social groups. Students will develop a contextual understanding of how social monitoring and listening is practised by different types of organisations and its relevance for media and communication professionals.
learning_outcomes: Formulate and justify appropriate social monitoring and listening strategies for organisations and governments to connect with their key stakeholders and reach out to their target publics and audience.
Describe the ethical issues associated with social monitoring and listening and connect these issues to their social, political economic, and cultural contexts.
Explain and give examples of theories and current applications relating to the practice of social monitoring and listening for social media measurement and public relations social strategies.
Critically examine and evaluate the potential and implications of social monitoring and listening for individuals, organisations, and governments.

title: Media Production Project
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Completing a capstone course offers a tangible way for students to showcase the skills and knowledge learned and complete a project that is aligned with their career aspirations. In this course, students will create a substantial professional work or portfolio of work that applies the skills they have learnt in their Media Production major. Students will draw on skills including story ideation, research, writing, interviewing, cinematography, sound recording, and editing to develop and create quality industry-standard media content for a target audience. Students may create one audiovisual work or a series of work (portfolio) suitable for online distribution. Students will reflect on the process of creating their project in the context of contemporary industry practices including ethical approaches to media production and distribution. The integration of theoretical and practical knowledge will prepare students for the transition to professional practice in media production or for further study.
learning_outcomes: Create a substantial media production work or portfolio of work that comprises industry-standard audiovisual media content for a target audience.
Describe strategies and approaches for creating industry-standard content.
Identify ethical issues and propose solutions in the context of contemporary Australian media production.
Evaluate works in the context of industry practices and processes using media and communication theories and concepts.

title: Public Relations and News Media Project
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Completing a capstone course offers a tangible way for students to showcase the skills and knowledge learned and complete a project that is aligned with their career aspirations. In this course, students will create a substantial professional work or portfolio of work that applies the skills they have learnt in their Public Relations or News Media major. Students will develop quality industry-standard journalistic content or public relations content for a target audience. The integration of theoretical and practical knowledge will prepare students for the transition to professional practice in public relations or news media, or for further study. Public Relations major students will draw on skills including story ideation, research, situational analysis, writing, social media listening and monitoring, campaign evaluation and social media content creation in their project. Students may create one work or a series of work (portfolio) that addresses an identified communication problem and opportunity for an issue, a person, or an organisation. They will reflect on the process of creating their project in the context of contemporary industry practices including ethical approaches to public relations, dialogic communication, and digital public relations. News Media major students will draw on skills including story ideation, research, interviewing, writing, editing and digital production in their project. Students may create one work or a series of work (portfolio) that addresses an issue of news value, for one medium – text/digital, audio or video – or for a combination of media (multimedia). They will reflect on the process of creating their project in the context of contemporary industry practices including ethical approaches relevant to contemporary journalism practice.
learning_outcomes: Create a substantial work or portfolio of work that comprises industry-standard content for a target audience.
Employ oral and written communication skills to describe strategies and approaches for creating industry-standard content.
Evaluate works in the context of industry practices and processes using media and communication theories and concepts.
Identify ethical issues in contemporary professional practice and propose solutions to explain creative and communication practices.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Public Relations or News Media Project

title: Advanced Media Production
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will work together in groups and individual contexts to create a media project that draws on interdisciplinary skills and frameworks. Students are invited to develop an original collaborative media piece that reflects on different social and media issues and practices. Weekly workshops will explore collaborative and individual creative processes through bringing together diverse stories and knowledges, media skills and questions into relation with each other. Suitable for students who are interested in expanding their knowledge, skills and creativity that can be applied in professional contexts.
learning_outcomes: Propose creative research questions for different social and media issues
Examine different individual and collaborative approaches for professional contexts
Produce a substantial creative work based on interdisciplinary knowledges and media production skills.
Critically reflect on knowledge and skills gained in audio-visual contexts

title: Database and Information Management
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with theoretical knowledge and practical skills in the use of databases and database management systems. The conceptual and logical design and implementation of relational databases are covered.
learning_outcomes: Convert conceptual models to logical data models
Implement a database solution using contemporary database management systems (DBMS)
Understand data security and data quality management
Design conceptual models encapsulating data requirements for business and organisational scenarios
Develop expertise in database languages (e.g. SQL) including the ability to develop sophisticated queries to extract information from large datasets

assessment_tasks.task_name: Assignment 2, Database Project - Logical Database Design
Assignment 1 Database Project - Description and EER model
Practical Test - Lab test on SQL
Assignment 3 - Database Project - Physical Database Design

title: Theory of Computation
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Information and Physical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course introduces formal models of computation and the problems that they can solve. It presents Turing machines and equivalent models of computation. It also discusses the fundamental limitations of what can be computed. It covers finite state machines, regular expressions and regular grammars as well as context-free languages and grammars and non-context free grammars. It includes algorithms and decision procedures for regular and context-free languages, Turing machine, decidability and complexity analysis
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of context-free languages and their limitations
Explain the importance of automata as modelling tools and apply them to computational problems
Discuss the limitations of computational procedures
Explain the basis of theory of computation, in particular the role of key problems in defining classes of equivalent problems from a computational perspective

title: Algorithms
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the notion of efficiency and computational complexity. The basic data structures encountered in first year, such as lists, trees and graphs, are reviewed in light of their efficiency and common usage scenario. Asymptotic measures of complexity are covered, and recurrence relations are introduced as an analytical tool. Problem-solving techniques such as the greedy strategy, divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming, and graph searching are covered. These techniques are illustrated upon optimization problems chosen for their practical relevance.
learning_outcomes: apply efficient algorithm design techniques and understand the limitations of algorithms.
apply basic techniques to analyse the performance of algorithms
explain the most important algorithms used in various common computer science applications;

title: Data Security
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Information and Physical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course deals with topics in cryptography and data security. Students learn fundamental technical tools for cryptography and data security, as well as how to combine the tools to support various security requirements in computerised data processing, data storing and communication.
learning_outcomes: Break classical ciphers
Implement a modern cryptosystem
Analyse and evaluate modern cryptographic systems
Apply number and information theories to modern cryptography
Assess privacy in data publishing

title: Operating Systems
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students are introduced to modern operating systems, the most prominent system software, focusing on their purposes, principles and functionalities. The course will explore different components of operating systems and the services offered by them to increase the productivity, efficiency and convenience of users. Topics include processes and threads, process synchronisation, starvation and deadlocks, resource scheduling, physical and virtual memory organisation and their management, file systems, disk management and scheduling, and security issues. Real operating systems are used for case study where appropriate.
learning_outcomes: Connect how OS abstractions are realised on conventional hardware.
Examine the central issues and methods/algorithms employed in operating systems design.
Discover the structure, functions and components of modern operating systems.
Gain familiarity with some popular operating systems and identify their functional features.
Develop essential skills of programming with consideration of concurrency and multithreads.

title: Compiler Design
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: Compiler Design will teach students the fundamental concepts and techniques used for building a simple compiler. Focusing on both theory and practice, we will use a sample language to explore the lexical, syntactic and semantic structures of programming languages, and learn to use those structures in implementing a demonstrative compiler. The discussion will also include the examination of intermediate code states, machine code optimisation techniques and support for advanced language features. At the end of the course, students will understand different considerations and phases of compilation, the impact of language attributes upon the compilation process, the effect of hardware feature on the generated code and the practical fundamentals of compiler implementation.
learning_outcomes: Specify and analyse the lexical, syntactic and semantic structures of advanced language features
Describe techniques for intermediate code and machine code optimisation
Turn fully processed source code for a novel language into machine code for a novel computer
Separate the lexical, syntactic and semantic analysis into meaningful phases for a compiler to undertake language translation
Design the structures and support required for compiling advanced language features.
Write a scanner, parser, and semantic analyser without the aid of automatic generators

assessment_tasks.task_name: Project Part 1 - Programming in Source Language and Scanner
Project Part 3 - Semantic Analyser & Code Generator

title: Computer Graphics
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: Studies issues related to the displaying of objects, which may include: 2D drawing primitives, homogeneous coordinates, curves and surfaces, 2D & 3D geometrical transformation, projections, geometric models, 3D viewing, visible-surface determination, illumination and shading, ray tracing, real time rendering, colour modes, computer vision.
learning_outcomes: Understand and appreciate computer graphics concepts.
Employ selected software to achieve interactive computer graphics.
Work within a group to complete a graphics project.
Appreciate mathematical fundamentals of computer graphics techniques.
Implement graphics effects.

title: Machine Intelligence
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course provides an introduction and overview of important concepts and applications in the fields of Machine Learning and Artificial Intelligence (AI). With the availability of fast computers, machine intelligence methods have found widespread applications in areas such as in Language Processing, Computer Vision and Autonomous Robots. This course will explore some of them, including systems where machine intelligence methods led to significant advancements, often surprising solutions, and sometimes triumphal success.
learning_outcomes: Produce reports and presentations suitable to explain methods and outcomes of a Machine Intelligence project to others.
Analyse a given task or data and select suitable Machine Learning and AI methods for processing.
Implement relevant code or apply standard libraries for Machine Learning and AI to selected tasks.
Critically reflect on ethics, opportunities and risks of current and future developments of Machine Learning and AI.
Explain central concepts of Machine Learning and AI.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Project Check-ins A and B (multi component)

title: Data Engineering and Mining
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course introduces the processes involved in preparing and analysing data to discover patterns and generate insights for prediction, classification, and data-driven decision making. It covers key concepts in data engineering and data mining, including data acquisition, preprocessing, data quality management, feature engineering, and the preparation of AI-ready datasets for analytics workflows. Students are exposed to established techniques in predictive analytics, machine learning, and pattern discovery, along with methods for model evaluation and interpretation, motivated by practical data analytics problems in business and real-world data science applications.
learning_outcomes: Communicate and collaborate to develop, interpret, and present data analytics solutions while considering responsible and ethical use of data and AI.
Evaluate the processes and techniques used in data engineering and data mining within modern data analytics workflows, including AI-ready data pipelines and data quality considerations.
Prepare, integrate, and transform data for analytics using appropriate data engineering methods, including data ingestion, feature engineering, and data quality management.
Apply well-established data mining and predictive analytics methods to analyse data, develop models, and extract useful patterns for data-driven decision making.

title: Advanced Database
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Information and Physical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with theoretical knowledge and practical skills in modern database systems and data-intensive applications. It covers conceptual and logical database design, SQL and its procedural extensions, storage structures, indexing and query optimisation, transaction and concurrency management, and Object Relational Mapping. Contemporary topics such as OLAP, data warehousing, datamarts, business intelligence, data mining, and big data and distributed databases are also discussed.
learning_outcomes: Design and implement relational databases using EER modelling, normalisation, basic SQL, and object–relational mapping.
Apply storage, indexing, and query processing techniques to improve the performance of database systems.
Apply transaction, concurrency, and crash-recovery management techniques to ensure data integrity and consistency.
Apply concepts of data warehousing, datamarts, and OLAP for analytical data processing and decision support.
Use basic techniques in business intelligence, data mining, big data, parallel, and distributed databases in modern information systems.
Work effectively in teams and communicate professionally when working on database development.

title: Security Attacks: Analysis and Mitigation Strategies
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Information and Physical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to techniques that are used by attackers to exploit computer systems and networks. Security attacks such as injection, rootkits and denial of service attacks will be discussed along with the detailed analysis of defending security technologies such as firewalls, host/network-based security tools and signature/anomaly-based security tools. Students who complete this course will have a good understanding of security technologies that are used for securing systems and networks. Furthermore, students should be able to perform attack detection and security anomaly analysis and manage the security aspect of a network.
learning_outcomes: Apply security mechanisms to mitigate cyber attacks
Identify security risks in enterprise network infrastructures
Demonstration and communication skills of security risks and technologies.
Analyse security threats and methods for exploiting systems and networks to generate attacks
Investigate security technologies used to counteract the attacks

title: Computing and Information Sciences Work Integrated Learning Part A
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Information and Physical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course is Part A of a multi-term sequence incorporating Work Integrated Learning (WIL). Part B must also be completed to meet the requirements of the sequence. This Work Integrated Learning course allows you to apply the theoretical knowledge and skills obtained during your studies with and for an organisation. Through these courses (Part A and Part B), you will work on a project related to the fields of computer science, data science, and/or information technology. The work is undertaken in an organisation (industry, research groups or laboratories) or as an innovative proposal that has been approved by the course coordinator. In your project you will develop an entrepreneurial prototype which requires you to incorporate computer science, data science, and/or information technology skills into their practices. This direct experience exposes you to the project management practices of managers and/or researchers. Under supervision and in a group work environment, you will undertake 240 hours of project-based work, and a Work Integrated Learning Experience within the year, with one or more appropriate organisations. For the Work Integrated Learning Experience, you will undertake 140 hours (equivalent to nominally 4-weeks full-time) in a role relevant to the professional context of your program. This experience may be undertaken within a range of settings, including the private sector, government, other relevant organisations, or with an industry project partner. The student will have an active role in organising this experience, however, students will need to consult with the Course Coordinator prior to approaching companies or organisations. The Course Coordinator will ensure the experience is appropriate and does not adversely affect other existing activities or courses of the University. A nominated supervisor within the host organisation will be required.
learning_outcomes: Apply theoretical knowledge to practical workplace tasks
Critically reflect on the ethical and technical issues faced in the workplace
Critically set objectives and evaluate partial outcomes to enhance developing capabilities and skills required in an evolving placement context
Identify and plan the application of a suite of computer science, data science and/or information technology skills learnt in the program to a specific project
Demonstrate and reflect upon the skills required for the workplace, including both written and verbal communication, and teamwork

title: Cyber Security Governance, Risk, and Compliance
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: Developing and maintaining a sound cybersecurity strategy is important in our digital-first world. Organisations need to adopt strong governance measures to help develop strategies for effectively managing risk and meeting their compliance obligations. Students will learn about the different risk management techniques used in cybersecurity and adopt methods for quantifying and making threat-informed decisions. Students will also learn about the regulatory environment and compliance frameworks that organisations adopt to improve their overall cybersecurity posture. These concepts are then reinforced with practical examples from industry and government to help demonstrate their importance across different industry verticals.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the legal and privacy aspects of cyber security.
Report on an organisations maturity against industry and regulatory standards.
Evaluate and control cybersecurity risks in an organisation.
Report on the differences for governance, risk, and compliance across finance, government, and critical infrastructure verticals.
Develop cybersecurity program metrics and reporting for effective cybersecurity governance.

title: Computing Honours Part 1
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Information and Physical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course is the first part of the CS Honours project. It provides preparation for completion of a supervised research project. In part 1, students carry out a preliminary literature review of the material relevant to their project, develop a research proposal and timeline and begin their research project. They summarise and discuss their proposal in an intermediate report and present a seminar. The Honours project (part 1 and 2 together) comprises a substantial project usually involving a detailed literature review together with a theoretical and/or practical investigation of a computer science problem. Technical content will be dependent on the project undertaken.
learning_outcomes: Improve capacity to undertake postgraduate research
Understand in-depth knowledge in a specific area of ICT
Improve communication skills

assessment_tasks.task_name: Intermediate Project Report of Proposal and Literature Review
Presentation (seminar) of the Project Proposal and Literature Review

title: Computing and Information Sciences Work Integrated Learning Part B
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Information and Physical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course is Part B of a multi-term sequence. Part A must also be completed to meet the requirements of the sequence. Through these courses (Part A and Part B), you will work on a project related to the fields of computer science, data science, and/or information technology. The work is undertaken in an organisation (industry, research groups or laboratories) or as an innovative proposal that has been approved by the course coordinator. In your project you will develop an entrepreneurial prototype which requires you to incorporate computer science, data science, and/or information technology skills into their practices. This direct experience exposes you to the project management practices of managers and/or researchers. Under supervision and in a group work environment, you will undertake 240 hours of project-based work.
learning_outcomes: Identify and plan the application of a suite of computer science, data science and/or information technology skills learnt in the program to a specific project
Critically reflect on the ethical and technical issues faced in the workplace
Apply theoretical knowledge to practical workplace tasks
Critically set objectives and evaluate partial outcomes to enhance developing capabilities and skills required in an evolving placement context
Demonstrate skills required for the workplace, including both written and verbal communication and teamwork

title: Computing Honours Part 2
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course is the second part of the CS Honours project. Parts 1 and 2 together comprise a substantial individual research project usually involving a literature review together with a theoretical and/or practical investigation of a computer science or information technology problem. In part 2, students complete their project building on the foundations and the plan developed in part 1. Under the supervision of a member of the academic staff, each student will complete an individual research project and at the end provide a written exposition (research dissertation in the style of the discipline) of their research. Technical content will be dependent on the project undertaken.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate coherent and advanced communication skills.
Demonstrate capacity to undertake postgraduate research.
Prepare a research dissertation that displays an in-depth knowledge in a specific area of computer science or information technology.

title: Human Factors Engineering
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: Human factors professionals prevent accidents from happening by designing and changing products, systems and processes to best suit a user. This course provides an understanding of some of the major areas of human factors, starting with an overview of psychological capabilities and limitations, followed by how the operational environment can be optimised over a range of contemporary applications. In this course, you will be exposed to a range of human factors in contemporary areas of human factors engineering such as cyber security, workplace design and emerging technology. This will enable you to design and implement user-centred solutions, mitigate risks stemming from human behaviour, and contribute to more effective and holistic products, systems and processes.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and apply scientific solutions to human problems in diverse environments.
Develop and implement educational programs that promote human factors and behaviours.
Critically evaluate contemporary studies on the application of human factors engineering to real world applications and contexts.
Analyse the role of cognitive and perceptual factors in human performance.

title: Contemporary Topics in Artificial Intelligence and Cyber Security
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this course you will investigate and research contemporary topics in both Artificial Intelligence and Cybersecurity. The content is driven by leading literature, case studies and modern breakthroughs in each of the key domains. You will gain a keen insight into both areas while also seeing how the two fields impact upon each other.
learning_outcomes: Formulate, structure, and communicate technical information to scientists, engineers, and other professionals in a clear and professional manner using various mediums.
Investigate, apply and evaluate Generative AI technologies.
Research, critically analyse, and evaluate technical information in Cyber Security and Artificial Intelligence.
Demonstrate effective and collaborative team skills to achieve shared objectives in professional contexts.

title: Databases and Information Management
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: Modern enterprises depend on the effective storage and management of data. Organisational data is essential not only for daily operations but also for building knowledge repositories that support long-term learning and strategic planning. Well-structured corporate data systems form the foundation for informed decision-making and provide a sustainable competitive advantage. This course introduces the fundamental concepts of databases and database systems, alongside their practical implementation through elementary programming skills. Students will learn the principles of information storage and management, beginning with the conceptual modelling of organisational data requirements using the relational model. These concepts are then extended to implementation techniques such as SQL programming and relational normalisation. The course also addresses practical challenges in database systems, including issues of security, transaction management, and concurrency control.
learning_outcomes: Master fundamental relational database concepts including entity relationship diagrams, data normalisation and relational operators.
Design, develop and implement a mid-scale relational databases for an application domain using a commercial-grade Relational Database Management System (RDBMS).
Create, query, and maintain databases in SQL for real-world applications.
Explicate system implementation issues such as data views, data independence, indexing, security and transaction management.
Design and implement physical database based on logical database representation.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Assignment 1: Database Project - Description and EER model
Assignment 3: Database Project - Physical Database Design
Practical Test - Lab test on SQL
Assignment 2: Database Project - Logical Database Design

title: Storytelling with Data
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: In today's data-driven environments, effectively communicating the outcomes of data analysis is crucial for ensuring that decision- makers can understand and act upon the insights presented. This course explores the art and science of data storytelling, integrating it with fundamental principles of data visualisation. Students will learn how to transform complex data into compelling and actionable narratives fulfilling the essential role of a data translator across various applied settings.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate past and current methods used to effectively communicate data insights
Assess the ethical implications of visual and narrative data presentation.
Critically analyse the challenges data scientists and analysts encounter when using data to justify decisions in organisational settings.
Develop interactive visualisation strategies to enhance audience engagement and understanding.
Design and implement a visual story to effectively convey complex data insights to a non-technical audience.

title: Operating Systems
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: Students are introduced to modern operating systems, the most prominent system software, focusing on their purposes, principles and functionalities. The course will explore different components of operating systems and the services offered by them to increase the productivity, efficiency and convenience of users. Topics include processes and threads, process synchronisation, starvation and deadlocks, resource scheduling, physical and virtual memory organisation and their management, file systems, disk management and scheduling, and security issues. Real operating systems are used for case study where appropriate.
learning_outcomes: Explain and evaluate the structure, functions, and components of modern operating systems.
Gain familiarity with some popular operating systems and recognise their functional features.
Apply synchronisation techniques for solving concurrency problems in a multi-process or multi-threaded environment.
Interpret the central issues and methods/algorithms employed in operating systems design.
Analyse and evaluate various strategies used by an operating system for managing system resources and utilising them efficiently.

title: Data Engineering and Mining
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course introduces the processes involved in preparing and analysing data to discover patterns and generate insights for prediction, classification, and data-driven decision making. It covers key concepts in data engineering and data mining, including data acquisition, preprocessing, data quality management, feature engineering, and the preparation of AI-ready datasets for analytics workflows. Students are exposed to established techniques in predictive analytics, machine learning, and pattern discovery, along with methods for model evaluation and interpretation, motivated by practical data analytics problems in business and real-world data science applications.
learning_outcomes: Communicate and collaborate to develop, interpret, and present data analytics solutions while considering responsible and ethical use of data and AI.
Apply well-established data mining and predictive analytics methods to analyse data, develop models, and extract useful patterns for data-driven decision making.
Design and evaluate integrated data engineering and data mining solutions for modern AI-enabled analytics workflows, including AI-ready data pipelines and predictive analytics systems.
Evaluate the processes and techniques used in data engineering and data mining within modern data analytics workflows, including AI-ready data pipelines and data quality considerations.
Prepare, integrate, and transform data for analytics using appropriate data engineering methods, including data ingestion, feature engineering, and data quality management.

title: Advanced Database
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Information and Physical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with theoretical knowledge and practical skills in modern database systems and data-intensive applications. It covers conceptual and logical database design, SQL and its procedural extensions, storage structures, indexing and query optimisation, transaction and concurrency management, and Object Relational Mapping. Contemporary topics such as OLAP, data warehousing, datamarts, business intelligence, data mining, and big data and distributed databases are also discussed.
learning_outcomes: Design, implement, and manage relational databases using EER modelling, normalisation, advanced SQL, and object–relational mapping.
Apply storage, indexing, query processing, and optimisation techniques to improve the performance of database systems.
Analyse architecture and applications of big data, parallel, and distributed databases in modern information systems.
Apply concepts of data warehousing, datamarts, and OLAP for analytical data processing and decision support.
Apply advanced business intelligence and data mining techniques to derive insights from structured data.
Work effectively in teams and communicate professionally when working on database development.
Apply transaction, concurrency, and crash-recovery management techniques to ensure data integrity and consistency.

title: Computer Graphics
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: Studies issues related to the displaying of objects, which may include: graphics hardware, windows programming, 2D drawing primitives, 2D & 3D geometrical transformation, projections, geometric models, 3D viewing, visible-surface determination, illumination and shading, ray tracing, and computer animation.
learning_outcomes: Work within a group to complete a graphics project
Employ selected software to achieve interactive computer graphics
Implement graphics effects
Appreciate mathematical fundamentals of computer graphics techniques
Understand and appreciate computer graphics concepts

title: Machine Intelligence
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Information and Physical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course offers a postgraduate-level introduction to Machine Intelligence, emphasising clear conceptual understanding and the practical skills required to design and implement intelligent systems. Rather than relying on advanced mathematical prerequisites, the course builds intuition for how machine intelligence methods work, why they succeed, and in which contexts they are most effective. Students will explore a range of foundational and advanced approaches, including artificial neural networks and deep learning, support vector machines, search and prediction methods, autonomous robotic systems, evolutionary algorithms, automated reasoning, logic-based AI, and selected topics in modern machine learning. Throughout the course, these techniques are presented in a grounded and accessible manner, enabling students to implement solutions and critically evaluate AI methods in real-world scenarios. Using case studies across areas such as computer vision, language processing, robotics, and strategic decision-making, students will analyse the strengths, limitations, and ethical implications of contemporary machine intelligence systems. By the end of the course, students will be able to design, implement, and assess a variety of AI techniques, and articulate how conceptual principles translate into computational architectures and intelligent behaviour.
learning_outcomes: Produce detailed professional reports and presentations suitable to support specialised research or business decision-making.
Design innovative solutions to complex challenges applying advanced concepts and incorporating recent developments in AI and machine learning.
Implement relevant code or apply standard libraries for Machine Learning and AI to selected tasks.
