Explain central concepts of Machine Learning and AI using a professional communication format.
Critically reflect on ethics, opportunities and risks of current and future developments of Machine Learning and AI.
Independently analyse a given task or data and select suitable Machine Learning and AI methods for processing.

title: Data Security
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Information and Physical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course deals with topics in cryptography and data security. Students learn fundamental technical tools for cryptography and data security, as well as how to combine the tools to support various security requirements in computerised data processing, data storing and communication.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and evaluate modern cryptographic systems
Break classical ciphers
Design a system that will provide encryption, decryption, signature and forward security
Assess security and privacy in data publishing, social networks, electric voting and digital cash
Apply number and information theories to modern cryptography

title: Cyber Security Governance, Risk, and Compliance
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: Developing and maintaining a sound cybersecurity strategy is important in our digital-first world. Organisations need to adopt strong governance measures to help develop strategies for effectively managing risk and meeting their compliance obligations. Students will learn about the different risk management techniques used in cybersecurity and adopt methods for quantifying and making threat-informed decisions. Students will also learn about the regulatory environment and compliance frameworks that organisations adopt to improve their overall cybersecurity posture. These concepts are then reinforced with practical examples from industry and government to help demonstrate their importance across different industry verticals.
learning_outcomes: Analyse, evaluate, and control for cybersecurity risks in an organisation.
Design and quality test cybersecurity program metrics and reporting for effective cybersecurity governance.
Critically assess and report on an organisations maturity against industry and regulatory standards.
Review and advise on the legal and privacy aspects of cyber security.
Report on the differences for governance, risk, and compliance across finance, government, and critical infrastructure verticals.

title: Security Attacks: Analysis and Mitigation Strategies
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Information and Physical Sciences
syllabus_overview: The course covers leading techniques currently used by attackers to exploit systems and networks. Students are introduced to various attack strategies including injection, rootkits and denial of service attacks as well as underpinning security defence techniques such as signature based analysis, anomaly-based analysis and traceback techniques for detection of attacks. Students are required to critically analyse the characteristics of various security tools such as firewalls, host/network-based security tools, and signature/anomaly-based security tools. Students who complete this course gain a practical knowledge of security attack detection and analysis, which is highly beneficial for carrying out security incident analysis in organisations.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate security technologies used to counteract security attacks in networked infrastructures.
Analyse the methods employed by attackers to exploit vulnerabilities in networked systems.
Design and develop advanced security mechanisms to counteract attacks in networked systems.
Demonstration and communication skills of security risks and technologies.
Identify and analyse security risks in heterogeneous network infrastructures.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Assignment 1: Risk Analysis and Attack Methods Presentation

title: Introduction to Criminology
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the study of crime and deviance through an exploration of criminological theories, both historically and from contemporary perspectives. Topics may include: strain theory, labelling theory, Marxist theories, feminist theories, left realism, new right theory, and critical criminology. Key criminological concepts will be used to examine and understand relationships between the social construction of crime, transgression, and deviance. Discussion will include consideration of how crime affects marginalised populations, those suffering social inequality, as well as sub-groups such as women.
learning_outcomes: Outline key criminological theories.
Analyse public representations of crime.
Apply criminological theories to real-world case scenarios.
Demonstrate an understanding of a range of criminological perspectives, concepts, and research approaches.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Multiple choice quiz in two parts.

title: Computing Project
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: The Computing Project course offers students the opportunity to apply and deepen their understanding of concepts, skills, and techniques learned throughout their program, encompassing areas of computer science, IT, data science, and/or cybersecurity. Assessment includes the submission of a project final report and a piece of applied work. Projects can span a diverse range of topics such as data management, data analysis, cybersecurity strategies, theoretical computer science work, simulations, software development, and other computing solutions. The range of projects can vary from year to year, with a selection of topics, including those in data science and cybersecurity, provided annually. The emphasis is on facilitating student learning in technical and project management skills across these multifaceted domains of computing.
learning_outcomes: Research, critically analyse, and evaluate technical information in computing and information technology topics.
Plan, justify, and reflect on time and resource management strategies to produce realistic and effective project outcomes.
Apply, adapt, and integrate technical knowledge to address complex computing and information technology problems.
Formulate, structure, and communicate technical information to scientists, engineers, and other professionals in a clear and professional manner.
Demonstrate effective and collaborative team skills with peers and/or industry partners to achieve shared objectives in professional contexts.

title: Media Criminology
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Media criminology is a developing sub-discipline of criminology, as the public's interest in consuming true crime increases in every format. This subject examines representations of crime in the media, including news, journalism, online discussions, film, TV, and podcasts. Using relevant criminological and sociological theories, it relates media representation to wider understandings of crime and deviance. Key areas covered include representations of class, gender and race in relation to crime, urban, suburban and rural distinctions; institutional relations between advocates, journalists and key figures in the justice system; the role of moral panics; and the connections between youth cultures, labelling and social problems.
learning_outcomes: Recognise the influence of ‘framing’ in relation to representations of crime in the media.
Analyse deviance and its function in constructing cultures of crime.
Understand the relationship between crime, class, and social disadvantage.
Identify different types of media influence, as applied to understanding crime and criminality.
Critique practices of social control and the use of power through media outlets.

title: Criminal Justice in Practice
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: The course applies criminological theory to real-world scenarios and will enable students to develop a vocational understanding of the criminal justice system (CJS) through direct exposure to practitioners working within the CJS. The class will analyse issues of corruption in policing, human rights in prisons, and the use of risk assessments in the CJS. The provision of guest lectures with industry partners will greatly assist those students who wish to undertake the final course in this sequence, CRIM3002: Criminal Justice Placement. In CRIM3002, students will be exposed to appropriate organisations involved in criminal justice research, education, or community engagement, through an 140 hour work placement. Divided into various components of working with offenders and working with victims, as well as the importance of community participation, CRIM2001 will build on the foundation provided in CRIM1010: Introduction to Criminology and CRIM1020: Victimology through the provision of case examples and workshops to illustrate how criminological theory is applied in practice.
learning_outcomes: Apply criminal justice skills relevant to working with offenders and victims in the CJS
Identify core elements that should be included in an offender's case report
Demonstrate professional knowledge gained through experiential learning by undertaking criminal justice tasks
Critique issues facing criminal justice practitioners when working with offenders and victims of crime
Prepare a case report to a professional standard

title: Victimology
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: A grounding in criminology requires the understanding of the interplay of two core components: the offender and the victim. Victimology, as the study of all aspects of victims and victimisation, has therefore developed as a sub-discipline of criminology, as the importance of the victim profile has been increasingly recognised both within academia and the criminal justice system more broadly. This course will help students cultivate a theoretical and practical understanding of the role of the victim in a variety of criminological contexts, with a focus on the human rights of victims, disparities in justice system responses, social justice, and social inequality
learning_outcomes: Critique the victim's role in the criminal justice system, looking at various aspects of primary, secondary, and tertiary victimisation;
Outline key criminological theories that help to explain victimisation;
Contrast the different victim typologies within criminal contexts;
Apply theoretical notions of victimology in real-world case scenarios.

title: Criminal Justice Systems
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Curious about how the justice system operates and its impact on society? This course offers essential insights into the criminal justice system, equipping you with the critical knowledge needed for a career in criminology’s allied professions. You will develop an understanding of the organisation and structure of federal, state and local enforcement agencies; organisation and function of the courts; interplay of probation, parole, restorative justice and victim services; and overview of penology and prison administration. You are also encouraged to critically reflect on the meaning and implication of the words “criminal”, “justice”, and “system”, while developing your understanding of the agencies and actors within the criminal justice system, as well as the historical, and contemporary social and political contexts that shape the criminal justice system. Students begin to develop a critical understanding of the concepts of “crime”, “justice”, and “system”.
learning_outcomes: Compare historic and contemporary approaches to crime, justice, and the role of institutions.
Describe how the key organisations in the criminal justice system interact with each other.
Explain the various objectives of the justice system and its constituent parts.
Identify the key organisations that make up the criminal justice system.
Analyse the types of conduct considered criminal and non-criminal, and how justice system responses reflect differing power dynamics

title: Media Criminology
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Media criminology is a developing sub-discipline of criminology, as the public's interest in true crime increases in every format. This course examines representations of crime in the media, including news, investigative journalism, online discussions, film, TV, and podcasts, and their relationship to social justice. Using relevant criminological and sociological theories, it relates media representation to wider understandings of crime, deviance, and community engagement. Key areas covered include representations of class, gender and race in relation to crime, urban, suburban and rural distinctions; institutional relations between advocates, journalists and key figures in the justice system; the impact of media amplification; and the connections between youth cultures, labelling and social inclusion.
learning_outcomes: Understand the relationship between crime, class, and social disadvantage.
Critique practices of social control and the use of power through media outlets.
Analyse deviance and its function in constructing cultures of crime.
Identify different types of media influence, as applied to understanding crime and criminality.
Recognise the influence of 'framing' in relation to representations of crime in the media.

title: Criminal Psychology
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Criminal psychology analyses the thoughts and action of criminals, including those engaging in anti-social behaviours. This course will take students through a step-by-step analysis of various crime types, looking at the psychological, biological, and environmental influences that lead to criminal and anti-social behaviour in regional, national and international contexts. Topics covered in this course include criminal profiling in violent crimes, predicting who will be the victim of personal violence, and strategies for threat and violence intervention. The course has been developed to appeal to students studying a range of social science disciplines, including criminology, psychology, law, and social work, as it will augment and build upon content within those discipline areas. The material covered will be trans-disciplinary in nature, and particularly relevant for students wishing to work within, or with an interest in, the criminal justice system.
learning_outcomes: Compare the key causes of criminal victimisation
Apply the core criminal psychological elements in a criminal profiling case study
Interpret the psychological, biological, and environmental factors that lead to criminal and anti-social behaviour
Evaluate violence intervention strategies
Explain the fundamental principles involved in understanding threat

title: Restorative Justice
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Restorative justice and practices provide an alternative approach to conflict resolution where relationships are placed at the centre. This course will introduce key concepts of restorative justice, with an emphasis on how it applies within the criminal justice system. We will examine conflict resolution that actively involves the victims, offenders, and community members in joint decision-making processes, building relationships rather than traditional legal and court-based mechanisms. We will explore how restorative practices can help build stronger communities, and consider the wider applicability in child welfare, youth justice, education, health, and business settings. Strengths and limitations will be critically examined, to better understand where restorative justice options may be applicable or when they might not be possible to implement.
learning_outcomes: Identify what key aspects must be present for a process to be restorative
Apply a restorative justice framework to scenarios in the criminal justice system
Compare restorative justice to other approaches to justice.
Evaluate issues arising from the broad application of restorative justice and practice.
Analyse the strengths and weaknesses of restorative practice in the criminal justice system .

title: Criminology in the Legal Context
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students (or graduates) without a legal background to the key concepts and principles that underpin criminal laws in NSW. The course covers essential knowledge of state law for non-lawyers working in the criminal justice system. It provides an important legal foundation for other courses offered in the Criminology and Human Services majors, and Social Work, Psychological Science, and Communication Programs, through theoretical examination of the elements of major substantive criminal offences and defences, within the wider historical, social, and political context. Students will examine the way criminal responsibility: attaches to certain behaviours, is processed via the agencies of the State, and, finally, the disposition of offences by way of sentencing, bail, and parole. We examine these issues by highlighting certain criminal laws in NSW and Australia that demonstrate challenges in how we criminalise behaviours and conduct and how we process people through the criminal justice system. Utilising case studies of specific criminal offences, students develop an understanding of the political and social forces that influence criminal law, procedure, and sentencing
learning_outcomes: Explain the sources of Criminal Law in NSW
Define the nature of criminal law, and describe perspectives on the meaning of crime
Explain how the court system functions, and examine arguments around the application of bail, sentencing, and parole
Identify 'conduct' and 'mental' elements of crime

title: Criminal Justice Placement
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Through this course criminal justice students will engage directly with organisations that require criminological input into their policy, evaluation, and professional practices. Under supervision, students will complete a 140 hour work placement with appropriate organisations involved in criminal justice research, education, or community service. This direct experience will expose students to the discourses and practices of researchers and managers, in order to consider the many complex factors that influence criminological research and policy. The importance of understanding cultural diversity of offenders and victims in the criminal justice system (CJS) will also be highlighted.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate outcomes for offenders and victims in a vocational setting, demonstrating expertise.
Apply advanced criminal justice skills relevant to working with a range of criminal justice stakeholders in a vocational setting.
Show advanced professional knowledge through the undertaking of case-based tasks related to working with offenders and victims of crime in a vocational setting.
Employ professional knowledge gained within your own professional practice.
Critique issues facing criminal justice professionals in the workplace.
Construct a report relating to working with offenders or victims of crime.

title: Cybercrime: Crime and Digital Landscapes
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Threats posed by cybercriminals to individuals, businesses, and nation states are growing in volume and sophistication. Preventing, disrupting, and prosecuting cybercrime is a priority focus for police, and is a national and global research priority. This course introduces students to the fundamentals of cyber-offences, notably fraud scams for financial gain, which range from cyber fraud and identity theft, to malware and ransomware attacks. Knowledge of these offences, how to successfully investigate and prosecute them, and their impact on victim-survivors will be valuable for anyone wanting to work in, or already working in the criminal justice system, as well as investigators in private practice, and NGOs that respond to related issues. A theory-based and applied understanding of cybercrime will emphasise the impacts of cybercrime as a driver of social inequality, particularly for Indigenous communities, and the integral role that community engagement plays in comprehensive responses to harms generated through digital technologies.
learning_outcomes: Analyse police and criminal justice responses to cybercrime and their effectiveness for victim-survivors
Use criminological theory to analyse cybercrimes
Communicate knowledge of criminal justice issues and theory via a range of modes for varied audiences
Define different types of cybercrime
Explain the prevalence of and trends in cybercrime

title: Criminal Justice Placement
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Through this course criminal justice students will engage directly with organisations that require criminological input into their policy, evaluation, and professional practices. Under supervision, students will locate and undertake an 80-hour work placement with appropriate organisations involved in criminal justice research, education, or community service. This direct experience will expose students to the discourses and practices of researchers and managers, in order to consider the many complex factors that influence criminological research and policy. The importance of understanding cultural diversity of offenders and victims in the criminal justice system (CJS) will also be highlighted.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate outcomes for offenders and victims in a vocational setting, demonstrating expertise
Critique issues facing criminal justice professionals in the workplace
Show advanced professional knowledge through the undertaking of case-based tasks related to working with offenders and victims of crime in a vocational setting
Apply advanced criminal justice skills relevant to working with a range of criminal justice stakeholders in a vocational setting
Employ professional knowledge gained within your own professional practice
Construct a report relating to working with offenders or victims of crime

title: Crime, Power and the State
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course applies criminological theories to analyses of contemporary crime and deviance and their relationship with social justice and human rights. It equips students with an understanding of the intersection of knowledge, discourse, power, forms of state governance, and community participation. Topics may include risk society, governmentality, class and gender, and how aspects of globalisation and science have transformed the nation-state’s engagement with crime, deviance and security. The course provides the opportunity for students to integrate and consolidate knowledge and skills learned throughout the criminology and combined degrees and the criminology major. This enables students to articulate a clear analysis of crime, criminality, and victimisation as influenced through institutional power, and subsequent impacts on social inclusion.
learning_outcomes: Explain the connection between state power and definitions of crime and deviance.
Contrast primary and secondary source material in the study of crime and criminality.
Understand the different approaches to the study of power and crime.
Evaluate the impact of crime on people of varying gender, race, class, and social economic status.
Articulate a clear analysis of crime, criminality, and victimisation within society as influenced by institutional power.
Identify bias within source material.

title: Forensic Evidence
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course will illustrate how various evidence types can be utilised in a legal context, to provide students with a general understanding of the breadth and application of forensic evidence. This course will explore the journey of physical evidence (including electronic evidence) from its collection at a crime scene to its explanation in the courtroom. Various sub-fields will be discussed, including crime scene processing, forensic toxicology and chemistry, forensic biology, evidence recovered from cybercrime investigations, and the relevance of novel and evolving evidence techniques. The weekly lectures will address the various sub-fields of forensic science, with the tutorials using a mock homicide as a teaching tool to contextualize the lecture information and the readings. This course will provide students with a holistic view of the importance of forensic evidence to the criminal justice system.
learning_outcomes: Recognise the strengths and weaknesses of using novel forensic techniques in forensic investigations.
Effectively communicate the stages at which problems can occur with evidence collection, evaluation, and retention.
Describe the utilisation of different types of forensic evidence.
Critique the role of the expert witness.
Critically evaluate the weight and admissibility of different types of forensic evidence.

title: Crime, Power and the State
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course applies criminological theories to analyses of contemporary crime and deviance. It equips students with an understanding of the intersection of knowledge, discourse, power, and forms of state governance. Topics may include risk society, governmentality, class and gender theories, and how aspects of globalisation and science have transformed the nation-state’s engagement with crime, deviance and security. The course provides the opportunity for students to integrate and consolidate knowledge and skills learned throughout the criminology and combined degrees and the criminology major. This enables students to articulate a clear analysis of crime, criminality, and victimisation as influenced through institutional power.
learning_outcomes: Produce written knowledge for public dissemination on criminal justice issues.
Evaluate the impact of crime on people of varying gender, race, class, and social economic status.
Apply criminological theory to analyses of power and crime.
Articulate a clear analysis of crime, criminality, and victimisation as influenced by institutional power.
Demonstrate critical thinking skills through explaining the connection between state power and definitions of crime and deviance.

title: Miscarriages of Justice
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Curious about why our criminal justice system sometimes gets it wrong? Are you passionate about ensuring our justice system is, in fact, just? Miscarriages of Justice is the course for you. This course examines the factors that lead to miscarriages of justice, through a review of cases that reflect failures of the criminal justice system. These failures range from wrongful convictions to cold cases where families are not provided resolution or answers following a suspected crime, as well as international crimes and the challenges of transparency, accountability, and impunity. Students will analyse systemic issues in domestic and international justice systems that contribute to miscarriages of justice, including bias, prejudice, and professional cultures. Examples will be set within a legal framework, through an evaluation of post-conviction review processes, as well as the work of innocence projects, and the functions of Criminal Case Review Commissions.
learning_outcomes: Explain the causes of miscarriages of justice.
Investigate key debates related to the reduction of miscarriages of justice and clearly communicate findings.
Identify various types of miscarriages of justice.
Evaluate the suitability of external bodies in providing transparency and accountability, where miscarriages of justice have occurred.

title: Cybercrime: Tools, Tactics and Traps
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: There is a growing emphasis on cybersecurity as a crime prevention tool locally and internationally by police, government, corporations, and individuals. This course provides students with an in-depth, critical understanding of cybersecurity as a harm-prevention strategy. Students will gain an understanding of common cybersecurity prevention measures through case studies used to illustrate practical, legal, and regulatory tactics available to a range of stakeholders, including communities more susceptible to digital exclusion such as Indigenous populations. The course equips students with the knowledge to be able to identify cybersecurity measures, evaluate their effectiveness from a range of stakeholder perspectives, and foregrounds responses to threats arising from emergent technologies, such as the metaverse and artificial intelligence. Students will apply their critical thinking skills to live issues in cybersecurity, and develop online policing and security strategies to address cybersecurity problems. This will include analysis of community participation to address social justice issues facilitated through digital technologies.
learning_outcomes: Apply criminological theory to explain a cybersecurity policy issue
Analyse police and criminal justice responses to cybersecurity and their effectiveness for victim-survivors
Analyse the stakeholder relationships necessary to effectively prevent crime through approaches to cyber security
Present empirically based research as the basis of an effective presentation to a criminal justice audience
Define various approaches to cyber security

title: Honours I: Contextualising Criminological Research
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Through this course, students will gain an understanding of how research problems are conceived and acted upon in criminology. The course contextualises criminological research and theory within key debates on criminal justice. Students will consider the philosophical underpinnings of criminological research, as well as ethical and political components of research in response to vital questions, such as: 'what is criminological knowledge?', 'how do we know what we know about crime?’, and what are the causes and range of approaches to responding to criminal justice issues? The core concept of the course is 'epistemology’ – the kind of knowledge that researchers are producing. A central learning objective is for students to gain insight into how epistemology – the theory of knowledge, especially with regard to its methods, validity and scope – features in their own research.
learning_outcomes: Present and defend an epistemological viewpoint in relation to a criminal justice research project.
Identify the criteria used to evaluate the quality of research conducted in criminology.
Explain in writing how knowledge production in criminology is influenced by, and influences, philosophical and political perspectives and practices on criminal justice issues.
Select and synthesise key intellectual issues and debates in criminology to justify the scope and method for a research study.
Critically evaluate the quality of research conducted in criminology.

title: Honours II: Criminological Research Methods
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course is the second of two honours level courses that build knowledge and understanding about the philosophy and history of criminological research. This course focuses specifically on the practice of research and explores the idea of research as design. The course enhances digital research skills and capacities in reading and reviewing literature, critical reasoning and argument. The course includes – discussions of pure and applied research methods in criminology, ethics, research design, and on-line bibliographic searches and writing techniques.
learning_outcomes: Use advanced features of reference, data analysis and data management software to systematically manage and organise quantitative and qualitative information.
Critically evaluate the relevance of research methods when presenting a position.
Systematically and methodically analyse own and others' assumptions through analysis of own and others' written work.
Use professional academic writing conventions for the purposes of communicating complex ideas and procedures.
Demonstrate the capacity to identify high quality research at an honours level.

title: Honours III: Thesis I
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: CRIM4030 part one of the thesis component of the Bachelor of Criminology (Hons), the second being CRIM4040. The honours thesis gives students the opportunity to put the skills they have acquired over the course of their undergraduate studies and the honours coursework into advanced practice in the form of a substantial project.
learning_outcomes: Maintain a professional relationship with a mentor and develop interpersonal and teamwork skills.
Communicate research design that illustrates the alignment of research problems and research methods with an explanatory theoretical and epistemic framework.
Apply independent data collection skills and procedures necessary to generate defendable research findings.
Show progress in structuring and formulating arguments at macro and micro levels through developing the equivalent of a 15,000-20,000 words thesis (in conjunction with CRIM4040).
Apply disciplinary specific conventions to communicate research methods and procedures to an academic audience.

title: Honours IV: Thesis II
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: CRIM4040 is part two of the thesis component of the Bachelor of Criminology (Hons), the first being CRIM4030. The honours thesis gives students the opportunity to put the skills they have acquired over the course of their undergraduate studies and the honours coursework into advanced practice in the form of a substantial project.
learning_outcomes: Conclusive use of independent data collection skills and procedures to generate defendable research findings.
Demonstrated capacity to argue at macro and micro levels to the equivalent of a 15,000-20,000 word thesis (in conjunction with CRIM4030).
Apply disciplinary specific conventions to communicate research methods and procedures to an academic audience.
Effective articulation of a research design that illustrates the alignment of research problems and research methods with an explanatory theoretical and epistemic framework.
Demonstrated interpersonal and teamwork skills through maintaining a professional relationship with a mentor.

title: Criminology in Context: Miscarriages of Justice
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course examines the factors that lead to miscarriages of justice, through a review of cases that reflect failures of the criminal justice system. These failures range from wrongful convictions to cold cases where families are not provided resolution or answers following a suspected crime, as well as international crimes and the challenges of transparency, accountability, and impunity. Students will analyse systemic issues in domestic and international justice systems that contribute to miscarriages of justice, including bias, prejudice, professional cultures. Examples will be set within a legal framework, through an evaluation of post-conviction review processes, as well as the work of innocence projects, and the functions of Criminal Case Review Commissions.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse the causative factors of miscarriages of justice
Investigate and effectively communicate the differentiation of key debates in the reduction of miscarriages of justice
Evaluate and critique the suitability of external bodies (such as innocence initiatives and Criminal Case Review Commissions) to provide transparency and accountability
Identify and explain types of miscarriage of justice

title: Cybercrime: Tools, Tactics and Traps
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: There is a growing emphasis on cybersecurity as a crime prevention tool locally and internationally by police, government, corporations, and individuals. This course advances students’ critical analysis of cybersecurity as a harm-prevention strategy. Students will critique common cyber threats and responses through case studies used to illustrate the practical, legal, and regulatory measures available. The course equips students with the knowledge to be able to analyse cybersecurity measures, evaluate their effectiveness from a range of stakeholder perspectives, and foregrounds responses to threats arising from emergent technologies, such as the metaverse and artificial intelligence. Students will apply their critical thinking skills to live issues in cybersecurity, and develop online policing and security strategies to address cybersecurity problems, including the impacts of digital exclusion on Indigenous communities. This will include analysis of community participation to address social justice issues facilitated through digital technologies.
learning_outcomes: Assess the stakeholder relationships necessary to effectively prevent crime through approaches to cybersecurity
Critically analyse approaches to cybersecurity
Prioritise police and criminal justice responses to cybersecurity and their effectiveness for victim-survivors
Critique a cybersecurity policy issue using criminological theory
Apply rhetorical techniques to persuade a criminal justice audience of the importance of funding research into a topical cybersecurity issue

title: Cybercrime: Crime and Digital Landscapes
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Threats posed by cybercriminals to individuals, businesses, and nation states are growing in volume and sophistication. Preventing, disrupting, and prosecuting cybercrime is a priority focus for police, and is a national and global research priority. This course introduces students to the fundamentals of cyber-offences, notably fraud scams for financial gain, which range from cyber fraud and identity theft, to malware and ransomware attacks. Knowledge of these offences, how to successfully investigate and prosecute them, and their impact on victim-survivors will be valuable for anyone wanting to work in, or already working in the criminal justice system, as well as investigators in private practice, and NGOs that respond to related issues. A theory-based and applied understanding of cybercrime will emphasise the impacts of cybercrime as a driver of social inequality, particularly for Indigenous communities, and the integral role that community engagement plays in comprehensive responses to harms generated through digital technologies.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse types of cybercrime
Explain trends in cybercrime
Reframe knowledge of criminal justice issues and theory to compose varied responses for a range of audiences
Critique a cybercrime issue using criminological theory
Appraise criminal justice responses to cybercrime and their effectiveness for victim-survivors

title: Visual Culture
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Visual Culture introduces students to foundational principles of design by integrating theory with hands-on practice. Students will explore key theoretical concepts including design history, social contexts of design and semiotics, examining how these ideas shape—and are shaped by—technological progress. Students will engage with practical projects from analogue techniques to digital design that encourage critical and creative thinking, analysing how graphic design and artistic practices extend across social, environmental and political domains. Through project work, students will gain understanding in how historical and cultural contexts impact visual communication, to highlight the evolving role of the contemporary designer – who, through a negotiation process proposes prospective solutions for commodities, products, messages, promotions and technologies, to connect with consumers, communities, businesses and governments.
learning_outcomes: Apply design principles to design artefacts
Employ technical capabilities in the use of relevant materials, technology and software
Evaluate visual sources
Interpret visual communication and image research
Create design artefacts that show an understanding of visual design history and culture

title: Typography
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Typography is an essential component of visual communication; it not only delivers message, but establishes tone, directs hierarchy, and shapes how the viewer engages with and experiences a text. This course introduces students to the fundamentals of typography and takes a playful approach to exploring the relationships between typographic form, language, images, and graphic elements. Through a series of experimental projects students will develop an understanding of type in relation to scale, colour, form, juxtaposition and context of usage.
learning_outcomes: Employ technical capabilities in the use of relevant materials, technology and software
Present typographic design visually and verbally;
Identify and manipulate key structural features in the design of a typeface;
Outline the role typeface design plays in establishing a tone of voice in visual communication.
Design effective typographic layouts for various forms of publication;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Multi-part design project: Design a Typographic Publication
Multi-part design project: Design a Typeface

title: Design Imaging
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Designing images is a key aspect of graphic design process and practice. This course introduces students to key image making techniques commonly used in graphic design practice. Students will experiment with image-making forms, techniques, technologies and visual strategies through research, conceptualisation, execution and presentation of visual ideas.
learning_outcomes: Employ technical capabilities in the use of relevant materials, technology and software
Integrate iterative ideation with technical competency to achieve design outcomes
Apply manipulated design elements of images to design tasks using common design principles
Use digital, analogue and hybrid image-making processes for graphic design outcomes
Explain design research findings through design practice

title: Studio: Motion and Interactive
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Motion and interactive elements are core to contemporary visual communication design. This course introduces students to the creative potential of motion and interactivity in screen-based design, bringing together narrative development with hands-on experimentation. Students learn foundational technical skills in motion, basic coding and interaction principles enabling them to create participatory experiences. Through projects that explore interactive design principles, timing and transitions, students discover how to create narratives and guide user engagement. This course emphasises creative making and technical exploration, encouraging students to design time-based interactive visual works to connect with audiences.
learning_outcomes: Create time-based media using motion as a design element
Employ technical capabilities in the use of relevant technology and software
Develop animated interactive works to provide engaging user experiences
Construct basic screen-based interactive elements
Design simple animations for online interactive environments

title: Visual Abstraction
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Visual abstraction allows the designer to focus on the elements and principles of design, including shape, line, colour, direction, rhythm, pattern and the relationships between. This course focuses on developing visual abstraction skills as an aspect of visual communication design practice. Through participation and completion of practical tasks, discussion of case studies and referenced works students will acquire skills in the conceptual development, iteration and articulation of visual abstractions. This approach seeks to shape works outside the bounds of explicit representational imagery leading to a broader capacity to visually communicate and interpret concepts, ideas and emotions. This course focuses on the development of visual materials with diverse graphic expressions and outputs.
learning_outcomes: Apply concepts of visual abstraction in the development of design imagery
Employ technical capabilities in the use of relevant materials, technology and software
Apply colour theory to visual design outcomes
Implement iterative ideation with technical competency to achieve design outcomes
Explain design abstraction principles and apply to design practice

title: Drawing Foundations
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Drawing is a foundation skill for illustration, animation and design process and practice. This course focuses on developing drawing skills to visually articulate subjects, themes and events. Through applied studio classes students will develop knowledge of and experience with drawing principles and techniques. Using both traditional and digital approaches students will develop drawing project outcomes that respond to prescribed briefs and individual creative ideas.
learning_outcomes: Apply design drawing practices and process in the development of finished drawings.
Analyse image forms and design briefs in developing drawing concepts.
Communicate ideas effectively through applied drawing practice.
Employ appropriate drawing skills to the design process.

title: Character Design
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Character design is an essential part of story development and storytelling for the fields of illustration and animation, and for broader design contexts. In this course students will learn the process of designing characters through conceptualisation and iteration. Using imaginative and observational skills students will create a narrative around their created character and produce visual outcomes to communicate character designs.
learning_outcomes: Identify character design considerations related to illustration and animation contexts.
Evaluate their own work and the work of others through peer assessment and critique.
Apply technical information and techniques related to character design.
Communicate character design ideas, concepts, process and related practices.
Create believable characters in a narrative setting.

title: Image Making
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Image making is an essential visual communication tool for graphic designers, illustrators, animators, game designers and those contributing to the visual communication industry. This course focuses on the development of 2D and 3D image making skills as an aspect of visual communication design practice. Through participation and completion of practical tasks, discussion of case studies and referenced works, students will acquire skills in the conceptual development, iteration, realisation and articulation of images. This course focuses on the development of core image-making skills including concept, composition, form, lighting, colour and texture. This approach seeks to shape the development of an image-making practice as a core function of students developing visual communication design practice.
learning_outcomes: Describe image making principles and approaches, and apply to design practice
Use analogue and digital image-making techniques and processes
Apply iterative ideation with technical competency to achieve novel design outcomes
Employ technical capabilities in the use of relevant materials, technology and software
Outline the importance of copyright and design authorship in professional visual communication design

title: Interaction Design (IxD) Fundamentals
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Interaction is a key feature of contemporary visual communication design. This course introduces students to the key principles of Interaction Design (IxD), with a focus on developing interactive design solutions. Students will learn about User-Centred Research and Methods, and process techniques applied to real-world projects. The course will explore the scope of screen-based interactive projects from ideation to prototype building.
learning_outcomes: Employ technical capabilities in the use of relevant materials, technology and software
Investigate the relationships between interactive media and user experiences
Design logical Information Architecture (IA) and navigation structures
Implement industry standard methods and processes
Apply principles of Interaction Design

title: Materials and Making
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Materials and Making introduces foundational skills needed to understand and explore the creative potential of tactile materials in image making practice. Students will work with a variety of media including textiles and paper to experiment with processes including felting, screen printing and relief printing to create illustrations or time-based media. This foundation experience embraces contemporary art practice, introducing students to the theoretical and conceptual dimensions of expanded image-making techniques.
learning_outcomes: Apply basic technical, theoretical and conceptual principles of image making practice.
Explain the historical, conceptual and contemporary contexts of material image making practices.
Use foundational expanded image-making techniques and processes to creatively respond to project briefs
Employ tools and materials in a competent and safe manner while engaged in material processes

title: Digital Photography
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Capturing photographic imagery for creative and design documentation purposes is a key aspect of graphic design process and practice. This course introduces students to the creative and technical potentials of working with DSLR cameras (available for loan) for digital photography. You will be taught how to master camera controls, work with lighting, and understand exposure to inform the creation of digital source photographs that can be applied to a wide range of design and media scenarios. This foundation experience considers historical, ethical, technical and conceptual dimensions of photography to inspire creative practice, and to facilitate current discourse on photomedia.
learning_outcomes: Describe historical, ethical and contemporary perspectives in photomedia practice
Show a working knowledge of the processes involved in producing digital photographs
Use digital cameras in a professional design context
Apply photographic compositional techniques
Employ safe and responsible work practices

title: Animation Thinking
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Animation, no matter the technology, is primarily about timing and spacing. This course introduces students to the foundational animation principals of timing, movement and space that are used in 2D animation, 3D animation and motion graphics. This will be done through an exploration of key historical animation styles and movements and practical studio work. Students will use a variety of analogue techniques to apply these principles to their work and locate them in relation to animation methods and forms.
learning_outcomes: Apply foundational animation principles to creative work.
Identify key animation genres and styles in contextualising their own work.
Create animated movement works that demonstrate the principles of animated space.
Analyse motion and create breakdowns of animated movement.
Develop different forms of animated movement using analogue techniques.

title: Design Thinking and Innovation
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The world is full of ‘wicked problems’, issues of great complexity with multiple overlapping concerns and stakeholders. The Design Thinking suite of methods and techniques assists the lay designer as well as the expert to untangle systemic and service design problems across a wide range of sectors and disciplines. Using inclusive and empathetic approaches that foster innovation, this course will produce critically, pedagogically and creatively informed research that generates real-world impact. In this course, students will explore various methods and techniques related to Design Thinking, applying these to inform their own disciplinary practices, in ways that respond to the experiences of end users, and the needs of multiple stakeholders.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on their own disciplinary practice through the lens of Design Thinking and/or Art Thinking;
Apply user centred research methods that appropriately respond to an area of practice to generate a solution to a specific real-world problem;
Collaborate effectively in group based work
Interpret established Design Thinking theories, concepts and processes, as well as analyse new directions in the field;
Communicate an understanding of various problem-solving methods and their relationship to Design Thinking strategies;

assessment_tasks.task_name: A Visual Poster Presentation to an Audience

title: Visual Process
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Visual process is the foundation that enables design outcomes from discovery through ideation, experimentation and development to finalisation of a design. This course provides a deep dive into visual process, examining models of the design process and their related stages and techniques, and their relevance to visual communication design in theory and professional practice. Students will learn about established and emergent models of design process and engage in experimentation to explore their own process, applying theory to practice in the articulation of design concepts and projects.
learning_outcomes: Employ technical capabilities in the use of relevant materials, technology and software
Describe the stages of design process related to design practice
Evaluate experiments with design process
Apply design process techniques to their own design practice
Develop a design proposal that critically engages with design theories and situates them within broader cultural, social, economic political and legal contexts

title: Studio: Global
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Professional visual communication design, illustration and animation practice involves working in teams and connecting with a local, national and global community of creative practitioners and audiences. This course seeks to link and apply key concepts of visual design practices to address and challenge environmental and social phenomena. Projects, and the articulation of process and creative decisions made in the development of outcomes underpins this course. In industry multiple practitioners work collaboratively to contribute to studio outputs, and working in teams, developing and pitching concepts, managing client relationships and communication, and delivering creative outcomes to meet client briefs and industry standards is essential. In this course students will undertake visual design projects to apply theoretical knowledge through practical skills. Emphasis will be placed on collaboration and participation in creative design team strategies.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate strategies for working across cultural differences
Develop strategies for conducting research and development for design projects
Apply key concepts of visual communication design to creative problem solving
Analyse group dynamics and collaborative processes
Employ technical capabilities in the use of relevant materials, technology and software

title: Prototyping
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Prototyping is an important aspect of design process and visual communication design practice. This course introduces students to the techniques and processes used in the creation of 3D objects, models and prototypes for a wide range of applications in the creative industries including animation, film, art and installation, graphic and product design. Students will design and make objects using production processes and techniques such as 3D printing, digital modelling and the application of digital techniques to traditional materials. The course will develop foundational skills in designing for rapid prototyping and the creative application of digital fabrication technologies to contemporary object making. The course will explore a broad range of materials, practices and equipment requiring students to utilise UON’s Makerspaces as a primary studio context for completing course work. This approach seeks to shape an inventive, innovative and adaptable 3D-making practice as a core function of students developing visual communication design process and practice.
learning_outcomes: Determine the conceptual rationale for making works using applied processes
Complete project-based research and documentation of work
Design resolved and finished 3D material outcomes
Apply 3D or 'spatial' research to production of objects
Employ technical knowledge and practical skills in 3D production

title: Design Futures
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Your design future starts now. In this course students will use speculative design and iterative design concepts to reflect upon, plan and design their career trajectory. The course will explore current industry trends and challenges that indicate future opportunities for emerging practitioners. Students will engage with industry professionals and peers to shape the emerging landscape of work in their preferred area/s of visual communication practice.
learning_outcomes: Employ technical capabilities in the use of relevant materials, technology and software
Analyse industry and workforce research data and case studies
Apply speculative and iterative design concepts to creative outputs and projects aligning with professional practice.
Interact with relevant design communities of practice
Design an industry relevant professional project

title: Illustration
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Investigate an exciting and varied range of illustration projects within a commercial context. This course explores the professional approaches and design processes associated with commercial illustration practice. It will examine a variety of commercial contexts where illustration is the key visual communication form. Students will be introduced to the conceptual and aesthetic qualities that inform how ideas and impressions are expressed through illustration.
learning_outcomes: Employ technical capabilities in the use of relevant materials, technology, and software
Analyse ideas, contexts and references sourced through visual research.
Create illustrations that visually communicate ideas and concepts.
Apply an iterative design process in developing illustration outcomes.
Interpret design briefs in developing illustrations for professional applications.

title: Scientific Illustration
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Visualising natural and realistic subjects, themes and events is a critical part of constructing visual narratives for the fields of science, education, and visual communication. This course focuses on the development of representational illustration skills, methods and approaches used in industry for visualisation within the sciences. A range of applied tasks and projects will enable the development of illustrative outcomes using traditional and digital media. The course will consider the development of sequential imagery in the visual communication of narrative and message.
learning_outcomes: Analyse image forms and design briefs in developing representational illustration concepts and finished outcomes.
Apply illustration methods and processes related to scientific and representational illustrations and visualisation.
Show the ability to apply representational illustration methods in the development of visual communication materials.
Collect field/lab resources and compile contextual research relevant to a specified topic

title: Visual Narrative
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Design is storytelling. This course applies established theories and practices of visual narrative design through tools such as drawing, storyboarding, image making, layout and prototyping to create visual stories for print, screen and/or motion outcomes. Students will engage with visual narrative theory and practice, story design research and planning, analogue and digital image-making techniques and industry standard prototype design. Students will undertake visual exercises and narrative design projects to apply theoretical knowledge to practical skills with a variety of media and techniques.
learning_outcomes: Show visual narrative concept development, planning and process through pre-visualisation, storyboarding and journal reflection
Design sequential imagery and layout for visual narratives
Evaluate the results of visual planning and design development with respect to visual narrative theory in social cultural contexts
Employ technical capabilities in the use of relevant materials, technology and software
Select appropriate illustration and/or type design styles, techniques and platforms of dissemination in context of the narrative

assessment_tasks.task_name: Visual Narrative Concept Guide and Storyboard

title: Graphic Brand Identities and Spaces
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Identity design is a core component of professional graphic design practice. This course explores visual design approaches to the development, construction and communication of brand identities. It examines how brand identity operates within historical, social, and commercial contexts, and looks at the application of brand identity design to conceptual and physical spaces, experiences, campaigns and environments. Through a combination of research and project-based learning students will develop the creative, theoretical, and technical expertise required to effectively communicate identified philosophies and strategic brand messages of organisations, events, and individuals.
learning_outcomes: Complete brand identity projects to production ready standards;
Participate in ongoing testing, reflection, critique, and refinement during the design process;
Implement self-directed visual and contextual research for branding and identity design outcomes;
Apply visual identities to spatial and environmental contexts;

title: Designing for Game Play
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Game art is an exciting area of game design. This course introduces students to conceptualising game aesthetics for designing and prototyping gameplay. Students will become capable of evaluating the structural aspects of game development, including environment, character animation and mechanics, and the relation between those and the desired aesthetics.
learning_outcomes: Employ technical capabilities in the use of relevant materials, technology, and software
Describe game structure and aesthetics
Develop level design prototypes to show autonomy in the game design process
Create selected assets to determine game aesthetics

title: User Interface (UI) Design
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: User Interface (UI) Design governs the look, feel, interactivity and responsiveness of screen and product interfaces, and determines how a user engages with and experiences the screen or product. This course develops skills and knowledge to design interactive experiences for different types of screen-based outputs across a broad range of devices and situations. Students are taught visual design and layout for screen, navigation and prototyping. Students will learn about User Interface (UI) patterns and industry best practices in implementing the correct patterns for different screen types, platforms and target audiences. User friendly design practices will be examined in the context of implementing usability heuristics, accessible and inclusive design, and user testing.
learning_outcomes: Implement correct UI patterns in interface design, specific to platform and device best practices.
Test User Interface designs through an iterative process.
Apply usability heuristics to evaluate user experiences and functionality requirements of interactive projects and their interfaces.
Design paper prototype interfaces for user testing.
Create a working digital proof-of-concept prototype for a specified user group using industry standard software.

title: Commercial Studio Photography
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The studio setting allows the photographer full control, with the option to craft light, backdrop, angle and perspective. This course introduces students to photography as an art-directed design practice, with an emphasis on the creation of strong photographic source material that can be used for a variety of outputs. Students will gain a clear working knowledge of photographic pre-visualisation, art direction, studio image construction and studio lighting. Camera skills and studio technologies will be applied to a range of creative ‘client’ briefs.
learning_outcomes: Construct creative photographic works within a set of challenges or constraints
Apply a variety of studio-based photographic processes and/or studio lighting techniques to achieve specific effects
Plan and art direct photographic images
Employ technical capabilities in the use of relevant materials, technology and software

assessment_tasks.task_name: Studio Photography Demonstration - Product / Still Life

title: Animation Process
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Animation offers significant opportunity for creative expression, storytelling, and visual communication. This course introduces students to various forms of animation practice, providing students with an introduction to animation design, techniques and story development including movement, timing, materials and design for animation and interaction.
learning_outcomes: Describe animation ideas, concepts, process, and related practices.
Employ technical capabilities in the use of relevant materials, technology, and software
Interpret technological information related to animation processes.
Analyse key animation forms and identify animation styles.
Analyse animation processes/principles and design briefs in developing creative project outcomes.

title: Motion Graphic Design
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Motion Graphic Design explores animated motion through procedural and algorithmic animation. Students learn to create dynamic, animated type, graphics and illustrations using rules and code. They will be introduced to designing and animating graphics, objects, type, and data to create motion graphics, data visualisations or animated content for online or video projects. Students learn foundational techniques for designing real-time dynamic animations with creative outcomes in a wide variety of motion graphic or illustrated areas including title design, advertising, games, and social media.
learning_outcomes: Use motion as a narrative and graphic communication tool.
Design for procedural animation outcomes.
Employ technical capabilities in the use of relevant materials, technology and software
Implement procedural and algorithmic motion in digital animation.
Apply animation principles in 2D and 3D digital animation.

title: Commercial Illustration
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Commercial Illustration offers a broad range of projects with a focus on using illustration skills in a commercial context. This course explores of various modes of representation used in the development of commercial and editorial illustration. Students will critique industry practices and processes to develop a professional approach to the application of skills and knowledge in illustration practice. Students will consolidate the core skills of observation, visual narrative, and storytelling through the execution of creative projects. Student projects may involve work integrated or research integrated learning opportunities; projects that involve external stakeholders; group/collaborative projects; speculative or more theoretically oriented projects; professionally oriented projects; projects based on competition or award briefs.
learning_outcomes: Implement an iterative design process.
Communicate ideas and concepts effectively through finished illustrations.
Incorporate collaborative visual research into commercial illustration practices.
Create and present illustrations for commercial contexts.

title: Constructed Image
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Truth, power, ethics and the manipulation of meaning are all embedded in the mediums of photography and image making. This is increasingly the case in the digital and online domains. This studio-based course builds on students’ skills in image analysis and encourages advanced, critical photographic image making. Web technologies, screen-based imagery and timeline methods for display and audience interaction will be investigated, along with dissemination and critique of the still and moving image. Digital composition, design and image construction, enriched by the student’s independent research lead to a portfolio of sophisticated and conceptually rich photographic work.
learning_outcomes: Construct photographic work with a sophisticated conceptual basis
Create screen-based images using a range of production techniques
Employ technical capabilities in the use of relevant materials, technology and software
Critique images in relation to contemporary and historical forms of persuasion and meaning
Apply appropriate research methods to underpin the production of photographic works

title: Publication Design
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Publication design is an art; combining type and image across sequential layouts with considerations of materiality and/or interactivity. This course explores contemporary and experimental approaches to the design of longform publications such as books, magazines and newspapers in both print and online contexts. The course focuses on page layout and typography as core components of a publication’s effectiveness, as well as exploring the use of tactile materials and physical processes through the university’s technical equipment and Makerspaces. The assessments take an experimental approach to the physical presence of a publication through innovative and prototype-oriented bindings, materials and construction, and explore the relationship between materials and design voice.
learning_outcomes: Constructively critique design concepts and outcomes
Apply experimental techniques with print materials, construction methods and outcomes
Construct professional level typography and page layout in a publication context
Incorporate appropriate production processes for different print applications
Design content for print to production-ready standards

title: Visual Research Practice
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Research, design and development are essential skills for visual communication design practitioners. This course requires students to undertake visual research to inform the development of practical design outcomes. Emphasis will be placed on developing knowledge and skills in visual research design and development as an aspect of professional practice. A constantly evolving and ethically aware design practice is essential in maintaining technical currency in a landscape that is undergoing continual and significant progression. Students are also provided with a foundation in creative and visual research methodologies for those who may wish to pursue careers in design research or to apply these methodologies to research questions that provide design solutions for other disciplines.
learning_outcomes: Employ technical capabilities in the use of relevant materials, technology and software
Critique practice-based and practice-led research methods used in design
Develop design research in the form of a design project proposal
Formulate design research findings to practical design outcomes
Generate a design project for professional presentation

title: Studio: Professional Portfolio
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Developing a professional design portfolio and/or showreel is the cornerstone of contemporary design education and gateway to industry practice. This course will focus on the research, development and design of a professional portfolio. Students will investigate existing creative studios and practices, plan for and create new work, and reiterate existing work to curate a professional portfolio. Emphasis will be on the documentation of design projects, including completing case studies to promote student’s knowledge and skills.
learning_outcomes: Determine a personal design practice and/or research direction in relation to industry-standard roles and terminology
Integrate visual communication theory and practice to exhibition and promotional design
Employ technical capabilities in the use of relevant materials, technology and software
Develop professional visual communication design documentation, including proposals and timelines
Design a professional portfolio and online component

title: Physical Experience (PxD) Design
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Physical Experience Design (PxD) involves moving beyond screen-based interaction to interactions with physical objects and the world. This course explores the design potential of emerging technologies in creating interactive design. Students will be introduced to designing playful interactions that extend beyond screen, to learn about and experiment with sensors, actuators, microcontrollers and the communication of those items with computers. Knowledge acquired through experimentations will focus on interaction problem solving for user design engagement.
learning_outcomes: Critique new directions in non - screen based interaction design
Design an experimental user interface
Apply experimental methodology within an iterative design approach
Develop skills in simple physical computing
Construct a prototype of a sensor-based interactive experience

title: Production Studio
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Production Studio teaches creative pathways to production. Through fast-paced project briefs, students will explore a variety of creative strategies as production pathways in illustration and animation including teamwork, creative pitching and critique as ways of arriving at dynamic creative solutions.
learning_outcomes: Organise a team production workflow.
Respond creatively to a design brief.
Employ technical capabilities in the use of relevant materials, technology and software
Implement collaborative strategies as a member of a team and use feedback processes to achieve team goals.
Analyse professional production examples and connect insights to the development of personal work.

title: Environment Design
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Understanding space, light and perspective is key to a wide range of image making. With a focus on miniatures and model making, Environment Design explores designing objects, dioramas, and scenarios for a range of physical and virtual applications. Students will learn techniques suitable for a variety of outcomes including animation, illustration, games, and motion graphics with a primary focus on designing environments, set design and landscapes. The course introduces students to fundamental concepts related to creating virtual and physical spaces through designing experimental three-dimensional environments. There is a strong focus on analysing and critiquing both historical and contemporary examples of virtual design, installation, miniatures, and light projections.
learning_outcomes: Create 3D sets, environments and landscapes.
Apply the fundamentals of environment design to a creative production concept.
Employ industry standard technical capabilities in the use of relevant materials, technology, and software.
Design physical and virtual spaces for animation, installation, film and games.
Critically analyse professional examples of virtual and physical environment design.

title: Digital Production
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Understanding digital effects workflows and techniques is key to working in illustration and animation. Digital Production explores the processes and techniques for creating optical and digital effects with all forms of digital media, using still and moving images. This course encourages experimentation and exploration of digital image making skills using a variety of compositing tools to create new and engaging visuals in film, photography, illustration, motion graphics and animation applications.
