Student projects may involve work integrated or research integrated learning opportunities; projects that involve external stakeholders; group/collaborative projects; speculative or more theoretically oriented projects; professionally oriented projects; projects based on competition or award briefs.
learning_outcomes: Analyse professional compositing and visual effects examples.
Create visual elements suitable for compositing as optical and visual effects
Design workflows and pipelines for digital production.
Construct digital images and effects that explore both experimental and conventional digital production techniques.
Employ technical capabilities in the use of relevant materials, technology, and software.

title: Major Project
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Creative projects inspire the Visual Communication industry. In this capstone course, each student will undertake a substantial creative project in their chosen Visual Communication Major. Students will execute a design project from concept to completion, including research and concept development, project planning and scheduling, design and production. Students develop their final project outcome to be included in their portfolio and/or exhibited in the Graduation Show.
learning_outcomes: Plan an original major visual communication project, including design research, scheduling and development of a design proposal
Complete a major visual communication project to industry ready standards
Apply iterative ideation with technical competency in the production of a substantial creative project
Explain design choices relating to professional practice and/or creative application of proposed design outcome
Employ industry standard technical capabilities in the use of relevant materials, technology and software

title: Transmedia Product and Campaign Design
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Design in contemporary context involves embracing transmedia design responses to creatively engage audience. This course involves applying critical thinking in design and visual communication creative process in response to the design brief. Students will explore visual communication approaches across print, motion, interactive and experimental or future media, and be encouraged to make informed media choices to enable successful transmedia design outcomes for products and/or campaigns.
learning_outcomes: Generate graphic imagery and/or prototype responses for a given brief
Evaluate a brief and provide an appropriate creative response.
Apply a variety of graphic design and imaging techniques and materials, and technologies
Creatively translate text, ideas and concepts into a visual form in transmedia practice
Design projects to creatively target specific audiences in transmedia platforms

title: Business Intelligence
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Information and Physical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Business intelligence (BI) refers to the technologies, applications and practices needed for the collection, integration, analysis, and presentation of business information. This course provides an overview of BI and demonstrates how it facilitates effective implementation of organisational strategies through better business decision making.
learning_outcomes: Describe the concepts and components of Business Intelligence (BI).
Critically evaluate use of BI for supporting decision making in an organisation.
Plan the implementation of a BI system.
Understand and design the technological architecture that underpins BI systems.
Understand and use the technologies and tools that make up BI (e.g. Data warehousing, Data reporting and use of Online analytical processing (OLAP)).

title: Business Intelligence in Practice
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Information and Physical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Business Intelligence (BI) plays a critical role in helping business professionals make better, evidence-based decisions. It transforms complex business data into meaningful insights by drawing on software tools, databases, and analytical models. This course offers a comprehensive overview of BI components, combining conceptual knowledge with practical skills. Students will engage with real-world problems and apply data-informed solutions that support decision-making in diverse business contexts.
learning_outcomes: Describe the structured process involved in developing a BI solution.
Analyse business data using contemporary tools to identify and address current decision-making problems.
Describe the core components of Business Intelligence (BI).
Evaluate the use and effectiveness of BI solutions in addressing business challenges in different organisational contexts.

title: Systems Design for the Digital Economy
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: Information and Communication Technology (ICT) has fundamentally changed how people communicate, work, and engage with organisations. In this rapidly evolving digital economy landscape, it has become vital for ICT professionals to effectively design, implement, and evaluate systems (e.g., in the form of chatbots, digital platforms, mobile apps). Against the backdrop of the development of IT solutions during the 20th century, this course identifies the fundamental driving forces and core principles for effective systems design in the digital economy. Building on these foundations, it equips ICT professionals with contemporary skills and practices to pro-actively develop approaches for designing, testing, and evaluating innovative ICT applications in different application areas (e.g., recommender systems, streaming platforms).
learning_outcomes: Identify societal and ethical concerns that arise during the design and evaluation of systems in the digital economy.
Recognize the fundamental ICT driving forces and core principles for effective systems design in the digital economy.
Apply contemporary ICT methods and frameworks to pro-actively design innovative ICT systems for the digital economy.
Evaluate the usability and usefulness of systems solutions for the digital economy.

title: Basic Econometrics and Quantitative Modelling
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Businesses are increasingly faced with today’s toughest economic and financial problems. This course is designed to foster the development of foundational skills and knowledge required to assist in business contexts. Students are equipped with statistical and econometric concepts and tools to provide a deeper understanding of the quantitative methods required to collect real-world data in the field of business and commerce and to analyse the data within an MS Excel spreadsheet environment. Emphasis is placed on problem-based learning and drawing on inferences to make effective business decisions, both highly valued attributes within the business environment.
learning_outcomes: Apply appropriate statistical and econometric techniques to analyse real-world data for predicting future trends of data series within an MS Excel spreadsheet environment.
Demonstrate the importance of statistical inference in establishing the relationship between variables using estimation and hypothesis testing frameworks;
Apply appropriate analytical techniques to summarise and present real-world data in a manner that informs business decision-making.
Use basic quantitative methods to draw inferences from real-world data and to present and interpret results;
Employ analytical techniques to coherently and logically illustrate the underlying assumptions in establishing relationships between variables;

title: Economics for Business Decisions
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Economics for Business Decisions course offers a comprehensive understanding of the economic forces that impact individuals, businesses and the global economy. Throughout this course, students will explore the economics of life, delving into the concepts of specialisation and exchange, which are as pertinent to personal life as they are to the global economy. Students will gain a deeper insight into supply and demand dynamics, how they determine the prices of goods and services, and the different market structures, uncovering the reasons behind varying levels of competitiveness. The course will also explore the role of government, market efficiency, production costs, and macroeconomic concepts such as GDP, inflation, and financial crises to understand their impact on business decision-making. The course also explores the functioning of labour markets, economic growth, and the influences of fiscal and monetary policy in shaping the economy. By the conclusion of this course, students will have a solid grasp of how economic concepts and principles inform business decisions, empowering you to make well-informed choices. Whether you aspire to launch your own business, pursue a career in the industry, or seek a deeper understanding of the economic landscape, this course equips you with the essential tools for success.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the impacts of government fiscal and monetary policies on individual and business activities.
Apply principles of supply, demand, and pricing in different market structures.
Apply economic tools and principles in written communication to analyse economic, financial and business data.
Evaluate different market structures and their effects on business strategies and decision-making.
Explain the fundamental concepts of microeconomics and macroeconomics.

title: Microeconomics for Business
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Intermediate microeconomics expands on the concepts and ideas developed in first year economics, building applicable models and tools for empirical analysis. Students are introduced to microeconomic models of the market - including the individual decision-maker, the household and the firm - to develop understanding of market forces, constraints and failures. Additionally, students analyse the impact of Market Failure, Behavioural Economics, Public Policy, Market Power, Poverty and Welfare. By the end of the course, students should have an intermediate (i.e., more advanced) understanding of economic models and how to apply them to different economic problems, from business, industry, politics, society and the environment. This course is designed for students who have successfully completed introductory economics). Importantly, ECON2001 extends microeconomic principles to analyse and model economic events at the local, national and international levels. While the mathematics requirement for this course is not advanced, basic math is essential to be able to fully grasp and apply the material. This subject is the entry point into the study of the more advanced economic specialisations such as behavioural and experimental economics, industrial organisation, labour economics, health economics, property economics and game theory.
learning_outcomes: Apply microeconomic concepts to inform business-decisions and governance in the workplace and develop an appreciation of synergies with other disciplines.
Apply microeconomic theory to explain real-world economic events and debates.
Critically assess traditional approaches to theories of consumer and producer behaviour, market structure theories and have insights into alternate perspectives.
Demonstrate a proficiency in utilising numerical and graphical techniques.

title: Intermediate Macroeconomics
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course builds on the first-year course by extending and deepening the analytical and policy framework. New analytical approaches are developed to examine the important debates about the operation of the labour market and employment determination, the role of financial markets in the changing global economy and the conduct of macroeconomic policy. Students are equipped with the tools, skills and knowledge base necessary to understand the operation of the macroeconomy and to critically evaluate competing views about the conduct of policy.
learning_outcomes: Collaborate with fellow students in the evaluation and presentation of arguments about macroeconomic theory and policy.
Discuss competing theoretical arguments about the operation of the macroeconomy.
Engage in critical thinking through the comparative assessment of competing macroeconomic models and policy frameworks.
Access and analyse macroeconomic data which are pertinent to contemporary macroeconomic debates in Australia and overseas.

title: Predictive Modelling in Business
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course builds upon the first-year course (BUSN1010) through: (i) the development and application of quantitative methods and techniques; and (ii) the introduction of key concepts, models and issues in the classical linear regression model, as well as the introduction of recent developments of time-series econometrics and their applications to economics and finance. Accordingly, the course first provides a brief review of linear models; matrix algebra; rules of differentiation; constrained optimisation; integration and differential equations; and other related topics. This is followed by the introduction of the classical linear regression model; hypothesis testing; forecasting; issues in the violations of classical linear regression model. Other topics include: dynamic econometric models; simultaneous equation models; time-series econometrics; variance modelling; vector autoregressive models; and panel data models.
learning_outcomes: Formulate and apply quantitative methods and techniques to such disciplines as accounting, economics and finance.
Use econometric software such as Python for estimation of econometric models, diagnostic testing of models, and forecasting.
Develop and apply econometric models and techniques to undertake research in economics and finance.

title: Health Economics and Finance
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Health Economics is the application of economic principles to health and health care. Students apply core concepts of supply and demand theories to health and healthcare examples and learn about the importance of information (and information asymmetry) in healthcare markets; the crucial role of insurance; hospital financing and delivery; and private/public mix in finance and provision of healthcare. In this course students are introduced to key conceptual frameworks of health economics and decision making and examine how Australian and international healthcare systems are designed and organised, including the critical components of long-term care and pharmaceutical markets.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the effects of a health policy or intervention.
Appraise health economics/policies and apply them to address specific types of market failure.
Identify the key economic trade-offs involved in different healthcare allocation decisions and analyse the implications for payers, providers and consumers.
Apply knowledge of relevant economic concepts to the healthcare industry and healthcare provision.
Apply analytical skills to interpret and synthesise data from a variety of sources and communicate information effectively individually and in groups.
Examine the economic rationale associated with trends in health system development.

title: Global Trade and Finance
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the fundamental theories of international trade and finance, emphasising contemporary global policy issues including sustainability and development. Students will examine why and how nations gain from international trade in goods, services and assets. Simple models are used to analyse the current problems in foreign trade concerning commercial policies, tariff and non-tariff barriers, economic integration, regional trade arrangements, and new trade issues such as labour standards, human rights, and environmental protection. The political economy of agricultural price support, export subsidies, and other issues are examined. This course's second interrelated part illustrates key models and issues in international finance. This includes an analysis of global capital markets, international parity relations and foreign investment. The contentious nature of international trading rules, exchange-rate regimes, monetary unions, capital movements, financial crises, labour migration, and the roles of the World Trade Organisation, the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank are explored.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the operations of global capital markets and their implications for domestic trade-oriented businesses with respect to production, investment and employment.
Use economic models and principles, including trade models, to analyse the impacts of changes in commercial policies, trade and non-tariff barriers, and taxes and subsidies.
Use international finance theories and models to explain the evolution of global capital markets and policy issues.
Analyse sector- and industry-specific implications for an economy of changes in the international trading system.
Demonstrate an understanding of the reasons behind the rapid increase in global trade and its differential implications for standards of living internationally.

title: Economics of Sports and Entertainment
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Sport and entertainment has become a multi-billion-dollar industry across the world, including the Hunter region, which is very passionate about its sports and teams. Students will gain an opportunity to apply basic economic processes to the world of professional sports. They not only analyse sport as big business, but also look at finance, market structures, public policy and globalisation. Students will combine their understanding of economics to the field of sports. Blending together economic theory and applying it to the professional sport market, students gain a range of transferable skills that can be used from government and tourism to statistical analysis of labour markets.
learning_outcomes: Use specialised cognitive skills to communicate in oral and written form
Demonstrate an advanced and integrated understanding of economic concepts relative to the area of sport
Examine the 'peculiar' characteristics of sports markets and the policy conclusions that follow
Analyse the role economic incentives play in determining the behaviour of controlling bodies, leagues, clubs, players, fans, sponsors, the media and government
Use economic analysis to understand how appropriate policies could be formulated to address economic problems in the sports industry
Provide detailed knowledge of the content of the particular topic area

title: Econometrics
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course is designed to introduce core econometric techniques that are used to analyse business, finance, and economic data. The course covers the properties of linear regression models, as well as the consequences of violating classical regression assumptions. Diagnostic testing and econometric remedies are discussed, including heteroscedasticity, autocorrelation, omitted variable bias, measurement error, and the use of instrumental variables. The course explores simple linear and multiple regression modelling and then progresses to time-series models, panel data models and limited dependent variable modelling, and the use of dummy variables and instrumental variables. Emphasis is placed on understanding the theory behind econometric modelling and critically analysing the strengths and weaknesses of econometric techniques. Additionally, students will learn about collecting real-world data and using an econometric package to analyse the data and interpret the empirical results to address business, finance and economic policy issues relevant to business decision-making.
learning_outcomes: Implement hypothesis testing and inference in linear regression models.
Employ collaborative problem-solving, information literacy and inquiry skills.
Explain the specification issues of linear regression models.
Use appropriate econometric models and techniques to analyse business, finance and economic data and interpret the results.
Develop econometric skills to critically analyse applied economic research.

title: Environmental Economics
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course introduces you to an economic and policy-oriented approach for exploring the environmental system and the role of government in using natural and environmental resources. The course is designed to provide a deeper understanding of the global perspectives on contemporary environmental and natural resource issues and appropriate economic concepts, models, and tools for analysing environmental and natural resource problems and exploring the strengths and weaknesses of alternative viewpoints to inform policy decision-making. Drawing on case studies, the course will delve into how underlying economic concepts and principles informed policy decision-making concerning environmental and natural resources. The course covers a broad range of issues pertaining to natural resource scarcity, market failure, the economics of pollution control locally, nationally, and internationally, efficient use of exhaustible and renewable resources, market-based instruments, environmental cost and benefit analysis, environmental evaluation, global environmental challenges, and the role of government in achieving sustainable economic growth and development.
learning_outcomes: Explain the economic and policy-orientated approach to externalities, benefit-cost analysis, valuation methods and ecosystem goods and services.
Critically analyse public policy debates relating to climate change, water, forests, land, transportation and ecosystem services as it pertains to sustainable development and environmental justice.
Undertake a critical analysis of theoretical and empirical literature and comparative assessment of competing theoretical and policy issues using real-world data in a team environment.
Evaluate the contemporary environmental and natural resource debates.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Group Project Report and Narrated Video Presentation

title: Intermediate Econometrics
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course builds on the basic econometric and quantitative techniques studied in the first year. It extends students' knowledge and understanding of a range of econometric methods and techniques used to analyse data sets in economics, business and finance. This course introduces the student to a thorough and critical coverage of econometric methods in a program of graduated complexity. It studies the properties of linear regression models under classical assumptions and explores the implications of potential violations of these assumptions. Diagnostics for detecting violations are discussed and econometric remedies are derived. The basic theory of estimation of time-series models, systems of linear regression equations and instrumental variables, and panel data modelling are canvassed. The course proceeds by firstly acquiring understanding of the methods involved; secondly describing the appropriate use of econometric software to provide valid, reliable results; and thirdly interpreting and commenting on the results. Assessment is made about the strengths and weaknesses of econometric techniques and methodologies in addressing specific applied economic policy problems of critical interest to economists and business-and financial researchers and professionals.
learning_outcomes: Engage in collaborative processes (formal or informal group works) to complete econometric modelling inquiry, employing statistical techniques, analysing data and communicating results.
Demonstrate an extended understanding of a range of econometric modelling techniques;
Critically analyse and evaluate the results of studies that have been undertaken by others using econometric techniques;
Demonstrate skills in 'hands-on' modelling, estimation and diagnostic testing, utilising economic and business data;

title: International Macroeconomics
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course extends intermediate macroeconomic theory and policy analysis to the advanced examination of both historical and contemporary issues in international macroeconomics. Global economic interdependence means our lives – consumption, investment, labour market outcomes, policies, technology, and culture among other things, are constantly affected by economic developments in other countries. How is Australia affected by open macroeconomic events and how are other countries affected by Australia’s open macroeconomic activities and policies? The national and international macroeconomic aspects shaping current global interdependence are emphasised in this course. The impact of both domestic and international economic institutions and policy constraints on the conduct of policy, equity, integration of indigenous knowledge and culture into sustainable development are emphasised and illustrated by drawing on international case studies. Students will learn by accessing, analysing, and synthesising relevant open macroeconomic theories, policies, models, data and other information, and will continue to build sector specific skills.
learning_outcomes: Access, analyse, evaluate and synthesise both quantitative and qualitative economic information pertinent to contemporary macroeconomic and labor markets debates internationally;
Review information on the challenges and advantages of international economic interdependence from business and national performance;
Participate in groups to analyse and communicate developments in international macroeconomic events both orally and in written form.
Demonstrate a deep analytical understanding of concepts and models for international macroeconomic operation and policy analysis;

title: Urban and Regional Economics
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course focuses on contemporary challenges of building sustainable cities and regions with competitive advantage for driving positive economic and societal impact. The economics of the built environments of cities, models of land use and growth, education, healthcare, housing, infrastructure, regulation, planning and global megatrends continue to shape the growth and development of cities and region. Students are introduced to economic models of property and land use in cities and regional areas, with a focus on NSW, especially the Lower Hunter Region and Sydney, in addition to international examples to help build skills for sustainability of future business and environment. By using case studies, students will gain an understanding of the complex economic, environmental, social, indigenous affiliations and political processes that shape land use in urban and regional cities. Immersive and interactive workshop sessions are integrated into the course to help students bring their own experiences of urban and regional development challenges, broaden perspectives, question the status quo and develop collaborative approaches to sustainable development. Urban and regional economics complements degrees in business, finance, economics, planning, geography, urban design among others in the job market and is applicable in the real estate industry, management and delivery of development projects including transport, health and defence infrastructure planning, civil and electrical engineering, urban or town planning, social infrastructure and contribute to environmental protection.
learning_outcomes: Apply economic theories to explain the dynamics of urban and regional property economics, using both Australian and international case studies.
Evaluate the role of government, policy, and planning on urban property economics through a range of appropriate methodologies.
Analyse the roles and motivations of key stakeholders in urban and regional economics, and demonstrate confidence in engaging with these stakeholders through practical examples.
Apply knowledge of private and public roles involved in urban and rural economic development to relevant local issues.

title: Introduction to Health Economics and Finance
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Health Economics is the application of economic principles to health and health care. Students apply core concepts of supply and demand theories to health and healthcare examples and learn about the importance of information (and information asymmetry) in healthcare markets; the crucial role of insurance; hospital financing and delivery; and private/public mix in finance and provision of healthcare. In this course students are introduced to key conceptual frameworks of health economics and decision making and examine how Australian and international healthcare systems are designed and organised, including the critical components of long-term care and pharmaceutical markets.
learning_outcomes: Examine the economic rationale associated with trends in health system development.
Appraise health economics/policies and apply them to address specific types of market failure.
Identify the key economic trade-offs involved in different healthcare allocation decisions and analyse the implications for payers, providers and consumers.
Apply analytical skills to interpret and synthesise data from a variety of sources and communicate information effectively individually and in groups.
Evaluate the effects of a health policy or intervention.
Apply knowledge of relevant economic concepts to the healthcare industry and healthcare provision.

title: Behavioural Economics
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course is designed to provide applications of behavioural economics in a variety of business settings. Students are exposed to the economic paradigms, decision under risk and uncertainty, time and distributional preferences, status concerns, inter-temporal choices, human rationality, heuristics and biases, and behavioural game theory.
learning_outcomes: Summarise and explain major insights generated in the field of behavioural economics including risk and uncertainty, time preferences and distributional preferences.
Identify and explain standard and behavioural economic approaches relevant to a variety of contexts.
Employ technical skills in applying methodological approaches and analytic tools used in the field of behavioural economics to interdisciplinary research problems.
Apply theoretical and empirical behavioural economic approaches to evaluate and critically analyse economic problems in a variety of contexts.

title: International Economics and Payment Infrastructure
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course will equip students with the theory and practice of payments and payment infrastructures within the context of the international monetary system. Students will be able to understand how financial market operations (including those by the central bank) are implemented in the global context. The topics will include the basic functioning of payments (in addition to Indigenous aspects to payments, such as barter), including key payment infrastructures. Students will also learn the operational mechanics of various monetary regimes, balance of payment issues, in addition to payment innovations, including Bitcoin, stablecoins and Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC).
learning_outcomes: Explain the challenges of macroeconomic policymaking in the open economy.
Identify the operations of the central bank within the context of the open economy.
Analyse and assess the potential for payment innovations to disrupt and drive change in payments and/or financial stability.

Communicate an analytical understanding of concepts and models relating to the operation of payment infrastructures and the international monetary system in both oral and written formats, individually and in groups.
Recognise the various risks and evolutions in payments and the importance of payment infrastructure.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Group Case Study and Oral Presentation

title: PE Studies 1: Motor Development and Skill Acquisition
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with an opportunity to gain knowledge, understanding and skills in movement skill acquisition to facilitate the planning, assessment, implementation and evaluation of a fundamental movement intervention program in a primary school setting. Students will gain valuable theoretical and practical experience while attending lectures and participating in tutorials as well as learn a variety of planning, assessment and teaching techniques for the implementation and evaluation of a fundamental movement skills program in a primary school setting.
learning_outcomes: Document the progress of the learners, the process of implementation and complete an evaluation of the intervention program; and

Demonstrate skills, knowledge and understanding of relevant content and pedagogy enabling the application of content in ways that are responsive to the particular characteristics of learners, curricula and teaching environments;
Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the processes of motor skill acquisition in children and adolescents;
Gain knowledge, understanding and skills to detect motor skill deficiencies and design programs to correct and evaluate the motor skills of children in a primary school setting;
Become familiar with recent research and understand the implications for motor skill acquisition in children and adolescents.
Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the principles of growth, development and motor behaviour in children and adolescents;

title: PE Studies 2: Court and Striking Games
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to a range of court and striking sports and to the application of theoretically-based teaching and coaching strategies used to facilitate effective learning in these sports. The sports to be covered are: cricket, softball, netball, basketball, volleyball and tennis. Students will be given the opportunity to apply teaching and coaching strategies to practical game situations and to develop their knowledge, skills and understanding in each sport. PDHPE curriculum links will be made and practical assessment techniques will be explored for each of the sports.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a range of movement skills relating to court and striking sports;
Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of a range of court and striking sports (including the rules and tactics used in each sport);
Make effective links between learning court and striking sports and the PDHPE syllabus; and
Demonstrate the ability to analyse and apply theoretically based coaching and teaching practices and strategies;
Demonstrate understanding of effective assessment techniques used to evaluate performance in court and striking sports.

title: K-6 Pedagogies
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course provides an introduction to effective teaching practices in K-6 contexts and an understanding of the various discourses and disciplines that inform teachers' practice in primary contexts.
learning_outcomes: Identify structures to support teaching and learning in K-6 contexts
Demonstrate effective professional oral, written and technological skills
Transform learning activities through understandings of new technologies
Identify elements of the Quality Teaching model through classroom observation
Understand the diversity of primary contexts and learners

title: Foundations of Secondary Education
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Through undertaking this course students will be expected to: Develop and apply academic skills to succeed at university Understand teaching as a profession Understand education as a field of study Understand how student and teacher wellbeing can be supported Develop an understanding of your emerging professional identity
learning_outcomes: Develop an understanding of your emerging professional identity
Understand education as a field of study
Understand teaching as a profession
Understand how student and teacher wellbeing can be supported
Develop and apply academic skills to succeed at university

title: Becoming a Teacher: Primary and Early Childhood Context
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Through undertaking this course students will be expected to: Develop and apply academic skills to succeed at university Understand teaching as a profession Understand education as a field of study Understand how student and teacher wellbeing can be supported Develop an understanding of your emerging professional identity
learning_outcomes: Understand teaching as a profession
Develop an understanding of your emerging professional identity
Understand how student and teacher wellbeing can be supported
Develop and apply academic skills to succeed at university
Understand education as a field of study

title: Lifetime Physical Activities
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course focuses on lifetime physical activity participation and will include: fitness and exercise activity instruction, athletics, recreation and outdoor activities and adapted physical education.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and critique fitness activities, exercise programs and physical activities using exercise science and fitness principles;
Apply and evaluate effective teaching and coaching principles/strategies to correct and extend performances in a variety of physical activity settings;
Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the importance of promoting a variety of physical activities to children and adolescents in a school and community setting;
Demonstrate knowledge, understanding and skill competencies relating to a range of lifetime physical activities for individuals of all abilities;
Demonstrate the importance of risk assessment and the safety and legal issues regarding school-aged participation in a variety of physical activities

title: Foundations of Child Development
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Examines development from conception through to infancy and early childhood to age twelve. Students develop an understanding of developmental concepts, principles and processes and various theoretical perspectives relating to child development, and the implications for early childhood education. Particular attention is paid to critical engagement with research and theory within the Australian socio-cultural context.
learning_outcomes: Explain how these relate to children's learning and how to support children's wellbeing and health, emotional and social learning and lives
Observe, document, implement and review in order to assess and reflect on children's learning for planning within early childhood settings
Identify contemporary theoretical perspectives and approaches to different domains of development, including language development and learning
Apply knowledge of the relationship between theory, children's learning, documentation for learning and intentional teaching

title: Foundation of Creative Arts for Early Childhood and Primary Teachers
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to foundational knowledge and skills of visual art, music, drama, media and dance. It examines ways in which these art forms can be integrated to create art that is dynamic and expressive. Students will be given the opportunity to develop an appreciation, knowledge, skills, teach and evaluate creative art frames involving music, art, drama, media and dance experiences for early childhood and primary educational contexts, 0-12 years of age.
learning_outcomes: Plan, implement and evaluate learning activities that promote creativity in children aged 0-12 years
Communicate understanding of creativity as an integral aspect of the Early Childhood Learning Framework (EYLF) and NSW creative arts syllabus K-6;
Demonstrate knowledge of different approaches to implementing creative arts within early childhood and primary education settings;

title: Junior Mathematics Curriculum Methods
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course explores the principles and practices of teaching and learning junior Mathematics. Students will consider the role and value of mathematics in contemporary society and the broader school curriculum. Students will explore lesson planning and programming for Stages 3 - 5 Mathematics and Stage 6 Standard Mathematics curriculum; and a range of strategies and resources for teaching and assessing junior Mathematics at school level.
learning_outcomes: Develop lesson plans, programs and assessment tasks for Junior Mathematics.
Use, compare and contrast a range of strategies, technologies and resources for teaching and assessing Mathematics.
Articulate the role and value of Mathematics education in contemporary society and the broader school curriculum.

title: Curriculum, Assessment and Pedagogy
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course provides an introduction to curriculum studies as a field of scholarly inquiry and professional practice. The course extends upon curriculum studies to explore how the Stage 4 and 5 curriculum manifests within the students' major specialisation. The course explores conceptual frameworks for understanding curriculum, pedagogy and assessment discourse and design. It will introduce students to lesson planning formats,and assist them to begin building a pedagogical repertoire relevant to the New South Wales and National Curriculum requirements of their major teaching specialisation.
learning_outcomes: Understand the NESA requirements and multiple discourses that inform curriculum design;
Implement an engaging micro-teaching session that demonstrates their developing understanding of appropriate teaching and assessment methodologies;
Conduct research to inform teaching practise and the development of resources in their teaching specialisation area.
Critically reflect upon own and peers micro-teaching performance with an aim to improve future teaching practise for self and provide feedback for peers .
Plan a lesson and associated resources focusing on a concept and/or skill drawn from the Stage 4 syllabus in their specialised teaching area;

title: Schooling, Society and Inequality
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course will examine the interconnections between schooling, society and inequality. It examines schooling and early childhood education as foundational social institutions that serve multiple social, cultural, and civic functions, with particular attention to how these institutions reproduce and challenge educational inequality. Drawing on sociological theories, concepts and research, the course explores how social structures, institutions, and policy shape educational experiences in unequal ways while also recognising schools as important sites of change. Through critical analysis, applied case studies, and a field study, the course develops students’ capacity to understand how teachers can reshape and challenge educational inequality for a more just society.
learning_outcomes: Examine the interconnections between schooling, society and inequality
Analyse how educational inequality is shaped by social, economic, cultural, and spatial structures using sociological theories and concepts
Describe how educators use policy, practice, and curriculum to enact transformative pedagogies that support diverse learners in varied educational contexts.
Critically reflect on the role of teachers in addressing issues of educational equity
Draw on sociological understandings to describe experiences in a community setting

assessment_tasks.task_name: Field Study Plan and Field Study Report

title: Foundations of TESOL
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course provides fundamental knowledge and skills of teaching English as a second language (ESL) in secondary schools. A wide range of theoretical concepts and practical issues will be explored in four interrelated aspects including pedagogical, technical, cultural and institutional domains. This introductory course lays a foundation for undergraduates who wish to be an ESL and/or LOTE teacher both domestically and internationally.
learning_outcomes: Produce an ESL lesson plan and develop ESL curriculum
Evaluate approaches to, and methods and techniques of, ESL and LOTE teaching
Critically analyse theories of second language acquisition and its application
Apply core knowledge of TESOL into teaching practice
Demonstrate an understanding of the nature and structure of language
Provide examples showing how culture is integrated into second language teaching

title: Knowledge and Communication Technologies
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In this course students will explore the ways in which new technologies can be used to support and extend student learning. Through project-based tasks students will develop the capacity and confidence to employ digital devices and software applications to construct and communicate new knowledge in and beyond the classroom. Attention will also be given to the social impact of technology; frameworks for thinking about the pedagogical use of new technologies; digital, visual and media literacy; and information literacy processes.
learning_outcomes: Display an understanding of critical, digital, visual, media, and information literacy.
Construct and communicate new knowledge using digital devices and software applications.
Relate relevant pedagogical frameworks and curriculum models to classroom use of new technologies.
Use technology as a tool to facilitate quality teaching and learning.
Demonstrate a capacity to work collaboratively on a technology-focused project-based learning task.
Explain the social impact of new technologies.

title: Junior HPE Curriculum Methods
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course explores the principles and practices of teaching and learning in Personal Development, Health and Physical Education (PDHPE) in secondary schools focusing on the Year 7 to 10 syllabi. Students will experience programming, assessment, evaluation and reporting for Stage 4 and 5 PDHPE and all other PDHPE related, elective courses. Students will explore legal and ethical conduct of teaching and learning and also explore ways of differentiating curriculum to meet the diverse needs of learners in the secondary school setting.
learning_outcomes: Understand the legal and ethical ramifications of the PDHPE teaching profession.
Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the Stage 4 and 5 PDHPE and elective courses syllabi;
Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of PDHPE pedagogies that cater for the diverse needs of learners and increase cultural understanding in a secondary school setting;
Demonstrate knowledge, understanding and skills of teaching and learning pedagogies that increase engagement across secondary school curriculum.
Demonstrate knowledge, understanding and skills in planning and programming strategies in Stage 4 and 5 PDHPE mandatory and/or elective studies courses;

title: Junior History Curriculum Methods
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In this course students will explore the role and value of History education; lesson planning and programming for Stage 4/5 History; course and assessment requirements; the literacy and numeracy demands of History as an area of study; strategies, technologies and resources for teaching and assessing History; processes of historical investigation and inquiry; key historical concepts; and ways of differentiating curriculum to meet the diverse needs of learners. Attention will also be given to civics and citizenship education, and strategies for teaching about Australia's social, political and cultural history.
learning_outcomes: Develop lesson plans, programs and assessment tasks for Stage 4/5 History curriculum;
Support the literacy and numeracy demands of History as an area of study;
Differentiate the curriculum to meet the diverse needs of learners in the History classroom;
Select appropriate strategies for teaching about Australian and Aboriginal social, political and cultural history.
Define processes of historical investigation and inquiry;
Discuss the role of History in civics and citizenship education; and
Use a range of strategies, technologies and resources for teaching and assessing History;
Articulate the role and value of History education in contemporary society and the broader school curriculum;
Explain key historical concepts (such as sources, evidence, explanation and interpretation);

title: Junior English Curriculum Methods
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In this course students will consider the role and value of English education in contemporary society and the broader school curriculum; explore planning and programming for Stage 4/5 English curriculum; course and assessment requirements for junior English; and ways of differentiating curriculum to meet the diverse needs of learners in the English classroom. Specific attention will also be given to Australian literature, and texts that give insights into Aboriginal and multicultural experience; as well as a range of strategies, technologies and resources for teaching and assessing reading, writing, listening, speaking, viewing and representing.
learning_outcomes: Develop lesson plans, programs and assessment tasks for Stage 4/5 English curriculum.
Support the literacy and numeracy demands of English.
Differentiate the curriculum to meet the diverse needs of learners in the English classroom.
Select appropriate Australian literature, and texts that give insights into Aboriginal and multicultural experience.
Articulate the role and value of English education in contemporary society and the broader school curriculum.
Use a range of strategies, technologies and resources for teaching and assessing reading, writing, listening, speaking, viewing and representing.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Analysis and alteration of an existing unit plan and assessment task design

title: Junior Science Curriculum Methods
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course will develop students' pedagogical understanding of a variety of teaching strategies suitable for use at the secondary school level. Students will investigate these strategies with reference to current Science syllabi. They will consider the rationale of the syllabi and use knowledge of a variety of teaching strategies introduced in this course to develop suitable lesson and unit plans that draw on their own discipline minor, and gather resources that will help them to teach that minor in Stage-appropriate ways that are consistent with quality teaching.
learning_outcomes: Develop science lesson plans and programs for their discipline minor at the Stage 4/5 level of the 7-12 curriculum;
Articulate the role and value of Science education in contemporary society and the broader school curriculum;
Support the literacy and numeracy demands of their discipline minor as an area of study; and
Use a range of strategies, technologies and resources for teaching their discipline minor.

title: PE Studies 3: Performance Activities
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Students will apply movement principles and develop skill competencies and teaching techniques across a range of core physical activities. Specifically, students will examine the areas of dance, gymnastics and aquatics.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate understanding of how to plan and deliver quality physical education lessons focusing on dance, gymnastics, aquatics and contemporary physical activities using relevant and evidence-based teaching and delivery frameworks
Demonstrate an understanding of the safety issues regarding school-aged participation in dance, gymnastics, aquatics and contemporary physical activities
Display a capacity to apply appropriate teaching/coaching strategies to dance, gymnastics, aquatics and contemporary physical activities
Demonstrate skill competences relating to a range of dance, gymnastics, aquatics and contemporary physical activities

title: PE Studies 4: Invasion Games
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Students will develop knowledge and teaching skills relating to the principles and practices of teaching a range of invasion games. Students will apply movement principles and develop both performance and teaching skill competencies across a range of core team sports that focus on invasion as the major game strategy. Specifically, students will examine the rules, tactics and appropriate pedagogical strategies that enable the design and delivery of learning experiences in Soccer, Touch, Rugby League, Rugby Union and Australian Rules.
learning_outcomes: demonstrate an understanding of the rules and tactics that apply to a range of invasion games;
demonstrate key teaching skills of particular movement/motor skills used in invasion games;
demonstrate an understanding of the key pedagogical strategies relating to the presentation of activities for invasion games in school and community settings;
demonstrate an ability to identify effective teaching practices relating to invasion games;
demonstrate an ability to perform various motor skills related to invasion games;
demonstrate an understanding of the role and value of invasion game learning experiences in the broader school curriculum.
demonstrate relevant safety issues relating to the teaching of invasion games;

title: Junior Geography and Commerce Curriculum Methods
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In this course students will explore the role and value of Stage 4 and 5 HSIE courses - Geography & Commerce; lesson planning and programming for Geography/ Commerce in Stage 4/5; course and assessment requirements for Stage 4/5 Geography/Commerce; the literacy and numeracy demands of Geography and Commerce; key concepts, tools and inquiry skills within Geography/Commerce; strategies, technologies and resources for teaching and assessing Geography and Commerce; ways of differentiating curriculum to meet the diverse needs of learners; links to civics and citizenship education; and strategies for teaching the NSW Syllabus for the new Australian Curriculum in Geography: Stage 4 -Landscapes and Landforms, Water in the World, Place and Liveability, Interconnections; Stage 5 - Sustainable Biomes, Environmental Change and Management, Changing Places and Human Wellbeing.
learning_outcomes: Explain key geographic and economic processes of inquiry, including the use of concepts, tools, and skills
Using a range of strategies, technologies, and resources, develop lesson plans, programs and assessment tasks for Stage 4/5 Geography and Commerce curricula
Articulate the role and value of Geography and Commerce education in contemporary society and the broader school curriculum, including civics and citizenship education
Support the literacy and numeracy demands of Geography and Commerce as an area of study
Differentiate the curriculum to meet the diverse needs of learners in the Geography and Commerce classroom

title: Creativity in practice: drama pedagogies for imaginative learning
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with an understanding of the way drama pedagogies transform and generate creative and imaginative learning experiences for students. This practical course with an embedded school-based teaching project at its core, investigates the ways in which drama learning processes dynamise students critical thinking, collaborative and empathic skills through role based enactments and devised performance. The course explores knowledge and skills that support innovative approaches to teaching and learning, covering concepts and strategies for creativity, performative and embodied learning, process drama and playbuilding. This elective is suitable for all pre-service teachers, primary and secondary, particularly those wanting to use drama as pedagogy to teach across KLAs and to delve into dramatic processes in more depth.
learning_outcomes: The exploration of dramatic inquiry projects and their significance for learners and school communities
A practical understanding of Drama as a pedagogy, mode of inquiry, subject and art form
A drama learning project to plan, implement and evaluate in a school context.
Knowledge of the creative processes involved in leading and transforming learning using drama pedagogies and strategies
A critical understanding of theories and concepts of creative learning and teaching in and through drama

title: Teaching, Learning and Play in Early Childhood
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Students will have the opportunity to explore, plan, teach and review play and learning experiences in early childhood sites 0 - 5 yrs, drawing upon contemporary early childhood education theories and curriculum documents.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of contemporary early childhood curriculum documents, namely the Early Years Learning Framework;
Critically reflect on their own teaching practice, based on action learning methodologies.
Create a challenging, engaging and safe learning environment for young children;
Plan and implement a range of play and learning experiences for young children, based on children's interests skills and need;
Apply contemporary early childhood education theories in their professional and ethical practice, including guiding appropriate child interactions with others and with adults;
Critically evaluate the learning experiences of young children;

title: Educational Psychology: Learners and the Learning Process
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course examines concepts and theories from developmental and educational psychology as they pertain to learning. The course provides opportunities for pre-service teachers to develop knowledge and understanding of learners and the process of learning, and their implications for educational planning and practice. This is a core course for undergraduate Education students and may also be taken electively by students in other disciplines who are interested in the psychology of learning.
learning_outcomes: Consider how social contexts influence individual behaviour
Understand typical developmental trends
Explain individual differences that affect learning
Compare and apply current theories of learning

title: Junior Drama Curriculum Methods
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In this course students will consider the role and value of Drama education; lesson planning and programming for Stage 4/5 Drama curriculum; course and assessment requirements of the NSW School Certificate for Drama; the literacy and numeracy demands of Drama as an area of study; ways of differentiating curriculum to meet the diverse needs of learners; a range of strategies, technologies and resources for teaching and assessing drama; and current issues and trends related to the teaching of Drama in schools. Students will also be introduced to drama processes relating to improvisation, play building, scripted drama, and theatre.
learning_outcomes: Engage in Drama processes relating to improvisation, play building, scripted drama, and theatre.
Use a range of strategies, technologies and resources for teaching and assessing drama.
Articulate role and value of Drama education in contemporary society and the broader school curriculum.
Differentiate curriculum to meet the diverse needs of learners in the Drama classroom.
Articulate current issues and trends related to the teaching of Drama in schools.
Support the literacy and numeracy needs of students studying Drama.
Develop lesson plans, programs and assessment tasks appropriate for Stage 4/5 Drama curriculum.

title: Junior Languages Curriculum Methods
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course explores the principles of teaching and learning languages, including English as an Additional Language/Dialect (EALD) in secondary schools. Students will consider the role and value of language education; lesson planning and programming for Stage 4/5 languages, and EALD across the curriculum; course and assessment requirements of the NSW School Certificate; the literacy and numeracy demands of languages as areas of study; strategies, technologies and resources for teaching and assessing languages; and ways of differentiating curriculum to meet the diverse needs of learners. Attention will also be given to theories of second language acquisition.
learning_outcomes: Apply theories of second language acquisition to the design and planning of coherent, theory informed language learning experiences for Stage 4/5 learners
Support the literacy and numeracy demands of languages and EAL/D as curriculum areas through effective instructional and assessment practices
Select, justify, and use a range of assessment strategies, technologies, and resources to monitor and support student learning in languages classrooms
Differentiate curriculum, pedagogy, and assessment through the informed use of strategies, technologies, and resources to address learner diversity in languages and EAL/D contexts
Design and implement pedagogically sound language lessons that integrate receptive and productive macro skills in alignment with curriculum requirements

title: Junior Technology Curriculum Methods
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course provides an introduction to curriculum, pedagogy and assessment for teaching the Stage 5 Elective Technology Syllabi including: Food, Textiles, Industrial Technology and IST. It provides students with an opportunity to understand the various discourses that inform teachers' knowledge and pedagogical practice as well as critically engaging with models of pedagogy. Students will also develop vital practical skills required in teaching Stage 4 and 5 Technology Syllabi
learning_outcomes: Apply a range of teaching strategies to a teaching situation.
Design challenging, engaging, and supportive programs for teaching the Stage 5 Elective Technology Syllabi.
Develop and complete Project Based learning activities and assessment tasks for Stage 4 and 5 Technology.
Critically evaluate various approaches to pedagogy / theories that capture the complexities of the TAS curriculum.

title: Multiliteracies
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In this course students will explore key principles and evidence-based practices that support the teaching and learning of literacy and numeracy in secondary education. They will investigate the nature and role of multiple literacies, alongside effective scaffolding and differentiation strategies for diverse learners, and apply these concepts to the specific demands of their teaching areas. Throughout the course, students engage in practical activities that provide consistent opportunities to apply and consolidate these principles within authentic classroom contexts.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of approaches to scaffolding and differentiation that respond to the languages, cultures and abilities of diverse learners, including EALD learners and Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students.
Understand and explain how multiple literacies, including print, visual, digital, media and critical literacies, shape meaning and influence learner engagement in secondary curriculum contexts.

Demonstrate knowledge of a range of evidence-based teaching strategies, including explicit instruction, to support the development of students' literacy and numeracy skills within secondary subject disciplines.
Apply knowledge of and justify effective digital design principles by producing a discipline specific, student facing ICT resource that expands curriculum learning opportunities for students.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Digital Resource Design and In-Class Participation

title: Quality Teaching and Student Learning K-6
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course is focused on students' knowledge and skills in the areas of professional knowledge and professional practice. A key focus is on gathering evidence aligned with the Australian Institute for Teaching and School Leadership (AITSL) standards to demonstrate an intermediate understanding of the profession. This course builds on classroom observations of teaching and learning undertaken by students in the first year of their teacher education program. It also helps students to recognise and understand how coursework/research forms the foundation of high quality teaching and assessment practice by connecting what is studied at university and how that plays out in classrooms and schools.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate effective communication skills to support classroom discussion; and
Apply frameworks and models for understanding and responding to a range of challenging student behaviours;
Relate child development theory, and student well-being and mental health research, to the management of learning;
Critically analyse and apply principles, policies, and practices for establishing and maintaining a productive learning environment;
Demonstrate progress towards the attainment of Graduate Teacher Standards through professional experience.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Professional Experience Report on performance in classrooms

title: Managing the Learning Environment
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course is focused on developing students' knowledge and understanding in the field of student learning, encompassing the topics of: managing the student learning environment (including classroom management); inclusive education and transformative pedagogies. These topics are explicitly connected to contemporary school settings across all key learning areas. This course provides a lead-in to the first and second secondary practicums, EDUC2196 and EDUC3196. During this course, students reflect and critically engage with the NSW Quality Teaching model as a professional learning tool, demonstrate an understanding of the principles, policies and practices for establishing and maintaining a productive learning environment; and promote equity in classrooms through inclusive education. A key focus is on gathering evidence aligned with the Australian Institute for Teaching School Leadership (AITSL) standards to demonstrate a coherent understanding of all elements of the profession, apply frameworks for understanding and interpreting classroom management, inclusive education and core concepts of transformative pedagogies. This course includes the use of the simSchool online website classroom simulation to develop teaching skills and understandings.
learning_outcomes: Promote equity in classrooms through inclusive education.
Reflect and critically engage with the NSW Quality Teaching model as a professional learning tool;
Demonstrate an understanding of the principles, policies, and practices for establishing and maintaining a productive learning environment; and
Apply frameworks for understanding and interpreting professional practice, particularly through classroom management, inclusive education and core concepts of transformative pedagogies;

title: Quality Teaching and Student Learning 7-12
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course is focused on students' knowledge and skills in the areas of professional knowledge and professional practice, particularly in the areas of student learning and classroom management. A key focus is on gathering evidence aligned with the AITSL standards to demonstrate an intermediate understanding of the profession. This course builds on observations of teachers, teaching and learning undertaken by students in the first year of their teacher education program. It also helps students to recognise and understand how coursework/research forms the foundation of high quality teaching and assessment practice by connecting what is studied at university with how that plays out in classrooms and schools.
learning_outcomes: Apply frameworks and models for understanding and responding to a range of challenging student behaviours;
Relate child development theory, and student well-being and mental health research, to the management of learning;
Critically analyse and apply principles, policies, and practices for establishing and maintaining a productive learning environment;
Demonstrate effective communication skills to support classroom discussion; and
Demonstrate progress towards the attainment of Graduate Teacher Standards through professional experience.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Professional Experience Report on performance in classrooms

title: The Future of Teaching and Learning
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course will overview the current research in the learning sciences and its implications for equity, learning and teaching. It will provide opportunities for students to explore new learning platforms, educational innovations, and alternative models of education in a variety of contexts, communities and settings, from the early years through to adulthood.
learning_outcomes: Design innovative equity-based solutions for contemporary educational problems.
Present an alternative future-focused vision of education.
Critically evaluate current research in the learning sciences and its implications for equity, learning and teaching.
Describe alternative models of education from a variety of contexts, communities and settings.

title: Specialist Studies in Technology 2
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course provides an introduction to curriculum, pedagogy and assessment for teaching the Industrial Technology Syllabi. It provides students with an opportunity to understand the various discourses that inform teachers' knowledge and pedagogical practice as well as critically engaging with models of pedagogy. Students will also develop practical skills using and teaching timber, as well as building upon workplace health and safety practices.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the use of timber/metal/plastic skills in creating a product/system/environment and digital folio.
Design challenging, engaging, and supportive project-based learning activities and assessment for teaching the Stage 5 Design/Industrial Technology Syllabi.
Critically engage with various discourses / demands/ approaches to pedagogy / theories that capture the complexities of the curriculum.
Demonstrate the teaching of numeracy skills when measuring, cutting to size and calculating quantities to manufacture timber/metal items.

title: Australian Early Childhood and Primary Education
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Students will have the opportunity to explore, experience, and review Early Childhood and Primary Education as it occurs in Early Childhood centres catering for 0-5 year olds, and K-6 Primary schools. The course provides an experiential basis for reflecting upon the application of contemporary educational theories, and an opportunity for comparative analysis of curricular and pedagogical practices, examining Australian Early Childhood and Primary Education in comparison to that experienced in the pre-service teacher’s home culture and country. Students will complete 10 days of observation in an Early Childhood site, and 10 days of observation in a K-6 setting.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of contemporary early childhood curriculum policies (including the Early Years Learning Framework) and primary curriculum policies (including the Australian K-6 Curriculum);
Compare and contrast Australian curriculum policies against the student's home country's curriculum policies for Early Childhood and Primary education;
Critically evaluate the learning experiences of young children;
Design their own ideal learner-centred teaching space;
Identify the implementation of contemporary early childhood and primary education theories during their experience of an Early Childhood site, and a Primary classroom setting;
Critically reflect on their own teaching philosophy.

title: Australian Secondary Education
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Students will have the opportunity to explore, experience, and review Secondary Education as it occurs in Australian Secondary Schools. The course provides an experiential basis for reflecting upon the application of contemporary educational theories, and an opportunity for comparative analysis of curricular and pedagogical practices, examining Australian Secondary Education in comparison to that experienced in the pre-service teacher’s home culture and country. Students will complete 20 days of observation in a 7-12 setting.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of contemporary secondary curriculum policies (including the Australian 7-12 Curriculum);
Compare and contrast Australian curriculum policies against the student's home country's curriculum policies for secondary education;
Design their own ideal learner-centred teaching space;
Critically reflect on their own teaching philosophy.
Identify the implementation of contemporary secondary education theories during their experience in a Secondary classroom setting;
Critically evaluate the learning experiences of children 12-18 years old;

title: Australian Primary Education
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Students will have the opportunity to explore, experience, and review Primary Education as it occurs in Australian K-6 Primary schools. The course provides an experiential basis for reflecting upon the application of contemporary educational theories, and an opportunity for comparative analysis of curricular and pedagogical practices, examining Australian Primary Education in comparison to that experienced in the pre-service teacher’s home culture and country. Students will complete 20 days of observation in a K-6 setting.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the learning experiences of children aged 5-12 years;
Demonstrate knowledge of contemporary primary curriculum policies (including the Australian K-6 Curriculum);
Compare and contrast Australian curriculum policies against the student's home country's curriculum policies for Primary education;
Identify the implementation of contemporary primary education theories during their experience in a Primary classroom setting;
Design their own ideal learner-centred teaching space;
Critically reflect on their own teaching philosophy.

title: K-6 Science and Technology
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In this course students will explore the content and organisation of the NSW K-6 Science and Technology curriculum. The course examines strategies and resources for programming, teaching and assessing K-6 Science and Technology; the role and value of Science and Technology in contemporary education; and its place within the broader K-10 Science and Technology continuum, with particular attention to the transition between Stage 3 and 4. Students will consider the embedded literacy and numeracy demands, working across KLAs and explore approaches to differentiating instruction to meet the diverse needs of learners. The course will also address the purposeful integration and use of digital technologies and digital literacies across the curriculum, including online tools and platforms to support teaching and learning in the Science and Technology classroom.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of the principles and practices of teaching and learning K-6 Science & Technology;
Differentiate curriculum to meet the diverse needs of learners; and
Use the internet as a teaching tool in the Science and Technology classroom
Meet the literacy and numeracy demands, integrate Science and Technology across Key Learning Areas;
Discuss the role and value of Science & Technology in the broader school curriculum, and its place in the K-12 Science & Technology continuum (particularly the links between Stage 3 and 4;
Understand and use the NSW K-6 Science & Technology (2024) and incorporate the Australian curriculum syllabus document to plan for learning and teaching;

title: K-6 Society and Environment
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course provides an overview of teaching and learning in Humanities and Social Sciences subjects in K-6 contexts. Students will explore the various NSW syllabus documents in the area incorporating the Australian Curriculum and the role and value of the Humanities and Social Sciences in promoting citizenship values and actions.
learning_outcomes: Understand the underlying principles of the Humanities and Social Sciences area of the curriculum and be able to demonstrate that they can plan teaching and learning events to further these principles and practices;
Value and clarify the diversity of perspectives in the Humanities and Social Sciences with particular emphasis on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander, Asian and Sustainability perspectives;
Understand and use the NSW syllabus document in this area (incorporating the Australian Curriculum) to plan for learning and teaching in all aspects of Humanities and Social Sciences.
Appreciate the role and value of Humanities and Social Sciences in the broader school curriculum;

assessment_tasks.task_name: HSIE based ICT resource creation and lesson planning
Article to a teacher's professional magazine

title: K-6 PDHPE
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In this course students will explore the content and organisation of the NSW K-6 PDHPE curriculum; examine the knowledge base underpinning the principles and practices of teaching and learning in PDHPE; teaching strategies and resources for programming, teaching and assessing primary PDHPE; the role and value of PDHPE; the place of PDHPE in the K-12 PDHPE continuum (particularly the links between Stage 3 and 4); the literacy and numeracy demands of the PDHPE curriculum; ways of differentiating curriculum to meet the diverse needs of learners.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate appropriate teaching strategies for PDHPE.
Differentiate curriculum to meet the diverse literacy needs of learners.
Navigate the content, structure and organisation of the NSW K-6 PDHPE curriculum.
Demonstrate knowledge of the principles and practices of teaching and learning K-6 PDHPE.
Discuss the role and value of PDHPE in the broader school curriculum, and its place in the K-12 PDHPE continuum (particularly the links between Stage 3 and 4.
Understand the literacy and numeracy demands of PDHPE.

title: K-6 Literacy 1
