syllabus_overview: In this course, you will be introduced to significant literature on quality pedagogy, with a particular focus on dimensions of classroom practice identified in research as contributing to greater and more equitable student achievement. You will have the opportunity to engage in direct analysis of current classroom practice and will acquire a deep working knowledge of how the Quality Teaching Model can enhance your own educational practice.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse current classroom practice
Demonstrate a good understanding of pertinent research literature
Apply relevant knowledge, skills and critical thinking when using current and emerging tools and adapting solutions to be context-sensitive and suitable for the intended audience
Demonstrate a sophisticated understanding of pedagogy
Apply the Quality Teaching Model to improve classroom practice

assessment_tasks.task_name: Design and analysis of a lesson plan

title: Quality Curriculum
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will be introduced to significant literature on quality curriculum, with a particular focus on curriculum practice identified in research as contributing to greater and more equitable student achievement. You will have the opportunity to analyse curriculum through the lens of the Quality Teaching Model and design a unit of work using the principles of backward design.
learning_outcomes: Apply the Quality Teaching Model to improve curriculum practice
Apply relevant knowledge, skills and critical thinking when using current and emerging tools and adapting solutions to be context-sensitive and suitable for the intended audience.
Demonstrate a sophisticated understanding of curriculum
Critically analyse current curriculum practice
Demonstrate good understanding of pertinent research literature

title: Intermediate Curriculum Design
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: The course will provide students with the necessary knowledge and skills to design and implement curriculum practices at an intermediate level (that of a practicing educator).
learning_outcomes: Analyse and critique the links between assessment, curriculum and pedagogy;
Demonstrate the capacity to design curriculum units of differing models;
Articulate an understanding of current knowledge about different curriculum design principles;
Design a curriculum unit for use in a real institutional curricular context.
Articulate an understanding of current knowledge about the different curriculum theories and their design models;

title: Integrated Leadership Studies
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In this capstone course, students will examine teaching and learning through the lens of transformational leadership. Students will focus on the creation of learning-oriented organisations and develop interventions for international, national and local educational issues. This course is intended to develop a community of learners, leaders and scholars who embed research-informed practice in their learning organisations.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate contemporary regional, national and global issues affecting education.
Evaluate current learning organisations in terms of teaching and learning practices and policies, proposing research-based improvements.
Analyse characteristics of high-quality reaching and learning.
Design sustainable professional development systems that support high-quality teaching and learning.

title: Technology Assisted Language Learning
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course develops students' understanding of the theory about Computer Assisted Language learning (CALL) and its application in ESL/EFL classrooms. Topics include the basic theoretical foundation for CALL, the existing practice in language teaching in Australia and overseas, the current research finding and new trends in the use of information technology in language teaching and learning. The changing roles of ESL/EFL teachers in the technological environment of education will also be discussed.
learning_outcomes: Understand the foundations and key concepts of Computer Assisted Language Learning;
Design ESL/EFL courses by integrating information technology and curriculum materials to meet learners' needs.
Develop and evaluate CALL application including multimedia materials and internet tools; and

title: Leading Digital Learning in the 21st Century
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: To provide students with the opportunity to explore ways in which ICT can be transformative in terms of student learning. Students will also be given the opportunity to develop skills in the project based implementations of ICT technology.
learning_outcomes: Understand the ICT needs of students in modern educational contexts; and
Gain an understanding of project based learning in relation to ICT;
Develop meaningful learning experiences that utilize ICT in effective ways.
Broad overview of the use of specific ICT applications;

title: Sociocultural Context for ESL/EFL Teaching
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course develops students’ understanding of the socio-cultural contexts affecting ESL/EFL/EALD language teaching and learning. Topics include language policies used in Australia and internationally, the impact of language policies and community needs on language teaching in school curriculum, the cultural issues related to ESL/EFL/EALD and the educational environment for ESL/EFL/EALD teachers and students with various social, cultural, and linguistic backgrounds.
learning_outcomes: Understand the foundations and key concepts of socio-cultural contexts;
Analyse the cultural issues related to ESL/EFL/EALD, the interaction between teachers and students with various social, cultural, and linguistic backgrounds; and
Apply socio-cultural theories in the practice of ESL/EF/EALD teaching

title: Education and International Development: Global Perspectives
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course provides a general introduction to the forces that shape education systems and processes globally, and the associated nature, structure and practice of education systems. Concurrently, it reviews the historical development of International Educational Development (IED) as a subfield of Comparative and International Education (CIE) as a field, and its trajectories within academic research and educational practice, and explores the birth of the development project, and key institutions at the heart of this project including the World Bank, the United Nations, aid agencies, non-governmental organisations, etc.. Through this examination, the course develops insights into the key relationships between education and political, economic and social change, and their manifestation at multiple levels (local, national, regional, international and global), based on comparative and international research and evidence. The course uses an issue based approach to explore key educational phenomena and areas of reform. Basic critical descriptions of similarities and differences between education systems in different contexts are made, and associated explanations of these are developed.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a rigorous, broad and deep, understanding of the nature and historical development of education systems from a global perspective;
Interpret specific system and reform moments in their particular contexts and from a global perspective.
Describe a particular education system in its historico-political context as a case study; and
Identify forces that shape education systems and practices, from multiple levels of scale, and the ways in which they form the same;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Essays/Written Assignments - Discussion and analysis of CIE literature

title: Data Mining for School Leaders
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: With increasing pressure on school leaders to draw upon research and evidence in their decision-making, the need for effective management and critical engagement with school-based and system-wide data has become imperative. This course aims to assist school leaders in managing and mining data to make evidence-based decisions.
learning_outcomes: Apply data mining and/or knowledge management strategies to a real-world case; and
Link data mining and analysis to strategic decision-making.
Understanding and analyse school-based and system-wide data;

title: Australian School Leadership
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course brings together Australian education policy, research and practice to explore the nature of school leadership in contemporary Australia.
learning_outcomes: Investigate the impact of different policy players on schools and schooling; and
Critically engage with contemporary policy issues facing Australian school leaders.
Demonstrate an understanding of the Australian education policy context;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Discussion Board Tasks: Trends in Australian Education Policy
Presentation and interactive oral assessment: Analysis of the impact of policy on school leadership

title: Leading and Managing Educational Change
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course critically explores the leadership and management of educational change in the contemporary context.
learning_outcomes: Reflect upon and analyse educational change issues and the relationship to strategic management; and
Investigate and critically engage with the concepts, principles, and research findings relating to educational change processes;
Develop strategic planning for initiating change in an educational setting.

title: Engineering Studies 2
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course extends students' knowledge of the Engineering Studies syllabus, teaching and learning and curriculum development in engineering research skills and industry knowledge with a specific focus on engineering materials, testing, hydraulics, aerodynamics, pneumatics and aerodynamics. As part of this course, students will extend their knowledge of civil structures, transport, lifting devices, aeronautics and telecommunication. Students will explore engineering materials and mechanics, history and the scope of the engineers' professions from electrical, telecommunication and aeronautical engineering. Students will focus their study from the dimensions of: engineering materials, testing, hydraulics, pneumatics, and aerodynamics and develop engineering reports which are appropriate for the stage 6 NSW Engineering Studies syllabus.
learning_outcomes: Introduce students to engineering concepts related to materials, hydraulics, pneumatics and aerodynamics.
Explore the historical and contemporary engineering and the nature and scope of the engineering profession.
Differentiate engineering classrooms using quality teachings to cater for all NESB and male/female students.
Develop management and problem-solving skills in engineering contexts.
Investigate recent innovations, emerging technologies and technological developments in the areas of engineering studies.
Enable students to write appropriate engineering reports for a range of situations.
Analyse the inter-relationship of all concepts involved in the engineering curriculum including the quality teaching model.
Inform the students of the mechanics behind engineered products.
Explore through experimentation materials and testing relating to engineering concepts used in the stage 6 Engineering syllabus.
Develop teaching and learning lessons and programs that integrate engineering, problem based learning and the quality teaching model.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Problem Solving Activity - Formal Assessment Task and Marking Criteria

title: Engineering Studies 1
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to stage 6 of the Engineering studies syllabus. It is directed towards the application and advancement of skills associated with mathematics, science and technology and is integrated with business and management of ‘Braking systems’ and ‘Personal and Public Transport’. It will provide students with skills, knowledge and understanding associated with a study of engineering, its practices and associated methodologies in ‘Braking systems’ and ‘Personal and Public Transport’. The subject promotes environment, economic and global-awareness, problem-solving ability, engagement with information technology, self-directed learning, communication, management and skills in working as a team.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and synthesise engineering applications in specific fields and report on the importance of these to society.
Enable the students to explore the nature of engineering in specific fields and report of the importance of these to society.
Identify BOS assessment requirements for the HSC.
Explore and develop an appreciation of the responsibilities of engineers in society.
Determine through observation, testing and experimentation suitable properties, uses and applications of materials in engineering.
Study the relationship between properties, uses and applications of materials in engineering.
Introduce students to the profession of engineering and to the stage 5 and 6 syllabus for engineering studies, explaining the intent and requirement of the syllabus documents.
Extend the students' knowledge and understanding of engineering principles.

title: Engineering Studies 4
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to engineering studies providing a context within which to develop general competencies considered essential for the acquisition of effective, higher-order thinking skills necessary for further education, work and everyday life. Key competencies are embedded in the engineering studies syllabus to enhance student learning. The key competencies of collecting, analysing and organising information reflect core processes of inquiry and reporting which are explicit in the objectives and outcomes of engineering studies. The other key competencies are developed through the methodologies of the syllabus and through classroom pedagogy. In particular the course will focus on the historical development of engineering from it's origin to the role of engineers in society today as well as a study of the sociological and environmental factors that impact upon engineers and their work.
learning_outcomes: Study the social, environmental and cultural implications of technological change in engineering and apply them to the analysis of specific problems.
Critically analyse current worldwide innovations and emerging technologies and their possible impact on engineering practice and society.
Investigates the extent and influence of technological change on engineering and its effect on people and society.
Synthesise solutions to engineering problems by applying knowledge of history and technological innovation and change to engineering based problems.
Extend knowledge of developments in technology and an appreciation of their influence on people and engineering practice.
Explore the scope of engineering both nationally and from a global perspective.
Enable themselves to act in the role of the engineer to solve engineering dilemmas.

title: Engineering Studies 3
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to engineering mechanics and materials. In particular the course has a primary focus on the areas of communication through engineering reports including the materials and mechanics involved. The course will also provide essential information about the real world of engineering, informed through an industry study as well as providing an insight into the effect of technological innovation. The exploration of issues and investigation of the nature of engineered products and systems contributes towards the students' development of the key competency solving problems. Students work as individuals and as members of groups to conduct investigations into engineered civil structures and household appliances. Students focus their study from the communication and engineering report dimensions appropriate for the stage 6 NSW Engineering Studies syllabus.
learning_outcomes: Introduce skills used application of engineering knowledge and methodology.
Explore the knowledge and understanding of the developments of technology and an appreciation of their influence on people and engineering practice.
Enable students to develop and use a range of specialised communication skills and techniques in the application of graphics as a tool appropriate to engineering practices.
Communicate using written, oral and presentation skills in the preparation of detailed engineering reports.
Demonstrates proficiency in the use of mathematical, scientific and graphical methods to analyse, solve problems of engineering practice.
Apply knowledge and demonstrate skills in research and problem solving related to industry and engineering.
Demonstrates skills in analysis, synthesis and experimentation related to engineering.
Integrate computer based technologies into teaching and learning activities
Create a teaching and learning folio containing a range of engineering resources.
Proficiently use application software and graphics software including (CADD) computer aided design and drafting and electronic communications.

title: Curriculum for High Potential and Gifted Learners
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course empowers students to apply differentiation techniques high potential and gifted learners by examining the concepts, theories and issues related to curriculum differentiation for high potential and gifted students. Students will evaluate a range of models for the provision of educational services for high potential and gifted learners. Several research-based teaching models will be studied including but not limited to Bloom’s, Williams and the content, process, product model of Maker. Assessment for, of and as learning will be studied in relation to the teaching and development of appropriate curriculum for high potential and gifted learners. Additionally, students will explore the ways in which teachers can support the talent development and social-emotional well-being of high potential and gifted learners through differentiation.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the strengths and weaknesses of different teaching models.
Recognise the application of assessment for, as, and of learning in providing appropriate curriculum for high potential and gifted students.
Evaluate a range of models for the provision of educational programs for high potential and gifted students.
Review and critique a variety of relevant resources for meeting the educational needs of high potential and gifted students.

title: Meeting the Needs of High Potential and Gifted Students with a Disability
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Catering for the needs of learners who demonstrate both exceptional ability and a disability or learning difficulty can be one of the most complex challenges educators face.This course will examine the characteristics, identification and appropriate programs for high potential and gifted students with disability. These are students who are identified as high potential and gifted learners but also have disability or disabilities. Current research and practices in implementing education provisions for these students will be studied and evaluated.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate a range of methods for identifying high potential and gifted students with disability.
Describe the characteristics that high potential and gifted students with disability demonstrate.
Use research-based strategies and programs to meet the educational needs of high potential and gifted students with disability
Develop an appropriate Educational Plan for high potential and gifted students with disability.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Student engages in a professional activity in context for a real-world audience

title: K-6 English
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course provides an introduction to teaching and learning in English in K-6 contexts with a focus on children's reception, interpretation and interdependency of verbal, textual and visual literacies including an introduction to the sciences of reading. Students will explore the NSW English K-6 syllabus incorporating the Australian Curriculum and the role and value of English in the broader school curriculum.
learning_outcomes: Consider children's home and community literacy practices as a foundation for learning in K-6 contexts
Identify the key stages in children's early language acquisition
Understand and use the NSW English K-6 syllabus (2023) incorporating the Australian Curriculum (2012) to plan for learning and teaching in receptive literacy
Demonstrate an understanding of theory, concepts and 'sciences of reading' reading and learning related to the key stages of knowledge and skills in receptive and visual literacies (pre-K - 6)
Value children's literature as a context for teaching and learning in English

title: K-6 Mathematics
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course introduces pre-service teachers to the principles and practices of teaching primary mathematics, with a particular focus on Patterns & Early Algebraic Reasoning and Problem Solving. Through the exploration of patterning, early algebraic reasoning, and strategic problem-solving approaches, students will develop the knowledge and confidence to design and deliver effective mathematics lessons aligned with the NSW K–6 Mathematics Syllabus. There will be a particular focus on how to recognise and respond to common student misconceptions, plan learning sequences that promote mathematical thinking, and embed formative assessment in practice. Emphasis is placed on using rich tasks to develop numeracy, support diverse learners, and cultivate essential strategies such as algebraic reasoning, generalising, and working mathematically.
learning_outcomes: Describe and model patterns and relationships that can be generalised, and as a means of interpreting the world.
Demonstrate knowledge of the principles and practices of teaching and learning mathematics in K-6 school contexts (including strategies for planning, teaching and assessing).
Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of central ideas in Mathematics and common student misconceptions
Demonstrate knowledge of Mathematical thinking, working mathematically and problem-solving techniques.
Explore range of strategies for teaching and assessing primary mathematics
Navigate the content, structure and organisation of the NSW K-10 Mathematics curriculum and explore its relationship to the Numeracy.
Demonstrate knowledge of the development of numeracy skills through the stages of primary schooling.

title: K-6 Creative Arts
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course explores the principles of teaching and learning K-6 Creative Arts. Students will consider the role and value of Creative Arts in the broader school curriculum; the place of creative arts in the K-12 Creative Arts continuum (particularly the links between Stage 3 and 4); the relationship between creative arts, literacy and numeracy; and ways of differentiating curriculum to meet the diverse needs of learners in the Creative Arts classroom. Students will explore the content and organisation of the NSW K-6 Creative Arts curriculum; models of pedagogy for programming, teaching and assessing dance, drama, music, media and visual arts.
learning_outcomes: Differentiate curriculum to meet the diverse literacy needs of learners.
Engage in dance, drama, music and visual arts.
Navigate the content, structure and organisation of the NSW K-6 Creative Arts curriculum.
Select strategies for teaching dance, drama, music and visual arts.
Discuss the role and value of Creative Arts in the broader school curriculum, and its place in the K-12 Creative Arts continuum (particularly the links between Stage 3 and 4.
Demonstrate knowledge of the principles and practices of teaching and learning K-6 Creative Arts.
Understand the literacy and numeracy demands of Creative Arts.

title: Students with Diverse Needs
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course introduces Initial Teacher Education Students (ITES) to issues, policies and practices relating to the provision of effective inclusive education that meets the diverse learning needs of all students, including those with disabilities, behaviour disorders and difficulties in learning. During the course students will develop the skills required for collaborating with families and other professionals, for assessing and monitoring student learning, and for making reasonable adjustments to curriculum materials so that all students have access to learning.
learning_outcomes: Identify and discuss issues, attitudes and concepts relevant to the education of students with diverse needs within the social context of the school.
Utilise a range of teaching and learning practices designed to maximise the social and learning experiences of students with diverse needs in primary and secondary settings.
Demonstrate knowledge of legislation, educational policies and provisions as well as syllabus documents relating to students with diverse needs including those with a disability.

title: K-6 Science and Technology
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In this course Initial Teacher Education Students (ITES) will explore the content and organisation of the NSW K-6 Science and Technology curriculum, incorporating the Australian Curriculum; strategies and resources for programming, teaching and assessing primary Science and Technology; the role and value of Science and Technology; the place of Science and Technology in the K-12 Science and Technology continuum (particularly the links between Stage 3 and 4); the literacy and numeracy demands of Science and Technology curriculum; ways of differentiating curriculum to meet the diverse needs of learners; and the use of the internet as a teaching tool in the Science and Technology classroom, and ways of developing positive attitudes and motivation techniques for developing intellectual and problem solving skills in all students.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the role and value of Science & Technology in the broader school curriculum, and its place in the K-10 Science & Technology continuum (particularly the links between Stage 3 and 4;
Differentiate curriculum to meet the diverse needs of learners;
Understand the literacy and numeracy demands of Science and Technology;
Demonstrate knowledge of the principles and practices of teaching and learning K-6 Science & Technology;
Navigate the content, structure and organisation of the NSW K-6 Science & Technology syllabus (2024)
Use a range of digital technologies to enhance teaching and learning

title: K-6 HSIE
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In this course Initial Teacher Education Students (ITES) will explore the content and organisation of the NSW K-6 HSIE Syllabus and curriculum; strategies and resources for programming, teaching and assessing primary HSIE; the role and value of HSIE; the place of HSIE in the K-12 HSIE continuum (particularly the links between Stage 3 and 4); the literacy and numeracy demands of HSIE curriculum; ways of differentiating curriculum to meet the diverse needs of learners. Particular attention will be given to Aboriginal history and culture, and concepts emerging from the HSIE curriculum that relate to civics and citizenship.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the underlying principles of Human Society and its Environment (HSIE) and design learning experiences that apply these principles using the Quality Teaching Framework and inquiry-based learning cycle;
Explain the role and value of HSIE within the broader school curriculum; and
Evaluate diverse perspectives in HSIE to inform inclusive teaching approaches that incorporates Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander, Global, and Sustainability perspective;
Plan for effective classroom learning and teaching using the NSW HSIE syllabus and incorporating the Australian Curriculum

assessment_tasks.task_name: Article for a teacher's professional magazine
HSIE-based ICT lesson planning and validation

title: Advanced Literacy Studies
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course will explore current research on children's language acquisition, and the teaching, learning and assessment of reading (including phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, and text comprehension); instructional approaches for developing children's concepts of print, grammar, punctuation, spelling and handwriting; and strategies for teaching and assessing the composition of digital and multi-modal texts. Students will learn how to interpret school-based and system-wide literacy data and to consider related issues of literacy practices in the home, child language development, the diverse language backgrounds of students, intercultural awareness and inclusiveness, in order to make informed decisions about student literacy needs.
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of providing timely and appropriate feedback to students about their learning
Describe the importance of home and community literacy and numeracy practices across the span 0-12 years
Analyse evidence-based research and apply findings to support the interpretation of school-based and system-wide literacy data

Apply a range of models of pedagogy for teaching and assessing the components of reading (including strategies for teaching and assessing phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, and text comprehension)

Apply the principles and practices of teaching English as an Additional Language or Dialect (EAL/D) and supporting students with learning difficulties to design and implement units of work for diverse K-6 contexts
Apply instructional approaches for developing children's concepts of print, grammar, punctuation, spelling and handwriting

title: K-6 PDHPE
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In this course Initial Teacher Education Students (ITES) will explore the content and organisation of the NSW K-6 PDHPE curriculum; strategies and resources for programming, teaching and assessing primary PDHPE; the role and value of PDHPE; the place of PDHPE in the Physical Literacy Continuum K-10 (particularly the links between Stages 3 and 4); the literacy and numeracy demands of PDHPE curriculum; and ways of differentiating curriculum to meet the diverse needs of learners.
learning_outcomes: Differentiate curriculum to meet the diverse needs of learners.
Analyse the role and value of PDHPE in the broader school curriculum, and its place in the K-12 PDHPE continuum (particularly the links between Stage 3 and 4).
Navigate the content, structure and organisation of the NSW K-6 PDHPE curriculum to plan for effective classroom teaching and learning.
Demonstrate knowledge of the principles and practices of teaching and learning K-6 PDHPE.
Understand the literacy and numeracy demands of PDHPE.

title: Managing the K-6 Learning Environment
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In this course Initial Teacher Education Students (ITES) will explore child development, student well-being, mental health, and their relationship to the management of learning; principles and practices for establishing a productive learning environment; and frameworks and models for understanding and responding to a range of challenging student behaviours (including bullying and cyber-bullying). The course provides opportunities for ITES (primary) to analyse school policies; to plan and teach lessons using a variety of technologies and strategies; assess student learning; and to evaluate their own classroom management beliefs and practices through a full-time, 20 day block of professional experience in a primary school setting.
learning_outcomes: Relate child development theory, and student well-being and mental health research, to the management of learning;
Demonstrate progress towards the attainment of Graduate Teacher Standards through professional experience.
Critically analyse and apply principles, policies, and practices for establishing and maintaining a productive learning environment;
Demonstrate effective communication skills to support classroom discussion; and
Apply frameworks and models for understanding and responding to a range of challenging student behaviours;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Professional Experience Report on performance in classrooms and eportfolio

title: Effective Pedagogies for Primary Mathematics
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course deepens students' understanding of the impact of the principles and practices of teaching and learning mathematics in primary schools. Students will explore the numeracy demands of all key learning areas in the primary curriculum. They will also learn about different models of pedagogy for teaching, differentiating and assessing in Primary Mathematics to meet diverse needs of students. With a focus on helping students to reason and "work mathematically", this course will place particular attention upon instructional strategies and educational technologies for teaching and assessing the foundational mathematical concepts in the strands of number and algebra, measurement and geometry, and statistics and probability.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a thorough understanding of appropriate instructional strategies and educational technologies for teaching and assessing in Primary Mathematics
Demonstrate a deep understanding of mathematical concepts of number and algebra, measurement and geometry, statistics and probability in the primary curriculum.
Identify instructional requirements that assists students to work mathematically
Design for differentiated instruction to meet the diverse learning needs of students
Demonstration of Understanding of Aboriginal and Torres Strait islander histories and cultures
Identify the numeracy demands of everyday life and demonstrate the knowledge of the development of numeracy skills through the stages of primary schooling

title: Professional Experience 1 (7-12)
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In this course Initial Teacher Education Students (ITES) will explore child and adolescent development, student well-being, mental health, and their relationship to the management of learning; principles and practices for establishing a productive learning environment; and frameworks and models for understanding and responding to a range of challenging student behaviours (including bullying and cyber bullying). The course provides opportunities for ITES to analyse school policies; to plan and teach lessons using a variety of technologies and strategies; assess student learning; and to evaluate their own classroom management beliefs and practices through a full time 20 day block of professional experience in a Secondary school setting.
learning_outcomes: Relate child and adolescent development theory, and student well-being and mental health research, to the management of learning;
Demonstrate progress towards the attainment of Graduate Teacher Standards.
Evaluate their classroom management beliefs and practices in the light of theory and professional experience;
Critically analyse and apply principles, policies, and practices for establishing a productive learning environment;
Apply frameworks and models for understanding and responding to a range of challenging student behaviours; and

title: Curriculum Method 1 (7-12)
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In this course students will interrogate the role and value of their major teaching area in contemporary society and the broader school curriculum. The specialised knowledge and skills of the teacher, in particular, planning, teaching and assessment and ways of differentiating curriculum to meet the diverse needs of learners will be explored. Specific attention will also be given to Indigenous students and multicultural experience; as well as a range of strategies, technologies and resources for teaching and assessing the major teaching area.
learning_outcomes: Develop and evaluate lesson plans, programs and assessment tasks for secondary schools in the major teaching area.
Integrate strategies, technologies and resources for planning, teaching and assessing in the major content area.
Adapt and differentiate the curriculum to meet the diverse needs of learners in the secondary classroom.
Articulate and critically analyse the role and value of the major teaching area in contemporary society and the broader school curriculum.
Analyse the process and components of planning, teaching, assessment and reflection as related to the major teaching area.

title: Curriculum Method 2 (7-12)
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In this course Initial Teacher Education Students (ITES) will investigate the use of innovative and alternative teaching approaches for either their additional teaching area or their area of interest for specialist skill development. The specialised knowledge and skills of the teacher for planning and programming; course and assessment requirements for using cross-curricular, innovative approaches and technologies; and ways of differentiating curriculum to meet the diverse needs of learners, including Indigenous and multi-cultural students, will be explored. Specific attention will also be given to developing a research agenda for the development of a range of strategies, technologies and resources for teaching and assessing in the student’s chosen minor teaching area or area of specialist skills.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse the role and value of the major teaching area in contemporary society and the broader school curriculum.
Explain effective strategies for working effectively with parents/carers and the community
Develop and evaluate lesson plans, programs and assessment tasks for secondary schools in the major teaching area
Adapt and differentiate the curriculum to meet the diverse needs of learners in the secondary classroom
Integrate strategies to support the delivery of general capabilities from the Australian Curriculum in the chosen teaching area

title: Educational Foundations
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Learn the foundational knowledge and skills needed to become a primary or secondary teacher. This course examines concepts and theories from educational, social, and developmental psychology and sociology. Pre-service teachers develop an understanding of how students learn and how teachers can help students learn. By investigating the relationships among the individuals, society, social diversity, and contemporary education systems, students learn how this complexity impacts on students’ development and achievement. Students will investigate equity issues, including Indigenous issues, in schooling, reflect on education policy and teaching practices and identify ways in which educators can create socially and culturally inclusive educational environments.
learning_outcomes: Define the multiple discourses and theoretical fields that inform educational practice;
Interpret and critically analyse contemporary policy, current issues, values, practices and ethical considerations in their area of specialisation; and
Identify typical developmental trends (physical, cognitive, social, emotional, moral) in students as they move through primary and secondary school;
Research and plan socially just pedagogical and curricular practices for diverse student populations in their specialisation.
Describe the social nature of schooling and the ways in which socio-cultural factors can affect students experiences of schooling;
Apply current theories of learning and motivation and explain ways in which teachers can assist students to learn;
Synthesise a broad research base and communicate their understanding of the foundations of quality teaching in schools;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Individual Task - Teaching for Equity in Module 3
Individual Task - Literature Review in Module 1
Individual Task - Belonging in Schools in Module 2

title: Introduction to Higher Education
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course is designed to introduce students to three aspects of higher education: orienting to institutional requirements; curriculum design (inclusive of teaching, learning, and assessment alignment); and supervision and support of higher degree by research candidates. Students will learn through a variety of teaching approaches informed by inquiry learning, scholarship of teaching and learning, learning design instruction, and mentoring. This course is designed for both novice and experienced academic and professional staff working in higher education institutions.
learning_outcomes: Appraise a variety of curriculum development frameworks to their teaching and learning context in relation to the scholarship of teaching and learning
Apply the scholarship of teaching and learning to prepare teaching and learning activities and resources in their teaching
Prepare a research-informed approach to research by higher degree supervision
Explain and practically demonstrate the orientation requirements of their institution

assessment_tasks.task_name: Introduction to Scholarship of Teaching Learning
Supervision of research higher degree students

title: Contemporary Literacies
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course will explore language as a social practice and discover its significance in learning and development. Initial Teacher Education Students (ITES) will analyse the literacy demands of different subject areas, and learn strategies for assessing and teaching reading, writing, speaking, listening, viewing, and representing in the secondary classroom. Specific strategies to address intercultural competence and cater for the learning needs of multilingual students or students who require additional language and literacy support are introduced. This course will detail the ways in which new technologies can be used to support and extend student learning. Through a project-based task, ITES will develop the capacity and confidence to employ digital devices and software applications to construct and communicate new knowledge in and beyond the classroom. Attention will also be given to the social impact of technology; frameworks for thinking about the pedagogical use of new technologies; digital, visual and media literacy; and information literacy processes
learning_outcomes: Explain the social nature of language and how it impacts student learning and development.
Demonstrate teaching and assessment strategies aligned with identified contemporary literacies within varying school contexts and secondary school subject areas
Apply pedagogical frameworks and curriculum models for technology usage to facilitate quality teaching and learning to prepare their students for subsequent endeavours.

Apply strategies (including the use of assistive technologies) to cater for the learning needs of students for whom English is an additional language or dialect and those who require additional language and literacy support.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Project: Literacy planning, pedagogy, and assessment.

title: K-6 Literacy 2
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course develops a deep understanding of how children learn to produce written, visual and multimodal texts, drawing on key theories, developmental progressions and research-informed practice. Students learn to design explicit and differentiated literacy instruction, assess writing and visual literacy using a range of strategies, and analyse data to guide responsive teaching. The course also builds knowledge of digital, visual and media literacy, with a focus on effective, ethical and purposeful use of multimodal tools in K-6 contexts.
learning_outcomes: Explain and apply key concepts in digital, visual and media literacy in alignment with the NSW English K-10 syllabus, incorporating digital and multimodal tools to enhance communication and knowledge construction

Explain key theories, concepts and development progressions in children's writing, visual and multimodal literacy, and interpret research evidence informing effective and differentiated literacy instruction in K-6 contexts.

Apply principles and practices of effective English teaching to design and justify explicit instruction in writing, visual and multimodal literacies, including text structure, language features, vocabulary, spelling and handwriting.
Select and use appropriate assessment strategies to evaluate students' writing and visual literacy development and provide constructive, differentiated feedback that supports literacy growth.
Analyse individual student literacy data to identify strengths and learning needs, and use this evidence to inform responsive whole class, small group and individual literacy instruction.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Micro-teaching video and Annotated Reflective Commentary
Literacy Case Study & Instructional Design Portfolio

title: Quality Teaching in Higher Education
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Delivering high quality teaching is critical to the student experience at university. This course provides a conceptual and practical introduction to quality teaching, grounded in evidence of positive effects for teachers and students. By addressing core aspects of quality teaching, students are guided in how to enrich their teaching, course design, and assessment.
learning_outcomes: Analyse, discuss and refine teaching and learning using the language and structure of the Quality Teaching Model.
Design and use relevant strategies to achieve quality learning environments.
Design and use relevant strategies to achieve high levels of intellectual quality in teaching and learning.
Formulate and explain their ideas about quality teaching in higher education.
Design and use relevant strategies to ensure teaching and learning are meaningful to students.

title: Scholarship of Teaching and Learning
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course is designed to explore and evaluate the scholarship of teaching and learning in higher education contexts, including learning theories, evidence-based teaching and learning strategies, and action research. Students will engage with inquiry approaches to the scholarship of teaching and learning, and consider how this informs teaching and learning in their own professional practice.
learning_outcomes: Document reflective practice in your teaching context
Design an action research project to evaluate your teaching
Develop your own research-based philosophy of teaching
Analyse and apply key concepts from scholarship of teaching and learning

title: Emerging Technologies: Planning teaching and assessing
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: To move forward in the modern education sector, higher education providers must move beyond traditional educational paradigms in order to engage students and to prepare them for contemporary working and learning contexts. Technological solutions offer educators a range of tools to assist in teaching and learning approaches, content delivery, and assessment in ways to make their courses more engaging and with greater opportunity for feedback. This course will cover a range of technological tools and give tertiary educators knowledge and skills to practically apply and integrate emerging technologies into their own educational programs.
learning_outcomes: Design appropriate formative assessments specific to their area of teaching using appropriate technologies.

Identify, describe and implement methods that can be used for the purpose of reducing the risk of student cheating through the use of modern and emerging technologies including Large Language Models (LLMs).
Describe a range of technologies available for formative and summative assessment.
Ensure appropriate technologies are implemented into their learning programs that enhance student learning.
Design and implement appropriate methods for content delivery using technologies include Video calls, Canvas, and other Digital Technologies.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Creation of a Formative Assessment Task
Creation of a Summative Assessment Task and Rubric

title: Professional Experience 2 (7-12)
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course will introduce Initial Teacher Education Students (ITES) to approaches for building commitment to the profession of teaching and shaping reflective practices for ongoing professional learning throughout their career. This course is the culminating placement course of your degree and is focused on consolidating your knowledge and skills in the areas of professional knowledge and professional practice, across all secondary Key Learning Areas (KLA’s). The primary focus is preparing ITES to complete the Newcastle Teaching Performance Assessment (NTPA). During their 40 days professional experience opportunity, ITES will demonstrate their attainment of Graduate Teacher Standards and have an opportunity to engage in student sport, playground supervision, faculty/grade/stage meetings and school activities and functions, as required. They will demonstrate the impact of their teaching on the learning of their students in their NTPA.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate progress towards the attainment of Graduate Teacher Standards through professional experience.

Develop strategies for identifying professional learning strengths and needs, critical reflection, individual and collegial support, engagement with the wider school community and the world beyond the classroom/school.
Engage in critical reflection on their development and learning as an ethical teacher in productive professional learning communities.
Engage in the full life of school including student sport, playground supervision, faculty/grade/stage meetings and school activities and functions.
Construct, implement and evaluate unit/s of work.

title: Australian Primary Education
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Students will have the opportunity to explore, experience, and review Primary Education as it occurs in Australian K-6 Primary schools. The course provides an experiential basis for reflecting upon the application of contemporary educational theories, and an opportunity for comparative analysis of curricular and pedagogical practices, examining Australian Primary Education in comparison to that experienced in the pre-service teacher’s home culture and country. Students will complete 20 days of observation in a K-6 setting.
learning_outcomes: Design their own ideal learner-centred teaching space;
Compare and contrast Australian and home country's curriculum policies for Primary education;
Identify the implementation of contemporary primary education theories during their experience in a Primary classroom setting.
Demonstrate knowledge of contemporary primary curriculum policies (including the Australian K-6 Curriculum);
Critically reflect on their own teaching philosophy.
Critically evaluate the learning experiences of children aged 5-12 years;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Document the learning experiences of a child aged 5-12 years while on observation placement
Develop 3D Model of Ideal Teaching Space

title: The Global Primary Professional
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course will introduce Primary Initial Teacher Education Students (ITES) to approaches for designing integrated curriculum that they will implement using multi-level pedagogies during a 40-day block of full time professional experience in a school setting. During their professional experience opportunity, ITES will demonstrate their attainment of Graduate Teacher Standards and have an opportunity to engage in student sport, playground supervision, faculty/grade/stage meetings and school activities and functions, as required. ITES will reflect upon, and produce a Teacher Performance Assessment (NTPA), their professional learning during the program with a particular focus on one of the program’s overall learning themes. They will learn about how to integrate curriculum, explore the legal, social and ethical responsibilities associated with being a member of the teaching profession. This course allows reflection on and consideration of their responsibility as participants in local, national and global teaching communities.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate attainment of Graduate Teacher Standards through professional experience.
Engage in critical reflection on their professional practice and be able to articulate a personal philosophy of teaching incorporating moral dimensions of the work of teachers;
Adapt and differentiate curriculum and instruction to personalise the learning for students in their care;
Engage in the full life of school including student sport, playground supervision, faculty/grade/stage meetings and school activities and functions; and
Construct and implement an integrated unit of work.
Develop a teaching portfolio that demonstrates critical reflection on their professional learning over the entire program, at a level commensurate with graduate teacher standards;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Professional Experience Report (incorporating Teacher Performance Assessment)

title: Introduction to Electrical Engineering
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to fundamental electrical elements including voltage, current, resistance, inductance, capacitance and ideal operational amplifier. It provides students with an understanding and appreciation of techniques for analysing and designing simple dc and ac circuits. It also introduces the principles behind simple electrical machines, and provides hands on experience in using a electrical and electronic laboratory and prototyping equipment.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate familiarity with the problems and theoretical tools to be further developed in the electrical engineering degree
Apply knowledge and gain practical 'hands on' experience through a design exercise in the laboratory
Explain the operating principles of electrical machines
Analyse and design ac and dc circuits using fundamental techniques
Demonstrate safe working practices in laboratories

title: Digital and Computer Electronics 1
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the principles of digital computer design, particularly the fundamentals of modern digital logic design including logic gates, Boolean algebra, Karnaugh maps, flip-flops, and sequential circuits (state-machines). It examines the binary number system, hexadecimal notation and computer arithmetic. This course then introduces the basic elements of a modern computer, its organisation and architecture. Students are introduced to assembly and machine language programming at the interface of computer software and hardware.
learning_outcomes: Solve problems using binary numbers, hexadecimal and octal notation, and the representation of information using digital codes
Write low level assembly language
Apply state diagrams, flip-flops, logic gates and Karnaugh maps to design and analyse sequential circuits
Employ logic gates, Boolean algebra, truth tables and Karnaugh maps to design and analyse digital logic circuits
Solve problems using computer arithmetic including signed number representations in 1's and 2's complement form
Formulate solutions to real-world problems using discrete digital components, medium-scale integrated circuits, and software tools
Discuss the fundamentals of computer architecture and its interaction with software

title: Electric Energy Systems
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course introduces the theory of magnetic circuits, transformers and electromagnetic energy conversion and applies these fundamental principles to systems which rely on them. Topics considered may include three phase circuits, magnetic circuits, transformers, electromechanical energy conversion, transmission lines and power systems.
learning_outcomes: Interpret AC circuit theory in relation to three phase circuits in steady state, balanced and unbalanced.
Identify the theory necessary to analyse magnetic circuits.
Combine elements into a complete system and perform elementary analysis of the system as a whole.
Perform power and efficiency calculations for major components of the electromagnetic system and for the system as a whole.
Recognise the principles of electromagnetic energy conversion.
Apply the fundamental theories to the operating principles of and to model. a. Transformers; b. Relays and solenoids; c. Transmission lines.
Recognise the nature of power losses in major elements of an electromagnetic system.
Identify and adopt safe practices when working with electric systems containing energy conversion elements.

title: Introduction to Embedded Computing
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Students in ELEC2720 will learn about microcontrollers, their low level architecture, and the techniques of programming a microcontroller using the C programming language. Students will develop a practical product by programming a microcontroller with C and will learn to use modern peripheral devices used in embedded systems, including interrupt controllers, direct memory access, communication devices such as SPI and I2C. The assessments for this course are broken into a number of progressive practical assignments contributing towards a final demonstrable product. There will also be a final exam component to examine the basic concepts presented during the course. Students are encouraged to familiarise themselves with the materials available online. The lectorials and supervised laboratory sessions are interactive sessions for the students to discuss their questions with the instructors. All materials for this course will be available online prior to face-to-face sessions.
learning_outcomes: Program analogue-to-digital converters and general-purpose input/output ports on microcontrollers
Configure peripheral devices using special function registers
Interface a microcontroller with peripheral devices using serial communication protocols such as I²C and SPI.
Program microcontrollers for developing practical products
Apply direct memory access for fast data transfer
Write C programs on PC and microcontrollers

title: Electrical and Electronic Circuits
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course explores the fundamental concepts of electrical circuits. Content includes mesh/loop analysis (with super meshes), nodal analysis (with super nodes), Thevenin, Norton and maximum power transfer and superposition theorem applied to circuits, circuits based on ideal operational amplifiers, simple non-linear circuits employing diodes and transistors. These include basic amplifiers, buffers and switching circuits.
learning_outcomes: Design and analyse circuits containing ideal operational amplifiers
Apply circuit theorems in practical work
Analyse simple non-linear circuits containing discrete components such as diodes and transistors
Analyse circuits using node and mesh analysis
Design filters and analyse circuits in the frequency domain

title: Circuits and Signals
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course starts from the frequency dependent behaviour of alternating current circuits and filters, and shows how Fourier series and Fourier Transform can be used to analyse a circuit's response. Subsequently, differential models and linear system interpretation of linear circuits are discussed, and the first and second order transient behaviour of circuits is analysed using Laplace transforms. Some fundamental concepts of system theory such as transfer functions, impulse response and convolution are introduced. The course also covers the basic building blocks of a digital system including sampling, frequency domain analysis and elementary filters.
learning_outcomes: View linear circuits as examples of linear systems
Apply sampling theory to properly sample analog signals for digital processing in computers
Use Fourier methods to analyse circuits and signals in frequency domains
Analyse the physical processes governed by linear equations using basic techniques of linear system theory
Design simple digital signal processing systems
Apply Laplace transform techniques to compute the responses of linear circuits and systems driven by commonly encountered signals

title: Electric Machines and Power Systems
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Analyses the steady state performance of D.C. and A.C. (single and polyphase) machines in the context of their application. Space vector theory is introduced. Fundamental power system topics are introduced including transmission line parameters and steady state operation and power system representation.
learning_outcomes: Solve electrical engineering problems associated with electric machines and power systems.
Perform experiments, collect data using appropriate measurement equipment and analyse these data so that reasonable conclusions can be made.
Perform work safely and be aware of the workplace health and safety implications of the tasks carried out.
Perform as a member of a team in performing laboratory tasks in a setting which approximates an industrial environment.
Write technical reports associated with the laboratory exercises

title: Analog Electronics
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course deals with transistor amplifier circuits, multi-stage transistor amplifiers, differential amplifiers, power amplifiers, operational amplifiers, feedback amplifiers, and non-linear analogue circuits. The above areas along with analogue-to-digital and digital-to-analogue conversion are developed with view to interfacing sensors to computer equipment. Practical issues when implementing high-performance analogue electronic systems are also discussed.
learning_outcomes: Identify the structure, describe the operating principle, and perform analysis of multi-transistor, power amplifier, feedback and operational amplifier circuits.
Demonstrate the ability to perform signal and frequency response analysis of analogue transistor circuits.
Produce evidence-based documentation of complex analogue circuit analysis.
Avoid the common practical mistakes when implementing high-performance analogue circuits.

title: Principles and Design of Off-Grid Power Systems
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Off grid power systems offer many advantages over traditional electric power systems especially in areas where the cost of transmission is very high. Off grid systems are of particular importance in remote areas of Australia, in mining applications and in areas where electrical power may only be required transiently. Off grid systems whilst attractive in these and other scenarios offer up their own challenges in system stability, reliability and availability of supply. I.e. power quality. This course offers students the requisite knowledge to understand the particular issues associated with the design of off grid power systems and gives them the tools to tackle and solve these issues. Problems associated with long and short term energy storage, the use of renewable and non-renewable energy sources, load scheduling and shedding, etc are typical problems which will be investigated in this course. Students will become proficient in modelling electrical power systems and their components, solving the steady state power flow problem and investigating transient stability of modern off grid power systems which may or may not utilise traditional generation techniques.
learning_outcomes: Solve engineering problems associated with off grid power systems.
Write technical reports.
Perform as a member of a team whilst performing tasks in a setting which approximates an industrial environment.
Perform simulations, collect data using appropriate tools and analyse these data so that reasonable conclusions can be made.

title: Control System Design
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course covers both classical as well as optimal control design methods widely used in the industry. The topics include internal model control, state feedback control, noise modelling, observer design, and constrained optimal control.
learning_outcomes: Design optimal controllers by minimising quadratic costs.
Design state feedback controllers and associated observers.
Tune controllers for optimal performance.
Identify noise models from experimental data.
Incorporate application driven linear constraints in optimal control design.
Design internal model controllers.
Implement the designed controllers in practical applications.

title: Power Electronics and Renewable Energy Systems
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Power electronic circuits are an essential component of renewable and distributed energy sources including wind turbines, photovoltaic, marine energy systems and energy storage systems. This course covers the design and implementation of power electronic devices for off-grid and grid connected renewable energy systems. Power quality issues in renewable energy systems are investigated and some solutions are presented.
learning_outcomes: Justify the concepts of zero voltage and zero current switching as used in switched mode power supply converters
Explain the merits of switching electronic circuits over non-switched circuits in renewable energy power applications.
Classify power quality issues in renewable energy systems; recommend the use of power electronic systems to alleviate power quality problems.
Evaluate and design off-grid and grid connected converter systems for renewables.
Explain the use of power converters in photovoltaic and wind turbine applications.
Appraise the design implications of the relevant semiconductor physics issues that impinge on the practical use of power semiconductor devices.
Recognise the national and international safety standards that are relevant to grid connected inverters for renewable applications.
Analyse, design and construct switch mode power supply circuits, specifically the buck, boost and buck-boost converters.
Explain the main issues associated with the use of feedback control loops for switched mode power supplies.
Explain the operational principles of single and three phase PWM inverters.

title: Telecommunication Networks
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course provides an introduction to the principles & techniques of design, implementation, and analysis of communication networks which is the key technology for the modern ICT systems. Topics include: basis of voice, video, data and internet communications. network topologies, architecture. switching techniques, network design, basic queuing analysis, protocols. local and wide area networks, cellular wireless networks, TCP/IP/UDP/DHCP protocols, routing techniques, multicasting techniques. network security, Performance analysis and network simulation.
learning_outcomes: Develop problem solving approaches as applied in telecommunications networking areas.
Understand basic and some advanced concepts and techniques of telecommunications networks.
Understand the basic properties of internet and telecommunications traffic properties.
Understand telecommunication network design techniques and practical implementation issues.
Able to analyse performance of basic communication networks using both analytical and simulation techniques.

title: Analog and Digital Communications
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course introduces you to the basic principles and techniques used in analog and digital communications. You will learn analog and digital modulation techniques, communication receiver and transmitter design, baseband and bandpass communication techniques, line coding techniques, and noise analysis in various transmission environments. After completing the course, you will be able to use analytical techniques to evaluate the performance of analog and digital communication systems.
learning_outcomes: Identify the basic elements of a communication system
Analyse baseband signals in time domain and in frequency domain
Explain the importance of synchronisation in communication systems
Compare and contrast various analog and digital modulation and demodulation techniques
Evaluate the performance of modulation and demodulation techniques in various transmission environments

title: Digital and Computer Electronics 2
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will be introduced to the basic building blocks of an embedded system. You will design and develop software for commonly used peripheral devices as well as analyse and modify embedded software to make it fit for purpose.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and modify embedded software written by other professional developers
Identify the building blocks of an embedded system (hardware and software)
Develop software for commonly used peripheral devices
Perform a functional hardware design for an embedded system
Write application software using simple looping executives and real-time operating systems

title: Electrical Systems
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: In this course you will explore the operation and behaviour of electrical power systems. You will develop your knowledge of the physical and electrical properties of equipment used in power systems, and develop the analytical techniques and practical skills required to plan, design, operate and evaluation of electrical power systems.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the issues associated with the operation of power systems, including technical and non technical.
Use computer based simulation to analyse power systems. Discuss the limitations of analysis tools in terms of planning, design and operation.
Identify types of equipment used in power systems and describe the physical and electrical properties of equipment.
Plan, design, operate, analyse and evaluate power systems.

title: Signal Processing
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Provides an introduction to the fundamentals of signal processing with an emphasis on filtering and spectral measurement. Both continuous and discrete time processing methods are covered.
learning_outcomes: Design, implement and test digital filters
Collaborate effectively in group projects, integrating sophisticated signal processing solutions into practical applications.
Apply different transform domain techniques for signal processing
Execute signal processing applications with a deep understanding of underlying principles
Evaluate the fundamental uses, distinction and trade-offs between analog and digital signal processing methods
Demonstrate expertise in analog and digital filter design methodologies for demanding specifications

title: Advanced Drives and Power Electronics
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Analyses the dynamic behaviour of D.C. and A.C machines in the context of their application. Space vector theory is utilised to develop control strategies for these machines especially vector control and torque and flux control. Advanced topics in power electronics, including design of gate and base circuits, multilevel converters, and electric utility applications are investigated.
learning_outcomes: Solve electrical engineering problems associated with electric drive systems and electric machines.
Solve electrical engineering problems associated with grid connected power electronics.
Function effectively as an individual, and as a member or leader in diverse teams.
Perform as a member of a team in a high level engineering project making engineering design; resource allocation; component selection and algorithm applicability decisions.
Perform work safely and be aware of the workplace health and safety implications of the tasks carried out.
Perform experiments on AC and DC drives, collect data using appropriate measurement equipment and analyse this data so that reasonable conclusions can be made.

title: Programmable Logic Design
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the principles and practices of digital logic design using programmable logic devices and CAD tools. Topics include programmable logic devices and structures, design tools, hardware description language, datapath design, and control-unit design.
learning_outcomes: Design digital circuits using HDL and CAD tools
Understand and design pipelined circuits and processors
Gain experience in working in a group
Design a single cycle MIPS processor

title: Internet of Things
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course provides a sound introduction to the Internet of Things (IoT) technologies and system design concepts. The course will focus on important IoT topics, which includes: industrial standards, sensor/actuator/data devices, hardware, software, security, system design and performance analysis techniques.
learning_outcomes: Interpret and apply national and International IoT standards.
Apply professional skills to solve industry problems using IoT approaches.
Implement IoT firmware using embedded systems.
Design IoT system hardware and software.
Analyse performance of industrial IoT systems.

title: Final Year Engineering Project
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Final Year Projects represent the culmination of study towards the Bachelor of Engineering degree. Projects offer the opportunity to apply and extend material learned throughout the program. Assessment is by means of a seminar presentation, submission of a thesis, and a public demonstration of work undertaken. In contrast to the majority of courses studied elsewhere in the program, projects are undertaken individually or in small groups. This necessarily introduces the dimension of workload management into the program to enable completion of a large, relatively unstructured "assignment" over the course of the semester. The projects undertaken span a diverse range of topics, including theoretical, simulation and experimental studies, and vary from year to year. The emphasis is necessarily on facilitating student learning in technical, project management and presentation spheres. This course consists of a combination of Part A and Part B which reflects the full year multi term sequence program. As it is a single course of 30 units in one semester, approval by the Course Coordinator is required before enrolling in this course.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a sound technical knowledge of their selected project topic.
Communicate with engineers and the community at large in written an oral forms.
Undertake problem identification, formulation and solution.
Conduct an engineering project.
Demonstrate the knowledge, skills and attitudes of a professional engineer.
Design engineering solutions to complex problems utilising a systems approach.

faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
