Demonstrate a sound technical knowledge of their selected project topic.

title: Electrical Systems
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: In this course you will develop deeper learning of the physical and electrical properties of the equipment used in power systems. You will be able to discuss the analytical techniques used design, planning, operation and evaluation. You will develop higher-order analytical skills necessary to plan design and operate the various equipment used in power systems.
learning_outcomes: Research and present findings of a range of current issues associated with power systems.
Select an appropriate analysis tool to conduct the required mathematical analysis for planning, design, operation and evaluation of power systems.
Demonstrate expertise on the equipment used in power systems, and knowledge of the physical and electrical properties of this equipment.

title: Advanced Drives and Power Electronics
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course teaches students to analyse the dynamic behaviour of D.C. and A.C machines in the context of their application, and use the analysis to design electric drives. Space vector theory is utilised to develop control strategies for these machines, especially vector control and torque and flux control. Students investigate advanced topics in power electronics, including design of gate and base circuits, multilevel converters, and electric utility applications.
learning_outcomes: Perform work safely and be aware of the workplace health and safety implications of the tasks carried out.
Perform experiments on AC and DC drives, collect data using appropriate measurement equipment and analyse this data so that reasonable conclusions can be made.
Function effectively as an individual, and as a member or leader in diverse teams.
Solve complex problems associated with grid connected power electronics.
Solve problems associated with electric drive systems and electric machines, and design advanced drives
Perform as a member of a team in a high level engineering project making engineering design; resource allocation; component selection and algorithm applicability decisions.

title: Power Electronics and Renewable Systems
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Power electronic converters are essential for integration and utilisation of renewable and distributed energy sources including wind turbines, photovoltaic, marine energy systems and energy storage systems. This course covers the design and implementation of power electronic converters for off-grid and grid connected renewable energy systems. Control aspects and power quality issues in renewable energy systems are discussed and some solutions are presented.
learning_outcomes: Explain the merits of switching electronic circuits over non-switched circuits in renewable energy power applications.
Classify power quality issues in renewable energy systems; recommend the use of power electronic systems to alleviate power quality problems.
Explain the use of power converters in photovoltaic and wind turbine applications.
Justify the concepts of zero voltage and zero current switching as used in switched mode power supply converters.
Appraise the design implications of the relevant semiconductor physics issues that impinge on the practical use of power semiconductor devices.
Explain the operational principles of single and three phase PWM inverters.
Evaluate and design off-grid and grid connected converter systems for renewables.
Explain the main issues associated with the use of feedback control loops for switched mode power supplies.
Analyse, design and construct switch mode power supply circuits, specifically, the buck, boost and buck-boost converters.
Recognise the national and international safety standards that are relevant to grid connected inverters for renewable applications.

title: Medical and Industrial Electronic Product Design
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Industrial and commercial electronic products require the ability to sense physical quantities, communicate signals, and drive actuators and machinery. This course will introduce the principles required to build analogue and digital instrumentation electronics for industrial and commercial applications. Sensor types include electrochemical sensors, gas detection, pressure sensors, and flow rate sensors. The principles for designing these circuits will be combined with practical skills for fabricating and testing devices. Analogue circuit design topics include Radio Frequency (RF) signal transmission, filtering, signal conditioning, and data conversion. Analogue signals will be interfaced with industry-standard microcontrollers and communicated to supervisory systems using a fieldbus such as RS485 or industrial Ethernet. Drive and controller circuits for low-voltage actuators and motors are also investigated. By the end of the course, students will be able to design and build industrial electronic products that satisfy or optimise specifications such as accuracy, resolution, and cost.
learning_outcomes: Design robust industrial products that address industrial performance and safety standards.
Design analogue circuits for acquiring and conditioning physical measurements.
Design power management circuits for electronics, actuators, and motors.
Design high-frequency circuits and transmission lines for RF communications and digital signals.

title: Signal Processing
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with an advanced knowledge of signal processing with an emphasis on filtering, spectral analysis and applications such as image processing and signal compression.
learning_outcomes: Apply different transform domain techniques for signal processing
Design, implement and test digital filters
Demonstrate expertise in analog and digital filter design methodologies
Gain experience in working on a practical group project
Demonstrate skills and understand the principles of extensions and applications
Discuss the fundamental uses, distinction and trade-offs between analog and digital signal processing methods

title: Telecommunication Networks
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course introduces the principles and techniques used to design and develop computer and communication networks, including the Internet. Telecommunication networks are one of the core components of the ICT technology. Students in this course will learn telecommunication networking concepts and techniques including the network design techniques using industry standards. Network performance analysis and simulation techniques will be introduced in the course. Students should have background knowledge of computer architecture and basic statistics to understand the content of the course.
learning_outcomes: Design IP routers and multimedia networks.
Analyse performance of communication networks using both analytical and simulation technique
Develop problem solving approaches as applied in telecommunications networking areas.
Explain concepts and techniques of telecommunications networks.
Explain the basic properties of internet and telecommunications traffic.
Explain telecommunication network design techniques and practical implementation issues.

title: Control System Design
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course covers both classical as well as optimal control design methods widely used in the industry. The topics include internal model control, state feedback control, noise modelling, observer design, and constrained optimal control.
learning_outcomes: Tune controllers for optimal performance.
Design state feedback controllers and associated observers.
Design internal model controllers.
Incorporate application driven linear constraints in optimal control design.
Extend the concept learnt to design more advanced optimal control systems.
Design optimal controllers by minimising quadratic costs.
Identify noise models from experimental data.
Implement the designed controllers in practical applications.
Select appropriate control system architecture for a given practical application.

title: Final Year Project A
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Final Year Projects represent the culmination of study towards the Postgraduate Engineering degree. Projects offer the opportunity to apply the material learned throughout the program, extend and advance the knowledge through research. Assessment is by means of a seminar presentation, submission of a thesis, and a public demonstration of work undertaken. Projects are undertaken individually or in small groups. This necessarily introduces the dimension of workload management into the program to enable completion of a large, relatively unstructured "assignment" over the course of the semester. The projects undertaken span a diverse range of topics, including theoretical, simulation and experimental studies, and vary from year to year. The emphasis is necessarily on facilitating student learning in technical, project management and presentation spheres. This course consists of a combination of Part A and Part B which reflects the full year multi-term sequence program. Part A must be completed before Part B is commenced.
learning_outcomes: Undertake problem identification, formulation and solution.
Demonstrate a sound technical knowledge of their selected project topic.
Conduct an engineering project.
Design engineering solutions to complex problems utilising a systems approach.
Communicate with engineers and the community at large in written an oral forms.
Demonstrate the knowledge, skills and attitudes of a professional engineer.

title: Final Year Project B
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment

Projects offer the opportunity to apply the material learned throughout the program, extend and advance the knowledge through research. This necessarily introduces the dimension of workload management into the program to enable completion of a large, relatively unstructured "assignment" over the course of two semesters. The projects undertaken span a diverse range of topics, including theoretical, simulation and experimental studies, and vary from year to year. The emphasis is necessarily on facilitating student learning in technical, project management and presentation spheres. This course consists of a combination of Part A and Part B which reflects the full year multi term sequence program. Part A must be completed before Part B is commenced.
learning_outcomes: Conduct an engineering project.
Undertake problem identification, formulation and solution.
Demonstrate a sound technical knowledge of their selected project topic.
Communicate with engineers and the community at large in written an oral forms.
Design engineering solutions to complex problems utilising a systems approach.
Demonstrate the knowledge, skills and attitudes of a professional engineer.

title: Mindful Leadership
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Mindful Leadership supports participants towards the establishment of effective, sustainable leadership with a particular focus on self-awareness and self-management. It prepares participants for critical reflection, self-awareness, managing relationships and effective communication. The study of mindful leadership will support participants towards becoming less reactive and more focused in an ever-changing work environment. From a brain perspective this is at the core of all effective leadership behaviours towards engendering trust, strategic influence, clarity in decision-making, creativity and more. Leadership is key to effective global and intercultural interactions, identity and citizenship. Course content/case studies will include a range of international references and materials.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the strengths and limitations of their leadership behaviours and experiences.
Analyse how leaders shape organisational climate in their own organisation and compare and contrast findings with others in small groups.
Display an advanced awareness of their own predispositions, preferences and competencies in relation to exercising leadership.
Articulate how mindful leadership relates to their chosen profession.

title: Enterprise Strategy for Global Uncertainty
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Enterprise Strategy for Global Uncertainty focuses upon understanding and applying the critical enterprise processes of strategy creation and execution, innovation, entrepreneurship, management and leadership, in the pursuit of sustained enterprise success. International, contemporary case studies will be used to identify key issues and how theories, models, and principles explain (or fail to explain) various aspects of strategy. Participants will learn how to realise and grasp opportunities for ongoing growth in a world of constant, rapid, volatile change, so as to support ongoing, sustainable enterprise success. This course emphasises strategic thinking and action towards the creation, implementation and evaluation of both enterprise and operational-level strategies that can help an enterprise to keep ahead of competitors, while satisfying the demands of multiple stakeholders.
learning_outcomes: Research and communicate effectively (both written and orally through presentations) a range of leadership, innovation and entrepreneurship capabilities and ethical practices deemed critical for enterprise success.
Critically analyse and evaluate the competitive capabilities of an enterprise and its ability to maintain sustainable competitive advantage in turbulent environments.
Synthesise contemporary theories/principles to create, implement and evaluate strategies for sustainable effectiveness while meeting relevant stakeholder demands.
Identify and critically evaluate emerging trends, opportunities and challenges that impact enterprises in a range of environments;
Reflect on and articulate personal, team and workplace learning gained throughout the course.
Create, implement and evaluate enterprise strategies in complex, real-world case studies and a work-based project.

title: Sustainable Organisational Change
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Sustainable organisational change will be considered from a range of diverse perspectives: global and local; radical and minor; senior leadership and front line employees. The course emphasises the development of both analytical and procedural skills to assist participants in making important decisions about change while developing strategies to tackle the changes. Learning how to influence others and implement sustainable organisational change will enable student’s capabilities as a leader in their chosen field. Participants will identify an area for change within their own organisation, and work on a plan to operationalise the change, taking into account stakeholders, potential risks, budget constraints and more.
learning_outcomes: Cultivate capabilities required for leading and managing ongoing, long-term strategic, sustainable change including persuasive presentation skills.
Apply change theories, concepts and frameworks to analyse relevant aspects of their organisation.
Evaluate effective and ineffective organisational change and why change management programs often fail.
Reflect on organisational change principles and interventions in relation to individual, group and organisational change.

title: Innovation Management and Design
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Innovation Management and Design explores processes of innovation management from the perspective of both start-ups and established organisations. International and national case studies and current organisational examples will be used throughout. This course combines real world projects, bringing in external experts to help expand participants’ understanding of design thinking, new product and service innovation, entrepreneurial strategy, and the development of an entrepreneurial mindset. The course provides opportunities for participants to transform aspects of their workplaces. Specifically, it prepares managers and leaders for effective innovation within their organisations, building on their capabilities and knowledge as required for starting new ventures.
learning_outcomes: Analyse/synthesise and present information relating to the nature of new ventures and innovation within dynamic markets.
Reflect on and articulate personal, team and workplace learning gained throughout the course.
Research and plan for the role of people in facilitating and constraining innovation in organisational contexts.
Critically analyse innovation processes and the influence of organisational context on innovative activity.
Critically evaluate and utilize relevant innovation management and entrepreneurship concepts and models.

title: Tools, Techniques, and Transitions in a Digitally Changing Environment
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course provides executive-level insights into how technology, digitalisation, and digital transformation are reshaping industries, business models, and corporate strategies. It explores emerging technological trends, digital business tools, consumer behaviour shifts, and strategic frameworks for transforming conventional businesses into digital-first enterprises. Participants will engage in real-world case studies, strategic analyses, and interactive discussions to develop a digital transformation roadmap for their organisations. The course also covers cybersecurity, ethics, corporate governance, and regulatory challenges , ensuring leaders can navigate digital risks while driving sustainable business innovation. By the end of the course, students will be equipped with the strategic, operational, and leadership skills needed to lead digital transformation in their organisations and industries.
learning_outcomes: Develop strategic digital business model innovation.
Design & implement a digital business strategy.
Leverage on digital business tools & value chain transformation.
Understand and analyse the impact of technological & digitalisation trends.
Appraise cybersecurity, ethics & corporate governance in the digital age.
Understand digital marketing fundamentals & consumer behaviour in the digital world.

title: Project Design and Implementation
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course has been designed to encompass best practice project life cycles across international boundaries. It is intended to address the challenges faced by global and local project teams, providing participants with the knowledge to plan, create, implement, evaluate and modify projects designed to meet specific business goals and objectives. Participants will develop their skills and practices to manage projects that will support organisations in achieving sustainable outcomes for a range of projects. Participants will also develop the skills necessary to effectively manage team based business and technical projects.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the effectiveness of participant's own project planning, leadership and management skills.
Report, promote and communicate project outcomes including status reports.
Manage project, global and local stakeholders, as well as project suppliers.
Identify quality objectives and appropriate controls and measures to enable risk management.
Research and collate relevant information to prepare a project management plan for both a global and local program.

title: Strategic Financial Management
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Strategic Financial Management applies finance theory to the formulation and execution of an organisation’s strategy. International case studies, current organisational examples and reference to strategic financial management in industry contexts will be used throughout the course. With a focus on investment and financing decisions, the course equips participants with the tools necessary for managers to make and evaluate financial decisions in a competitive, changing and risky environment. This involves the analysis of data and the assessment of risk in valuing projects which inform strategic decision making in the creation of long-term shareholder value.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on the implications of strategic financial management in their own organisation's and their learning to date.
Critically analyse capital structure theory and the role of the financing decision in strategic management.
Perform a valuation on the basis of financial statement information.
Explain the role of asset pricing models and apply the concept of risk in project evaluation.
Practice strategic management to evaluate the role finance plays in strategic decision making.
Apply and evaluate analytical tools used in making investment decisions.

title: Executive Consulting for Managers and Leaders
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In this course participants will develop the capability required by executive leaders to design and consult on a strategic project to meet their organisation's needs. Participants will regularly confer with stakeholders in their organisations to deliver the project. International case studies and organisational examples in contemporary industry contexts will be used throughout the course. The consulting capstone project journey is transformative for participants and their organisations providing them with the opportunity to integrate, reflect on , and consolidate what they have learnt throughout the EMBA program.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the effectiveness of the project planning/design process through reflective reporting and peer review.
Generate a project progress report utilising stakeholder views that articulate a clear understanding of project requirements.
Apply interpersonal skills to effectively work in teams and communicate with stakeholders.
Create a project to address issues identified within their own organisations.

title: Introduction to Professional Engineering
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course is the first in a series of professional practice courses that introduces students to professional skills that are integral to an engineering workplace. The focus of all the courses is on integrating professional skills with technical skills. The courses also incorporate academic survival skills and support, particularly in first year. The course content is delivered by subject specialists and then students are asked to apply their theoretical learning to engineering-based assessments. This first year professional practice course explores a number of large-scale issues that are increasingly becoming the focus of engineering across the globe. Adding to this macro picture is a more micro examination of the day to day life of an engineer. The aim of exploring both the macro and micro perspectives is for students to not only gain a realistic picture of what to expect in their future career, but also an understanding of the myriad ways engineers can be part of the solution for some of the issues the world is currently facing. The course also focuses on developing underpinning skills such as practical problem solving, report writing, oral presentation skills, teamwork and W&HS that students will need in all years of their program. Students participate in a project of their choosing from provided options. Through the project, they demonstrate teamwork and other core skills. Each student is required to present a reflective learning journal as part of their assessment.
learning_outcomes: Utilise reflective tools to evaluate their own learning needs
Identify and discuss large and small scale engineering issues in the context of their engineering studies
Manage time as a resource and provide on-time deliverables in-line with industry-authentic client expectations
Experience working in environments with a structure and level of guidance representative of emerging industry
Construct written and oral communications in an accepted professional format
Identify the value and legal requirements of WHS by participating in WHS briefings and inductions and demonstrating safe workshop practice
Create a tangible engineering solution to a set problem
Identify team roles and work in teams to meet a specified purpose

title: Engineering Risk and Uncertainty
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the development and application of probability and risk concepts to provide solutions to common problems formulated in engineering practice. Its purpose is to provide the foundation material for later year courses so students are able to understand the risk and uncertainty that is part of engineering design.
learning_outcomes: Apply principles of making decisions under uncertainty.
Formulate and solve problems dealing with probability and statistics in engineering applications.
Apply risk management principles.
Develop practical skills in Monte Carlo simulation.
Employ the key concepts of probability, Bayesian inference and regression models to estimate uncertainty in engineering systems.

title: Introduction to Engineering Programming with Python
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the fundamentals of procedural programming and computational problem-solving using the Python programming language, with a focus on engineering applications. Designed for students with no prior programming experience, the course builds foundational skills in writing, testing, and debugging code to solve real-world engineering problems.
learning_outcomes: Describe the procedural programming approach and how it uses the input–process–output model to solve structured problems in engineering.
Translate real-world engineering problems into step-by-step algorithms suitable for implementation in Python.
Demonstrate effective use of PyCharm IDE and Jupyter Notebook for writing, running, and documenting code.
Write, test, and debug Python programs that implement computational algorithms to solve engineering problems.
Apply foundational programming constructs such as data types, variables, arrays/lists, operators, control flow, and functions.

title: Project/Directed Reading
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: The content of this course is variable, and depends on the context in which the course is to be taken. It may involve project, laboratory, literature search or theoretical work in a private study context under the direction of an appointed supervisor. Enrolment requires the permission of the relevant course coordinator and is based on project availability.
learning_outcomes: Outcomes are determined for the individual student depending on the circumstance in which they undertake the course.

title: Engineering Fluid Mechanics
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: In this course students are introduced to fluid mechanics concepts and their application in a range of engineering contexts. It lays the foundation for subsequent courses studied in the following years.
learning_outcomes: Conduct an experimental simulation
Solve fluid mechanics problems encountered by engineers
Demonstrate report writing skills commensurate with second year engineering students
Examine and analyse fluid systems

title: Modelling and Control
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to modelling and control of engineering systems. It presents tools that are fundamental for the analysis and design of such systems. The tools presented in the course use energy as a key element to develop modelling skills that can transcend physical domains and engineering specialisations. In addition, the course provides students with an understanding of the principle of feedback along with an introduction to classical control design techniques. Topics include fundamental limitations, stability of closed loop systems, control design for time domain and frequency domain specifications.
learning_outcomes: Perform numerical simulations of time-domain response of dynamic systems
Relate the frequency response of linear systems to transfer functions and system time response to sinusoidal excitation
Build computational models based on block diagrams and state-space equations
Demonstrate how different controller attributes influence the performance of a feedback control system
Formulate mathematical models of basic engineering systems with components from different physical domains (mechanical, electrical, hydraulic)
Design feedback controllers for typical response specifications in time as well as frequency domain
Analyse stability of equilibrium points of nonlinear systems via linearisation
Demonstrate how feedback can be used to control the response of a system in a desired manner, and recognize the limit of performance
Relate the time response of linear time-invariant systems to model structure and parameters

title: Sustainable Engineering Practice
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course is the second in a series of professional practice courses that introduces students to professional skills that are integral to an engineering workplace. The focus of all the courses is on integrating professional skills with technical skills. The course content is delivered by subject specialists and students are asked to apply their theoretical learning to engineering-based assessments. The second of the professional development courses introduces students to sustainability and `Green' engineering concepts. Students will continue their written communication skills building through the assignments and tutorials for this course.
learning_outcomes: Utilise reflective tools to evaluate their own learning.
Communicate the role of engineers and scientists within a resource-constrained world
Demonstrate effective oral and written communication skills for a purpose
Use the principles of Life Cycle Analysis to explain how sustainability applies to their personal and professional lives
Devise strategies for responding to complex, sustainable engineering demands
Articulate the founding principles of sustainable engineering and their application to open-ended problem scenarios

title: Engineering Work Integrated Learning
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: By completing this course students will have an exposure to a range of industry relevant topics and issues associated with contemporary professional practice. ENGG3000 is intended to support students moving into an industrial experience (IE) position and completing the degree requirements of professional placement which falls within the companion course ENGG3050. ENGG3000 will be a fully online core course common to all engineering programs at the University of Newcastle.
learning_outcomes: Identify the processes and benefits of Industrial Experience within the educational framework of an engineering career in Australia
Complete document preparation skills typical of job seeking
Gain a foundation in application and limitations of contemporary tools
Recognise and respond to issues around WH&S and personal wellbeing and safety

assessment_tasks.task_name: Personal alignment assessment against EA Stage 1

title: Work Experience in Industry
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Testing your knowledge, application of skills and improving graduate employability, Industrial Experience (IE) allows students to integrate real world skills and experience with theoretical concepts and knowledge obtained during studies in the Bachelor of Engineering (Honours), and Surveying (Honours) degrees and is assessed in reference to Engineers Australia Accreditation Requirements. Students will undertake a 12 week (full-time equivalent) relevant placement in a professional context. It is the student's responsibility to organise this placement or similar external activity for this course. Proposed placements will be subject to a review and approval process, and students must not proceed with a placement until it has been formally approved by the University.
learning_outcomes: Contribute as part of a team to achieve workplace tasks and resolve workplace problems.
Communicate effectively in the workplace, both verbally and in writing.

title: Machine Learning for Engineers
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This introductory course on statistical machine learning is intended to offer foundational concepts in both the theory and practice of this exciting area. It is intended for students with some background in physics, calculus and linear algebra and focuses on supervised learning, i.e., classification and regression, and introduces nonparametric Bayesian methods. A major theme of this course is to introduce flexible model structures, and incorporate fundamental limits (such as physical conservation laws) - where appropriate - so that predictions obey these limits. The course will cover a range of methods used in statistical machine learning and will review relevant areas of statistics and probability theory as required. These methods will be studied and applied to real data from various applications throughout the course. The course also covers important practical considerations such as cross-validation, model selection and the bias-variance trade-off. The course includes theory (e.g., derivations and proofs) as well as practice (labs and assignments) and is delivered using a problem-based format. The practical aspects are implemented using the industry standard programming language, MATLAB, which will be introduced in context throughout the course.
learning_outcomes: Design solutions that adhere to fundamental limits, where appropriate
Propose appropriate flexible models for different problem domains
Design and train deep neural-networks for classification
Construct Gaussian Process models for nonparametric modelling
Apply machine learning methods to large-data problems
Select a model using cross-validation and bias-variance trade-offs
Quantify the uncertainty of predictions and estimates
Implement solutions in MATLAB

title: Managing Engineering Projects
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course is the third in a series of professional practice courses that introduces students to professional skills that are integral to an engineering workplace. The focus of all the courses is on integrating professional skills with technical skills. This third professional practice course strongly focuses on project management tools and techniques as defined by the Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK). The course runs in a 'flipped' classroom mode where students are required to read/watch a variety of project management resources prior to each week's lecture . Where possible, each lecture will include a seminar by an external senior practicing project manager on that week's topic. As these external guests are giving up their time for the benefit of the student body, and in the spirit of professionalism, 100% attendance is expected at all presentations. Due to the 'commercial in confidence' nature of some aspects presented, any recordings captured will (by necessity) be edited before release. Students who are not located at the Callaghan Campus will have access to lecture presentations via UoN Capture. In relation to program completion for continuing students, ENGG3500 is a direct replacement for GENG3830.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate effective interpersonal, communication and management skills to plan a project and meet a specified purpose
Apply the most appropriate tools and techniques to effectively plan and manage a project
Reflect on and evaluate their own input and output during the course

Develop a range of project management documents that address project scope, schedule, quality, communication, procurement, costs, risk, stakeholders, work breakdown, ethical issues, and resource breakdown
Demonstrate a working knowledge of the key concepts and theories of project management as per the Project Management Body of Knowledge (PMBOK)

title: Nonlinear Control and Estimation
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course is intended to introduce students to a range of techniques for control and estimation for nonlinear systems. Specifically, the course will cover some basic concepts of nonlinear systems and control theory; nonlinear model predictive control; and modern estimation and observer techniques for nonlinear systems. The course includes laboratory and simulation experiments to apply the concepts taught.
learning_outcomes: Design and implement observers and estimators for nonlinear systems
Design and implement systems to improve nonlinear system performance in the presence of constraints
Configure, implement and test Nonlinear Model Predictive Controllers for simple nonlinear systems
Design and implement simple feedback control systems for regulating a nonlinear system

title: Engineering Final Year Project A
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Working under broad direction of a chosen academic supervisor, students undertake a substantial and open-ended engineering project that encompasses research, problem solving, oral communication, and report writing. Projects vary from highly theoretical research, through to applied engineering projects, but in all projects a high level of personal drive is required to optimise a substantial outcome. The ‘FYP’ is your ‘Capstone’ educational experience allowing you to draw elements from across your degree to a single point of focus, you will need to demonstrate exceptional self-management and need to clearly demonstrate you are in control and leading the project through all stages. Your Part A performance, reflecting the initial 150 hours of work carries a Compulsory Component such that if your Part A performance does not demonstrate sufficient commitment or progress in the project, you can be excluded from the Part B component.
learning_outcomes: Engage in self-directed learning to acquire new knowledge and skills for solving emerging engineering problems.
Organize and manage information and documentation effectively to support engineering projects.
Communicate technical and non-technical information clearly and effectively to diverse audiences, including engineering teams and the wider community.
Design and implement creative and innovative solutions to address challenges encountered in engineering contexts.
Analyse complex engineering problems and devise appropriate, evidence-based solutions.
Plan, execute, and manage engineering projects, ensuring adherence to deadlines and timely submission of deliverables.

title: Introduction to English Literature
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course introduces key skills in the study of English literature and creative writing. It will examine a variety of texts written in different genres in order to develop an understanding of how writers across literary history have deployed the resources of language to convey their ideas and concerns. The course will focus on developing skills in literary analysis as preparation for further study of literature and/or creative writing. In addition to practice in essay writing, you will be offered the opportunity to experiment with creative writing in response to the material studied.
learning_outcomes: Construct persuasive arguments about literary narratives, informed by existing scholarship, at a basic level.
Interpret and analyse literary works from different genres and eras at a basic level.
Recognise a variety of literary forms and key terms appropriate to understanding of works in those forms.
Apply core linguistic concepts and principles important in the analysis of literature in English.
Communicate key literary concepts and findings in appropriate written forms.

title: Australian Stories
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to Australian literature and culture through consideration of constructions of Australian identities in a broad range of texts including fiction, non-fiction, poetry, plays, film and television.
learning_outcomes: Recognise the different discourses of nationhood and citizenship attached to these representations.
Provide in-depth analysis and critique of selected course texts.
Develop core skills in written and oral communication.
Identify different representations of Australian cultural identity in popular literature, film and television.

title: Critical Reading and Writing
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course will introduce students to key skills in the English major by developing their expertise in reading, writing, and critical thinking. It will promote an appreciation of the multi-faceted resources of language, and of the challenges and satisfactions entailed in writing, and in writing about, literature and culture.
learning_outcomes: Integrate research with critical analysis and argument;
Write research essays using critical analysis and argument;
Outline a research project in the discipline of English;
Employ terms and techniques necessary for the analysis of literature in English;
Identify a range of cultural and linguistic issues important in the analysis of literature in English.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Reading summary and Author Q&A: summary and reflection

title: Creative Writing: Introduction
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course offers entry-level training in creative writing. Through a close reading and discussion of texts across the major literary forms, as well as through developing their own writing, students are familiarised with the techniques and strategies used by creative writers and are trained to adapt these tools to produce their own work.
learning_outcomes: Use the workshop model of critiquing to develop their own written work and that of others.
Develop original creative works that reflect their engagement with writing craft and the work of contemporary creative writing practitioners.
Edit and refine written language in terms of grammar and sentence construction.
Identify a range of techniques and elements of writing craft in poetry, creative nonfiction and fiction.

title: Stories in Context: Fiction, Drama, Film
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Provides introductory-level study of narratives of various kinds (fiction, drama, film) drawn from various periods, focusing on the transformation of particular stories, characters, and situations between texts created in different genres or at different times. We shall examine how form itself conveys meaning, and thus how literary forms have been employed to represent private and public concerns in a variety of cultural contexts.
learning_outcomes: Communicate literary ideas in appropriate written and digital forms at basic level.
Explain the significance of cultural contexts in shaping specific literary narratives.
Analyse and interpret narratives from different genres and eras at basic level.
Construct persuasive arguments about literary narratives, informed by existing scholarship, at basic level.
Demonstrate close acquaintance with a number of literary and dramatic works from a range of periods and genres.

title: Classics of World Literature
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course gives you the opportunity to familiarise yourself with some of the classic texts of world literature - mainly works by foreign-language authors in English translation. You will hone your skills in textual analysis and critical thinking by engaging in careful analysis of the individual texts, aiming to identify their main features as well as the historical and cultural frameworks within which they were produced. You will also develop an understanding of some of the key challenges involved in reading world literature: national vs global reading strategies, the circulation of literary texts across borders, and reading literature in translation. Course readings will, where possible, be arranged thematically. Past themes include “Origins of the Novel” and “Cultural Meetings” (on travel and migration literature).
learning_outcomes: Discuss the literary, historical, social and cultural backgrounds of these texts.
Identify some of the main theoretical and methodological issues involved in reading World Literature.
Analyse literary texts in English or English translation in terms of their main stylistic and thematic features.
Communicate findings clearly and engagingly.

title: Shakespeare & Co
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course offers an introduction to literature from the English Renaissance, or Early Modern Period, covering poetry, prose, drama, and other forms prevalent in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. It will provide training in the set of scholarly skills necessary for the study of the distinctive styles and concerns of this literature, including close reading, textual analysis, and the assessment of central critical debates. The course will permit students to reflect on their personal and intellectual relationship to texts from the period.
learning_outcomes: Compare cultural and intercultural concerns between the early modern period and our own;
Effectively interpret and analyse Renaissance literary works at intermediate undergraduate level;
Use communication skills appropriate to intermediate undergraduate level, including personal reflection;
Recognise and discuss aspects and forms of Renaissance Literature;
Apply critical and theoretical debates and approaches to readings of Renaissance Literature;
Develop skills in information literacy and use technology to perform research.

title: Literary Theory and Practice
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course will take your understanding and appreciation of literary texts to the next level. You will become familiar with a range of key concepts and theoretical problems of Literary Studies and will thereby acquire a solid foundation for your further studies in English & Writing and beyond. Equipped with an expanded conceptual toolbox, you will be able to reflect on your own reading practice and ask new and more advanced questions of literary texts. Rather than simply internalising the tenets of various schools of criticism, you will learn to engage actively and critically with theoretical ideas while also developing your ability to argue for and against specific theoretical positions. Ultimately, the course aims to enhance your ability to think independently about literature and the various ways in which it engages with the world.
learning_outcomes: Construct reasoned arguments for and against a theoretical position;
Critically analyse theoretical texts;
Explain a range of key concepts and problems in Literary Studies;
Communicate theoretical ideas in clear and effective language.

assessment_tasks.task_name: 1 reflective journal due at the end of semester

title: Novel Ideas: Selves and Worlds
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Novel Ideas: Selves and Worlds explores the many different voices of the novel from the eighteenth century to the present day, and considers how these voices are assimilated by readers and reading communities. It looks at how this literary form, sometimes regarded as trivial entertainment, has developed into a powerful and highly theorised literary genre, capable of handling complex cultural and psychological material, and of effecting profound social impact.
learning_outcomes: Examine the key formal, thematic, and contextual characteristics of individual novels.
Conduct research independently and express clear and informed arguments.
Develop persuasive written responses both individually and in groups.
Outline the history of the novel from the eighteenth century to the present day.

title: Mind and Monstrosity: Victorian Novel
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to an exciting range of Victorian novels. Our study of key texts and their contexts will explore connections between Gothic monstrosity and psychological realism in the long nineteenth century. Focusing primarily on novels from the period 1837 to 1901, with some attention to precursor texts and other genres (such as the short story) as well as more recent responses to or adaptations of the nineteenth-century novel, we will investigate the ways that cultural anxieties and scientific and technological developments have historically affected literature (and vice versa). What does it mean to be human? How has this question been raised within the Gothic and realist traditions at different cultural moments? What sorts of monsters terrify or haunt us and how do they evolve to keep pace with the gaps in our certainties? From doubling to degeneration, madness to the metropolis, villain to vampire, empire to the threat of extinction, this course examines the work of writers such as Mary Shelley, Charles Dickens, Edgar Allan Poe, Charlotte and Emily Bronte, Wilkie Collins, George Eliot, Bram Stoker and H.G. Wells.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of a range of texts, authors and contexts of the long nineteenth century, as well as the ways in which literature of this important period has shaped our modern sensibilities.
Construct convincing analyses of primary and secondary texts.
Reflect through both critical and creative activities upon the cultural, social, historical and aesthetic concerns of literature of the long nineteenth century.
Develop cogent written responses both individually and in groups.
Apply interpretive skills to complex issues concerning the Victorian novel and Gothic and realist literature.
Conduct research independently and express clear and informed arguments.

title: Modernisms
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course provides an introduction to literary Modernism as an artistic movement that transformed literary production in Europe and the United States from the end of the nineteenth century and across the first half of the twentieth century. In response to the unsettling social, political, and cultural changes brought about by an era of 'modernity', writers sought to create art that would engage with and reflect these changes. Through the study of key Modernist texts (prose and poetry), students will learn about the diverse innovations in form, style, and subject matter characteristic of the movement. Works studied may be British, American, or both.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and interpret a range of Modernist texts;
Communicate key literary concepts and findings in appropriate written forms.
Recognise and discuss features of Modernist literary texts;
Construct persuasive arguments, informed by existing scholarship, about the operations of Modernist literary works;
Explain how specific Modernist literary works reflect on social and artistic developments and concepts from the era;

title: Contemporary Australian Literature
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Examines recent writing of fiction in Australia from 1990 to the present. It covers a range of genres, including novel, short story, autobiography and metafiction, and explores the tension between postmodernism and politics in the field through an examination of the discourses of gender, class, race and sexuality in each text.
learning_outcomes: A detailed understanding of the theoretical concepts informing recent shifts in the field.
A detailed knowledge of the texts on the course and of the literary field under examination;
The ability to analyse literary texts in their social contexts; and

title: Sex and Death on the Renaissance Stage
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course offers an in-depth exploration of English Renaissance theatre and its representations of desire and death on stage. Through studying five plays central to the period, students will learn about genres such as revenge tragedy and tragicomedy, understandings of sexuality and gender, and death and mourning. There will also be a focus on London's theatres and publishing industry. Students will be introduced to major theoretical and methodological approaches to the field and will be encouraged to undertake advanced research in the topic area.
learning_outcomes: Develop written communication skills by reflecting on the cultural impact of Renaissance literature;
Develop understanding of Renaissance concepts of genre and gender.
Demonstrate an understanding of Renaissance modes of cultural production such as performance and print, different literary genres, and themes;
Interpret Renaissance literary works at advanced undergraduate level;
Analyse critical and theoretical debates surrounding Renaissance Literature;

title: Children's Literature
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course provides a representative survey of children's literature. Topics investigated will include the nature and social context of children's literature, the relationship between text and illustration, the presentation of social issues in writing for children, the role of imagination and fantasy, and the representation of Australian childhood.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the inter-relationship of text and illustrations.
Interpret the presentation of cultural variation, human relationships and social tensions in children's literature.
Identify different genres of children's literature.
Apply reading and critical analysis skills at an intermediate level.
Discuss linguistic and literary properties common in literature written for children.

title: Writing Short Fiction
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Short fiction is often the first challenge in the creative writer’s career and has become a vital component of major writing programs across the world. This course offers a practice-led approach to understanding and applying the techniques used to create short stories. Both the work of Australian and international writers, as well as the original writing of students, will be used to explore this foundational literary form.
learning_outcomes: Create works of short fiction that reflect an understanding of writing craft.
Identify key writing elements used in short fiction.
Explain the techniques used by fiction writers.
Apply editorial processes to the development of written work.

title: Creative Writing: Life Writing
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Do you want to learn how to turn your life experience into compelling narrative? This course explores various forms of life writing such as memoir (including family memoir, graphic memoir and medical memoir), personal essays on aspects of culture and identity, place, environmental and travel writing. Students learn about the creative possibilities in the blending of fact and fiction that occurs in creative nonfiction and how to master the subjective voice in their own writing.
learning_outcomes: Experiment with key writing techniques used to shape creative nonfiction text
Apply core skills in written communication, in both critical analysis and creative practice.
Identify forms of life writing across an array of voices both local and global

title: Writing for Social Change
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Writing for Social Change is both a longstanding literary tradition and a current professional practice, used in a myriad of careers from politics, policy and non-profits, to advocacy, activism and the arts. This course will explore ways that authors and other artists have used songs and slogans, sci-fi and social protest, memoir and manifesto, to articulate social critique. Texts may include important works from First Nations, People of Colour, feminist, queer, and anti-capitalist traditions, as well as more recent writing from the Black Lives Matter, #MeToo and environmental movements. Students will learn to analyse and employ the rhetoric of persuasion, with the option to work on a collaborative social change campaign or an individual critical or creative work.
learning_outcomes: Recognise different traditions of social change literature in historical contexts;
Create publishable content for creative, critical or collaborative social change projects.
Interpret and employ the conventions of persuasive rhetoric;
Critically examine contemporary social change literature in current cultural contexts;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Written Assignment – Critical, Creative, or Collaborative Project

title: Creative Writing: Writing Sci-Fi and Fantasy
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The course will introduce students to a practice-based understanding of the genres of science fiction and fantasy. Students will engage with a range of writing techniques and strategies appropriate for all forms of fiction and learn how to combine the conventions of the genre with their own writing style and ambitions. This course is designed both for aspiring writers of science fiction and fantasy and those who are interested in taking a hands-on and creative approach to understanding these genres.
learning_outcomes: Identify key features of the literary genres of fantasy and science fiction.
Develop original works that use key features of the science fiction and fantasy genres.
Use a range of creative writing strategies to turn ideas, concepts, and knowledge into compelling fiction.
Construct and edit written language that is impactful and grammatically correct.

title: Crime Fiction: Mutations of a Genre
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will gain detailed knowledge of one of the most popular and widely read literary genres: crime fiction. You will become familiar with the evolution of the genre from the early nineteenth century to the present day and will develop advanced skills in analysing and contextualising crime fiction texts from the UK, the US, Australia and beyond. The course as a whole challenges the traditional view of crime fiction as formulaic “genre fiction”, seeing instead the genre as a form of literature defined by its diligent investigation of some of the key issues of modern society: justice, inequality, urban life, gender, sexuality, race and many others.
learning_outcomes: Outline the history of crime fiction and some of the key crime fiction subgenres.
Debate the concept of â€œpopular literatureâ€�, its significance in modern culture and its limitations.
Examine the key formal, thematic and contextual characteristic of individual crime fiction texts.
Analyse crime fiction texts as investigations of specific political, social or philosophical issues.
Investigate crime fiction texts in relation to their genre and the idea of genre evolution.

assessment_tasks.task_name: 1500 word essay and interactive oral component

title: Women's Writing
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will read literature written by women from the 14th century CE to today. The course focuses on writing produced in the English-speaking world but may include significant works in translation. You will learn about the formal features of women’s writing, including the ways women adopt, adapt, and challenge broader literary traditions. The course explores the conditions under which women wrote and published as well as how their works were received by their first readers. It provides opportunities not only to explore key issues and debates in contemporary scholarship on women’s writing but to contribute to them through a collaborative class project. Together, we will think about what constitutes “women’s writing” and the effects (both positive and negative) of categorizing literary works in this way.
learning_outcomes: Explain and participate in critical and theoretical debates surrounding women's writing at advanced undergraduate level;
Explain cultural, intercultural, and transhistorical concerns relating to women's writing;
Locate and compile selections from primary and secondary sources relevant to women authors.
Interpret literary works by women at an advanced undergraduate level;

title: Creative Writing: Emerging Writers’ Toolkit
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Students in this course will explore contemporary creative writing practices and contexts, including new media literary cultures. The course aims to enable our graduates to become successful industry practitioners who are engaged with the broader emerging writers' community, locally, nationally and on-line. The course will also prepare students who wish to take an academic pathway to advance to honours and further study.
learning_outcomes: Conduct research independently, and to express clear and informed arguments, orally and in writing, on aspects of Creative Writing;
Demonstrate awareness of contemporary debates and issues in Creative Writing;
Apply practical skills learnt in Creative Writing to industry contexts.
Apply advanced interpretive skills to comprehension of contemporary practice in Creative Writing;

title: Satire and Its Forms
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course will explore satire across a range of historical contexts, modes, and media. It looks at verse satire, the satirical novel, and satirical TV shows and movies. It will primarily be concerned with understanding the forms that satire takes. This includes an examination of the various forms of irony, as well as an understanding of the various forms of parody, such as burlesque, travesty, and persiflage.
learning_outcomes: Incorporate a diverse range of relevant creative and critical perspectives on topics of contemporary interest.
Communicate Humanities research to varied audiences using a variety of forms at an advanced level.
Apply critical reasoning, creative thinking, and problem-solving skills to answer complex questions in areas of the Humanities.
Interpret literary and media works at an advanced undergraduate level.

title: Imagination, Nature, Freedom: Romantic Literature
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Imagination, Nature, Freedom: Romantic Literature explores some of the key voices of British and American Romanticism from the 1780s to the 1860s. The course introduces students to Romantic poetry and fiction in relation to its intellectual, philosophical, artistic, cultural, and societal contexts: including revolution, urbanisation, industrialisation, slavery, and empire. It looks at how the Romantic movement - with its rebellion against pure rationalism - redefined ideas about thought, feeling, nature, selfhood, the role of the writer, and the humanitarian impulse which have much to say to our present cultural moment.
learning_outcomes: Outline the history and contexts of Romanticism.
Conduct research independently and express clear and informed arguments.
Examine the key formal, thematic, and contextual characteristics of individual literary works.
Develop persuasive written responses both individually and in groups.

title: Indigenous Australia in Literature: Listenin' Up
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course centres stories written, told and shared by Aboriginal Australians for the benefit of all readers. Through "listening"/reading to these stories that come from Country, the course employs Marcia Langton's notion of "intersubjectivity" so that students, Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal, can engage with Aboriginal ways of knowing through stories that share public knowledge about this land. This course uses both Indigenous and non-Indigenous texts to examine the ways in which "Aboriginality" and "whiteness" interact in fictional and non-fictional texts.
learning_outcomes: Critique representations of Indigenous and non-Indigenous relationships in Australian literature.
Identify issues related to "race" relations in Australian literature.
Recognise how representations of identity are constructed and used in Australian literature.
Analyse the construction of "whiteness" in Indigenous and non-Indigenous representations.
Develop responses to local, national and global ways of telling stories.

title: Reading Across Borders: Modern World Literature
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will gain skills in reading contemporary literature across borders as well in navigating a literary world that is increasingly transnational and defined by the international circulation of texts. You will become familiar with the main theoretical positions within the field of World Literature Studies and will develop a keen understanding of both the challenges and the potentials of reading literature outside national frameworks. Above all, you will engage in detailed analysis of a range of exciting contemporary texts from around the world. The aim will be to understand these texts in terms of their key formal and thematic aspects as well as to read them transnationally as they travel across national borders. The readings will be selected in such a way that they speak to each other and lend themselves to comparative analysis. The focal point may be a specific genre or theme that bring to light the internationalisation of the literary field. Texts written by foreign-language authors are examined in English translation.
learning_outcomes: Apply critical/creative thinking skills in planning and writing an analytical essay.
Analyse individual texts with the aim of identifying their major formal and thematic aspects.
Debate some of the key theoretical ideas and problems of World Literature Studies.
Interpret examples of World Literature in translation in terms of the wider cultural and political contexts to which they respond.
Communicate evidence-based arguments and findings in speech and writing.

title: Creative Writing: Poetry and Poetics
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course explores the various forms of poetry and the poetic ideas which inform them. Traditional as well as open forms are examined in detail, supplemented by readings of poetic theory from a historical range of sources. Students will learn about the nexus between theory and creative practice. They will study the specialised skills and techniques that turn an experience or memory into a compelling poem.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the poetic ideas and theories which inform particular kinds of poetry.
Identify a range of different forms of poetry.
Discuss key techniques involved in shaping a poem.
Apply core skills in written communication, in textual analysis and in creative practice.
Develop a creative voice of their own through exposure to an array of local and global texts.

title: The Novel Writing Toolkit
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course offers advanced training in fiction writing for students aiming to write their first novel. Through a study of different genres and the development of their own work and ideas, students will explore the narrative options available in the writing of a novel. With a focus on scene and chapter writing, they will learn how to edit, redraft and shape a larger work both collaboratively and independently.
learning_outcomes: Describe and analyse the technical decisions made by novelists writing in different genres.
Develop scenes and opening chapters that reflect the technical features of novelistic writing.
Use a range of writing techniques common to prose fiction.
Edit and refine written language in terms of grammar and sentence construction.
Identify through independent research and class discussion, issues relating to the writing of novels such as genre, target audience and writing process.

title: Creative Writing: Fiction, Medicine, Psychology
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course offers students the opportunity to develop their understanding of, and practical skills in, the writing of prose fiction. By taking narratives of medicine and psychology as the focus, this course enables a close consideration of strategies for representing the body, the mind, pain, and healing in fiction. The course contributes to students' future career potential – whether as creative or other kinds of professional writers – and provides them with a better understanding of how literary works are constructed. Students will develop a narrative-based understanding of experiences of illness and healing. Using the workshop model of creative writing, students will develop the tools to write creatively about traumatic or difficult topics in a sensitive and engaging way. Topics will be explored theoretically and with the aid of exemplars, but the main focus of both class work and independent study will be the practical application of creative and aesthetic principles. Students in this course will use the workshop model of critiquing to develop their own written work and that of others.
learning_outcomes: Apply a range of techniques and elements of writing craft in fiction, with particular emphasis on interactions between narrative, medicine, and psychology.
Edit and refine written language in terms of grammar and sentence construction; voice and point of view; plot and structure; creative balance of nuance and detail.
Develop original creative works that reflect their engagement with the fields of medicine and psychology.
Critique their own written work and that of others.

title: Creative Writing: Science Fiction and Fantasy
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The course will introduce students to a practice-based understanding of the genres of science fiction and fantasy. Students will engage with a range of writing techniques and strategies appropriate for all forms of fiction and learn how to combine the conventions of the genre with their own writing style and ambitions. This course is designed both for aspiring writers of science fiction and fantasy and those who are interested in taking a hands-on and creative approach to understanding these genres.
learning_outcomes: Identify and analyse key features of the literary genres of fantasy and speculative fiction.
Effectively construct and edit written language in terms of grammar and impact.
Use a range of creative writing strategies to turn ideas, concepts, and knowledge into compelling fiction.
Develop original works that demonstrate an engagement with the conventions and features of the genres of fantasy and science fiction.

title: Children's Fantasy Literature
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Examines fantasy literature for children and young adults from the "Golden Age" in the late nineteenth century to the present time. We will consider such issues as ideas of the hero and the child's sense of identity; attitudes to race and power and other areas of broader cultural concern; the location of imaginary spaces; and the values attached to art and the imagination.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate interpretive and analytic skills necessary to comprehend the practice of children's fantasy writing since the late nineteenth century;
Reflect on social and cultural concerns in children's fantasy literature;
Demonstrate developed understanding of a number of important works of children's fantasy literature from the late nineteenth century to the present;
Demonstrate essay-writing and research skills at advanced undergraduate level.
Show familiarity with critical debates about children's fantasy literature;

title: Principles of Editing and Publishing
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to appropriate theories and methods for editing and designing a book for publication. It is practice-based with a strong emphasis on grammar, technical aspects of editing, creation of style guides and principles of book design. The practical outcome of the course is the creation of a print-ready pdf.
learning_outcomes: Identify and correct common grammatical errors
Apply basic skills in book design and layout
Demonstrate a critical understanding of ethical, theoretical and practical considerations of editing and publishing
Design a style guide appropriate for a publishing project
Apply basic copy editing skill using editing marks in manual mark-up, and Track Changes in Microsoft Word

assessment_tasks.task_name: In Term Test - in-class editing test

title: Young Adult Literature: Storying the World through Young Adult Voices
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course focuses on popular, speculative, and realist young adult (YA) literature and other YA texts that engage with and shift dominant narratives of the world. In particular, we will examine how human relationships with their environment are storied in YA genres. Students will consider how positive and negative images of societies are constructed in the literature, and will examine representations of power and authority and rebellion against these. Students will learn how to identify, engage with, and contribute to contemporary discussions about subjectivity, agency and authority.
learning_outcomes: Interpret the relationships between different historical, socio-economic and cultural contexts in YA literature, including Aboriginal ways of knowing;
Synthesise YA scholarship to create and apply literary approaches to YA literature.
Identify and explain literary movements in the representation of YA voices;
Evaluate a range of theoretical issues relating to YA texts;
Analyse in both formal and informal academic writing, different representations of YA literature;

title: Adaptations: Books, Films, Shows and Games
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The course will explore traditional adaptations from novel to film, or Shakespeare to screen, alongside translations of texts across different media types, including television, comics, games, and poetry. Students will be encouraged to identify differences and similarities between a text and its adaptation(s), as well as looking beyond the concept of ‘fidelity’ to ask how else an adaptation might be working.
learning_outcomes: Design and deliver an effective and efficient oral presentation.
Apply critical reasoning, creative thinking, and problem-solving skills to ask and answer complex questions about adaptation.
Interpret literary and other texts at an advanced undergraduate level.
Identify distinct techniques of different forms and genres.
Analyse and describe the process of adaptation as revealed in specific examples.

title: Environmental Science Concepts and Methods
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: The earth is facing unprecedented human-induced pressures that threaten the functioning of our ecosystems. Environmental Science attempts to explain how life on Earth is sustained, what contributes to our many environmental problems, and how these problems can be solved. Environmental Science & Management stands at the interface between humans and the Earth and explores the interactions and relations between them. This course introduces students to a number of the basic multidisciplinary concepts which are fundamental to understanding these interrelationships. Students will explore the methods which environmental scientists use in monitoring, measuring and assessing environmental variables. The course develops a firm understanding of scientific principles as applied to these variables and the necessary grounding for continuing studies in the Environmental Sciences.
learning_outcomes: Apply methods to sample and specimen collection, field observation, recording, laboratory techniques and experimental design;
Summarise core and fundamental knowledge of concepts and methods appropriate to environmental science;
Manipulate data, interpret trends, analyse and communicate results associated with the measurement of environmental variables;
Monitor, measure and assess a variety of environmental variables;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Practical examination based on practical activities
Practical exercises in the lab and field written assignments based on practical activities

title: Physical and Chemical Environmental Systems
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Environmental Science is a multidisciplinary approach to understanding and solving the interactions between humans and the Earth. This course introduces students to a number of the basic physical and chemical environmental systems which are fundamental to understanding these interrelationships.
