EPEDUC101 and EPEDUC201 are complementary courses and students can choose to study one or both courses in their program.
learning_outcomes: Define key introductory concepts in the fields of educational sociology, philosophy and psychology and explain the contribution of seminal thinkers to the study of education.
Recount key points in the historical development of schooling and education policy in Australia including Indigenous knowledges.
Reflect knowledgeably and critically on their own and others' educational experiences using insight gained during the course.
Define basic features of pedagogy, curriculum and assessment.

Employ a range of academic reading, writing and oral skills and attitudes, including reflective, analytical and critical thinking, at a level suitable for successful university study at the undergraduate level.

title: Foundations in Education: Contemporary Issues in Schooling
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: EPEDUC201 provides enabling students with the opportunity to deeply explore some of the challenges related to educating in Australia. The course guides students through an exploration of critical issues in education. EPEDUC101 and EPEDUC201 are complementary courses and students can choose to study one or both courses in their program.
learning_outcomes: Define basic features of pedagogy, curriculum and assessment, and evaluate how these impact on the experiences of diverse learners.
Define and apply key introductory concepts and theories in the fields of educational sociology, philosophy and psychology to aspects of contemporary schooling.
Reflect knowledgeably and critically on their own and others' educational experiences, as well as the social and professional role of teachers, using insight gained during the course.
Recount key points in the historical development of schooling and education policy in Australia including Indigenous pedagogies, and evaluate how they have impacted on contemporary education.
Employ a range of academic reading, writing and oral skills and attitudes, including analytical and critical thinking, at a level suitable for successful university study at the undergraduate level.

title: Engineering Physics
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: EPENGG101 introduces students to the problem solving skills that are integral to an engineering workplace. The focus of the course is on integrating critical thinking with an introduction to physics and physics problem solving. The course will develop practical problem solving, report writing, oral presentation skills and teamwork, as essential skills for future undergraduate study. Students will participate in a range of learning activities including tutorials, laboratories, and a group project. These activities will further their understanding of the engineering problem solving cycle and the professional and technical skills engineers require. Students who intend to study engineering and meet the assumed knowledge for EPPHYS152 and EPPHYS252 should enrol in EPPHYS152 and EPPHYS252 instead of EPENGG101.
learning_outcomes: Create a tangible engineering solution to a set problem.
Construct written and oral communications in an accepted professional format.
Explain the key elements of the engineering problem solving cycle.
Choose and apply appropriate problem solving and decision-making processes and methods.
Identify team roles and work in teams to meet a specified purpose.
Solve problems using the principles of physics with appropriate mathematics.

title: Foundational Studies in Mathematics
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Many relationships in the real world can be modelled via a function. The course introduces common functions used in the sciences, equips students with the tools of differential and integral calculus to analyse the properties of functions, and develops an understanding of the role of functions and calculus in real-world systems. This course is suitable for students with a background in high-school algebra but who have not studied, or who have not succeeded in, the 2-Unit or higher mathematics courses at the HSC level. Academic skills and support are embedded into each diploma course.
learning_outcomes: Apply skills in algebra, differential calculus and integral calculus to solve mathematical problems.
Use mathematical functions and their graphs to clearly specify relationships between variables.
Recall and apply properties of common functions of a single real variable to solve mathematical problems.

title: Research in Action
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: EPFNLT108 is running in place of FNLT1008 Research in Action. If FNLT1008 is core in your Diploma, you will enrol in EPFNLT108 instead. This course has the same content and allows you to complete the course fee free. For more information see our free Diploma course page. Research in Action allows students to pursue their passion for their discipline by completing an independent research project on an issue of interest to them. Undertaking this project and engaging with the core learning in this course will allow students to demonstrate knowledge and skills related to research methodologies, research processes, and a range of academic literacies including producing and communicating research in appropriate academic formats. This course will also prompt students to consider the ethical implications of research and the connection between theory and action research. This allows students to demonstrate the skills of analysis and critical thinking that underpins all scholarship and active citizenship. These introductory skills and key learning areas will assist students in participating in further undergraduate studies regardless of their degree destination.
learning_outcomes: Apply academic research processes and methodologies to the development of an independent research project.
Apply effective academic writing and speaking skills to demonstrate an understanding of research processes.
Demonstrate an understanding of academic literacies, including referencing and academic integrity, in the construction of academic texts.
Critically analyse primary and secondary information in order to support an argument.

title: Academic Literacies for Studies in Education
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: EPFNLT106 is running in place of FNLT1006 Academic Literacies for Studies in Education. If FNLT1006 is core in your Diploma, you will enrol in EPFNLT106 instead. This course has the same content and allows you to complete the course fee free. For more information see our free Diploma course page. Through exploration of a number of contemporary issues in education and beyond, this course aims to challenge students’ thinking and to develop the critical reasoning and written and oral language skills required for study at an undergraduate level and in teaching practice.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the academic skills of close analysis, critical reading and note taking.
Understand academic integrity and apply academic referencing skills.
Generate independent research.
Construct an argument in written and oral form.
Analyse, evaluate, and synthesise ideas as represented in academic and non-academic texts.
Reflect knowledgably and critically on their own and others’ experiences in education.

title: Foundational Studies in Mathematics 1
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: EPFNMT103 is running in place of FNMT1003 Foundational Studies in Mathematics 1. If FNMT1003 is core in your Diploma, you will enrol in EPFNMT103 instead. This course has the same content and allows you to complete the course fee free. For more information see our free Diploma course page. Many relationships in the real world can be modelled via a mathematical function of one or more variables. This course introduces common functions of one variable used in the sciences, equips students with the tools of algebra and graphing to analyse the properties of such functions, and develops an understanding of the role of functions in real-world systems. This course is suitable for students with a background in high-school mathematics who have not studied, or who have not succeeded in, HSC Mathematics Advanced or higher.
learning_outcomes: Recall and apply properties of common functions of a single real variable to solve mathematical problems
Apply skills in algebra and graphing to solve mathematical problems
Use mathematical functions and their graphs to clearly specify relationships between variables

title: Foundational Studies in Mathematics 2
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: EPFNMT104 is running in place of FNMT1004 Foundational Studies in Mathematics 2. If FNMT1004 is core in your Diploma, you will enrol in EPFNMT104 instead. This course has the same content and allows you to complete the course fee free. For more information see our free Diploma course page. Many relationships in the real world can be modelled via a mathematical function of one or more variables. This course introduces common functions of one variable used in the sciences, equips students with the tools of differential and integral calculus to analyse the properties of such functions, and develops an understanding of the role of functions and calculus in real-world systems. This course is suitable for students with a background in high-school mathematics who have not studied, or who have not succeeded in, HSC Mathematics Advanced or higher.
learning_outcomes: Apply skills in differential calculus and integral calculus to solve mathematical problems
Recall and apply calculus of common functions of a single real variable to solve mathematical problems
Use mathematical functions and their graphs to clearly specify relationships between variables

title: Engineering Physics
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: EPFNPS103 is running in place of FNPS1003 Engineering Physics. If FNPS1003 is core in your Diploma, you will enrol in EPFNPS103 instead. This course has the same content and allows you to complete the course fee free. For more information see our free Diploma course page. For engineers, a knowledge of physics is essential to understand and transform the world around us. This course is designed for students in the Diploma in Engineering program with no or little physics background. The course covers introductory physics and lays the physical foundations essential for further studies in engineering. Academic skills and support are embedded into each diploma course.
learning_outcomes: Explain the basic principles of physics and mathematics and how they apply to practical situations and engineering problems.
Solve qualitative and quantitative problems using mathematics and the principles of physics.
Communicate the results and significance of both theoretical and experimental work in written form.
Perform laboratory and computational experiments and interpret the significance of the results with regards to the principles and applications of physics.

title: Introductory Skills in Mathematics and Statistics
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: EPFNMT121 is running in place of FNMT1201 Introductory Skills in Mathematics and Statistics. If FNMT1201 is core in your Diploma, you will enrol in EPFNMT121 instead. This course has the same content and allows you to complete the course fee free. For more information see our free Diploma course page. Quantitative methods are used in many areas of business, finance, information technology, the built environment as well as in education. This course will explore the essential mathematical and statistical skill to analyse and work with data to get a better understanding of the world around us. Mathematical skills include algebra, equations and application to real world problems. Statistical skills include representing, analysing and interpreting data to find probable solutions when an exact one can’t be found. This course is suitable for those students who have not studied, or who have not succeeded in, mathematics courses at the HSC level. Academic skills and support are embedded into this diploma course.
learning_outcomes: Identify different data sets and interpret tables and graphs.
Use mathematical skills in real world applications.
Demonstrate a sound knowledge and an understanding of numbers and arithmetic.
Explain and work with basic concepts in algebra.
Apply basic mathematical and statistical concepts to real world problems.

title: Academic Survival Skills for STEM
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: EPFNSC103 is running in place of FNSC1003 Academic Survival Skills for STEM. If FNSC1003 is core in your Diploma, you will enrol in EPFNSC103 instead. This course has the same content and allows you to complete the course fee free. For more information see our free Diploma course page. This course will explore the essential skills needed to survive and succeed at university, including understanding assessments and their rubrics, researching and evaluating sources, and understanding referencing conventions. This course will cover time management, planning, and study skills and familiarise students with the university’s support systems. Fundamental numeracy skills which are critical for studies in STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics) will also be covered. These include an understanding of and competence in the skills of numeracy, arithmetic, fractions, decimals, percentages, ratio and scale measurement, units of measurement and basic concepts of statistics.
learning_outcomes: Apply basic mathematical and statistical concepts to real world problems.
Identify different data sets and interpret tables and graphs.
Demonstrate a sound knowledge and an understanding of numbers and arithmetic.
Analyse an assignment question and interpret a rubric.
Demonstrate an understanding of the concepts of mathematics relevant to STEM degrees.
Evaluate the appropriateness and reliability of information sources and apply academic integrity and referencing conventions.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Quizzes on academic skills, maths, statistics

title: Academic Literacies and Social Analysis
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: EPFNSO110 is running in place of FNSO1110. If FNSO1110 Academic Literacies and Social Analysis is core in your Diploma, you will enrol in EPFNSO110 instead. This course has the same content and allows you to complete the course fee free. For more information see our free Diploma course page. Academic Literacies and Social Analysis offers an introduction to academic skills in the context of the discipline of sociology, the study of people, societies and cultures. Students will develop a sociological imagination that challenges their taken-for-granted and common sense understanding of the world and use sociological theory to critically investigate how social structure, social roles, social inequality, power and class impact people's lived experience. Students in this course will develop techniques and strategies to prepare them for tertiary study and for work in a range of professional fields by learning how to use a social science approach to examining issues in contemporary society.
learning_outcomes: Critically assess academic and non academic texts.
Use library research skills for academic research.
Critically analyse social problems using sociological theory in written forms.
Identify and evaluate social issues, institutions and social structures which exist in everyday life using a critical social scientific approach.
Apply academic planning, research and referencing skills to academic writing.
Understand and implement academic feedback.

title: Science Essentials for Nursing and Midwifery
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: This course will introduce students to basic mathematics, biochemistry, anatomy and physiology of the human body relevant to studies in the health sciences. Using relevant examples, students will understand how these theoretical concepts underpin the science informing nursing practice and interventions. Topics will cover a range of processes that are important to the maintenance of life and some of the medical methods used to measure and understand these.
learning_outcomes: Carry out calculations related to health and medical sciences.
Communicate scientific knowledge in a variety of formats appropriate for health and medical sciences.
Gather, summarise, and interpret scientific information related to the basis of life and disease.
Recognise and recall key features of the cellular basis of life and the biochemical basis of disease.
Define and describe key scientific concepts related to health and medical sciences.

title: Society Unmasked: Sociology for our Times
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Ever wondered why the world works the way it does? Society Unmasked: Sociology for our Times is your gateway to understanding the forces shaping societies—both locally and globally. This course explores the social, political, and economic structures that influence our daily lives, challenging you to think critically about issues like inequality, power, and culture. We’ll explore historical transformations and their impact on contemporary society, unpacking key topics such as gender, race, health, education, media, technology, youth culture, and the role of the state . You’ll develop and apply your critical imagination —the ability to see beyond “common sense” explanations and question the world around you. Along the way, you'll sharpen essential academic skills, including critical reading, research, essay writing, and oral presentation . Whether you’re looking to make sense of today’s biggest challenges or just want to see the world differently, this course equips you with the tools to analyse society in a new light. Get ready to challenge assumptions, explore new perspectives, and build the skills to make a difference in a range of personal and professional settings.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse social problems using theory in written and oral forms.
Use library research skills for academic research.
Apply academic planning, research and referencing skills to academic work at a foundational level.
Identify and evaluate social issues, institutions and social structures which exist in everyday life using a social scientific approach.

title: Bioscience for Nursing and Midwifery
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: This course will introduce students to the major body systems and their role in health and disease. It will focus on how anatomy (structure) and physiology (function) and biochemistry (molecular interactions) interact in health, medicine and disease. A systems approach will be used to explore how biosciences underpin normal and pathophysiological functioning, and nursing practices.
learning_outcomes: Define and explain the relationship between structure and function in the major human bodily systems.
Summarise, and interpret scientific information related to the scientific basis of health and disease.
Conduct research relevant to understanding the science behind human health, disease, nursing practice and interventions.
Recall and describe key scientific concepts explaining normal function and health problems for the major human bodily systems.
Communicate scientific knowledge in a range of formats related to human health sciences.

title: Media and Communication Studies
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Communications and Media will provide students with an overview of the function and influence of the media industry. The course will examine the various segments of the industry, considering their history, structure and contemporary development. It will also consider how diverse media outlets are interconnected, both nationally and global, and the influence that media has on social and cultural understanding.
learning_outcomes: Describe the development of the media, including both national and global media structures.
Identify and describe technological developments impacting the media industry.
Interpret media output in written and verbal forms.
Analyse and critique diverse media output; particularly news media, and identify their political influences.
Write an essay at a level suitable for successful study at the introductory undergraduate level.

title: Australian History to Federation
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the study of Australian history at the tertiary level. Topics covered include race and gender relations, convict society, and the growth of self-government. Emphasis is placed on academic skills, such as note taking, research, analysis and essay writing, which are widely applicable to the tertiary study of history and to humanities subjects in general.
learning_outcomes: Practice effective note taking skills and oral and written methods of communication at the tertiary level, to demonstrate familiarity with the study of Australian history including the factors that affect change and continuity in the modern world.
Construct a coherent, well-structured and sustained argument in a written academic work incorporating different historical interpretations and perspectives.
Use a number of relevant historical sources and evaluate their reliability.
Analyse and evaluate issues in Australian history using historical terms and concepts, and a set of conceptual tools.
Analyse a range of key ideas and events in Australian history before Federation, and evaluate the role of key individuals, groups, events and ideas.

title: Research in Action
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Research in Action allows students to pursue their passion for their discipline by completing an independent research project on an issue of interest to them. Undertaking this project and engaging with the core learning in this course will allow students to demonstrate knowledge and skills related to research methodologies, research processes, and a range of academic literacies including producing and communicating research in appropriate academic formats. This course will also prompt students to consider the ethical implications of research and the connection between theory and action research. This allows students to demonstrate the skills of analysis and critical thinking that underpins all scholarship and active citizenship. These skills and key learning areas will assist students in participating in future undergraduate studies regardless of their degree destination.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of academic literacies, including referencing and academic integrity, in the construction of foundational level academic texts.
Apply academic research processes and methodologies to the development of an independent research project at a foundational level.
Critically analyse primary and secondary information in order to support an argument at a foundational level.
Apply effective academic writing and speaking skills to demonstrate an understanding of research processes.

title: Literature Foundations
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: EPHUMA144 provides students with foundational knowledge of the academic study of literature through a variety of critical approaches related to genre and adaptation. The course focuses on the development of foundational skills in critical analysis.
learning_outcomes: Write an academic essay at a level suitable for successful study at the introductory undergraduate level.
Select and employ the skills necessary to think critically and respond appropriately in written form to a variety of fictional texts.
Explain terminology used in the analysis of written and visual texts, and ways it can be used.
Identify the structures and techniques used in various forms of written and visual texts.
Identify and understand a variety of critical approaches that may be employed in the study of written and visual texts.
Develop independent responses to a variety of imaginative texts.

title: Language in Society
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: This course is an introduction to the study of language in relation to society, known as sociolinguistics. Studying sociolinguistics, and more specifically the use of language in its social context, allows students to have a proper understanding of the social role of language. Local and global perspectives are taken in this course, as we explore how language differs between speakers separated by social variables including social status, ethnicity, gender, and age. Furthermore, we will be exploring how language is used as a marker of social identity and often utilised as a tool of social power. Another aim of this course is to equip students with language awareness skills in multilingual societies and the application of these skills in everyday life. Some of the methods used include case studies from different communities around the world, which demonstrate how social relationships are established between these communities. Students are encouraged to engage in objective analysis of various aspects of the social role of language. The main aim is to provide them with an opportunity to develop critical skills necessary for undergraduate study through the embedded teaching of academic literacies.
learning_outcomes: Explain how social factors, including gender, age, regional and cultural background, social status, and attitude influence language choice and language style.
Demonstrate an appropriate level of academic literacies for tertiary study.
Demonstrate awareness of language variation, shift, and maintenance among Indigenous and multilingual communities in local and global contexts.
Accurately utilise and demonstrate an understanding of sociolinguistic terminology, concepts, and methodology.

title: Law in Australia
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Law in Australia is an introduction to the Australian legal system which examines the sources of Australian law, legal institutions and their processes and gives an overview of basic legal concepts, terminology and principles. It also aims to explain and develop writing, researching and referencing skills needed for undergraduate study at university.
learning_outcomes: Identify the major sources and categories of law in Australia.
Describe the Australian legal system, key legal concepts and terminology.
Locate, organise, analyse and orally communicate legal information from a variety of sources including legislation and cases.
Apply academic, research, referencing and essay writing skills.

title: Academic Literacies and Language Enhancement for Culturally and Linguistically Diverse Students
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: This course has been designed for students from a culturally and linguistically diverse background, who would benefit from focused language and academic literacy development, to support their discipline based study. Students will develop institutional, digital, social and cultural, critical, language and academic literacies skills which are required for success in their enabling and undergraduate degree studies. Students will use and interact with University software, systems and processes. Academic literacies will be analysed, practised and applied in a forum that is discipline specific.
learning_outcomes: Apply academic vocabulary, grammar and skills, and feedback to produce authentic text types.
Demonstrate an understanding of institutional and digital literacies including adherence to the principles of academic integrity and referencing.
Critically analyse information from academic texts in order to evidence an argument.
Apply critical reading techniques to academic texts.
Apply effective speaking skills to discuss course issues and engage an audience to demonstrate an understanding of academic vocabulary and grammar.

title: Screen and Cultural Studies
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the various thematic issues presented through film; specifically examining historical, political and cultural studies. The course will provide a basic understanding of various techniques available to filmmakers to create cinematic representations. It will also consider the influence and relevance of film in creating cultural understanding.
learning_outcomes: Describe and explain basic cinematic techniques.
Recall, describe, and explain the language and terminology of film studies.
Analyse and illustrate the transmission of meaning through film.
Analyse and discuss how social/cultural issues are represented through film.
Demonstrate academic writing, analysis, and critical thinking skills.

title: Social Enquiry
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Social Enquiry offers an introduction to the critical analysis of everyday life to engage students in the application of a wide range of academic skills, language, and literature through sociological and historical insights. This course begins by exploring historical changes in social, political, and economic arrangements of cultural groups. It will examine the impact of structure, roles, functioning and inequality, and awareness of this on people's lives. Students will learn to develop a critical imagination to enable them to view the world in a way that challenges the taken-for-granted, or common-sense, view of the world. This is an enabling course which provides students with techniques and strategies to prepare them for tertiary study by learning to take an analytical approach to examining contemporary society.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse problems using theory in written forms.
Identify and evaluate social issues, institutions and social structures which exist in everyday life using a social scientific approach.
Use library research skills for academic research.
Apply academic planning, research and referencing skills to academic writing.

title: Reading, Writing and Critical Thinking
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: This course has been designed to assist students in their ongoing development of the academic literacies necessary for success in their enabling studies and in preparation for their entry into undergraduate study. This course aims to engage students in the processes and practices of university reading, writing, and speaking, with a focus on helping students enter into academic disciplinary communities. The course aims to challenge students’ thinking and to develop the critical reasoning and written and oral language skills required for study at an undergraduate level.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the ability to source and critically analyse and evaluate information in support of their point of view.
Demonstrate membership in an academic community by adhering to the principles of academic integrity and referencing.
Apply technique of critical reading to a variety of texts.
Demonstrate knowledge of the conventions of speaking in an academic context.
Demonstrate academic skills of close analysis and critical reading.

title: Introduction to Linguistics: The Science of How Language Works
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Whenever people get together, they communicate through language. Although humankind could not exist without it, most of us are unaware of the many language choices we make every day. This course will provide students with insight into some of these choices. This course provides an introduction to the scientific study of language, known as linguistics. It investigates language as a human communication system, specifically examining the technical features that all languages have in common, how we construct the components of language into meaningful words and utterances, how children acquire language, and how our brains organise and interpret language. The course also explores the use of language in its social contexts, examining how language functions as a marker of social identity and as a tool of social power. By the end of this course, students will have developed foundational skills in linguistic analysis and language awareness, preparing them for further study and careers in a broad range of fields such as education, speech pathology, artificial intelligence, translation, advertising, communications, and forensic linguistics.
learning_outcomes: Apply formal linguistic analysis to spoken and written language data.
Use linguistic and sociolinguistic terminology to describe and analyse language structure and use.
Explain how social factors, including gender, age, and social status, influence language choice and style.
Describe the structural levels of language, including the classification, structure, and creation of words and sentences.
Explain the causes and effects of language contact in Indigenous and multilingual communities within local and global contexts.
Identify the relationships between language, society, culture, and cognition, including the main areas of the brain associated with language processing.

title: Creative Writing and Reading
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Through a close reading and discussion of texts, students are familiarised with the techniques and strategies used by creative writers and trained to apply these techniques to produce a range of creative written forms. The work of Australian and international writers, as well as the original writing of students, will be used to analyse and critique literary form.
learning_outcomes: Create projects that reflect an understanding of the literary conventions and techniques of creative writing in its relevant form.
Apply the conventions of editing and refining written language in terms of grammar and sentence construction.
Identify a range of writing techniques in poetry, creative nonfiction and fiction.
Develop and practice skills in critiquing other people's work and through this, develop the ability to recognise issues within their own writing.

title: Australian History from Federation to Present
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the study of Australian history at the tertiary level. Topics covered include race and gender relations, war and society and postwar developments. Emphasis is placed on academic skills, such as note taking, research, analysis and essay writing, which are widely applicable to the tertiary study of history and to humanities courses in general.
learning_outcomes: Construct a coherent, well-structured and sustained argument in a written academic work incorporating different historical interpretations and perspectives.

Practice effective note taking skills and oral and written methods of communication at the tertiary level, to demonstrate familiarity with the study of Australian history including the factors that affect change and continuity in the modern world.
Use a number of relevant historical sources and evaluate their reliability.
Analyse a range of key ideas and events in Australian history after Federation, and evaluate the role of key individuals, groups, events and ideas.
Analyse and evaluate issues in Australian history using historical terms and concepts, and a set of conceptual tools.

title: Law in Action
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Introduction to three specific areas of law: crime, consumer guarantees and the tort of negligence. Students learn about these legal areas and also how to assess legal problems and structure and answer hypothetical questions in law. The course also aims to explain and develop the critical analysis, researching and referencing skills needed for undergraduate study at university.
learning_outcomes: Describe two civil law areas in which legal disputes commonly arise: negligence and consumer guarantees.
Apply problem solving methods to identify, analyse, and explain areas of law covered in the course.
Define the categories, elements, defences and causes of crime.
Apply academic, research, referencing and writing skills needed for undergraduate study at university.
Locate, organise, and analyse legal information from a variety of sources including legislation and cases.

title: Foundations of Linguistics
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Humankind would not be possible without language. This course provides an introduction to the scientific study of language, known as linguistics. Most of us are not aware of the enormous number of language choices we make every day and this course will give students insight into some of these choices. It investigates language as a human communication system, specifically: the technical features that all languages have in common; how we construct the components of language into meaningful words and utterances; how children acquire language; and how our brains organise and interpret language. Although English is the main focus, examples from other languages may be used with the intention of providing an understanding of the fundamental features that all languages share. The course aims to engage students in a learning experience of language through various approaches catering for different learning styles. Students are encouraged to engage in objective analysis of various aspects of language, and they will be given the opportunity to develop skills necessary for undergraduate study through the embedded explicit teaching of academic literacies.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse theories of language acquisition.
Apply formal analysis to a variety of spoken and written language data.
Employ an appropriate level of academic literacies for tertiary study.
Accurately use linguistic terminology.

title: Social Insights
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Social Insights offers an introduction to developing understanding of the complex contexts of local and global issues through grounding critical analysis in topics that impact us. The course introduces critical approaches to understanding the world around us, importantly expressed and experienced through academic language and literature. It develops students’ skills in critical reading of a text, oral presentation skills, academic research skills, integrating research into an academic essay, and critical analysis. It critically examines a range of topics which include: gender; race/ethnicity; health; media; research methods; youth and youth cultures; environment; crime and deviance; consumption and lifestyles; cities, regions and globalisation; leisure, recreation and sport.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse social problems using theory in written and oral forms.
Use library research skills for academic research.
Identify and evaluate issues, institutions and social structures which exist in everyday life using a social scientific approach.
Apply academic planning, research and referencing skills to academic writing.

title: Fundamentals of Epidemiology
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview: Introduces students to the basic concepts of epidemiology. Epidemiology is the study of the distribution and determinants of disease in specific populations and the application of this knowledge to the evaluation and control of health problems in the community.
learning_outcomes: Recall common population health/social indicators and calculate common measures of disease/death frequency, and crude, specific and standardised rates.
Interpret a forest plot, pooled effect size, and measures of heterogeneity and publication bias from a systematic review and meta-analysis.
Apply the Bradford Hill criteria of causation to an association to evaluate if this is likely to be causal.
Identify strengths and limitations related to the quality of a case control study, cohort study, randomised controlled trial and/or systematic review and meta-analysis.
Recall the range of sampling strategies and determine which is optimal to recruit subjects for a particular study.
Distinguish between association and causation, and identify the errors that can weaken the demonstration of a causative link.
Differentiate between the types of descriptive studies, and identify their importance and limitations.
Construct and use a 2X2 table to calculate and interpret measures of effect from cross-sectional studies, case control studies, cohort studies, and randomised controlled trials.

title: Clinical Epidemiology
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview: This course applies the principles of Epidemiology and Biostatistics in a very practical manner to improve clinical decision-making. Students are provided with an opportunity to develop research skills and apply epidemiological concepts which are essential for investigating important clinical and population-based health problems. The course is delivered in topic specific modules. Each module includes a video that focuses on the key objectives. In addition, other content specific videos are provided by the Course Coordinator. Students also contribute to facilitated discussion questions after reading relevant sections of the textbook and other articles. Students are expected to read all recommended texts and contribute to discussion forums on Canvas.
learning_outcomes: Describe the relationship between the natural history of disease and prognosis and the factors that influence the natural history of disease.
Analyse variations in clinical practice and understand ways to reduce variations in clinical practice to improve health outcomes.
Define and apply concepts relating to the selection and interpretation of diagnostic tests.

Discuss the ways that the risk of various disease precursors and their interaction might be used to identify groups amenable for prevention. Consider factors that influence the natural history of a disease.

Apply concepts relating to the principles and practice of screening for early diagnosis of disease. Describe the role of screening and early diagnosis in preventing diseases. Critically appraise studies that evaluate screening programs
Locate and interpret evidence-based information to inform clinical practice.
Evaluate evidence in relation to a specific clinical question and patient population.
Give examples of the properties and evaluation of health outcomes at an individual and population level.
Describe how prognosis may vary according to factors (injury, disease, age, sex, race and treatment) that influence the natural history of disease.
Describe the use of health outcomes in clinical decision-making, management, quality improvement and public health research.

title: Infectious Disease Surveillance
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview: Covers the principles and conduct of Public Health surveillance. Presented in association with Hunter New England Population Health.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate a surveillance system (existing or proposed)
Discuss the roles of health care workers and government agencies in the surveillance process
Apply the principles of surveillance to healthcare associated infection
Explain the flow of surveillance data in Australia
Discuss the uses of surveillance data
Identify the roles and functions of communicable disease surveillance

title: Advanced Epidemiology
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview: Extends the points, analyses and designs covered in EPID6420 Fundamentals of Epidemiology.
learning_outcomes: Defend and critique longitudinal study designs.
Perform sample size and power calculations for advanced study designs.
Explain and recommend an appropriate advanced epidemiological method for a given research plan.
Create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) to document causal relationships and use it to decide on confounding for a designated exposure-outcome relationship.
Differentiate between advanced study designs and recommend an appropriate design for research questions.
Demonstrate and apply mediation and how to test for this.
Explain interaction and effect modification and demonstrate how to test for these.

title: Research Project
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview: This course will enable students to take a research project on a topic of interest to themselves. It will provide the opportunity to conduct epidemiological research under the guidance of a supervisor from the School of Medicine and Public Health academic staff. A learning contract will be negotiated between the student and their supervisor at the commencement of the semester when the student is enrolled. It is envisaged that a minimum of monthly meetings will be held with the student's supervisor. The research project will involve planning and development of research protocol, literature review and data collection. Once data is collected, the student will analyse the data and write up the work completed either as a research project report or journal manuscript for publication.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the ability to conduct a literature review
Demonstrate the ability to conduct research
Demonstrate the ability to plan and develop a research protocol
Demonstrate the ability to write up the work completed as either a research project report or a journal manuscript for publication

title: Research Protocol Design
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview: Develops a research protocol in an area of student interest. This research protocol framework may be preparatory work for a Masters, PhD, EPID6630 Research Project, or a workplace project.
learning_outcomes: To design or select appropriate measures, and to discuss one of these measures in detail (reliability, validity, acceptability)
To identify appropriate sampling procedures and sample size
To develop a testable hypothesis
To select appropriate statistical tests for different types of data; and to understand the assumptions underlying different statistical tests (where appropriate)
To consider ethical and logistical issues in research
To design research methodology appropriate to test the hypothesis and/or answer the research question.
To provide a brief rationale for that research question
To select an appropriate area of research and a relevant research question

title: Information and Communication Technology
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Information and Communication Technology is designed to develop computing knowledge and skills for university study and beyond. The course covers a range of digital literacies that will assist students entering any field of study. The course also covers a variety of foundational and contemporary computing topics, offering a broad overview of the field.
learning_outcomes: Recall, describe, explain, and apply a range of computer terminologies and concepts.
Describe the tertiary computing environment and use it proficiently.
Utilise software applications to meet study, communication, or business needs.
Deliver professional computer supported presentations and/or produce digital videos.
Apply group work skills effectively in an ICT context and evaluate group performance.

title: Programming Fundamentals
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Programming can be considered a literacy for the 21st century, with an increasing number of roles requiring some programming knowledge. Learning to program also develops logical thinking and analytical problem solving skills that are valued across industries. This course introduces students to programming using object-oriented programming languages. Students will apply computational thinking to a range of problems and learn to code, test, and document solutions at a foundational level.
learning_outcomes: Apply computational thinking to real-world problems and draft solutions.
Code using object-orientated programming languages at a foundational level.
Document and test object-oriented code
Recognise and discuss issues related to software development.
Recall, identify, and apply programming concepts.

title: Managing People in Organisations
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: EPMANC120 provides an introduction to organisational theory and the behaviour of groups and individuals within organisations, including the processes of team building and team work. These concepts are explored with particular reference to the fundamentals of management within the business context. Through case studies students develop an understanding of the practical application of theoretical concepts.
learning_outcomes: Locate, read and critically evaluate scholarly sources relevant to the assessments.
Explain and discuss fundamental management concepts using relevant terminology.
Analyse a case study requiring application of relevant management concepts and theories to recommend solutions.
Contribute in team work during class in an effective manner and to reflect on personal learning on how to manage a team.
Organise and present information effectively in in various academic formats.

title: Project Management
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: EPMANC220 provides an introduction to project management, including international dimensions and the impact of culture in a globally connected world. The course introduces students to fundamentals of project management, such as planning, organising and controlling resources. The course teaches basic soft, transferable skills such as communication and working in teams.
learning_outcomes: Organise and present information in oral presentations, essays and reports.
Explain the basic fundamentals of project management and organisational theory, including ability to recognise and use relevant terminology.
Contribute to a team project in an effective manner.
Analyse and critically evaluate case studies in at least one of the topic areas, including its relevance to course topics.
Read, understand, and critically evaluate the information contained in relevant academic texts.
Describe the processes underlying diversity as it relates to management of a project and team.

title: Fundamental Mathematics
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Fundamental Mathematics is a partially non-calculator introductory mathematics course which covers mathematical skills relevant to degrees requiring a basic level of mathematical knowledge and ability. The learning outcomes include an understanding of and competence in the skills of numeracy, arithmetic, fractions, decimals, percentages, ratio and scale measurement, basic statistics and units of measurement.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the concepts of mathematics relevant to degrees requiring a basic level of mathematical ability.
Apply basic mathematical and statistical concepts in real world problems.
Demonstrate a sound knowledge and an understanding of numbers and arithmetic.
Use the skills of basic arithmetic without the use of a calculator competently and accurately.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Mid-Term Test and End of Term Test - Quiz Components
End of Term Test - Written Component

title: Advanced Mathematics 1
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: This course prepares students for the commencement of undergraduate study in those courses that require a sound knowledge of mathematical principles. The depth and content of the course is similar to HSC 2 unit Mathematics. The course covers number systems, basic algebra, simultaneous and quadratic equations, functions and graphs, sequences and series. The course aims to develop the algebraic and graphical skills necessary for calculus. Recommended for degrees in Mathematics, Engineering, Computer Science, Surveying and Biotechnology.
learning_outcomes: Formulate and solve real world problems in the language of mathematics
Use algebraic skills to solve real world problems
Use graphical skills to solve real world problems
Communicate mathematics in oral and written forms
Explain the different number systems and how they are used within various scientific disciplines
Determine the correct use of mathematical notation

title: Intermediate Mathematics
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: This course is an intermediate level mathematics course which covers the introductory concepts as well as further skills in algebra and functions and further practice in problem solving. The course content includes skills in numeracy, algebra, linear and non-linear functions, graphing, exponential and logarithmic theory. The course aims to provide a sound foundation in a wide range of basic mathematical skills and in their application to problem solving.
learning_outcomes: Solve mathematical problems using critical reasoning and problem solving skills.
Explain and apply number theory, algebra, functions, graphing and exponential and logarithmic theory.

title: Applied Mathematics
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Applied Mathematics is a calculator based mathematics course for those who have competence in the basic skills of numeracy, arithmetic, fractions, decimals and percentages. The course further develops skills in mathematics and its application to the real world. The content includes units and prefixes, algebra, trigonometry, proportionality, linear functions, sketching, logarithms, exponential functions and an introduction to statistics.
learning_outcomes: Understand basic skills of mathematics and statistics and their application, relevant to undergraduate study requiring these abilities.
Apply sound reasoning and to use a variety of strategies to solve mathematical problems and analyse statistics.
Use mathematical concepts, skills and techniques accurately.
Understand the application of basic mathematical and statistical concepts in the real world.

title: Statistics
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: This course provides a foundation for concepts in statistics and probability and is a good preparation for students wishing to proceed with further study in statistics or to study in field where statistics is an important component.
learning_outcomes: Apply probability theory to solve specific problems.
Present data and conduct analysis of statistics at a basic level.

title: Advanced Mathematics 2
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: This course aims to develop the trigonometric and calculus skills necessary for entry to an undergraduate science or mathematics degree and covers the topics of trigonometry, and differential and integral calculus, with some applications in the physical sciences.
learning_outcomes: Use integration theory and skills to solve real-world problems.
Communicate mathematics in oral and written forms.
Use differentiation theory and skills to solve real-world problems.
Identify and use trigonometric skills sufficient for the understanding and practice of calculus.
Formulate and solve real world problems in the language of mathematics.
Determine the correct use of mathematical notation.

title: Modern Physics
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Modern Physics prepares students for undergraduate study in science and engineering by developing a broad understanding of physics at the introductory level. It covers the basic concepts of force and energy, electromagnetism, atoms and space.
learning_outcomes: Develop hands-on experimental skills of measurement and analysis in a laboratory setting.
Communicate problem solving ideas and methods through diagrams, words, and logical mathematical processes.
Solve problems using the principles of physics with appropriate mathematics.
Identify, describe, and explain the fundamental principles of physics.

title: Physics Essentials
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Physics Essentials prepares students for undergraduate study in science and engineering by developing an introductory understanding of physics and its fundamental principles. The course covers the basic concepts of mechanics, forces, energy and waves.
learning_outcomes: Develop hands-on experimental skills of measurement and analysis in a laboratory setting.
Solve problems using the principles of physics with appropriate mathematics.
Identify, describe and explain the fundamental principles of physics.
Communicate problem solving ideas and methods through diagrams, words and logical mathematical processes.

title: Maths for Health, Medicine and Wellbeing
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Please refer here for information about when this course is running and how to enrol in NUPrep courses. The aim of this introductory course is to improve and practise existing maths skills and begin to develop the ability to transfer these skills into medical calculations. This course focusses on building elementary mathematical skills to build numeracy skills. Numeracy is a key skill for the study of health, medicine, and wellbeing. Correct and safe administration of medication depends upon the ability to both calculate and measure medications correctly. Every branch of health, medicine, and wellbeing is the same in that you need mathematical skills.
learning_outcomes: Calculate Flow rates in mL/hr and drops per minute, the time taken or the volume to be used.
Demonstrate competent numeracy skills.
Use a calculator to check calculations for tablets and liquids.
Perform unit calculations (ml, L, mcg, mg, and g).
Perform conversions between mcg/hr, mL/hr, and mcg/min with a 1mg/1mL solution.
Calculate dosages using basic mental arithmetic.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Oral Dosages, BMI and Injection Calculations Worksheet

title: Academic Survival Skills
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Please refer here for information about when this course is running and how to enrol in NUPrep courses. This course will explore the essential skills needed to succeed at university and provide students with the opportunity to apply these skills. These essential skills include: understanding assessments and their rubrics, researching and evaluating sources, critically reading and paraphrasing academic texts, and understanding referencing conventions. In addition, in order to not just survive university but to enjoy university, this course will cover time management, planning, and study skills to make studying more efficient and less stressful. Furthermore, an important element of doing well at university is knowing when to ask for help and whom to ask. To aid this, this course will familiarise students with the university’s support systems. This preparation course is appropriate for all students who wish to improve their academic performance.
learning_outcomes: Write a paragraph, using paraphrasing and in-text referencing
Access the university's support services
Search an online library catalogue
Evaluate the reliability and relevance of an academic text
Create a reference list
Analyse an assignment question and interpret a rubric

title: Writing for University
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Please refer here for information about when this course is running and how to enrol in NUPrep courses. This preparation course is designed for students who are about to commence studies at foundation or tertiary level and who want to be sure they are starting with the written communication skills required for successful course work. Whatever the study program, the ability to plan a well-organised piece of work and to present it in a coherent and informative way is critical for success at tertiary level. Students do not need to write and submit a full academic piece of writing during the course. Rather the course aims to provide the fundamental skills, knowledge and approaches that will give you a head start in developing your writing abilities during your foundation or undergraduate studies.
learning_outcomes: construct grammatically correct sentences.
use correct referencing systems.
use evidence to support arguments.
organise ideas in order to structure the argument in response to the question.
determine what the question is asking.
edit drafts.
devise a reading plan and take notes.

title: Foundation Chemistry
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Please refer here for information about when this course is running and how to enrol in NUPrep courses. This preparation course is designed for students who have limited prior studies in chemistry and are not confident that their experience is adequate for the requirements of the Open Foundation Chemistry & Life Sciences courses. The course can also be taken as preparation for the course EPPREP940 Introduction to Undergraduate Chemistry for students who intend to enrol in the undergraduate courses CHEM1010 or CHEM1020 and have limited chemistry background. The course is organised to present fundamental chemical concepts with particular emphasis on problem solving and is a skills based course.
learning_outcomes: Outline basic atomic structure
Explain the structure of the periodic table, distinguish metals, non-metals, liquids and gases
Distinguish between elements, compounds and mixtures
Write chemical formula and name different classes of compounds
Write and balance chemical equations
Use scientific notation, covert SI units and identify significant figures
Determine molar masses for elements and compounds.

title: Mathematics for Beginners
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Please refer here for information about when this course is running and how to enrol in NUPrep courses. Mathematics for Beginners is an introductory course for students who are enrolling in programs requiring some level of numeracy and algebraic skills, for example, Primary Teaching, Construction Management, Architecture, Biotechnology or Information Technology. We recommend this preparation course for students with limited prior studies in mathematics.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate competent numeracy skills
Build a number plane plotting points, graphing straight lines, gradients and solving equations for straight lines.
Use scientific notation and identify significant figures
Solve linear equations involving fractions and brackets

title: Grammar for Linguistics
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: This is an introductory preparation course in English grammar designed for native speakers of English. It will provide a basic introduction to grammatical terminology and aims to demystify the area for students who feel they missed out on an understanding of grammar at secondary school or would like to refresh their knowledge. Grammar is the study of the structure of language. It is an essential part of our understanding of how language works and is used as a system of communication, including the importance of sentence construction and punctuation. There is a growing awareness of the need to understand grammatical terms in many areas such as learning languages (modern and/or classical), in education (especially primary education, and secondary English and language teaching), in Linguistics and Speech Pathology. Understanding grammar and the ability to use it correctly is also an important skill for all university programs.
learning_outcomes: Identify sentence structure.
Analyse sentences for tense and aspect.
Identify phrase structure.
Analyse word classes and criteria used for word classes in English.
Define the study of linguistics.

title: LANTITE: Literacy for Preservice Teachers
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Please refer here for information about when this course is running and how to enrol in NUPrep courses. LANTITE: Literacy for Preservice Teachers is designed as a starting point for education students to prepare for their LANTITE literacy test. As such, we focus on assisting students in developing literacy skills necessary to achieve teacher accreditation.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of syntax and grammar (including punctuation).
Demonstrate ability to use different reading processes including: access, identify, integrate, interpret, evaluate, and reflect.
Communicate effectively by using language conventions appropriate to audience and context.
Read and comprehend texts of different lengths and formats, topics, and levels of complexity.

title: LANTITE: Numeracy for Preservice Teachers
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Please refer here for information about when this course is running and how to enrol in NUPrep courses. LANTITE: Numeracy for Preservice Teachers is designed as a starting point for education students to prepare for their LANTITE numeracy test. As such, we focus on interpreting and communicating important non-technical mathematical information and using such information to solve everyday problems.
learning_outcomes: Interpret, evaluate, communicate and represent mathematics.
Use and apply mathematical knowledge and problem-solving processes.
Identify mathematical information and meaning in activities and texts.

title: Mathematics Bridging for Education
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Please refer here for information about when this course is running and how to enrol in NUPrep courses. This course will provide students wishing to enter the Master of Teaching (Primary) with the prerequisite requirement of Band 4 Mathematics. This prerequisite applies to all students entering a postgraduate primary teaching degree from 2023 onwards and is required by the NSW Education Standards Authority (NESA).
learning_outcomes: Work with basic concepts in algebra.
Demonstrate a sound knowledge and an understanding of numbers and arithmetic.
Understand and apply principles of measurement to real world problems.
Identify and apply geometric properties and express different data sets in graphical form.
Understand and apply statistical concepts to real world problems.

title: Auditioning and Public Presentation
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Please refer here for information about when this course is running and how to enrol in NUPrep courses. This course is designed for students wishing to gain admission to studies in the BMusPA at UoN through live auditions and others wishing to enhance their skills in live public presentation. Students will develop knowledge and confidence in preparing for auditioning and live public presentations, skills in presentation and communication, managing changed circumstances and improvisation. They will be lead through the process of preparing for an audition/presentation and have the opportunity for an initial audition/presentation performance at the end of the course with a written response from the tutor allowing students to further craft their work.
learning_outcomes: Identify introductory characterisation skills and techniques
Identify appropriate preparation methods for an audition
Reflect on their performance and apply self-assessment skills following an audition
Demonstrate improved vocal and gestural skills for auditions and public presentation
Apply strategies for choosing appropriate audition pieces

title: Songwriting
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Please refer here for information about when this course is running and how to enrol in NUPrep courses. This course is intended for any student who wants to explore song as a musical form. Students will engage with songs from a range of traditions, identifying musical techniques and enhancing their understanding of form, tonality, and musicality. They will have the chance to work individually and with others and utilise emerging digital tools to support them in the creation of their song. At the end of the course students will showcase their work (or a part thereof) in a course concert and will take away a recording of their work.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on their own creative process.
Identify different kinds of song from a range of traditions.
Use digital technologies to create music.
Use musical notation to express a musical idea.

title: Digital and AI Literacies
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Please refer here for information about when this course is running and how to enrol in NUPrep courses. This course has been designed for students to undertake prior to commencing their enabling or undergraduate studies, who would benefit from focused digital literacy development, to support their tertiary study. Communication and access to information in higher education is increasingly through digital technologies, that require specific skillsets. Similarly, online, blended and hybrid learning necessitates a broader set of practical skills in content creation, to engage with online tutorial activities, assessments and exams. These skillsets will continue to be critical beyond the classroom, as students move into the professional world. Students will develop institutional, digital, information, and communication skills which are required for success in their enabling and undergraduate degree studies. Students will use and interact with University software, systems and processes. Digital literacies will be analysed, practised and applied in a forum that is university specific.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate their own digital identity.
Engage in appropriate online communication via a variety of channels.
Create a digital media product.
Apply critical thinking techniques to digital texts.

title: Exploring Photography
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Please refer here for information about when this course is running and how to enrol in NUPrep courses. This course is intended for any student that wants to learn more about creative and technical photographic practices. Students will learn about photography’s role in culture, mass and social media and reflect on this in their own work. Through learning about photographic fundamentals and how to print and present photography, students will develop a small body of work. At the end of the course, students will have the opportunity to showcase their best images in a small group exhibition. At the same time students will engage in group discussions about some of the issues raised by photography today.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on their own and others’ photographic practice.
Work collaboratively to present their work to best practices in photography.
Implement basic image digital correction techniques to refine photographic images
Discuss the issues raised by the creation and circulation of photographic work in contemporary society.
Apply their knowledge of camera techniques to create photographic works for different outputs.

title: Foundation Physics
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Please refer here for information about when this course is running and how to enrol in NUPrep courses. This preparation course is designed to introduce students to the range of topics that will be covered in Undergraduate or Open Foundation physics courses. The course is recommended for ALL students who have not undertaken a physics course before or require a refresher of the introductory ideas and concepts underpinning modern physics.
learning_outcomes: Use algebra to solve physics problems eg motion along a line
Demonstrate strategies for problem solving in physics
Use units, metric prefixes and significant figures in calculations
Solve two dimensional problems
Construct vectors and do vector calculations

title: Introduction to Foundational Mathematics
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Please refer here for information about when this course is running and how to enrol in NUPrep courses. EPPREP920 is a preparatory course for students intending to commence their undergraduate mathematical studies in MATH1002 Foundational Studies in Mathematics. The course assumes a high level of competency in numeracy and algebra at Stage 4 level (Year 7 and 8), and revises topics in algebra, graphing and trigonometry at the Stage 5 level (Year 9 and 10) to ensure students entering MATH1002 have a strong foundation in those areas.
learning_outcomes: Solve equations by changing the subject of the formula
Solve quadratic equations by factoring or by using the quadratic formula
Simplify expressions involving algebraic fractions
Apply the distributive law to expand or factorise algebraic expressions
Use Pythagoras' Theorem and trigonometry to find unknown sides and angles in right angled triangles
Recognise perfect squares and difference of squares, in expanded and factored form
Recognise the equations and graphs of straight lines and parabolas
Calculate with surds in exact form

title: Physics for Engineers and Scientists
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: This preparation course will introduce physical concepts applicable to those students entering or continuing engineering and/or a science degree (with physics). The course includes concepts involving kinematics, forces, work and energy, waves and electromagnetism. The mathematical framework for the course will involve some basic understanding of calculus and vectors and will introduce some "new" mathematical concepts needed to fully describe real world situations. These include such ideas as unit vector notation, "dot" and "cross" vector products and path integrals which are NOT covered in HSC physics or extension mathematics courses. This course is applicable for all students enrolling in PHYS1205 and PHYS1210. If you have not done any previous physics or require a refresher course, then it is highly recommended you first do the "Foundations of Physics" EPPREP900 course before this. This course is designed to introduce students to the range of topics that will be covered in Undergraduate or Open Foundation Physics courses. The course is recommended for ALL students who have not undertaken a physics course before or require a refresher of the introductory ideas and concepts underpinning modern physics.
learning_outcomes: Explain the concept of work and energy
Describe the basic structure of the atom
Use units and dimensions in problem solving in physics
Explain electric potential charges and electric fields
Apply the laws of motion
Describe magnetism, vibration and simple harmonic motion
Indicate where forces are acting and apply Newtons laws

assessment_tasks.task_name: Problem Set 3 - Electric Force and Fields

title: Introduction to Mathematics for Engineering, Science and Technology
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Please refer here for information about when this course is running and how to enrol in NUPrep courses. EPPREP930 is a preparatory course for students intending to commence their undergraduate mathematical studies in MATH1110 Mathematics for Engineering, Science and Technology 1. This course assumes students have previously completed 2 Unit HSC Advanced Mathematics (or equivalent). It revises topics in algebra, graphing, trigonometry, and differential and integral calculus to ensure students entering MATH1110 have an adequate background in those areas.
learning_outcomes: Find trig values for angles of any size
