Solve exponential growth and decay problems
Differentiate any combination of common functions
Write algebraic expressions in index form using negative and fractional indices
Antidifferentiate common functions, and use this to find areas of curved regions
Convert between degrees and radians
Find unknown sides and angles in non right-angled triangles
Find equations of tangent lines, relate displacement to velocity and acceleration, find local maxima and minima
Recognise and graph equations of polynomials, circles, sine and cosine functions

title: Introduction to Undergraduate Chemistry
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Please refer here for information about when this course is running and how to enrol in NUPrep courses. This preparation course aims to introduce students to a broad range of topics within the field of chemistry and develop basic skills in chemical calculations. It is designed for students who are not confident that their prior studies in chemistry are adequate for the demands of undergraduate science and is a useful review for students planning to study chemistry in engineering. Students intending to study the biological or life sciences are advised that an understanding of chemistry is beneficial. This course is organised to present fundamental chemical concepts with particular emphasis placed on topics required for CHEM1010/CHEM1110 or CHEM1020/CHEM1120.
learning_outcomes: Calculate pH and understand acid/base strength
Name, draw, and identify carbon compounds, functional groups, chiral centre and isomers.
Understand the concept of equilibrium in chemical reactions and Le Chatelier's principle
Explain the effect of pressure, temperature and volume on gases
Determine bond order and molecular shape
Balance chemical equations and use stoichiometry
Draw Lewis structures and describe intermolecular forces
Calculate molarity and solve solution concentration problems
Solve redox equations

assessment_tasks.task_name: Solution Concentration, pH and Acid/Base Strength
Redox reactions, Gases and Chemical Equilibrium
Lewis Structures, Molecular Shape and Intermolecular Forces

title: Introduction to Undergraduate Chemistry (Advanced)
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Please refer here for information about when this course is running and how to enrol in NUPrep courses. This preparation course aims to build on and refresh the chemistry skills already gained from the study of HSC 2 Unit Chemistry. The course covers a broad range of topics within the field of chemistry and builds further skills in chemical calculations. The course is organised to present fundamental chemical concepts with particular emphasis placed on topics required for CHEM1010/CHEM1110 or CHEM1020/CHEM1120. Students intending to study the biological or life sciences are advised that an understanding or chemistry is essential.
learning_outcomes: Write equilibrium expressions and calculate equilibrium constants
Identify the limiting reagent when chemicals are mixed and calculate the theoretical yield for the chemical reaction
Use specific and molar heat capacities
Understand that there are exceptions to VSEPR
Determine the empirical formula of a substance from the % mass contribution
Determine the oxidation number of atoms within compounds and molecules
Perform calculations using the ideal gas equation
Convert between chemical and empirical formulas
Calculate enthalpy change for a chemical reaction using Hess's Law
Calculate percentage yield
Calculate the standard electrode potential for redox reactions
Identify chiral centres in an organic compound.
Identify isomers of an organic compound
Calculate partial pressures
Calculate the concentration of an unknown solution using titration

title: Introduction to Human Biology
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Please refer here for information about when this course is running and how to enrol in NUPrep courses. This preparation course will be valuable to students entering Medical Radiation Science, Nursing, Occupational Therapy, Nutrition and Dietetics, Human Nutrition, Speech Pathology, Health and Physical Education, Podiatry, Oral Health, Biomedical Science and Physiotherapy who have limited prior studies in biology or who feel that their knowledge in these areas is not sufficient.
learning_outcomes: Describe the use of prefixes, roots and suffixes.
Define the four types of tissue and 11 organ systems in the body.
Describe the key structures and functions of the cardiovascular, respiratory and renal systems.
Describe the structural organisation of the human body.
Define eponyms, acronyms and abbreviations.
Explain why we use specific terminology.
Explain the structure of DNA.
Describe the key structures and functions of the skeletal, muscular, and digestive systems.
Discuss the human body's four types of macromolecules.
Define the monomers and construction methods of the four main molecules found in the human body.
Explain why knowledge of anatomy and physiology is important.
Discuss the anatomical position and sectional planes.

title: Surviving Statistics for Tertiary Study
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Please refer here for information about when this course is running and how to enrol in NUPrep courses. This preparation course is an introduction to a range of concepts encountered during a statistics course at university and aims to build a fundamental understanding of these concepts and their application. The course assumes no background knowledge of statistics, however basic numeracy and algebraic skills are required. Although limited emphasis is placed upon mathematical calculations, students will be required to perform simple statistical procedures to demonstrate their skills and understanding. Course notes will be available. The course can be taken as preparation for Enabling Statistics and undergraduate studies in STAT1060 and STAT1070. Students with limited mathematics experience should also consider enrolling in EPPREP920 Introduction to Foundational Mathematics.
learning_outcomes: Write up a hypothesis test and interpret the results
Explain why we standardise data
Identify the different data types
Define variability, its measures and their uses
Explain the difference between descriptive and inferential statistics
Explain the basis for different hypothesis tests
Construct and interpret tables and graphs from a set of data
Explain the use of correlation, linear regression and Chi-squared analysis in assessing relationships
Calculate the mode, median and the mean from a set of data
Explain the normal distribution and be able to apply it

title: Physics for Medical Radiation and Health Sciences
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Please refer here for information about when this course is running and how to enrol in NUPrep courses. This preparation course will examine the basic principles of nuclear physics and how it applies to Medical Radiation and Health Sciences. Concepts such as the electromagnetic spectrum, sources and types of radiation, as well as how we quantify radiations effect on biological samples will be discussed. This course is recommended to students enrolled in MRSC1010 (and PHYS1250) but also students undertaking studies in the Health Sciences (Bachelor of Oral Health and Bachelor of Physiotherapy).
learning_outcomes: Name the 3 types of radiation levels of penetration and detection of radioactive emissions.
Give examples of serious early effects of high radiation doses
Define and name different isotopes and unstable nuclides
Use appropriate units to solve basic physics principles e.g. Force , work, energy
Explain the effect of ionising radiation on biological systems
Define radiopharmaceuticals
Describe radiation doses using rad, Sievert

title: Introduction to Programming
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Please refer here for information about when this course is running and how to enrol in NUPrep courses. With the appropriation of digital technologies across all industries, the use of programming knowledge and computational thinking has become a requirement within tertiary studies. This course introduces programming concepts and Python syntax applied to intuitive, real-world scenarios. It aims to highlight key skills such as: Abductive reasoning Critical and logical thinking Professional communication Documentation Design, and Teamwork Students will experience Integrated Development Environments (IDE) and formulate an understanding of the System Development Life Cycle (SDLC) as a standardised approach for application to a wide range of varying disciplines.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and deconstruct briefs into a logical simplification
Design solutions using logical communication
Understand Integrated Development Environments (IDE)
Understand the System Development Life Cycle (SDLC) and how it fits into any project design process
Test and troubleshoot developed programs
Apply Python syntax and appropriate communicative documentation to designed solutions

assessment_tasks.task_name: Programming Concepts, Basic Syntax and Functions

title: Psychology and Human Behaviour in Everyday Life
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: This course introduces the study of psychology and human behaviour and how it can be applied in the understanding of everyday life. This course covers the key conceptual and theoretical approaches to psychology including the latest research findings. This introductory course will provide students with an overview of the discipline of psychology and an understanding of how the study of the mind and human behaviour can be applied in various real world contexts. This course emphasises a scientific understanding of human behaviour and psychology.
learning_outcomes: Recognise foundational concepts in selected content areas of psychology.
Apply psychological concepts, theories, and research findings to interpret various aspects of everyday life.
Apply scientific reasoning for the evaluation of psychological research.
Recognise the historical and contemporary approaches to the psychological investigation of the interaction between mind, body, and society.
Use critical thinking to effectively evaluate the scientific evidence in the digital world.
Employ a range of academic reading, writing, and research skills, including analytical and critical thinking, at a level suitable for successful university study at the undergraduate level.

title: Academic Language Skills for International Students
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Designed for international students who are native speakers of languages other than English. The course focuses on the further development of students' academic English skills in writing, speaking, listening and reading. Lectures, tutorials and oral activities are presented on an appropriate range of topics which will help students to develop a higher language proficiency that will be of benefit to them at all levels of their University studies. During all sessions, students will be encouraged to participate actively in order to practise their increasing spoken-language skills. Problem based learning, discussions and individual talks presented in class will help students to efficiently absorb the material that is being taught.
learning_outcomes: Apply effective presentation skills to deliver a presentation related to their field of study
Critically and independently discuss a range of issues related to the course
Present a well-structured and cohesive argument
Adhere to standard academic standards of communication and written presentation
Critically analyse information for use as evidence and support for arguments

title: Fundamentals of Exercise and Sport Science Practice
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: The exercise and sport science profession encompasses a range of skills aimed at primarily creating a safe and effective exercise environment. This course will expose students to the broad nature of the exercise and sport science discipline and its career pathways and opportunities. Students will learn about the pre-exercise screening assessments and professional behaviours that are expected by Exercise and Sport Science Australia. Students will learn about the theory and application of health-related assessments and how to interpret the results. This course will introduce students to the concept of research in exercise and sport science, exploring both qualitative and quantitative data as well as how to source and differentiate between research information. By the end of the course, students will have developed a greater understanding of the exercise and sport science profession, undertake pre-exercise screening to stratify medical risks and develop an ability to access and interpret research within the discipline.
learning_outcomes: Identify and critique common processes and equipment required to conduct accurate and safe health, exercise and sport-related assessments for various populations.
Explain the scientific rationale, purpose, reliability, validity, assumptions and limitations of common assessments, as well as the need for the calibration of equipment.
Conduct appropriate pre-exercise procedures with respect to the Exercise and Sport Science Australia pre-exercise system.
Explain the scope of practice for an exercise scientist, a sports scientist, and an exercise physiologist with respect to the ESSA Code of Professional Conduct and Ethical Practice.
Access peer-reviewed scientific literature through appropriate databases and differentiate between high and lower quality sources of information to inform evidence-based practice.
Describe the types and applications of qualitative and quantitative research study designs.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Bibliography of primary and secondary information of a selected topic
Workbook of activities relating to the weekly content
Demonstration of competency in applying health screening and assessments

title: Functional Anatomy for Exercise Science
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: Functional anatomy extends the knowledge of structural anatomy and integrates basic neuromuscular concepts to improve understanding and analysis of human movement. The properties and functions of the musculoskeletal system are explored to enhance knowledge of the factors related to muscular strength, posture and stability, as well as how some common injuries can occur. The practical component of this course requires application of this knowledge to prescribe and deliver exercise aimed at achieving specific adaptations.
learning_outcomes: Analyse basic and complex movements to identify joint actions and the muscles involved in producing and controlling these actions
Describe the planes of motion, joint actions and fundamental neuromuscular concepts
Describe the importance of posture and stability during movement
Identify joint actions and neuromuscular factors that may contribute to injury risk during movement
Integrate knowledge of functional anatomy and resistance training to prescribe exercise targeting specific adaptations
Explain the factors affecting force, stability and function of the musculoskeletal system during movement

title: Fundamentals of Exercise Prescription and Delivery
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: Exercise can provide health, fitness and performance benefits for a number of populations if prescribed and delivered correctly. This course will teach across a range of exercise modalities and how students can effectively coach them. Students will also learning about risk stratification, basic exercise programming, and monitoring training loads to guide changes in fitness and fatigue. By the end of this course, students will be able to understand the risks associated with exercise, as well as prescribe and deliver a range of exercise modalities.
learning_outcomes: Explain the various components of a resistance training program and demonstrate the ability to write an exercise program
Identify, describe, analyse and demonstrate a broad range of exercise modalities, and their progressions and regressions

Employ a range of tools and methods to monitor and evaluate exercise load and progress, including mechanical, physiological and perceptual methods that are appropriate for the specific needs of clients
Select and employ simple exercise assessments that are relevant to the needs of the client and explain how data obtained can inform exercise prescription
Identify, explain and employ a range of learning cues and appropriate verbal and non-verbal communication techniques

Identify and explain in simple, comprehensible language the risks of performing exercise and determine appropriate action regarding adverse signs and symptoms during exercise and physical activity, within the professional scope of practice

assessment_tasks.task_name: Coach and demonstrate selected exercise modalities as well as be able to monitor training loads
Online written tasks relating to lecture and laboratory content
Completion of exercise programs for case studies

title: Physical Activity and Exercise Across the Lifespan
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: Exercise and physical activity are important across all stages of life; however, exercise participation and abilities vary greatly across the lifespan due to changes in individual constraints. This course will explore the stages of growth and development across the lifespan, and the benefits and risks of different exercise interventions in very young to elderly populations. The course will also explore sub-populations most at risk of being inactive and the Australian systems, policies and guidelines responsible for promoting physical activity and exercise. Students will evaluate population-level interventions and Australian guidelines for optimising physical activity and sedentary behaviour in diverse populations. By the end of the course, students will understand the structural, physiological, motor and psychosocial changes that occur across the lifespan, and how they shape physical activity and exercise interventions and guidance.
learning_outcomes: Identify assessments to monitor changes in growth and development and apply the results to guide the development of exercise and physical activity interventions
Describe the broad structure of the Australian health system, and identify agencies tasked with physical activity and health promotion across diverse Australian populations
Illustrate the role of physical activity and sedentary behaviour in the aetiology, prevention and management of chronic disease

Describe the physical, motor and psychosocial stages of growth and development across the lifespan, from conception through to death (including pregnancy in women), and the effect of exercise on such changes
Define physical activity, exercise and sedentary behaviour, and identify and evaluate methods to assess these behaviours in different contexts and populations
Apply population-level guidelines for physical activity and sedentary behaviour recommendations to inform physical activity and exercise interventions across the lifespan

title: Exercise Physiology
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: A fundamental understanding of exercise physiology is required to understand the performance and health benefits of exercise. This course will advance fundamental knowledge about exercise physiology and discuss the acute responses and adaptations of major body systems to exercise training. Furthermore, it will explore how environmental stressors effect human physiology and introduce sport-specific applications of exercise physiology. By the end of this course, students will have a greater understanding of the underlying physiological determinants of physical performance and how to assess physiological adaptations that occur with exercise.
learning_outcomes: Select effective communication strategies, including interpreting or explaining normative data where appropriate, to support clients and service users from diverse populations in understanding assessment outcomes.
Identify and use current Australian guidelines to provide appropriate general advice on physical activity and nutrition in the context of health, performance, and recovery;

Explain the scientific rationale, reliability, validity, assumptions, and limitations of common health and exercise assessments and select appropriate equipment and digital practices based on individual needs;
Describe the physiological functions of the broad range of human cells;
Analyse and interpret physiological data obtained during acute exercise, and compare that data between time points, individuals, populations and environments;

Select and apply contextually appropriate verbal and non-verbal communication strategies in a timely and respectful manner to engage effectively with clients, service users, colleagues, and relevant others;

Differentiate between the individual and integrated physiological responses and adaptations to acute and chronic exercise under normal conditions, in different environments, and by external influences;
Describe the function and interaction of physiological systems and how they respond to movement;
Apply informed consent procedures, gather relevant medical and activity history, and conduct a pre-exercise risk assessment to ensure safety and suitability for activity;
Analyse and interpret information and results from assessments, including the accuracy and limitations of the assessment;

title: Psychological, Nutritional and Injury Foundations for Exercise and Sport Science
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: Improving health, injury outcomes and performance through exercise requires an integrated understanding of nutrition, injury mechanisms, and evidence-based exercise prescription. Professionals must demonstrate a strong foundation in human nutrition, including dietary assessment and interpretation, macro- and micronutrients, energy balance, and nutrition strategies for chronic disease prevention, sports performance, and injury management. In parallel, practitioners require knowledge of injury types, mechanisms, and exercise screening and management to safely prescribe and progress exercise across acute and chronic conditions. Within professional settings, students are expected to apply clinical skills such as understanding scope of practice, conducting client consultations, and formulating appropriate client plans. By the end of this course, students will demonstrate an understanding of fundamental nutrition principles as applied to health, performance, and injury, alongside core competencies in injury prevention, and return-to-play decision making through applied case studies and practical assessment.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate competence in practising within scope of practice, identifying reasons for referral and collaborating with multidisciplinary teams
Demonstrate competence in identifying, analysing, and interpreting health, nutrition, and exercise assessments to manage health, performance, and injury across diverse populations.
Identify and describe common risk factors, including physical, psychological and social, for chronic disease and acute and chronic exercise or occupational-related injuries.
Critically evaluate and interpret nutrition, injury and health data using contemporary digital technologies in accordance with professional and ethical standards.
Develop and deliver evidence-based nutrition and exercise recommendations using effective communication for diverse populations
Explain the basic functions and common food sources of macronutrients and micronutrients in general health and performance, including injury

assessment_tasks.task_name: Practical skill competency from activities in workshops

title: Sport, Exercise and Performance Psychology
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: Sport, Exercise and Performance Psychology is a fundamental element in empowering learning, well-being and athletic performance of different individuals and teams. This course introduces students to various fundamental constructs that impact on adherence, participation and performance in sport, exercise and physical activity. The content provides a basic overview of key concepts that help to recognise, explain and interpret human behaviour within sport, exercise and physical activity settings. The course will provide students with an ability to recognise the broad and inter-linked influences that psychological factors have within sport, exercise and physical activity settings. Students will need to demonstrate an ability to interpret and modify such factors to enhance one’s performance and wellbeing. By the end of this course, students will develop sound understanding of key concepts in Sport, Exercise and Performance Psychology and will be able to identify and apply evidence-based behavioural techniques needed to increase exercise adherence, improve health and fitness, and performance needs.
learning_outcomes: Identify, interpret and apply behavioural strategies in relation to client's needs, preferences and goals in an exercise, physical activity, sport and performance setting
Identify and analyse psychological factors and behavioural strategies that influence and predict participation and adherence to exercise, physical activity, sport and performance settings
Describe the role of exercise, physical activity and sport in mental health and wellbeing, and best practices in the delivery of health, exercise and performance advice
Explain and interpret behavioural theories in relation to common social determinants of health that influence health, physical activity, exercise and sport for individuals and groups/teams

Select and employ the appropriate methods and tools, including professional and communication skills, to evaluate client's needs and monitor their progress towards achieving realistic goals in exercise, physical activity, sport and performance settings
Apply self-reflective practices to provide a critical evaluation of contemporary issues in health, sport and exercise psychology

title: Biomechanics
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: Biomechanics is the study of the science of motion via the application of the mechanical branch of physics to a living organism. To understand motion, the internal and external forces acting on a body (kinetics) and the effects produced by these forces to create motion (kinematics) will be taught. By examining the principles of the theoretical mechanics applicable to the study of human motion, this course will teach practical skills on how to qualitatively and quantitatively analyse human movement relevant to a client’s needs. It will introduce selected biomechanical techniques available for quantifying movement patterns important for performance improvement and injury reduction.
learning_outcomes: Identify and describe how mechanical principles affect and direct performance and injury prevention in human movement and sport
Quantify the kinematics and kinetics of human movement using the mathematics of mechanics
Explain what biomechanics is and how it can be used to analyse human movement
Apply the processes of qualitative and quantitative movement analysis to identify specific aspects of movement patterns important for performance improvement and injury reduction

title: Motor Control
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: Motor control encompasses an area of study that explains how we coordinate and control voluntary movement. This course explores the underlying neurophysiology of motor control and the concepts and processes that underpin controlled movement. Students gain a greater understanding of the structure of the nervous system and how it affects motor control following the completion of this course. In addition, students gain a better understanding of how motor performance can be measured and of the associated theories and concepts that underpin the control of voluntary movement such as attention, memory and sensory information.
learning_outcomes: Interpret, analyse, and design experiments demonstrating concepts of motor control;
Describe the structure and function of the neuromuscular and sensory systems as they relate to motor control and learning
Integrate and apply knowledge of and skills in motor control with other sub disciplines of exercise science in health, exercise, and sporting contexts
Design and implement safe tests to assess aspects of motor function in physical activity and exercise contexts
Describe common theoretical models proposed to explain motor control
Plan and produce reports as part of a collaborative team.

title: Performance and Data Analysis for Exercise and Sport Science
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: Recent technological advances have provided exercise and sport scientists with an advanced ability to capture and analyse quantitative performance data. Students must develop an understanding of the technologies used to assess performance and an ability to critique and justify their selections. Further, given the large data sets generated by the technology, students must understand the fundamentals of data analysis and development an ability to synthesis and communicate the data. By the end of the course, students will be able to select and employ the appropriate technology to analyse performance, as well as treat, analyse and communicate the resulting data.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate proficiency in collecting and interpreting data to quantify physical and technical demands in training and competition, which guides evidence-based decisions and supports ethical, legal, and professional standards.

Evaluate the application of technologies used in assessments of physical and technical demands of training and competition, and critically appraise their strengths, limitations and practical implications.

Analyse, interpret and adapt exercise and sport performance data to develop reporting methods, and effectively communicate findings to diverse audiences (including practitioners, coaches, clients and service users), demonstrating empathy and cultural competency when presenting performance analysis findings.
Compare different data types and select appropriate analysis methods relevant to exercise and sport performance data.

Examine research designs and methodologies, critically evaluating their application, strengths, and limitations in informing decision-making and evidence-based practice in exercise and sport contexts.

title: Exercise Prescription and Delivery
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: Prescribing and delivering exercise to a wide range of apparently healthy populations is a fundamental skill of exercise and sport scientists. The course will develop students abilities to use data from initial assessments and desired outcomes to prescribe exercise programs across a range of populations. Students will be expected to be able to competently demonstrate and deliver a range of exercise modalities using professional skills and communication. By the end of this course, students will be able to prescribe and deliver exercise programs aimed at developing health, fitness or performance outcomes across a range of populations.
learning_outcomes: Employ suitable health and performance assessments to provide data to inform the development of exercise programs.
Demonstrate competency in prescribing and delivering exercise programs to both individuals and groups across a range of populations.
Facilitate effective communication and risk management strategies in a professional exercise and sport science context.
Employ a range of monitoring tools to monitor exercise load and progress to help determine if it is safe for an exercise program or session to continue.

Prescribe exercise programs according to best-practice models utilising appropriate in-person and remote service delivery practices, to facilitate health, fitness and performance benefits across a range of populations.

Identify, select, and demonstrate a range of exercise modalities that are suitable to be prescribed and delivered to a range of populations across both in-person and digital platforms (including telepractice).

assessment_tasks.task_name: Practical competency in exercise prescription through various case-studies
Record of student engagement and supervisor competency assessment

title: Applied Sport Science
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course offers a comprehensive examination of the key principles and practices essential for analysing athletic performance in sport. Students will learn how to conduct detailed needs analyses, design and implement effective testing protocols, and administer reliable and valid assessment practices. Through practical, hands-on experience students will develop the skills to create evidence-based and data-informed strategies that enhance performance across all levels of sport, from recreational to elite. Emphasis is placed on critical thinking, scientific reasoning, and the application of evidence-based practices to real-world sporting contexts.
learning_outcomes: Conduct a comprehensive athletic performance analysis to identify and evaluate key requirements of athletes.
Design and explain a testing protocol tailored to assess the key performance requirements for an athlete.
Describe the key factors that affect athletic performance.
Analyse and interpret performance testing data to develop evidence-informed performance solutions.
Demonstrate appropriate testing procedures to ensure the collection of reliable and valid data.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Professional Task- presenting a needs analysis

title: Practicum in Exercise and Sports Science
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: An Exercise Scientist can apply their exercise science knowledge and skills to practice effectively in an ethical, professional and responsible manner. This course allows students to integrate and apply the knowledge and skills obtained during their degree toward a real world practicum experience within exercise science. Students will undertake work-integrated learning to consolidate development of competency in exercise assessment, prescription and delivery across a variety of settings. The course involves a minimum of 120 hours of exercise and sports science industry practicum that is supervised by an appropriate professional in line with the Exercise and Sport Science Australia Practicum requirements. By the end of the course, students will demonstrate competency in exercise assessment, prescription and delivery as well as various professional behaviours and tasks.
learning_outcomes: Identify risks and apply appropriate risk management strategies to the professional practice of exercise science
Critically evaluate how the Exercise Science practicum experience developed the professional attributes of an Accredited Exercise Scientist (AES).
Apply Exercise Science knowledge and skills in a work context to support clients to meet their goals
Display integrity through professional behaviour and effective communication
Demonstrate competency in exercise assessment, prescription and delivery at the completion of a minimum of 100 hours of Exercise Science practicum

title: Nutrition for Health, Fitness and Sport
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: The course covers a range of topics including dietary guidelines and measuring dietary intake, the role of macro- and micronutrients in health and exercise performance, identifying athletes at risk of nutrition-related health conditions, weight management and body composition assessment, hydration and nutritional considerations before, during and after exercise, and nutritional supplements. By the end of this course, students will have the foundational knowledge and skills to provide general advice on nutrition to support general health, well-being, fitness and performance.
learning_outcomes: Identify risk factors for nutrition-related health conditions commonly seen in athletes and understand the process for referring on
Appraise the basic functions of macro and micronutrients and evaluate how diet plays a role in disease prevention and exercise performance
Describe the strengths and limitations of commonly used dietary and body composition assessment methods and interpret the impact of body composition on health and performance.
Apply Australian dietary guidelines in the context of health and performance and critically evaluate the accuracy, relevance, and potential biases of AI-generated nutrition information.
Critique the evidence on the efficacy and potential side-effects of supplements and key supplement safety messages
Demonstrate evidence-based approaches that support appropriate delivery of dietary information by Accredited Exercise Scientists

title: Applied Exercise Physiology and Training
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: Continued advancements in refined training methods, technology and monitoring practices on exercise across a range of populations has widened the scope and resources available to exercise scientists when working with clients and athletes. The application and interpretation of assessments and responses to exercise training requires a detailed understanding of physiological system function and supporting evidence to maximise training adaptations. The prescription of training programs should be led by the available evidence and initial assessments and guided through training monitoring and adaptation data. By the end of this course, students should be able to write a detailed exercise program targeted at improving performance that is under-pinned by evidence and current technology. Prior to Semester 2 2021, this course was named Applied Exercise Physiology.
learning_outcomes: Interpret and communicate assessment data to inform physical activity and exercise-based approaches, selecting appropriate exercises and equipment based on individual needs and abilities.
Describe the function and interaction of physiological systems and how they respond to movement;

Differentiate between the individual and integrated physiological responses and adaptations to acute and chronic exercise under normal conditions, in different environments, and by external influences;
Analyse and interpret physiological data obtained during acute exercise, and compare that data between time points, individuals, populations and environments;
Analyse and interpret information and results from assessments, including the accuracy and limitations of the assessment;

Apply evidence-based approaches to prescribe, monitor, manage, progress and regress exercise programs based on individual needs, including principles related to growth, development, pregnancy, disability, and ageing;

Explain the scientific rationale, reliability, validity, assumptions, and limitations of common health and exercise assessments and select appropriate equipment and digital practices based on individual needs;

title: Advanced Biomechanics
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course assumes an understanding of biomechanics and builds on the students’ understanding of biomechanical principles and practical skills to analyse movement patterns taught in EXSS2020 Biomechanics. Students are afforded the opportunity to scientifically measure the physical attributes of human motion. This includes the quantitative analysis of human motion through the use of bioinstrumentation during dynamic performance. A detailed analysis of the gait pattern of human locomotion, from both a clinical and sport science perspective, and investigations into the mechanics of tissues and their function, are integral features of this course. These skills and knowledge are integral to the problem-solving nature of human movement science. Students will learn industry-relevant practical biomechanical skills to identify specific aspects of movement patterns important for performance improvement and injury reduction: including how to measure and analyse three-dimensional motion using biomechanical equipment; and how to interpret and apply this data to inform exercise prescription practices relevant to the client’s needs.
learning_outcomes: Communicate recommendations for improving performance, reducing injury likelihood and/or enhancing rehabilitation based on their biomechanical assessment of their client's motion
Evaluate the biomechanical factors during human motion that interact and contribute to mechanisms of sporting injury and optimise performance
Capture and critically analyse three-dimensional human movement analysis using industry standard biomechanical methods and equipment to aid in exercise prescription
Discriminate how the biomechanical properties of tissue adapt to loading
Classify and quantify normal and pathological gait movement

title: Skill Acquisition and Development for Exercise and Sport Science
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: Skill acquisition encompasses an area of study that explains how we acquire, adapt, and retain skilled movements. This course emphasises motor skill acquisition and development, such that students will understand the processes behind motor skill acquisition that are relevant to the role of the exercise and sports scientist. By the end of this course, students will have the knowledge and capability to assess motor skill proficiency and design training and development programs that optimise the quality of skill acquisition in a range of exercise and sport contexts.
learning_outcomes: Describe and assess changes to motor performance that occur with learning and development;
Evaluate theories and models proposed to explain motor learning and skill acquisition;
Facilitate training activities that adhere to best-practice principles of skill acquisition;
Design safe learning environments to optimise the acquisition, adaptation, and retention of motor skills in health, exercise, and sporting contexts;
Communicate the results of both theoretical and experimental work in various forms including written reports, oral presentations and multimedia presentations.
Work in small groups to produce reports;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Practical demonstration of facilitating training activities
Written report on skills training project

title: Behavioural Change for Physical Activity and Health
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: The decline in physical activity is having an adverse effect on health in many populations globally, and much of the decline has a behavioural cause. Successful interventions that improve physical activity and address sedentary behaviours are built on an understanding of the Australian health care system, recommendations and guidelines for diverse populations, health determinants and evidence-based behaviour change strategies. This course will cover the key psychological theory as well as explore the tools and strategies that underpin successful interventions aimed at improving physical activity behaviours and health outcomes. Further, this course will provide an understanding of the Australian health care system and policies around physical activity and health and explore the impact of poor physical activity behaviours. The course will expand upon past interventions targeted at improving physical activity behaviours for review and critique. By the end of the course, students will be able to use psychological skills to assess, evaluate and recommend population-level interventions based on evidence-based principles aimed at improving physical activity behaviours across the lifespan.
learning_outcomes: 2. Describe the epidemiology of physical activity and sedentary behaviour and explain how policies and organisations support health and well-being in diverse populations;
6. Develop effective communication skills for clients from diverse populations and propose innovative strategies to support and maintain physical activity behaviour.
3. Examine social determinants of health and analyse the factors that influence physical activity and exercise adherence;
1. Examine the influence of physical activity and sedentary behaviour on physical health, mental health and well-being;
4. Evaluate populations at risk of insufficient physical activity and design evidence-based population interventions that apply behaviour change theories to support physical activity;
5. Apply Australian guidelines and population-level recommendations that optimise physical activity in diverse populations across the lifespan;

title: Thesis Creation
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: Thesis Creation forms part of the Honours Program in Exercise and Sport Science. This course is part of the multi-sequence research component of Honours which requires the development of original research under the supervision of a member of academic staff from the School of Environmental and Life Sciences. It is a continuation from research undertaken in EXSS4003A with the students completing their final Thesis.
learning_outcomes: Apply constructive feedback to improve thesis.
Demonstrate scientific writing skills.
Critically analyse and evaluate published research material.
Use research skills to undertake higher-level and post-graduate research and writing.
Communicate research findings that positions conclusions within the overall field of enquiry.
Present information in written and verbal formats in a logical and comprehensive manner.

title: Presenting Research
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: Presenting Research forms part of the Honours Program for Exercise and Sport Science. This course allows students to showcase their presentation and communication skills, and knowledge of research process and outcomes. Students will share their findings to a range of audiences, communicating the results of their theoretical and/or experimental work through a Research Presentation.
learning_outcomes: Effectively communicate research methods and results to an audience.
Demonstrate professionalism in presentation of thesis to an audience.
Structure and formulate responses to questions by written, graphic and oral means.

title: Foundations of Exercise Physiology Practice
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: Practicing exercise physiologists are required to work within integrated health care teams under a variety of legislative, practice and ethical frameworks. This course will assist students in developing an understanding of the scope of practice and regulations surrounding the profession and practice environment of an accredited exercise physiologist. Students will develop an understanding of the role of an exercise physiologist relative to other health disciplines in managing chronic and complex disease.
learning_outcomes: Identify the professional roles and scope of practice of an accredited exercise physiologist;
Analyse the health care needs of the community and design an exercise physiology intervention to meet these needs.
Recognise the role of an exercise physiologist in patient care and refer to other appropriate medical allied health profession;
Critically assess legislation relevant to exercise physiology practice within the national compensation schemes;
Clearly communicate with key stakeholders within national health care framework in both written and verbal forms;

title: Foundational Assessments and Interventions for Exercise Physiology
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: The ability to design and deliver appropriate exercise programs for people requires a thorough understanding of foundational and contemporary skills in assessment and exercise intervention within an integrated health system. Specifically, practicing exercise physiologists are required to understand how exercise can be utilised to assess and improve physiological capacities. This course will provide students with fundamental insights into the clinical rehabilitation process and develop student’s critical evidence-based thinking in the selection of key assessment and exercise interventions. Students will be required to design exercise programs and assessment schedules to improve physical and physiological function of complex cases. At the completion of the course students will be able to successfully select, administer and interpret results from a variety of exercise assessment techniques as well as apply clinical frameworks to design exercise training for a broad array of populations.
learning_outcomes: Appraise and summarise the evidence for exercise across a broad array of common chronic health conditions.
Justify the rationale for specific assessment and exercise intervention strategies, in accordance with a patient's history;
Conduct subjective and objective assessments of health, exercise, and physiological function;
Apply motivational change for patient management according to human behaviour;
Undertake and interpret a patient history in the scope of exercise physiology practice;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Written Report and Case Study Interpretation

title: Thesis Preparation
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: Thesis Preparation forms part of the Honours Program for Exercise and Sport Science. This course provides students an opportunity to advance the skills and knowledge they acquired throughout their undergraduate studies through thesis formulation. It covers advanced topics in research methodologies and ethics relevant to the projects undertaken by the cohort of students at this level. This course is part of the multi-sequence research component of honours which requires the development of original research under the supervision of a member of academic staff from the School of Environmental and Life Sciences. In Part A, students will undertake preparation work for their thesis, completing this final body of work in Part B.
learning_outcomes: Present information in written and verbal formats in a logical and comprehensive manner.
Select appropriate research principles (including ethics where applicable), procedures and capacity to obtain appropriate approval for a research project.
Critically analyse and evaluate published research material.
Establish the aims, objectives and boundaries of the thesis, methodology and research plan, and an appropriate timetable for completion.
Demonstrate scientific writing skills.

title: Exercise for Metabolic and Kidney Disease
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: In Australia, two thirds (67%) of adults are overweight or obese, and therefore at high risk of metabolic complications such as diabetes and chronic kidney disease. This costs the Australian government $8.6 billion annually, but regular exercise has been proposed as a cost-effective intervention to improve societal health. This course will develop the clinical exercise physiology expertise of students in safely and effectively prescribing and delivering exercise for clients with obesity, diabetes, liver disease, kidney disease, polycystic ovary syndrome and gastrointestinal disease. The pathophysiology, medical and clinical considerations (including management/treatment avenues and common co-morbid conditions), and the role that exercise may play in the various stages of these conditions (including enhancing physical function & quality of life and preventing/managing complications & disease progression) will be explored. Students will also learn to apply techniques to modify behaviour both within and beyond supervised exercise interventions, as well as the roles of other health professionals in delivering multi-disciplinary care to clients with these conditions.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate appropriate verbal and non-verbal communication to suit different stakeholders (i.e. client and/or general population, versus other health and exercise professionals);
Design, justify and deliver safe and effective assessments and exercise interventions for people with metabolic and kidney disease, in consideration of clinical and psychosocial factors;
Implement effective behaviour change strategies to improve exercise adherence and self-management in metabolic and kidney disease;
Recognise and respond to adverse clinical signs and symptoms that typically present during and between exercise sessions in people with metabolic and kidney disease;
Describe the aetiology, pathophysiology and pharmacological/medical management of metabolic and kidney disease, including the implications for exercise prescription;
Describe the role of accredited exercise physiologists in managing metabolic and kidney disease within a multi-disciplinary team.

assessment_tasks.task_name: End of Semester Formal Written Exam

title: Exercise for Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Diseases
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: For people with cardiovascular and pulmonary disease, progressive exercise is a key element of clinical management to improve physical and emotional function and increase capacity for participation in activities of daily life and occupation. This course will develop students’ expertise in designing, delivering and evaluating safe and effective evidence-based exercise interventions for people with common cardiovascular and pulmonary conditions. Students will develop knowledge in the aetiology and pathophysiology (including symptoms, comorbidities and systemic complications) of a range of cardiovascular and pulmonary conditions and learn about the role of exercise and clinical exercise physiologists in the broader, interdisciplinary medico-pharmacological disease management. Different strategies to promote exercise adherence and disease self-management will be explored, with a focus on long-term physical activity maintenance. Students will also learn and practice specific clinical physiological, perceptual and functional assessments for evaluation of disease and exercise status. Prior to Semester 2 2021, this course was named Exercise in Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Disease Rehabilitation.
learning_outcomes: Modify exercise according to outcomes of assessments of clinical status;
Design, justify and evaluate exercise assessments and interventions for people with common cardiovascular and pulmonary diseases in consideration of individual clinical and psychosocial factors;

Identify barriers and enablers to exercise for people with common cardiac, vascular and pulmonary conditions, apply evidence-based behaviour change strategies to improve exercise adherence and self-management;
Describe pharmacological, medical and surgical management strategies for a range of common cardiac, vascular and pulmonary conditions and the implications for exercise responses and prescription;
Explain the aetiology and pathophysiology of common cardiac, vascular and pulmonary conditions, including implications for exercise responses;
Adapt and apply appropriate verbal and non-verbal communication to suit different audiences and stakeholders, for instance client and/or population, versus other health and exercise professionals.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Written report and case study interpretation

title: Exercise for Cancer and Mental Health Conditions
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: According to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare (AIHW, 2020), one in two men and women will be diagnosed with cancer before the age of 85; that equates to one new cancer diagnosis every four minutes. Further, one in five Australian adults aged 16-85 years experience at least one mental health condition per year (AIHW, 2021). Regular exercise is known to not only be an effective management strategy for cancer and mental health conditions, but also reduces the risk of developing these conditions in the first instance. This course will develop the clinical exercise physiology expertise of students in safely and effectively prescribing and delivering exercise for clients with cancer (breast, prostate, colorectal, other) and/or mental health conditions (anxiety, depression, psychoses/severe mental illness, PTSD). The pathophysiology, medical and clinical considerations (including management/treatment avenues and common co-morbid conditions/health behaviours), and the role that exercise may play in the various stages of these conditions (including enhancing physical function and quality of life and preventing/managing complications and disease progression/survivorship) will be explored. Students will also learn to modify exercise prescription and assessments to suit the delivery of interventions via telehealth.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate appropriate verbal and non-verbal communication to suit different stakeholders and the method of service delivery (i.e., face-to-face versus telehealth);
Describe the aetiology, pathophysiology and pharmacological/medical management of cancer and/or mental health conditions, including the implications for exercise prescription;
Implement effective behaviour change strategies to improve exercise adherence and self-management in cancer and/or mental health conditions;
Recognise and respond to adverse clinical signs and symptoms that typically present during and between exercise sessions in people with cancer and/or mental health conditions;
Design, justify and deliver safe and effective assessments and exercise interventions for people with cancer and/or mental health conditions, in consideration of clinical and psychosocial factors;
Describe the role of accredited exercise physiologists in managing cancer and/or mental health conditions within a multi-disciplinary team.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Written Report and Case Study Interpretation

title: Exercise for Ageing and Neurological Conditions
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: Exercise is important for healthy, successful ageing helping to maintain functional independence and quality of life years. For people with musculoskeletal or neurological conditions due to ageing or other factors, exercise is also a key element of clinical management. This course will develop students’ knowledge and clinical decision making around designing, delivering and evaluating safe and effective exercise interventions for people with age-related complications and neurological conditions. Students will develop knowledge in the aetiology and pathophysiology (including symptoms, comorbidities and systemic complications) of a range of common age-related and neurological conditions and learn about the role of exercise and clinical exercise physiologists in the broader, interdisciplinary medico-pharmacological management. Different strategies to promote exercise adherence and disease self-management will be explored, with a focus on long-term physical activity maintenance. Students will also learn and practice specific clinical assessments for evaluation of disease and exercise status. Prior to Semester 2 2021, this course was named Geriatric Exercise Physiology.
learning_outcomes: Explain physical, functional and cognitive changes associated with ageing, as well as the aetiology and pathophysiology of common age-related and neurological conditions, including implications for exercise responses;
Adapt and apply appropriate verbal and non-verbal communication to suit different audiences and stakeholders, for instance client and/or population, versus other health and exercise professionals.

Identify barriers and enablers to exercise for people with common age-related and neurological conditions and apply evidence-based behaviour change strategies to improve exercise adherence and self-management;
Modify exercise prescription and/or delivery according to outcomes of assessments of clinical status;
Design, justify and evaluate exercise assessments and interventions for people with common age-related and neurological conditions in consideration of individual clinical and psychosocial factors;
Describe pharmacological, medical and surgical management strategies for a range of common age-related and neurological conditions and the implications for exercise responses and prescription;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Written report and case study interpretation

title: Exercise for Musculoskeletal Injury Rehabilitation
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: An understanding of musculoskeletal injury aetiology and the ability to implement musculoskeletal rehabilitation programs are key elements of exercise physiology practice. Specifically, exercise physiologists are expected to be able to use targeted exercises to prevent and rehabilitate injuries that occur due to a range of occupational, domestic and sporting activities. This course will provide students with an advanced understanding of the risk factors, pathology and management of a range of common musculoskeletal injuries. In addition, key assessment and exercise intervention frameworks to manage injuries and rehabilitation will be presented. At the end of this course, students will be able to practically implement evidence-based frameworks to improve musculoskeletal health for a wide range of populations throughout the rehabilitation process.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the evidence base for exercise relative to other treatment approaches in the integrated rehabilitation of musculoskeletal injuries.
Outline the risk factors, aetiology and integrated medical management of common sport and work related musculoskeletal, disorders and conditions;
Develop advanced exercise programs integrating multiple information sources and applying a client-centred approach;
Design and rationalise the development of exercise interventions in the prevention and treatment of acute traumatic and chronic overuse injuries;
Plan and deliver resistance and range of motion exercises in the correction of musculoskeletal pain, abnormality and secondary conditions in work and sport related settings;
Demonstrate clinical decision-making ability by selecting and applying evidence-based musculoskeletal exercise and functional assessments;

title: Evidence Supported Practice in Exercise Science
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: Evidence supported practice refers to the integration of available scientific evidence into decision-making processes that guide the delivery of exercise assessment and intervention. In this course, students will enhance their understanding of research design and methodology, contemporary practice guidelines, and knowledge translation strategies to clients and colleagues. An emphasis of this course is to develop advanced skills in primary research retrieval and evaluation, synthesis of research findings across studies towards evidence-based decision-making across core areas of exercise science practice. Students will have opportunities to practice discussing research and knowledge with various audiences (researchers, practitioners, clients and the public) through various media.
learning_outcomes: Integrate research findings and outcomes into exercise science practice toward a specific pathology or population.
Develop research questions and select study designs and research processes that are suitable to providing outcomes in exercise science practice.
Review and critically evaluate a published study or literature review using a recognised critical appraisal instrument.
Explain the general principles of research ethics, design, and methodologies focused toward interpretation and application relevant to exercise science practice.
Demonstrate advanced communication skills to present evidence guidelines and recommendations relevant to exercise science practice.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Online presentation of evidence-based exercise guidelines

title: Translating Research into Practice within Exercise Science
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: The translation of scientific evidence into best-practice guidelines is crucial to practitioners being able to provide clients with the most effective exercise programs. In this course, students will learn how to synthesise and effectively communicate the available scientific evidence to a variety of populations. Students will apply communication techniques to translate scientific knowledge through a variety of mediums such as social media, infographics and traditional scientific publications.
learning_outcomes: Develop contemporary media to effectively translate evidence-based outcomes.
Concisely report scientific evidence to rationalise evidence-based exercise programs specific to a population or pathology.
Design a research project to further the research evidence in providing best-practice exercise guidelines.
Source and critique different evidence sources in relation to exercise for a specific pathology or population.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Infographic of evidence-based exercise guidelines specific to a pathology or population

title: Exercise Physiology Professional Practicum 1
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: Practical experiences in exercise assessment and prescription for clients with chronic disease is important to prepare students for transition into an exercise physiologist role in private or public health care practice. The practicum courses (EXSS6210, EXSS6220 and EXSS6230) within this program allow students to observe the health care environment and have guided opportunities to develop the skills of an exercise physiologist. Specifically, these skills will include development of clinical reports and communication skills, as well as assessment and exercise design and delivery in population groups with common or complex conditions. During the practicum, students will have the opportunity to apply skills and knowledge learnt in the pathology areas of the accredited exercise physiologist. Students will also gain practical insights into health care systems that support exercise physiologists and other health care providers. Students will be expected to complete a 1 hour online activity per fortnight and record experiences demonstrating critical reflection of practice. The placement will be for a minimum of 120 hours in one of the following practice domains of cardiovascular, metabolic or musculoskeletal or another priority condition.
learning_outcomes: Conduct an exercise focused client history or evaluate a medical history relevant to an exercise intervention;
Monitor exercise responses and modify exercise prescription in clients with a broad range of target pathological conditions;
Design, rationalise and deliver client-centred exercise programs for a given pathology;
Record case-notes and reflect on personal practicum experiences.
Use motivational and behaviour change techniques to improve client exercise compliance, heath education and lifestyle choices in patients with disease;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Students must demonstrate competency in all listed assessments

title: Exercise Physiology Professional Practicum 2
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: Practical experiences in exercise assessment and prescription for clients with chronic disease is important to prepare students for transition into an exercise physiologist role in private or public health care practice. The professional practicum courses: EXSS6210, EXSS6220, and EXSS6230 allow students to observe the healthcare environment and have guided opportunities to develop the skills of an exercise physiologist. Specifically, these skills will include the development of clinical reports and communication skills, as well as assessment, exercise design and delivery in population groups with common or complex conditions. During the practicum, students will be able to apply skills and knowledge learnt in the pathology areas of the accredited exercise physiologist. Students will also gain practical insights into health care systems that support exercise physiologists and other health care providers. Students will be expected to record experiences demonstrating their reflection of practice throughout the placement. The placement will be for a minimum of 120 hours across multiple pathologies and client complexity levels
learning_outcomes: Monitor exercise responses and modify exercise prescription in clients with a broad range of target pathological conditions;
Use motivational and behaviour change techniques to improve client exercise compliance, heath education and lifestyle choices in clients with disease;
Conduct an exercise-focused client history and critical evaluation of a medical history relevant to an exercise intervention;
Record case-notes and reflect on personal practicum experiences.
Design, rationalise and deliver client-centred and individualised exercise programs for a given pathology;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Students must demonstrate competency in all listed assessments

The professional practicum courses: EXSS6210, EXSS6220, and EXSS6230 allow students to observe the healthcare environment and have guided opportunities to develop the skills of an exercise physiologist. Record case-notes and reflect on personal practicum experiences.

Use motivational and behaviour change techniques to improve client exercise compliance, heath education and lifestyle choices in patients with disease;

title: Fundamentals of Finance
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Effective financial management is essential in creating and managing value within a business. This course develops the necessary practical skills within financial management to make informed investment, financing and dividend decisions to facilitate value creation. Students first learn the importance and role of financial management, and how the time value of money underpins the valuation of risky assets and facilitates the investment decision. The course then examines the relationship between risk and return, dividend policy and how businesses finance their investment decisions through an examination of capital structure.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and apply the concepts of market efficiency, risk and return in the pricing of risky assets.
Apply knowledge of appropriate financial techniques to evaluate the financing and dividend decisions.
Use discounted cash flows to generate solutions to financial problems, investment decisions and value financial assets.
Explain the role and importance of financial management to create value for business.

title: Financial Management
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: All firms must determine how the firm will be financed, and which projects offer the greatest return on investment. This course helps students acquire the knowledge of relevant finance theory and financial techniques to evaluate a firm’s investment, financing, and payout decisions. Additionally, the course covers an array of topics on modern portfolio theory, asset pricing models, and the impact of mergers and acquisitions. Upon completing this course, students will have the analytical and problem solving skills to critically evaluate financial problems reflective of contemporary professional practice in financial management.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse theories relevant to the financing and dividend decision of firms.
Use analytical tools to evaluate a firm’s cost of capital with the effect of imputation tax.
Apply advanced capital budgeting techniques to evaluate investment options.
Explain and apply the capital asset pricing model and multi factor models in pricing financial assets.
Communicate financial information to inform independent investment decision making.
Evaluate the evidence of mergers and acquisitions and explain their implications for management.

title: Financial Technologies and Innovations
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course delves into the effects of FinTech on the financial sector, encompassing its historical evolution, current state, and prospective developments domestically and internationally. It scrutinises the challenges and prospects inherent in the digital finance era, with particular attention to how FinTech shapes the digital transformation within financial markets. Legal and ethical aspects are discussed, encompassing the regulatory landscapes and ethical dimensions tied to technology's role in managing financial transactions and data. The course hones communication abilities, with a particular focus on refining presentation and report crafting skills to proficiently convey essential discoveries and recommendations to various stakeholders. By course completion, students will possess a fundamental grasp of FinTech, innovation, and their ramifications, coupled with the proficiency to assess, navigate challenges, and communicate insights effectively within finance, technology, and related domains.
learning_outcomes: Critically examine the challenges, prospects and resolution of issues related to the use of FinTech and digital transformations within financial markets and applications.
Present discoveries to relevant stakeholders.
Evaluate the legal and ethical facets of employing FinTech in the sphere of blockchain technologies, machine learning, and artificial intelligence.
Assess the historical, present, and future trajectory of financial technology and innovation.

title: Debt Securities and Bank Management
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course covers the theory and practice of Bank Management, broadly construed to include a wide range of depository and non-depository institutions. The course will also cover the role of financial intermediaries in developing debt markets and an analysis of debt securities. The topics will include models and techniques to measure and manage different types of risks (such as interest rate risk, credit risk, market risk, liquidity risk, sovereign risk and operational risk) and concepts required to understand investment in debt markets (for example, duration, convexity, bond volatility and term structure of interest rates). Additionally, the course will provide an overview of financial institutions regulations, issues in international banking and international perspectives on risk management with a focus on developing problem solving and decision-making skills.
learning_outcomes: Analyse debt markets and appraise the most recent developments in these markets.
Explain the role of banks in an economy and the trends in banking and bank regulations in Australia.
Apply core risk measurement and management tools to a variety of risks faced by financial institutions in general and banks in particular.
Describe key risks applicable to banks, including the conversion of risks into required capital buffers.
Calculate bond prices, yields, duration and convexity to structure and manage a debt securities portfolio.

title: Financial Modelling
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Financial modelling plays a significant role in corporate decision-making and investment analysis. This course offers students an opportunity to develop an understanding of modelling approaches along with quantitative skills to build financial models and analyse data in Excel and Python.
learning_outcomes: Describe and critically analyse financial models.
Present recommendations based on results of the data analysis.
Apply modelling techniques to analyse financial problems and inform decision making.
Effectively communicate findings and recommendations to relevant stakeholders.
Create programs and models using Python.

title: International Finance
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In today's business world, awareness of the most important dimensions of international finance is vital. This course exposes you to the advanced aspects of corporate financial management in an international setting such as currency loans hedged with options and real exchange rates. International Finance equips you with both the knowledge and the technical skills required to understand and analyse a range of relevant financial issues within the global environment.
learning_outcomes: Explain the problems of dealing in foreign currency and the advantages and disadvantages of overseas funding.
Analyse the range of hedging strategies including forward rate hedging and contingent hedging along with the use of futures and option contracts in hedging foreign exchange exposure.
Synthesise the foreign exchange market and the relationships between interest rates, spot and forward rates and expected inflation rates by applying relevant theories and models.
Analyse, evaluate and synthesise both quantitative and qualitative financial information to influence problem solving and decision-making.
Identify market conventions on exchange rate quotation and correctly calculate those quotations.

title: Investment Analysis and Portfolio Management
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
