syllabus_overview: This course provides students with an overview of the investment environment, modern portfolio theory, and its applications to portfolio management. Students will be introduced to various valuation methods and alternative asset allocation/pricing models in finance to assist them in developing and implementing investment strategies. Financial technology will be used to control portfolio risk and evaluate the portfolio performance. The course takes students beyond investment theories and trains them to perform portfolio management with real world data.
learning_outcomes: Critically assess the “efficient market hypothesis” and discuss it’s implications within investment.
Develop mean-variance efficient portfolios using financial technologies.
Effectively plan and present analyst research on equity evaluation as a team.
Critically estimate the equity value with different valuation models.
Summarise the investment environment, institutional investment and empirical evidence on security performance.
Apply critical analysis and problem solving skills in the context of portfolio construction, management and evaluation.

title: Derivative Securities
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Investment concerns financial decision-making about where to place wealth to provide for future returns. Students will develop an understanding of binomial option pricing, the Black-Scholes option-pricing model, put-call parity for European and American options on a diverse range of asset classes. The use of futures and options, payoff structures for options and arbitrage bounds will also be examined. Students will engage in independent or collaborative work processes and develop effective profesional communication skills.
learning_outcomes: Identify the major types and characteristics of options, distinguish between options and futures, explain the factors that affect option prices, and apply basic option pricing theorems, including put-call parity.
Explain what a futures contract is, how futures markets are organised and the determinants of futures prices.
Apply the Black-Scholes and binomial option pricing models in pricing options.
Interpret and explain speculation and hedging strategies using futures contracts, inclusive of reasons for imperfection.
Analyse and communicate financial information leading to independent investment decision making.

title: Alternative Investments
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: The aim of this course is to acquaint students with alternative investments as a unique category of assets. Within this course, students will gain insights into the distinctive attributes, risk-reward evaluations, essential technology, strategies, and tactics associated with alternative investments domestically and internationally. Through the examination of concrete instances involving superannuation and sovereign wealth funds, students will acquire the ability to scrutinise the application of alternative investments as an asset category, encompassing event-driven, convergence, and market-neutral strategies, as well as property, infrastructure, futures, commodities, venture capital, cryptocurrencies, and non-fungible tokens. Furthermore, students will grasp the significance of disclosing information, conducting investment performance assessments, and conducting extra due diligence before capital allocation. The ethical considerations pertinent to both fund managers and investors will also be explored.
learning_outcomes: Collaborate effectively as a team member.
Appraise alternative investment tactics through risk and reward evaluations and performance gauges.
Identify the prospective beneficiaries of alternative investment tactics.
Formulate solutions using technology for investment analysis.
Critically evaluate the significance of thorough investigation in asset allocation and resolve ethical predicaments stemming from the implementation of alternative investment tactics.

title: Music and Culture
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Music is everywhere: on our phones, in film and TV, on YouTube and in our living rooms. Music shapes and informs our media consumption, our relationships, our identity, and our experience of the world. This course examines how music provides not only entertainment, but a common space for personal, social, and political experiences. We will consider what is music beyond sound and noise. This course explores the cultural role of music and the music industry and unpack how music culture circulates. This course is about describing and analysing the shared conventions and associations that allow music and sound to have meaning, and how that culture around music and music culture creates meaning. This course encourages students to think “beyond the music itself” to consider what makes music a powerful and pervasive force in our culture.
learning_outcomes: Illustrate the significance of concepts like genre, authenticity, and identity to music culture.
Describe the relationship between music and culture.
Analyse the relationship between music and culture.
Combine scholarship with original analysis in a music culture case study.

title: Social Media and Digital Culture
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: All aspects of contemporary culture are increasingly mediated by digital technologies. This course examines how digital communication affects everyday life, culture, institutions, communities and identity. The course introduces various scholarly frameworks, theories and perspectives on social media and digital culture. In this course you are encouraged to analyse the complexities of social media and digital culture and their social and cultural function. You will examine social media, video-on-demand platforms and mobile apps; discuss critical issues such as ethics, politics and histories; and use case studies to connect theory and practice.
learning_outcomes: Articulate an argument about current digital cultures.
Identify the relationship between digital technologies and contemporary culture.
Use scholarly literature to analyse social media and/or digital culture case studies.
Examine key issues and debates emerging in contemporary digital culture research.

title: Hollywood and Beyond: American Cinema in Context
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course studies Hollywood films in the wider context of cinema from continental America within and beyond the USA. Each week, it examines a specific feature film and its historical, industrial, national, social, economic, political, and cultural dimensions, covering key moments in Hollywood history and select other American cinema. The course charts the connections and stark differences within films from this part of the world and the similarly diverse nature of cinema studies from the region, gaining both inside and outside perspectives on the most powerful country in history and its equally dominant commercial cinema.
learning_outcomes: Situate Hollywood films within their historical, spatial, geopolitical, industrial, socio-cultural contexts.
Demonstrate intermediate research, analytical and communication skills in the area of screen studies.
Apply appropriate interpretive and theoretical models to the discussion of American cinema within and beyond the USA.
Analyse the narrative and aesthetic form of Hollywood and other American films.

title: Preparatory Studies in Human Bioscience for Nursing and Midwifery
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Preparatory Studies in Human Bioscience for Nursing and Midwifery introduces students to the organization and control of the human body from cells to the entire organism in the context of the discipline of nursing and midwifery. Students will learn the anatomical, physiological and biochemical principles that underpin the development and treatment of disease in the human body. Students in this course will also develop techniques and strategies to prepare them for tertiary study.
learning_outcomes: Apply critical thinking to interpret anatomical, physiological and biochemical information about the human body in the form of diagrams, graphs, tables and text.
Apply theoretical knowledge to relevant practical experiences.
Use library research skills for academic research.
Apply research and referencing skills to academic writing.
Demonstrate competency in performing measurements and calculations in a nursing context.
Explain anatomical, physiological and biochemical concepts underpinning disease and nursing interventions in oral and written formats appropriate for the health sciences.
Appraise their knowledge of the course and relevant tertiary study skills.

title: Engineering Computations and Procedural Programming
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the use of computers in engineering. The course assumes that students have basic computer literacy but no prior exposure to computer programming. It has the objective of achieving basic competency in a high-level programming language as well as improving problem-solving skills.
learning_outcomes: Translate a simple problem into an algorithm suitable for solving on a computer.
Apply knowledge of mathematics, science and engineering in the use of spreadsheets to perform engineering calculations and prepare graphs/tables/etc for inclusion in engineering reports.
Describe a programmer's perspective of how computers work using an "input-processing-output" model.
Use the basic elements of programming languages including data types, variables, arrays, operators, program flow control, and functions.
Write, run and debug programs implementing computer solvable algorithms.

title: Fundamentals of Engineering Mechanics
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: This course introduces some basic principles of engineering mechanics in as simple a manner as possible. Emphasis is placed upon students gaining a real understanding of the laws and principles of mechanics. This course provides essential foundation knowledge for all disciplines of engineering and surveying.
learning_outcomes: Recognise the assumptions and limitations of the approaches used.
Formulate, analyse and solve simple problems in mechanics.
Apply the laws and principles of mechanics to a basic level.

title: Introduction to Electrical Engineering
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to fundamental electrical elements including voltage, current, resistance, inductance and capacitance. It provides students with an understanding and appreciation of techniques for analysing and designing simple DC and AC circuits including balanced 3 phase circuits. It also introduces the principles behind simple electrical machines, and provides hands on experience across several aspects of introductory electrical engineering.
learning_outcomes: Identify fundamental electrical circuit analysis theories and tools.
Apply knowledge and demonstrate practical skills through exercises in the laboratory.
Demonstrate safe working practices in laboratories.
Analyse and design AC and DC circuits using fundamental techniques.
Demonstrate competence with electrical simulation software and its applications.
Explain the operating principles of electrical motors.

title: Working with Technology
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: This course will develop knowledge and skills in the use of technology by exploring a range of theoretical concepts and practical applications for study, communication and work.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate foundational skills in a range of software applications for study, communication and work.
Demonstrate awareness of a range of computer terminologies and theoretical concepts.
Show growing capacity to utilise technology well in professional contexts.

title: Introduction to Mechanical Engineering Design
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: This course enables students to develop basic spatial skill by using a solid modelling system. Students develop skills in interpreting and visualising 3D objects in 2D format. They create and assemble solid model representation of machine components and create 2D engineering drawings from solid models. Students develop advanced technical sketching skills to aid communication in engineering design.
learning_outcomes: Interchange engineering graphical information from 2D to 3D and back.
Demonstrate a foundational skill set with 3D solids modelling.
Communicate through technical sketching.

title: Foundations in Australian Criminal Justice
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Foundations in Australian Criminal Justice is an introduction to the legal, social and political processes involved in criminal law making, enforcement and punishment in Australia with a focus on the New South Wales criminal justice system. Students will consider what distinguishes criminal conduct, which has State sanctioned punishment consequences, from other conduct and how and why this can change over time, place and population. They will also develop writing, researching and referencing skills.
learning_outcomes: Locate, organise and analyse legal information from a variety of sources including legislation and cases.
Outline key elements and types of crime
Describe the major actors and procedures involved in the criminal justice system
Demonstrate an understanding of the Australian legal system
Demonstrate an understanding of the political, moral and ethical dimensions of criminal law
Apply academic research, referencing and essay writing skills

title: Academic Literacies for Integrated Aged Care 1
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: This course will provide teaching and learning activities that are designed to develop a range of competencies required of participants working within an aged care related industry, including effective critical thinking, communication and leadership skills.
learning_outcomes: Develop ability to analyse, evaluate and synthesise ideas as valid representations of 'fact'.
Develop academic skills of close analysis, critical reading and note taking in a health context.
Develop awareness of key ideas and issues within a variety of texts.
Develop capacity for independent, applied research into a chosen industry.

title: Academic Literacies for Integrated Aged Care 2
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: This course will continue to provide teaching and learning activities that are designed to develop a range of competencies required of participants working within an aged care related industry, including engagement with relevant scholarly literature to both inform contemporary practice and for use as evidence within independent research.
learning_outcomes: Continue to develop capacity for independent, applied research into a chosen industry.
Read critically to develop capacity for deeper understanding of academic text types.
Write in the different discourses of their required health field.
Conduct independent research through effective use of the university library and digital research technologies.
Develop formal oral presentation skills.

title: Academic Literacies for Studies in Education
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: This course is not currently running. If FNLT1006 is core in your Diploma, you will enrol in EPFNLT106 Academic Literacies for Studies in Education instead. This course has the same content and allows you to complete the course fee free. Please view the EPFNLT106 course page for more information. Through exploration of a number of contemporary issues in education and beyond, this course aims to challenge students’ thinking and to develop the critical reasoning and written and oral language skills required for study at an undergraduate level and in teaching practice.
learning_outcomes: Understand academic integrity and apply academic referencing skills.
Construct an argument in written and oral form.
Analyse, evaluate, and synthesise ideas as represented in academic and non-academic texts.
Reflect knowledgably and critically on their own and others’ experiences in education.
Generate independent research.
Demonstrate the academic skills of close analysis, critical reading and note taking.

title: Research in Action
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: This course is not currently running. If FNLT1008 is core in your Diploma, you will enrol in EPFNLT108 Research in Action instead. This course has the same content and allows you to complete the course fee free. Please view the EPFNLT108 course page for more information. Research in Action allows students to pursue their passion for their discipline by completing an independent research project on an issue of interest to them. Undertaking this project and engaging with the core learning in this course will allow students to demonstrate knowledge and skills related to research methodologies, research processes, and a range of academic literacies including producing and communicating research in appropriate academic formats. This course will also prompt students to consider the ethical implications of research and the connection between theory and action research. This allows students to demonstrate the skills of analysis and critical thinking that underpins all scholarship and active citizenship. These introductory skills and key learning areas will assist students in participating in further undergraduate studies regardless of their degree destination.
learning_outcomes: Apply academic research processes and methodologies to the development of an independent research project.
Apply effective academic writing and speaking skills to demonstrate an understanding of research processes.
Demonstrate an understanding of academic literacies, including referencing and academic integrity, in the construction of academic texts.
Critically analyse primary and secondary information in order to support an argument.

title: Preparatory Studies in Mathematics
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Quantitative methods are used in many areas of science, business and information technology. The course FNMT1001 introduces and develops those areas of arithmetic, algebra and elementary geometry necessary for an understanding and use of basic quantitative methods. This course is suitable for those students who have not studied, or who have not succeeded in, mathematics courses at the HSC level. Academic skills and support are embedded into each diploma/undergraduate certificate course.
learning_outcomes: Explain and work with the concepts from basic algebra and coordinate geometry
Use mathematical theory and skills in real world applications
Use mathematical software to support mathematical work.

title: Foundational Studies in Mathematics
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: Many relationships in the real world can be modelled via a function. The course introduces common functions used in the sciences, equips students with the tools of differential and integral calculus to analyse the properties of functions, and develops an understanding of the role of functions and calculus in real-world systems. This course is suitable for students with a background in high-school algebra but who have not studied, or who have not succeeded in, the 2-Unit or higher mathematics courses at the HSC level. Academic skills and support are embedded into each diploma course.
learning_outcomes: Apply skills in algebra, differential calculus and integral calculus to solve mathematical problems.
Use mathematical functions and their graphs to clearly specify relationships between variables.
Recall and apply properties of common functions of a single real variable to solve mathematical problems.

title: Foundational Studies in Mathematics 1
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: This course is not currently running. If FNMT1003 is core in your Diploma, you will enrol in EPFNMT103 Foundational Studies in Mathematics 1 instead. This course has the same content and allows you to complete the course fee free. Please view the EPFNMT103 course page for more information. Many relationships in the real world can be modelled via a mathematical function of one or more variables. This course introduces common functions of one variable used in the sciences, equips students with the tools of algebra and graphing to analyse the properties of such functions, and develops an understanding of the role of functions in real-world systems. This course is suitable for students with a background in high-school mathematics who have not studied, or who have not succeeded in, HSC Mathematics Advanced or higher.
learning_outcomes: Recall and apply properties of common functions of a single real variable to solve mathematical problems
Apply skills in algebra and graphing to solve mathematical problems
Use mathematical functions and their graphs to clearly specify relationships between variables

title: Mathematics for Engineering, Science and Technology 1
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: FNMT1110 covers the parts of calculus and algebra which have proved fundamental to all of mathematics and its applications. In algebra, students learn concepts and symbolic manipulation when calculating with large numbers of variables. In calculus, they learn concepts used when working with continuously changing variables. Academic skills and support are embedded into each diploma course.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate improved analytical ability, in particular their skills at problem-solving.
Demonstrate competence to study further university level mathematics as required in their program of study.
Demonstrate mathematical knowledge and skills in the areas of calculus, functions, vectors and complex numbers.

title: Introductory Skills in Mathematics and Statistics
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: This course is not currently running. If FNMT1201 is core in your Diploma, you will enrol in EPFNMT121 Introductory Skills in Mathematics and Statistics instead. This course has the same content and allows you to complete the course fee free. Please view the EPFNMT121 course page for more information. Quantitative methods are used in many areas of business, finance, information technology, the built environment as well as in education. This course will explore the essential mathematical and statistical skill to analyse and work with data to get a better understanding of the world around us. Mathematical skills include algebra, equations and application to real world problems. Statistical skills include representing, analysing and interpreting data to find probable solutions when an exact one can’t be found. This course is suitable for those students who have not studied, or who have not succeeded in, mathematics courses at the HSC level. Academic skills and support are embedded into this diploma course.
learning_outcomes: Explain and work with basic concepts in algebra.
Use mathematical skills in real world applications.
Identify different data sets and interpret tables and graphs.
Demonstrate a sound knowledge and an understanding of numbers and arithmetic.
Apply basic mathematical and statistical concepts to real world problems.

title: Foundational Studies in Mathematics 2
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: This course is not currently running. If FNMT1004 is core in your Diploma, you will enrol in EPFNMT104 Foundational Studies in Mathematics 2 instead. This course has the same content and allows you to complete the course fee free. Please view the EPFNMT104 course page for more information. Many relationships in the real world can be modelled via a mathematical function of one or more variables. This course introduces common functions of one variable used in the sciences, equips students with the tools of differential and integral calculus to analyse the properties of such functions, and develops an understanding of the role of functions and calculus in real-world systems.This course is suitable for students with a background in high-school mathematics who have not studied, or who have not succeeded in, HSC Mathematics Advanced or higher.
learning_outcomes: Apply skills in differential calculus and integral calculus to solve mathematical problems
Use mathematical functions and their graphs to clearly specify relationships between variables
Recall and apply calculus of common functions of a single real variable to solve mathematical problems

title: Engineering Physics 1
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: For engineers, knowledge of physics is essential to understand and transform the world around us. This course is designed for students in the Diploma in Engineering program with no or little physics background. The course covers introductory physics essential for further studies in engineering. Academic skills and support are embedded into each diploma course.
learning_outcomes: Communicate the results and significance of both theoretical and experimental work in written form.
Perform laboratory and computational experiments and interpret the significance of the results with regards to the principles and applications of physics.
Explain the basic principles of physics and mathematics and how they apply to practical situations and engineering problems.
Solve qualitative and quantitative problems using mathematics and the principles of physics.

title: Engineering Physics 2
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: For engineers, knowledge of physics is essential to understand and transform the world around us. The course examines some of the core topics in physics essential for further studies in engineering such as mechanics, vibrations and waves, electricity and magnetism, and optics. It builds on content from FNPS1001. Academic skills and support are embedded into each diploma course.
learning_outcomes: Solve qualitative and quantitative problems using mathematics and the principles of physics.
Perform laboratory and computational experiments and interpret the significance of the results with regards to the principles and applications of physics.
Communicate the results and significance of both theoretical and experimental work in written form.
Explain the basic principles of physics and mathematics and how they apply to practical situations and engineering problems.

title: Engineering Physics
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: This course is not currently running. If FNPS1003 is core in your Diploma, you will enrol in EPFNPS103 Engineering Physics instead. This course has the same content and allows you to complete the course fee free. Please view the EPFNPS103 course page for more information. For engineers, a knowledge of physics is essential to understand and transform the world around us. This course is designed for students in the Diploma in Engineering program with no or little physics background. The course covers introductory physics and lays the physical foundations essential for further studies in engineering. Academic skills and support are embedded into each diploma course.
learning_outcomes: Explain the basic principles of physics and mathematics and how they apply to practical situations and engineering problems.
Communicate the results and significance of both theoretical and experimental work in written form.
Perform laboratory and computational experiments and interpret the significance of the results with regards to the principles and applications of physics.
Solve qualitative and quantitative problems using mathematics and the principles of physics.

title: Foundations of Environmental Chemistry and Biology
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: One of the most pressing issues in today’s society is the human-induced pressures that are placed on earth’s ecosystems and resources. Environmental Science is a multi-disciplinary approach that endeavours to explain how life on Earth is sustained, what contributes to our many environmental problems, and how these problems can be solved through understanding of interactions between humans and the Earth. This course introduces students to a number of the basic multidisciplinary concepts, such as chemistry, biology, botany and atmospheric chemistry which are fundamental to understanding these interactions. Students will be introduced to the role of chemistry in environmental studies and develop the skills to be able to monitor, measure and assess environmental variables.
learning_outcomes: Summarise core and fundamental knowledge of chemical concepts and methods appropriate to environmental science.
Apply theoretical knowledge to an environmental problem and develop a viable solution.
Express chemical ideas in a logical, coherent fashion.
Demonstrate competency in the analysis of biological and chemical properties of environmental systems.
Apply methods to sample collection, recording, analysing statistical data to environmental contaminants.
Demonstrate competency in the analysis for analytes in water and soil samples.
Describe the key chemical processes of Earth's atmosphere and the contribution to climate change.

title: Academic Survival Skills for STEM
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: This course is not currently running. If FNSC1003 is core in your Diploma, you will enrol in EPFNSC103 Academic Survival Skills for STEM instead. This course has the same content and allows you to complete the course fee free. Please view the EPFNSC103 course page for more information. This course will explore the essential skills needed to survive and succeed at university, including understanding assessments and their rubrics, researching and evaluating sources, and understanding referencing conventions. This course will cover time management, planning, and study skills and familiarise students with the university’s support systems. Fundamental numeracy skills which are critical for studies in STEM (Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics) will also be covered. These include an understanding of and competence in the skills of numeracy, arithmetic, fractions, decimals, percentages, ratio and scale measurement, units of measurement and basic concepts of statistics.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a sound knowledge and an understanding of numbers and arithmetic.
Identify different data sets and interpret tables and graphs.
Apply basic mathematical and statistical concepts to real world problems.
Demonstrate an understanding of the concepts of mathematics relevant to STEM degrees.
Analyse an assignment question and interpret a rubric
Evaluate the appropriateness and reliability of information sources and apply academic integrity and referencing conventions.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Quizzes on academic skills, maths, statistics

title: Academic Literacies and Social Analysis
faculty: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
school: Pathways and Academic Learning Support Centre
syllabus_overview: This course is not currently running. If FNSO1110 is core in your Diploma, you will enrol in EPFNSO110 Academic Literacies and Social Analysis instead. This course has the same content and allows you to complete the course fee free. Please view the EPFNSO110 course page for more information. Academic Literacies and Social Analysis offers an introduction to academic skills in the context of the discipline of sociology, the study of people, societies and cultures. Students will develop a sociological imagination that challenges their taken-for-granted and common sense understanding of the world and use sociological theory to critically investigate how social structure, social roles, social inequality, power and class impact people's lived experience. Students in this course will develop techniques and strategies to prepare them for tertiary study and for work in a range of professional fields by learning how to use a social science approach to examining issues in contemporary society.
learning_outcomes: Apply academic planning, research and referencing skills to academic writing.
Critically analyse social problems using sociological theory in written forms.
Critically assess academic and non academic texts.
Understand and implement academic feedback.
Use library research skills for academic research.
Identify and evaluate social issues, institutions and social structures which exist in everyday life using a critical social scientific approach.

title: French Language and Culture Beginners 1 (A0 to A1.1)
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Designed for those with little or no previous knowledge of French, this course introduces basic vocabulary and structures through a communicative approach. Students will also gain awareness and understanding of the French and Francophone cultures.
learning_outcomes: Use basic vocabulary, pronunciation and grammar at an elementary level, in written and spoken French.
Use technology at an elementary level in the online assessments environment.
Demonstrate knowledge of key aspects of French culture.
Demonstrate understanding of simple texts and dialogues in French.

title: French Language and Culture Beginners 2 (A1.1 to A1.2)
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: A semester language unit designed as the continuation of the Introductory course FREN1100. The course provides vocabulary extension and further fundamental sentence patterns, still placing emphasis on communication skills. Students will also develop their awareness and understanding of the French and Francophone cultures.
learning_outcomes: Speak and understand simple spoken every day French.
Recognise and reproduce French sounds and intonation patterns.
Correctly use French grammatical structures appropriate to the Elementary level 2.
Use technology at an elementary level in the online assessments environment.
Identify main characteristics of the cultures of French-speaking countries.

title: French Language and Culture Elementary 1 (A1.2 to A2.1)
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course further develops students’ knowledge of the French language and culture, enhancing vocabulary, pronunciation and grammar beyond the beginner level. The goal is to achieve an A2 level or above in communicative competence (Common European Framework of Reference for Languages) by the end of FREN2620.
learning_outcomes: Communicate effectively in French in a variety of everyday speaking or writing situations.
Understand simple French texts in a variety of listening situations and written materials.
Identify some aspects of the culture(s) of Francophone societies.
Utilise an elementary standard of French grammar and vocabulary.
Use technology at an elementary level in the online assessments environment.

title: French Language and Culture Elementary 2 (A2.1 to A2.2)
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course aims to enable students to reach an Elementary level of communication in French (A2 level or more in the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages) while enhancing their cultural awareness of the Francophone world. As a sequel to FREN2610, this course further develops students' proficiency in the four language skills: Listening, Speaking, Reading and Writing, empowering them to communicate effectively in both spoken and written contexts.
learning_outcomes: Communicate effectively in French in oral or written interactions in a variety of everyday situations.
Understand French documents in a variety of listening situations and written materials corresponding to this upper elementary level.
Utilise an upper elementary standard of French grammar and vocabulary, commensurate with A2 of the Common Framework of Reference for Languages.
Use technology at an elementary level in the online assessments environment.
Identify key elements of the culture(s) of Francophone societies.

title: French Language and Culture Intermediate 1 (A2.2 to B1.1)
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course provides further intensive study of the French language to improve vocabulary, pronunciation and grammar, aiming to develop self-expression in both writing and speaking. The goal is to achieve a B1 level or above (“Independent user” in the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages) by the end of FREN3620. It also expands knowledge of French and Francophone cultures.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a clear understanding of the culture(s) of Francophone societies.
Communicate effectively in the foreign language in a variety of speaking or writing situations.
Demonstrate understanding of spoken and written French in a variety of listening situations and written materials corresponding to this level.
Use technology at an elementary level in the online assessments environment.
Utilise an intermediate standard of French grammar an vocabulary.

title: French Language and Culture Intermediate 2 (B1.1 to B1.2)
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The aim of this course is to enable students to reach an Upper Intermediate level of communication in French (B1 level or above - “Independent user” in the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages) and to develop their cultural awareness of the Francophone world. It is designed as a sequel to FREN3610; it builds on the four skills of language acquisition: Listening, Speaking, Reading and Writing.
learning_outcomes: Identify key aspects of the culture(s) of Francophone societies.
Utilise an upper Intermediate/Advanced standard of French grammar and vocabulary commensurate with B1 or above of the Common Framework of the Reference for Languages.
Communicate effectively in the French language in a variety of speaking or writing situations.
Demonstrate understanding of documents in French in a variety of listening situations and written materials corresponding to this level.
Use technology at an elementary level in the online assessments environment.

title: Extended French: Grammar
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course offers a consolidation and extension of the knowledge of French grammar through an in-depth study of French structures that are often difficult to master, especially for English speakers, using these in order to translate sentences from English into French.
learning_outcomes: Adapt grammatical and lexical constructions to suit different linguistic scenarios.
Select and use the appropriate register to ensure effective written communication.
Correctly use complex sentence constructions in written French.
Identify linguistic differences between English and French in complex sentence constructions.

title: Introduction to Food Science and Technology
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: The supply of safe, high quality food is essential in our modern society. This course will examine the food supply chain and factors contributing to the quality of food commodities. Students are introduced to the principles of the scientific study of food through case studies and experiential laboratory learning, and will explore the chemical, physical, sensory and microbiological properties of food commodities. Principles for the safe supply of food are established, as are mandatory requirements and voluntary aspects of food product labelling. At the completion of this course students will have gained an appreciation of the scope and breadth of food science, and be able to work safely and effectively in kitchen and laboratory environments.
learning_outcomes: Compare the contributions of individual, cultural and religious differences to food selection and preparation;
Discuss the global management of food commodities and issues in the supply of a safe and adequate daily intake;
Apply the scientific method of enquiry as it relates to the measurement of sensory, chemical and physical properties of foods;

Implement safe laboratory & kitchen practice, including wearing of appropriate personal protective equipment, safe handling of chemicals and laboratory equipment and safe disposal of chemicals according to the relevant safety data sheets (SDS).
Match the principles of food science and laboratory based evaluation of food properties to constituents, their reactions and applications;

title: Extended French through Translation
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course will introduce students to the translation of short texts of different genres from French into English and from English into French. It will allow them to further improve their knowledge of the French language and culture while learning some common translation strategies.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate higher-order grammatical and translation skills;
Translate simple literary and journalistic texts to and from French.
Use varying registers of language appropriately;

title: Introduction to the Nutritional, Physical and Psychological Aspects of Wellness
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course provides an introduction to the triad of nutrition, physical activity and psychological health and how they are linked and interact to impact on overall wellness. The importance of food and nutrition, physical activity and exercise and of emotional and mental health in the overall concept of wellness and their contribution to conditions and disease states such as obesity, diabetes, heart disease, cancer and dementia, will be covered. The modern lifestyle will be explored to investigate how it has impacted on the nutrition, physical activity and psychological health triad and thereby on overall wellness.
learning_outcomes: Describe the nutrients and other food components and the impact they can have on wellness.
Describe important psychological factors which can impact on wellness.

Explore the evidence based links and interactions between nutritional, physical and psychological factors which impact on wellness and the equally important roles they play in terms of the currently common societal conditions and diseases such as obesity, diabetes, heart disease, cancer and dementia.
Apply the evidence based nutritional, physical activity and mental health factors that improve wellness on case studies and in real life.
Describe physical activity, exercise and fitness and the impact these can have on wellness.

title: Introduction to Nutrition Science and Applications
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: Nutrition science is used to determine our dietary needs, recommended intakes, and our food regulations and policies. This course provides an introduction to food and the nutrients they contain and will cover the concepts and use of food analysis and food databases. The government and food industry bodies which regulate and/or inform food professionals and consumers on foods and nutrients will also be covered. At the end of this course students will have a solid foundation in the basics of nutrition science and it’s applications, which will assist in future studies or interactions with nutrition information.
learning_outcomes: Explain how food composition tables are generated and used and how to apply them to record and analyse food intake;
List and describe the nutrients we need from foods, summarising their related health issues, digestion and absorption.
Identify the requirements and regulation for food labelling and apply these to the generation of labels;
Describe dietary guidelines, nutrient reference values and models for healthy eating; how they are generated and regulated and explain how they are used as tools for improving food consumption;
Identify the various sectors of the government and food industry and recognise their role in providing safe and nutritious food;

title: Essential Nutrients
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: The micronutrients (vitamins, minerals, and trace elements) and macronutrients (fat, protein, carbohydrate and alcohol) are the essential nutrients in our foods. They play an important role in our body and impact our health and wellbeing. This course will discuss the biochemistry, food sources, absorption, metabolism, physiological functions, genetics, development and consequences of deficiency, dietary requirements and assessment, therapeutic use and toxicity. In the tutorial activities students will discuss dietary intake and learn about how suboptimal nutrition may affect human health, with particular attention to malnutrition and global hunger. This course includes traditional Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander foods and ways of learning. On successful completion of this course, students will be able to explain the nutrient contents of food and the role and function of macronutrients and micronutrients in the body and their impact on health.
learning_outcomes: Apply their knowledge of biochemistry, physiology and other sciences in the understanding of the principles of nutrition with emphasis on micronutrients and macronutrients.
Explain the forms in which nutrients are present in foods.
Explain the role of nutrients in maintaining normal body metabolism and functions, as well as in the prevention and treatment of chronic diseases.
Match foods with specific nutrients.
Discuss digestion, absorption, transport and metabolism of nutrients by human beings.
Present and communicate scientific content.

title: Plant Food Products
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: Commodities of Plant origin constitute the staple diet for people worldwide, providing essential nutrients - such as proteins, carbohydrates and fibre - through fresh, minimally processed and fully processed products. The structure, composition, properties, uses, processing and technology of cereal grains, with emphasis on wheat, will be studied. The post-harvest technologies of horticultural produce is studied in relation to their biochemistry, physiology, composition and response to changes in the physical environment. Properties and methods of processing of other food plant materials such legumes, nuts, coffee, teas and herbs will also be addressed. By completing this course, students will appreciate the properties of plant-based foods and explain methods for processing plant food materials.
learning_outcomes: Identify and explain the product composition, product quality, production process of commercially available selected plant food products.
Identify the various methods of processing that can be used for plant food materials;
Collect and interpret the data and results of experiments on the effect of processing conditions on quality parameters of plant food products;
Identify the structure, composition and uses of cereal, oilseed, horticultural produce and leguminous foods;
Explain the effect of different storage conditions on horticultural produce in relation to structure, composition, biochemistry and physiology;

title: Food Marketing and Consumer Behaviour
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Psychological and environmental (physical and social surroundings) factors influence our food choices, often beyond physiological signals such as hunger and satiety. In this course you will learn about basic marketing and consumer psychology principles, which can help promote new food products and create healthier food environments in the long term. This course includes traditional Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander ways of learning. Upon completion of this course, students will be able to identify and apply basic consumer behaviour and food marketing concepts.
learning_outcomes: Describe marketing concepts behind food advertisement
Identify ambient influences on consumer behaviour and choice
Describe and discuss drivers that influence food choice
Apply learned principles to conducting food market research and developing a marketing strategy
Explain marketing and consumer behaviour principles

title: Animal Food Products
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: Commodities of Animal origin constitute a major component of the diet of people worldwide, providing essential nutrients, such as proteins and fat, through fresh, minimally processed and fully processed products. The physicochemical properties of milk are studied, as are the processing methods involved in the conversion of milk to other dairy products such as cheese, yoghurt and butter. The chemistry, structure, composition, properties, uses, and method of processing of animal food such as eggs, fish meat and meat products are also examined. By completing this course, students will appreciate the properties of animal-based foods and explain the processing methods of animal foods.
learning_outcomes: Identify and explain the product composition, quality and production process of commercially available selected animal food products.
Explain the composition, structure and function of meat, eggs, milk and fish;
Collect and interpret the data of experiments on the effect of processing conditions on quality parameters of animal food products;
Identify and describe the physical and biochemical changes occurring during the conversion of muscle to meat;
Describe and evaluate the implication of storage and processing operations on the quality of selected foods of animal origin;

title: Food Processing and Quality Management
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: The current patterns of food consumption indicate a strong consumer preference for processed food products, as they are very economical and last much longer than fresh produce which are not compatible with today's lifestyle. It is, therefore, very important to have a clear understanding of the principles of the processes involved as well as the methods employed to ensure quality standards. This course examines food processing systems and food quality management systems. Particular emphasis is on the principles of the various operations including pre-processing, food processing operations and post-processing, as well as on the application of Hazard Analysis Critical Control Point (HACCP) to food production with the aim of producing quality food that meets consumer expectations and food safety standards regulated by the authorities. By completing this course, students will appreciate the principles of food processing and food quality management.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the quality parameters of food products from different food processing operations;
Describe and outline the principles of food processing design and production techniques;
Identify and explain issues relevant to food processing and food quality management systems.
Generate a quality management system based on the Hazard Analysis Critical Control Point (HACCP) principles to food processing;
Collect and interpret the data from experiments in different food processing operations;

title: Microbiology, Food Safety and Immunology
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Focuses on the understanding of introductory microbiology and immunology for application to food and nutritional sciences. The course provides foundation concepts in microbiology and immunology that leads to a thorough understanding of these disciplines relevant to a broad range of sciences. It covers issues relevant to the food and nutrition industry including Microbial diversity, metabolism, microbial genetics and human microbiology and immunology.
learning_outcomes: Develop awareness of the importance of microorganisms in food production, health, gene technology, and probiotics.
Demonstrate advanced skills in laboratory methods and understanding of occupational health and safety procedures in scientific work.
Demonstrate familiarity with common food microbiology issues and food safety practices.
Apply Knowledge of the diversity of microorganisms, microbial metabolism, and immune function to common pathological disease processes.

title: Future Food: Technologies, Issues and Trends
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: The world population will always need feeding, but the food production, consumption and regulatory environments are constantly evolving in the face of new technologies and challenges. This course will address the contemporary knowledge, trends, debates and controversies that shape current and future food systems, production, regulation, utilisation and sustainability. By the end of this course, students will have developed the skills to engage with and reflect on these key issues, readying them to engage with future challenges and opportunities in the food sector.
learning_outcomes: Integrate information on contemporary issues in food to make predictions on future trends.
Interpret and evaluate current government rules and regulations related to food labelling, manufacture, and claims.
Critically analyse and engage with contemporary issues, trends and controversies important to the future of food.
Apply critical and reflective thinking to contemporary issues in food.

assessment_tasks.task_name: In-class presentation on future food trends
Case study of a novel product or food company
Analysis of the contemporary media portrayal of a novel or controversial food issue

title: Nutrition in Health and Disease
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: Nutrition is a key factor that can reduce disease burdens and optimise health outcomes – with benefits for individuals and society. In this course students will explore the evidence base for the role nutrition plays in health status, and the prevention and management of major chronic and acute diseases. By the end of this course students will be able to apply and critique a variety of information relevant to the relationships between nutrition, health and disease; this will include methodologies, evidence and interactions with other factors influencing nutrition, health and disease outcomes. This will prepare students to engage with various stakeholders in nutrition, health and disease including health, government and public health sectors, and the food industry.
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of genetics in diet-related diseases and disease susceptibility;
Apply dietary, energy and physical assessment methodologies;
Evaluate evidence for the relationship between diet, nutrition and disease;
Synthesise, interpret and communicate information on interactions between diet, nutrition and other key determinants of health in the aetiology, prevention and treatment of key diseases;

title: Nutrition for the life cycle
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Provides a detailed view of the nutritional foundations necessary for human growth, development, reproduction, health and well-being in each stage of the human life cycle. The life stages covered are preconception, pregnancy and lactation, infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood, and old age. Recommendations and consequences for health and disease will be addressed for each life cycle stage.
learning_outcomes: Explain, compare and contrast the nutritional requirements of humans during different stages of the life cycle
Generate resources to summarise and communicate nutritional information compiled from official recommendations and scientific sources
Relate foods and nutrients to the biological requirements of humans at different stages of the life cycle
Explain and reflect upon the consequences of physical, biochemical, physiological, social and psychological factors impacting nutritional intake and status during each stage of the human life cycle
Relate the nutrition-related concerns specific to each stage of the human life cycle to consequences for health and disease

title: Research Methods
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Provides a detailed view of the methods used in scientific research. It covers access to and critical evaluation of the literature, the design and conduct of experiments, the handling and analysis of experimental data and the reporting and publication of results. Aspects such as generation and testing of hypotheses based on existing knowledge, generation of aims, animal and human ethics considerations and applications, health and safety issues, importance and choice of methodology including power analyses, preparation of data and statistical analyses, interpretation and publishing of results, the grant application process and the patent application process.
learning_outcomes: Access, review and critically evaluate the scientific literature in a specific field;
Recognise and explain the importance and use of statistics in the scientific process;
Understand the grant and patent application processes.
Understand the process of the scientific experimental method from the generation of a hypothesis to the publishing of results including ethics and safety considerations;

title: Food Product Development
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: New food products are continually evolving and being added to the marketplace. This course involves going through the process of developing a new food product from concept, through to market analysis, design, development and evaluation, and finally to market release. On successful completion of this course, students will gain a wide range of knowledge and skills that can be applied for the improvement or development of food products to satisfy consumers’ changing demands and to improve business related outcomes.
learning_outcomes: Design and apply packaging for food products;
As part of a team, create and evaluate a product using the development process;
Combine theoretical knowledge and practical skills to reproduce existing food products.
Evaluate product quality and sensory properties;
Design a food product through the application of knowledge of food ingredients and functional foods;
Reflect on the role of food trends in the new product development process;

title: Food Analysis
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: Foods are analysed for purposes of trade, compliance, quality assurance, authentication, complaint investigation, nutritional attributes and scientific research. In this course students will undertake and compare various food analysis techniques, followed by analysis, interpretation and presentation of the results. Upon completion of this course, students will have the knowledge and skills to apply and assess the principles and practices required for the analysis of foods.
learning_outcomes: Analyse, interpret and report on results obtained in a scientific format.
Compare advanced and conventional techniques and instruments to analyse chemical and physical properties of foods;
Apply a range of chemical analyses of food components;
Select appropriate analytical techniques for specific food components;
Apply valid sampling techniques to food materials having widely diverse properties and volumes;

title: Professional Practice
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: The transition from the university learning context into the professional workplace environment and the integration of theoretical concepts and knowledge to real world skills and experience is an important component of any student's professional career commencement. This course allows students to implement the theory and learning obtained during their degree program in real-life work settings by providing the opportunity to apply their knowledge and skills through the completion of a Work Integrated Learning (WIL) experience, to be completed in a setting and environment relevant to practicing Nutritionists and Food Technologists. On successful completion of this course, students will improve their skills in job application, career planning, professional conduct and behaviour, teamwork, organisation and management in professional atmospheres. Students will have an active role in organising their WIL experience, however, students will need to consult with the Course Coordinator prior to approaching companies or organisations. The Course Coordinator will ensure the WIL experience is appropriate and does not adversely affect other existing WIL activities or courses of the University. A nominated supervisor within the host organisation will be required. In addition to the 140 hours of WIL, students will be expected to complete up to 40 hours of addition study load, which includes the completion of assessments, and on-campus contact hours.
learning_outcomes: Communicate effectively and display professional behaviour in actions, attitudes, and demeanour.
Identify required knowledge and skills in the chosen field of work to contribute effectively as part of a team, set goals for WIL, and assess potential workplace risks
Identify, synthesize, and reflect on the application of theoretical knowledge to the practical requirements of a discipline-specific workplace
Evaluate and report their work experience performance, including their roles, professional strengths and weakness.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Students must demonstrate competency in all listed assessments

title: Food Science and Human Nutrition Honours 4110
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course builds knowledge and understanding about research in the discipline of food and/or nutritional sciences. The course aims at enhancing the skills and capacities in reading and reviewing literature, critical reasoning and argument, and verbal communication. Students will enhance their skills through discussions of theoretical and applied directions in food science or human nutrition studies; student-based presentations of key issues; and training in computing skills, on-line bibliographic searches, risk assessment and oral presentation techniques.
learning_outcomes: Application of skills and methods needed to critically analyse scientific literature and communicate scientific issues in verbal form.
Advanced understanding of the theory and practice of research in the discipline of food science and/or human nutrition.
Advanced understanding of the use of the scientific method to examine problems.
Knowledge of research ethics and safety principles and procedures associated with food and/or nutritional research and a capacity to obtain the appropriate approvals for a research project.
Advanced comprehension of contemporary issues in food and/or nutritional science.

title: Industry Placement II
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course will enhance students’ knowledge and skills through an extended Work Integrated Learning (WIL) experience in a food-related environment. Students will participate in a range of work practices as negotiated with the host organisation. Upon successful completion, students will use critical reflective thinking and writing to strengthen identified areas of professional practice. Students will build on their identified strengths and demonstrate growth in areas needing development. Students are expected to spend at least 200 hours on WIL and complete additional study activities related to the course. The University's placement system, SONIA, will be used to facilitate student placement.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the ability to fluently adapt to a changing workplace setting taking into consideration, role, workplace policies and operating procedures, workplace culture and structure and workplace purpose and business model
Enhance professional skills in the workplace, such as effective oral and written communication, teamwork, time management, independent work, and ethical practice
Use a reflective practice framework to set achievable and professionally relevant learning goals for a defined period of study
Communicate with impact and efficiency in the workplace.
Critically evaluate and report on work placement performance, in relation to stated goals, professional standards and work placement setting

title: Industry Placement I
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with real-world experience through the completion of a Work Integrated Learning (WIL) component in a food-related environment. Students will observe and participate in a range of work practices as negotiated with the host organisation. Students will develop introductory skills in job application writing, career planning, professionalism and safety in the workplace, and teamwork. Students are expected to spend at least 200 hours on WIL and to complete additional study activities related to the course. The University's placement system, SONIA, will be used to facilitate student placement.
learning_outcomes: Develop a cover letter and CV that align with the job description and reflect relevant experience and motivation
Develop skills in analysing and managing potential workplace risks to minimise their impacts
Design and deliver a presentation on the skills and experience obtained from a workplace setting.
Apply teamwork and time management skills in a workplace environment
Identify the required knowledge, skills, and selection criteria from a job description

assessment_tasks.task_name: Written Assignment: Expectations and Goal Setting/Risk assessment

title: Research Project I
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course helps students develop the knowledge and skills necessary to identify research problems, review relevant literature, identify research gaps, formulate research questions, establish research aims and objectives, and select and modify methodologies to conduct experiments that address the research questions.
learning_outcomes: Choose from a range of recommended approaches to design study and identify the appropriate methods for collecting data
Justify a research need, establish research questions, and develop aims and objectives for a study
Discuss, write, respond to feedback and present processes, knowledge and implications of research to an informed audience.
Collaborate with a senior researcher to develop a scientifically sound research proposal for the chosen topic
Analyse trends or themes in information/data and synthesise to establish current state knowledge of a research problem

title: Research Project II
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course helps students advance their knowledge and skills in research and scientific communication by conducting an original research project under the guidance of an academic supervisor. It enables students to carry out experiments, collect and analyse data, and interpret and present their findings in a scientific manner, thereby strengthening both their research and communication skills.
learning_outcomes: Select appropriate statistical methods to analyse data to fill knowledge gaps that are stated by others.
Independently design and conduct experiments or surveys to obtain the necessary data to meet the research aims and objectives
Communicate research process and findings using oral and written communications following the discipline-specific format.
Evaluate information/data and the inquiry process using self-determined criteria

title: Nutrition for the Life Cycle
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: It is essential to understand the nutritional requirements across various life stages, including preconception, pregnancy, lactation, infancy, childhood, adolescence, adulthood, and older adulthood. This course provides advanced knowledge of human growth, development, reproduction, health, and well-being throughout the life cycle. Additionally, it addresses nutritional recommendations and their implications for health and disease at each stage of life.
learning_outcomes: Synthesise and communicate nutritional information derived from official guidelines and scientific literature
Critically evaluate the nutritional needs of humans at various life stages, highlighting key differences and similarities
Assess the nutrition-related concerns specific to each life stage and their implications for health and disease
Explain the relationship between foods, nutrients, and the biological requirements of humans across different stages of the life cycle

title: Animal Food Products
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: Commodities of Animal origin constitute a major component of the diet of people worldwide, providing essential nutrients, such as proteins and fat, through fresh, minimally processed and fully processed products. The physicochemical properties of milk are studied, as are the processing methods involved in the conversion of milk to other dairy products such as cheese, yoghurt and butter. The chemistry, structure, composition, properties, uses, and method of processing of animal food such as eggs, fish, meat and meat products are also examined. By completing this course, students will have knowledge and skill to assess the properties of animal-based foods and explain the processing methods of animal foods.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse the composition, structure, and function of meat, eggs, milk, and fish
Interpret experiments to assess the impact of processing conditions on quality parameters of animal food products
Examine and describe the physical and biochemical transformations occurring during the conversion of muscle to meat
Collaboratively evaluate the composition, quality, and production processes of commercially available animal food products.
Accurately quantify the implications of storage and processing operations on the quality of selected animal-derived foods

title: Plant Food Products
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: Commodities of plant origin constitute the staple diet for people worldwide, providing essential nutrients - such as proteins, carbohydrates and fibre - through fresh, minimally processed and fully processed products. The structure, composition, properties, uses, processing and technology of cereal grains, with emphasis on wheat, will be studied. The post-harvest technologies of horticultural produce is studied in relation to their biochemistry, physiology, composition and response to changes in the physical environment. Properties and methods of processing of other food plant materials such legumes, nuts, coffee, teas and herbs will also be addressed. By completing this course, students will have knowledge and skills to assess the properties of plant-based foods and explain methods for processing plant food materials.
learning_outcomes: Collect, analyse and interpret the data and results of experiments on the effect of processing conditions on quality parameters of plant food products
Demonstrate scientific writing skills.
Explain the effect of different storage conditions on horticultural produce in relation to structure, composition, biochemistry and physiology
Identify the appropriate methods of processing that can be used for plant food materials
Critically analyse and evaluate the product composition, product quality, production process of commercially available selected plant food products
Describe the structure, composition and uses of cereal, oilseed, horticultural produce and leguminous foods

title: Food Processing and Quality Management
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: Food processing is involved in food preservation and alteration of eating quality, where quality management systems are used to ensure food products meet consumer expectations for quality and safety, as well as compliance with food standards regulations. In this course, students will examine advanced food processing and food quality management systems. Emphasis is on the principles of the various operations including pre-processing, food processing operations and post-processing, as well as on the development of Hazard Analysis Critical Control Point (HACCP) to food production with the aim of producing quality food that meets consumer expectations and food safety standards regulated by the authorities. By completing this course, students will have knowledge and skills to apply food processing principles and to develop quality management systems in food processing.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate and optimise quality parameters of food products from various processing operations
Conduct complex experiments in food processing operations, utilising advanced statistical tools to interpret and present data effectively
Critically assess and address current and emerging issues in food processing and quality management, including regulatory compliance, sustainability, and technological advancements.
Develop and evaluate a comprehensive quality management systems based on Hazard Analysis Critical Control Point (HACCP) principles
Critically analyse and synthesise advanced principles of food processing design and production techniques

title: Future Food: Technologies, Issues and Trends
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: The world population will always need feeding, but the food production, consumption and regulatory environments are constantly evolving in the face of new technologies and challenges. This course will address the contemporary knowledge, trends, debates and controversies that shape current and future food systems, production, regulation, utilisation and sustainability. By the end of this course, students will have developed the skills to engage with and reflect on these key issues, readying them to engage with future challenges and opportunities in the food sector.
learning_outcomes: Apply critical and reflective thinking to food science practice
Develop and implement strategies for sustainable food systems and products, considering novel food processing technologies and underutilized food resources.
Integrate and synthesize information on contemporary issues in food to inform strategic business and research investments
Interpret, evaluate, and apply government rules and regulations to evaluate to food labelling, manufacture, and health claims
Critically analyse and engage with advanced issues, trends, and generative AI in manufacturing and development of novel food products

assessment_tasks.task_name: Case study of a novel product or food company
In-class presentation on future food trends

title: Food Product Development
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: New food products are continually developed to meet market demand. This course provides advanced knowledge and skills in developing a new food product, from concept and market analysis to design, development, evaluation, and final market release. Students are required to develop a new food product and showcase it at the food expo at the end of the course.
learning_outcomes: Collaboratively apply theoretical knowledge and skills to develop a new food product and showcase it to hypothetical customers
Communicate effectively in a professional manner with a knowledgeable audience.
Demonstrate advanced knowledge in major steps to develop a new food product
Critically reflect on the trends in food science and technology
Explain the roles and properties of ingredients in foods

title: Food Marketing and Consumer Behaviour
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Consumer behaviour and food marketing involves exploring the psychological, social and economic factors influencing food choices and purchasing decisions. In this course, students will examine and apply key theories of market research and consumer behaviour, the role of branding and advertising, and the impact of marketing strategies on the consumer’s food choices. By the end of the course, students will be able to apply consumer insights to design effective marketing strategies that promote both commercial success and public health outcomes.
learning_outcomes: Apply advanced strategies to influence consumer behaviour in the food industry
