syllabus_overview: In a global marketplace where "borderless organisations" are quickly becoming the norm, employees have an increasingly important role in the cultivation of company capability. This course examines the management of people in organisations across different countries and cultures. The primary aim is to discriminate the varying roles and functions of the various HRM activities within an international context. The course considers the challenges of managing expatriates in home and host countries, in the context of multinational and transnational corporations as well as other types of international organisations. In doing so, it draws on a cross-section of the literature in human resource management, organisational behaviour and comparative management.
learning_outcomes: Differentiate between and asses the key HRM issues arising from organisations operating in an international context.
Engage critically with recent research in the literature in order to gain a deeper understanding of ongoing developments in the international human resource management function.
Recognise and evaluate the key requirements for managing people in an international context.
Apply the theories and concepts learned to real international management scenarios and cases.
Work collaboratively in teams to produce cohesive group reports/projects on international HRM.
Describe the impact that culture has on management in the international context.

title: Entrepreneurship and Innovation
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Entrepreneurship refers to the process of developing new business ventures or growing existing ones. Central to this activity is entrepreneurs: innovative and risk-taking individuals who seek to bring about change and new opportunities, both for themselves and the business communities in which they operate. Entrepreneurs play an important role in commence, trade, and economic growth in many nations. Entrepreneurship will be explored in the course in terms of analysing new venture opportunities and ideas as well as building and assessing entrepreneurial characteristics. A key element of entrepreneurship, innovation, will also be a focus of the course. Innovation is an important prerequisite for gaining a competitive advantage and building a strong and sustainable business. Modern thriving enterprise demand constant levels of innovation. The scope and richness of theoretical developments in the discipline of innovation, offers students the potential to develop substantial skills in understanding the discipline, its role in entrepreneurship and in the development of successful, contemporary organisations. The course provides a framework for understanding the process of creating and managing innovative organisations. This will enable students to deal successfully with dynamic demands from markets and customers, that are becoming even more sophisticated and knowledgeable.
learning_outcomes: Critically discuss and analyse the concepts of entrepreneurship and innovation.
Demonstrate an ability to engage in entrepreneurial and innovation processes.
Create a well-structured and concise innovation plan.

title: Global Business and Innovation Management
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course focuses on the management of international business organisations, comprising both equity (wholly-owned and JV) and non-equity business organisations (strategic alliances). The course is organised around theories and approaches to international management. Major topics include the organization and management of multinational corporations (MNCs) as the leading type of international business organisation; MNC headquarter-subsidiary relationships; the organisation and management of business networks; MNCs as learning organisations; and critical perspectives on international businesses. Functional areas of management are examined in their international contexts, including international human resources management; international operations and supply chain management and international marketing.
learning_outcomes: Comprehend how the management of cross-border operations impact upon the management functions of human resource management, marketing, operations and supply chain management.
Think critically about underlying theories, concepts, assumptions and arguments relating to the multinational form of organisation.
Engage in inquiry processes to understand the management and organisational challenges of coordinating cross-border operations.
Work independently and collaboratively to analyse strategies to manage multiple cross-border operations.
Develop the essential international perspectives which inform professional management standards and ethical practice in international management.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Group Research Project (Written Report & Oral Presentations)

title: Cross-Cultural Management
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course examines the ways in which cultural differences impact on the process of doing business and managing internationally. A range of conceptual frameworks are developed, including mental models and schemata as the source of cultural differences and difficulties in managing intercultural interactions. Using evidence and business practice, the course explores the nature of culture and how cultural differences impact on interpersonal interactions, intergroup interactions and the management of multi-cultural workforces (including expatriates). This course analyses the practice of management and negotiation in an international cross-cultural context, and the challenges of managing international business relationships are critically analysed. Topics include the nature and dimensions of culture, issues relating to cross-cultural problem solving, the dynamics of multi-cultural teams, managing global teams and leadership across cultures. How culture impacts on managerial decision-making of ethical and social responsibility issues is explored.
learning_outcomes: Identify, analyse, evaluate and communicate information reflective of negotiation and management formats and in cross cultural contexts.
Apply analytical and theoretical frameworks to cross-cultural management.
Effectively engage in a cross-cultural negotiation exercise.
Demonstrate an integrative understanding of the ethical and social issues in cross-cultural management and negotiation.
Incorporate theories, concepts and models relevant to the global and cultural context of an international business issue or case.
Identify the key issues raised by international business cases in cross-cultural management.
Interact with team members within a problem-based learning structure to effectively coordinate and communicate project and case study outcomes.

title: Consumer Psychology and Behavior
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Understanding how and why consumers make decisions is a critical skill for marketing leaders shaping strategies in a competitive, rapidly changing marketplace. Students critically examine how consumer behaviour theories and research can be applied to design effective marketing strategies. Emphasis is placed on evaluating how individuals interpret, respond to and are influenced by diverse marketing approaches, with a primary focus on individual consumers making purchase and consumption decisions. By engaging with current theory, empirical research, and applied case studies, students develop the ability to analyse, interpret, and predict consumer behaviour - and to translate these insights into innovative, evidence-based marketing strategies that deliver impact at both strategic and operational levels.
learning_outcomes: Develop evidence-based marketing recommendations that address consumer identity and ethical considerations.
Predict adoption patterns for innovations using consumer psychology frameworks.
Interpret consumer behaviour data and case evidence.
Generate consumer behaviour insights and outline implications for managerial decision-making.
Explain psychological, social and cultural influences on decision-making using consumer behaviour theories.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Group Strategic Insight Report for an Innovation and Presentation

title: Digital Marketing Strategy
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: As global business increasingly operates in real-time digital environments, organisations must adapt their marketing strategies to remain competitive. This course provides students with a thorough understanding of how digital technologies influence marketing practice and consumer engagement. Students will explore the strategic use of digital platforms including web, mobile applications, online advertising, and social media. The course examines the technological foundations of these platforms and their role in delivering marketing content effectively. Key topics include globalisation, localisation, real-time communication, and emerging approaches to market segmentation. Students will critically assess how digital environments shape consumer behaviour and learn to develop marketing strategies that are responsive to rapid technological and cultural change.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the role of conversion and digital relationship marketing in achieving strategic marketing objectives.
Investigate the challenges of adapting marketing strategies to globalised and networked digital markets.
Conduct online market research to assess and select digital marketing opportunities.
Analyse the integration of marketing operations, and technology in delivering value through real-time digital channels.

title: Customer Experience Management
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In an era where customer expectations are shaped by digitalisation, omnichannel interactions, and emerging technologies, managing customer experience (CX) has become a critical driver of competitive advantage. This course builds on the foundations of services and relationship marketing to explore how organisations design, deliver, and optimise customer experiences across physical, digital, and hybrid environments. Students will examine the principles, frameworks, and strategies that underpin exceptional customer experiences, including the role of service design, customer journey mapping, and experience innovation. Emphasis is placed on understanding customer behaviour in experience-centric contexts, leveraging data and technology for personalisation, and managing relationships to foster loyalty and advocacy. The course also addresses the strategic and ethical considerations of CX management, including the integration of AI, automation, and analytics in shaping customer interactions. The course also critically examines ethics, privacy, accessibility, and inclusion in data-driven experiences. Graduates will be able to diagnose journey pain points, prioritise CX investments using evidence, and build actionable CX roadmaps that align with strategy and performance. By the end of the course, students will be equipped to develop and implement customer experience strategies that enhance value creation for both customers and organisations in a rapidly evolving marketplace.
learning_outcomes: Analyse CX data and metrics to prioritise improvements, justify investments, and address ethical, privacy and inclusion considerations.
Apply service design and customer journey mapping tools to diagnose and improve omnichannel experiences.
Critically evaluate customer experience (CX) theories and frameworks ground in services and relationship marketing.
Design omnichannel engagement strategies integrating CRM, automation and AI in alignment with ethical and strategic goals.
Develop actionable CX roadmaps and governance frameworks that support organisational strategy and foster a service-led culture.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Omnichannel Customer Experience Audit and Quality Analysis

title: AI and Data Insight in Business Decisions
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In today’s data-driven world, it is essential to understand the application of AI and machine learning to gain insight and inform business decisions. This course fosters students' conceptual and practical grasp of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly machine learning, across diverse business scenarios where AI plays a pivotal role. Students learn fundamental concepts, key AI technologies, and basics of machine learning techniques exploring its impact on diverse businesses and industries in making decisions. Additionally, students gain proficiency in applying AI and machine learning techniques and tools to address challenges in various business settings. Please note: This course is offered in alternate terms. Students should plan their enrolment accordingly.
learning_outcomes: Explain core concepts, essential techniques, and prevalent tools in AI and machine learning with a focus on their application in business contexts.
Communicate ideas proficiently in a professional manner and function as a capable leader or team player.
Critically evaluate the significance of machine learning across diverse business scenarios.
Apply suitable machine learning methodologies and tools to address business challenges.

title: Cybersecurity and Risk Management in Banking
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Effective risk management is critical for the viability and success of financial institutions. This course provides an insight into measuring and managing cybersecurity risks and other financial risk exposures of firms operating in the financial services industry. Students will be introduced to cybersecurity risks and gain an understanding of the cyber threat landscape for banks, including cost assessment of security risks and threat and vulnerability management. Additionally, students will be equipped with analytical tools for measuring and managing other financial risks for banks such as interest rate risk, market risk, credit risk, sovereign and off-balance sheet risk, liquidity risk, and technology and other operational risk. Please note: This course is offered in alternate terms. Students should plan their enrolment accordingly.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate risk exposures of financial institutions in a simulated environment.
Develop solutions to challenges faced by financial intermediaries in terms of risk measurement and management using case studies and excel based modelling.
Outline cybersecurity risks from the perspective of practitioners in the financial services sector.
Explain the cyberthreat landscape for banks and how to manage cyberthreat and vulnerability.
Identify and measure different types of risks financial institutions are exposed to.

title: Digital Payments and Blockchain Technology
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In today’s rapidly evolving digital landscape, it is essential to understand the application of blockchain technology in the financial sector. This course covers the fundamentals of payments as well as blockchain technology and its applications in the context of payments, payment systems, crypto-assets, and financial services. Students will develop knowledge of payments and payment systems as well as skills in leveraging and managing the risk associated with utilising blockchain technologies and other technological innovations to support payments and the delivery of financial services. Please note: This course is offered in alternate terms. Students should plan their enrolment accordingly.
learning_outcomes: Work individually or in teams to communicate and present information in a proficient and professional manner.
Analyse the mechanics of payments and the infrastructures that support payments in both domestic and cross-border contexts.
Critically analyse the opportunities and challenges in deploying blockchain technologies.
Evaluate the transformative impact of blockchain technologies to payments and the delivery of financial services.
Explain the key principles that underpin payments, blockchain technologies and crypto-assets.

title: Marketing Analytics and Emerging Technologies
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Understanding analytical tools, marketing metrics, and emerging technologies is critical for a career in the dynamic world of marketing. Students will gain an in-depth understanding of how data analysis, performance measurement, and the application of new technologies can enhance marketing effectiveness. Emphasis will be given to developing student skills in evaluating market data, applying marketing metrics, forecasting trends, and integrating advanced approaches such as AI agents and agentic marketing into strategic management.
learning_outcomes: Analyse company, competitor, and customer metrics to assess marketing performance in digital and physical contexts.
Evaluate the effectiveness of digital and social media marketing analytics in measuring campaign outcomes.
Interpret customer behaviour and digital marketing metrics to inform marketing decisions.
Apply product, pricing, distribution, and promotion metrics to evaluate strategic marketing decisions.
Generate data-driven marketing recommendations by integrating traditional metrics with emerging technologies.

title: Human Resource Management
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course provides an introduction to human resource management (HRM), and to frameworks explaining the core functions of HRM i.e. planning, recruitment, development, reward, voice and exit. In particular, students will consider how responsibility for people management is distributed inside and outside the organisation. The course takes a very practical view of HRM, using many examples, exercises, and cases. Students are encouraged to think about what HRM means - how it differs according to the nature of work, by organisation, by industry sector, and in different regions and countries - and to consider what constitutes ethical human resource management.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate various HRM theories and frameworks to assess their fundamental assumptions, intellectual rigour, and practical value.
Communicate how and why HRM policy and practice differs according to context.
Consider the range of competencies and roles required of HRM practitioners and other managers of people within various organisational settings.
Develop an appreciation of the ethical challenges inherent in managing people in an equitable way.
Develop skills in framing, researching and presenting solutions to workplace problems.
Define and examine fundamental HRM concepts.

title: Global Marketing Strategy and Planning
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In contrast with growing their domestic market, businesses often engage in strategic market expansion to other countries, involving alternative processes that range from exporting to internationalisation, multinationalisation, and globalisation. Each of these expansion strategies is unlike the others in the capabilities and competencies needed by the business, as well as in the core marketing considerations of segmentation, targeting and positioning it involves. Guided by the global marketing imperative, the course is designed to provide students with a thorough grounding in all facets of global marketing strategy, A framework is developed that focuses on such key issues as the global market environment, the global marketing mix, and the strategic consideration of global market segmentation, targeting and positioning decisions. The overall focus is on the identification of global marketing opportunities, and on the subsequent planning and development of global marketing strategies aligned to the identified opportunities. Case studies dealing with global marketing issues assist in the application of learning to practical situations and in the development of a global marketing plan for a product or product line.
learning_outcomes: Justify the importance of studying global marketing and explain the challenges that influence global marketing decisions.
Distinguish between international, Multinational and global marketing management.
Develop effective global marketing strategies and determine the method of entering a market.
Develop and justify an in-depth global marketing plan.
Demonstrate cognitive knowledge of the skills required in identifying, assessing and selecting global market opportunities.
Apply global marketing concepts to gain strategic insights from case studies of real global marketing issues.
Recognise key factors in running effective global businesses and the managerial challenges facing global marketing managers.
Develop and justify global marketing mix programs for different environments.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Case Analysis Live Presentation and Q&A

title: Employment Relations
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: The course Employment Relations explores the management of employment relations in Australia, exploring both laws and institutions beyond the workplace and management strategies within the organisation. Important points of departure are the different ideological and intellectual perspectives on the employment relationship. The course will be especially valuable to managers seeking a better understand Australia's system of employment relations, and the strategic options available in the Australian context, and their potential risks and benefits. Several guest speakers will add practical insights.
learning_outcomes: Analyse a range of laws, institutional structures and managerial practices in employment relations in Australia.
Apply the skills necessary to analyse employment relations problems and develop managerial solutions.
Identify and explain key concepts in employment relations.

title: Strategic Management
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Strategic Management informs students of issues and perspectives in strategic management and corporate policy. This course also tests knowledge and skills through a range of relevant challenges such as debates, case studies and participation in a corporate policy game or a management consultancy in addition to an exam.
learning_outcomes: Critically discuss the concepts and models of strategic management.
Develop and present a critically reflective, well-structured case analysis.
Integrate the tasks of management and planning in an organisation within a competitive environment.

Think strategically about an organisation, its present business position, its long-term direction, its resource and competitive capabilities, the effectiveness of its strategy, and its opportunities for gaining sustainable competitive advantage.

Utilise strategic management tools to conduct strategic analysis of organisations in a variety of industries and competitive situations and understand the challenges and opportunities of the global market environment.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Group Project Written Report and Group Presentation

title: Strategic Intervention Project
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Students will be involved with the identification and framing of a real business intervention project and problem. The Strategic Intervention Project is designed to help students hone, integrate and internalise the competencies developed throughout the Master of Business Administration by applying those competencies to the solving of strategic challenges for client firms and organisations. The course is also designed to produce useful, professional-level results for clients, who in turn provide a rich and consequential learning opportunity for students. Enrolment into the course is via application to the course coordinator. Students will be required to address a set of selection criteria.
learning_outcomes: Propose solutions to identified business challenges by implementing advanced innovation and entrepreneurial strategies.
Critically evaluate key theories, concepts and models that underpin strategic management and intervention within organisations.
Formulate evidence-based actions for organisational application.
Work collaboratively to challenge and develop ideas, and to communicate outcomes in written and oral contexts.
Examine an organisation’s environmental conditions in order to identify challenges, opportunities and emerging trends.

title: Negotiation and Conflict Resolution
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Using a workplace and organisational perspective, this course analyses the nature of conflict and how it is "resolved" from a variety of theoretical and applied perspectives. Students will be able to describe and apply a range of conflict resolution methods including mediation, negotiation, and advocacy. The course is practically oriented. Students develop conflict resolution skills particularly through group-based formal negotiations within the general context of business organisations and the specific context of employment relations law and practice. Adopting a problem based learning approach, the course emphasises the importance of student’s communication skills as an essential attribute in effective conflict resolution.
learning_outcomes: Explain the nature and sources of conflict in organisations and workplaces.
Develop the strategy formulation, planning and research skills required for mediation, negotiation and advocacy.
Describe the features of resolution methods including mediation, negotiation, advocacy and other alternatives.
Apply, both individually and collaboratively, skills in the practice of negotiation within the contexts of workplace employment relations.

Explain the employment relations framework as it affects conflict resolution particularly, but not exclusively, the rights and obligations on employers, employees and their collective representatives to mediate and negotiate, and the use of third-party intervention.
Measure and reflect on the development of their conflict resolution skills and demonstrate their recognition of the factors that enable and sustain such skills.

title: Investment Analysis
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with a solid foundation in theories and methods of pricing securities. It provides an overview of the operation of the securities markets and the mechanics of trading securities. The fundamental valuation tools, including models of risk and return, discounted cash flows and relative valuation are examined and applied to the pricing of securities.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge and skills in the core investment concepts, collecting financial information from electronic databases and employing analytical tools to value financial securities.
Demonstrate critical thinking, analytical and problem solving skills in the context of investment theories and practices.
Analysis and evaluate ordinary shares and fixed income securities.
Examine the relationships between returns and risks.

title: Derivatives and Financial Modelling
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: A broad range of derivative products are examined with a primary focus on how to use these for the management of financial risks. The course introduces standard models of pricing forward, futures and options on diverse underlying assets. The course then explores hedging methods to conduct risk management for business operations, speculative trades, and issued financial instruments. After completing this course students will be familiar with derivatives valuation and their use in risk management. In addition, this course offers students with an opportunity to develop quantitative skills to build financial models to price derivative contracts and inform decision making. Please note: This course is offered in alternate terms. Students should plan their enrolment accordingly.
learning_outcomes: Explain the binomial model and its extension in continuous time to the Black-Scholes model.
Apply financial modelling to price derivative contracts and inform decision making.
Analyse and price diverse derivatives products to generate an optimal risk management strategy.
Demonstrate critical thinking, analytical and problem solving skills in the context of derivatives pricing and hedging practice.
Demonstrate an understanding of pricing forwards, futures and options contracts.

title: Applied Portfolio Management
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Applied Portfolio Management deals with the construction and management of an institutional investment portfolio. It provides students with a thorough understanding of procedures involved in portfolio management - setting portfolio objectives, determining investment policy, formulating investment strategies, devising rules for updating portfolio, evaluation performance and protecting portfolio. Students will be provided with various management investment products and fund management practices in Australia.
learning_outcomes: Measure and manage risk exposure of a portfolio.
Develop and demonstrate ability to construct and evaluate a portfolio from internationally traded assets under changing market conditions.
Display an understanding of taxation, legal, regulatory and ethical issues relevant to fund management.
Evaluate the portfolio performance.
Demonstrate critical thinking, analytical and problem solving skills in the context of portfolio construction and management.
Critically examine both the active and the passive strategy of portfolio management

title: Financial Institutions Management
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course provides an insight into measuring and managing risk exposures of firms operating in the financial services industry. Introducing analytical tools for measuring interest rate risk, credit risk, liquidity risk, operational risk, and sovereign risk. Please note: This course is offered in alternate terms. Students should plan their enrolment accordingly.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of a broad spectrum of financial products and competence in measuring risk exposures of financial institutions.
Demonstrate critical thinking, analytical and problem solving skills in the context of methods of measuring and managing risks faced by financial intermediaries.
Identify the off-balance-sheet activities of financial institutions.
Function as a finance team member to address operational risk.
Explain the structure and regulation of the financial services industry.

title: International Financial Management
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: The course undertakes an in-depth examination of international financial markets and instruments, foreign exchange regimes and exchange rate determination. A significant part of this course also covers alternative methods of financing international operations and strategies for foreign direct investment and alternative methods. Please note: This course is offered in alternate terms. Students should plan their enrolment accordingly.
learning_outcomes: Explain the use of futures and option contracts in hedging foreign exchange exposure.
Identify market conventions on exchange rate quotation and correctly calculate those quotations.
Recognise and calculate forward exchange rates given spot rates.
Apply appropriate formats and technologies to financial communication.
Comprehend the range of hedging strategies including forward rate hedging and contingent hedging.
Analyse, evaluate and synthesise both quantitative and qualitative financial information to influence problem solving and decision making.
Analyse, apply and evaluate information within the global financial environment of foreign exchange to solve problems and make informed decisions.
Review the problems of dealing in foreign currency and the advantages and disadvantages of overseas funding.
Demonstrate an integrative understanding of the foreign exchange market and the relationships between interest rates, spot and forward rates and expected inflation rates.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Group Assignment Written and Oral Presentation

title: Investment and Portfolio Management
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with a foundation in modern portfolio theory and methods of pricing securities. It also provides an overview of the operation of the securities markets and in-depth analysis of fundamental valuation tools. Students will link theory to practice by constructing an investment portfolio that applies a specific investment strategy with real-world data. Upon completion of this task, students will have a thorough understanding of procedures involved in portfolio management. They will also be equipped with the knowledge and skills to effectively communicate their managed portfolio performance to potential investors. Please note: This course is offered in alternate terms. Students should plan their enrolment accordingly.
learning_outcomes: Construct and manage a portfolio of internationally traded assets.
Critically analyse and solve problems within portfolio management individually and as a part of a team.
Explain the core investment concepts and employ analytical tools to value financial securities.
Explain investment theories and apply critical thinking to investment practices.
Evaluate the portfolio performance and manage risk exposure of a portfolio.
Effectively communicate investment portfolio decisions to potential investors.

title: Human Resource and Organisational Development
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to human resource development (HRD), a field of study and practice that an organisation can draw upon for improving its effectiveness at an individual level, group and process level and organisational systems level. This course also introduces organisation development (OD), a process designed to improve the effectiveness of an organisation by incorporating individual, group and system level requirements. Further, it is a planned and longer-term systematic approach often driven by an expert practitioner (internal or external) working in conjunction with senior management. HRD and OD consider how the wider contextual environment impacts on the organisation's need to manage change effectively. Combining the foundational theoretical disciplines contributing to HRD and OD, the course introduces students to a range of learning interventions for improving the performance and effectiveness of a system.
learning_outcomes: Apply and synthesise a range of human resource and organisation development competencies.
Comprehend and synthesise the theoretical foundations of HRD and OD.
Review the learning processes of self and others.
Analyse and evaluate the role of HRD and OD in relation to organisational outcomes such as organisational effectiveness, productivity and quality of working life.
Collaborate effectively with others for sharing and extending knowledge to complete complex HRD tasks.

title: Digital Innovations in Financial Markets
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course provides an in-depth analysis of FinTech's impact on the financial industry, covering its past, present, and future landscape. We explore challenges and opportunities in the era of digital finance, including FinTech's influence on digital transformation in financial markets. Legal and ethical considerations are emphasised, encompassing regulatory environments and ethical implications of technology in managing financial transactions and data. Communication skills are refined, focusing on effective presentation and report preparation to convey key findings and recommendations to stakeholders. Upon completion, students will have gained a comprehensive understanding of FinTech, innovation, and its impact, along with skills to evaluate, navigate challenges, and communicate findings effectively in finance, technology, and related fields. Please note: This course is offered in alternate terms. Students should plan their enrolment accordingly.
learning_outcomes: Assess the legal and ethical considerations in using fintech in the context of blockchain technologies, machine learning and artificial intelligence.
Analyse the past, current and future landscape of financial technology and innovation.
Effectively communicate findings to stakeholders.
Critically analyse and solve problems on the use of fintech and digital transformation in financial markets including banking models, crowdfunding and other applications in finance.
Explain and apply critical thinking to challenges and opportunities of fintech in the era of digital finance.

title: Media and Advertising Strategy
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Developing expertise in media and advertising strategy is essential for marketers who want to craft campaigns that influence audiences and shape brand reputation. Students in this course learn to analyse local and international campaigns, evaluate ethics and cultural impacts, and develop targeted, responsible strategies aligned with communication objectives. Through real-word case studies and creative projects, students will explore emerging media trends, audience segmentation, and cross-platform integration. Designed for future marketing leaders, this course fosters critical thinking, strategic insight, and an understanding of advertising's role in shaping brand reputation and societal outcomes.
learning_outcomes: Examine the effectiveness of local and global advertising strategies.
Examine the role of advertising and media strategy within marketing communications and identify key trends.
Develop advertising and media strategies that effectively target key segments and align with communication objectives.
Evaluate the ethical, cultural, and societal impacts of advertising and media strategies.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Part B: Full Advertising and Media Strategy
Part A: Campaign Idea and Justification

title: Financial and Management Accounting
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course introduces financial and management accounting to non-accountants. It aims to provide an understanding of the main accounting concepts and the practical use of accounting and financial information for decision making and the achievement of business goals.
learning_outcomes: Apply cost accounting concepts in decision making.
Explain the ways in which accounting contributes to management decision making.
Demonstrate knowledge of the application of capital budgeting methods.
Construct and analyse budgets.
Demonstrate knowledge of the main principles behind the preparation and interpretation of financial statements.
Analyse the cash flow, financial performance and financial position of a business using published financial statements.
Apply cost-volume-profit analysis.

title: Strategic Human Resource Management
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Strategic HRM and ER is the capstone course in the Master of HRM degree and provides a strategic framework for integrating and applying HRM and ER concepts. The need for sustained competitive advantage has made the strategic management of HRM and ER increasingly important to long term business success as it focuses on linking all HRM and ER activities with an organisation's business objectives. As such, Strategic HRM will require students to work at an advanced level to critically analyse HR and ER strategies in relation to their application in the workplace.
learning_outcomes: Apply critical thinking skills in analysing theoretical and applied perspectives of strategic HRM and ER.
Communicate knowledge of SHRM and employment relations in both written and verbal formats reactive to both audience and purpose.
Investigate and communicate the professional values of HRM including the ethical problems inherent in HRM and ER professional roles, including managers and consultants.
Demonstrate the application of problem solving and evaluation skills in HRM and ER through exercises and case study work.
Analyse problems and develop managerial solutions to employment relations problems at both national and workplace level.

title: Brand Value Creation
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Drawing on established frameworks and contemporary practice, students will learn to build and measure customer-based brand equity, design brand architectures, and evaluate brand performance. The course integrates traditional and digital branding, including influencer strategies, social media communities, and the use of analytics and emerging technologies in brand management. Through brand audits and a strategic brand launch project, students will apply theory to practice, developing actionable insights and strategies for building strong, resilient brands in both domestic and global contexts.
learning_outcomes: Critically appraise branding strategies, marketing programmes, and digital metrics to identify strengths, weaknesses, and opportunities for strategic improvement.
Generate branding insights and strategic recommendations effectively in professional written formats.
Interpret and evaluate foundational theories, principles, and models of brand management.
Design a strategic brand launch plan that integrates positioning, identity, communications, and emerging technologies to create brand value.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Individual Brand Plan and Live Interactive Presentation
Individual Brand Audit Report (Part A and B)

title: Health Economics and Finance
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Health economics is the application of economic principles to health and healthcare. Students apply core concepts of supply and demand theories to health and healthcare examples and learn about the importance of information (and information asymmetry) in health care markets; the critical role of insurance; hospital financing and delivery; and private/public mix in finance and provision of healthcare. In this course students are introduced to key conceptual frameworks of healthcare economics and decision making, and examine how Australian and international healthcare systems are designed and organised, including the critical components of long-term care and pharmaceutical markets.
learning_outcomes: Understand the economic concepts relevant to health and healthcare.
Understand how health economics/policies can be used to address specific types of market failure.
Critically evaluate the effects of a health policy or intervention.
Apply analytical skills to interpret, analyse and synthesise data from a variety of sources and communicate information effectively.
Critically examine the economic rationale associated with trends in health system development.
Identify the key economic trade-offs involved in different healthcare allocation decisions and analyse the implications for payers, providers and consumers.

title: Health Plan Design and Payments: Theory and Practice
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Health Plan Design and Payments provides an overview of the practice of health insurance and financing in advanced health systems and healthcare systems in transition. The course is a comprehensive journey through a crucial element of healthcare systems, which pertains to the complexities of health insurance and financing of health economics: health plan design and payments. Students will gain knowledge in the regulatory frameworks and institutional designs of risk sharing, risk adjustment, premium regulation, and payments schemes from both a conceptual and applied perspective.
learning_outcomes: Describe and understand risk sharing, risk adjustment, and incentive mechanisms.
Demonstrate an understanding of the key conceptual frameworks adopted in health plan design and payment schemes including the options available from regulatory and institutional perspectives.
Identify the advantages and limitations of the in-place regulatory tools in different regulated health systems.
Critically assess the effects of the regulatory tools on the objectives of the health system and universal health coverage.
Track and delineate the historical development and evolution of regulation in health plan design and payment.
Critically compare and assess difference between prospective and retrospective risk adjustment, pay-for-performance and activity based/fixed funding.
Design an evaluation framework for the health plan payment.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Research Report and Live Interactive Performance

title: Applied Economic Evaluation in Healthcare
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: The study of economics introduces a unique perspective on healthcare service and system evaluation. Resources are finite for the range of a society's healthcare needs and wants. As a result, choices must be made about how available resources will be best used. This course will introduce participants to economic evaluation principles and their application to real life scenarios in healthcare. The course is designed as an introduction to applied economic evaluation in healthcare. Students will gain knowledge of core economic principles before learning the necessary steps leading up to the conduct of an economic evaluation. The course provides students with the opportunity to apply practical experience in a range of economic evaluations used in front line healthcare. Students will gain an understanding of how economic evaluation can, and is used to inform health care decision-making.
learning_outcomes: Explain the complexity of decision-making in healthcare and the role of economic evaluation in informing decisions and policy design.
Understand the principles and perform steps of cost-effectiveness, cost-utility and cost-benefit analysis.
Critically appraise a randomised controlled trial and a health economic evaluation and be familiar with a range of priority setting techniques.
Understand and use preference elicitation measures for a value-based approach to economic evaluation.
Use economic data to construct a Budget Impact Statement.
Synthesise evidence to develop and strengthen an economic evaluation.

title: Health Systems, Policy and Governance
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Health Systems, Policy and Governance examines national and international health systems and policies from a governance perspective. Conceptual frameworks in governance rely on multidisciplinary (e.g. political sciences, public policy, management, industrial relations and economics) approaches to understand the complexities of dynamic industries such as the health and social care sector. Students will be exposed to healthcare governance frameworks and to applications in the Australian and health countries' systems and policy. Students will examine the principles of healthcare organisations, institutions, and policy design and development in a comparative perspective, and will discuss recent healthcare reform efforts in developed and developing countries. Historical, political, economic and stakeholders' influence on current and emerging health reforms and policy will be analysed to enable students to recognise and design best practices.
learning_outcomes: Critically examine the stakeholders' approaches and positions within governance structures.
Examine different models and regulations of governance in healthcare systems and services.
Apply theoretical knowledge and critically analyse specific cases from different perspectives for health policy.
Examine different types of health care systems and policies and analyse their implications for efficiency and equity.
Critically analyse contemporary reforms in healthcare nationally and internationally.
Apply analytical skills to interpret and analyse data from a variety of sources, and communicate information effectively.
Assess the comparative performance of healthcare systems and use such analysis to infer implications for health policy.

title: Strategic Health Leadership and Management
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: The healthcare sector is in continuous evolution with complex simultaneous dynamics involving demographic and epidemiologic transitions, health technology and new models of healthcare, changes in healthcare funding algorithms and governance, and consumers and societal expectations about health outcomes and optimal mix of healthcare workforce. Strategic Health Leadership and Management introduces students to leadership and managerial approaches pertaining to health and social care organisations. Participants gain information on the implications of key challenges for strategic health leadership and management, and the skills to effectively anticipate and manage structural changes in health industries locally, nationally and internationally. The course distinguishes between Management, described as the production of acceptable results within known constraints and conditions; and Leadership, described as harnessing individual and organisational capacity, collaboration and character to facilitate strategic and productive changes within health organisations. Through the use of case studies presented by industry leaders and academic staff, theoretical and practical issues in healthcare leadership and management in Australian and global health industries will be discussed.
learning_outcomes: Apply competencies in communicating health policy development and review.
Demonstrate understanding of strategic tactical planning in health and social care organisations.
Identify and develop their leadership style in relation to individual characteristics.
Explain the fundamental theories and models of health leadership and management.
Examine the styles and attributes of current leaders in health and social care.
Develop adaptable leadership and management skills for the complex and ever-changing healthcare system.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Research Report and Live Interactive Performance

title: Healthcare Data Analytics
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Healthcare data analytics is the application of data analytics and statistics techniques to healthcare data. Students learn how to apply core concepts of data analytics to healthcare examples, and about the implications for the purposes of policy evaluation, design, development and implementation in healthcare. This course is designed to provide an understanding of the management, analysis and interpretation of diverse healthcare data. Students will be exposed to a broad range of topics, including an in-depth exposure to fundamental analytic and biostatistical concepts; a range of different methodologies used to collect data; a variety of techniques to appropriately analyse data; and information on how to assess the results of such analysis.
learning_outcomes: Conduct descriptive and analytic studies in health management and health policy research.
Explore the tools and techniques used to analyse and extract value from healthcare data.
Assess the roles and challenges of data analytics in healthcare research.
Develop strategies for data collection and management of healthcare data.

title: Research Thesis in Health Economics, Management and Policy
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course is designed for students with an interest in health economics, management and policy research. Students combine and synthesise their learning from Master of Health Economics, Management and Policy courses to prepare a research thesis. The research thesis is based on a contemporary research topic grounded in the literature and implemented through an appropriate research design incorporating effective research methods within the required time period. Students may also be required to develop an ethics application based on their proposal and gain an understanding of the skills required to manage their research and work with supervisors and potentially with healthcare sector stakeholders.
learning_outcomes: Develop and articulate a research problem.
Link the research problem to an appropriate body of literature, identifying specific question(s) to be addressed.
Prepare thesis or article corresponding to outcomes 1, 2, 3, and 4.
Conduct research analysis and synthesise findings.
Select and execute an appropriate research design.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Definition of Research Problem and Literature Review
Thesis or Article in Collaboration with Supervisor

title: Economics of Competitive Advantage
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In the dynamic global economy, managers are increasingly faced with multifaceted problems where a working knowledge of economic principles can provide useful insights. This course develops economics skills and competencies for problem solving by offering experiential analysis of the challenges that managers face and by demonstrating how the application of economic principles informs managerial decision-making. Students are encouraged to use the insights provided by this course - with its emphasis on concepts of competitive advantage and the economics of strategy - to investigate how competitiveness is created in industries and firms. Students develop an understanding of microeconomic principles and their practical application, and use this knowledge to analyse various issues including the impacts of government regulation and policies and the production and pricing decisions within an international business environment.
learning_outcomes: Develop and present a critically reflective, well written case analysis.
Apply the microeconomic concepts, theories and models to case studies.
Identify recent developments in applied microeconomics, especially concepts about competitive advantage and strategy, and contemporary policy debates.
Access and analyse on-line microeconomic data sources.
Demonstrate critical understanding of the assumptions, tools, theories, models and the language of microeconomics.

title: International Business Strategy
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course analyses how multinational enterprises (MNEs) develop and leverage their capabilities and competencies to create competitive advantages in international markets. A key purpose of this course is to understand how managers design and implement international business strategies. The motivations for international expansion are examined with a particular emphasis on the need to understand the unique characteristics of emerging and transition economies. A range of internationalisation theories and frameworks are used to analyse strategy formulation; decisions regarding to the foreign direct investment; selections of foreign investment locations; forms of international involvement and modes of market entry; and the concept of 'liability of foreignness'. Topics include assessing firm capabilities, institutional differences, industry attractiveness, and international competitive dynamics.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate strategic thinking and conduct strategic analysis of business opportunities in an international context.
Develop the essential international perspectives which inform professional standards and ethical practice in global business strategy design and implementation.
Engage in inquiry processes to understand the integration of planning and implementation of international business strategies.
Engage in critical analysis of the underlying theories, concepts, assumptions and arguments in international business strategic management.
Work both independently and collaboratively to analyse international business strategies, reflect upon, and communicate the outcomes of a multi-stage project orally and in writing.
Comprehend how national institutional frameworks impact upon multinational strategies.
Analyse the competitive environment facing global corporations and identify country specific institutional factors for the development and implementation of international business strategy.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Group Consulting Project Written Report and Oral Presentation

title: Corporate Governance and Social Responsibility
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Corporate Governance and Social Responsibility examines how corporations respond to ethical dilemmas whilst considering the needs of their various stakeholders. This requires an understanding of the social responsibilities of business in a global environment. Expectations of corporate behaviour by stakeholders changes constantly and must be viewed through the lens of corporate governance, risk management and the legal requirements made of company executives and directors.
learning_outcomes: Describe ethical theories and practices and the influence of these issues on society, management decision making, behaviour and policies.
Practice appropriate business responses and management approaches for dealing with social, political, environmental, technological and global issues.
Define governance in business and discuss the legitimacy of business as an institution in a global society.
Distinguish the various expectations and demands that emanate from stakeholders on organisations.
Evaluate the extent to which social, ethical, public and global issues be considered by organisations from an accountability perspective in contrast to purely commercial interests.

title: Financial Statement Analysis
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course introduces key valuation theories for fundamental analysis. The primary emphasis is on equity valuation, with a focus on developing and applying methods for valuing firms using financial statement analysis. Topics include the residual earnings model and the abnormal earnings growth model. Please note: This course is offered in alternate terms. Students should plan their enrolment accordingly.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate critical thinking, analytical and problem solving skills in the context of financial statement analysis.
Describe and apply the techniques of financial statement analysis and security valuation.
Identify information contained within financial statements to conduct fundamental analysis.
Demonstrate an understanding of various different valuation models.

title: Data Driven Marketing Research
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course examines how data-driven research generates insights to guide marketing decision making. Students will learn to design and conduct research projects that integrate both traditional methods and digital data sources. The course spans the full research process, from defining problems and designing research through to measurement, questionnaire design, sampling, data collection, and analysis. Practical experience with survey platforms, experiments, and statistical software will enable students to prepare, analyse, and interpret consumer and market data. Emphasis is placed on applying appropriate techniques to deliver valid, reliable, ethical, and responsible insights that inform marketing strategy. Through applied assessments, students will develop the ability to translate business problems into research questions, apply suitable research methods, and communicate insights in a professional format for managerial decision making.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and interpret consumer and market data using statistical techniques to generate valid, reliable, ethical, and responsible insights.
Apply research tools, including survey and experimental design, measurement scales, and sampling techniques.
Explain the role of marketing research and data-driven insights in marketing decision making.
Communicate research processes, findings, and recommendations in professional formats that inform marketing strategy.
Design a marketing research project by formulating research problems and opportunities, developing research questions, and selecting suitable qualitative or quantitative methods.

title: Professional Practice in Human Resource Management and Employment Relations
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Professional Practice in HRM&ER provides students with the opportunity to apply foundation learning in human resource management and employment relations to manage organisational and workplace issues. Following the principles of problem-based learning, students consider, research, and propose solutions to challenges which are commonly the responsibility of HRM and ER professionals either directly, in an internal advisory role to line managers, or as external consultants or advisors. Combining theoretical considerations and practice, students engage in a selected range of HRM and ER cases and activities. The course provides students with essential experience in professional practice to support the effective conduct of HRM and ER functions in organisations.
learning_outcomes: Gain experience in designing or improving HRM and ER policy, practices and methods for the mutual gain of employees and the organisation.
Reflect on the experience of participating in the management of people in order to better understand some of the common errors and challenges in HRM and ER practice.
Apply theoretical knowledge of specific HRM and ER methods to 'real-world' examples and situations.
Demonstrate the development of advanced skills in issue definition, research, critical thinking and problem solving in the HRM and ER domain.

title: Project in Enterprise Development
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Project in Enterprise Development is a capstone course in the Master of Innovation Management and Entrepreneurship. This course builds on theory but also puts into practice what has been learnt from the courses undertaken in the Master of Innovation Management and Entrepreneurship. Students will work with their current employer or identified business (the enterprise) to create and implement a major new product (good or service) or new process (the innovation), which will be run and managed by an internal corporate venture (together, the innovation and organisational vehicle to create and implement the innovation are known as the project). The course provides mentorship and support for their respective projects. This course focuses on students having the ability to apply their skills to real world problems. The major outcomes of this course are a written final report and presentation of the proposed project.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate relevant theories, concepts and models underpinning new products/ processes development;
Evaluate enterprise strategy and the impact of a new project on the strategy
Evaluate key ingredients involved in taking a product or process to market.
Evaluate project organisation and resource requirements to develop and launch a major new innovation

assessment_tasks.task_name: Project Report Brief, Objective and Structure

title: Leadership in Contemporary Organisations
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with an in-depth analysis of leadership styles, behaviours and achievements in the context of contemporary organisations. Situational and contingency approaches to determining the effectiveness of leadership are evaluated from a practical perspective, and leadership competency frameworks are explored as diagnostic tools and as precursors to leadership development initiatives. Competing perspectives in organisational leadership practices are highlighted, and the concept of leaders as architects of climate and culture is considered through a series of case-studies. The case study method is used throughout this course to emphasise the practical applications of theory.
learning_outcomes: Apply the theoretical paradigms to provide an analysis of how leaders shape organisational climate in contemporary settings, and evaluate their potential effect on the culture of an organisation over time.
Display an advanced awareness of their own predispositions, preferences and competencies in relation to exercising leadership in contemporary organisational settings.
Demonstrate an advanced understanding of the prominent leadership paradigms that assist in the analysis of leader effectiveness.
Critically examine the organisational contextual features that help to determine the efficacy of a range of leadership styles and approaches.
Identify the stages of group development, and display an advanced awareness of the barriers to team effectiveness.
Identify a wide range of leadership styles evident in today's organisations, and articulate their distinctive features.
Critically evaluate the strengths and limitations of their leadership behaviours and experiences.
Present advanced analytical material professionally and convincingly, in a manner that is supported by reasoned argument.

title: Organisational Behaviour in Sport
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Understanding the dynamics of human behaviour within the context of sports organisations is foundational to effective sport management practice. The course explores the psychological and sociological factors that influence individual and group behaviour, leadership styles, organisational culture, and decision-making processes within the sports industry. Learning through case studies, experiences, and academic research, students develop a deep understanding of how to effectively manage and lead diverse teams in the global sports business landscape.
learning_outcomes: Assess the influence of organisational culture and climate on behaviour and decision-making processes within sports organisations.
Propose effective decision-making strategies and conflict resolution techniques to resolve issues and enhance organisational performance in sports contexts.
Identify individual behaviour factors such as motivation, personality, and attitudes, and their impact on performance in sport-related roles.
Evaluate group dynamics, teamwork processes, and leadership styles within sports organisations to enhance team effectiveness.
Define key concepts and theories of organisational behaviour as they relate to the sports industry.

title: Financial Management and Decision Making in Healthcare
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Financial Management and Decision Making in Healthcare is the application of accounting and finance principles to assist decision making in healthcare. Students apply the main accounting and finance concepts of the time value of money and the investment decision, cost accounting, financial statement analysis, budgeting and performance evaluation in assisting managers allocate scarce resources in healthcare decision making.
learning_outcomes: Apply financial statement analysis on financial statement information from healthcare organisations.
Apply and appraise analytical tools used in making investment decisions in healthcare.
Evaluate financial management and the role finance plays in decision making in healthcare organisations.
Implement and evaluate cost accounting concepts used in healthcare decision making.
Prepare and analyse budgets to assist in decision making.

title: Global Sports Marketing
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Globalisation is profoundly impacting the sports industry as a direct result of increased exposure through broadcasting and social media. Many sports brands are increasingly targeting overseas markets to reach new fans and customers, develop new revenue streams and gain competitive advantage. Marketing is central to contemporary business, and this course provides students with a foundation on which to better understand the sport marketing discipline. Students learn that the consumer is at the heart of all buying decisions and will explore consumer needs and the psychological processes that effective marketing addresses. The course explores the key principles and practices involved with identifying new markets and creating an effective marketing strategy. It also addresses how digital and social media communications strategies have revolutionised the connection between sports brands and consumers.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the relationship between digital platforms and sport marketing principles across different sport business contexts.
Analyse sport marketing ideas and social media concepts to inform effective marketing strategies.
Propose marketing strategies that incorporate techniques and practices relevant to the global sports industry.
Assess the major theories, principles, and concepts surrounding sport marketing.

title: Sports Economics
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Mastery of sports industry economics equips future leaders with knowledge and skills needed to navigate and influence a multi-billion-dollar global market. In this course students explore the intersection of economic principles with the dynamic knowledge and practices of the sport business world. Learning spans unique theoretical applications, such as supply and demand dynamics in sports ticket pricing, the economics of stadium financing, and the impact of player salaries on team performance. Students gain a deep understanding of how economics shapes decision-making in the sports industry, empowering the analysis of complex issues like revenue sharing agreements and the economic impact of sport mega-events.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and apply economic principles to contemporary issues within the sport and fitness industries.
Examine how economic theories influence decision-making in the sport industry.
Develop evidence-based strategic recommendations using economic theory, industry data, and analytical tools
Evaluate labour markets, commercial structures, governance systems, and regulatory frameworks influencing sport organisations.

title: Sports Integrity
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Understanding and upholding integrity is crucial in the world of international sport, where ethical challenges impact players, organisations, and entire communities. Through examination of theoretical frameworks and real-world case studies, students analyse integrity issues such as match-fixing, doping, governance transparency, and ethical conduct. By developing critical analysis and ethical reasoning skills, this course provides students with tools to help navigate complex integrity dilemmas. The course also develops student knowledge of ethical business practices and social responsibility within international sport business contexts.
learning_outcomes: Outline integrity principles and their relevance to the promotion of ethical conduct and governance transparency in sport organisations.
Apply critical analysis and ethical reasoning skills to navigate complex integrity dilemmas in the sports sector and propose ethical business solutions.
Analyse the multifaceted challenges to integrity within the global sports industry.
Evaluate the ethical implications of key integrity issues in sport business, such as match-fixing, doping, and governance transparency.

title: Sports Sponsorship
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: With sport sponsorship revenue surpassing billions annually, students explore the multifaceted decisions involved in sponsorship agreements, from selecting the right partners to negotiating deals that align with organisational objectives. Understanding the strategic positioning of sponsorship within sports marketing, students analyse how brands leverage sponsorships to enhance visibility, engage audiences, and build brand equity. Through in-depth examination of sponsorship activation measures and evaluation techniques, students learn to assess the effectiveness of sponsorships in achieving marketing goals.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the effectiveness of sponsorship activation measures using key performance indicators and ROI analysis to assess brand impact.
Evaluate sports sector partnerships and identify negotiation tactics that are well-suited to the context/situation
Design comprehensive sport sponsorship activation plans, integrating diverse marketing channels.
Analyse sponsorship decision-making strategies to determine their effectiveness in achieving marketing goals.
Outline the historical significance and contemporary relevance of sport sponsorship within the sports industry.

title: Leadership and Sustainability in Sport Enterprises
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Many factors influence organisational sustainability in sport, including governance, workforce, funding and finances, integrity, infrastructure, participant experiences, and environmental impacts. To fully examine sport leadership in a such a multi-faceted context, this course draws on two interpretations of “sustainability”. The first interpretation considers both the broader global impacts of the sport sector and engagement by sport leadership with sustainable development principles to manage social, environmental, and economic issues. The second interpretation relates to sustainability in the context of business continuity management, organisational performance management, and strategic planning. Understanding and application of both these sustainability interpretations is demonstrated to be essential for effective contemporary sport leadership.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the principles of sustainable development and their relevance to sports leadership and international sport business.
Apply planning approaches that optimise sustainability and organisational performance in the sports sector.
Propose sustainable sport business solutions that address environmental, social, and economic factors.
Evaluate the role of sports leadership in embedding sustainability into the design, management, and operations of sports facilities and events.

title: Athlete and Agency Management
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Explore the contemporary world of athlete representation and agency management within the sports industry. This course engages with multi-disciplinary knowledge spanning talent scouting, contract negotiation, brand management, legal considerations, and ethical responsibilities in athlete representation. By fostering critical thinking and strategic decision-making skills, this course empowers students to navigate the complexities of athlete agency management and excel in advocating for the holistic development and success of athletes in the global sports landscape.
learning_outcomes: Examine the legal, ethical and regulatory frameworks governing athlete representation, risk and safeguarding.
Design holistic athlete career management and transition strategies covering welfare, finance, and post-sport planning.
Critically evaluate strategic principles, governance challenges and commercial dynamics in athlete representation.
Design athlete branding, digital media, sponsorship and reputation management strategies.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Athlete Career and Brand Development Portfolio

title: Introduction to Sports Analytics
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In a world where ‘data is everywhere’, contemporary sport increasingly requires the use of analytical techniques. This course explores the key aspects of sports analytics, both ‘on the field’ and ‘off the field’. It examines the application of analytics in sports for purposes of in-game strategy, player performance, team management, sports operations, business development, fan engagement, sponsorship evaluation and other selected topics.
learning_outcomes: Explain key concepts and terminology in sports analytics.
Evaluate real-world applications and case studies of sports analytics to identify best practices and emerging trends.
Collect various types of sports data using appropriate tools and techniques.
Interpret analytical findings effectively to inform decision-making in sports contexts.
Apply analytical methods to assess player performance, team strategies, and operational efficiency.

title: Sport Business Statistics and Analytics
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: With data playing a pivotal role in modern sports, understanding statistical analysis and visualisation is key to uncovering insights that underpin success on and off the field. This course draws on statistical analysis and data visualisation to explore how data is used in sport to make evidence-based decisions. The course covers three areas. First, it provides a foundational understanding of quantitative analysis. Second, various data visualisation techniques are outlined (including exposure to relevant software programs) to develop skills in understanding and presenting complex data. Third, an applied understanding of the importance of data in identifying insights and trends in the sport sector. Recent examples from the sport industry, including ‘on-field' performance and in commercial activities, will be used to illustrate these complex concepts.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate proficiency using analytic software and data visualisation techniques commonly employed in the sport business sector.
Apply quantitative analysis to solve problems in a data-driven sport business context.
Evaluate how analytical techniques can address sport business problems.
Interpret multi-dimensional data sources to make evidence-based decisions.
Assess the role of data visualisation in supporting evidence-based decision making within sport business environments.

title: Talent Identification and Recruitment
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Identifying and recruiting the right talent is essential to building competitive, successful sports teams and sports organisations. This course engages with the methodologies and analytical techniques used in the identification and recruitment of athletic talent. Students explore the principles of talent identification, including physiological, psychological, and performance metrics. The course covers various models and approaches used by sports organisations to scout, assess, and recruit athletes. Using case studies and practical applications, students gain insights into the strategic importance of effective talent identification, recruitment, and development in the sports industry.
learning_outcomes: Investigate methods to appropriately distinguish higher performers in sport.
Critique the limitations and fallibility of talent identification procedures with consideration of ethical issues.
Investigate common talent development frameworks and their applicability across different sports.
Examine the conceptual and applied underpinnings of athlete expertise and talent in the context of sport.
Evaluate traditional and contemporary methods of measuring and identifying talent in sport.

title: Applied Performance Analytics
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In high-performance sports, the ability to turn data into actionable insights is essential to player development and delivering competitive advantage. This course provides an in-depth exploration of performance analytics in sports, focusing on the practical application of data analysis techniques to enhance individual and team performance.
