Students learn how to collect, interpret, and apply performance data in real-time settings to inform coaching decisions, improve player development, and optimise team strategy. The course integrates theoretical frameworks with hands-on projects using real-world datasets, enabling students to understand the analytical tools and technologies used in performance analysis. Emphasis is placed on ethical data use, communicating insights effectively, and adapting analytical approaches to different sports contexts.
learning_outcomes: Analyse team performance data to assess tactical and strategic effectiveness
Interpret performance data from various sources to assess athlete workload, biomechanics, and game performance.
Create data visualisation reports and predictive models that communicate performance insights to coaches, athletes, and stakeholders.
Describe key metrics and technologies used in performance analytics
Apply analytics techniques to develop data-driven strategies for improving athlete performance

title: Global Study Tour
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Experiencing the global sports industry firsthand provides invaluable learning opportunities that can only be gained by exposure to diverse cultural and professional settings. This course expands the theoretical knowledge and skills developed in the classroom, immersing students in international sports business practice. In this course, students will undertake educational activities at a range of international sporting related venues and organisations and also engage in a range of other activities designed to require engagement in and increased understanding of the social, political, cultural and sports business practices in other countries.
learning_outcomes: Synthesise and compare cultural perspectives related to sport
Critically analyse the varying effects of globalisation in different countries or contexts, drawing on direct experiences from the overseas study program.
Apply sports related knowledge and insights gained through the overseas study experience.
Communicate orally and in writing with confidence about cultural differences and similarities related to sport.
Use visual/pictorial and journal writing techniques to record and reflect on their overseas study experience.

title: Applied Placement Workplace Learning
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Having an opportunity to apply skills and knowledge acquired through study is essential to students being ‘career-ready’. This course builds student employability by providing in-person exposure to the working world of sport businesses. Students undertake 140 hours of supervised work placement (work integrated learning) in partnership with a host organisation. Students observe and participate in a range of work practices as negotiated with the host organisation.
learning_outcomes: Establish professional networks for future career development.
Reflect on work placement experience to improve personal and business outcomes.
Co-design and complete a professional workplace placement by applying knowledge, skills and competencies attained through education and experience.
Apply professional behaviour and ethical practices.
Develop new skills and knowledge to improve employability.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Professional Skills Audit and Placement Learning Outcomes

title: New Media Analytics in Sport Business
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In an era where digital engagement shapes fan loyalty and brand success, mastering new media analytics is central to sport business operations. This course explores the impact of new media on the sports industry, focusing on the use of digital communication technologies to enhance interaction between users and content. Students will learn how to analyse and leverage data from various new media platforms to increase engagement, enhance fan experiences, and support business decision-making. The course content includes social media analytics, content performance metrics, and the role of digital marketing in sports. Through practical applications and case studies, students develop skills to critically evaluate and utilise new media analytics in sport business contexts.
learning_outcomes: Develop digital marketing strategies to enhance fan engagement and brand presence.
Analyse social media data to assess engagement and performance metrics.
Describe the role of new media in the sports industry and its impact on user interaction.
Critically evaluate the effectiveness of new media campaigns and content.
Apply ethical principles in the collection and use of new media data.

title: BA Futures
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course examines the history and learning principles of the Humanities and explores how critical and creative thinking occurs inside and across disciplines. Students will consider the complexity of today’s world and engage in intellectual debates on the big ideas and major concepts underpinning the Humanities, including power, language, storytelling, and representation. This course provides innovative research skills in Humanities disciplines, informed by traditional and new perspectives. It also highlights new awareness of the relevance of digital research tools in the Humanities. It fosters a learning environment that enables students to develop skills in problem solving, making convincing arguments, and intercultural awareness through language and cross-cultural communication. At the conclusion of this course, you will have developed written, oral and digital research and communication skills that are vital for success in the Bachelor of Arts and a range of potential career paths. You will also have demonstrated foundational understanding of the role of the Humanities in knowledge creation and ethical problem solving.
learning_outcomes: Apply core academic reading, writing, and presentation skills to communicate research findings.
Conduct scholarly research using appropriate resources, including library materials and digital platforms.
Demonstrate knowledge of Humanities disciplines, including how humans use language and communicate.
Analyse local and global problems and ideas and recognise how Humanities disciplines can interact to produce new knowledge.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Weekly Learning Task Reflecting on Lectures and Tutorials

title: BA Practice
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The Bachelor of Arts degree program encompasses a diverse field of specialised practices. This course is the second-year core course in the BA and builds on HASS1000 BA Futures by developing student awareness of becoming a practitioner within these interconnected specialisms. Students begin by identifying a practice standpoint. They move onto considering the origins and emergence of values that are common to inquiring into, continuing and changing human culture, behaviour and society. Students reflect on the concepts of ethics, truth, evidence, integrity and originality that shape practice in the humanities and adjacent disciplines. Being a BA practitioner involves technology use. This course develops skills in information literacy and we debate what it means to read, think, write, speak and work with technologies now. Students completing this course will have an understanding of methods for asking informed questions about topics that matter to them.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate scholarly and other sources of evidence to ask a research question.
Identify theories and concepts for practice in the humanities and related fields.
Reflect on cultural and information literacies that are common to the humanities and related fields.
Communicate the purpose, background and significance of a research question in oral and written forms.

title: Business Project Management
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This unit is designed to develop and apply the knowledge and skills required for the effective management of business projects incorporating practical problem-solving and critical analysis . Students will apply core principles of project management to functional business areas noting the importance of effective leadership, project communication, human resource management, and processual aspects of managing change . It also highlights the skills needed and key tasks in leading and managing change in organisations.
learning_outcomes: Apply the principles of communication management to the core tasks of managing change.
Evaluate the role of leadership at different stages of managing projects.
Manage resources and risks in the project management environment.
Apply a programmatic approach to managing business projects.
Monitor, review and critically evaluate projects.

title: Professional Career Ready Placement
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: In this course you will apply your learning to a real-world work situation by undertaking a work placement (140 hours). In preparing for your work placement, you will research opportunities connected to your area of study, reflect on the skills and knowledge you have built in the course of your degree and identify areas for further professional development. You will be supported in the course by the School’s Placement Co-ordinator, the University’s Careers Team, a work placement supervisor and a mentor with an understanding of your discipline or area of work. In this course you will take responsibility for your own professional development, building a personalised plan for the next phase in your career journey.
learning_outcomes: Assess strengths and identify areas for further development and use this insight to develop a professional development plan.
Apply knowledge and skills to successfully undertake an identified role within a work place.
Identify employment opportunities that are relevant to their course of study and to skills.
Critically reflect on the importance of their disciplinary expertise in the workplace and the implications of work experience for disciplinary understanding

title: BA Project
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This capstone course will give you the freedom to explore your interests in depth. This is the third core course in the BA program, bringing together Humanities students from all disciplines and subfields to put into practice the critical reasoning and research skills studied in HASS1000 and HASS2000. You will hone your knowledge and skills through practical application and a major research project. This individual project can take the form of a traditional research paper or a creative, applied or digital outcome. It will demonstrate your capabilities in a range of areas that are demanded by employers in the knowledge economy, including digital communication, complex problem solving, initiative or enterprise, and creative thinking.
learning_outcomes: Apply critical reasoning, creative thinking and problem-solving skills to answer complex questions in areas of the Humanities.
Implement evidence-based Humanities research methods in a practical research project.
Communicate Humanities research and the relevance of BA studies to varied audiences using a variety of forms at an advanced level

title: Honours Research
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The course introduces Honours research methods by exploring forms of critical, analytical and creative thinking in the production of research knowledge in humanities, creative arts and social sciences. The course provides essential scholarly grounding for students wishing to pursue academic study beyond Honours, while those headed for other employment futures will acquire a range of flexible research and communication skills adaptable to a wide variety of work. Throughout, we explore the dual benefits of disciplinary and interdisciplinary knowledge in the form of advanced research and skills development. Students will co-design their learning through weekly supervision with a discipline expert and scaffolded assessment tasks related to relevant methodologies applied to their larger Honours project.
learning_outcomes: Design and present a research proposal.
Complete a literature review relevant to their discipline;
Apply advanced research skills;
Effectively communicate knowledge resulting from research;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Project Proposal and Short Annotated Bibliography

title: Honours Theory and Practice
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with the opportunity to develop the research skills that enhance their humanities, creative arts, and social sciences research capacity in present and future. Differing methodologies are examined in the context of their application to a specific project. In this course students deepen their understanding of the nature and importance of research methodology, and further develop the theoretical framework and overall research design of their Honours projects. The subject's interdisciplinary context also encourages students' engagement with diverse approaches to knowledge creation. Student projects may include, but are not limited to: theoretical explorations and reviews; speculative design practices; professionally oriented projects; work-integrated learning and research-integrated learning opportunities; group / collaborative projects; external stakeholder based projects.
learning_outcomes: Design a substantive project on their discipline methodology.
Respond to contemporary philosophies which inform current practice in the humanities, creative arts and social sciences.
Explain the theoretical foundations of their Honours research project.
Apply advanced communication and information technology skills appropriate to the professional presentation of concepts, issues, and ideas.
Analyse complex ideas, texts, visual and sonic material in the humanities, creative arts or social sciences.

title: Honours Thesis 1
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: HASS4003 is the first part of the thesis component of the Honours degree, the other component being HASS4004. The honours thesis gives students the opportunity to put the skills they have acquired over the course of their undergraduate studies to practice in the form of a substantial project. This project can be in one of three formats: 1) Academic, 2) Work-Integrated Learning, and 3) Creative/Digital. The Academic option involves a15,000 word thesis on a topic determined in consultation with a supervisor with appropriate expertise. The thesis is expected to engage critically with recent scholarship in the field, offer a comprehensive account of the topic, and embody the standards of argumentation, writing and referencing in the field. The Work-Integrated Learning option allows students to undertake a substantial research-based project for, or in collaboration with, an approved workplace wholly or largely dedicated to issues of concern to the discipline. Students compile a 5,000-8,000 word portfolio documenting the findings and outcomes of the project. Additionally, students produce a description of the workplace and its key characteristics, to be endorsed by the workplace supervisor as accurate (500 words), as well as a reflective journal with weekly entries (2,000 words). Identifying an external partner and negotiating terms is the responsibility of the student. The Creative/Digital option enables students to engage in practice-led research resulting in a creative work or, alternatively, to use digital tools to develop and communicate their research. The work undertaken under this option is expected to be a substantial individual research effort within the chosen discipline and requires pre-approval by the supervisor. The thesis will consist of a creative/digital portfolio equivalent to 12,000 words, accompanied by a 3,000 word reflective statement outlining the background, aims, methods and theoretical foundation of the research.
learning_outcomes: Apply relevant theories and methods to carry out an extended independent research, creative or digital project;
Formulate an extended critical argument drawing on discipline and/or interdisciplinary knowledge;
Demonstrate advanced skills in communicating research.
Design a research project utilising skills developed over the course of the honours program;
Apply advanced disciplinary and/or interdisciplinary research skills;

title: Europe and the World
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course explores the history of European encounters with the wider world, from the 'discovery' of the Americas in 1492 to the present. It investigates the people, events, myths, and ideas that have shaped European and world history. While adhering to a chronological structure, the overall approach will be thematic, covering topics that have informed Europe's complex and often troubled interactions with the peoples and places beyond its borders.
learning_outcomes: Identify the main themes of Europe's encounters and interactions with the wider world.
Communicate clear and concise arguments in written form relevant to the history discipline.
Apply basic historical research and information literacy skills.
Critically evaluate relevant primary and secondary sources.

title: Honours Thesis 2
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: HASS4004 is the second part of the thesis component of the Honours degree, the first component being HASS4003. The honours thesis gives students the opportunity to put the skills they have acquired over the course of their undergraduate studies to practice in the form of a substantial project. This project can be in one of three formats: 1) Academic, 2) Work-Integrated Learning, and 3) Creative/Digital. The Academic option involves a 15,000 word thesis on a topic determined in consultation with a supervisor with appropriate expertise. The thesis is expected to engage critically with recent scholarship in the field, offer a systematic and comprehensive account of the topic, and embody the standards of argumentation, writing and referencing in the field. The Work-Integrated Learning option allows students to undertake a substantial research-based project for, or in collaboration with, an approved workplace wholly or largely dedicated to issues of concern to the discipline. Students compile a 5,000-8,000 word portfolio documenting the findings and outcomes of the project. Additionally, students produce a description of the workplace and its key characteristics, to be endorsed by the workplace supervisor as true and accurate (500 words), as well as a reflective journal with weekly entries (2,000 words). Identifying an external partner and negotiating terms is the responsibility of the student. The Creative/Digital option enables students to engage in practice-led research resulting in a creative work or, alternatively, to use digital tools to develop and communicate their research. The work undertaken under this option is expected to be a substantial individual research effort within the chosen discipline and requires pre-approval by the supervisor. The thesis will consist of a creative/digital portfolio equivalent to 12,000 words, accompanied by a 3,000-word reflective statement outlining the background, aims, methods and theoretical foundation of the research.
learning_outcomes: Apply advanced disciplinary and/or interdisciplinary research skills in written form;
Apply relevant theories and methods to carry out an extended independent research, creative or digital project;
Design a research project utilising skills developed over the course of the honours program;
Demonstrate advanced skills in communicating research.
Formulate an extended critical argument drawing on discipline and/or interdisciplinary knowledge;

title: The United States from Civil War to Superpower
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course surveys the domestic history and foreign relations of the United States since 1865. It looks broadly at social movements and developments in American society and culture over 150 years of American history as well as the main political developments in that period.
learning_outcomes: Communicate clear and concise arguments in written and oral forms that address problems and issues in American history
Employ basic research skills to identify suitable scholarly sources in the field of American history.
Critically analyse interpretations of America's past, and the primary source documentation that underpins them.
Articulate core knowledge of American history in the period since the Civil War.

title: The Foundations of America
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This early modern History of the Atlantic World surveys the history of this region including western Europe, Africa and the Americas from pre-Columbian times, through European discovery and settlement to the founding of new, distinctly modern republics (including that of the United States) from the late eighteenth century into the early decades of the 19th century. Using a combination of case studies and themes, this course explores the world that Europeans, Africans and native peoples forged together from the late 15th century to the founding of the modern era.
learning_outcomes: Present arguments in written form.
Summarise the development of the 'Atlantic World' from the mid fourteenth century to the mid nineteenth century.
Evaluate historical documents concerning the history of the Americas, Europe and Africa.
Identify key research documents and reflect on their research capacities.

title: The Australian Experience
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course provides an introduction to Australian history. It treats the development of Australian society to the present through the lenses of Aboriginal deep time history; convicts and colonialism; war and conflict; migration and multiculturalism; landscape and the environment; and the development of democratic institutions. The course looks to Australian history to contextualise issues in contemporary Australia and introduces the skills and approaches employed in the study of the Australian past.
learning_outcomes: Situate the Australian past within a local and global context.
Show a developing understanding of core historical concepts.
Demonstrate basic knowledge of key themes, events, and people in Australian history.
Use scholarly sources (both primary and secondary) to construct and communicate clear and informed arguments about Australian history.
Explain why there are differing interpretations of Australian history.

title: Origin of Controversies
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Controversial topics inevitably arise in our society. Each has a history that can stretch back hundreds and sometimes thousands of years. This course explores the historical origins of contemporary controversies to better understand their significance. Such explorations are designed to introduce students to foundational concepts addressed in the study of history and to provide insight into the methods that they typically employ.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate communication skills appropriate to the presentation of historical issues.
Show basic competence interpreting historical and contextual factors at work within the topics in question;
Employ skills in studying and analysing concepts and issues in the study of history;
Identify the historical origins of key controversial issues of contemporary relevance;

title: Fact or Fiction? Reading the Past
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Why study history? Can we really know about the past? Is history fiction? Why is the past so frequently and bitterly contested? This course focuses on the craft of history to explore how varied and controversial historical writing can be. We focus on landmark events in international contexts and in a range of time periods. We employ diverse methods to interpret them, from the empirical to the theoretical to the unconventional. In doing so, we will interrogate the process by which the past is recovered, constructed and debated. In this course, you will join a discussion about the nature and practice of history as a basis for understanding the contested nature of human experience.
learning_outcomes: Use a range of sources effectively in scholarly writing about the past.
Evaluate a range of approaches and methods used by historians and related scholars.
Assess the use of a range of historical sources in scholarly argumentation.
Apply a number of methodologies employed by historians and scholars in related fields, taking account of ethical and intercultural issues as they arise.

title: The History of Slavery
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This global history course surveys the idea of slavery in theory and practice from the ancient world to the present day. Using case studies based on a specific theme or event, the course explores the culture of servitude and labour relations within the framework of slavery. This course also explores contemporary notions of involuntary servitude and how they relate to the way slavery has been understood in the past.
learning_outcomes: Summarise the history of global slavery from ancient times to the present
Critically evaluate key historical documents concerning slavery
Formulate and present arguments in written or oral form.
Apply historical research materials relevant to the study of slavery;

title: Australian Underworlds: Histories of Crime in Australia
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Crime holds a special place in Australian history, having facilitated colonisation, provided its most celebrated anti-hero in Ned Kelly and been used to sell millions of newspapers, books and movie tickets. Drawing upon a rich array of digital history resources, this course will examine the back stories of Australia's best known crimes and criminals, setting this underworld in its historical context. It will address the role of sex, class, race and ethnicity in decisions about which behaviours are defined as crimes and why certain people become criminals.
learning_outcomes: Integrate primary and secondary sources into a research outcome, drawing on digitised sources as appropriate;
Reflect on their learning and express an ethical stance towards the history of crime in Australia.
Evaluate information, ideas, and arguments about the history of crime, including those from cultures other than their own;
Outline key historical debates, themes and concepts around the history of crime in Australia;
Demonstrate intermediate written and visual communication skills, and information literacy skills relevant to history;

title: History, War and Film
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Cinema is a powerful medium for the interpretation of the past. Some film biographies, period pieces, and documentaries have provided us with insightful information about human history; others have distorted issues or served as propaganda. This course will study the challenges and promises of film as cultural artefact, introducing students to its contested nature. It draws on theoretical perspectives and critical tools to support the study of history.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the historical value of film as a site of cultural expression and conflict with the potential to influence cultural change.
Conduct research independently and express clear arguments, either orally or in writing.
Identify historical debates in the contested nature of historical representation.
Critique the complex relationship between cinematic invention and historical knowledge.

title: Communicating History to Public Audiences
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The course offers students the opportunity to combine historical research with applied public history practice and to acquire preparatory skills in communicating history to public audiences. It will provide an overview of the field of public history and the gallery, library, archive and museum (GLAM) sector with case studies from the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand. It will also highlight legislation and major cultural collecting institutions' policies. Students will learn basic oral history interviewing skills and go on a local field trip as part of their assessment.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the field of public history with reference to the gallery, library, archive and museum (GLAM) sectors.
Practice research and information technology skills appropriate to studies of history.
Analyse essential texts in the field of preservation and display of the past.
Explain historical knowledge to public audiences.

title: A Sunburnt Country: Australian Environmental History
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course treats the environmental history of Australia, examining the impact of humans on the continent from ancient times to the present and attempting to understand the cultural assumptions about the environment which guided human practices. It will engage with contemporary debates within the literature on environmental history and provide students with opportunities to conduct original research in the field.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse issues in Australian environmental history in both written and oral form.
Demonstrate intermediate written and visual communication skills, and information literacy skills, relevant to history.
Evaluate the historical impact of Australians on their environment and the attitudes which underpin the human use of the environment.
Design and conduct research projects in Australian environmental history

title: Medieval and Renaissance Europe
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course chronologically and thematically explores the medieval and early modern world, from the fall of the Western Roman Empire to the Renaissance and the Reformation. It focuses on the key issues and events which defined the medieval world, and which still resonate in our society today. The course is divided into four periods: Early, High and Late Middle Ages, and the Early Modern period. The Early Middle Ages will introduce the themes which will be continued and expanded in the later periods, namely the role of the Christian Church in politics and society, the emergence of the modern state, the fall and recovery of urban life, trends in education and learning, interaction between Europe and other cultures through trade, invasion and cultural exchange, and the evolution of social and gender relations. Students will learn how to evaluate the events, people and ideologies constituting this colourful period of European history.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and comprehend a variety of Medieval and Early Modern sources.
Explain the key themes in the history of Medieval and Early Modern Europe from the fifth to the fifteenth century.
Employ research and reflective skills relevant to the study of history.
Apply social, economic and cultural approaches to Medieval and Early Modern history.

title: Things that Made the Modern World
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Computers, clothes, coal, cars, cosmetics, and Coca-Cola are commodities that shape people’s daily lives. The development of modern globalised commodity industries since the 1850s has connected people in many places around the world. For this reason, changes in making, selling, buying and consuming commodities offer valuable insights into human ingenuity, protection and conservation, and cruelty. This course considers the history of environmental, social and economic costs and benefits of globalised things. It does so by exploring how the development of things has played out in the actions of governments, corporations and protest movements through the politics of nature, labour, race, trade, education and science.
learning_outcomes: Understand concepts that historians use to interpret the role of things in their explanations about the modern world;
Effectively examine and discuss selected primary sources to make an argument about commodities and the modern world.
Communicate clearly in oral and digital formats about how things are related to nature and the choices that people made in the past;
Accurately locate specific commodity histories in time and place;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Multiple short online tasks and reflections

title: Bodies and Brains: Histories of Illness, Disability and Disease
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Medical and psychiatric diagnosis, treatment and care have developed over past centuries through increasing clinical understanding of the human body, as well as expectations of how society and the people within it should behave. From pox, consumption (tuberculosis) and hysteria to HIV/AIDS, post-traumatic stress disorder and ‘gut health’, this course will examine a range of medical conditions alongside social changes within the modern historical world to show how illness, disability and disease have been approached by medical and political authorities, as well as local communities and the individual patient.
learning_outcomes: Outline how social, medical and political worlds collectively impact the development of disease categories, diagnosis and treatment.
Integrate both primary and secondary sources to form well-written historical arguments about medical and psychiatric histories.
Critically analyse historical texts about human illness, disability and disease.

title: The Russian Revolution: From the Tsars to Putin
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: “Revolution” denotes a dramatic period of seminal change in history. This course investigates the processes of revolution with a focus on the Russian Revolution from the late 19th to the late 20th century. It encompasses the Russian Empire and its immediate neighbourhood, including the conditions that made Russia ripe for revolution, the events of 1917, the Civil War, Stalin’s dictatorship, the catastrophe of World War II, the Cold War years, the collapse of the Soviet Union and the revolution’s ongoing legacies in Putin’s Russia.
learning_outcomes: Apply different theories and approaches to the study of political, cultural and social history;
Identify and explain the key issues in the history of revolution in 19th and 20th century Russia;
Critically reflect upon a variety of primary and secondary source materials;
Synthesise source materials in oral and written form.

title: War and Trauma
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The history of trauma is bound up with the history of warfare and its impact on combatants and noncombatants. Drawing on Australian and international examples from the World Wars, the Vietnam War and the War on Terror, this course examines changing theorisations of trauma in response to the major conflicts of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. It also considers the medical, political, social and cultural responses to traumatized individuals and communities in the aftermath of conflict. This course will be of interest to students who want to gain a deeper understanding of the evolution of ideas about trauma, the impact of war on societies, and the long running debates over whether it is possible to resolve the mental damage of war.
learning_outcomes: Employ high-level skills in scholarly research and written, visual and verbal communication;
Demonstrate understanding of the history of ideas about trauma and their relationship to major wars in the modern period;
Apply historical knowledge to present-day discussions of trauma and the aftermath of wars in Australian and international contexts.
Critically analyse primary sources and secondary scholarship relevant to the study of war and trauma;

title: Israel and the Middle East: Roots of the current conflict
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course examines the historical origins of the current conflict in the Middle East with particular reference to Israel and Palestine. On completion of the course, you will be able to identify major developments of post-Ottoman history. You will understand the importance of the late Ottoman, European and global contexts. You will be able to historically discuss main aspects of the Arab-Israeli conflict and see the interconnections with other conflicts in the Middle East.
learning_outcomes: Identify major issues pertaining to post-Ottoman conflicts, the Arab-Israeli issue at the first place;
Employ research and information literacy skills to identify relevant scholarly sources according to the ethical standards of the field of history;
Discuss historiographical issues pertaining to the Middle East conflict;
Communicate clear and concise arguments in written and oral forms at an intermediate level.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Personal book review in written or oral form in the style of an interview with another person

title: Global Perspectives on the First World War
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The First World War was a devastating conflict that transformed the lives of millions of people around the world and left a legacy of violence and conflict that continues to resonate today. This course takes advantage of the rich sources that have emerged since the centenary of the First World War to explore themes and concepts related to the prosecution, impact, representation and aftermath of the war from a global perspective. By examining the major events and turning points of the war alongside new research on the global dimensions of the conflict, this course will provide students with a broader and more nuanced understanding of the war.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate critical understanding of complex themes and topics in global First World War history;
Analyse primary sources from a variety of repositories (including digital);
Demonstrate familiarity with differing conceptual approaches and their methods to the study of the First World War.
Identify, evaluate and synthesise issues and debates in international First World War literature;
Apply advanced communication skills appropriate to the evaluation of primary and secondary source material;

title: The History of Violence
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: What is violence? What do we mean by it? Is it innate or learned? Are we becoming more or less violent? These are all questions that we will ask throughout this course. A History of Violence will examine the different types of violence that humans have practiced over the centuries, put them into historical context, and try to understand why those different forms of violence are used at particular times, and not others; why some kinds of violence are accepted in some parts of the world but not others? This course will explore aspects of human violence in world history from pre-history to the present. Major topics to be addressed within this overview include: Inter-personal violence; state violence; crime and criminality; sexual violence; religious and ritual violence; warfare; massacre and genocide; theories and thinkers of violence; and representations of violence in film and literature.
learning_outcomes: Synthesise primary and secondary source material in oral and written form at an advanced level.
Develop an understanding of the different theories and approaches to the study of the history of violence.
Identify key issues in the history of violence.
Analyse and reflect upon a variety of historical source materials relevant to the study of violence.

title: Power in the Asia Pacific: Conflict and Alliances
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course begins by tracing major shifts in the concentration of power in what is now referred to as the Asia-Pacific or Indo-Pacific region. The initial focus extends from Genghis Khan’s amassing of an enormous land empire centred on Central Asia in the twelfth century to British imperial domination of the Indian and Pacific Oceanic worlds by the nineteenth century. In the context of these histories the course proceeds to explore key turning points in the centring and recentring of power from the Anglo-Japanese war in the early twentieth century to the rise of China as a superpower in a globalised world order at the turn of the twenty-first century. Students will encounter the historical diversity of the Asia Pacific and identify the extent to which Australia as a modern nation-state based on settler colonialism has influence in the region.
learning_outcomes: Recognise different historical themes (Indigenous, diplomatic, military, economic, social, cultural, gender, and environmental) in secondary sources.
Communicate clear and concise historical arguments about the Asia Pacific region, including Australia, in written form.
Evaluate key issues in the history of polities and power in the Asia Pacific region, including Australia.
Analyse international relations in historical documents and other primary source materials.

title: The History of Racism
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course traces the history and culture of racism since World War II, focusing on individuals as well as social trends that informed the twentieth century struggle for racial equality.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate scholarship in the context of the history of racism.
Understand the key issues and themes in the history of racism from World War II to the present.
Demonstrate knowledge about the history of racism from a wide range of historical sources, photographs and film.
Transmit knowledge of the history of racism in written and oral forms.

title: Global Food History: From Bunya Nuts to French Fries
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Eating and drinking are the basis of every human society and culture. Each society has their own beliefs and practices surrounding these essentials of life. Since the fifteenth century, food and drinks production, trade and consumption have also disrupted and connected people and places in ways that have globalised the world. This course will explore how food and drinks globalisation has come about from colonisation, capitalism, the law, cultural power and changes to the environment. Students will gain a deeper understanding of the origins and consequences of the planet’s food and drink systems and choices in shaping the present and future. You will co-learn with students from Aotearoa New Zealand and participate in weekly in-class food challenges.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate advanced information literacy, reading, writing, and/or oral communication skills relevant to history.
Explain disruptions and connections between people and places with case studies from food and drinks history.
Analyse evidence of changing food and drink cultures among Indigenous and non-Indigenous peoples.
Evaluate sources on environmental impacts from changing practices in food production, trade and consumption.

title: A History of Protest in Australia
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The historian George Rudé defines protest as a ‘social act (generally a collective act) that seeks to rectify an injustice, to ventilate a grievance of public concern, or to offer a more fundamental challenge to society or its established norm’. This course uses this definition as its basis to explore how protest has been employed as an expression of ideological, political and cultural belief in Australia from the period of European settlement on Aboriginal lands until the present. It explores global influences on changing popular understandings of protest from a historical perspective to analyse why people in Australia have protested and continue to protest.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the changing reasons for mass protest in Australia alongside societal changes;
Develop arguments about the history of protest in Australia and express these in a variety of written and creative assessments.
Articulate protest as a historical form of self-expression;
Evaluate global influences on Australian protest movements;

title: Global Women's History: From Boadicea to Barbie
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the rich scholarly literature of histories of women across a range of nations, periods and geographical regions. It provides a chronological and thematic survey of the field, informed by sources written in women's own words, as well as classic and more recent studies of women's history. It covers periods from ancient to postmodern times, to explore both women’s lived experiences and constructions of women that continue to shape our views of them. Topics will include aspects of women's lives from childhood to old age.
learning_outcomes: Employ advanced research, analysis, writing and information literacy skills relevant to history.
Apply methodologies appropriate to the study of women's history and gender studies.
Critically discuss themes and topics in women's history across a range of geographical locations and time periods.
Compare the range of influences which impact on women in diverse social, historical and cultural contexts.

title: Global Age of Revolution: Russia, Germany and Modern Turkey
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The course investigates revolution in modern history with focus on the "global age of revolution" in the first third of the 20th century in Greater Europe. It encompasses Russian, Young Turk, Kemalist and post-WWI German revolutions, paying attention both to socialist and ethno-national rightist revolutionaries.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate understanding of the key issues in the history of revolution in 20th century Europe, Russia and Turkey;
Critically reflect upon the rhetoric and use of violence;
Analyse a variety of primary and secondary source materials and synthesise it in oral and written form.
Apply different theories and approaches to the study of historical revolutions;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Personal book review in written or oral form in the style of an interview with another person

title: Maps and Dreams: Aboriginal-Colonial Relationships in Australian History
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The experiences of Indigenous Australians since colonisation are among the most searing, contested and engaging themes in the Australian past. This course considers the causes and effects of encounters and interactions between Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal people through histories of violence and dispossession, love and intimacy, and law and culture. Some tensions and pressures keep Indigenous and non-Indigenous people separate from each other and some other circumstances bring them together. This shared history is viewed through intersections between gender and class, questions of degrees of agency and power in these interactions, and differing perspectives on sovereignty and the natural environment.
learning_outcomes: Develop ideas in advanced written and/or oral expression relevant to the study of history.
Analyse relevant primary and secondary sources on cross-cultural Indigenous Australian history.
Recognise key themes in historical relationships between Indigenous and non-Indigenous people in Australia.
Evaluate information, ideas, and arguments containing diverse cultural assumptions.

title: The Rise of Fascism: From the ‘March on Rome’ to Hitler’s ‘Seizure of Power’
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The emergence of fascist movements after the First World War propelled Europe into its most violent age. Why did this dangerous new ideology emerge on the political stage in the interwar period? What did fascism stand for? Why were European societies polarised between extremist ideologies of the left and right? How were the two most “successful” fascist movements, Fascism in Italy and National Socialism in Germany, able to come to office, and how did they cement their regimes in power? This course answers these questions by taking an in-depth look at Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy. It looks at the economic, social and political forces that gave rise to fascism, the path of fascist leaders to power and fascist methods of rule. In this context, it also considers debates about the nature of fascism, and whether it is possible to speak of ‘generic fascism’ at all.
learning_outcomes: Identify and explain key themes in the early history of fascism and National Socialism.
Apply historical research and critical analysis skills at an advanced level in oral and written forms.
Interpret and evaluate a variety of primary sources at an advanced level.
Explain and interpret the origins, nature, popular appeal and impact of fascism and Nazism.

title: The Downfall of Fascism: The Third Reich, War and Genocide
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The interwar fascist dictatorships, especially National Socialism in Germany, propelled Europe into its most violent age. Focusing on National Socialism in power (1933-1945), this course asks what role did Hitler play in the Third Reich; was he the master or the prisoner of circumstances? How did National Socialism seek to transform German society? To what extent did “ordinary” Germans internalise National Socialist values? What was the relationship between National Socialism and other fascist movements in Europe? What links were there between fascist repression and militarist expansionism? How do we explain the genocidal impulses of National Socialism? This course considers these questions by looking at the economic, social, and political forces that shaped National Socialism, National Socialist methods of rule, and the ideology’s drive to total warfare, particularly on the Eastern Front. In this context, it also looks at the debates concerning genocide (particularly the Holocaust and Porajmos), and at differing interpretations of fascism and its representation
learning_outcomes: Identify and explain key themes in the history of fascism and National Socialism in office;
Explain and interpret the nature, impact, and legacy of fascism and Nazism, the Second World War and genocide;
Interpret and evaluate a variety of primary sources at an advanced level;
Apply historical research and critical analysis skills at an advanced level in written form.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Academic Article Plan and Literature Review

title: The Future of the Middle East
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The course analyses the contemporary history of the Middle East in order to understand why this region is today’s global hotspot. The course will place particular emphasis upon the early 21st century and Turkey, the successor state of the Ottoman sultanate-caliphate, and Turkey’s neighbours Syria, Iraq, Iran and Armenia. The Ottoman Empire ruled the Middle East for four centuries, ending in war and genocide during the decade before the Republic of Turkey was founded in 1923. The course will lead back many of today’s issues to this pivotal background of the contemporary Middle East. On completion of the course, students will be familiar with major post-Ottoman developments, related historical narratives and sources of political, social and religious history. Topics include the Kurdish question, political Islam, the Sunni-Shia divide and the challenge of egalitarian, supra-religious social contracts. Students will acquire in-depth knowledge about current conflicts, their historiography and the potential for future peace in today’s Middle East.
learning_outcomes: Debate the major historiographical issues relating to the Middle East region;
Construct clear and concise arguments in written and/or oral forms.
Formulate fundamental questions pertaining to the contemporary Middle East as well as possible solutions;
Employ research and information literacy skills to analyse relevant scholarly sources according to the ethical standards of the field of history;

title: Global Age Of Revolution: The Middle East and Far East
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: “Revolution” denotes a dramatic period of seminal change in history. This course investigates revolution with focus on the 20th century in the Middle and Far East where revolutionary and anti-colonialist, “anti-imperialist” movements went hand in hand. It pays attention to the entanglement and diversity of revolutions worldwide, and thus to socialist, nationalist, religious and anti-colonialist revolutionaries.
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect upon the rhetoric and use of violence;
Identify and explain the key issues in the history of revolution in the 20th century with regard to the Middle and Far East;
Apply different theories and approaches to the study of historical revolutions;
Analyse a variety of primary and secondary source materials and synthesise them in oral and written form.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Personal book review in written or oral form in the style of an interview with another person

title: Transition to Health Sciences Education and Practice
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course is designed especially for health science students, and focuses on three main themes: Academic preparation topics; where students will examine a range of issues related to their transition to university learning and engagement, academic skills required for scientific reading and writing, and the associated policies and procedures in relation to academic responsibility and conduct. Fitness to practice topics; where students will look at the national framework for the recognition and maintenance of qualifications and registration, as well as a range of issues related to safe, effective and ethical professional practice. Core health science topics; where students will examine a range of foundation health and cultural issues that impact on all health professional education. This course is now delivered in blended format (both face-to-face and online delivery of learning).
learning_outcomes: Define Evidence Based Practice (EBP) and recognise the importance of critical appraisal skills in applying the EBP approach to health care.
Describe core health science concepts relating to resilience in clinical practice, and the national health priorities of Australia.
Describe the extent of workplace hazards and their associated risks, and demonstrate safe manual handling and effective hand hygiene practices relevant to the clinical setting.

Describe the professional responsibilities of health practitioners including national accreditation standards, legal and ethical issues, effective communication practices and inter-professional health care.
Identify the factors that differentiate health outcomes and the provision of health services to Australia's Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islanders, and other cross-cultural populations.
Demonstrate key components of introductory academic writing including library search skills, basic evaluative thinking, paraphrasing, coherent paragraph writing, and referencing.
Apply academic integrity requirements to a range of learning and assessment contexts.

title: Food Science 1
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to major foods/food groups/food categories with application to human health and food production, with a scientific approach in weekly written and laboratory content. The course explores different commodities and takes students through their structure, function and nutritional issues relating to processing and cultural aspects in the Australian context. This information is fundamental to further studies to nutrition and dietetics and is complimentary to studies in nutrition covered in Semester 1.
learning_outcomes: Participate in collaborative decision making, shared responsibility and shared vision within a team, recognising the diverse roles other team members play
Demonstrate appropriate food skills and techniques in completing practical exercises in a scientifically sound, safe and hygienic manner

Demonstrate and apply knowledge of food science and processing principles to commercial food production, focusing on major food groups and their impact on human health as well as the scientific principles behind food preparation and production
Critically analyse and evaluate information from diverse sources, including the ways in food science and culinary practices are influenced by determinants including culture
Demonstrates clear and concise verbal communication

title: Nutrition4Me
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: Introduces students to the study of nutrition including nutrients, requirements, food sources and food selection guides. It covers some aspects of food legislation, as well as proteins, carbohydrates, fats, vitamins and minerals, recommended dietary intakes, and nutrition as a contributor to health.
learning_outcomes: Understand Australian nutrition education tools
Critically appraise sources of nutritional information
Describe role of food and diet in good health and wellbeing
Be aware of safe and sustainable food practices

title: Nutrition in Childhood
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: The study of nutrition in childhood will focus on food and nutrition requirements for normal growth and development, as well as particular diet related concerns for children. It will examine nutrition education for children as well as the development of eating behaviours and barriers to change, especially in relation to the school setting. Students will be provided with the opportunity to integrate theory with skill based activities.
learning_outcomes: Describe the key diet related health issues for Australian children
State the nutritional requirements for growth and development in children.
Identify opportunities for modifications of the school environment to promote nutrition education and healthy eating in children.
Identify the role and significant food sources of nutrients essential to children.
Identify the ways in which the school environment contributes to the development of eating behaviours in childhood.

title: Interprofessional  Work Integrated Learning for Health
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This elective course will allow students to integrate the knowledge obtained during their health degree program in the ‘real world’ with an opportunity for interprofessional work-integrated learning (WIL) and engagement experiences in a health and wellbeing context. Interprofessional practice may encompass activities/projects that involve two or more professions where they can work and ‘learn with, from and about each other’ to improve collaboration and the quality of health care. Students will undertake an interprofessional WIL or engagement experience that may focus on: community-based projects, group learning and/or leadership activities to provide additional application of their knowledge and skills. Experiential workplace learning will be supported by appropriate readings and workplace guidance to suit the unique areas of the experience. Students will be able to undertake their interprofessional WIL or engagement experiences in a broad spectrum of work environments, both within or outside the University. Types of workplaces may include private businesses, government organisations, industry and/or volunteer/community-based organisations in Australia or in overseas locations. Students may undertake interprofessional WIL and engagement experiences with a focus on the following placement options: international, Indigenous, rural and remote or industry settings. WIL and engagement opportunities will be developed by the Course Coordinator (School of Health Sciences) in consultation with relevant Program Convenors, who will ensure that the interprofessional WIL experiences do not impact existing placement courses. Interprofessional WIL and engagement experiences will be supported by an appropriate workplace supervisor, not necessarily specific to the students program of enrolment. An EOI process will be used by the course coordinator to liaise with the students about existing interprofessional placements and provide an opportunity for students to indicate their placement requests. By the end of this course students will have extended their learning in a real-world context through an opportunity to develop interprofessional practice experience and develop a broad or specialised understanding of health care practice in their field or in a complementary area to their own field. Admission to this course is based the number of places available and may be restricted. Allocation to an interprofessional WIL placement is not guaranteed and is dependent on availability and the suitability of applications for each placement. Students should enquire through the Course Coordinator and/or Program Convenor for advice. To enrol in this course, students must obtain approval from the Course Coordinator in advance.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on the work integrated learning or engagement activities and how they relate to interprofessional practice in the health context
Develop a learning agreement with work/community site
Complete work integrated learning or engagement activities aligned with Learning Agreement

title: Research Project A
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course is Part A of a multi-term sequence. Part B must also be completed to meet the requirements of the sequence. Students will undertake an individual supervised research project, incorporating self-directed learning, with assistance from their supervisor. Projects will address a health sciences related research question. Students will use evidence based techniques to develop and test a hypothesis. This will ideally be in an area where there is sufficient published literature so that the student is able to critically appraise the topic. In research Project A, students will initiate and progress their project in consultation with their supervisor; they will complete their project in Research Project B.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate advanced oral and written communication skills including the presentation of a research report.
Critically appraise the literature related to the research question.
Collect data appropriately.
Analyse and interpret data.
Demonstrate the application of research strategies.
Develop a research question.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Part A - Introduction and Method of the research project

title: Research Methodology and Design
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course advances the student's understanding of health-related research methods and concepts. The course will explore human research ethics, qualitative research methods, and quantitative research methods. Students will read and critique both qualitative and quantitative published research.
learning_outcomes: Critically appraise qualitative, quantitative and mixed methods research
Describe ethical considerations pertaining to human research
Select appropriate methodologies to address a research question
Evaluate the appropriateness of common qualitative, quantitative and mixed methods research methodologies
Define, compare and contrast the common qualitative, quantitative and mixed methods research methodologies

title: Research Project B
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course is Part B of a multi-term sequence. Part A must also be completed to meet the requirements of the sequence. Students will undertake an individual supervised research project, incorporating self-directed learning, with assistance from their supervisor. Projects will address a health sciences related research question. Students will use evidence based techniques to develop and test a hypothesis. This will ideally be in an area where there is sufficient published literature so that the student is able to critically appraise the topic. Students completing this course will have successfully completed Research Project A where they will have initiated and progressed their research project, which is completed in this course, Research Project B.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate advanced written communication skills including the presentation of a research report.
Demonstrate advanced oral communication skills including the presentation of a research report.
Demonstrate the application of research strategies.
Analyse and interpret data.
Critically appraise the literature related to the research question.
Collect data appropriately.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Part A - Introduction and Method of the research project

title: Health, Medicine and Wellbeing Honours Research Skills
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course focuses on developing the tangible skills required to embark on a career as an independent researcher. These include grant writing, preparing a conference abstract that concisely describes research in order to generate interest and discussion, and the development of an academic profile. It is recognised that the outputs required in completing the HLSC4404A&B, HLSC4406 and HLSC4301A&B sequence will be based on the same body of material and involve considerable overlap.
learning_outcomes: Network and present as an independent contributor to the research community.
Develop skills in grant writing.
Disseminate and promote research, and engage professionally with peers.

title: Foundations of Health Promotion
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview: This course provides an introduction to the theory and practice of health promotion.
learning_outcomes: describe and apply underpinning principles and elements of effective health promotion, such as population reach and evidence-based practice;
describe the concepts of health and determinants of health;
describe and apply in context key frameworks of health promotion, such as relevant WHO charters and declarations;
understand the difference between health promotion and health education;
critically appraise strategic policies and plans for health promotion.
apply a systematic process for the determination of priorities; and
understand and apply organisational change and capacity building theory to influence change in organisations;
understand and apply behaviour change theories and models to influence change in individuals;

title: Managing Talent
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Human Resource Management links people-related activities to business strategy. The course develops a critical understanding of the role and functions of the various human resource activities in an organisation, providing students with a comprehensive review of key HRM concepts, techniques and issues. Working with contemporary case studies, students not only engage in collaborative and individual work processes but use communication and discourse characteristic of the HRM context and environment.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and evaluate significant contemporary issues in human resource management including Human Resource Management's contribution to organisational performance.
Investigate and evaluate the key procedures in recruitment and selection.
Explain key Human Resource practices and activities necessary for an organisation's value creation and success.
Demonstrate understanding of key concepts and theories to develop effective performance management and rewards systems that reinforce desired employee behaviours.
Recognise diversity in the workplace and its value in attracting and retaining employees, boosting productivity and fostering innovation.

title: Dynamics of People and Work in Organisations
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: People are an organisation’s most dynamic resource, and managing people well is essential to achieving an organisation’s purposes. Yet people are a fundamentally different kind of resource from others. Understanding how people do work that contributes to organisations, and how organisations in turn affect the lives of their workers, is challenging and important. This course equips students with the foundational concepts, theories, and evidence they need to identify, connect, and interpret these issues, and to eventually become managers of people, work, and workplaces. Drawing on established and emerging international perspectives and frameworks, illustrated by contemporary Australian examples, the course explains how and why work takes different forms and what determines its value. Students will compare and engage critically with diverse academic and practitioner views of work as a core concern of management and as a major part of organisational life.
learning_outcomes: Compare multiple perspectives on people and work as dynamic organisational resources.
Evaluate how contemporary work practices and arrangements deliver value for organisations and evaluate the consequences of those practices.
Explain how various factors, both inside and outside organisations, affect what work is done and how it is organised, managed, and valued.
Contrast different types of work in different organisational contexts.
Analyse work holistically, as a source of value (income, connection, meaning) for workers, beyond managerial concern.

title: HR Analytics
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course is designed to introduce the evolving field of Human Resource (HR) analytics, combining key aspects from human resource management (HRM), behavioural sciences, and statistics. Positioned at the intersection of quantitative analysis and human capital management, the course navigates through both tactical and strategic dimensions, emphasising the potential impact of analytics on organisational objectives. The subject matter delves into the theoretical foundations of HR analytics, investigating its role in shaping contemporary HRM functions. Complementary to this, the course scrutinises ethical considerations, underscoring the responsible use of HR data, and casts a prospective eye on the future trends shaping the field. The course offers hands-on exercises focusing on the management, analysis, and interpretation of HR data sets, thereby equipping students with the requisite skills to perform elementary to intermediate statistical analyses.
learning_outcomes: Translate analytical insights into human resource management decisions.
Describe the core concepts of human resource analytics and explain how human resource analytics can add value to an organisation.
Assess ethical and responsible data management and use within the human resources environment.
Apply quantitative methods to resolve human resources challenges.

title: Introduction to Employment Relations
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: The effective management of complex employment relationships is a critical function in contemporary organisations. This course introduces the theory and practice of employment relations, delineating its essential concepts. It considers the historical dimensions of work and the employment relationship, and the origins and the development of the field of employment relations up to the present day. Students will learn to recognise and describe the structures and characteristics of employee representation, management, and relevant state agencies. This is complemented by an examination of the main rule-making processes in contemporary employment relations, from individual bargaining to collective agreement-making and direct regulation by the state. Through practical activities and problem-based assessments, students will develop the foundational skills needed to interpret and effectively manage employment relations situations and issues.
learning_outcomes: Investigate and outline solutions to employment relations problems, based on research and assessment of current practices.
Define and discuss the theory and practice of employment relations.
Communicate knowledge of employment relations in written and verbal formats appropriate to both audience and purpose.
Recognise and analyse the social, historical and equity issues within employment relations.
Apply the essential concepts of employment relations and their interrelationship at the individual, organisational, and national levels.

title: Future of Work
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Gone are the days of a linear career path. Today, a confluence of global factors - digital transformation, globalisation, and emergent organisational cultures - have redefined the very meaning of 'work.' The dual forces of automation and information explosion are reshaping job roles, creating novel career avenues even as they challenge existing ones. This course is designed to reflect on the complex terrains of tomorrow's workplace. In a world dynamically shaped by technological breakthroughs, global interconnectedness, and evolving employment paradigms, this course aims to prepare for a deeper understanding of a shifting landscape that defies traditional understandings of career, labour, and value creation.
learning_outcomes: Apply current academic theories and research to solve challenges via solutions that reflect the changing nature of work.
Asses the critical characteristics and skills required to influence workplace culture and practice.
Explain how organisational paradigms and cultures have evolved over time.
Evaluate the key competencies needed to lead the Future of Work.

title: Negotiation and Conflict Management
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Many business and people management problems are complex and challenging, requiring skill and sensitivity in dealing with sometimes conflicting interests, perspectives, and agendas. In these situations, there are rarely easy solutions; effective managers must use constructive problem-solving methods and develop sustainable stakeholder relationships to achieve positive outcomes. This course introduces the concepts and techniques of negotiation and conflict management, from theoretical basis to practical application. Adopting a problem-based and experiential learning approach, and using a wealth of international cases, simulations, and hands-on activities to bring concepts to life, the course develops students’ skills and their confidence as aspiring managers and leaders. Through participation and reflection, both as individuals and in groups, students will learn to interpret, evaluate, and respond effectively to real conflict situations.
learning_outcomes: Collaboratively construct and defend a plan (written and verbal) that responds to a workplace negotiation scenario.
Incorporate and apply the language and theory that underpins negotiation and conflict management.
Reflect critically on individual and group negotiation processes and experiences using concepts, theories, and readings introduced in the course.
Develop and implement the skills required for strategy formulation, planning and research for a real negotiation.
Apply and evaluate skills related to the practice of negotiating, in workplace and other employment relations contexts.

title: Strategic HR
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Contemporary human resource management (HRM) defines a holistic approach to employment relations (ER). The concepts and theories of HRM and ER and their subsequent application to the current cooperation of HRM and ER are examined. Students will draw upon their prior learning from previous HRM and ER courses, applying this to real-world industries and enterprises. Through experiencing relevant case studies of selected industries and enterprises, and responsiveness with local practitioners, students will strengthen and enhance their independent and collaborative work processes and problem solving & decision-making skills. This will enable students to further their practical skills and expertise in the areas of HRM and ER.
learning_outcomes: Collectively engage in prolonged group assignments that encourage diverse collaborative outcomes.
Access, evaluate and apply current publicly-available data and information sources to inform Human Resource Management and Employment Relations problem solving.
Communicate in oral and written formats employing subject specific terminology and context.
Apply and critically analyse Human Resource Management and Employment Relations concepts in the study of selected industries and enterprises, both unionised and non-unionised.
Design a solution that demonstrates an integrative awareness of contemporary professional standards, practice and effective implementation.
Individually and collectively engage in projects that require reflection on personal knowledge, skill and ability.

title: Musculoskeletal Anatomy
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
