school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: Provides an introduction to the functional anatomy of the human body with emphasis on the musculoskeletal system, peripheral vasculature and major nerve trunks. This course contributes to the broad biomedical science foundation required for health graduates. In addition, it provides a firm basis for later courses in organ-based anatomy.
learning_outcomes: Identify and describe the bone and joint structure, musculature, vasculature and innervation of the head and torso.
Apply the knowledge gained in this course to describe functional anatomy of the human musculoskeletal system.
Identify and describe the bone and joint structure, musculature, vasculature and innervation of the lower limb.
Identify and describe the bone and joint structure, musculature, vasculature and innervation of the upper limb.
Apply correct anatomical terminology when describing the musculoskeletal elements of the human body.

title: Human Capital Development
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Managing and developing human capital within organisations for sustained performance is key to achieving long-term competitive advantage. Human Capital Development examines the activities and core processes that impact in developing organisational and individual level human capital. This course focuses on interventions which will change and improve the ability of individuals', groups' and the organisation’s human capital. Interventions may range from strategic to the functional areas of human capital development and its core processes. Communication and group management techniques are emphasised as important attributes for Human Capital Development (HCD) professionals. All students engage in trainer competencies through developing and implementing experiential sessions for small groups.
learning_outcomes: Develop, apply and evaluate core HRD processes.

Explain human capital development (HCD) and its underpinning theories, the difference between human resources development (HRD), education, training, learning and the concept of the transfer of learning.
Evaluate the role of HRD in dealing with contemporary challenges.
Critique the relationship between organisational development (OD) and HRD contribution to organisational effectiveness.

assessment_tasks.task_name: In Person - End of Term Assignment

title: Head and Neck Anatomy
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course aims at providing students with a thorough understanding of head and neck anatomy with emphasis on those structures associated with the oral cavity. The course focuses on the anatomy, design and function of structures in the head and neck as they pertain to oral health.
learning_outcomes: Describe the structure and function of the musculoskeletal elements of the skull, face, ear, nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, oral cavity, and cervical and thoracic regions
Apply the knowledge gained in this course to identify and describe the anatomical and neural mechanisms involved in mastication, swallowing, respiration, and hearing
Describe the structure and function of the brain, spinal cord, neural pathways and cranial nerves; in particular the course and distribution of the facial and trigeminal cranial nerves
Identify the major blood vessels which supply the features of the head and neck
Understand and apply anatomical terminology when identifying and describing the anatomy of the head and neck region
List and identify major musculoskeletal elements of the skull, face, ear, nasal cavity, pharynx, larynx, oral cavity, and cervical and thoracic regions
Describe the structure and biomechanics of the temporomandibular joint, and briefly describe some common disorders of this joint.

title: Neuroscience and Head and Neck Anatomy
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course aims to provide students with a thorough understanding of the anatomy of the structures that are involved in the production of speech. The course focuses on the anatomy, design and function of structures in the head, neck and thorax as they pertain to speech pathology. The course also includes the neural basis of sound production.
learning_outcomes: Describe the structure and function of the musculoskeletal elements of the skull; face; cervical and thoracic regions of the vertebral column; nasal cavity; oral cavity; pharynx and larynx.
Describe the structure and function of the brain, spinal cord, neural pathways and cranial nerves.
Identify and apply anatomical terminology when describing the anatomy of the head and neck regions.
Apply the knowledge gained in this course to describe the anatomical and neural mechanisms involved in respiration; swallowing; speech and hearing.
Identify major musculoskeletal elements of the skull; face; cervical and thoracic regions of the vertebral column; nasal cavity; oral cavity; pharynx and larynx.

title: Anatomy for Biomedical Science
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course aims to provide students with an overview of the anatomical structures of the human body. It consists of a series of lectures and laboratories covering functional anatomy of the human body including the musculoskeletal system, nervous system, cardiovascular system, thorax, abdomen and pelvis. Areas emphasised are those that will prepare students for an understanding that focuses on the major body systems. The course will also prepare students for subsequent careers in any of the health and biomedical sciences, and bioengineering fields.
learning_outcomes: Describe, for major organs and structures in the head, chest, abdomen, pelvis and limbs: - their structure (Gross Anatomy), - their relationship to other organs and their surface anatomy, - their blood supply, nerve supply, as well as its venous drainage, and - how the organ's structure relates to its basic function (i.e. it's physiology).

title: Fundamentals of Human Anatomy
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course aims to provide students with an understanding of the functional anatomy of the human body with emphasis on the musculoskeletal system, nervous system and major nerve trunks, vascular system, thorax, abdomen and pelvis. It contributes to the broad biomedical science foundation required for health graduates, and provides a firm basis for subsequent courses in advanced anatomy.
learning_outcomes: Describe the general anatomy of the thorax, abdomen and pelvis and identify the structures and organs located in these regions
Name, identify and describe the bones of the human skeleton
Identify and describe the joint structure, musculature, vasculature and innervation of the upper limb
Understand and apply the appropriate use of anatomical terminology when identifying and describing structures of the human body
Identify and describe the joint structure, musculature, vasculature and innervation of the lower limb
Describe the anatomy of the head and neck region, including the structure and function of the brain
Describe the structure of the vertebral column and spinal cord, and identify and describe the axial musculature of the human body

title: Human Genomics and Biomolecular Analysis
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course represents a blend between fundamental concepts and current issues in molecular medicine. The course focuses on the relationships between structure, function and analysis of proteins and nucleic acids as applied to human disease and provides an introduction to modern concepts of genomic structure, function and analysis.
learning_outcomes: Perform basic experimental methods for analysis of proteins and nucleic acids.
Discuss the relationship between molecular structure and function.
Explain the importance of molecular structure as it applies to fundamental biomedical analytical techniques.
Describe the structural features of proteins and nucleic acids.
Describe, with examples, the main types of human genetic disorders, how they arise, and their patterns of inheritance.
Communicate effectively using scientific writing and standardised notation.
Outline the organisation of the human genome, and methods of genome analysis.
Solve problems related to inheritance of traits and diseases.
Explain the principles of Mendelian genetics and their relationship to inheritance of traits and diseases.

title: Human Bioscience
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course provides an integrated introduction to the anatomy (structure), physiology (functioning) and biochemistry (molecular interactions) of the human body. Core concepts are: - the principles of homeostasis and the significance of a breakdown in homeostasis as a threat to health - the organisation of the human body from atoms to organism - the processes that are critical to the maintenance of life and the processes that help defend threats to life - the complementarity of anatomy and physiology, and interrelationships between body organ systems. In addressing these concepts the course covers the cell, cell cycle and basic cellular chemistry; atomic structure; molecules of life; protein synthesis; water, acids, bases and pH balance. The course introduces the 4 primary tissue types and the 11 body systems - integumentary, skeletal, muscular, nervous, endocrine, cardiovascular, lymphatic, respiratory, digestive, renal and reproductive systems. The course also presents an introduction to immunity, infectious microbiological agents, genetics and human evolution. HUBS1401 cannot be undertaken in B. Nursing or B. Midwifery as an Elective.
learning_outcomes: Develop strategies for self-learning and critical reasoning
Identify and apply the correct terminology in relation to human anatomy and physiology
Define the major aspects of biochemistry relating to reactivity and the formation of chemical bonds
Develop an understanding of the organ systems and how they contribute to life
Demonstrate strategies for infection prevention and control in line with NSQHS standards
Identify and explain the levels of biological organisation
Explain homeostasis and negative feedback

title: Biomedical Science Part 1
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: Provides a comprehensive introduction to aspects of human anatomy, physiology, biochemistry and evolution. Covers the concepts of molecules and their behaviour within cells, the transition from cells to tissues to organs, the control of homeostasis through the nervous and endocrine systems, movement, an introduction to genetics and drugs and their modes of action.
learning_outcomes: To understand the structure (Anatomy), function (Physiology) and the molecular interactions (Biochemistry) of the human body.
To understand the structure and functions of the cell.
To understand how homeostasis is achieved in terms of feedback control of bodily function.
To understand the principle of homeostasis in the context of a healthy functioning human body.
To develop critical reasoning skills, particularly in relation to the application of knowledge in the human biosciences.
To develop strategies for independent learning.
To understand the organisation levels of the body from cells, tissues, organs, systems and organism.

title: Biomedical Science Part 2
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course follows on from Biomedical Science Part 1 (HUBS1403). We will investigate the control of several systems which are vitally important to normal human functioning. We will study the cardiovascular system, the respiratory system, the reproductive system, how the body digests and assimilates food, controls fluid balance and protects itself from disease.
learning_outcomes: Employ critical reasoning skills in relation to the application of knowledge in the Human Biosciences area.

Understand the function and regulation of: The cardiovascular system The respiratory system The digestive system and energy metabolism Excretion and fluid and electrolyte balance Immunity and defence against infection Reproduction and development
Build on the strategies for self learning gained in first semester in Biomedical Science Part 1.
Appreciate that the above systems do not act in isolation but must interact with each in order to ensure optimal function.

title: Human Bioscience for Nursing and Midwifery
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course provides an introduction to the anatomical, biochemical and physiological bases of health and illness. It provides an integrated approach to understanding body function, and, where possible, places the learning in the context of the nursing and midwifery professions, in order to reinforce the relevance and importance of this underpinning knowledge to the nursing and midwifery student's future study and career. The course material is structured around the National Health Priority areas of Cardiovascular Health, Diabetes, Asthma, Obesity, Cancer Control, Mental Health, Arthritis & Musculoskeletal conditions and Injury Prevention & Control. This course cannot be counted as credit for HUBS1401 Human Bioscience.
learning_outcomes: Use knowledge and understanding of the basic function of these systems to interpret and solve clinical problems
Briefly describe the mechanisms of energy metabolism
Provide an overview of the functions of the Endocrine, Nervous, Immune, Cardiovascular, Respiratory, Renal and Reproductive systems
List the major functions and repair methods of the major tissue types
Describe the basic biology of the cell and functions of its structures
Describe the role of Blood as a tissue
Explain the basic chemistry underlying the maintenance of life, reproduction and homeostasis

title: Advanced Human Bioscience
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: HUBS1416 provides students with a background of core concepts in gastrointestinal system, microbiology, immunology, neurophysiology and genetics. Integral to this course is an understanding of homeostasis, the complementarity of anatomy and physiology, and the interrelationships between body organ systems. Relevant clinical examples are introduced and discussed where possible around the National Health Priority areas of Cardiovascular Health, Diabetes, Asthma, Obesity, Cancer Control, Mental Health, Arthritis & Musculoskeletal conditions and Injury Prevention and Control. Knowledge, comprehension and application of these core concepts is essential for understanding both physiological and pathophysiological processes in the patient which students will encounter in future studies and career.
learning_outcomes: Explain the basic mechanisms of action of vaccines and their importance in disease prevention
Outline the components and arms of the immune response
Use knowledge and understanding obtained in objectives 1-7 to interpret and solve clinical problems
Describe the main neurotransmitters and receptors of the nervous system
Explain the function and control of the digestive system including the roles of accessory organs in nutrient digestion & absorption
Describe the basis of human inheritance and genetic variation and use pedigrees and punnet squares to predict inheritance patterns and calculate risk of inheriting genetic disorders
Describe the characteristics of some clinically important microbes and the clinical manifestations of the diseases they produce and concepts in infection control and epidemiology
Describe the structural and functional divisions of the nervous system and broadly, how they operate

title: Professional and Communication Skills in Biomedicine
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course introduces the student to the preclinical and clinical nomenclature used to efficiently communicate in health professions and biomedical science. It will also introduce the student to strategies for reporting observations and findings accurately and concisely, both in a clinical and a scientific context.
learning_outcomes: Recognise and appropriately use biomedical terminology, abbreviations and signage across professional and clinical contexts, considering audience and clarity.
Communicate biomedical concepts clearly in written, oral, and collaborative formats, adapting style to different audiences and providing constructive feedback.
Recognise ethical and legal boundaries in biomedical communication and apply best practices across professional, media and public forums.
Locate, evaluate and reference biomedical information accurately and ethically, demonstrating academic integrity and critical judgement.
Apply principles of patient-centred and cross-cultural communication, including culturally safe practices with First Nations Australians and diverse communities.
Use AI literacy skills to evaluate, critique and refine generative AI outputs in biomedical contexts, recognising applications, limitations and ethical considerations.

title: Foundations of Health and Disease
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: The course provides an integrated introduction to Human Biosciences: the anatomy and physiology of the major organ systems will be explored including the mechanisms of disease. Students will gain exposure to potential future health careers including Medical Radiation Science, Nutrition and Dietetics, Pharmacy, Occupational Therapy, Nursing and Biomedical research. The course will be taught in a blended mode that includes face to face instruction in lectures and interactive tutorials/practical exercises, in conjunction with online teaching and interaction. This course is only offered to high school students accepted into the High Performing Students program.
learning_outcomes: Develop an understanding of how to use physiological testing equipment
Define the key organ systems of the human body and describe their basic anatomy and physiology
Develop strategies for self-learning and critical reasoning
Explain homeostasis and describe examples of a breakdown in homeostasis and its role in disease/pathophysiology

title: Critical Thinking and Scientific Process in Biomedicine
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course is intended to develop a student's ability to understand and logically evaluate arguments typically found in biomedicine, giving them the ability to think clearly and critically. This course also introduces the students to the scientific process used in biomedicine and develops their technical skills in the laboratory
learning_outcomes: Measure basic properties of the human body and molecules.
Begin to appropriately format, interpret, analyse and report on simple data from biomedical experiments.
Identify cognitive bias and fallacious thinking.
Begin to formulate the right question or hypothesis to ask.
Begin to understand how to conduct biomedical experiments.
Recognise hazards and describe safe practices for biomedical laboratories.
Apply basic logical principles to the evaluation of arguments.
Analyse and critically evaluate arguments, ideas and theories in biomedicine.

title: Neural and Visceral Anatomy
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: The course consists of a series of lectures and laboratories on the functional anatomy of the nervous system, thorax, abdomen and pelvis. Areas emphasised are those most important in Medical Radiation Science, Occupational Therapy and Physiotherapy practice.
learning_outcomes: Describe the blood supply, venous and lymphatic drainage.
Describe the structure of the major organs in the head, chest, abdomen and pelvis (Gross Anatomy).
Understand how the organ's structure relates to its function, i.e. its physiology.
Describe the relationship to other organs and its surface anatomy.

title: Human Biochemistry and Cell Biology
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with knowledge and understanding of the structure and function of the cells with an emphasis on molecular aspects. It involves integrated learning between the areas of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology. Practical sessions develop core skills that prepare students for a career in laboratory-based research in the biomedical sciences.
learning_outcomes: Describe the translation of messenger RNA into protein
Demonstrate how to research topics, seek out information and solve problems in cell biology and biochemistry
Describe the replication and transcription of DNA
Explain how cells communicate and respond using signal transduction
Describe the structure and function of cells
Demonstrate practical skills necessary to conduct laboratory-based investigations of cell biology and biochemistry
Analyse, discuss and present laboratory-based data and scientific information written and oral forms of communication
Describe the structure and function of proteins including enzymes

title: Cancer Biology and Oncology
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course will cover the underlying molecular and cellular biology involved in carcinogenesis, tumor growth, and metastasis, and the implications of the basic biological findings on cancer prevention, diagnosis, and treatment. It involves integrated learning between the areas of Biochemistry, Cell Biology, Molecular Biology and Human Genetics. Students will also learn about the biologic hallmarks of cancer, genomic instability, dysregulated cancer cell metabolism, and the role of microenvironment, lifestyle factors, and immune system in cancer development and progression. The course is organised as a series of modules that include lectures and practical classes that provides students with a solid background in general cancer biology and prepares them for a career in laboratory-based research in areas of the biomedical sciences.
learning_outcomes: Describe how cellular processes including cellular metabolism are altered during cancer initiation, progression and metastasis.
Describe how cancers are modelled and studied in the laboratory.
Describe how cell growth and differentiation occurs and what happens when the control of these processes is altered.
Demonstrate practical skills necessary to conduct laboratory-based investigations of human cancers.
Describe how basic biology research helps design novel therapeutics.
Describe the role of tissue microenvironment, obesity, aging, and lifestyle factors in cancer development.
Discuss the concepts of cancer stem cells and clonal evolution of cancers.
Describe the biologic hallmarks of cancer.
Describe how genetics and epigenetics drive cancer initiation and progression.

title: Introductory Pharmacology
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with knowledge of the basic pharmacological mechanisms underlying the action of drugs on the body systems and indications of medicines in the management of diseases and disorders.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge and understand the pharmacology and accepted indications of selected drug classes that act on the body systems
Relate the physiology of selected disease processes to the identification of targets for pharmacological intervention
Demonstrate knowledge of medication safety in line with NSQHS standards
Demonstrate knowledge and understand the basic concepts of pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics
Demonstrate knowledge and understand the pharmacology and accepted indications of selected classes of chemotherapeutic and antimicrobial drugs

title: Experimental and Clinical Design in Medical Research
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course provides an introduction to the skills and knowledge needed to design, execute and analyse the results of experimental work. The course will focus on (i) why experimental and clinical research should be undertaken (ii) experimental and clinical design failures and repercussions (iii) ethical and safety considerations and their influence on study design (iv) blinding, randomisation and repeatability in study design (v) experimental noise and other sources of variance and their influence on study design and (vi) the influence of social, political, career, and economic factors on the study design process. This course will give students a framework to plan and execute scientifically and ethically sound experimental work involving both human and non-human subjects.
learning_outcomes: Understand statistical approaches as they relate to the design and interpretation of clinical and experimental study results.
Understand how ethical frameworks, legislation, safety and consumer needs influence experimental designs.
Understand how social, political and professional incentives shape clinical and experimental study design.
Effectively critique clinical and experimental study designs.
Understand the consequences of good and bad experimental design.
List and understand the principles of clinical and experimental study design.
Understand the limitations of biological models and assays and how these limitations need to be factored in during clinical and experimental study design.

title: Human Metabolic and Nutritional Biochemistry
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: By building upon the knowledge of the structure and function of cells developed in HUBS2206, this course provides students with knowledge and understanding of the delivery and function of cellular nutrients and metabolism in the human body. It involves integrated learning, including practical skills, between the areas of Biochemistry and Nutrition.
learning_outcomes: Identify and explain how nutrients are delivered to the body
Demonstrate how to research topics, seek out information and solve problems in metabolic and nutritional biochemistry
Analyse and present laboratory-based data and scientific information in a written form of communication
Demonstrate practical skills necessary to conduct laboratory-based investigations of metabolic and nutritional biochemistry
Identify and explain how nutrients are important in disease pathology
identify and describe the function of various nutrients including how they are metabolised to form energy used by the human body
Understand how energy metabolism varies between tissues

title: Clinical Exercise Physiology
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: The course is designed to enhance students' understanding of human physiology and develop their understanding of physiological responses to single bouts of exercise as well as the adaptations that occur following regular exercise training. Students will participate in practical sessions to gain an understanding of exercise and physical fitness testing.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the physiological responses and adaptations to physical activity
Demonstrate knowledge of the impact of clinical conditions on capacity to perform physical activity
Demonstrate skills in conducting basic fitness physical assessments and exercise tests
Describe the roles and recommendations for specific types of exercise programs for people with different clinical conditions
Describe the role of regular physical activity in the maintenance of health and physical fitness
Demonstrate an understanding of the role of pre-exercise screening and exercise testing
Apply knowledge of the principles of exercise training to selection and appraisal of the different types of exercise training programs

title: Human Pathophysiology
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course provides an introduction to the concept of human disease and the pathophysiological mechanisms underlying the causes. Students will be provided with an introduction to pathophysiology of the immune, endocrine, circulatory, respiratory, gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal, renal and nervous systems. Associated pathologies of these systems will be introduced and explored.
learning_outcomes: Develop an understanding of the pathology and pathophysiology associated with disorders of the immune, endocrine, circulatory, respiratory, gastrointestinal, musculoskeletal, renal and nervous systems.
Develop an understanding of the pathophysiological mechanisms and processes underlying human diseases.
Develop an understanding of the concept of human disease.

title: Integrative Physiology for Biomedical Science
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course builds upon the basic human physiological concepts introduced in HUBS1403 and HUBS1404 by presenting in more depth the physiology of the major body systems and with greater emphasis on the regulatory roles of the neural and endocrine systems. Practical sessions will demonstrate and reinforce physiological concepts and extend the student's knowledge base providing students with the capacity to use research skills to address biomedical science questions of importance to world health. Areas emphasised are those that prepare students for a career in research that focuses on physiological mechanisms and also for careers in any health science discipline.
learning_outcomes: Describe the application of animal models of physiology and their relationship to the understanding of human disease
Describe how these systems are integrated in the human body to maintain homeostasis
Use written and/or oral skills to report on the variance in body systems
Describe the physiological function and control of the major organ systems
Use physiological measurement and analysis to demonstrate the variability in response by the human body to stimuli that disturb the homeostatic balance

title: Human Infection and Immunity
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course will build on the knowledge gained in the Year 1 Human Bioscience course: HUBS1404 Biomedical Science Part 2. Students will learn general principles of infection and immunity including the growth and metabolism of human microbial pathogens, mechanisms of microbial pathogenesis and infection control strategies. Students will also learn about host defence mechanisms to combat microbial infections.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate how to research topics, seek out information and solve problems in microbiology and immunology.
Analyse, discuss and present laboratory-based data and scientific information in written and oral forms of communication.
Demonstrate practical skills necessary to conduct laboratory-based investigations in microbiology and immunology.
Demonstrate knowledge of contemporary biomedical and molecular techniques to diagnose and characterize infectious microbes.
Describe the basic structures and growth characteristics of bacteria and viruses.
Describe human immunity and the development of immune responses that are important in the prevention and development of disease.
Describe prevention and treatment strategies for infectious diseases.

title: Bioinformatics and Functional Genomics
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: The development of high throughput techniques for sequencing nucleic acids and proteins has resulted in an explosion of molecular information, and new computational tools for seeking, storing and analysing this information have also been developed. The challenge is to use the information accessible from databases to solve biological problems and to inform hypothesis generation and future experiments in biomedical sciences. This course will focus on functional genomics (genomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics) and how to use bioinformatics in different physiological and pathological situations.
learning_outcomes: Use the knowledge and skills gained to logically, critically and creatively analyse real-life questions in biomedicine.
Demonstrate knowledge of the extent of international biological databases and use them to investigate important biomedical questions.
Work to solve research problems and acquire, organise and present information.

title: Sports Science 1
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: Examines aspects of general physiology important during exercise and introduces students to exercise physiology. It covers both theoretical knowledge and the development of basic skills in exercise testing. The physiological responses to a bout of exercise are examined first, followed by principles of exercise training, and an examination of adaptations to exercise training.
learning_outcomes: Describe the role of physical activity plays in the maintenance of overall health and physical fitness
Demonstrate skills in conducting basic exercise tests
Discuss the physiological systems necessary for exercise
Apply the principles of exercise training to distinguish between different types of exercise programs
Analyse the physiological responses to a bout of exercise
Identify the appropriate types and levels of fitness required for different sports
Predict the physiological adaptations to regular exercise training

title: Biomedical Research Integrated Learning
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course is intended to provide students with an overview of both general and personal professional skills required to enter into, and succeed in, the field of biomedical science. These skills are intended to complement the theoretical and practical skillsets provided by traditional academic courses and practical classes. Emphasis will be on determining the accuracy of information, with the importance of effective presentation of a graduate's skill sets which include critical analysis and communication of scientific information to target audiences. This course aims are to enable students to develop skills important for professional life (including teamwork, problem solving, communication, and critical thinking/evaluation skills). Students will also gain invaluable exposure to real-world cutting-edge scientific problems, and through developing scientific thinking skills, enhance their critical analysis and teamwork capabilities. The aim is to ensure that students develop the ability to integrate their learning through a combination of academic and research-related activities. This course is designed to provide an overview of the key research skills that are essential for medical research. Students will develop these skills in a collaborative environment through interactive group activities and engagement with leading medical researchers in the School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy.
learning_outcomes: Work effectively in a group.
Explain the difference between being a consumer and a practitioner of scientific research.
Critically review information.
Understand the importance/responsibility of conducting research ethically.
Communicate scientific information to a target audience in written format.
Appreciate the range of approaches and techniques involved in addressing a research question.
Evaluate the accuracy of scientific information.
Orally communicate a scientific topic to a non-specialist target audience.
Identify and explain how a study fits into the wider research area.
Understand the role of media and communication in science.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Spot the rubbish and scientific literacy
Short answer Assignment (review of example paper)

title: Neuroscience
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: The purpose of this course is to provide the student with a broad understanding of neuroscience. In covering cellular, behavioural, and pathological aspects of neuroscience, the student is introduced to some of the most challenging issues in the field today, along with the most advanced research tools used to probe these issues. Students will gain knowledge of neuroanatomy, molecular and physiological features of the nervous system through exposure to lectures, workshops/discussions and laboratory classes. The course is divided into 4 major blocks: 1. Basic Organisation and Function of the Nervous System 2. The Sensorimotor Systems 3. Neurobiology of Aging-Relate Diseases: Dementia and Stroke 4. Neurobiology of Mental Health Disorders. Particular emphasis will be placed on neuronal and non-neuronal function, plasticity and degeneration, on important neurotransmitter systems, on the organisation of the central nervous system and methods to study the nervous system. Students will be expected to apply the basic knowledge developed above to understand processes involved in normal and pathological nervous system function. Students will have weekly workshops that will allow them to apply and consolidate the knowledge taught in lectures and have an opportunity to conduct basic neuroscience experiments, collect and analyse data, and interact and discuss course content with their peers and neuroscientist lecturers.
learning_outcomes: Recall & understand the basic anatomical (gross and cellular) organisation of the brain and spinal cord, and have a basic understanding how these developed (neurodevelopment) and an appreciation of how they evolved (neuro- evolution).
Apply the knowledge developed in Learning Outcomes 1 and 2 to understand processes involved in major nervous system functions, pathologies, and disorders.

Through the course workshops, be able to apply the knowledge gained from Learning Outcomes 1-3 to basic neuroscience experiments and discussions. Be able to understand how to carry out a neuroscience experiment, and interpret that data in the context of course content taught and with an appreciation of the limitations of the study.

Recall & understand the anatomical, biochemical and physiological features of neural transmission. Understand the principles of plasticity and appreciate the importance of plasticity to cognition and behaviour.

title: Regulatory skills for the Pharmaceutical and Therapeutic Goods Industries
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: Employers in pharmaceutical, therapeutics, and medical technologies prefer to hire staff who are future-ready; who have a working knowledge and understand the regulations applied to the research, development and manufacturing of pharmaceuticals, therapeutics, foodstuffs, and personal use products. While this may appear to add complexity to the manufacture and marketing of these products, it ensures that the product is safe, effective and meets a minimum measure of quality. Whether you wish to work in a large multinational enterprise, small-medium enterprise, or your own small business, you will need to be aware of the relevant statutory regulations, understand how to comply with these obligations and assure that your product is safe, effective, and able to be sold in relevant markets! This course is designed to introduce you to the statutory regulations applied to the development, evaluation, manufacture, storage, distribution, and post-marketing vigilance of pharmaceutical and therapeutic products in clinical and consumer sectors, expanding your core knowledge and providing career flexibility between these sectors. In this course you will be shown how to identify and find the relevant regulatory framework that applies to specific industries, how to comply with regulatory oversight, and how to ensure that your manufactured goods meet consumer expectations. You will be exposed to strategies and practical solutions to help meet these commercial–legal obligations, contemporary manufacturing standards, and to assure the quality and safety of pharmaceutical, therapeutic and consumer products. This course will focus on contemporary regulations applied in the Indo-Pacific and SE Asia (APEC, ASEAN) regions.
learning_outcomes: Justify and effectively communicate with other stakeholders in the pharmaceuticals and therapeutics sector.

Outline and explain the ethical obligations, OECD-mandated regulations, and rationale underpinning the regulatory requirements in the good manufacturing practice (GMP) for pharmaceuticals and therapeutics.
Provide advice on how to implement. meet and maintain Quality Management Systems, consistent and efficient product manufacture and delivery, and ensure compliance with ISO and GMP standards.
Identify, evaluate and rectify non-compliance and deviations from QMS/ISO/GMP in the manufacture of pharmaceuticals, therapeutics, and foodstuffs.

title: Work Integrated Learning in Biomedical Science
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course is an industry placement course with a focus on research and professional skills development. This course will provide an opportunity for a student to work within a setting that is an employer of biomedical science graduates.
learning_outcomes: Understand and be able to communicate the purpose and importance of the work within a wider context
Demonstrate the ability to adapt to a new environment and to take responsibility for learning within that environment
Function effectively in an industry-relevant workplace settting
Demonstrate the ability to apply knowledge and skills in biomedical science to the work
Demonstrate a professional and ethical approach to the work

title: Anatomical Pathology
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course aims to provide students with knowledge of the cellular architecture of the human body, including the ability to detect and identify structural changes associated with acute and chronic diseases. Workshops will allow students to build upon prior anatomical and physiological studies to develop an appreciation for the role of anatomical pathology in diagnosing disease states. By the end of the course students will have an understanding of the processes used in anatomical pathology to detect disease, be able to identify structural elements of the human body and detect and interpret structural abnormalities.
learning_outcomes: Outline stages of tissue preparation, from biopsy to microscopy
Demonstrate microscopic assessment of tissues prepared by standard and specialised staining techniques
Apply knowledge of anatomical pathological techniques in the diagnosis of acute and chronic disease states
Detect and interpret structural evidence for acute and chronic disease states
Describe the cellular architecture of normal tissues in healthy organs

title: Clinical Immunology and Infection
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course provides integrated learning in human infection and immunity with major focus on the techniques and approaches used to study and understand and diagnose infection- and immune-associated disorders of the human immune system that cause disease. Students will study the pathogenesis of infection-associated and immunological disorders, including bacterial and viral diseases, autoimmune and allergic diseases and inflammatory diseases of the mucosa. Immune deficiency, hypersensitivities, tumour immunology, transplantation and transfusion immune reactions will also be addressed. The course is organised as a series of modules, which include practical labs, lectures and workshops/tutorials. This course prepares students for a laboratory-based career in the study and/or diagnosis of infection- and immune-associated diseases of major importance.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate how to research topics, seek out information and solve problems in clinical immunology.
Analyse, discuss and present laboratory-based data and scientific information in written and oral form.

Demonstrate knowledge of the utilisation of contemporary biomedical and molecular techniques to diagnose and characterise immune disorders and in the development of new diagnostics and treatments for immune disorders.
Describe the pathogenesis of microbial and viral infections and apply this knowledge to the diagnosis and treatment of infectious disease.
Demonstrate practical skills necessary to conduct laboratory-based investigations in clinical immunology.
Describe, at an advanced level, human immunity and the development of immune responses.

title: Human Reproduction and Pregnancy
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course explores the biology and physiology of reproduction and pregnancy, encompassing how sperm and eggs are made; the events that result in fertilisation and conception; and how a baby develops and is born. The course will focus only on human reproduction.
learning_outcomes: Describe factors limiting human fertility, and how they can be overcome
Discuss a variety of diseases affecting human reproductive health and development
Demonstrate an in-depth understanding of the basics of reproduction including conception, contraception and fetal development
Convey complex biomedical information using language that an average non-professional can understand
Describe the endocrinology of reproduction and pregnancy
Compare male and female reproductive development in humans and describe the maturation process of both male and female gametes from early embryonic development to puberty
Describe and apply biomedical perspectives related to fertility, pregnancy, birth and perinatology including an awareness of the latest technological advances
Describe the stages of labour and discuss birth-related complications
Discuss factors contributing to abnormal fetal development
Outline placental development and function
Collaborate effectively with peers to create an educational health resource
Examine and critique current research findings relating to the topics covered in this course

title: Medical Data Management
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This advanced course is designed to introduce you to key concepts associated with the management of medical data, covering areas such as confidentiality, associated ethics and research utilising medical data within Australia. Through a series of interactive content and case studies, you will explore the infrastructure required, and processes associated with, the storage, maintenance and access of large medical data sets. Importantly, all aspects of medical data management will be considered from the perspective of under-represented populations, with students being guided to consider what constitutes an "under-represented group" and identify situations relevant to individual populations. Upon completion of this course, students will have a deep understanding of the collection, storage and access of medical data with an appreciation for the complexity surrounding data from under-represented groups.
learning_outcomes: Describe the primary infrastructure in place to record, maintain and archive medical data, and acknowledge the ownership of the medical data.

Outline the confidentiality and legal requirements associated with storing and accessing medical data, and describe the unique considerations applied to data from First Nations people and other under-represented populations.

Demonstrate knowledge of the ethical protocols, including how to locate said protocols, associated with research conducted on medical data, including the additional stages required to work with data collected from First Nations people and other under-represented populations.
Critically evaluate emerging digital technologies for remote access to, and integration of, multi-disciplinary, medical data.

title: Biomedical Sciences Honours Part A
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: The Honours Program provides students with advanced knowledge and skills in specialised areas of biomedical science and provides an introduction to research. The courses together comprise a program of approved supervised research.Candidates present a project report in the form of a thesis. The project report is also presented and defended orally. Candidates are required to submit an assignment on an approved topic and to attend seminars.
learning_outcomes: Present both written and oral summaries of the research program.
Review the literature relevant to the research specialty and an area outside the research specialty.
Carry out original research under supervision of a member of the academic staff.

Present both written and oral summaries of the research program

learning_outcomes: Review of the literature relevant to the research specialty and an area outside the research specialty.

Present both written and oral summaries of the research program.

title: Preanalytical Laboratory Medicine
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course will introduce students to the intricacies of medical science laboratories, including specimen collection and distribution through a diagnostic pathology laboratory. A major focus will be on national accreditation requirements, occupational health and safety and compliance associated with diagnostic pathology, and how these differ from non-accredited laboratories. Through engaging in workshops, students will learn about maintaining records, confidentiality and data entry of medical specimens, and further explore this learning with an introductory placement within a medical science laboratory. By the end of the course students will have a deep understanding of the functionality of a medical science laboratory, and be able to outline the processes required for accreditation of both laboratories and staff, and maintaining accurate and confidential records.
learning_outcomes: Accurately enter data into database management software to industry standards for a standard operating protocol.
Distinguish between quality assurance and quality control, and demonstrate how each would be applied in a laboratory.
Order the correct movement of pathology specimen, from collection to point of testing and describe the key elements of patient confidentiality required at each stage
Differentiate between NATA accredited and non-accredited laboratory standards and outline the key occupational health and safety requirements of each

title: Medical Microbiology
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: Throughout this course, students will develop a theoretical and practical understanding of pathogenic bacteria common to key organ systems, and the associated laboratory testing and antimicrobial therapy. Students will gain an appreciation for the appropriate collection, handling and isolating of infectious bacteria, with a focus on obtaining practical skills relevant to a diagnostic laboratory.
learning_outcomes: Interpret, troubleshoot and effectively communicate outcomes of laboratory testing for microbial samples
Accurately describe the pre-analytical requirements for the collection and transport of microbial samples, including adequate infection control
Use aseptic techniques to process common types of clinical specimens from a range of sterile and non-sterile sites, and undertake antimicrobial susceptibility testing
Understand and apply the principles of quality control and occupational safety where applicable to medical microbiology
List common pathogenic bacteria, and outline the pathogenesis of their associated infectious disease

assessment_tasks.task_name: Prepare a standard operating procedure for handling microbial samples

title: Genomic Pathology
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course focuses on the the architecture of the genome and how this is implicated in health and disease. Students will learn how these variations are detected and diagnosed in laboratory medicine, and how these laboratory results are applied to genetic epidemiology. Students will learn about existing and emerging technologies in genomic pathology, and consider their application within a multi-disciplinary diagnostic setting. By bringing together workshops, practical classes and engagement with industry, this course will allow students to develop theoretical knowledge and practical skills in the field of diagnostic genomics.
learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge of practical molecular techniques in the diagnosis of disease
Evaluate new and emerging technologies in genomic pathology
Demonstrate an in depth understanding of the association between genomic variations and health and disease
Interpret genomic diagnostic data in the context of health and disease

title: Haematology and Haemostasis
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: Throughout this course, students will learn about the cellular and non-cellular components of blood, and gain practical skills in the diagnostic tests utilised to examine clinical blood samples. Students will also obtain experience in point of care testing, and develop communication skills relevant to haematology and haemostasis.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate current and emerging point of care testing for whole blood samples
Process whole blood, including the preparation of cells, serum and plasma, and prepare and analyse blood films
Effectively communicate diagnostic results from haematological tests and reports
Understand and apply the principles of appropriate quality control of automated haematological and haemostatic analysers
Describe the elements of whole blood, including the production and physiology of each component and cell type

assessment_tasks.task_name: Complete a white blood cell differential

title: Transfusion Science
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with theoretical and practical knowledge of the major blood groups, antibody identification and screening and selection of compatible products for transfusion. Students will gain practical skills by preparing and testing samples, and develop excellent communication skills for transfusion of donated blood products.
learning_outcomes: Describe the pathophysiology of and methods used to detect adverse transfusion reactions
Describe the pathophysiology of and methods used to detect haemolytic diseases of the foetus and newborn
Outline the major blood group systems and describe the diagnostic methods used to identify them
Successfully prepare, assess and report the blood group and antibody classification for clinical samples
Apply the principles of emergency and remote transfusion to appropriate case studies
Explain the importance of accuracy and quality control in collection of and processing of blood and blood products

assessment_tasks.task_name: Case study for a remote emergency requiring transfusion

title: Clinical Chemistry
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with an understanding of the biochemistry of health and disease, and how biochemical changes are detected in a diagnostic laboratory. Students will learn the common clinical chemistry tests, explore the automated systems utilised in a diagnostic laboratory, and develop the skills required to effectively prepare and communicate clinical chemistry laboratory results.
learning_outcomes: Interpret and troubleshoot outputs from clinical chemistry analysers
List common clinical chemistry tests, and correctly describe the appropriate sample required for each test
Explain, and provide examples of, biological variations and matrix effects in common clinical chemistry tests
Understand and apply the principles of appropriate quality control of automated clinical chemistry analysers
Effectively communicate diagnostic results from clinical chemistry tests and reports

assessment_tasks.task_name: Interpret outputs from clinical chemistry analysers

title: Advanced Haematology & Haemostasis
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This advanced course outlines inherited and malignant haematological diseases, and diseases arising from disordered haemostasis. Students will learn the underlying pathophysiology of these disorders, with a focus on the associated genomic and epigenetic variants and appropriate diagnostic tests. This course presents cutting edge technologies through a series of interactive workshops and laboratory classes. Students will be equipped with the knowledge and foundational skills required to undertake laboratory testing, and effectively communicate clinical reports to facilitate diagnosis.
learning_outcomes: Describe the laboratory tests required to diagnose malignant and inherited haematological disorders, and correctly identify the samples required for these tests.
Critically evaluate innovative research in the field of haematology and haemostasis
Identify key haematological diseases driven by changes in genomics and epigenetics
Successfully prepare haematological samples for further testing

assessment_tasks.task_name: Case study presentation of laboratory results

title: Histotechnology
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course focuses on the processes involved in preparing tissue for microscopic examination. Students will learn the underlying principles, and develop technical skills required for non-surgical cut-up, fixation, tissue processing, embedding and sectioning. Students will also gain knowledge in the principles of staining and immunohistochemistry.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the relevance of various types of histology and cytology staining and immunohistochemistry techniques, and accurately describe their use in a modern medical laboratory
Identify biopsies and samples of a wide variety of tissues, and accurately describe the appropriate fixation requirements.
Apply knowledge of tissue processing, embedding and sectioning techniques to a range of tissue biopsies
Competently use a microscope to distinguish between various tissue types and staining techniques

assessment_tasks.task_name: Demonstrate adequate tissue embedding and microtomy
Presentation of a case study following a biopsy from collection to final reporting
Utilise microscopy to distinguish between differently stained tissue

title: Advanced Medical Microbiology
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This advanced course outlines the communication, infection and pathogenesis associated with medically important viruses, parasite and fungi. Students will learn the relevant methodologies for each microbial agent, including current and emerging technologies. This course presents cutting edge technologies through a series of interactive workshops and laboratory classes. Students will be equipped with the knowledge and foundational skills required to participate in specialist medical microbiology laboratories.
learning_outcomes: Describe and justify the use of molecular assessment of microbial agents
Critically evaluate innovative research in medical microbiology
Differentiate between diagnostic techniques associated with virology. parasitology and mycology
Identify and outline diagnostic serological assays associated with infectious disease
Prepare microbial samples for further testing, and analyse and report results of these tests

assessment_tasks.task_name: Prepare a methods paper for molecular assessment of microbial agents

title: Laboratory Medicine Placement A
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: In this course, students will complete a supervised placement based around the knowledge they have gained in laboratory medicine. Students will explore the skills outlined within the Australian Institute of Medical and Clinical Scientists (AIMS) Competency-based Standards for Medical Scientists, and critically evaluate their placement based on these Standards.
learning_outcomes: 1. Demonstrate an understanding of the AIMS Competency-based Standards for Medical Scientists within the workplace.
2. Demonstrate the practical knowledge and technical skills required to operate in a medical science laboratory
3. Apply analytical and technical skills to prepare reports to the standard required in a medical science laboratory.

title: Laboratory Medicine Placement B
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: In this course, students will complete a supervised placement based around the knowledge they have gained in laboratory medicine. Students will follow the journey of a sample from collection to report, and develop effective communication strategies required for reporting clinical results.
learning_outcomes: 2. Generate and communicate clinical reports from technical data obtained in a medical science laboratory.
1. Identify key roles and responsibilities of AIMS-accredited Medical Scientists within medical laboratories.
3. Effectively communicate clinical results in both oral and written format.

title: Laboratory Medicine Placement C
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: In this course, students will complete a supervised placement based around the knowledge they have gained in laboratory medicine. In this final placement course, students will have the opportunity to prepare themselves for employment by developing a curriculum vitae (CV) and a relevant job application.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the ability to prepare an effective application for a medical scientist position, and reflect on key skills that align with the requirements of employment as a medical scientist
Demonstrate capacity to work safely and effectively in a medical science laboratory environment
Provide examples of appropriate quality control practices in a medical science laboratory

title: Research in Laboratory Medicine 1 Part A
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: The Research in Laboratory Medicine Program provides students with advanced knowledge and skills in specialised areas of laboratory medicine and provides an introduction to research. The courses together comprise a program of approved supervised research, undertaken within a research team affiliated with the University of Newcastle. Students will develop skills in reviewing current scientific literature and synthesising research proposals. This suite of Research in Laboratory Medicine courses will provide students the opportunity to design and conduct research protocols and collate research data utilising cutting edge platforms. Upon completion, students will have extensive experience in medical laboratory research, including high level communication skills in both oral and written presentation of data.
learning_outcomes: Propose original research under supervision of a member of the academic staff
Present both written and oral summaries of the research problem
Review the literature relevant to the research specialty and an area outside the research specialty

integrate independent research with relevant existing literature
present the findings of independent research using both oral and written communication

title: Global Experiences
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course enables you to undertake a pre-approved global experience while gaining credit towards your degree. It also allows you to add an international dimension to your profile and put the skills and knowledge acquired during your studies to the test in an overseas setting. Experiences include international study tours, virtual and physical internships, in-country language programs, international short courses, summer schools, and volunteering for international NGOs or community projects. Students can plan their own experience or choose between a range of pre-approved options advertised on the course website. Experiences should be equivalent to 80-100 hours of full-time study. Enrolling in the Midyear Session allows you to undertake a global experience at any point between 1 March and 30 August, while students completing overseas activities between 1 September and 28 February can enrol in either the Semester 2 or (preferred option after 11 September 2026) the Global Experience Term offering. For more information, please see the HUMA2001 webpage
learning_outcomes: Apply skills and knowledge obtained in their degree studies in an international setting
Demonstrate appropriate knowledge of the international location
Organise a successful international experience
Effectively communicate their global experience across different media and formats

title: Local Placements
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course enables students to undertake a placement with a local/regional employer while gaining credit towards their degree. It connects the world of university study to the workplace, enabling students to acquire new skills and networks while also putting the skills and knowledge they have acquired in their studies to the test in an authentic setting. The course provides a practical platform for students to develop areas of study into careers. Students can organise their own placement or apply for one of the pre-defined roles listed on the HUMA2000 webpage.
learning_outcomes: Apply skills and knowledge obtained in their degree studies in the workplace.
Effectively communicate their placement experiences.
Demonstrate understanding of the local career pathways available for Bachelor of Arts graduates.
