present the findings of independent research using both oral and written communication
conduct research in laboratory medicine under supervision of an academic staff member

title: Auslan Language and Culture Beginners 1
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course is a starting point for you to learn Australian Sign language (Auslan). You will become aware of the deaf and hard of hearing community and its culture. No prior knowledge of Auslan or contact with deaf people is assumed. You will learn fingerspelling and signs, and by the completion of the course you will be able to participate in short dialogues. You will also investigate elements of Auslan linguistics and explore issues related to Deaf culture, community and history.
learning_outcomes: Recognise and respond effectively to Auslan vocabulary and grammatical constructions in simple everyday situations.
Identify and describe issues affecting Australian Deaf Community, Culture and history.
Identify and apply appropriate linguistic elements of Auslan.
Produce and deliver a range of accurate Auslan vocabulary and grammatical constructions in simple everyday situations.

title: Introduction to Human Services
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course provides an overview of the human services sector and the role of the human service worker within it. It examines macro and micro level influences on the historical developments of the Australian Welfare State and service delivery models. It explores the knowledge, skills and values required of the human services worker in dealing with a range of complex social issues. It highlights the structural disadvantage of many service users and explores progressive approaches to human service practice. It covers the theories and knowledge that underpin different types of practice undertaken by human service workers and establishes the importance of ethical and professional standards in practice.
learning_outcomes: Apply, at an introductory level, distinct practice approaches that might be used in human services with individuals, groups and communities.
Identify key aspects of the human services sector including: its history and social context; forms of practice; the influence of beliefs, values, attitudes, ethics and practice standards.
Apply introductory level reflective strategies to their experiences in order to extend learning about human services and their personal response to the content.
Describe the social conditions experienced by one or more groups of people in Australia and human services responses to these groups.

title: Auslan Language and Culture Beginners 2
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course provides continuing study of Australian Sign Language (Auslan), building on the foundations provided in HUMA2070 Auslan 1. You will expand your ability to use Auslan in a variety of forms and settings. You will also continue to investigate elements of Auslan structure in greater detail and further explore issues related to accessibility that impact Deaf people.
learning_outcomes: Explain key accessibility issues affecting the Australian Deaf community.
Recognise and apply basic linguistic features of Auslan and frequently used expressions.
Develop basic conversational skills in Auslan on familiar topics in various situations.
Utilise basic receptive Auslan skills to understand familiar topics in various situations.

title: Shaping Human Services: Social Policy and the Political Process
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course examines key dimensions of social policy and policy-making, particularly the understanding of social policy as a political process. It looks at the influential and competing ideas that have underpinned the historical and contemporary development of the role of the state in social policy; the links between ideas and sectional 'interests'; the wider factors that drive social policy change; and the distributional consequences of policy change. It examines the role of political actors and governmental institutional architecture in forging the content of social policy and programs and explores the extent to which administrators and practitioners can modify policy in program delivery.
learning_outcomes: Identify policy within a field of human services
Analyse the main ideas and values underlying policy
Critique the role of government and governance institutions in mediating policy formation
Demonstrate an understanding of the welfare system and its stakeholders
Assess and examine the impact of policy on workers, service users and other sections of the population

title: Gendered Violence
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course examines the policies, practices, people and institutions involved with gendered violence and places issues of gendered violence within a social and political context. It explores the response of state institutions to gendered violence through an examination of the process of policy development and implementation, and practice methods utilised by various agencies including the police, the courts, refuges and prevention programs.
learning_outcomes: Outline and analyse the issues in defining gendered violence
Identify and critique current definitions and understandings of the effect of gendered violence
Assess state policy responses to gendered violence, including the assumptions, values and decision-making processes involved
Describe the various state interventions in the lives of those experiencing violence, including the social and historical origins of these interventions
Evaluate the adequacy of local service networks for responding to gendered violence

title: Person-centered practice and casework skills
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course prepares students for working with individuals and families across a range of human services. It focuses on person-centred and strengths-based approaches to casework - collaborating with, supporting and coordinating services for, people with multiple and often complex needs. Drawing on theory and practice models, emphasis is given to developing an empowering and anti-oppressive strategy to working with people as partners, and fellow stakeholders in the community.
learning_outcomes: Discuss critically the use of casework in contemporary human services, including the role and influence of the state on this form of practice.
Reflect critically on experiences in the course to extend learning.
Apply specific strategies and skills to a fictional case study to demonstrate application of person-centred practice principles.
Distinguish between different casework approaches and identify a personally preferred practice model based on values, beliefs, aims and context.

title: Child Protection Work
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course covers the knowledge and skills required to practice in services that form part of child protection services such as: prevention and early intervention services; tertiary and statutory agency work; domestic violence services; health services; and the family law system. It introduces students to: explanatory theories; definitions and effects of child abuse and neglect; examining assessment; risk of harm and responding to child abuse; out of home care systems; outcomes and effectiveness; working with Indigenous families; and practice frameworks. Issues of child protection are placed in a social and political context and the impact of class, gender and ethnicity are highlighted in terms of the process of policy development, implementation and practice frameworks.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the complex and multi-layered issues involved in defining child abuse and neglect
Demonstrate an understanding of the effects of child abuse
Identify and critique types, purposes and effectiveness of services (early to late intervention) available in the local area for responding to child welfare
Evaluate current perspectives on the effects of child abuse
Describe and critique the social, political and cultural context of responses to child abuse

assessment_tasks.task_name: In class discussion - response to scenario
History and definition of child abuse

title: Youth Justice
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course examines the theories, processes, practices, people and institutions involved in the Australian youth justice system. It explores the social and political context of youth justice issues and highlights the impact of class, gender and ethnicity on young people who encounter the youth justice system and its representatives. It covers the experiences of First Nations youth, ethnic youth, young women, and young people with difficult behaviours within the system of juvenile justice. The course will cover the way policy and practice interact in context by analysing a range of areas including the role of youth/corrections workers, youth conferencing, the courts and the diversion of young offenders.
learning_outcomes: Critique the different theoretical positions and models of youth justice
Explain and critique the role and impact of the courts, media and police in the diversion of young offenders
Demonstrate knowledge of current policies, service delivery systems, and programs directed at young people
Communicate an understanding of the history, processes and contemporary dimensions of youth justice
Analyse and critique human service practice approaches with young people in youth justice settings

title: Essential Community Services: Disability and Aged Care
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course will provide an overview of policy trends and practice issues in the field of disability and aged care services, with a focus on material relevant to roles undertaken by human service staff with a social science and community welfare background. It will highlight developments in policy and practice philosophy in these two fields, at a time of rapid growth in disability and aged care services and employment opportunities. The course will emphasise high care disability services and services oriented to the frail aged
learning_outcomes: Evaluate key policy and funding trends in the disability and aged care sectors and their implications for practice.
Identify key shifts in the conceptual understanding, sociology, demographics and politics of disability and ageing.
Identify and analyse key skills and challenges relevant to working in disability and aged care services.
Demonstrate an understanding of the interaction between policy and practice in a disability or aged care setting.
Appraise methods of practice in the disability field for their effects on professionals and service users.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Major essay, policy or literature analysis

title: Working with Groups and Communities
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the theories and practices of community development and group work within the context of human service agency practice. It examines community development and group work approaches to social issues and social problems within Australia. This course shifts the focus from people as clients to people as community and group members and citizens, who can and should have the capacity to act on issues collectively and speak out about issues that affect them. Working collaboratively and effectively with communities, service users, colleagues and teams are key skills in human service practice particularly when working across diverse settings with vulnerable and marginalised groups. This course provides a platform for developing and integrating knowledge and skills necessary for effective group and team practice. Community development and group work are explored as empowering strategies, grounded in the notion that people with common experiences, issues or problems, can gain some control over their lives through collective action.
learning_outcomes: Implement the theory and practice of community development and group work as approaches to social issues and social problems
Demonstrate a critical understanding of the philosophy, policies and practice of community development based on concepts of community care and group work
Demonstrate advanced knowledge of community consultation and participation structures and practices
Display small and large group process skills and related expertise
Apply knowledge and advanced skills in the identification of community and group needs associated with social issues

assessment_tasks.task_name: Written analysis of group work activity - summative

title: Human Rights, Social Justice and Real Lives
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course examines the value of human rights as instruments for achieving social justice. It recognises the contribution of, and critiques, human rights from a range of theoretical perspectives. It considers the ways in which human rights shape, and are shaped by, people and communities at global and local levels. The course engages with key debates and emerging challenges in human rights discourse and encourages students to critique their own worldviews. In this course students will explore the ways in which they might apply their emerging skills and knowledge to contribute to social justice at local and international levels via activism, advocacy, policymaking and practice.
learning_outcomes: Identify and communicate the theoretical foundations and challenges to the concepts of human rights and social justice.
Analyse the ways in which international human rights conventions impact national social policies, diverse global communities and individual lives.
Assess the extent to which particular examples of social policies are consistent with or violate principles of human rights.
Develop responses, informed by human rights principles, which work towards more socially just outcomes for users of human services.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Group role play and individual written reflection

title: Social Policy and Planning in Regional Contexts
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course examines how place-based social planning is influenced by wider social policy and how it interacts with community engagement at the regional and local level. Students will develop knowledge and skills in social planning techniques and practices and will explore aspects including locational disadvantage, community development and the relation to other professions, and the relevance of ecological sustainability to the social services sector
learning_outcomes: Distinguish between different levels of government and their responsibilities in relation to social policy and planning at a regional level.
Reflect on experience in this course to extend learning.

Research and then communicate the current circumstances of different groups of people in a specific location and the impact of regional social policy and planning on human services responses to these people.
Describe key concepts related to regional social policy and planning and show their relevance to human services concerns and purposes.
Use research and analysis to participate in community engagement or lobbying in relation to a location-specific social issue. environmental quality, political processes and cultural experience

title: Human Services from the user perspective
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course centres on the knowledge, views and experiences of people who use human services. Students will consider the diversity, complexity and strengths of individuals’ lives and what this means in relation to human services practices, policies and politics. In this course service users provide opportunities for students to think deeply about the role and methods of human services when working with Indigenous and non-indigenous people from various equity groups, as well as providing tools that can facilitate ongoing critically reflective practice. Students learn how professionals may need to be good recipients of challenging communication. Interwoven with lived experience knowledge, the course provides historical context, including the consumer movement and the change from providing services to as opposed to providing services with. The course draws together many threads of critical Human Services teaching including theoretical debates about terminology (client/consumers); rights-based access to services; the marketisation of services; peer work and user-lead services. Central to the course is the theme of equity, inclusion and diversity (EID).
learning_outcomes: Integrate service user perspectives with theoretical perspectives and practice approaches to answer 'how can this understanding inform my approach to human services?'
Demonstrate a capacity to listen to, engage with and be informed by the perspectives of service users.
Identify the tensions and alignments in practitioner and service user perspectives on human services

title: Managing International Business Risk
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Global companies continually face an increasing variety of business, political, economic and security risks that can directly impact both operation and profit. This course identifies and analyses the multi-level risk environments facing today's global businesses and investigates strategies to identify, assess, manage and mitigate international and geopolitical risk. Focusing upon multinational enterprise and expropriation; sovereign risk and corruption; political and regulatory risk; brand and corporate reputation risk; financial and economic risk; risk from NGOs; consumer, human right and protest group risks; and terrorism risk, students investigate the various analytical approaches involved in designing risk identification systems, reporting and monitoring protocols, and how risk is able to be assessed, prioritized and effectively managed.
learning_outcomes: Explain and apply risk management frameworks when operating in global business environments.
Communicate an awareness of the political, economic, social and cultural factors which influence international business operations in written form.
Illustrate an awareness of ethical issues in international business.
Identify and explain theories of risk and risk management in international business environments.

title: International Trade Logistics in a Digital Age
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course introduces you to practical operational issues in International Trade Logistics in the era of digital trade and advanced technologies. The focus is on problem solving and appreciation of contemporary issues in International Trade Logistics in the digital age. Through the analysis of case reports and the exploration of cutting-edge technologies, you will develop a comprehensive understanding of international logistics operations and process design, with a particular focus on the transformative impact of digital trade Group work is employed to enhance knowledge and skills in analysis, problem solving, and team work.
learning_outcomes: Explain international trade logistics operations and process designs in a digital era.
Apply valid academic information to analyse and solve problems in international trade logistics in a Digital World.
Evaluate contemporary issues in international trade logistics.
Collaborate with peers to produce an analysis of an international trade logistics case study.

title: Cross-Cultural Management and Negotiations
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: National as well as organisational culture plays an important role in managerial effectiveness and business performance of firms engaged in cross-border operations. The theory and practice of management and negotiation in a cross-cultural international context are examined with models of cross-cultural management critiqued and applied to contemporary business cases. The challenges of operating international business relationships with diverse workforces are critically analysed. Course topics include understanding decision-making and sense-making by managers in terms of their mental models; organising and managing diverse teams; conflict management and negotiations; understanding cultural differences; and mapping institutional differences across countries. Focus is directed upon cross-country and cross-institutional negotiations; leadership types; and the concept of 'global managers'. Adopting a problem-based learning approach using relevant cases and experiences, the course emphasises the importance of communication as an essential attribute and provides practical examples of cross-cultural negotiation in relevant business environments.
learning_outcomes: Collaborate effectively with team members during case analysis and negotiation simulations.
Reflect critically on negotiation performance, strategy and tactics using relevant theories and concepts.
Apply strategic thinking and conduct strategic analysis of business opportunities across cultural environments.
Analyse ethical, social, and cultural issues that shape cross cultural management and negotiation practices.
Apply and reflect upon analytical and theoretical frameworks in cross cultural settings.
Identify the key issues raised by international business cases in cross cultural management and negotiations.

title: Managing International Business
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Understanding the international environment is critical to ensuring that businesses remain productive, resilient and innovative. In this course, students will be exposed to the frameworks and theories necessary for assessing opportunities, managing challenges and capturing value for organisations engaging in international business. Particularly, the course explores economic, political, and social factors at national, regional and global levels and their implications for the internationalisation of firms. Students will explore the range of strategies available for firms to compete more effectively globally and apply international business theories and frameworks to solve real-life problems faced by global business manager
learning_outcomes: Apply the core principles of contemporary international business theory to real-life international business problems.
Identify ethical issues in international business.
Analyse key decisions made by multinational firms regarding market choice, market entry strategy, global business organisation and people management.
Evaluate political, economic, social and cultural environments at country level and supernational institutions for international business.
Describe the risks and opportunities presented by globalisation for international business.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Case Study Report and Board of Directors Consultation

title: Corporate Social Responsibility for Global Business
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: The interconnectedness of economic, political, ecological, and social spheres of human activity is undeniable in our complex world. These realms are intertwined and have profound impacts on one another. To address contemporary business problems effectively, it is imperative to apply ethical and sustainable frameworks that take into account this interconnectedness. This course is designed to equip students with the knowledge and skills necessary to address non-financial spheres of human activity within the international business context. By delving into ethical issues, ethical decision-making, and sustainability considerations, students will be better prepared to make informed, responsible, and ethical business decisions. Ultimately, this course aims to produce future business leaders who are not only financially savvy but also socially and environmentally conscious, contributing to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
learning_outcomes: Explain how the business world can contribute to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
Critically reflect on personal values, practices and role as a potential agent of positive change.
Identify the key features of corporate social and environmental responsibility.
Apply ethical and sustainability frameworks to contemporary business problems.
Discuss the interconnectedness of the economic, political, ecological and social spheres of human activity.

title: International Business Alliances
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: The formation and implementation of successful global business strategies involves alliances with a range of stakeholders including international customers and suppliers, overseas agents, international franchisors and franchisees, international joint venture partners, and international merger relationships. The aim of this unit of study is to provide conceptual frameworks and evidence from practice that will develop an understanding of the motivations underlying international alliances, the alternative approaches to alliance formulation and development, and the problems involved in promoting effective alliance management.
learning_outcomes: Apply and integrate international business alliance knowledge, concepts, and principles in a range of business contexts.
Identify, analyse, and solve business challenges reaching conclusions using fundamental concepts, principles, and knowledge from international business alliances.
Effectively contribute to a team-based project.
Explain the need for, locate and evaluate business information.

title: International Human Resource Management
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course aims to develop a critical understanding of the role and functions of the various human resource activities within multinational corporations (MNCs). It provides an overview of the impact of globalisation and varieties of capitalism in shaping international human resource management practices in MNCs. The course addresses the literature in International Human Resource Management and the strategic management of human resources in MNCs by drawing on case studies and selected readings.
learning_outcomes: Asses the effectiveness of human resource management systems within the context of international organisations by drawing on relevant literature to form a cohesive argument.
Evaluate the impact of cultural, ethical and global factors in shaping human resource practices in multinational corporations.
Describe the role of the Human Resources Manager and Human Resource activities in an international context.
Utilise concepts, models and theories to demonstrate the differences between domestic and international Human Resource Management.
Explain the importance of cultural sensitivity in a contemporary international business case.

title: International Business Strategy
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course analyses how multinational firms leverage their capabilities and competencies to create competitive advantage in international and global markets. A key purpose is to understand how managers design and implement international business strategies. Informed by an integrated knowledge of international business, political and cultural interaction, students develop the valued attributes of inquiry, team processes and communication to form international business strategies.
learning_outcomes: Identify the key business, political and social issues raised by international business strategy.
Explain how national and international economic, political, legal and institutions impact international business strategy.
Think critically about underlying theories, concepts, assumptions and arguments in international business strategic management.
Work collaboratively to analyse international business strategies, reflect upon, and communicate the implications for international business strategy.

title: Foundations of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview: This course provides an opportunity for students to enhance their knowledge of historical and contemporary issues relevant to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. This course will explore the tenets of culturally capable and safe health practice and its development by exploring the dynamics between Australia's health practice and contemporary social and healthcare policies, and the current health status for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.
learning_outcomes: Outline the principles of ethical research when working with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities.

Explore the relationship between Australia's history of colonisation, relevant social and healthcare policy and the multiplicity of experiences of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples including health status and life expectancy.
Discuss strategies that hold the potential to improve the burden of illness and life expectancy for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people.
Discuss Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples history, cultural identity, beliefs and values with a particular focus on the burden of disease.
Identify key social determinants of health and their trends for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people including access, funding, housing, employment, infrastructure and education.

Describe the principles of cultural capability and cultural safety in order to provide culturally competent health care to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. This must include identifying the impact of racism and effective communication strategies.
Examine and reflect on their personal lens and potential biases about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people.
Identify and discuss ways of redressing health care inequities including the burden of illness for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Reflections based on Case study Part A and Part B
Case study - Part A and Part B

title: International Business in Emerging Markets
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Emerging markets are rapidly changing the global business landscape as they present tremendous growth opportunities. The rise of emerging economies as a new competitive force has strategic implications for global managers. This unit focuses on emerging markets to develop understanding and strategic tools to succeed in the emerging global competitive environment.
learning_outcomes: Choose strategies to leverage emerging markets for international business and communicate these in a group presentation.
Construct concise strategy analysis reports.
Apply concepts and theoretical frameworks covered in this unit to formulate strategies to leverage emerging markets for international business.
Evaluate and interpret information to identify relevant issues and new business opportunities for international managers in emerging markets.

title: Foundations of Nursing Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview: This course provides an opportunity for nursing students to enhance their knowledge of historical and contemporary issues relevant to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people. This course will explore the tenets of culturally capable nursing practice and its development by exploring the dynamics between Australia's historical and contemporary social and healthcare policies, and the current health status for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate and apply culturally responsive communication strategies and health promotion approaches into professional practice to improve health outcomes for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.
Critically analyse Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples’ histories, cultural identities, and values in relation to colonisation, health and social policy, and the burden of disease.
Engage in critical self-reflection to recognise and address personal biases, assumptions, and positionality to provide culturally responsive care.
Evaluate and apply ethical research practices that uphold Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultural integrity, self-determination, and community-led decision-making.
Apply culturally safe and trauma-informed practices, including evidence-informed anti-racism strategies, to deliver equitable nursing and midwifery care.

Evaluate and synthesize evidence on the social and cultural determinants of health and identify strategies to reduce health inequities and improve health outcomes for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.

title: Foundations of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Midwifery Care
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview: This course contributes to the overall aims of the Bachelor of Midwifery program by developing an understanding of woman centred cultural competent care for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people with a particular practice focus on childbearing women and their families. The content in this course includes an examination of historical and contemporary issues which assist the development of an understanding of the socio-historical context of life for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, and the provision of culturally safe midwifery services.
learning_outcomes: Identify and discuss barriers to adequate health care, and inequities including the burden of illness for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women and babies.

Critically analyse the historical relationship between Australia's history of colonisation, and social and healthcare policies relating to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples health status and life expectancy.
Examine and reflect on your personal lens and potential biases about Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people.

Critically analyse and discuss culturally safe continuity models of midwifery care that focus on the needs of the women and her family in the following contexts: Preconception and conception, Pregnancy, Birth, Postnatal care of the woman and neonate.
Identify key social determinants of health and their trends for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people including access, funding, housing, employment, infrastructure, and education.
Discuss Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples' history, cultural identity, beliefs and values with a particular focus on health and wellbeing.
Investigate historical and contemporary issues relating to women's business about birthing and mothering.

Describe the principles of cultural competence and cultural safety in order to provide culturally competent midwifery care to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women and families. This must include identifying the impact of racism and effective communication strategies.

title: Working with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Childbearing Women
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview: This course contributes to the overall aims of the Master of Midwifery (Graduate Entry) program by developing an understanding of woman centred culturally capable care for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people with a particular practice focus on childbearing women and their families. The content in this course includes an examination of historical and contemporary issues which assist the development of an understanding of the socio-historical context of life for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, and the provision of culturally safe midwifery services.
learning_outcomes: critically analyse culturally safe continuity models of midwifery care that focus on the needs of the women and her family
discuss the impact of racism in the Australian health system on the health and wellbeing of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
clearly articulate the barriers to adequate health care, equality and equity for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander women and babies
critically analyse the historical relationship between Australia's history of colonisation, and social and healthcare policies relating to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
demonstrate deep understandings of the multi-factorial issues affecting current health outcomes for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
investigate historical and contemporary issues relating to women's business about birthing and mothering

title: Investigating Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Health in the public health context
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview: This course will deepen your understanding of cultural, psychosocial and other determinants of health outcomes for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples. You will explore the different methods of assessing health and the acceptability of these approaches to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health prevention and intervention strategies will be investigated in terms of changing patterns of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health. This course will strengthen the work you do, not only with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples, but with all populations moving forward.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate ethical research and methodology with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities.
Apply the principles of co-designing, implementing and evaluating culturally appropriate health programs and health promotion for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander patients.

Identify and explain the impacts of colonisation, racism and the implementation of government policies and programs have had on health and cultural determinants of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.
Develop a knowledge of services, programs and resources for Aboriginal patients including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islanderâ€¯community-controlledâ€¯health services.â€¯

Critically reflect on your own culture, beliefs and biases, your life experience and professional practice and how these interplay with your current and future relationships with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.

title: Indonesian Language and Culture Beginners 1 (A0 to A1.1)
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course is designed for students with little or no previous knowledge of Indonesian, formerly known as Bahasa Indonesia. It provides beginners with a basic level of communicative competence in Indonesian language and culture.
learning_outcomes: Participate competently in every day social conversation in Indonesian within a range of topics covered.
Read and respond to simple authentic Indonesian language sources.
Demonstrate and apply a basic understanding of the grammatical system of Indonesian language.
Demonstrate an understanding of many fundamental aspects of Indonesian cultures and compare these to Australian thinking and practices.
Participate competently in pair and group interaction in Indonesian.
Write basic compositions in Indonesian.

assessment_tasks.task_name: 1 x written response to set task

title: Indonesian Language and Culture Beginners 2 (A1.1 to A1.2)
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: A course in late-beginning level Indonesian
learning_outcomes: Participate competently in pair and group interaction in Indonesian.
Participate competently in everyday social conversation in Indonesian within the range of topics covered.
Demonstrate an increased understanding of many fundamental aspects of Indonesian cultures and compare these to Australian thinking and practices.
Read and respond to authentic Indonesian language sources.
Demonstrate and apply an increased elementary understanding of the grammatical system of Indonesian language.
Write elementary compositions in Indonesian.

assessment_tasks.task_name: 1 x written response to set task

title: Indonesian Language and Culture Elementary 1 (A1.2 to A2.1)
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: A course in early-intermediate level Indonesian
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate and apply an early intermediate understanding of the grammatical system of Indonesian language.
Participate competently in everyday social conversation in Indonesian within the range of topics covered.
Demonstrate an early intermediate understanding of many fundamental aspects of Indonesian cultures and compare these to Australian thinking and practices.
Write developed compositions in Indonesian.
Read and respond to authentic Indonesian language sources.
Participate competently in pair and group interaction in Indonesian.

title: Database Management 1
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Information and Physical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Modern enterprises depend on the effective storage and management of data. Organisational data is essential not only for daily operations but also for building knowledge repositories that support long-term learning and strategic planning. Well-structured corporate data systems form the foundation for informed decision-making and provide a sustainable competitive advantage. This course introduces the fundamental concepts of databases and database systems, alongside their practical implementation through elementary programming skills. Students will learn the principles of information storage and management, beginning with the conceptual modelling of organisational data requirements using the relational model. These concepts are then extended to implementation techniques such as SQL programming and relational normalisation. The course also addresses practical challenges in database systems, including issues of security, transaction management, and concurrency control.
learning_outcomes: Design and implement physical database based on logical database representation.
Create, query, and maintain databases in SQL for real-world applications.
Master fundamental relational database concepts including entity relationship diagrams, data normalisation and relational operators.
Explicate system implementation issues such as data views, data independence, indexing, security and transaction management.
Design, develop and implement a mid-scale relational databases for an application domain using a commercial-grade Relational Database Management System (RDBMS).

assessment_tasks.task_name: Practical Test - Lab test on SQL
Assignment 3 - Database Project - Physical Database Design
Assignment 2 - Database Project - Logical Database Design
Assignment 1 - Database Project - Description and EER model

title: Indonesian Language and Culture Elementary 2 (A2.1 to A2.2)
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: A course in late-intermediate level Indonesian
learning_outcomes: Read and respond to more complex authentic Indonesian language sources.
Demonstrate a late intermediate understanding of many fundamental aspects of Indonesian cultures and compare these to Australian thinking and practices.
Participate competently in everyday social conversation in Indonesian within the range of topics covered.
Demonstrate and apply a late intermediate understanding of the grammatical system of Indonesian language.
Participate competently in pair and group interaction in Indonesian.
Write well developed compositions in Indonesian.

title: Business Intelligence for the Enterprise
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: Business intelligence (BI) is an umbrella term that combines architectures, tools, databases, analytical tools, applications and methodologies. The major objectives of business intelligence are to enable interactive access to data and to give business managers the ability to conduct analysis and make better decisions. The course covers how to design, implement and integrate business intelligence techniques and systems into the enterprise.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the use of BI for supporting decision making in an enterprise.
Describe the concepts and components of Business Intelligence and how they are relevant to an enterprise.
Describe and use the technologies, applications, tools and methodologies that make up Business Intelligence.
Demonstrate an understanding of the technological architecture that underpins BI systems in an enterprise.
Conceptually implement parts of a BI enterprise system.

title: Systems Analysis and Design
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: The course covers the development of information systems and of their software components. Whilst the course introduces students to the whole systems development process, it focuses on the elicitation and initial modelling of information systems requirements that enable identification of information problems and the subsequent analysis and modelling of an efficient solution to those problems. The approach follows the object-oriented (OO) methods expressed by the Unified Process software development life-cycle. The course addresses the complete methodology of the Unified Process, including its methodological deliverables and models and tools, with exposure to manual and automated diagramming and modelling techniques. It critically examines the issues and professional responsibilities that need to be considered at different phases in the development of information systems for an organization; including the impact of the systems on intended users and maintenance of quality. Students gain experience in requirements elicitation and modelling and systems analysis and feasibility estimation within a system development project setting aimed at developing an event-driven information system. They also gain practical experience in the use of a CASE tool to produce object and class definitions and to create models.
learning_outcomes: Experience in developing information systems models;
Experience in developing systems project documentation;
An understanding of the ways in which an analyst's interaction with system sponsors and users play a part in information systems development;
A firm basis for understanding the life cycle of a systems development project;
An understanding of the object-oriented methods models as covered by the Unified Modelling Language.
An understanding of the analysis and development techniques required as a team member of a medium-scale information systems development project;

title: Database Management 2
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with theoretical knowledge and practical skills in modern database systems and data-intensive applications. It covers conceptual and logical database design, SQL and its procedural extensions, storage structures, indexing and query optimisation, transaction and concurrency management, and Object Relational Mapping. Contemporary topics such as OLAP, data warehousing, datamarts, business intelligence, data mining, and big data and distributed databases are also discussed.
learning_outcomes: Analyse architecture and applications of big data, parallel, and distributed databases in modern information systems.
Apply concepts of data warehousing, datamarts, and OLAP for analytical data processing and decision support.
Design, implement, and manage relational databases using EER modelling, normalisation, advanced SQL, and object–relational mapping.
Apply advanced business intelligence and data mining techniques to derive insights from structured data.
Apply storage, indexing, query processing, and optimisation techniques to improve the performance of database systems.
Apply transaction, concurrency, and crash-recovery management techniques to ensure data integrity and consistency.
Work effectively in teams and communicate professionally when working on database development.

title: Introduction to Programming
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Information and Physical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course introduces the key skills of problem solving and computer programming, including the elementary programming concepts of documentation, data elements, sequence, selection, and iteration.
learning_outcomes: Comprehend the concepts of programming;
Analyse a programming problem and design a solution;
Code a solution to a problem;
Test and document program solutions.

title: Systems and Network Administration
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Information and Physical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the foundational concepts and experience in networking and systems administration. The course provides the basic theory, concepts and practical experience in the design, installation and configuration of personal computers, peer-to-peer networks and client-server networks meeting user requirements.
learning_outcomes: Develop an IP addressing scheme for a given scenario.
Configure a peer-to-peer network to share resources.
Configure an IP addressing schemes for a given scenario.
Develop a design for a local area network for a given scenario.
Describe network communication methods and protocols.
Develop a design and configure a client-server network and required network services for a given scenario.
Develop and present a design for a peer-to-peer networks to share resources.

title: Cybersecurity Fundamentals
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: In this course, you will develop an in-depth introduction to cyber security suitable for all domains of study. You will explore the fundamentals of security, privacy and risk, including core principles, cyber security controls and technologies, policies, procedures, and best practices. Through real world case study examination and assessment based on organisational-focused cyber security frameworks, you will develop a foundational knowledge base in cyber security that can be leveraged and built upon in both academia and industry.
learning_outcomes: Describe how Cyber Security policy and procedure mechanisms support organisations.
Identify Cyber Security threats and risks in accordance with organisational processes.
Identify technologies for managing cyber security risks.
Explore legal, ethical, and professional issues in the context of Cyber Security.
Apply introductory Cyber Security skills from the perspective of different stakeholders.

title: Application Programming
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Information and Physical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Continues the development of programming concepts and skills that was begun in INFT1004 Introduction to Programming. A different programming language is used, broadening the students' experience. Students' understanding of problem solving and of program design, implementation, and testing will be reinforced and extended, with the development of applications more advanced than those in INFT1004.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate advanced application programming skills.
Understand the role of computer programming in information technology applications for solving problems within organisations;
Select the appropriate language, and algorithm for a given task;
Create programming applications in a different language from that used in INFT1004.

title: Mobile Application Programming
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course builds on students’ basic programming skills to develop the knowledge and skills used to develop applications utilising touch interfaces, mobile platforms and event-driven programming.
learning_outcomes: Apply their knowledge of effective mobile app design and demonstrate their understanding of the challenges of implementing these designs
Design and develop a robust, aesthetic, and intuitive user-interface that applies the concepts of touch-driven applications
Organise and plan the development of mobile applications for deployment on mobile technologies
Implement and deploy robust mobile apps to a mobile device using iterative development and testing methodologies

title: Applied Artificial Intelligence
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: If data is the oil of the 21st Century, then artificial intelligence (AI) is its engine. Across a wide range of application areas, system designers leverage the advances in machine learning to process large volumes of data (e.g. audio, image, video) in an attempt to extract meaningful information from data, automate complex tasks, and support human decision making. This course equips students with the practical skills to apply existing AI tools and libraries to practical application areas such as business, education, and health.
learning_outcomes: Interpret, validate, and integrate AI outputs.
Define principles of artificial intelligence and machine learning.
Explain the application of AI tools and libraries to practical application areas (e.g. business, education, health).
Critically explain the limitations and issues of applying AI in practice.
Use AI tools and libraries to extract information from data (e.g. audio, image, text, video).

title: Web Programming
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: Introduces concepts and skills needed to develop and manage small to medium web facing server systems. Covers API techniques, event-driven programming, development or effective user interfaces, database integration and client side scripting.
learning_outcomes: Create a prototype Component-Based client-side, end-user focused web-application that can pass data between components to present reports from a database.
Demonstrate both team and self-management principles typically seen in the industry to deliver a prototype Component-Based web app solution
Design and develop a robust web-browser based, aesthetic and intuitive user-interface that applies the concepts of Component-Based Architecture.
Implement a comprehensive Component-Based web app capable of connecting to a prototype server-side web-application that displays editable information from a database in a web browser.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Mid-Term Project Updates, Demos, and Reflections

title: ICT Business Analysis
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course introduces the skills and techniques which contemporary ICT professionals need if they are to effectively design and utilise Information and Communication Technologies (ICT) in industry. In doing so, the course aligns with the IT occupation of an ICT Business Analyst and draws upon the business analysis body of knowledge defined by the International Institute of Business Analysis (BABOK). Three major areas are covered: ICT business systems analysis (including problem-solving techniques), defining and documenting ICT business system requirements, and ICT business system design and implementation.
learning_outcomes: Determine and document business requirements for information in the modern organisation.
Conceptually describe the role of ICT in the day-to-day management of an organisation.
Explain the key issues that arise when business information systems are being developed and implemented.

title: Cloud Computing
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the foundational concepts and experience in Cloud Computing. The course provides the theory, concepts, and practical experience in configuring, deploying, managing, maintaining, and securing cloud environments. By the end of the course students will be able to deploy, manage and test secure cloud solutions.
learning_outcomes: Automate basic cloud management tasks
Manage and monitor cloud storage and performance
Prepare and deploy a cloud solution
Plan, identify and assess management for cloud deployments
Design a secure network for cloud deployment

title: ICT Project Management
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: Information and Communication Technology (ICT) projects are pivotal for new technology adoption and digital transformation to achieve organisational strategic objectives. Delivery of successful ICT projects requires practical knowledge and the effective use of adequate tools for analysis, planning, implementation, and monitoring. It is essential that all ICT professionals, regardless of the industry domain they operate in, have the skills and knowledge to work in and manage complex ICT projects. This course introduces students to the foundational principles, methodologies, and tools of ICT project management. With a focus on the practical application of the PMBOK® principles, students will learn how to initiate, plan, execute, monitor, and close ICT projects. The course explores how organisational structure, team dynamics, and stakeholder communication affect project outcomes. Students will gain experience using project management software and techniques to address typical ICT project challenges and will explore agile practices to build adaptability and effective teamwork in technology-driven environments.
learning_outcomes: Use modern project management tools and techniques to solve practical problems in ICT project planning and delivery.
Describe how social, organisational, and technological factors can affect the success of ICT projects.
Apply PMBOK principles to effectively manage ICT projects across their lifecycle.
Apply agile approaches to improve flexibility and teamwork in ICT project environments.

title: Professional Practice in IT
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course covers in-depth ICT professional knowledge, including professional practice responsibilities, the role of certifications, and ICT professional ethical and legal issues. It further develops skills in interpersonal and organisational communication, as well as a comprehensive understanding of IT governance and ICT service management that ICT students will need in their future professional practice. It also provides a theoretical grounding of innovation and entrepreneurship methods and provides practice in the implementation of some of their underlying techniques. As part of this course, students will experience a recognised industry certification process.
learning_outcomes: Decide on appropriate certifications for ICT career development.
Apply the ICT professional code of conduct, and illustrate the roles and expectations of an ICT professional.
Differentiate between legal, ethical and social obligations of an ICT professional and be able to differentiate ethical and un-ethical behaviours.
Demonstrate skills for organisational communication within the roles that IT professionals will need in their professional practice.
Apply principles of innovation and entrepreneurship and their application in the context of ICT.
Synthesise contemporary and future ethical and social impacts of ICT.
Outline contemporary ICT governance in organisations.

title: Games Design
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Information and Physical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Introduces the techniques of designing games for the digital entertainment industry. Students will analyse key game design elements including game genres, concepts, virtual worlds, storytelling, character, user interface design, and core technologies with a focus on the conceptual component of games design. Students will assimilate and expand upon the key theories and practices associated with games design via a series of written and practical projects.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an informed knowledge of screen-based interactivity
Produce a visual presentation towards a games concept proposal.
Produce industry standard documentation towards a games concept proposal
Demonstrate an informed knowledge of concepts fundamental to games design
Communicate using the terminology specific to games design
Critically evaluate using the key concepts involved in games design
Describe the processes involved in the games production cycle
Describe emerging trends within the games industry
Demonstrate an awareness of the ethical dimensions relevant to games design

title: Process Analysis and Problem Solving
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course introduces tools and techniques used to observe, understand and describe workflows and processes within organisations. Students then utilise traditional and emerging techniques to identify problems and opportunities for improvement within these workflows and processes.
learning_outcomes: Use innovative problem-solving approaches to define improvements and alternatives to present methods.
Work within groups in ways that create synergies and facilitate high quality outcomes in each of the areas above.
Demonstrate expertise in using a set of tools and techniques that allow them to identify and clearly explain the strengths and weaknesses within these processes and procedures.
Gather information on workplace processes and procedures, and document these in a clear and unambiguous manner.

title: Games Production
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Information and Physical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Building on prior programming knowledge, students will use available game engine technology to construct the operating elements of a game design. This course examines the techniques used in bringing a game to the point of distribution and transforming a design into a reality. Students will also come to experience and understand the relevance of other implementation issues such as physics engines, rendering tools, audio components, and the integration of the output from the art production tools used to create the game objects, world elements and backgrounds.
learning_outcomes: State the objectives and define the design requirements for a computer game
Integrate and use existing development tools in the construction of an original computer game
Implement a game based on design requirements
Explain the impact of different development tools and key technologies that may be used in game development
Compare and contrast the different technologies used in game development
Recognise and follow the keys phases of computer game development.

title: Computing Directed Studies II
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Information and Physical Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course provides an in-depth study of a topic in computing at an advanced level. The topic is individually chosen to suit the student's background and aspirations, and will be offered either as a lecture course or as a reading course under the supervision of a member of the academic staff. Each student's topic must be approved by the relevant Program Convenor.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the theoretical foundations, methodologies, and contextual relevance of an advanced topic in computing.
Design and implement innovative solutions to complex problems in computing, demonstrating autonomy and advanced technical proficiency.
Communicate complex ideas, analyses, and findings effectively using advanced communication skills appropriate to computing research and practice.

The course also introduces to students advanced topics in computer programming.
learning_outcomes: Test and document program solutions.
Implement a solution to a problem.
Analyse a programming problem and design a solution.
Work along side suitable AI infrastructure to implement advanced programming concepts.
Comprehend and implement concepts of computer programming.

title: Mobile Application Development
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: The focus of this course is on building Mobile Applications and their use across a range of contexts, both personal and professional. It will provide students with the knowledge and skills required to use, design, and implement such applications and recognise their utility focusing on providing solutions to real-world problems.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate capacity in mobile application technologies.
Develop and communicate plans and prototypes for implementation of mobile applications.
Apply this knowledge to use and create relevant software in mobile applications leveraging cloud based environments, including user interfaces that are aesthetic, intuitive and easy to use.

You will explore the fundamentals of security, privacy and risk, including core principles, cyber security controls and technologies, policies, procedures, and best practices. Through real world case study examination and assessment based on organisational-focused cyber security frameworks, you will develop a foundational knowledge base in cyber security that can be leveraged and built upon in both academia and industry.
learning_outcomes: Source and evaluate technologies for managing cyber security risks.
Evaluate legal, ethical and professional issues frequently encountered in a Cyber Security risk management environment
Respond to Cyber Security threats and risks in accordance with organisational processes.
Apply introductory Cyber Security skills from the perspective of different stakeholders.
Interpret the ways in which Cyber Security policy and procedure mechanism support organisations

title: Systems Design for the Digital Economy
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Information and Physical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Information and Communication Technology (ICT) has fundamentally changed how people communicate, work, and engage with organisations. In this rapidly evolving digital economy landscape, it has become vital for ICT professionals to effectively design, implement, and evaluate systems (e.g., in the form of chatbots, digital platforms, mobile apps). Against the backdrop of the development of IT solutions during the 21st century, this course identifies the fundamental driving forces and core principles for effective systems design in the digital economy. Building on these foundations, it equips ICT professionals with contemporary skills and practices to pro-actively develop approaches for designing, testing, and evaluating innovative ICT applications in different application areas (e.g., recommender systems, streaming platforms). Finally, the course equips ICT professionals with the skills to leverage contemporary research insights to inform systems solutions in this space.
learning_outcomes: Apply contemporary ICT methods and frameworks to pro-actively design innovative ICT systems for the digital economy.
Identify and critically evaluate societal and ethical concerns that arise during the design and evaluation of systems in the digital economy.
Evaluate the usability and usefulness of systems solutions for the digital economy.
Critically evaluate and apply research insights to analyse, design, and evaluate systems solutions in the digital economy.
Recognize and reflect on the key driving forces and core principles for effective systems design in the digital economy.

title: Big Data
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: The pervasion of information technology into every aspect of life and the recent explosion of social media have resulted in the creation of huge volumes (Big Data) of typically unstructured data: web logs, videos, speech, photographs, purchase patterns, e-mails, GPS data and Tweets. Organisations have understood that there is a strong need for professional data analysts who are able to manage big data, to apply appropriate data analytics techniques (e.g. statistical learning, classification, and dimension reduction methods), and to utilise the critical knowledge within these enormous amounts of data. This course brings together several key theories and technologies used in manipulating, storing, and analyzing big data.
learning_outcomes: Apply contemporary Big Data technologies to store, manipulate and analyse large unstructured data sets.
Analyse the business requirements and applications of Big Data technologies.
Investigate and explore the problems and limitations of existing enterprise technology in handling large datasets and how Big Data technologies can be used to overcome them.

title: ICT Project Planning and Management
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: Information and Communication Technology (ICT) projects play a critical role in achieving digital innovation and driving organisational transformation. Leading such projects successfully demands not only technical understanding but also strategic foresight and the ability to navigate complex socio-technical systems. Professionals in ICT must be equipped to manage projects that are shaped by diverse stakeholders, emerging technologies, and shifting organisational priorities. This course equips students with the strategic insight and professional capabilities required to lead ICT projects in dynamic and complex environments. Emphasising the application of PMBOK® principles, the course covers each phase of the project lifecycle while examining the influence of socio-cultural, organisational, and emerging technological factors on project success. Students will solve domain-specific challenges through project-based learning, simulations, and the use of modern project management tools. Agile methods are introduced as a flexible and collaborative approach to enhancing ICT project delivery, supporting responsiveness to change and iterative development.
learning_outcomes: Apply PMBOK principles to effectively manage ICT projects across their lifecycle.
Critically evaluate the influence of socio-cultural, organisational, and emerging technological factors on the success of ICT projects.
Use modern project management tools and techniques to solve practical problems in ICT project planning and delivery.
Implement agile methods to enhance ICT project delivery and adaptability.

title: Cloud Computing
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the foundational concepts and experience in Cloud Computing. The course provides the theory, concepts, and practical experience in configuring, deploying, managing, maintaining, and securing cloud environments. By the end of the course students will be able to deploy, manage and test secure cloud solutions.
learning_outcomes: Manage and monitor cloud storage and performance.
Automate basic cloud management tasks.
Critically analyse and synthesise information to design and deploy a secure cloud solution
Design and quality assure a management plan for the deployment of cloud security.
Design a secure network for cloud deployment

title: Applied Artificial Intelligence
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: If data is the oil of the 21st Century, then artificial intelligence (AI) is its engine. Across a wide range of application areas, system designers leverage the advances in machine learning to process large volumes of data (e.g. audio, image, video) in an attempt to extract meaningful information from data, automate complex tasks, and support human decision making. This postgraduate course equips students with advanced skills to explore and push the boundaries of existing AI tools and libraries in practical application areas such as business, education, and health.
learning_outcomes: Explain principles of artificial intelligence and machine learning.
Use advanced AI tools, frameworks, and libraries to extract nuanced information from complex data sources (e.g. audio, image, text, video).
Critically evaluate the limitations and issues of applying AI in practice.
Interpret, critically evaluate and seamlessly integrate AI outputs to achieve intended purposes.
Interpret and evaluate the application of AI tools and libraries to practical application areas (e.g. business, education, health).

title: Professional Practice in IT
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: Information technology (IT) professionals need to be aware of both societal and technical issues in their work and require a solid understanding of the Professional Code of Conduct relevant to their field of practice. Recent developments in the technical areas of IT, such as social media, mobile applications, data analytics and data mining, have introduced new problems for professionals in social areas. IT professionals need to be aware of the ethical problems and the legal challenges that may arise from the use of information technology, as well as their level of accountability for these issues. Such issues include cybercrime, privacy, security and safety, intellectual property and social responsibility. This course introduces students to ethical and legal issues and provides a basic understanding of research appraisal and validation that IT professionals will need in their professional practice.
learning_outcomes: Differentiate between legal, ethical and social obligations of an ICT professional and be able to differentiate ethical and un-ethical behaviours.
Synthesise contemporary and future ethical and social impacts of ICT and discuss best practice for the use of ICT for society.
Demonstrate professional-level skills for organisational communication within the roles that IT professionals will need in their professional practice.
Discuss contemporary ICT governance in organisations.
Apply the ICT professional code of conduct, and reflect on the roles and competencies of a contemporary ICT professional.

title: Information Technology Project
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Information and Physical Sciences
syllabus_overview: The Information Technology Project course offers students the opportunity to apply and deepen their understanding of concepts, skills, and techniques learned throughout their program, encompassing areas of computer science, IT, data science, and/or cybersecurity. Assessment includes the submission of a project final report and a piece of applied work. Projects can span a diverse range of topics such as data management, data analysis, cybersecurity strategies, theoretical computer science work, simulations, software development, and other computing solutions. The range of projects can vary from year to year, with a selection of topics, including those in data science and cybersecurity, provided annually. The emphasis is on facilitating student learning in technical and project management skills across these multifaceted domains of computing.
learning_outcomes: Formulate, structure, and communicate technical information to scientists, engineers, and other professionals in a clear and professional manner
Apply, adapt, and integrate technical knowledge to address complex computing and information technology problems
Plan, justify, and reflect on time and resource management strategies to produce realistic and effective project outcomes
Demonstrate effective and collaborative team skills with peers and/or industry partners to achieve shared objectives in professional contexts.
Research, critically analyse, and evaluate technical information in computing and information technology topics

title: Design Thinking: Creativity in Action
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Design Thinking: Creativity in Action immerses students in the dynamic world of entrepreneurial problem-solving. They will learn to tackle challenges with curiosity, empathy, and resilience, adopting the mindset of successful innovators. Through hands-on projects and collaborative activities, they will leverage GenAI tools to research and frame problems, identify opportunities, enhance creativity, and explore new possibilities. The structured design thinking process guides them from understanding their purpose (“why?”) to analysing the current context (“what is”) and imagining future solutions (“what if”). This course lays the foundation for impactful work, equipping students with essential entrepreneurial and GenAI skills to apply throughout the program and in their careers.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate ideas through convergent thinking, effectively presenting them using storytelling, visual, and verbal communication techniques
Generate innovative ideas using creative thinking within an entrepreneurial context.
Conduct empathy-based research to identify user needs and pain points in real-world contexts.
Demonstrate a growth-oriented entrepreneurial mindset for purpose-driven problem solving.
Apply entrepreneurial and design thinking skills to address Sustainability challenges.

title: International Exchange Studies
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
