title: Entrepreneurial MakerSpace
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This interactive, hands-on second-year course provides students with the opportunity to build functional digital prototypes using no-code tools and GenAI agents. Through guided learning students engage in Entrepreneurial creation from initial UX design through to user-tested, iterated products ready to pitch. Operating under the Human Centric AI First/3P (Product-Process-Person) framework, students direct AI rather than defer to it, documenting their decision making in an individual portfolio across the semester. The course culminates in a working prototype validated by real users, a brand and business model anchored in a Sustainable Development Goal, and the development of practical AI collaboration skills that employers are increasingly requiring of business graduates.
learning_outcomes: Apply generative AI tools and agents to support design decision-making, documenting AI interactions and exercising informed judgement about AI outputs.
Describe how the design thinking process uses divergent and convergent thinking techniques and rapid prototyping to generate innovative solutions.
Integrate user feedback to drive iterative design improvement.
Create a basic business model and essential branding elements.
Apply makerspace tools and techniques to produce functional prototypes.

title: Data Analytics in Digital Entrepreneurship
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In today's digital world, understanding data is crucial for entrepreneurs. This course demystifies data analytics and shows you how to use it to make smart business decisions. You'll learn the basics of collecting, analysing, and interpreting data using user-friendly tools and GenAI assistants. Through practical exercises and real-world examples, you'll see how data can help identify opportunities, understand customers, and improve products or services. By the end of the course, you'll be comfortable working with data and using it to drive your entrepreneurial ideas forward.
learning_outcomes: Describe data collection challenges specific to early-stage ventures and resource-constrained environments.
Design data collection strategies for startup validation and competitive intelligence.
Develop data-driven strategies for innovative and entrepreneurial ventures.
Evaluate ethical implications of data collection and usage in innovation contexts.
Apply analytical methods to validate business hypotheses and measure product-market fit.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Individual Reflection Journals: My Path to Better Decisions

title: Social Entrepreneurship for Impact
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course explores entrepreneurship as a tool for positive social change. Students will learn how modern social ventures combine the energy and innovation of private enterprise with the inclusiveness of nonprofits and government. The course will examine organizations prioritizing both profit and social impact, emphasizing that successful impact starts with purpose and sustainability. Using GenAI, students will analyse Sustainable Development Goals such as poverty, quality education, and climate change, and brainstorm innovative solutions and business models. The course will help them understand the challenges and rewards of business for impact, inspiring their own socially impactful entrepreneurial journey.
learning_outcomes: Align personal purpose with a social change initiative.
Critically evaluate social impact dilemmas within ecosystems for shared value creation.
Assess the impact, costs, and benefits of social ventures
Develop a logic- and business model for positive social change.
Effectively present solutions to secure buy-in from key stakeholders.

title: Prompt Engineering for Innovation
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In the evolving world of Generative Artificial Intelligence, prompt engineering has emerged as a pivotal skill for innovators and entrepreneurs. Generative AI models, like large language models, hold vast potential but demand co-creation skills and meticulous instruction to fully harness their capabilities. This course provides the foundational knowledge and skills in prompt engineering, enabling students to leverage the strength of LLMs for ideation, problem-solving, and pioneering new products and services. They will learn to co-create with Generative AI, enhancing their critical and creative thinking for productive collaboration, refining outputs, and ensuring genuine real-world application of their joint endeavours.
learning_outcomes: Apply prompt engineering techniques to foster co-creation, critical and creative thinking.
Collaboratively develop a Venture with GenAI, balancing autonomous and human-directed work processes.
Translate AI collaborations into real-world applications, presenting them persuasively to stakeholders in various formats.
Justify ethical and responsible GenAI practices through informed decision-making.
Demonstrate a comprehensive understanding of Generative AI and its applications for innovation.

title: Global Networking and Negotiation
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course equips students with the cultural intelligence, strategic insight, and interpersonal competence required to succeed in global innovation ecosystems. Students will develop the ability to build and sustain professional networks across borders and cultures, both online and in person. They will learn how cultural values shape communication, collaboration, and entrepreneurial strategy by drawing on leading research in global dexterity, cultural mapping, and negotiation styles. The course includes case studies, interactive simulations, and role-play exercises to develop cultural intelligence and negotiation fluency in cross-cultural contexts. Students will also harness generative AI tools to analyse stakeholder behaviour, cultural frameworks, and negotiation dynamics. By the end of the course, students will have the competence and confidence to navigate innovation partnerships and negotiate effectively in emerging global markets.
learning_outcomes: Reflect critically on personal development in cultural intelligence, global mindset, and professional competencies.
Justify strategic decisions using relevant academic literature, cultural frameworks, and real-world analysis, supported by appropriate use of GenAI tools where applicable.
Demonstrate adaptability, strategic thinking, and discipline relevant communication in cross-cultural business scenarios, both in prepared work and live, interactive settings.
Apply cross-cultural management and negotiation theories to analyse communication styles, institutional contexts, and trust-building practices across culturally diverse settings.
Design and communicate culturally informed strategies for international business through structured presentations, negotiation plans, and scholarly writing.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Global Business Adaptation Report and Reflection

title: Traction and Growth
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Traction and Growth is designed to equip aspiring entrepreneurs and business leaders with the insights and tools necessary for achieving sustainable growth in today’s competitive landscape. This course offers a deep dive into the intricacies of building traction and expanding your business efficiently while managing people and resources effectively. At the heart of the program is the exploration of the Traction Model with milestones, providing a clear framework for identifying and pursuing key objectives that drive business growth. The course goes beyond traditional growth strategies to incorporate the AARRR Marketing Plan, also known as the Pirate Metrics—Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, and Revenue. This customer-centric approach focuses on optimising the Customer Factory Model to master the art of acquiring, retaining, and expanding customer base.
learning_outcomes: Develop a plan for sustainable growth that balances long-term vision with short-term execution, while maintaining agility to adapt to market changes.
Apply the Traction Marketing framework (Acquisition, Activation, Retention, Referral, Revenue).
Use the Customer Factory Model to identify optimisation opportunities and areas for improvement across the customer journey.
Summarize the Growth Management and Traction Model in scaling innovation.
Explain the principles of lean growth management and its role in sustainable scaling.

title: Venture Funding
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Venture Funding offers aspiring entrepreneurs and business professionals a deep dive into the dynamics of securing funding for new ventures and innovation projects. This course provides an essential guide to understanding the variety of funding avenues available, from angel investments and venture capital to crowdfunding and government grants, tailored specifically for the opportunity. Students will explore the intricacies of each funding type, learning how to effectively match their business needs with the right funding source, and understanding the legal and financial implications of venture funding agreements. Emphasis will be placed on developing an understanding of entrepreneurial finance building a financial model and presenting a compelling pitch. Participants will gain practical insights through case studies, real-world scenarios, and interactive sessions with industry experts, equipping them with the skills to navigate the complex landscape of venture funding. By the end of the course, students will not only be able to identify the most suitable funding options for their ventures but also understand how to approach investors with confidence and secure the capital needed to fuel their business growth.
learning_outcomes: Design strategic relationships with investors, financial institutions, and industry partners to secure venture funding and create sustainable financial partnerships.
Construct detailed financial models that demonstrate the economic viability of ventures.
Evaluate various funding avenues for ventures.
Discuss the core principles of entrepreneurial finance.
Develop compelling pitches for different investor audiences using the core principles of venture funding (business models, market analysis, funding needs).

title: Acceleration for Student Entrepreneurs (I2N)
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Acceleration for Student Entrepreneurs provides students with a hands-on approach to testing, improving, and advancing a business idea utilising Gen AI and lean startup methodology. Students start by mapping a problem landscape and their initial assumptions of their business idea and then test these hypotheses with customers and partners outside the classroom to build a Minimal Viable Product (MVP). The goal is for students to test their business model, understand which of their assumptions were wrong, and figure out what they need to validate the business model. The objective is to get students using the tools including Gen AI that help startups test their hypotheses and adjust when they learn that their original assumptions are wrong. Students experience faulty assumptions not as a crisis, but as a learning event called a pivot - an opportunity to change the model. More than just for use in startups, these problem-solving skills are increasingly crucial in today’s increasingly complex world.
learning_outcomes: Work and communicate effectively as part of a team across a range of activities and contexts.
Create and criticise a range of value based on a thorough analysis of customer problems, needs and wants.
Identify and apply key principles of problem discovery utilising tools and frameworks coupled with secondary research.

Identify and apply key principles of lean startup-methodology to assess desirability, viability and feasibility of a new business model, including designing and evaluating an appropriate business model.

Reflectively analyse their understanding of class concepts, and how their perspectives of these concepts have changed after interacting with the classroom activities. Reflectively analyse their perspective and the perspectives of their peers when engaging in classroom activities.
Appraise and apply evidence of traction through experiments and the development of a Minimum Viable Product.

title: International Policy, Politics and the Economy
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the study of the interactions between international politics, policy, and the economy. It examines the reciprocal, interactive relationship between politics and economics or between states and markets in the contemporary international system. It does this through learning about four key perspectives in international politics - neo-classical, neoliberal institutional, feminist and Marxist - in relation to five key debates in global-local (glocal) international politics. Each theme will also address how Indigenous peoples and perspectives, in particular Indigenous women and kin, address these global issues. The use of different theories to explore these debates will help students to describe, explain and suggest policy and broader political solutions to these global-local (glocal) issues and challenges.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate theoretical and empirical preparedness for professional life in the global economic development sector.
Explain the operation of power and the role of major state and societal actors in the international economic system.
Apply knowledge of the major theoretical perspectives in international politics to the interactions and intersections between states, diverse political actors, and the economy and key global issues.

Describe the merits and demerits of these perspectives as they account for the changing political dynamics of international political and economic relations and policy and political strategies and practises.
Use key concepts and issues in contemporary global politics and policy to explain the interactions and intersections between states, diverse political actors, and the economy and key global issues.
Develop real world policy, political analysis and strategic solutions to global challenges.

title: Business and the Politics of Globalisation
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Globalisation is a phenomenon that shapes the interactions of our modern world. In this course students will critically engage with the ways that economies, societies and political systems influence the success of public and private organisations. Central to these discussions is an exploration of the diverse ways in which goods, services, people, ideas and technologies moves across borders. Globalisation creates new opportunities for trade, communication, and innovation. However, it also produces significant tensions, due to economic protectionism, political agendas, and the complexities of international cooperation and governance. Throughout the course students will explore these complexities considering the impacts of globalisation on business, international relations and global governance. By examining topics such as global governance, trade, transnational advocacy, and corporate social responsibility, students will develop a critical understanding of global power structures and their implications for business, policy, diplomacy and ethics.
learning_outcomes: Engage with key theories of international relations to examine global power dynamics and the changing role of the nation-state.
Develop a critical understanding of globalisation and its influence on the economy, ethics politics and society in our modern world.
Examine the roles of global institutions, multinational corporations and civil society in shaping global governance and ethical business practices.
Identify and analyse contemporary political and business events in global context.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Consultancy: Board of Directors Presentation and Q&A

title: The International Politics of Climate Change and the Future World
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Environmental challenges are a critical global issue, as the international community’s response now will profoundly impact future generations. Amongst these challenges, climate change sits at the centre, due to its far-reaching effects on ecosystems, Country, the atmosphere, and peoples. Cooperative strategies and solutions are needed to future proof and protect our natural and built environments. This course explores contemporary challenges in climate politics and policy and pursues questions of how interactions with our natural surroundings as kin and Country and ecology may be sustainably organised, implemented and justified. Students will be exposed to the business, economy, governance, civil society, climate change nexus, which is critical for understanding and evaluating the issues at stake for ensuring global, ecological futures.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the challenges and opportunities climate change presents to the realisation of ecologically sustainable futures.
Explain and apply diverse political frameworks of analysis to evaluate strategies to address contemporary environmental issues.
Describe and reflect on the role of key stakeholders in the production, governance and development of solutions to climate change.
Utilise effective written and oral communication of key concepts, frameworks and ideas in the international politics of climate change.
Analyse innovative strategies employed by different actors to respond to, mitigate and prevent climate change and its effects.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Case Study Live Podcast Presentation with Q&A

title: Diplomacy, Trade and Politics
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Sustainable and productive relationships are essential for the peaceful resolution of global conflicts, effective trade and the elimination of social justice issues. Building cooperative partnerships with diverse stakeholders, including indigenous populations, to address global issues requires individuals to engage in a wide range of strategies. In this course students will be introduced to the world of the diplomat and will have the opportunity to develop diplomatic skills, including negotiation and mediation. Students will learn how diplomacy is used to: create substantive social justice policy, develop trading relationships, meet the needs and interests of individuals and communities, harness technologies for innovation, and to resolve and transform conflicts.
learning_outcomes: Identify challenges to successful diplomacy and trade.
Create a collaborative diplomatic strategy for the successful resolution of a simulated global issue.
Apply diplomatic strategies and principles to current problems to generate socially sustainable, and ethical financial and political outcomes.
Explain the social, cultural, economic and political impacts of different types of diplomacy.
Evaluate the tools of diplomacy used by relevant actors during public and political events.

title: Public Diplomacy and Social Media
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: People, their perspectives and interactions are central to understanding international events. How transnational relationships are formed and strengthened is often critical for ensuring mutual understandings and collaborations between governments and other key international stakeholders. Increasingly, new media and emerging network approaches are at the core of how dialogues are negotiated and political interests are pursued. This course offers students an opportunity to discover how social media shapes international policy, deliberations and outcomes. Students will explore topics including the impacts of social media on civil society, the role of social media in cultural dissemination, the emergence of new social movements and transnational identities, and the evolution of relationships in response to new networks and technologies.
learning_outcomes: Assess the relationship between public diplomacy and social media.
Design and defend a strategy for building cooperative relationships through diplomacy and social media.
Utilise digital platforms and emerging technologies to design, deliver and evaluate diplomatic messaging strategies for diverse global audiences.
Identify and evaluate the principles of public diplomacy.
Apply public diplomacy concepts and ideas to global issues and events.

title: Global Data Governance for Just and Sustainable Futures
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course explores the complex and multifaceted nature of the Fourth Industrial Revolution (the Data Revolution) and its differentials. Increasingly, data is leveraged to produce often unequal and arguably undemocratic access to information. At the same time, the Fourth Industrial Revolution is evidence that data has the capacity to be deeply democratic, enhancing the participatory potential of individuals and communities in ways that revolutionise lives, and improve well-being globally. Throughout the course students will critically examine how data is utilised to make key government, civil society and business decisions. They will explore the factors and stakeholders needed for a just and sustainable system of global data governance across our economic, social and political institutions. The course will introduce students to some of the key debates central to understanding the (mis)use of data, and the regulation, democratisation and ethics of data governance. Specifically, they will engage with critical questions around who gets to decide the parameters of data construction and use; data sovereignty for Indigenous peoples; who regulates the use of data for distinct purposes; and how might the (inter)national community develop systems of democratic access to and control over data construction, data use and data evaluation.
learning_outcomes: Apply critical analysis in a data governance scenario to inform global professional/political practice.
Identify key issues and challenges in data governance.
Critically analyse solutions to challenges in data governance.
Develop solutions to challenges in data governance.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Short Answer and Long Answer Test

title: International Relations in a Changing World Order
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course examines the institutions, processes, narratives and actors that shape outcomes in international politics. It does this through an exploration of current and emerging global issues including: the international politics of resource management; the dynamics of peace and conflict; refugees and migration, space colonisation and future frontiers; and economic governance for sustainability. To understand how these global issues and events shape our changing world students will engage critically with key principles and frameworks of international relations. Throughout the course students will examine the core relationships central to global politics. They will consider how interactions between State and non-state actors (including for example civil society organisations, transnational economic actors and multilateral organisations) produce diverse outcomes in often complex contexts. They will also engage critically with the impact of these interactions on questions of justice, sustainability, conflict resolution and governance.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the core concepts and actors central to the study of international relations.
Critique the factors that influence international order and the relationships between states and non-state actors.
Utilise primary and secondary resources to analyse international relations issues and events.
Apply IR principles and frameworks to evaluate and critically address real world problems in international politics.

assessment_tasks.task_name: International Relations Expert Presentation & Interactive Response

title: Indigenising International Politics, Policy and the Economy
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course is award winning at both national and international levels and is recognised by local Indigenous community and knowledge holders as exemplifying Indigenous educational practise in responsibility relation for justice, reconciliation and healing. The course is embedded in a strengths-based Indigenous framework and uses Indigenous ways of learning that can include story, weaving, song, poetry and mapping that invites the student into a journey of (un)learning, connection to Country and remembering. During the course we explore two main themes: firstly, the ways in which (global) institutions of governance, economy and state have and continue to discriminate and exclude Indigenous peoples and how this might be rectified. Secondly, we explore the ways that Indigenous modes of governance, economy and citizenship provide new-ancient ways for thinking about and developing solutions to the pressing global issues of sustainability, precarity, disillusionment with democracy and citizenship, questions of well-being and mental health, community conflict and polarisation, and revitalising housing and education systems. The experiences and knowledges from Indigenous peoples in various parts of the world are taught using a comparative lens that is developed in respectful relation and in responsible ways. Students have the opportunity to develop the skills with which to contribute to Indigenising and offsetting discrimination and exclusion in their area of professional /political practice.
learning_outcomes: Identify, interpret and analyse the way that Indigenous perspectives have relevance for key challenges facing the global polity, society and economy.

Develop reflexive skills to foster an engagement with scholarship and professional/community practice that is attentive to difference, diversity and power and which Indigenises knowledge-production and practice.
Describe, interpret and suggest solutions to examples of Indigenous exclusion or marginalisation in a broad range of topics within the remit of International politics.
Describe, interpret and apply Indigenous perspectives to a broad range of topics within the remit of International politics.
Develop an analysis of key issues in the study of global Indigenous politics through Indigenous political science theory lenses.

title: Dynamics of People and Work in Organisations
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: People are the most dynamic resource an organisation has at its disposal. Understanding how people undertake work that contributes to organisations and how organisations affect the lives of the people who work in them is complex. This course introduces some of the concepts that help to understand these issues. Topics include diverse perspectives on people and work, the impact of technology and generational trends on work, gender and ethnicity at work, organizational culture, employee voice and its impact on organisational performance. All topics will develop key generic skills and have a strong emphasis on practitioner-based knowledge from human resource management and employment relations.
learning_outcomes: Identify and compare multiple perspectives on people and work in organisations
Demonstrate how work in organisations is managed in order to improve organizational culture, organizational performance and employee outcomes

Apply at an introductory level several generic skills important for future academic study and professional practice, including: critical analysis; the reading, interpretation and reporting of descriptive statistics; interviewing as a data-gathering technique; and the use of evidence to support an argument.
Explain the impact of factors outside organisations (like technology, the law, labour markets and social institutions) on the way people work in organisations
Describe and compare different types of work in different types of organisations and industries

title: Introduction to Industrial Relations
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: The effective management of complex employment relationships is a critical function in contemporary organisations. The course introduces industrial relations delineating its essential concepts. In so doing, it considers the historical dimensions of work and the employment relationship, and the origins and the development of industrial relations up to the present time. Particular detailed attention is given to the present day structures and characteristics of employee representation, management and employers' associations. This is complemented by an examination of the role of the state, and how recent systemic changes affect state regulation and the workplace. The problem based learning structure allows you to develop your inquiry and communication skills.
learning_outcomes: Apply the essential concepts of industrial relations and their interrelationship at the personal, organisational and national levels.
Communicate your knowledge of industrial relations inwritten and verbal formats appropriate to both audience and purpose.
Demonstrate descriptive knowledge of the field of industrial relations.
Investigate solutions to industrial relations problems based on research and assessment of current practices.
Recognise and consider the social, historical and equity issues within industrial relations.

title: Introduction to Human Resource Management
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Human Resource Management links people-related activities to business strategy. The course develops a critical understanding of the role and functions of the various human resource activities in an organisation, providing students with a comprehensive review of key HRM concepts, techniques and issues. Topics include job analysis and design, recruitment and selection, evaluation, performance management, occupational health and safety, and the strategic contribution of HRM to organisational performance and evaluating HRM effectiveness. Working with contemporary case studies, students not only engage in collaborative and individual work processes but use communication and discourse characteristic of the HRM context and environment.
learning_outcomes: Understand key concepts and theories to develop effective performance management and rewards systems that reinforce desired employee behaviours.
Analyse human resource planning and forecasting techniques.
Understand diversity in the workplace and its value in attracting and retaining employees, boosting productivity and fostering innovation.
Illustrate the essential features of a human resource information system and discover data that can be used to improve the effectiveness of HR functions and decision-making.
Investigate and evaluate the key procedures in recruitment and selection.
Analyse and evaluate significant contemporary issues in human resource management including HRM's contribution to organisational performance.
Develop an understanding of key HR practices and activities necessary for an organisation's value creation and success.

title: Applied Human Resource Management and Employment Relations
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Contemporary human resource management defines a holistic approach to employment relations. The concepts and theories of HRM and ER and their subsequent application to the current cooperation of HRM and ER are examined. Through experiencing relevant case studies of selected industries and enterprises, and responsiveness with local practitioners, students apply and enhance their independent and collaborative work processes and problem solving & decision making skills.
learning_outcomes: Access, evaluate and apply current data and information sources to inform HRM and ER problem solving.
Critically analyse selected key concepts in HRM and ER
Apply HRM and ER concepts in the study of selected industries and enterprises, both unionised and non-unionised
Utilise these research methods to gather publicly-available data about HRM and ER practices in selected industries and enterprises
Demonstrate an integrative awareness of contemporary professional standards, practice and effective implementation.
Individually and collectively engage in independent projects that encourage reflection on personal knowledge, skill and ability.
Communicate in oral and written formats employing subject specific terminology and context.
Collectively engage in prolonged group assignments that encourage diverse collaborative outcomes

title: Managing Diversity
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Management of diversity impacts both organizational performance and environment. This course aims to introduce you to a range of theoretical and applied approaches from various disciplines, so you can analyse workforce diversity in modern organisations and then design, evaluate and implement strategies to manage workforce diversity. Federal and state interventions which address labor market inequality and issues of gender, culture, disability, age and work/life balance etc, especially in Australia, are analysed. How diversity is managed at an organisational-level is the principal focus of the course. The social, legal and equity issues relevant to managing diversity in enterprises from both a national and international perspective will be addressed.
learning_outcomes: Identify relevant legislation, case law and government policies that relate to anti-discrimination, harassment, equal employment opportunity, pay equity and privacy.

Based on an assessment of "the business case" for diversity, determine, justify and recommend, professional best practice with regards to technical, organisational and process elements to be included in an organisation's strategy for managing diversity.
Examine different theories used to explain labour market segregation, segmentation, equity and diversity.
Compare and contrast characteristics of workforce diversity both nationally and internationally.
Explore and reflect on individual/personal opportunities and challenges when pursuing diversity in the workplace.
Employ macro and organisational-level data to critically analyse the success of state and firm-based diversity interventions.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Board Paper on Preventing and Handling Discrimination/harassment in the Workplace

title: Negotiation and Advocacy
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: To address business problems, the key is not just to solve them short term but to employ the most sustainable, workable and productive solutions. This course analyses negotiation, mediation and advocacy from a theoretical basis to practical application. It addresses issues in the immediate workplace and in the wider system of enterprise bargaining, awards, and industrial tribunals. Topics include: the nature and sources of conflict, the skills of negotiation, mediation and advocacy, distributive bargaining and interdependence, planning and strategy, communication and persuasion, power in negotiations, third party intervention and the ethics of negotiation and advocacy. Adopting a problem and experiential based learning approach using relevant cases and experiences, the course emphasises the importance of communication and emotional intelligence as essential attributes within the context of Australian workplaces. Due to the nature of teaching methods, enrolments in this course will be limited to a maximum of 40.
learning_outcomes: Develop and implement the skills required for strategy formulation, planning and research for negotiating and advocacy.
Engage in effective research and communication processes both individually and collaboratively.
Incorporate and apply both the language and theory underpinning negotiation, mediation and advocacy.
Utilise construction, connection and reflection processes to direct negotiation knowledge and application.
Apply and evaluate skills in the practice of negotiating and advocating at the workplace and in contexts relating to workplace employment relations.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Negotiation Plan and Research Dossier (Group assignment)

title: Human Resource Development
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: People performance within organisations is a source of long term competitive business strength. Human Resource Development examines the activities and processes that impact on organisational and individual learning. The focus is on interventions which change, or improve the ability to change organisational behaviour. Interventions can range from the strategic to the functional areas of training and development. Topics include the strategic role of human resource development, organisational and individual analysis, adult learning styles, technology and learning, management education, vocational education and training. Communication and group management techniques are emphasised as important attributes for the HRD professional. All students engage in trainer competencies through developing and implementing experiential sessions for small groups.
learning_outcomes: Explain human resources development (HRD) and its theories, the difference between education, training, learning and the concept of the transfer of learning;
Critique the relationship between organisational development (OD) and HRD contribution to organisational effectiveness;
Evaluate the HRD role dealing with contemporary challenges.
Apply and evaluate a learning process starting with training needs analysis to assessment and evaluation process;

title: Legal System and Method I
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Legal System and Method I introduces the foundation and structure of the institutions and processes of the Australian legal system, including its origins and cultural contexts. Students are introduced to the sources of authoritative law (including statutes and case law), Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander legal systems, and fundamental legal concepts such as the rule of law, separation of powers, and doctrine of precedent. The nature and function of law is analysed and contextualised. The course provides essential knowledge and skills in reflective practice, legal research, legal writing, referencing, case reading, problem solving, and legal reasoning. Students develop a growing awareness of legal practice as a distinctive element within the Australian legal process.
learning_outcomes: Recognise and apply conventions for legal writing and referencing, including in a manner that is audience-appropriate.
Read and analyse legal cases effectively, and apply principles of the doctrine of precedent to interpret case law for the purpose of deriving legal rules and principles.
Demonstrate an understanding of the foundational elements of the Australian legal system and a growing understanding of key legal terminology.
Apply principles of reflective practice, including in relation to one’s own learning, legal practice, and sources of law.
Demonstrate the capacity to locate primary and secondary sources of law accurately and efficiently using online databases and library sources.
Develop coherent and persuasive written arguments using legal data.

title: International Human Resource Management
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Aims to develop a critical understanding of the role and functions of the various human resource activities within multinational corporations (MNC). It provides an overview of the impact of globalisation and varieties of capitalism in shaping international human resource management practices in MNCs. In doing so, the course addresses the literature in International Human Resource Management and the strategic management of human resources in MNCs. The field of International HRM is a relatively new area of academic/professional interest and the course will draw on case studies and selected readings. Case studies will be used to expose students to the various human resource management issues in the management of people in MNCs in an international context.
learning_outcomes: Describe Human Resource activities in an International Context.
Critically appraise the impact of cultural and contextual factors in shaping human resource practices in MNCs.
List and explain the differences between domestic and international HRM.
Explain the importance of cultural sensitivity in an international assignment.
From the literature form an opinion and express a logically argued view regarding the adequacy of HR systems in international organisations.
Describe the role of the HR Manager in an International context.

title: Japanese Culture and Identity
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course examines aspects of Japanese society and culture using English-language texts only.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate important themes in this field through the reading of major texts.
Demonstrate an understanding of Japanese culture and society.
Organise their ideas in a logical form in an essay.
Show a capacity for independent research.
Identify conceptual problems involved in studying a culture other than their own.

title: Japanese Language and Culture Beginners 1 (A0 to A1.1)
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Designed for those with little or no previous knowledge of Japanese, the course provides a foundational understanding and practice in pronunciation, vocabulary, grammar, the writing system and Japanese culture at a beginner's level.
learning_outcomes: Understand simple sentences related to daily life.
Converse in Japanese at a beginner’s level, including asking and answering questions, and initiating and responding to simple statements.
Write short sentences using kana and kanji and their compound words.
Read and understand simple sentences.
Recognize Japanese customs and cultural practices in different social settings and act appropriately in different contexts.

title: Japanese In Context 1 (A1.2 to A2.1)
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the study of contemporary Japan through the use of a variety of elementary level 1 Japanese-language materials.
learning_outcomes: Write short messages and paragraphs using kanji and their compound words.
Read and understand various styles of Japanese writing, such as short stories and articles.
Understand short, paragraph-length statements related to Japanese society and culture.
Recognise Japanese customs and cultural practices in familiar settings, such as at work, cultural events, school, or home, and act appropriately.
Converse in Japanese at a beginner to elementary level, with the ability to perform tasks such as looking for a job, planning a trip, sharing experiences and expressing hopes and wishes.

title: Japanese Language and Culture Beginners 2 (A1.1 to A1.2)
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Designed for those with knowledge of Japanese equivalent to a pass or higher in JAPN1110, this course continues to develop basic skills in reading, writing, speaking, listening and cultural understanding.
learning_outcomes: Read and understand short paragraphs and stories related to Japanese culture and customs.
Write short paragraphs using kanji and their compound words.
Converse in Japanese at a beginner’s level, including expressing opinions, plans, and experiences using present continuous and plain past forms.
Understand simple sentences related to daily life.
Recognize Japanese customs and cultural practices in various social settings and act appropriately.

assessment_tasks.task_name: 4x Writing Tasks – Writing task 1, 2, 3 and 4 (2x written, 2x typed)

title: Japanese in Context 2 (A2.1 to A2.2)
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course builds on skills acquired in JAPN2501 and introduces students to the study of the Japanese cultural tradition and society through the use of a variety of elementary level 2 Japanese language materials.
learning_outcomes: Write letters, journals, and essays using kanji and their compound words.
Understand paragraph-length statements related to Japanese society and culture.
Converse in Japanese at elementary level 2, performing tasks such as asking and answering questions, and expressing thoughts in various settings, including at work, home, school, or shopping.
Read and comprehend various styles of written Japanese, including letters, stories and essays.
Recognise Japanese customs and cultural practices in various settings and act appropriately.

title: Advanced Spoken Japanese I
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course will focus on improving students' reading, writing, listening and speaking skills and building up their confidence to discuss issues of everyday life in conversational Japanese.
learning_outcomes: Understand cultural aspects of human interactions in Japan.
Use appropriate styles of speeches according to different situations.
Communicate effectively in Japanese.
Demonstrate knowledge of aspects of Japanese society.

title: Advanced Spoken Japanese II
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course focuses on improving students' reading, writing, listening and speaking skills and building up their confidence to discuss issue of everyday life in conversational Japanese.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of aspects of Japanese society.
Apply their knowledge about cultural aspects of human interactions in Japanese society.
Demonstrate proficiency in communicating in Japanese.
Demonstrate practical skills to use appropriate styles of speeches according to different situations.

title: Japanese in Context 3 (A2.2 to B1.1)
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course uses Japanese language multimedia to expose students to traditional and modern Japanese culture through a diverse range of socio-cultural topics. JAPN3501 provides comprehensive language training at intermediate level 1.
learning_outcomes: Recognize Japanese customs, culture and society, and act appropriately in different contexts.
Write short paragraphs, articles, short essays and letters using kanji, compound words, and intermediate level 1 grammar structures.
Understand conversations and speeches on familiar topics in Japan.
Converse in Japanese at an intermediate level, including topics related to daily life as an exchange student in Japan, and express thoughts and reasons in various settings.
Read and understand texts at an intermediate level, including articles, reports and opinion statements about Japan.

title: Japanese in Context 4 (B1.1 to B1.2)
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course uses Japanese language multimedia to expose students to traditional and modern Japanese society through a diverse range of topics. JAPN3502 provides comprehensive language training at intermediate level 2.
learning_outcomes: Converse in Japanese at an intermediate level 2, on topics including daily life in Japan as an exchange student, and express thoughts, suggestions and experiences in various settings.
Recognize Japanese customs, culture and society and act appropriately.
Understand long discussions or lectures about familiar topics.
Write short essays presenting arguments for or against a social topic, using kanji, their compound words, and intermediate-level 2 grammar structures.
Read and understand at an intermediate level 2, including articles, survey reports and essays.

title: Legal System and Method II
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Legal System and Method II examines the nature of the Australian legal system, the constitutional framework and the development of sources of law, including the common law and legislation. Through the use of advocacy this course develops analytical and interpretative skills. Students develop further skills in legal research, statutory interpretation and in written and oral communication as relevant to the study and practice of law.
learning_outcomes: Explain the legislative process and rules and principles of statutory interpretation in Australia.
Conduct legal research to locate documents relevant to statutory interpretation.
Interpret statutory provisions and provide well-reasoned advice on their likely application to problem scenarios.
Describe fundamental aspects of Australia’s constitutional framework.
Critically evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of Australia’s constitutional framework, and the processes for achieving constitutional change.
Communicate analysis and argument in logically structured and grammatically sound outputs that reflect the expectations of professional legal writing.
Observe and interpret court etiquette.
Orally present and defend arguments in interactive dialogue with the teacher and peers in a style consistent with professional client consultations and court appearances.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Open book Formal Exam: Legal system-Problem Solving in Statutory Interpretation & Constitutional Law

title: Torts I
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Torts I (together with Torts II) examines the rules of law by which liability for civil wrongs is imposed. Tort law examines a wide range of topics that are closely relevant to fundamental human rights, including bodily integrity and property rights. Tort law also provides an important mechanism to engage with the use of public power (such as the action for false imprisonment and the action for negligence) and address potential corruption issues (such as in the action for misfeasance in public office). Both common law and statutory schemes are considered, including defences, remedies and the assessment of damages, with a view to promoting the rule of law.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate competing policy considerations and their impact on the development of the law of tort.
Orally present and defend arguments in interactive dialogue with the teacher and peers in a style consistent with professional client consultations, mediation, negotiation and court appearances.
Reflect critically on the role of the law of tort in the civil justice system and contemporary Australian society more generally.
Analyse case law, statutes and secondary legal materials relevant to the law of tort and develop concise notes in relation to those materials.
Identify the key legal principles relevant to the substantive areas of the law of tort and apply them to resolve legal problems.
Create persuasive and appropriately structured legal arguments on tort law issues and problems, both orally and in writing.

title: Torts II
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Torts II (together with Torts I) examines the rules of law by which liability for civil wrongs is imposed. Tort law examines a wide range of topics that are closely relevant to fundamental human rights, including bodily integrity and property rights. Tort law also provides an important mechanism to engage with the use of public power (such as the action for false imprisonment and the action for negligence) and addresses potential corruption issues (such as in the action for misfeasance in public office). Both common law and statutory schemes are considered, including defences, remedies and the assessment of damages, with a view to promoting the rule of law.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate competing policy considerations and their impact on the development of the law of tort.
Analyse case law, statutes and secondary legal materials relevant to the law of tort.
Orally present and defend arguments in interactive dialogue with the teacher and peers in a style consistent with professional client consultations, mediation, negotiation and court appearances.
Reflect critically on the role of the law of tort in the civil justice system and contemporary Australian society more generally.
Identify the key legal principles relevant to the substantive areas of the law of tort and apply them to resolve legal problems.
Create persuasive legal arguments on tort law issues and problems, both orally and in writing.

title: Criminal Law and Procedure
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Criminal Law and Procedure is the foundational course in criminal law. Students typically study this course in the second year of the combined B Laws (Hons) programs, which means that this is the first time you learn about the role that the state plays in proscribing behaviours and regulating the conduct of its citizens through the criminal law. The course will take us on an intriguing exploration of human behaviour, the operation of legal institutions, community participation in criminal procedure, social justice and the way in which our criminal laws shape, and are shaped by, contemporary social issues. The course will allow you to develop foundational knowledge of the criminal law. We will foster a contextual and critical understanding of the application of the criminal law in practice. The course focuses primarily on the criminal laws of New South Wales, although comparative components (both within Australia and internationally) are included where appropriate. Much of the course is devoted to studying the major criminal offences listed below. Major defences and the rules and principles of criminal procedure will also be examined in some detail. We will also begin to develop a familiarity with the principal agencies, procedures and routines involved in the administration of criminal justice in contemporary New South Wales. Our learning activities and assessment items in the course have a connection to the practice-context, which means that we will work to develop both oral and written communication skills relevant to the practice of criminal law. Those activities will be largely case and problem-based, so that you can see how your developing skills in legal analysis and legal problem solving relate to your future professional careers. You will also further develop your skills in statutory interpretation, which are fundamental to the practice of criminal law in contemporary NSW.
learning_outcomes: Explain the major procedures involved in criminal law and its practice.
Use legal reasoning to generate solutions to hypothetical criminal law problems.
Employ developed oral and written communication skills to transmit knowledge and ideas in the criminal law context, including in forms relevant to its professional practice.
Identify social, political, moral and ethical dimensions of criminal law and its practice.
Apply primary and secondary materials to develop persuasive criminal law arguments.
Outline major concepts and principles in the criminal law.

title: Contracts I
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course is one of two courses (Contracts I and II) that together provide an integrated understanding of the concepts, doctrines and theories underpinning contract law. The topics covered in this course include the law relating to the formation of contracts, an introduction to the equitable concept of estoppel and contract excuses (i.e. vitiating factors that might prevent the contract from being enforced). These topics are explored in line with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals 8 and 16, as contracts promote economic growth and development while strengthening the rule of law. The course will also focus on developing skills in note-taking, problem-solving, and referencing. These skills will complement and reinforce your understanding of the course content areas and will build your graduate skills portfolio.
learning_outcomes: Express contracts concepts and problem-solving clearly using relevant and accurate referencing.
Analyse and critically evaluate modern Australian contract law, including the transactional and policy frameworks within which it operates.
Create notes by reading and synthesising cases and use those notes to resolve legal problems.
Draft reasoned and supported legal and factual arguments relating to contract disputes, including critical judgments about their likely resolution.

title: Contracts II
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Contracts II examines the principles of contract law, including the law relating to termination) and remedies. This course focuses on the function the law plays in facilitating the performance and enforceability of contracts and their limitations as supported by; theories, legal precedent and history shaping the development of the law of contract. The course contributes to the enhancement of legal skills in legal analysis, critical thinking and problem solving to build graduates' skill portfolio. This course supports the UN Sustainable Development Goals 8 and 16, as contract law supports economic growth and development and strengthens the rule of law.
learning_outcomes: Conduct high-level legal research and analysis of primary legal materials, presenting the results in a logical manner and in clear and concise English.
Create persuasive legal and factual arguments relating to contract disputes, and form critical judgments about their likely resolution.

Determine and gather the information needed to support the understanding of a specific problem, clearly presenting and justifying their own views while responding critically and thoughtfully to the ideas of others.
Use questioning strategies to gather the information needed to support understanding and develop research arguments.
Demonstrate the ability to manage risk by assessing and formulating possible courses of action and the range of likely outcomes in a context of commercial and business realities.
Explain, interpret and apply modern Australian contract law, including the policy framework within which it operates.

title: Constitutional Law
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course primarily deals with the study of the Australian Constitution . State constitutions receive limited attention. The aim of the course is to impart an understanding of the fundamentals of Australian constitutional law through the study of key judicial decisions on powers and prohibitions in the Commonwealth Constitution. In a one semester course it is neither possible nor desirable to study all aspects of constitutional law. The course is designed to provide a conceptual framework for solving problems about constitutional law by a detailed, analytical treatment of selected topics. Mastery of these should enable students to master all issues arising in constitutional law whether or not they are specifically dealt with in this course.
learning_outcomes: Using advanced legal research skills provide critical analysis of and reflection on primary and secondary materials;
Communicate constitutional law arguments clearly and persuasively to a variety of audiences.
Critically and with integrated understanding assess the adequacy of the Constitution as Australia's fundamental law and basic instrument of government and the scope for constitutional reform;

Demonstrate a coherent and advanced understanding of (i) the function of the High Court as the final arbiter of constitutionality in Australia and (ii) the techniques of judicial review as applied in Australia;
Using advanced legal skills, identify legal issues, adduce relevant legal principles and rules and apply these to solve problems (whether hypothetical or real) based on constitutional law;
Demonstrate contextual and advanced knowledge of constitutional law doctrine;

title: Administrative Law
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: The study of Administrative Law involves examination of the legal rules and institutions through which government decision-making is authorised, controlled, and challenged. This course examines the legal principles that regulate the exercise of executive power by administrative agencies and officials, and the means by which administrative decisions can be supervised, controlled and challenged. It explains the role of tribunals in providing merits review and the role of the courts in undertaking judicial review (which is a key vehicle in promoting the rule of law). Particular attention is paid to the grounds for judicial review and the consequences of unlawful decision-making. Consideration is also given to the role of independent statutory agencies such as the Ombudsman and anti-corruption bodies in investigating individual complaints about government decision-making as well as undertaking investigations into systemic problems in administration. Means of accessing information held by the administration are also evaluated.
learning_outcomes: Advanced skills in oral and written communication in the context of administrative law.
Advanced knowledge and understanding of the concepts and principles of administrative law.
Critical understanding of the values of administrative law, and of the avenues to seek review of decisions made by government bodies.
Advanced legal reasoning, statutory interpretation, and case analysis skills to solve administrative law problems
Advanced skills in statutory interpretation and in analysing case law as well as the ability to identify and analyse relevant secondary sources.
Critical awareness of ambiguities in administrative law, current issues in administrative law, and the contexts in which administrative law may be relevant.

title: Civil Dispute Resolution
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This core course examines the principles, processes, rules and participatory methods that shape how civil disputes are managed and resolved in New South Wales. This course develops core legal knowledge of litigation and alternative forms of dispute resolution (including mediation and negotiation) based on the relevant Prescribed Academic Areas of Knowledge required for admission to legal practice (see the Content section below). The course is also designed to develop legal skills in accordance with the School of Law and Justice's Graduate Skills Portfolio, focusing on proficiency in three areas: negotiation skills, skills in policy analysis and reform, and writing for a lay (non-legal) audience.
learning_outcomes: Select and apply appropriate approaches to communicate clearly and persuasively with legal and non-legal audiences, without compromising the accuracy of the legal information.
Practise and reflect upon the skills involved in ethically negotiating to resolve disputes.
Analyse and evaluate the policies and principles that underline the Australian civil justice system and propose meaningful law reform to litigation and other dispute resolution processes.

Apply a specialised and advanced knowledge and understanding of the roles of the civil justice system(s), dispute resolution processes (from the commencement of proceedings through to enforcement), and the operation of civil procedure rules to solve complex practical problems.

title: Evidence
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Introduces students to the legal rules and principles governing the adducing of evidence and proof of facts in civil and criminal trials. Topics covered include relevance, competence and compellability, privilege, kinds of evidence, the examination of witnesses, burdens and standards of proof, illegally obtained evidence and the various exclusionary rules, such as hearsay, opinion, admissions, credibility and tendency/coincidence. The Evidence Acts 1995 (NSW) & (Cth) form the backbone to the course.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate effective communication skills in the oral seminar discussions and written presentation of assessment tasks based on the course materials.
Demonstrate some critical appreciation of the way in which the rules of evidence operate and are applied in the context of the trial process.
Demonstrate a developing ability to use legal analysis effectively in application of the relevant principles and rules of evidence law to a range of factual problems.

Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the principles and rules of evidence law used in the process of fact-finding in both civil and criminal litigation in New South Wales and in the Federal jurisdiction

title: Company Law
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with an integrated understanding of the body of legal rules that regulate companies in Australia. Topics covered include the management and control of companies; the process by which companies transact; and the process by which companies are both initiated and brought to an end. Detailed consideration is also given to the notion of corporate personality; the means by which companies can be financed; and the rights of creditors, shareholders and other stakeholders. In addition to detailed knowledge of this complex area of law, this course also provides students with an understanding of the principles and assumptions that underlie the way companies are regulated in Australia; the social and economic implications of this approach to corporate regulation; and the potential implications of challenging these theoretical assumptions. For example, the course explores debates regarding the extent to which corporate law influences the impact companies have on economic development, human rights, social justice and environmental issues such as climate change
learning_outcomes: Explain the key aspects of the body of legal rules that regulate companies and contemporary developments in relation to this body of rules.

Identify and articulate complex legal issues that arise in business practice and demonstrate advanced analysis of statutory provisions and case-law; sophisticated legal reasoning; and well-developed skills in creative thinking to identify appropriate legal and practical responses to those issues
Interpret and critically analyse statutory provisions, including alternatives to the existing provisions.
Critically assess legal and policy analysis in academic journals and other secondary sources regarding the legal rules that regulate corporations.

Synthesise your critical assessment of the information and analysis found in relevant sources in order to interpret, critique and justify propositions about legal and policy issues relevant to the rules governing corporations.
Describe the theoretical assumptions that underlie the way companies are regulated in Australia and the way changes to those assumptions might result in law reform.

title: Professional Conduct
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Examines and critically reviews the role of the legal profession and the legal, ethical and professional conduct duties and responsibilities of lawyers. Students consider the history, structure and regulation of the legal profession, before focusing on the admission requirements to the legal profession. The course considers in detail the duties and obligations of a lawyer to the courts, clients, other legal practitioners, the public and other parties. The course will examine in detail the ethical and professional conduct issues and dilemmas that can arise for a lawyer in practice including in the area of law and technology. The course also focuses on the legal profession and its commitment to pro bono and social justice and considers a lawyer’s role in assisting marginalised persons to access justice and pursue human rights.
learning_outcomes: Conduct high-level research, explore primary and secondary materials, and provide critical analysis of problems and questions.
Critically examine the role of the legal profession and its service to the public
Identify professional conduct issues and apply the relevant professional conduct rules, principles and case law and to take action which complies with those professional conduct rules and principles.
Identify and avoid any potential or actual conflict of interest and take action to deal with a conflict which has arisen.
Apply the legislation, rules and case law to professional conduct problems in a problem based learning context
Demonstrate thorough knowledge of the law and the regulatory framework governing lawyers in relation to ethical and professional conduct issues and their cost disclosure requirements
Critically evaluate and reflectively engage with legal ethics and professional conduct issues and critically evaluate the institutional framework for regulating the legal profession

Identify and critically analyse the wider issues in legal practice including the importance of pro bono contributions by the legal profession, acting as an advocate for the just rule of law, critically evaluating the barriers that some people face in accessing justice and the legal system and respond to demands for reform in an analytical and public-spirited fashion.

title: Equity and Trusts
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: The course introduces the concepts and principles which have been developed by the courts in the exercise of the equitable jurisdiction. It examines the history of equity, the concept of the "fusion fallacy", assignments, equitable dispositions and the requirement of writing, confidential information, fiduciary obligations, the concept of the trust, express trusts, charitable trusts, resulting trusts, constructive trusts and equitable remedies.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the role of equitable interests within our legal system and evaluate the origins, principles, and justifications for equitable rights and actions.
Demonstrate a comprehensive knowledge of the history, concepts and principles of equity and trusts law.
Identify and apply legal principles using case law and statute to resolve practical problems in the area of equity and trusts law.
Identify the various types of equitable interest in NSW and explain how these interests are created, transferred and extinguished.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Formal examination run by exams in examination period (open book)

title: Property
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Introduces students to the notion of property and interests in property, covering such topics as distinctions between real and personal property, notions of title and ownership, legal and equitable interests in property, and the enforceability of proprietary interests. The bulk of the course addresses the area of real property, and the principles of the Torrens system in particular.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an aptitude for the acquisition, interpretation, analysis and scholarly utilisation of appropriate research sources
Write concise documents that accurately convey legal information relating to property law issues.
Identify policy issues as they apply to Property Law, critically analyse and synthesise a variety of policy arguments, and develop their own position on a policy issue.
Identify the various types of property interests protected by property law in New South Wales (particularly land), and explain how these property interests are created, transferred and extinguished
Apply legal principles (using case law and statute) to critically analyse and solve problems that may arise in practice - particularly where property interests overlap or conflict.
Read and analyse key cases and statutory provisions in Australian property law.

title: Public International Law
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Public international law (PIL) introduces you to a legal system that operates at the international level. Like the domestic legal system, international law has normative and institutional frameworks that regulate the relations between states, international organisations and other actors with the objective of promoting the rule of law in their encounters. PIL governs relations across a myriad of topics ranging from the moon to the deep seabed, from climate change to gender and social justice issues. The course explores the nature of international law, competing notions of sovereignty, the making and enforcement of international law and the dilemma of conflict resolution between parties under international law. Special attention will be paid to statehood and the recognition of states, the prohibition of the use of force and aggression, and topical issues in international law, such as criminal justice, the law of armed conflict, human rights and the law of the sea. Students will gain knowledge of the public international legal framework and be exposed to a range of controversial debates which reflect the highly politicised nature of international law. A blended learning format will enable active learning and encourage student engagement with topical issues.
learning_outcomes: A thorough and contextual knowledge of public international law doctrine, principles and the role of legal institutions, in the areas covered during the course.
A reflective understanding of the significance of notions of justice, sovereignty and rights within the international legal framework.
The ability to conduct high-level legal research, exploring primary and secondary materials, and provide critical analysis of problems and questions.
The capacity to identify contentious issues in public international law and apply legal doctrine to solve problems.
The capacity to prepare and present cogent arguments, orally and in writing, and make productive contributions to class debate and discussion.
A critical perspective on the relationship between public international law and the politics of the international community.

title: Legal Practice 1 - Part A
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: The course introduces the practice of law, focusing on litigation and legal transactions, legal actions and gives emphasis to professional responsibility and ethical behaviour. The course is made up of a modules which covers a variety of areas of practice where communication, research, advocacy and legal transaction skills are utilised. The legal placement requirements for Legal Practice require students to enrol in LAWS6888 in the mid term session of the year in which they take this course. The placement hours may be spread across the full year.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate effective oral and written communication skills.
Understand professional responsibility and professional ethics;
Demonstrate the attainment of knowledge and development of key skills required of entry level lawyers;
Build upon and apply earlier learning in both substantive and procedural law;

title: Legal Practice 1 - Part B
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: The course introduces the practice of law, focusing on litigation and legal transactions, legal actions and gives emphasis to professional responsibility and ethical behaviour. The course is made up of Trust Accounting and Civil Litigation Practice.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the attainment of knowledge and development of key skills required of entry level lawyers;
Understand professional responsibility and professional ethics;
Demonstrate effective oral and written communication skills.
Build upon and apply earlier learning in both substantive and procedural law;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Drafting Exercise for Civil Litigation Practice
Problem-based assessment task for Civil Litigation Practice

title: Legal Practice 2 - Part B
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course builds upon the course Legal Practice 1, focusing on the more advanced aspects of litigation and legal transactions. It gives emphasis to professional responsibility and relevant ethical behaviour. This course is made up of a number of components and modules which cover a variety of areas of legal practice where communication, research, advocacy and legal transaction skills are utilised. Students undertake advocacy simulation and drafting exercises.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate development of the oral and written skills needed to practice law;
Apply earlier learning in both substantive and procedural law;
Demonstrate knowledge and advanced skills required of an entry level lawyer;
Demonstrate an understanding of the management of legal practices, time management, professional responsibility and professional ethics.

title: Legal Practice 2 - Part A
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course builds upon the course Legal Practice 1, focusing on the more advanced aspects of litigation and legal transactions. It gives emphasis to professional responsibility and relevant ethical behaviour. The course is made up of a number of modules which cover a variety of areas of legal practice where communication, research, advocacy and legal transaction skills are utilised. Students undertake simulation and drafting exercises.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate development of the oral and written skills needed to practice law;
Demonstrate an understanding of the management of legal practices, time management, professional responsibility and professional ethics.
Apply earlier learning in both substantive and procedural law;
Demonstrate knowledge and advanced skills required of an entry level lawyer;

assessment_tasks.task_name: In Class Test - Completion of Contract For Sale

title: Law Review
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course develops knowledge and skills in the processes of writing, editing, publication and marketing for legal publishing. Through work on the School's journal, The Newcastle Law Review, students are exposed to the publication process and gain practical experience in all stages of legal publishing, including research, writing and practical tasks.
learning_outcomes: Produce an original and authentic piece of legal writing that meets the publisher’s requirements and is suitable for publication in terms of both style and substance.
Communicate sensitively and diplomatically with contributors and/or editorial team members when required.
Undertake legal research making appropriate and ethical use of available tools and technology.

Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the various types of academic publishing and the ethical and practical issues relating to the assessment of articles and other submissions to the journal or other medium.

title: International Clinical Legal Externship
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course requires students to integrate the theoretical concepts and knowledge obtained during their program with real world skills and experience in an international context. Students will undertake an international work-integrated learning placement, in block mode. This work-integrated, experiential learning will be supported by appropriate readings and academic guidance.
