Demonstrate specialised and advanced knowledge the sources of legal disputes or conflicts, and a developed capacity to understand and use the language of dispute resolution.
Demonstrate an advanced knowledge of the processes of non-litigious dispute resolution.
Identify all the options by which disputes can be resolved or managed and apply dispute resolution knowledge and a range of problem solving skills in dispute resolution processes.
Analyse critically and reflect on complex theories of non-litigious dispute resolution.

title: International Arbitration
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with an in-depth knowledge and critical understanding of the fundamentals of the practice of international commercial arbitration, a self contained international legal system based upon the will of the contracting parties and drawn together by the New York Convention and relevant National laws. The course is a combination of legal theory, practical and procedural analysis and will appeal to those students who wish to study law in an international setting. This course is comparative and will expose students to a range of international commercial arbitration laws and institutional rules, including in Australia, England, Switzerland, France, Singapore and Hong Kong. Students will learn how to draft arbitration agreements, commence and run arbitration proceedings, as well as enforce and challenge arbitral awards under the 1958 New York Convention and local National and State laws. Students will also learn about specialised forms of international arbitration and the Court of Arbitration for Sport including investor-state arbitration.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate and apply advanced, specialised knowledge of legal principles in the regulation and infrastructure of international arbitration;
Acquire a knowledge of the principles of international trade and commerce as they are configured in commercial arbitration disputes.
Apply acquired legal knowledge in solving practical problem cases in an international commercial arbitration context;
Acquire a knowledge of the growing corpus of 'soft law' in international commercial arbitration including the IBA rules on the Taking of Evidence.
Evaluate key policy and practice surrounding investor-state arbitration.
Demonstrate and apply advanced, specialised knowledge of the procedural and conceptual issues that may arise in international arbitration;

title: Human Rights and Climate Change-Induced Human Displacement
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Climate change is today one of the top agendas in both domestic and international politics. The broad range of actors and systems that it impacts, such as humans and life, the earth, the oceans, the atmosphere and all in between, has prompted an unprecedented attention on the issue. There is also an acute focus on the great concern it poses for human rights protection. However, though the science of climate change has been established for a while now, the political, economic and social context within which we deal with climate change has meant that responses are slow. The existence of a wide array of actors and interests represented in the climate change debate continues to affect mitigation and adaptation strategies. This hurdle relates both to dealing with climate change and its impacts. A recognition of the direct impact of climate change on current and future generations and the urgency with which the international community needs to act has therefore given rise to an advocacy strategy that puts human rights at the centre of policy debates. This course will focus on issues at the intersection of climate change and human rights as they relate to a particular impact of climate change: the forced displacement of people from their abodes. It explores the institutions and actors as well as the international legal frameworks on climate change, human rights and forcibly displaced persons. Students will gain specialised knowledge of the impacts of climate change and the debate arounds approaches to dealing with them. The course further involves case studies that highlight the themes and considers special issues related to climate change. The course is primarily concerned with international law; however, students will have several opportunities to explore the interaction between international and domestic human rights protections.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate advanced understanding and knowledge of the key international principles and rules on human rights law with a focus on climate change-induced human displacement.
Evaluate and critically analyse the role of key actors in the area of human rights, climate change and climate-induced displacement.
Make professional contributions to the future development of law and policy.
Demonstrate specialised understanding of existing human rights mechanisms and the gaps for addressing climate displacement.
Conduct high-level legal research, exploring primary and secondary materials, in order to generate and justify theoretical and practical legal propositions.
Prepare and present cogent arguments, orally and in writing, that are persuasive for a legal audience.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Participation: Active learning participation in seminars
Presentation: Individual presentation prepared & delivered either in seminar or in a video recording

title: Expert Evidence
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Experts play a very important and unique role in all areas of the law. This area of law is governed by its own provisions in the Evidence Act and the corresponding regulations and legislation that provides for procedures relating to experts. This course deals with the role of experts in legal proceedings. It considers the ways in which experts deal with their area of expertise in a legal context both in adversarial and non-adversarial settings. The course highlights the professional and ethical standards required of an expert to the Court and their duties when compiling their reports and giving evidence in a proceeding. The course will cover the role of experts in civil, criminal, family law, coronial inquests, and forensic jurisdictions such as domestic courts and tribunals. The course has a practical component where guest presenters will share their knowledge and experience firsthand as either experts preparing court reports or giving evidence, solicitors and barristers adducing the evidence, and judges’ perspective’s as hearing the expert evidence as the finder of fact or to guide a jury in how to use the evidence by way of directions. It considers the admissibly of expert evidence, alternative modes of expert evidence presentation, adversarial influences on expert presentations and jury responses to expert witnesses.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate specialised knowledge and skills necessary to comply with expert rules and principles and effectively deal with experts.
Integrate and analyse the theory and practice of expert evidence in legal proceedings.
Critically evaluate and reflect on the ethical and professional responsibilities of experts and the principles which apply to them when dealing with courts and tribunals and in legal proceedings

title: Advanced Communication Skills
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course aims to equip students with a mastery of communication skills to ensure they are excellent communicators and effective professionals, by focusing on high-conflict situations. Law is a discipline that involves conflict. Indeed, most business or professional settings involve some degree of conflict. Students will focus on high-conflict personality types, exploring the common features of this personality, and practice strategies about how to effectively communicate and handle people with high-conflict personalities. The dynamics of high-conflict situations faced in professional practice will be analysed, equipping students with the ability to identify high-conflict situations and determine the necessary approach required. Students will gain knowledge and skills through role plays, including client interviewing and coaching, mediation in high-conflict situations, managing high-conflict legal and workplace disputes, and implementing strategies to reduce conflict in organisational systems. This course will ensure our students have an advantage over other professionals and allow them to succeed and thrive in adverse legal and business situations.
learning_outcomes: Conduct research into high-conflict dispute resolution practices

Utilise effective communication skills in potential high-conflict situations, such as interviewing or coaching clients, collaborating with other professionals, and when involved in meetings or conferences.
Implement strategies to manage high-conflict situations whilst effectively collaborating and maintaining professional standards
Analyse high-conflict situations, including court hearings, meetings, and conferences.
Demonstrate an understanding of personality traits common to people with high-conflict personalities and apply strategies to effectively manage situations involving these people

title: Corporate Power and Corporate Accountability: Pathways to Socially Responsible Business
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Traditionally, states have primarily sought to ensure that business entities operate in a socially and environmentally responsible manner by using a 'command and control' approach: that is, they have established legal rules and put in place inspectorates and courts to monitor compliance and punish non-compliance. Globalisation has challenged this approach, … For more content click the Read More button below. Traditionally, states have primarily sought to ensure that business entities operate in a socially and environmentally responsible manner by using a 'command and control' approach: that is, they have established legal rules and put in place inspectorates and courts to monitor compliance and punish non-compliance. Globalisation has challenged this approach, and even for business activity wholly within state borders this model has not always proved effective. This course will critically consider the efficacy of legal and non-judicial alternatives, including: alternative legal structures for business (especially cooperatives), responsive regulation, multi-stakeholder initiatives, ethical investment and ethical consumerism. Case examples will focus on state and private initiatives designed to address the impact that businesses have on corruption, human rights, social justice, social inclusion, gender issues and environmental issues such as climate change.
learning_outcomes: Design appropriate and innovative strategies to influence corporations to move towards the organisational change required to address human rights abuse or environmental degradation that is linked to their business activity.
Critically reflect on different theoretical perspectives regarding the influence of business entities on respect for human rights and the environment and be prepared to comment on these perspectives.

Compare and critically evaluate efforts by business entities, including co-operatives, to implement human rights and environmental obligations, including through participation in non-state non-judicial mechanisms, such as multi-stakeholder initiatives.

Compare and critically evaluate efforts by states to ensure that business entities respect human rights and the environment through judicial and state-based non-judicial mechanisms and by providing scope for alternative legal structures, such as cooperatives.

title: Mediation Skills and Theory
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course enables students to develop and practice essential skills required in mediation. Students will explore the skills required for effective and successful mediation, including communication, negotiation and dispute resolution skills. Mediation processes will be explored to enable students to gain an understanding of the roles of the various parties in a mediation, and of the strategies that can be employed during a mediation. Students will participate in scenarios which assess their mediation skills and demonstrate how to address conflict through mediation and also allow the students to critically analyse scenarios to determine how resolution through mediation could be achieved. Working with a mediation model, students will learn alternative approaches to deal with varying circumstances and will also investigate theoretical issues and relevant empirical studies in mediation ethics, inter-cultural context, contingent 3rd party interventions, power and empowerment, as well as other topics. The course considers access to justice as well as rule of law issues.
learning_outcomes: Conduct research in current issues in conflict resolution based on knowledge of appropriate research principles and methods.
Demonstrate a range of skills and techniques in communication, negotiation and mediation.
Understand the importance of mediation and how it is applied throughout the legal profession
Demonstrate a theoretical understanding of mediation, and the roles of parties involved in a mediation.
Investigate, analyse and reflect meaningfully on complex information and problems in relation to the facilitative mediation model.
Demonstrate an ability to explain the different approaches to negotiation and when each might be appropriate
Apply knowledge of, and understanding of, the facilitative mediation model and the purpose of each stage in the process, with creativity and initiative, to new situations in professional practice.
Use cognitive, technical and creative skills to generate and evaluate, at an abstract level, complex ideas and concepts relevant to the facilitative mediation model.

title: Restorative Justice
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Restorative justice and practices involve an alternative approach to conflict resolution based on a framework where relationships are placed at the centre. This course will introduce students to the concept of restorative justice as a means of resolving disputes with a particular focus on the criminal justice system. The extension of restorative practices in the broader community to building collaborative, inclusive and resilient communities will also be explored. Through exploring this concept and the broader framework for restorative practices, the course will focus on conflict resolution that actively involves the victims, offenders, and community members in a joint decision-making process and building relationships rather than traditional legal and court-based mechanisms. The course, while focusing on the criminal justice system, will consider the wider applicability of restorative practices, such as in child welfare, youth justice, education, health, and business settings. The course will also explore the strengths and limitations that restorative practices may have in some applications, and where restorative justice options may not be applicable or possible to implement.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate research, oral and written communication skills in locating, discussing and evaluating issues arising from restorative justice and practice and the broad implementation of a such an approach and practice.
Explain and apply a restorative justice framework for effective practice in the criminal justice system
Explain and analyse the concept of restorative justice
Critically evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of restorative justice and restorative practice in the criminal justice system and other settings.

Critically analyse and discuss the use of restorative justice and practice approaches and programs in a variety of community settings and the future development of such an alternative justice paradigm and practice.

title: Food and Wine Law
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course examines a range law and policy issues relating to the production, consumption, and trade of food and wine. Its purpose is to introduce participants to the breadth of issues that impact the food we eat and the wine we drink, and to examine and critique their multiple roles as expressions of culture and identity; as daily necessities (at least in the case of food); and objects of commerce both locally and internationally. Note that this is not a 'how to' course for food and wine producers and does not cover aspects of the law where food and wine are treated like other commodities, such as contracts or tortious liability.
learning_outcomes: Compare the breadth of legal issues that regulate food and wine in Australia and internationally.
Identify and critically evaluate, through oral and written communication, the current laws that impact food and wine
Engage in debate about the consequences of current laws and areas for reform

title: Negotiation in a Legal Context
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: The course focuses on negotiation strategies, styles and skills within a legal context. The course is delivered in and intensive format with blended-learning which enables the theoretical and practical aspects of negotiation to be explored. Students will be introduced to the fundamentals of negotiation through Harvard Negotiation model and given the opportunity to build up their own negotiation capability. Particularly, through multi agent interactive models and case studies, students will practice negotiating with role-playing simulations that cover a range of topics, including difficult situations such as cross-cultural scenarios. In addition, students will focus on legal issues relating to confidentiality, good faith, the enforceability of outcomes and focus on the role of lawyers and experts in negotiation.
learning_outcomes: Apply advanced and specialised knowledge in managing conflicts and solving practical problem cases.
Evaluate personal styles and approaches in a bargaining context.
Demonstrate advanced and specialised knowledge about negotiation contexts.
Evaluate key policy and legal issues surrounding negotiation.

title: Law for Startups
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Law for Startups will take the class through the key legal steps of moving from an idea to an operating business. The course commences by highlighting some common legal mistakes commonly made by startups. The focus then shifts to key legal and regulatory issues behind the various stages of the startup. This includes both a practical focus on what can be done effectively on a tight budget at an early stage and identification of areas where a significant legal spend will add value as the startup matures.
learning_outcomes: Show an understanding of a specific practice area and demonstrate an ability to educate clients, with an understanding of the level of legal knowledge of most startup entrepreneurs and the fast-paced commercial environment of startups.
Provide a legal advice that gives an overview of the main issues facing a startup and gives suitable emphasis to the most relevant issues.
Demonstrate an ability to prepare in-depth, practical and detailed advice within a specific practice area.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Case Study / Problem Based Learning Exercises

title: Final-Year Workplace Experience
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Final-Year Workplace Experience provides students with a work-integrated learning experience to enable students to acquire the specialised technical knowledge and skills in litigation and transactions required of entry level lawyers seeking admission to the legal profession.
learning_outcomes: Apply specialised technical knowledge of the practice of law in litigation and transactions;
Identify and interpret the role of professional responsibility and judgment in the practice of law at an advanced level;
Explain and value the management of legal practices and time management in legal practice.
Use practical legal skills including communication with real clients, drafting letters and legal documents together with the ability to conduct relevant and detailed legal research;
Use judgment, creativity, adaptability and initiative in applying the relevant law to new factual situations in professional legal practice;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Mandatory attendance at all practicums with completion of 180 hours placement

title: Renewable Energy Law Clinic
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: The legal issues which arise during the life cycle of a renewable energy project will be explored in the innovative context of a specialist legal clinic where students will work, under supervision, on legal advice and resources to benefit the community or start-up organisations who are engaged in the renewable energy sector and who do not have the current capacity to pay for specialised legal assistance. The School of Law and Justice will call for expressions of interest from organisations interested in participating in the clinic prior to the commencement of the course and this EOI process will be publicised by relevant industry news sites and peak body social media. To support the work integrated learning experience, students will engage in online and in class learning focused on relevant aspects of the legal and policy framework which applies to renewable energy projects. The course will also give students the opportunity to practically apply the legal knowledge acquired in core courses such as property law and contract law.
learning_outcomes: Design and create a practical resource that provides value to an organisation or sector of the community that requires support to engage
Identify sectors of the community that require support to better engage in the renewable energy sector and justify why that support is needed.
Identify and articulate complex concepts in renewable energy law;
Explain and critique the specialised, complex and integrated body of laws and policies that govern renewable energy projects.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Presentation on the laws and policies that affect renewable energy projects

title: Torts I
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Torts I (together with Torts II) examines the rules of law by which liability for civil wrongs is imposed. Tort law examines a wide range of topics that are closely relevant to fundamental human rights, including bodily integrity and property rights. Tort law also provides an important mechanism to engage with the use of public power (such as the action for false imprisonment and the action for negligence) and address potential corruption issues (such as in the action for misfeasance in public office). Both common law and statutory schemes are considered, including defences, remedies and the assessment of damages, with a view to promoting the rule of law.
learning_outcomes: Critically read, analyse and reflect on case law and statutes, learning within a collaborative environment and develop appropriate notes in relation to those sources.
Orally present and defend arguments in interactive dialogue with the teacher and peers in a style consistent with professional client consultations, mediation, negotiation and court appearances.
Identify legal principles and employ legal techniques and approaches to resolve complex practical problems in the area of tort law.
Analyse critically, reflect on and synthesise information on the role of tort law in the civil justice system and contemporary Australian society.
Research primary and secondary legal materials in a timely and accurate fashion, so as to access recent developments in the area as well as the foundational doctrines.
Integrate an advanced understanding of legal process and methods, with substantive areas of the law of tort.
Structure and present a coherent and persuasive argument using legal data, both orally and in writing, in accordance with legal professional practice.
Present a clear and reflective analysis of complex competing policy considerations.

title: Torts II
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Torts II (together with Torts I) examines the rules of law by which liability for civil wrongs is imposed. Tort law examines a wide range of topics that are closely relevant to fundamental human rights, including bodily integrity and property rights. Tort law also provides an important mechanism to engage with the use of public power (such as the action for false imprisonment and the action for negligence) and addresses potential corruption issues (such as in the action for misfeasance in public office). Both common law and statutory schemes are considered, including defences, remedies and the assessment of damages, with a view to promoting the rule of law
learning_outcomes: Analyse critically, reflect on and synthesise information on the role of tort law in the civil justice system and contemporary Australian society.
Present a clear and reflective analysis of complex competing policy considerations.
Structure and present a coherent and persuasive argument using legal data, both orally and in writing, in accordance with legal professional practice.
Identify legal principles and employ legal techniques and approaches to resolve complex practical problems in the area of tort law.
Integrate an advanced understanding of legal process and methods, with substantive areas of the law of tort.
Research primary and secondary legal materials in a timely and accurate fashion, so as to access recent developments in the area as well as the foundational doctrines.
Critically read, analyse and reflect on case law and statutes, learning within a collaborative environment.

title: Principles of Construction Law
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course explores the key legal principles that apply to construction law and disputes. It begins with an introduction to the construction industry and the nature of construction law. It moves on to construction contracts and common issues during project delivery (focusing on the critical factors of time, quality and cost). It concludes with an overview of construction claims and disputes, including methods of dispute avoidance and resolution. Students will test their understanding of each of these topics by proposing solutions to problems based on real-world and hypothetical construction projects.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate and implement the key principles of construction law
Apply the principles of construction law to the selection, preparation, formation and interpretation of contracts
Identify and apply the legislative and regulatory framework to the delivery of construction projects
Formulate and argue claims and defences in relation to common construction disputes and recommend appropriate methods of dispute resolution and avoidance

title: Elder Law
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: A significant ageing population, the changing profile of older people in the Australian community and their relationship with the contemporary legal landscape presents a timely and strategic opportunity to support student learning of the key legal issues affecting our elders. A broad approach is taken in this course to the contemporary concept of ‘elder law’ in the context of making decisions, financial arrangements, living arrangements, equitable, fair and dignified treatment, and future considerations. There is a focus on developing necessary practical skills as well as deepening cultural awareness and understanding of ageing and its legal ramifications.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate relevant primary and secondary legal material in the specific context of the interaction of older people with the law.
Formulate relevant and cogent arguments in representing an older person in various legal practice and other settings.
Discuss the key legal issues affecting elders in our community.
Interpret legal issues affecting elders in our community and evaluate pathways to law reform in resolving such issues

title: Contemporary Issues In Australian Public Law
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: The effect of public law frameworks on government and society is the subject of increasing interest and debate. The Australian public law framework has proven capable of swift adaptation in the face of major challenges (such as the global financial crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic), yet is also stubbornly resistant to change. This course will explore a selection of hot topics and debates in Australian constitutional and administrative law. Topics will be selected for their potential to extend knowledge and understanding of the role of law in Australian government and politics, and to support critical analysis of the operation of public law in practice. Assessment items are designed to extend skills in sustained and persuasive written communication. Students will develop capacity to analyse and synthesise relevant primary and secondary sources and to communicate complex technical information accurately and succinctly. Although the course will focus primarily on the Australian context, it will include comparative, transnational and theoretical perspectives where those approaches aid critical evaluation of public law in contemporary Australia.
learning_outcomes: Produce written research outputs appropriate to specialist and non-specialist audiences.
Critically analyse the contemporary Australian public law framework and its application to complex problems in Australian law and government;
Explain concepts and principles relating to contemporary issues in Australian public law at an advanced level;
Implement research strategies to explore theoretical and practical dimensions of Australian public law and adapt these for implementation in practice;

title: Advanced Property Equity and Commercial Law
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Advanced Property, Equity and Commercial Law is an elective course for students who wish to enhance their knowledge of private law matters. It examines important legal subjects such as commercial chattels and fixtures, commercial sale of goods, part performance, equitable estoppel, unconscionability, undue influence, equitable priorities, the in personam exception to Torrens indefeasibility, adverse possession, commercial leasing, complex aspects of fiduciary law, and equitable remedies. Although the course primarily focuses on doctrinal matters, it also considers legal policy issues as and when appropriate.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse legal policy issues relevant to advanced equity, property and commercial law.
Critically evaluate relevant priminary and second legal material in the specific context of advanced equity, property and commercial law
Examine the history, concepts and principles of advanced equity, property and commercial law.
Employ expert legal judgement in advanced equity, property and commercial law issues through oral and written communication.

title: Private International Law (Conflict of Laws)
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Private international law is part of the local private law in every legal system concerned with legal issues containing foreign elements (a relevant connection between a fact or party and a foreign legal system). For example, private international law issues require consideration if a question arises in New South Wales concerning a breach of contract to be performed in New York, a civil wrong committed in Japan, or the distribution of the property of a person who died domiciled in France. This course aims to develop your understanding of the international dimension of private law and your appreciation of the fact that many legal questions arising in everyday life are not confined to one legal system. We will address the three persistent issues in private international law: jurisdiction, choice of law and the recognition and enforcement of foreign judgments.
learning_outcomes: Construct and communicate legal arguments on key areas of private international law, including jurisdiction, choice of law, and enforcement of foreign judgments, while exercising autonomy, expert judgment, adaptability and responsibility as a future practitioner and lifelong learner
Apply principles and rules of private international law to various civil and commercial scenarios, showing an advanced and integrated understanding of private law with foreign elements.
Analyse problems, methods and techniques of private international law related to cross-border or transnational legal issues

title: Contracts I
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course is one of two courses (Contracts I and II) that together provide an integrated understanding of the concepts, doctrines and theories underpinning contract law. The topics covered in this course include the law relating to the formation of contracts, an introduction to the equitable concept of estoppel and contract excuses (i.e. vitiating factors that might prevent the contract from being enforced). These topics are explored in line with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals 8 and 16, as contracts promote economic growth and development while strengthening the rule of law. The course will also focus on developing skills in note-taking, problem-solving, and referencing. These skills will complement and reinforce your understanding of the course content areas and will build your graduate skills portfolio.
learning_outcomes: Express contracts concepts and problem-solving clearly using relevant and accurate referencing.
Analyse and critically evaluate modern Australian contract law, including the transactional and policy frameworks within which it operates.
Draft reasoned and supported legal and factual arguments relating to contract disputes, including critical judgments about their likely resolution.
Create notes by reading and synthesising cases and use those notes to resolve legal problems.

title: Criminal Law and Procedure
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Criminal Law and Procedure is the foundational course in criminal law. Students typically study this course in the first year of JD/GDLP programs, which means that this is the first time you learn about the role that the state plays in proscribing norms of behaviour and regulating the conduct of its citizens through the criminal law. The course will take us on an intriguing exploration of human behaviour, the operation of legal institutions, community participation in criminal procedure, social justice and the way in which our criminal laws shape, and are shaped by, contemporary social issues. The course will allow you to develop foundational knowledge of the criminal law. We will foster a contextual and critical understanding of the application of the criminal law in practice. The course focuses primarily on the criminal laws of New South Wales, although comparative components (both within Australia and internationally) are included where appropriate. Much of the course is devoted to studying the major criminal offences listed below. Major defences and the rules and principles of criminal procedure will also be examined in some detail. We will also begin to develop a familiarity with the principal agencies, procedures and routines involved in the administration of criminal justice in contemporary New South Wales. Our learning activities and assessment items in the course have a connection to the practice-context, which means that we will work to develop both oral and written communication skills relevant to the practice of criminal law. Those activities will be largely case and problem-based, so that you can see how your developing skills in legal analysis and legal problem solving relate to professional practice. You will also further develop your skills in statutory interpretation, which are fundamental to the practice of criminal law in contemporary NSW.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the social, political, moral and ethical dimensions of the criminal law and its practice.
Apply legal knowledge and reasoning to generate solutions to hypothetical criminal law problems.
Evaluate the major procedures involved in criminal law and its practice.
Assess primary and secondary materials relevant to the study of criminal law.
Employ advanced oral and written communication skills to transmit knowledge and ideas in the criminal law context, including in forms relevant to its professional practice.
Explain major concepts and principles in the criminal law.

title: Contracts II
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Contracts II examines the principles of contract law, including the law relating to obligations, content, excuses from performance (invalidating factors and termination) and remedies. Students gain knowledge in the functions of contract law and its limitations, contract theories and the historical background to the law of contract together with the forces which are shaping its development. Overall the course provides students with specialised knowledge of an important area of law and also contributes to the enhancement of legal skills in legal analysis and problem solving. The course will also focus on the development of skills in the areas of questioning, critical thinking and risk management. These skills will complement and reinforce your understanding of the course content areas and will build your graduate skills portfolio.
learning_outcomes: Conduct high-level legal research and analysis of primary legal materials, presenting the results in a logical manner and in clear and concise English.
Create persuasive legal and factual arguments relating to contract disputes, and form critical judgments about their likely resolution.

Determine and gather the information needed to support the understanding of a specific problem, clearly presenting and justifying individual views while responding critically and thoughtfully to the ideas of others.
Explain, interpret and apply modern Australian contract law, including the policy framework within which it operates.
Use questioning strategies to gather the information needed to support understanding and develop research arguments.
Demonstrate the ability to manage risk by assessing and formulating possible courses of action and the range of likely outcomes in a context of commercial and business realities.

title: Native Title Law
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Explore the intricate landscape of native title law in Australia, delving into the recognition and protection of First Nations Peoples' rights to land and waters under their traditional laws and customs. This course provides a comprehensive examination of key legal frameworks, including the landmark High Court decisions in Mabo and Wik, and the Native Title Act 1993 (Cth). By situating native title within its broader social, cultural, and legal contexts, students are prepared for careers in native title, cultural heritage, environmental law, human rights law, and related fields. Gain a deep understanding of the complexities and contemporary issues surrounding native title, equipping yourself with the knowledge to contribute to the pursuit of social justice and sustainable resource management.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate case law, legislation and commentary in relation to native title and policy incorporating international legal frameworks, comparative contexts and First Nations Peoples’ perspectives;
Assess complex legal issues within the context of native title and propose strategies for law reform and development.
Employ strong oral and written communication skills to effectively address and resolve legal issues.
Explain key aspects of Australian law, policy, and practice concerning native title, and understand their connection to broader issues of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander culture and law.

title: Banking and Finance Law
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Australia’s banking and finance sector is a complex field where financial activities are regulated through legislation and codes of practice. The course will equip students with a thorough knowledge of the Australian Prudential Regulatory Authority (APRA), the main regulator of the financial services industry, as well as the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) and the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC), the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) and The Treasury. Topics covered will include the regulatory framework for banks and financial institutions, credit, crime and hardship. The course will also expose students to the tensions between existing legal provisions and new innovations pertinent to banking and finance in Australia
learning_outcomes: Construct reasoned solutions to practical legal problems in banking and finance law.
Critically evaluate key policy debates surrounding banking and finance such as interest rates, conflicts of interest and the resilience of banks
Apply specialised statutory provisions and case law relating to banking and finance.

title: Climate Change Law and Policy
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Climate change is already impacting most social and ecological systems on planet Earth. Existing legal and socio-economic frameworks are typically ill-suited to governance of complex problems that span the local and global scales. The course will survey the foundation and evolution of the international climate law regime (under the UNFCCC process) and complementary developments in intersecting areas of international law (eg trade law). It will also critically assess the trajectory of Australian domestic climate and law policy, including national level legislative responses to the threat of climate change, alongside relevant state and local level initiatives. Drawing on interdisciplinary perspectives including law, natural and social sciences, economics and politics, the course will offer students the opportunity to develop skills in collaboration and teamwork across areas of expertise necessary to address climate change.
learning_outcomes: Generate written outputs that convey complex information to specialist and non-specialist audiences..
Explain the causes and likely impacts of climate change and the range of legal and policy responses for mitigating emissions and adapting (or otherwise responding) to its impacts;
Apply technical knowledge to propose evidence-based legal and policy responses to climate change and related issues within diverse social, ecological and economic contexts.
Critically analyse the social, political, economic and ecological factors that shape international and Australian climate law and policy.

title: Gender and the Law
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Understandings of gender are embedded in the law and legal system in ways that are not always immediately obvious. Feminist legal theory challenges the practice and theory of law and provides insights in the law’s power to shape meaning and reinforce disadvantage. This course examines the role of the law in creating and perpetuating gender inequalities and considers strategies for reform. It examines key concepts such as gender, equality and intersectional discrimination and the public/private divide. The course is grounded in theory and practice and examines gendered constructions of law through a series of case studies such as gender and work, family and relationships, violence, reproduction, and representation and power. The aim is to provoke critical thought about law and to provide you with skills to understand and apply feminist and other critical theories to analyse law or legal issues and to generate new perspectives to address gender inequalities in society.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate factual, legal and theoretical issues relating to gender and law using primary and secondary legal and interdisciplinary research sources.
Crtique a selection of key feminist and other critical theories
Formulate cogent and nuanced arguments, both orally and in writing.
Analyse theoretical questions about the relationship between gender and law
Conduct advanced legal research tasks, both individually and in collaboration with others

title: Foundations of Law
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: The law impacts our daily lives in ways particularly evident for those engaged in business, commerce, public service, and professions. This course meets educational needs by introducing the Australian legal system, its legal sources, the rule of law and the court system. Then, it focuses on the law of contract as one of the building blocks of business transactions while introducing other areas of potential legal liability for businesses. A professional conducting business requires a basic understanding of the law regulating torts, consumer protection, employment, agency, and business structures. Students are equipped with tools for analysing and solving legal problems. These skills are transferable to other subjects relevant to business, commerce and industry professionals. This course provides foundational knowledge to identify opportunities and risks for business, and to navigate the Australian legal institutions and think globally.
learning_outcomes: Identify and explain the principal features of the Australian Legal System;
Identify the key areas of the law facilitating running a business and the sources of potential liabilities.
Apply a problem-solving method to key areas of law covered during the course.
Outline the main legal requirements for creating and enforcing a contract;

Outline some the main legal requirements for establishing the tort of negligence, a breach of consumer protection, the employment and the agent-principal relationship, and the key business organisations; and

assessment_tasks.task_name: A Case Law Summary and an IRAC problem question

title: Law of Business Organisations
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Law of Business Organisations introduces students to the registered company as the dominant legal form for carrying on a business. It compares the company with other types of business models, including partnerships, joint ventures, trusts, objectives ad incorporated associations. It considers the legal framework that determines how a company deals with the issues of registration, corporate liability, internal governance, directors duties, financing and insolvency. This course provides students with the theory and practice necessary to set up and operate a business, provide advice, meet regulatory compliance, discharge directors duties, plan business succession and navigate financial stress.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of the legal options available to shareholders and directors of a company in times of financial stress.
Evaluate the factors that influence the choice of legal form for a business enterprise.
Identify and compare the key legal features of the main legal forms of business organisations.
Identify the role of law in corporate management and governance.
Explain the legal relationship in a company between the board of directors, members and executive officers in a company.
Analyse the legal rules that enable and restrict business dealings including third party transactions and raising finance.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Tutorial Learning Activities and Revision tests (MCQ)

title: Workplace Experience 1
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Workplace Experience 1 provides students with an intensive supervised Work Integrated Learning experience to enable students to acquire the technical knowledge and skills in litigation, communication and transactions required of entry level lawyers seeking admission to the legal profession. Through Workplace Experience 1, students will be exposed to a range of clients in the University of Newcastle Legal Centre. All students will spend time with clients who present through a general in-take; additional placement opportunities are available in regard to areas of strategic focus being First Nations clients and/or through the Older Persons Legal Clinic.
learning_outcomes: Develop technical knowledge of the practice of law in litigation and transactions.
Explain the role of professional responsibility and judgment in the practice of law.
Integrate the management of legal practices and time management in legal practice.
Employ practical legal skills including communication with real clients, drafting letters and legal documents, legal problem solving and ability to conduct relevant and detailed legal research.
Demonstrate judgement, adaptability and initiative in applying the relevant law to new factual situations in professional legal practice.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Satisfactory completion of all professional placement tasks

title: Australian Business and Company Law
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course provides a comprehensive overview of the Australian legal system, focusing on contract law, tort law, business structures, and company law. Students will explore the formation and enforcement of contracts, the roles and duties of directors, corporate governance, and insolvency. The course also covers risk management, consumer protection, and various business structures, including sole proprietorships, partnerships, and corporations. These provide students with a holistic picture of the Australian business environment. Through practical assessments, students will develop skills in legal research, problem-solving, and risk assessment, preparing them to navigate the legal challenges faced by businesses in Australia.
learning_outcomes: Explain the structure and function of the Australian legal system, including the sources of law and the role of the Constitution.
Identify and compare the key legal features of the main legal forms of business organisations.
Identify and apply the principles of contract formation, enforceability, terms, and remedies to real-world business scenarios.
Explain the legal relationship in a company between the board of directors, members and executive officers in a company and their duties under the law.
Assess, analyze, and resolve business law issues using problem-based scenarios, focusing on tort law, risk management, and consumer protection.
Explain the processes and legal implications of corporate insolvency, including the roles of receivership and administration in managing financial distress.

title: Survey and Engineering Law
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: The course introduces students to the Australian legal system, including some aspects of basic legal research. It has a focus on legal issues arising in the profession and practice of engineering, with particular emphasis on surveying. It has a strong emphasis on the concepts and classification of real property as they relate to boundary surveyors. It also deals with statutory control of land use as well as the regulation and legal liability of engineers and surveyors. In general, this course provides a legal foundation for the engineer and surveyor of how the law creates opportunities and potential liabilities in their professional practice. This course aligns with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals 9 and 11 in building resilient infrastructure and making cities and urban development inclusive, resilient and sustainable.
learning_outcomes: know when to seek specialist legal advice about a particular area.
state the legal issues that arise in the practice of engineering and surveying, and apply the law to solve problems in specific, fact situations involving professional liability and real property;
in relation to those issues, locate relevant and up-to-date information about the law at an appropriate level, and communicate the results of their knowledge in a structured way;

understand (a) the constitutional framework of Australia as a federation; (b) the sources of Australian law, and basic techniques for finding and interpreting the law; (c) the basic principles underlying key areas of contractual and civil liability; and (d) the land title and planning system in NSW, in particular affecting boundary determination;
identify and avoid areas of potential legal liability or difficulty in practice; and,

assessment_tasks.task_name: Take Home Final Exam 3 Problem Questions

title: Child Law
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Child law is constantly evolving and is complex because it involves arguably one of the most vulnerable groups requiring protection in our community. Issues pertaining to youth justice, youth crime, child neglect, the age of criminal responsibility, immigration, gender dysphoria and family violence, are regularly making headlines in the media with advocacy groups constantly raising concerns for the law needing to change. In this way, child law brings together students in law, social work and other front line services, to look at how law impacts upon children and our social fabric. It builds a foundation for the study of specific laws (childcare and protection, juvenile justice and family law) by exploring human rights, social and legal perspectives. It considers broader legal and social issues that affect children, including: 1. When children are considered capable of making legal decisions (legal capacity). 2. International and human rights law applicable to children in Australia. 3. The nature of inter-professional collaboration on behalf of children in varied legal contexts. 4. Children's interaction with legal processes. 5. Differential impact of laws on certain groups of children, such as Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children.
learning_outcomes: Work more effectively in teams to solve problems.

Demonstrate understanding of: the different and complementary orientations of professionals who work with children; the skills required to develop collaborative interdisciplinary relationships; and an understanding of the importance of interdisciplinary and holistic responses to children and young people's legal issues.
Demonstrate understanding of family, criminal and child protection law, policy and processes as it relates to problem-scenarios concerning children;
Identify the elements of a children's rights approach to legal issues that affect children and young people.
Critically reflect upon legal material presented in the context of professional practice with children and apply this to problem scenarios, demonstrating awareness of a children's rights approach.
Critically analyse the role of law and the limits of the domestic legislative framework from a children's rights perspective.

title: Concepts and Issues in Property and Commercial Law
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with a general introduction to fundamental concepts and legal issues in the areas of property law and commercial law in Australia. This course adds to existing legal courses relevant to students undertaking a Bachelor of Commerce (Accounting).
learning_outcomes: Evaluate and compare approaches to the concepts of property and ownership in different legal systems.
Describe the key steps required to create registrable interests in land including mortgages and leases.
Apply basic legal concepts in commercial law to identify solutions to legal problems encountered by businesses in commercial dealings with consumers and other businesses.
Explain the purpose and effectiveness of the Torrens land title registration system, including the different types of land titling systems.
Identify the main features of legislative schemes for regulating different types of property rights in Australia.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Problem-Based and Short Answer Formal Examination

title: Commercialisation of Intellectual Property
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course introduces student to Intellectual Property law concepts and principles, and develops their knowledge of Intellectual Property commercialisation processes and strategies. It provides students with an intensive learning experience to enable students to acquire technical knowledge of Intellectual Property law and gain an understanding of the business and economics of buying, selling and licensing Intellectual Property.
learning_outcomes: Apply the key areas of Intellectual Property law that govern individuals and businesses to develop solutions to practical problems.
Explain key Intellectual Property concepts and problems underlying them to lay and professional audiences.
Understand the main legal principles and rules that apply to different areas of Intellectual Property law in Australia.
Demonstrate judgment and skill in the development of Intellectual Property commercialisation strategies.

title: Law for Social Work and the Social Sciences
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In the 21st century professionals of all kinds are drawn by their work and study into multidisciplinary contexts. For example, '[s]ocial work, as a profession, exists in a contested domain, within a framework of rights and duties that are defined and constrained by law' (and other things) (Rice, Day and Briskman 2018). An understanding of law by non-legal professionals helps them to recognise when the law may be a means to challenge oppression and when the law might be restrictive and limit value-based practice. This course is designed to support 3rd year Social Work students and Social Science students to gain knowledge and skills about the legal system and legal process in ways that will facilitate their more effective professional practice. This includes providing opportunities to learn how the legal system works in subject areas involving child and family law, criminal law, guardianship, disability and mental health. It has a focus on supporting persons who are marginalised, advocating for the just rule of law, human rights and enhancing social justice.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse the opportunities and challenges associated with the legal framework that regulates the practise of social workers and social science professionals.
Analyse the most common activities performed by social workers and social science professionals in the Australian legal system including in courts and tribunals.
Apply the relevant legal rules to problem based scenarios that are common in the practice of social workers and social science professionals.
Identify the elements of the Australia's legal system that are most relevant to the work of social workers and social science professionals.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Written/oral assessment on Courts, Procedure and Evidence

title: Law for Workplace Health and Safety
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Gives students an understanding of the impact of the legal and regulatory system on health and safety in the workplace. Topics covered include: structure and functions of law and legal institutions in Australia as they relate to WH&S; an introduction to the employer/employee relationship; Tort liability: Negligence, Breach of Statutory Duty; the Work Health and Safety Act 2011 (NSW) and related legislation; an introduction to the principles of Workers' Compensation; and WH&S and anti-discrimination laws
learning_outcomes: Discuss the concepts of negligence and liability in relation to workplace health and safety;
Demonstrate an understanding of the general principles of workers compensation and of the scheme of legislation applying in NSW;
Discuss the remedies available for breaches of legal standards;
Describe the common law requirements which relate to workplace health and safety, and their relationship to the contract of employment;
Demonstrate an understanding of the Australian Legal System in the context of workplace health and safety laws, and the ability to access recent developments in the law;
Appreciate some of the issues raised by other workplace laws such as those relating to discrimination as they relate to this area.
Demonstrate a critical understanding of the relevant statutory requirements with particular emphasis on the Work Health & Safety Act 2011(NSW);

title: Foundations of Language - Primary and Early Childhood contexts
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the study of language, with particular reference to children's language, to equip future teachers with an understanding of how children learn to read, write, speak, listen, respond and represent in supportive and stimulating environments. Teaching literacy skills in the digital age is a complex scenario in many Australia early childhood centres and schools, and it is important to ensure focus is given in teacher education courses to a wide range of socio-economic factors and cultural diversity. This course will provide grounding in language and literacy which is inclusive and which will serve as a foundation for a balanced approach to teaching and learning. As part of the course, students will take part in a second language learning experience with a language other than English.
learning_outcomes: Explain English sentence structure, including the analysis of simple and complex clause structures
Present both a descriptive and a prescriptive explanation for given examples of English variation
Apply knowledge of speech sounds and grammatical structure in assessing the suitability of learning materials for literacies development
Recognise both the advantages and challenges of multilingualism
Describe the relationship between English speech sounds and spelling and the differences between sounds of adult and children's speech
Evaluate the experience of being a second language learner

title: How Languages Work: Linguistics and the Structure of Language
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This unit introduces students to the study of language, and what language reveals about the nature of human beings and human behaviour. It introduces the basic theoretical concepts in the structural and social analysis of language. It presents the different levels of structural analysis of language. It examines language acquisition, and geographical and social variation in language.
learning_outcomes: Apply the basic principles for the analysis of the different structural levels of language.
Describe basic principles for the analysis of variation.
Discuss the range of synchronic variation in language.
Describe the different structural levels of language.
Discuss the nature of language as the human communication system.

title: Phonetics
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The linguistic study of speech sounds on a phonetic basis. It provides a detailed analysis and description of speech sounds, with particular emphasis on articulatory phonetics, with considerable attention also given to acoustic phonetics.
learning_outcomes: Identify speech sounds from audio samples of speech from a range of language sources.
Describe in detail the articulatory phonetics (i.e. pronunciation)of speech sounds from a range of languages and from disordered speech.
Interpret spectrograms (voiceprints) in order to analyse acoustic features of speech sounds.
Demonstrate an understanding of the instrumental acoustic analysis of speech sounds in theory and practice (i.e. measuring their physical properties).

title: Cross-cultural Communication
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: In a world where networks are increasingly international and global, communication between speakers from different cultural backgrounds is becoming politically, economically and socially essential. Because cultural values expressed through language often do not "translate" accurately, miscommunication may arise from a lack of awareness of cultural and linguistic differences. This course explores some of the ways in which languages embody cultural differences in word meanings, in sentence structures, and in norms of interaction.
learning_outcomes: Apply your knowledge of the research process to contribute to a research project
Demonstrate knowledge of different approaches to the study of cross-cultural interaction.
Demonstrate awareness of ways in which cultural diversity is encoded in language;
Demonstrate an understanding of underlying causes of problems in cross-cultural communication;
Demonstrate an understanding of relationships between linguistic communication and cultural contexts;

title: Issues of Bilingualism and Bilingual Education
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The course constitutes a general introduction to the topic. Bilingualism can broadly be described as having the knowledge of, and the ability to use, two languages. The course offers an overview of a wide range of important dimensions of bilingualism, incl. conceptual, cognitive, psychological, social, pedagogical, etc. A number of critical issues are considered, such as: What constitutes knowledge of two (or more) languages? How is such knowledge acquired and used? How does bilingual knowledge affect the bilingual speaker's general cognitive capacity? How does bilingual knowledge affect the bilingual speaker's social identity? From a pedagogical perspective, what are the most effective methods of attaining bilingual knowledge?
learning_outcomes: Identify the critical issues in this field of knowledge.
Summarise different competing theories and research methods of bilingualism.
Compare and discuss different cognitive, social, psychological and pedagogical dimensions of bilingualism.
Apply advanced research and general information literacy skills.
Describe the basic concepts and the significance of research in this field of knowledge.

title: Indigenous languages of Australia and the Pacific
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course explores the indigenous languages, language families, and language types found in Australia, New Guinea, island southeast Asia and the Pacific. It introduces the basic principles of linguistic typology, using languages of the Australia-Pacific region to illustrate general typological phenomena, and explores the structural nature of the languages of the Australia-Pacific region. Students will learn and practise methods of typological analysis.
learning_outcomes: Describe the distribution of the indigenous language families and language types of Australia and the Pacific region.
Apply principles of typological analysis
Describe the main typological characteristics of the indigenous language types of Australia and the Pacific region.
Describe the key concepts and principles of linguistic typology.

title: Languages in the World
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This unit introduces students to the way languages reflect and shape the societies, cultures and minds of the people who speak them. It introduces the Indigenous languages of Australia and our region, and the language families of the world. It examines the way languages change over time, and what that can tell us about the past. The course investigates how and why languages are alike, and how and why they differ from each other; how meaning is constructed, and how languages are used for effect; and the operation and location of language in the brain. It concludes by examining language endangerment, asking why languages die, and what can be done about it.
learning_outcomes: Describe the main ways in which languages interact with society, culture, and the mind, and the main areas of the brain associated with language.
Identify and classify semantic and pragmatic relations.
Identify the Indigenous languages of Australia and the Newcastle region, and the main language families of the world.
Apply your knowledge of the research process to contribute to a research project
Identify the main causes of language endangerment.
Apply basic principles of historical and typological classification.

title: The Design of Language
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course focuses on the foundations of language structure - the underlying principles of grammar that form the innate structure of language in the human mind. We look at the way these universal principles are applied by speakers to build phrases, clauses and sentences across diverse languages, and at the functional relationship between parts of phrases and clauses, such as subject and object. We attempt to understand these phenomena through the lens of Minimalism, the dominant theory of syntax. The course concentrates on basic concepts and methods of syntactic analysis, and focuses on the practical analysis and description of a wide range of phenomena from a variety of languages.
learning_outcomes: Apply analytic methods to analyse syntactic data.
Characterize syntactic diversity across languages.
Demonstrate an understanding of the structural characteristics of phrases and clauses.
Identify syntactic units such as heads, complements, adjuncts, and arguments.
Describe syntactic structures and relations in a formal way.

title: Language and Cognition
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The course studies language processing (psycholinguistics) and brain function related to language processing (neurolinguistics); competing views of the language acquisition process (e.g. nativist vs. cognitivist); the relationship between language development and the development of other cognitive capacities; and psycholinguistic and neurolinguistic research methods.
learning_outcomes: Conduct an advanced literature review on sentence processing and cognitive disorder and summarise the findings in a succinct manner.
Describe the neurological bases of language processing with the description of specific regions of the brain involved in language comprehension and production.
Construct and deliver a comprehensive academic presentation based on the literature review on a specific topic related to language and mind.
Discuss the differences between competing theories of language acquisition.
Explain how speech perception in infants and young children are tested and what the research results suggest about language universals.
Apply your knowledge of the research process to contribute to a research project

title: 2nd Language Acquisition
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The course provides students with linguistic, psychological and social perspectives on the acquisition of a second language, with particular emphasis on English as a Second Language. Topics include the concepts of 'interlanguage', 'error analysis', 'transfer' from first language, and 'natural order of acquisition', 'fossilisation', and 'critical period' for language acquisition.
learning_outcomes: Identify and classify learner errors and evaluate the significance of errors.
Formulate, support and effectively communicate own position on an issue in the field of SLA.
Compare and contrast competing theories of language acquisition as applied to the acquisition of a second language.
Recognise factors influencing "successful" outcomes in second language acquisition.

title: Introduction to Phonology and Morphology
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course is an introduction to the basic principles of phonology and morphology. We will look at the structure of segments, morphemes, simplex words, and complex words. The course concentrates on the basic concepts and methods of phonological and morphological analysis and description, and focuses on the practical analysis and description of a wide range of phenomena from a variety of languages.
learning_outcomes: Identify phonological units such as features, segments, syllables, and feet;
Apply analytic methods to analyse phonological and morphological data;
Describe phonological structures in a formal way;
Characterise phonological and morphological diversity across languages.
Demonstrate an understanding of the structural characteristics of morphemes and words;

title: Language and Meaning
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Explores the study of how meaning is expressed through language and how it is understood in different real world situations. Particular attention will be paid to lexical and sentence level semantics, and how languages encode time and space relationships (including deictic elements which are linked to the non-linguistic context).
learning_outcomes: Separate different forms of lexical semantic relationships.
Explain in detail the nature of tense, mood and aspect systems in English.
Identify cohesive devices in connected discourse.
Distinguish between presupposition and implicature.
Apply your knowledge of the research process to contribute to a research project.
Use basic semantic and pragmatic concepts to discuss the role of meaning in language.

title: Structure of English
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Provides the grammatical knowledge necessary for a descriptive analysis of the structure of contemporary English, from the level of word class through phrase structure analysis to the description of complex sentence patterns. On completion of the course students should be able to provide a grammatical analysis of English sentential structure.
learning_outcomes: Apply grammatical knowledge to the analysis of English sentential structure.
Examine sentences in terms of word classes, phrase structure, grammatical relations.
Apply your knowledge of the research process to contribute to a research project
Explain key grammatical concepts, such as syntactic constituent and embedding of syntactic structure.
Describe grammatical terminology and levels of grammatical analysis.

title: Our Oceans
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Australia's marine environment is globally significant, containing some of the world's most diverse ecosystems and species, many of which are unique to Australia. The economic value of Australia's marine environment exceeds A$30 billion annually and its social value (for sport, recreation, relaxation) is immense in Australia's culture. Addressing future challenges for our oceans needs a sound understanding of its living and non-living features, including how we both benefit from, and impact upon, these valuable marine ecosystems. This course provides students with an introduction to the marine environment, to some of the most important marine ecosystems (coral reefs, beaches, rocky reefs), and current conservation and management issues (inc. climate change, land-based pollution, fishing and aquaculture, shoreline changes, marine protected areas) and their solutions. The course will be taught through on-line delivery of learning materials.
learning_outcomes: Recognise the social, economic and environmental benefits from sustainable use of Australia's marine environment;
Integrate personal perspectives and evidence-based arguments for analysing contemporary issues in the marine environment;
Describe the physical marine environment, including the seafloor, oceanography and climate;
Describe key Australian marine ecosystems and species and their significance;
Recognise the current issues for the Australian marine environment and their social, economic and environmental costs;
Organise and communicate key concepts, using written and visual means.

title: Research Methdologies
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: Research Methodologies forms part of the Honours Program in Marine Science. This course covers advanced approaches to research methodology, with relevance to Honours projects undertaken by students at the 4000 level. Students enrolled in this course will explore contemporary perspectives in Marine Science research and focus specifically on; developing research skills; formulating research proposals; framing research questions; reviewing existing research; and choosing appropriate methodologies for different types of study. Methodologies are examined in the context of their application to their project (and associated research grouping), such as Marine and Coastal Science, Environmental Science, Climate Science and Sustainability.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate skills in information searching, selection, retrieval, and interpretation.
Design and develop a structured research plan using cognitive skills and critical thinking.
Interpret, summarise, and synthesise the literature of academic and professional literature.
Apply discipline specific theoretical and practical research skills.
Identify appropriate methods of quantitative and/or qualitative data collection as relevant to the research project undertaken.

title: Coral Reef Biology, Ecology and Sustainability
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Coral reefs are ecologically diverse and extremely complex habitats, supporting thousands of marine species, and are considered to be the richest and most complex of all marine ecosystems. This course will examine the biological, ecological and sustainability aspects of coral reefs in order to gain a better understanding of this complex and unique environment. In a small group setting students will develop and execute a research project to be conducted at a coral reef location. Students will gain an in-depth appreciation of the professional requirements to conduct a research project in a remote location. This course will be particularly beneficial to those students pursuing careers in Marine Science, Environmental Science and/or Sustainable Resource Management. The field component of this course requires a significant up-front fee, not covered by HECS. This may vary with each offering of the course, so interested students should contact the course coordinator for more information about price and location.
learning_outcomes: Assess the relevant literature and develop a research proposal on a current issue of coral reef ecology or sustainability;
Explain the complex ecology of coral reefs;
Work in a small group to collaboratively plan, problem solve and execute a research project;
Prepare and write a risk assessment for a field-based project in a coral reef environment to ensure the safety of themselves and other group members.
