exhibit advanced communication knowledge and skills, especially those required for educating, mentoring, role-modelling, leading and following
show evidence of appropriate professional relationships with midwives and other members of the interdisciplinary team
achieve a satisfactory level of practice to demonstrate midwifery competence and completion of minimum supervised requirements.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Students must demonstrate competency in all below listed assessments

title: Optimising Childbearing
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course builds upon basic knowledge provided in pre-registration midwifery courses and explores how to optimise the biological, environmental, social, emotional and psychological factors that interact to create the conditions that women and babies experience during the childbearing year. Topics review and extend students understanding of normal psychophysiology and factors which optimise maternal and fetal health prior to conception to six weeks postpartum. This encompasses pre-conceptual health and nutrition of both parents. Genetics and epigenetics are reviewed to consider the impact of the woman's environment on her physical and emotional health and the way in which this can affect the baby's growth and development. The ideal birth environment is critically examined with reference to the birth space, mindfulness and the role of the midwifery guardian in creating and maintaining a safe and nurturing environment. Inter-professional collaboration in optimising normal physiology of labour, birth, bonding and breastfeeding is examined with particular reference to cortisol, adrenaline, oxytocin, prolactin and endorphins. The provision of woman-centred midwifery care, design of birthing services and related policy and practice is evaluated.
learning_outcomes: Synthesise knowledge on the initiation and regulation of labour as a holistic phenomenon, with particular emphasis on the role that the autonomic nervous system and hormonal cascade play in mediating the physiology of labour, birth, breastfeeding and bonding.
Critically reflect on own midwifery practice to examine the care you provide that either honours or diverts a woman's pathway towards optimal birth in her particular circumstances.
Evaluate the policy and practice of implementing woman-centred care and birthing services and the ability to provide primary level midwifery care within a tertiary level facility.

Critically analyse the conditions that optimise the normal maternal and fetal psychophysiology during pregnancy, labour, birth and the immediate postpartum including the role of the midwifery guardian, birth territory and inter-professional collaboration.
Critically discuss pre-conceptual counselling in relation to the health and nutrition for both parents, and its impact on future offspring.
Identify the social, emotional, psychological and physical environmental factors that affect genetic expression and maternal/fetal well-being.

title: Foundations of Marketing
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Business success requires a constant review of marketing strategies and application of marketing knowledge. Foundations of Marketing introduces the foundational concepts/frameworks in marketing to develop an understanding of both strategic and short-term marketing activities. Topics include the marketing environment, market segmentation, the marketing mix and sustainable marketing practices. This course develops communication and team processes which are valued attributes within marketing environments.
learning_outcomes: Interpret real-world marketing strategies in different environments and contexts.
Collect, review, and analyse market information to examine real-world marketing strategies.
Analyse key marketing theories and conceptual frameworks.
Apply marketing concepts within a range of contexts, both individually and in collaboration with a group.

title: Digital and Social Media Marketing
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Developments in information and communication technologies coupled with a radical shift online by businesses and consumers has raised new questions about how marketers communicate with and create value with customers. This course focuses on understanding how businesses engage with customers and stakeholders in a digital environment and develops skills in applying social media marketing techniques. It also provides students with a thorough understanding of digital and social media marketing theory and incorporates practical and contemporary examples.
learning_outcomes: Articulate specialised knowledge of digital and social media marketing in written contexts.
Apply inquiry processes to complete marketing projects in both an independent and team based capacity.
Interpret today's digital and social media marketing landscape.
Employ digital and social media analytics tools and techniques to interpret digital marketing performance.
Investigate how user-generated content in social media can be collected and analysed to formulate marketing strategy.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Digital Marketing Performance Analytics Interactive Group Presentation

title: Marketing Research and Data-Driven Insights
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In today's competitive business landscape, successful marketing strategies are driven by data and insights. This course explores the critical role of data in making informed marketing decisions and provides hands-on experience in designing research and leveraging data to drive modern marketing strategies.
learning_outcomes: Interpret marketing research findings and data-driven insights and communicate their impact on marketing decisions.
Use marketing research principles and technology to formulate marketing research problems, select data collection methods, and design research tools.
Effectively convey research findings and insights using ethical data visualisation techniques and technology.
Use statistical, analytical methods, and technology to analyse marketing data, generate actionable insights, and recommend marketing strategies.
Assess ethical concerns in marketing research, data collection, and reporting, making informed ethical choices throughout the marketing research process.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Marketing Research Presentation Deck and Technical Appendices

title: Consumer Decision Making
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Ever wondered why you cannot resist your favourite snacks at the grocery store checkout, why you choose one brand of jeans over another or why you buy those irresistible items even when you don’t really need them? Get ready to embark on an eye-opening adventure into the realm of customer decision making. This course will blend psychology, marketing, and everyday experiences into an engaging journey to unravel the mysteries behind consumer decision making.
learning_outcomes: Apply consumer decision making theories to real-world marketing scenarios.
Explain the rationale for studying consumer decision making.
Demonstrate the ability to work both independently and in a team environment employing inquiry processes to complete marketing projects.
Communicate consumer decision making insights clearly, effectively and persuasively.
Identify and evaluate the impact of cultural and social influences on consumer decision making.

title: International Marketing
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Remaining competitive in today’s ever changing business environment requires organisations to continuously adapt to market forces. This course examines the complexities of marketing in an international environment while addressing local market characteristics. It builds upon marketing theory and consumer behaviour addressed in other marketing courses, incorporating theory specific to international and global marketing management. Emphasis is placed on effective communication and collaborative work processes as critical attributes for international marketing professionals.
learning_outcomes: Apply problem-solving and decision-making in international marketing through active and responsible participation in individual and collaborative learning experiences.
Analyse contemporary issues such as social and cultural factors influencing international marketing operations.
Analyse the environmental and organisational constraints in international marketing strategy development.
Effectively communicate marketing knowledge and outcomes in oral and written contexts reflective of both audience and purpose.
Apply marketing concepts, theories, and principles to international marketing.

assessment_tasks.task_name: International Marketing Cultural Analysis Report and Presentation

title: Digital and Social Media Marketing
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Developments in information and communication technologies coupled with a radical shift online by businesses and consumers has raised new questions about how marketers communicate with and create value with customers. The course focuses on understanding how businesses engage with customers and stakeholders in a digital environment and develops skills in applying social media marketing techniques. It provides students with a thorough understanding of digital and social media marketing theory and incorporates practical and contemporary examples.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate how user-generated content in social media can be collected and analysed to guide marketing strategy.
Articulate specialised knowledge of digital and social media marketing in both oral and written contexts.
Demonstrate advanced understanding of today's digital and social media marketing landscape.
Demonstrate the understanding of digital and social media analytics and the capability to use online analytical tools.
Demonstrate the capability to work both independently and in a team environment employing inquiry processes to complete marketing projects.

title: Advertising and Image Management
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Crucial to the success of any communication campaign is ensuring that a message is delivered to the target audience at the right time through appropriate media channels. In this course, the functionality of advertising and public relations (PR) in shaping the strategic approach to the communication mix for brands is examined. Students will engage in tasks designed to embed creative and media concepts, and explore storytelling, copywriting, and image management for external stakeholders in advertising and PR.
learning_outcomes: Integrate marketing communication and public relations theories to shape brand strategies.
Apply professional standards and ethical conduct to achieve strategic communication outcomes.
Incorporate professional written, oral, and visual skills that customises the communication mix to a target audience.
Propose a media communication process that aligns with campaign objectives.
Apply effective creative practices when designing communication and PR campaigns.

title: Creating and Managing Brands
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Branding is a means to create and deliver a promise of value to customers. Marketers use branding to enhance customers' understanding of their offering in a way that creates associations between the brand and their offering, which customers use as an input to decision-making. This course focuses on the development and management of brands as valuable assets in delivering value to customers. This course supports students to understand concepts, theories and models of brand development and management and incorporates practical branding examples, so that students can make and evaluate branding decisions in the future.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate components of a brand.
Apply branding principles and theory to analyse problems and propose solutions.
Design a brand strategy by applying the branding principles and theories.
Discuss branding strategies, and apply a strategic framework to branding issues and decisions.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Live Group Presentation of the Brand Launch

title: Strategic Marketing Management
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Strategic Marketing Management encompasses the utilisation and integration of marketing strategy elements to ensure the organisation’s success in an evolving marketplace. This course will develop students’ abilities to apply various strategic principles and theories to address specific marketing problems for global and national brands. Competitive marketing strategies are introduced, and theories are applied to different economic, political, cultural, and technological environments. Encouraging a practical approach to strategy, students engage in interactive problem solving and contemporary case analysis.
learning_outcomes: Formulate strategies to marketing problems employing methods of analysis specific to marketing.
Apply strategic concepts and theories to a range of internal and external marketing environments.
Design and criticise marketing strategies across a range of contexts.
Illustrate strategic marketing knowledge and outcomes in both written and oral contexts.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Group Situation Analysis and SWOT Report
Group Situation Analysis and SWOT Presentation

title: Services Marketing
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Dominating the global economy, services contribute to more than half of the GDP in advanced and developing economies. Exploring the unique characteristics and challenges faced by service organisations, this course addresses the essential nature of services and how to successfully design and manage service experiences that enhance value creation and long-term relationships with customers. Students will also acquire knowledge of contemporary service thinking both scholarly and practical and its implications in managing service organisation in the digital era.
learning_outcomes: Employ service marketing concepts and terminology to develop an omni-channel service blueprint.
Propose justified strategic options to improve service quality, customer relationships and satisfaction, and firm performance.
Critically evaluate service market offerings, identifying and analysing issues and making practical recommendations.
Develop service marketing plans and strategies that incorporate relevant services marketing theories.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Service Delivery System (SDS) & Customer Experience Analysis

title: International Marketing
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Remaining competitive in a changing environment requires organisations to continuously adapt to market forces. The complexities of marketing in an international environment are examined while addressing local market characteristics. Marketing theory and consumer behaviour addressed in other marketing courses is expanded upon as well as incorporating theory specific international/global marketing management. Communication and collaborative work processes are emphasised as important attributes for the international marketing professional.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an integrative understanding of the environmental and organisational constraints that act on the development of an effective international marketing strategy.
Research and analyse contemporary issues inclusive of social and cultural, which impact international marketing operations
Effectively communicate marketing knowledge and outcomes in oral and written contexts reflective of both audience and purpose.
Apply the basic concepts, theories, and principles of marketing to international marketing.
Apply problem-solving and decision-making to international marketing situations participating actively and responsibly in individual and collaborative learning experiences.
Evaluate the international marketing processes involved in a successful marketing effort.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Cultural Analysis Presentation and Q&A session (Group)

title: Introduction to Entrepreneurship and Innovation
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Entrepreneurship and innovation have never been more important in the 21st century at a time of global, turbulent environments involving discontinuous change. This course introduces the concepts of entrepreneurship and innovation and how they are distinguished. It further explores who is an entrepreneur and what are the entrepreneurial and innovation processes that are used to achieve successful business outcomes. Students will be sensitised to these important contemporary concepts and processes and will apply them to case studies and other real-world contexts.
learning_outcomes: Utilise models and theories to explain the concepts of entrepreneurship and innovation and apply them to a real-world context.
Communicate effectively the concepts of innovation and entrepreneurial ideas in a written format for a business audience
Demonstrate an understanding of the importance of innovation and the role of entrepreneurs in creating value in Australian and global contexts.
Demonstrate an understanding of the different forms of innovation and entrepreneurship.
Describe idea generation, idea sourcing and idea screening processes and apply them to a real world context.

title: Introduction to Management and Sustainability
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: The course introduces students to the foundations of contemporary management by exploring how organisations operate, how people behave at work, and how managers lead, communicate, and make decisions in diverse and dynamic environments. Key areas include managing individuals and teams, understanding organisational behaviour, evaluation of motivation and leadership theories, navigating ethical and cultural challenges, and exploring how organisations design structures solve problems, and operate globally. The course introduces students to perspectives from Management, Human Resource, Leadership, International Relations and International Business to help students develop the skills and knowledge needed to work effectively in contemporary organisations.
learning_outcomes: Apply foundational management theories to analyse real-world organisational problems and the strategies proposed for their resolution.
Compare management ideas and concepts to develop coherent and well-reasoned arguments.
Evaluate the roles and strategies of different stakeholders in diverse business contexts, and the implications for future business success.
Explain key theories, models, and concepts in management and sustainability, and their application in diverse organisational contexts.

title: Entrepreneurial and Innovation Diversity
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Entrepreneurial and Innovation Diversity focuses on the importance, diversity and means by which entrepreneurial and innovative behaviour take advantage of increasingly rapid change to pursue enterprise objectives. The course examines concepts of entrepreneurship and innovation in their numerous settings, including private sector, public sector, family and social entrepreneurial settings. The course places a heavy emphasis upon contemporary global and Australian case studies to illustrate key themes.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate, oral and written form, the knowledge, skills and motivation of successful, responsible entrepreneurs and innovators through case studies and other real-world settings
Examine and analyse the interrelationships between entrepreneurship, innovation and management
Identify, articulate and assess relevant theories underpinning entrepreneurship and innovation in multiple settings
Predict and analyse emerging trends that impact entrepreneurship and innovation, both nationally and globally
Analyse and distinguish between different processes of entrepreneurship and innovation practised in, and relevant to, the many different settings in which these processes are practised

title: Business Venturing
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: The review of business fundamentals and the basic ingredients of a business plan are vital for sustainable enterprises. Business Venturing examines the processes of creating new business enterprises bringing together many concepts including the business idea, relevant resources, personal commitment and entrepreneurial drive, and a marketable product or service. Emphasis will be placed upon understanding the most essential aspects of each concept and the implications for application in relevant business contexts.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an awareness of the standards necessary for appropriate professional practice and ethical conduct and their implementation.
Utilise models and theories to screen and develop business ideas.
Discuss the entrepreneurial process and the main components of a business plan.
Prepare a business plan, incorporating both autonomous and collaborative work processes.
Present the business plan to potential stakeholders in both oral and written formats conducive to audience and purpose.

title: Managing Innovation
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Innovation does not happen without people. Within and outside organisations, individuals are critical agents who can either help or hinder the management of innovation and, ultimately, determine whether it succeeds or fails. This course will progress students from understanding the various models and processes of innovation to understanding how to manage that process, particularly how to identify, navigate and manage the people-based complexities of implementing innovation. The course will examine a range of topical and critical aspects relating to the people management components of the innovation process, including: social networks; power and politics; interpersonal skills, influencing, selling and persuading; fostering creativity and innovation at individual, team and organisational levels; diffusing innovation; and the 'dark side' of innovation. Overall, this course will equip students with the 'soft skills' needed by any organisation looking to innovate.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and evaluate different strategies for (but not exhaustive to): engaging individuals and teams in the innovation process; developing an organisational culture and climate conducive to innovation; positively managing issues of power and politics in organisations to foster innovation; utilising social networks to develop and implement innovation; identifying critical agents that support (or potentially hinder) innovation; influencing, selling and persuading others to adopt ideas; and diffusing innovation through organisational systems
Demonstrate their own capabilities and behaviours to become effective and ethical participants in, and leaders of, innovation in organisations
Apply relevant theories, frameworks and strategies to case studies and other real-world settings involving the management of innovation in the workplace
Work independently and collaboratively on assessments while reflecting on individual and group behaviours relating to innovative activity
Identify and analyse the critical role of people at multiple stages of the innovation process using relevant theoretical frameworks

title: Leadership Models and Practices
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: The aim of this course is to empower students with the ability to recognise and nurture vital skills that enhance personal and collective performance, whether collaborating within organisations or across them. Additionally, it will shed light on potential managerial challenges and equip students with the tools to embark on a lifelong quest to devise strategies for sidestepping these obstacles while actively progressing towards realising their managerial and leadership capabilities. This course initiates students into essential management and leadership principles, fostering the cultivation of essential skills required for proficient leadership and management. It emphasises the development of interpersonal competence, ethical decision-making, social responsibility, and a heightened awareness of cross-cultural considerations.
learning_outcomes: Examine complex issues in business and management and identify solutions.
Critically analyse the demands of leadership and management.
Apply contemporary management strategy theories and practices to local and global contexts.
Evaluate ethical, social, cultural and environmental dimensions associated with leadership and business operations and decision making.

title: Management in Environmental Turbulence
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Decision making is at the heart of management and business activity. It introduces theories and models to understand behavioural dimensions of decision making. Students will examine the decision-making process through a multi-disciplinary lens and explore the multiple factors that affect choice and judgment by individuals, groups and as organisations. Throughout the course, students will be introduced to different decision-making challenges faced in circumstances of incomplete information, limited time, finite resources and bounded rationality.
learning_outcomes: Contribute effectively as a team member in applying decision-making skills to a group project.
Identify various types of decision and decision-making approaches.
Evaluate decision-making processes, outcomes and contingencies.
Apply decision-making theories to examine problems and their potential solutions.

title: Digital Business Applications
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In this course, students will conceptually and practically dive into the world of digital business in the Industry revolutions 4.0 and 5.0. Through the analysis of case studies, students will explore contemporary digital business models, trending technologies, and compare the traditional business models with existing ones. Students will learn how to craft and enact strong digital business plans that align with business goals. Our diverse modules will immerse students in the practical, as well as theoretical applications of electronic commerce (e-commerce), mobile-commerce (m-commerce), Web 2.0., metaverse, social platforms, and peer-to-peer economy, along with their benefits and potential risks. With a mix of engaging lectures, practical workshops, and a hands-on capstone project, students will tangibly face actual challenges of digital business transformation and develop robust digital business strategies. This course is a gateway to understanding the indisputable role of disruptive technologies in today’s business arena, preparing students for a rewarding career in either a managerial or technical pathway.
learning_outcomes: Identify emerging trends, technologies and evolutions occurring in the digital business landscape.
Analyse data to make informed business decisions.
Explain the sources and methods used to inform an analysis of diverse data types.
Assess the application of new digital technologies and their relevance for organisations.
Design via collaboration a digital business plan that is presented orally using appropriate business language.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Digital Business Plan: Presentation and Interactive Feedback

title: Knowledge Management
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Knowledge is a distinct key to competitive business advantage. Knowledge Management sensitizes you to the importance and practice of the development and management of non-tangible worth (principally human-based knowledge) in modern organizations. The need for reciprocal concern for both structures and processes is important for dealing with organizational change and development. Recognizing graduate needs expressed by industry, the development and application of both technical and people management skills within Knowledge Management environments is emphasised. Critical discussion and analysis of key theoretical and practical aspects of knowledge management enhances problem solving and communication attributes valued within the profession.
learning_outcomes: Inform your practice by understanding the ethical and legal implications in managing knowledge
Critically apply theory to organisations in order to identify and justify effective knowledge management strategies and activities
Apply theory related to creative organisations
Access and evaluate current literature and research findings relating to knowledge management
Reflect upon different knowledge management paradigms and their value to the organisation
Design problem solutions based upon research findings and critical assessment of current theory and practice
Explain the key theories and models that inform knowledge management
Communicate clearly and effectively incorporating varying formats and technologies

title: Ideation in Enterprise
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Embracing novelty implies comfort with uncertainty and the courage to explore creative paths in situations where detailed roadmaps are not available. This course will equip students with the insight and confidence to create novelty in any organisational context. Creating something “new” implies a comparison to something that already exists. Understanding the context within which new ideas are expected to take hold is an essential starting point for discovering insights into the elements where customer needs are poorly or not at all addressed.. The discovery process (Opportunity identification, Imaging solutions, Explore your opportunity, and Evaluating your solutions) in this course relies on a framework that moves from “what is” (context) to “what if” (possibilities) to “what wows” (concepts) to “what works” (launch). Overall, students will learn how to apply design thinking principles and ultimately turn problems into real-world opportunities.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate potential solutions, justifying the methods or processes used to reach them.
Articulate, investigate and reframe problems into opportunities;
Explain the importance of understanding the context for identifying and developing opportunities;
Apply design thinking principles in practice;
Develop solutions through the creative process of ideation;

title: Organisational Behaviour
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: In this course, students will explore the factors shaping behaviour in organisations, including individual traits and external influences. We will cover key concepts like group dynamics, organisational structure, motivation, communication, leadership, and conflict management. Students will learn how organisational behaviour impacts managerial decisions, develop critical thinking skills, and apply theories to real life organisational challenges. Students will gain the knowledge and skills to enhance organisational dynamics, improve employee satisfaction, and optimise performance.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the intricacies and uncertainties in managing behaviour within organisations.
Apply acquired knowledge to enhance and optimise organisational performance through verbal forms of communication.
Examine the factors influencing behaviour in organisations, encompassing individual traits and external influences.
Recognise and appraise the critical role of organisational behaviour in managerial functions and decision-making.
Apply established organisational behaviour theories actively to analyse and address organisational challenges.

title: Entrepreneurial Strategy
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Entrepreneurial Strategy is a 20 credit point capstone course in the Innovation and Entrepreneurship program. The focus is on advancing your knowledge of how to craft and improve key enterprise choices and outcomes. Sustaining enterprises in an environment of accelerated change is also a critical element of this course. This starts here with an identification and framing of a real innovation project and problem. A mix of design thinking and project management will also be incorporated. The course importantly examines the "why" and values behind a venture which are known key tenets of great enterprises and their success. What should also be getting clearer is that successful firms are not built around luck but are a result of evidence and crafted strategies to mastermind a better outcome. The capstone applies all your knowledge from the suite of previous courses but with the addition of a major industry based challenge and project that utilises the theory and hones your practical understanding.
learning_outcomes: Appraise the criticality of effective entrepreneurial planning, decision-making, communication and behaviours when operating in turbulent environments
Critically evaluate relevant theories, concepts and models underpinning entrepreneurial strategy
Evaluate a range of leadership skills and ethical practices critical for sustainable, responsible entrepreneurial strategic success
Strategically assess major emerging trends that may impact entrepreneurial success
Demonstrate an advanced ability to create, implement and evaluate entrepreneurial strategies to complex, real-world case studies and a major work-based project

title: Advanced Innovation Management
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: A critical aspect of a modern enterprise is to develop a holistic understanding of innovation management. Enterprise competitive advantage stems from a culture of continuous improvement and strategically driving this from an enhanced interpretation of user needs. This course explores why innovation management plays a pivotal role in such advancement and, in doing so, will include multiple interpretations of innovation management, including a resource based interpretation as well as strategic competitive and open innovation interpretations. Key aspects for students of this broader approach relate to the central role of consistently reviewing business models as well as enterprise functions and processes.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate understanding of the tools and frameworks of innovation management.
Demonstrate the effective application of theories, tools and frameworks to case study and/or real-world settings.
Critically analyse innovation concepts and context such as open innovation and the sharing economy.
Reflect on the processes for delivering improved innovation performance and critically analyse capability development to explore and exploit strategic innovation opportunities.
Analyse the importance of innovation for entrepreneurs, nations and modern enterprises.

title: Social Entrepreneurship
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Entrepreneurship and venture seeking do not only exist in for-profit businesses but they can equally exist in other sectors. Social entrepreneurship focuses on these other sectors where social enterprise, its formation and development as a pursuit of social objectives is practiced. The course explores the use of innovative methods (including different products, foundations and organisations) to invoke action to practice, yield and sustain societal benefits. The course examines contemporary examples of socially entrepreneurial organisations, their benefits and limitations and their varied organisational structures and designs.
learning_outcomes: Identify and critically evaluate relevant contemporary social entrepreneurship theories and philosophies.
Critique the relevance and significance of social enterprises in economic and social terms in the context of government policy and broader societal development.
Critically analyse current and emerging trends in the field of social entrepreneurship, locally, nationally and globally.
Demonstrate experiential learning acquired in developing social enterprise initiatives through the application of knowledge, skills and attributes drawn from the field of social entrepreneurship.

title: Leading Organisational Change
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Heraclitus (Greek philosopher) said some two thousand years ago that the only constant is change. Leading organisational change examines the theories, frameworks and models of change within the organisational setting and leadership theories, approaches and behaviours that facilitate effective organisational change. The course explores the demise of the rational organisation and the growth of planned and emergent change models within turbulent environments. It examines the critical role of the leader and their decision making in effecting sustainable change and evaluates the multiple human, structural, technological, cultural, political and symbolic factors that affect meaningful change.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate models and approaches critical for sustainable organisational change.
Analyse the influence of human, structural, technological, cultural, political and symbolic factors in sustainable organisational change.
Apply an integrated change model to case studies and other real-world organisational settings.
Critique the leader's role in effective and ethical individual, group and organisational change.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Group Assignment - Change Management Plan and Storyboard Consultation

title: Business Development and Growth
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Successful creation of an enterprise brings with it another challenge, that of sustained growth. This course builds on the 2000 level course Business Venturing by focusing on business development and sustainability (rather than the creation) of growth firms. The course examines concepts of entrepreneurship and key entrepreneurial processes, strategies and techniques that well- established firms may embrace to grow and succeed in this age of rapid, volatile, discontinuous change.
learning_outcomes: Identify core personal entrepreneurial traits and skills required to lead successful company growth and sustainability.
Identify, articulate and select relevant contemporary business sustainability strategies.
Demonstrate entrepreneurial decision making and rationale to ensure the long-term growth and sustainability of a business.
Recommend an appropriate business exit strategy when given a business scenario.
Predict, evaluate and select emerging trends that may impact company growth.

assessment_tasks.task_name: In-Class Sales Activity and Knowledge Reflection

title: Innovation Management
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Innovation does not happen without people. Within and outside organisations, individuals are critical agents who can either help or hinder the management of innovation and, ultimately, determine whether it succeeds or fails. This course will progress students from understanding the various models and processes of innovation, to understanding how to manage that process, particularly how to identify, navigate and manage the people-based complexities of implementing innovation. Students will examine a range of topical and critical aspects relating to the people management components of the innovation process, including: social networks; power and politics; interpersonal skills, influencing, selling and persuading; fostering creativity and innovation at individual, team and organisational levels; diffusing innovation; and the 'dark side' of innovation. Overall, this course will equip students with the 'soft skills' needed by any organisation looking to innovate.
learning_outcomes: Identify and analyse the critical role of people at multiple stages of the innovation process using relevant theoretical frameworks.
Independently and collaboratively analyse capabilities and behaviours with a focus on ethics, leadership and innovation in organisations.
Evaluate and apply various strategies for fostering and diffusing innovation in organisations.
Apply relevant theories, frameworks and strategies to case studies and other real-world settings involving the management of innovation in the workplace.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Innovation Strategy & Implementation Journal and Report

title: Business Strategy
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Business Strategy is the capstone course in the Leadership and Management major and brings together the analytical skills and knowledge acquired in the foundational courses within the major. The course provides a holistic understanding of contemporary strategic business management in terms of how firms can achieve a sustainable strategic advantage and above average returns. The Strategic Business Management course, therefore, places the growth and sustainability of the firm in the context of strategic choice, at both business and corporate levels, which derives from an analysis of the firm's resources and capabilities, the operating environment, customers and competitive rivalry.
learning_outcomes: Critique key concepts and models of strategic management.
Develop and present a critically reflective case analysis in collaboration with others.
Evaluate an organisation’s environment, competitive position, resources, and capabilities to assess strategic effectiveness and provide theory-guided recommendations for improvement.
Utilise strategic management frameworks to analyse and address the challenges and opportunities in domestic and international business environments.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Group Case Study Report and Viva

title: Managing Inclusion, Diversity and Equity in Organisations
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Management of diversity impacts both organisational performance and environment. This course aims to introduce you to a range of theoretical and applied approaches from various disciplines, so you can analyse workforce diversity in modern organisations and then design, evaluate and implement strategies to manage workforce diversity. Federal and state interventions which address labour market inequality and issues of gender, culture, disability, age and work/life balance etc, especially in Australia, are analysed. The social, legal and equity issues relevant to managing diversity in enterprises from both a national and international perspective will be addressed.
learning_outcomes: Employ macro and organisational-level data to critically analyse the success of state and firm-based diversity interventions.
Explore and reflect on individual/personal opportunities and challenges when pursuing diversity in the workplace.
Examine different theories used to explain labour market segregation, segmentation, equity and diversity.
Identify relevant legislation, case law and government policies that relate to anti-discrimination, harassment, equal employment opportunity, pay equity and privacy.
Compare and contrast characteristics of workforce diversity both nationally and internationally.
Determine, justify and recommend, professional best practice for managing diversity, including technical, organisational and process elements.

title: Innovation and Entrepreneurial Strategy
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Innovation and Entrepreneurial Strategy is the capstone course in the Innovation and Entrepreneurship program. You will be involved with the identification and framing of a real innovation project and problem. A mix of design thinking and project management will also be incorporated. The course importantly examines the 'why' and values behind a venture; these are known key tenets of great enterprises and their success. The capstone applies all your knowledge from the suite of previous courses but with the addition of a major industry based challenge and project that utilises theory and hones your practical understanding.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate major emerging trends that impact the innovation and entrepreneurial process.
Evaluate a range of leadership skills and ethical practices critical for sustainable, responsible entrepreneurial strategic success.
Demonstrate an advanced ability to evaluate and implement innovation and entrepreneurial strategies as applied to complex, real-world situations.
Work collaboratively to challenge and develop ideas, and to communicate outcomes in written and oral contexts.
Demonstrate and critically evaluate key theories, concepts and models underpinning innovation and entrepreneurial strategy.
Access, analyse, evaluate and synthesise information appropriate for innovation and entrepreneurial activities.

title: Diagnostic Radiography Professional Practice 1
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with the opportunity to begin developing foundational professional knowledge, skills, attitudes, and behaviours required for safe and effective radiographic practice. Through participation in structured clinical skills laboratories and supervised placement at accredited diagnostic radiography clinical sites, students gain early exposure to real-world healthcare environments. Students will develop competence and confidence in performing basic radiographic procedures, patient positioning, and equipment handling, while applying principles of radiation safety and infection control. Emphasis is placed on patient-centred care, including communication with diverse patient groups, professionalism, and teamwork within multidisciplinary healthcare settings. The course introduces students to the professional, legal, and ethical frameworks governing medical radiation practice, including AHPRA registration requirements, scope of practice, accountability, and standards of conduct. Students are expected to demonstrate appropriate professional behaviour, reflective practice, and adherence to workplace policies and clinical governance requirements. Through guided clinical experience and simulation, students will begin to integrate theoretical knowledge with practice, demonstrating responsibility and developing the foundational capabilities required for progression within the program and future professional registration.
learning_outcomes: Begin to develop clinical reasoning skills
Practice within an ethical and legal framework, particularly with regard to cultural safety.
Begin to develop and demonstrate a professional attitude towards members of the public and other health care workers
Be able to evaluate and critique his or her role within and during the clinical period, according to the level of experience
Begin to develop and apply communication skills with members of the public and other health care workers
Apply, participate in, and develop clinical skills in, MRS procedures at a level suitable to their current clinical experience

title: Medical Radiation Science 1A
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course provides Medical Radiation Science (MRS) students with a global perspective of 21st century MRS clinical practice issues. The course will explore the practice and science of MRS and its role in modern health care; its use in the diagnosis, staging, treatment and monitoring of acute and chronic illness and injury; the physical, radiobiological and radiation safety principles underlying imaging and therapy; and an introduction to the interpretation of medical images used in MRS.
learning_outcomes: Describe the principles of safe and high-quality patient care, and the delivery of comprehensive care, in line with NSQHS Standards 1 and 5.
Describe the different types of patient information and management systems used in health care settings.
Compare and contrast the differences between different imaging modalities, and their use in the care of patients.

Recognise the role that MRS staff have in modern health care, and the requirements for national registration and the ongoing maintenance of registration, including legislative requirements for care and practice (within and beyond MRS practice)
Identify and describe normal anatomical positions and movements related to medical radiation science.

Develop the ability to read and understand medical terms and abbreviations used in patient records, referrals and in verbal communication, with an emphasis on Communicating for Safety, in line with NSQHS Standard 6.
Discuss the impact and use of medical radiation science in a wide range of medicine and health applications, including patient advocacy.
Recognise the dangers associated with medical radiations, and describe the safe and ethical use of medical imaging and therapy interventions.

title: Diagnostic Radiography Methods 1
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course introduces the clinical science of Diagnostic Radiography; the roles and responsibilities of the diagnostic radiographer in the health care team; conventional diagnostic radiography approaches; and issues related to the management of a patient undergoing a radiographic examination. Fundamental safety considerations and practice are considered.
learning_outcomes: Develop clinical reasoning skills so as to provide optimal patient management and outcomes, based on clinical history, patient presentation and differential diagnosis to ensure the appropriate imaging pathway
To describe and apply diagnostic radiography practice and procedures
Develop pattern recognition and image interpretation skills so as to identify and describe imaging pathology
Develop a knowledge of the mechanisms of injury and/or the causes of disease
Identify key imaging anatomy

title: Basic Radiation Therapy Methods IB
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This foundational course introduces students to the essential principles and practices of radiation therapy. Students will explore the fundamental concepts of radiation physics, radiation biology, and radiation protection while developing an understanding of the role of radiation therapy in cancer treatment. The course covers basic simulation, planning, and treatment procedures, providing students with core knowledge of radiation therapy equipment, patient positioning, and immobilisation techniques. Emphasis is placed on understanding the multidisciplinary approach to cancer care, professional communication skills, and the ethical considerations in radiation therapy practice. This course establishes the groundwork for all subsequent radiation therapy courses. This course is mandatory and must be passed in order to progress in the Bachelor of Medical Radiation Science (Honours) (Radiation Therapy). This Course recognises the Professional Capabilities developed by the Medical Radiation Practice Board of Australia (MRPBA).
learning_outcomes: Identify key radiological anatomy features in medical imaging typically used in radiation therapy.

Demonstrate understanding of cancer fundamentals by recognising and describing the hallmarks of cancer, explaining the natural history and staging processes of malignant disease, and describing current approaches to cancer diagnosis and treatment.
Analyse the specialist roles of the multi-disciplinary health care team in oncology.
Develop written and verbal communication skills, with a focus on person-centred care in relation to patient management, quality of life and survivorship.
Identify and describe the safe use of equipment in radiation therapy.

Describe the role of radiation therapy simulation, planning and treatment, and apply radiation therapy techniques, including simulation, planning, plan evaluation, patient immobilisation and setup for treatment.

Describe the safe and ethical use of medical imaging and therapy interventions, incorporating cultural competence and inclusive care practices for patients from diverse backgrounds in radiation therapy.

title: Radiation Therapy Professional Practice 1B
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This foundational course introduces students to professional practice in radiation therapy through theoretical learning and practical application. Students will develop foundational clinical skills through laboratory sessions and supervised clinical placement in an accredited radiation therapy facility. The course explores basic patient care skills, radiation safety protocols, infection control procedures, and professional communication within the healthcare team. Students will learn to apply theoretical knowledge in clinical settings while developing competence in basic simulation, planning, and treatment procedures. The course focuses on building confidence in professional interactions and establishing a foundation for ethical, safe, and effective radiation therapy practice. This course is mandatory and must be passed in order to progress in the Bachelor of Medical Radiation Science (Honours) (Radiation Therapy). This Course recognises the Professional Capabilities developed by the Medical Radiation Practice Board of Australia (MRPBA).
learning_outcomes: Identify signs and symptoms of medical emergencies that may occur in radiation therapy departments and demonstrate appropriate management actions.
Develop foundational clinical reasoning skills and apply basic evidence-based approaches to decision making in healthcare practice.
Reflect upon, evaluate and critique one's role and performance during clinical practice according to level of experience.

Demonstrate an understanding of and practice safe and ethical use of medical imaging and therapy interventions, incorporating cultural competence and inclusive care practices for patients from diverse backgrounds in radiation therapy.
Demonstrate skills in the design, evaluation and implementation of basic level treatment plans, ensuring they meet ICRU criteria and recognised departmental standards and protocols.
Demonstrate understanding of practice and participate in basic level radiation therapy treatment, planning and simulation procedures
Identify and observe the role and function of medical radiation practitioners and the broader multidisciplinary health care team in oncology.
Demonstrate a professional attitude and effective communication with members of the public, patients and other healthcare workers, including information gathering, active listening and empathy.

title: Nuclear Medicine Professional Practice 1B
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to clinical Nuclear Medicine professional practice. Students will begin to develop professional knowledge, skills, attitudes and experience, by participating in professional skills labs at university and by attending a professional placement at an accredited Nuclear Medicine clinical centre. The labs and professional placement will facilitate the development of student confidence and competence in undertaking and participating in basic Nuclear Medicine professional procedures. The lab assessment must be passed to pass the course.
learning_outcomes: Apply developing clinical skills in, Nuclear Medicine procedures, including radiopharmaceutical practices, appropriate to their level of experience
Apply clinical reasoning and risk management skills, including recognition of medical emergencies and appropriate responses.
Critically reflect on personal clinical performance to identify strengths and areas for ongoing professional development.
Demonstrate professional and effective communication with patients, cares, and members of the health care team.
Practice within an ethical, legal, and culturally safe framework, recognising professional responsibilities in nuclear medicine.

title: Nuclear Medicine Methods 1
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This is the foundation professional methods course for the Bachelor Medical Radiation Science (Nuclear Medicine). This course introduces the basic concepts of nuclear medicine imaging and radiopharmacy, as well as nuclear medicine skeletal imaging.
learning_outcomes: Develop and apply academic skills to search, retrieve, and synthesise clinical and scientific information to support evidence-based practice.
Develop professional and effective communication techniques using medical terminology.
Apply clinical reasoning to select appropriate imaging pathways, informed by patient history, presentation, and differential diagnosis.
Describe fundamental concepts in nuclear medicine, including radiopharmacy, radiation protection, quality control, gamma camera instrumentation and imaging acquisition.
Explain and perform routine nuclear medicine procedures, with a particular focus on basic radiopharmacy skills and skeletal imaging.
Demonstrate skills in image pattern recognition, interpretation, and identification of anatomy, injuries, and pathology relevant to nuclear medicine.

title: Diagnostic Radiography Methods IIA
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course consolidates conventional diagnostic radiography approaches and introduces imaging of more complex areas of the appendicular skeleton and introducing the axial skeleton. Patient assessments for suitable imaging approaches are reviewed. Students will continue to develop clinical reasoning skills to manage patients/clients, and professional practice and procedures.
learning_outcomes: Further develop clinical reasoning skills with regard to patient management and image evaluation which reflects the understanding of the clinical history and/or the impact on differential diagnosis to ensure the appropriate imaging pathway.

To describe and apply profession specific diagnostic radiography practice and procedures for all patient presentations, including paediatric presentations in medical imaging. Consideration is given to all aspects of paediatric presentations in medical imaging.
Identify key imaging anatomy/surface anatomy to continue development of pattern recognition skills so as to identify radiographic pathology

Describe and apply profession specific diagnostic radiography practice and procedures for the regions being covered which includes the axial skeleton. Consideration is given to patient presentations such as Trauma, Paediatrics, Geriatrics, Mobile and Theatre Radiography in addition to higher modality instrumentation such as Computed Tomography, MRI, Ultrasound, Fluoroscopy and Digital Imaging.
Further develop their knowledge of mechanisms of injury and/or the causes of disease processes on varying patient presentations

title: Diagnostic Radiography Professional Practice 2A
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with the opportunity to consolidate basic professional knowledge, skills, attitudes and experience, by participating in professional skill labs at university and by attending a professional placement at an accredited diagnostic radiography clinical centre. The labs and professional placement will increase confidence and competence in undertaking and participating in basic to more complex professional procedures. Clinical placement occurs during Semester 1 for five weeks.
learning_outcomes: Be able to evaluate and critique their professional role and performance during clinical practice
Further develop and demonstrate a professional attitude towards and ability to communicate with members of the public and other health care workers
Continue to develop and use clinical skills in MRS procedures
Practice within an existing ethical and legal framework
Further develop their clinical reasoning skills

title: Diagnostic Radiography Methods IIB
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course further consolidates conventional diagnostic radiography approaches and introduces imaging of more complex areas of the axial skeleton, chest and abdominal viscera. The students are also introduced to the concepts of the role of contrast media in imaging. Patient assessments for suitable imaging approaches are reviewed. Students will continue to develop clinical reasoning skills to manage patients/clients, and professional practice and procedures.
learning_outcomes: Further develop and apply self learning skills.
Continue to develop communication skills (written & oral).

Identify key radiographic anatomy and perform radiographic as well as imaging critiques in written and oral formats to assist in developing pattern recognition skills so as to identify radiographic pathology.

Describe radiographic examinations and radiologic procedures for the regions being covered which includes the shoulder girdle and thoracic cage, and plain and contrast enhanced radiographic examinations of the abdominal tracts and thorax. Consideration is given to patient presentations such as Trauma, Paediatrics, Geriatrics, Mobile and Theatre Radiography in addition to higher modality instrumentation such as Tomography, CT, MRI and Fluoroscopy and Digital Imaging.

title: Diagnostic Radiography Professional Practice IIB
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with the opportunity to further develop professional knowledge, skills, attitudes and experience, by participating in professional skill labs at university and by attending a professional placement at an accredited diagnostic radiography clinical centre. The labs and professional placement will increase confidence and competence in undertaking and participating in professional procedures of increasing difficulty or complexity. The labs must be passed to be allowed to attend professional placement, and pass the course.
learning_outcomes: Be able to evaluate and critique his or her role within and during the clinical period, according to the level of experience
Apply and participate in MRS procedures at a level suitable to their current clinical experience
Practice within an ethical and legal framework, particularly with regard to cultural safety.
Further develop clinical reasoning skills
Further develop and apply communication skills with members of the public and other health care workers
Further develop and demonstrate a professional attitude towards members of the public and other health care workers

title: Radiation Therapy Professional Practice 2A
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This intermediate course advances students' professional practice skills through intensive laboratory training and extended clinical placement. Students will begin developing competence in standard radiation therapy procedures, including simulation techniques, treatment planning, and delivery systems. The course emphasises the development of clinical reasoning skills, patient assessment abilities, and quality assurance procedures. Students will learn to evaluate treatment plans against established criteria and implement safe, effective treatment protocols. Professional development focuses on communication skills, ethical practice, and evidence-based decision making within the radiation therapy team environment. This course is mandatory and must be passed in order to progress in the Bachelor of Medical Radiation Science (Honours) (Radiation Therapy). This Course recognises the Professional Capabilities developed by the Medical Radiation Practice Board of Australia (MRPBA).
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate competence in the design, evaluation and quality assurance of standard treatment plans, and their implementation into treatment
Reflect upon, evaluate and critique one's role and performance during clinical practice according to level of experience.
Demonstrate knowledge and apply skills by participating in standard radiation therapy treatment, planning and simulation procedures

Demonstrate an understanding of and practice safe and ethical use of medical imaging and therapy interventions, incorporating cultural competence and inclusive care practices for patients from diverse backgrounds in radiation therapy.
Demonstrate a professional attitude and effective communication with members of the public, patients and other healthcare workers, including information gathering, active listening and empathy.
Demonstrate clinical reasoning skills through patient assessment, applying evidence-based approaches to management and decision making in healthcare practice.
Evaluate plans against ICRU criteria and ensure that they meet recognised standards and department protocols

title: Radiation Therapy Methods IIA
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This intermediate course builds upon foundational knowledge to explore radiation therapy methodologies and treatment planning techniques. Students will develop competency in simulation procedures, treatment planning, and treatment principles. The course covers imaging techniques used in radiation therapy, quality assurance protocols, and plan evaluation methods. Students will examine various radiation therapy techniques and technologies while developing clinical reasoning skills for patient management. Emphasis is placed on understanding treatment protocols, dose prescription standards, and the integration of imaging technologies in modern radiation therapy practice. This course is mandatory and must be passed in order to progress in the Bachelor of Medical Radiation Science (Honours) (Radiation Therapy). This Course recognises the Professional Capabilities developed by the Medical Radiation Practice Board of Australia (MRPBA).
learning_outcomes: Describe radiation therapy clinical trials and treatment protocol development, including their purpose, design, and implementation in clinical practice.
Describe the process of diagnosis and staging of major anatomical cancer sites
Develop an understanding and apply knowledge of current radiation therapy treatment techniques as well as planning systems, skills in plan evaluation and quality assurance
Describe the epidemiology, etiology and natural history of oncological related illnesses of major anatomical sites

Develop an understanding of the safe and ethical use of radiation therapy interventions, incorporating cultural competence and inclusive care practices for patients from diverse backgrounds in radiation therapy.
Compare & contrast the mainstream treatments used in oncology
Demonstrate understanding and apply knowledge of multimodality imaging used in radiation therapy and identify cross-sectional anatomy relevant to treatment planning.
Develop clinical reasoning skills in patient management, patient quality of life assessment, treatment evaluation, and imaging/treatment assessment

title: Radiation Therapy Methods IIB
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This intermediate methods course explores sophisticated radiation therapy techniques and treatment approaches for advanced clinical scenarios. Students will master intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT), volumetric arc therapy (VMAT), and other radiation therapy techniques for the anatomical site of the breast. The course covers advanced treatment planning concepts, biological models of radiation response, and comprehensive plan evaluation methodologies. Students will develop expertise in multi- modality imaging applications and organ motion management approaches. Emphasis is placed on critical analysis of treatment options, research methodology, and the application of evidence-based practice in radiation therapy. title: Person-Centred Care in Medical Radiation Science
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course provides a comprehensive overview of supportive and integrated person-centred care, highlighting its role in enhancing patients' wellbeing and outcomes. It focuses on equipping learners with the communication and clinical reasoning skills needed to adapt their management approaches to various situations and environments across the continuum of chronic conditions, including cancer, in diverse settings. This course is designed to equip medical radiation science students with the skills to care for patients across a variety of situations and diseases, and to identify patients’ unmet needs. Additionally, it offers a unique opportunity for students to explore their own motivations and core values, fostering self-awareness and personal growth. By focusing on both professional and personal development, students will learn how to maintain their own health and well-being while providing compassionate care to others.

title: Introduction to Digital Music Making
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course is an open elective for students from all programs across the University excluding the excluding the Bachelor of Music, Bachelor of Teaching/Bachelor of Music, and related programs. It utilises standard computer hardware and commonly available computer software applications (freely downloadable from the internet).
learning_outcomes: An appreciation of a range of musical styles
Self-expression through the arrangement of sound
Musical creativity through technology (software)
A basic understanding of fundamental music concepts
Practical experience working with non-notational methods of music editing and arrangement
Technical skills in digital music editing

title: Introduction to Music Theory
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The course enables students to gain practical strategies for independent and self-directed learning easily adaptable to the study of musicianship. Students are introduced to fundamental music skills and concepts in listening to and notating music. They create short works based on each concept introduced. Cloud-based music production and aural/theory software is also used to develop students’ listening and musicianship skills.
learning_outcomes: Employ fundamental rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic concepts in music analysis and creative tasks.
Apply core music theory concepts in written and notated examples.
Compose short musical studies that demonstrate understanding of core music theory concepts.
Identify rhythms, intervals, chord qualities, and scales using appropriate musical terminology.

title: Collaborative Music Making 1
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with opportunities to develop foundational skills in music performance. Students will develop performance skills in both solo and ensemble contexts. Students may explore any music style or genre including contemporary, popular, classical, jazz and folk/world music.
learning_outcomes: Work effectively in a team within a creative context.
Perform technical work, demonstrating control of rhythm, articulation, timbre and intonation.
Apply foundational musicianship through performance.
Review a live performance event.

title: Creative Music Studio 2
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course fosters an evolving understanding of music creation and helps students reinforce and develop their song writing, composition and music production skills, individually and in groups. It encourages stylistic diversity and extends their creative ability through developing a broader range of music production and collaborative compositional techniques. A foundation in digital sound production is enhanced by further developing sound recording and production techniques.
learning_outcomes: Recognise different musical styles and types
Evaluate the creative aspects of their own or collaborative compositions
Use instrumental / vocal sound sources to produce music
Construct new and recontextualised pieces of music

title: Collaborative Music Making 2
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with opportunities to develop intermediate skills in music performance. Students will develop performance skills in both solo and ensemble contexts. Students will also learn skills in mixing live sound and microphone techniques. Students may explore any music style or genre including contemporary, popular, classical, jazz and folk/world music.
learning_outcomes: Perform technical live sound tasks.
Apply intermediate musicianship through performance.
Perform technical work, demonstrating control of rhythm, articulation, timbre and intonation.
Work effectively in a team within a creative context.

title: Creative Music Studio 1
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course inspires students individually and in groups to begin developing, creating and recording their own music. It cultivates both technical and creative practices that support the writing, arranging and recording of music with an emphasis on using technology as a creative tool. The course covers fundamental concepts of song writing, music composition and sound design in addition to digital production skills relevant to this level of study.
learning_outcomes: Employ sound studio technology and audio equipment to produce a music recording
Use music and sound design terminology in communication
Review existing music compositions and describe their musical elements
Evaluate the creative aspects of their own composition

title: Foundations in Digital Media
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Foundations in Digital Media explores the practical applications of digital technology in current music-making, performance-making and media-making practices. The course focuses on software-based approaches to media creation, content enhancement and creative production while providing fundamental skills in sound design, performance design, music creation and media production. Students will advance their level of digital media literacy, enhance their creative ability and broaden their understanding of media content development within the digital domain.
learning_outcomes: Creatively arrange media material within a software environment;
Recognise visual representations of media content through software.
Describe fundamental media production techniques in the digital domain;
Adapt media content in different digital formats
Competently operate relevant media software and hardware technologies;

title: Sound, Music and Texture
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course develops an understanding of musical and performing arts vocabularies, representation, and communication, focusing on texture and timbre and their various developments in historical and cultural contexts. Students will apply these tools analytically and creatively towards works in various genres and eras. The course teaches students to be active and analytical listeners of sound events, textures, and musical gestures, using examples from diverse cultures, genres, historical periods and styles including innovations in music and performance technology.
learning_outcomes: Recognise, create and analyse significant sonic structures with respect to timbre and texture;
Apply technology in the analysis of music and sound events.
Identify and explain the use of timbre and texture in a variety of musical styles and eras;
Demonstrate the ability to communicate about music and performing arts;

title: Introduction to Guitar
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to elementary guitar technique and musicianship. Students will develop a repertoire of songs and pieces in various styles and obtain a method to further their development on the instrument independently. This course will prepare the student to play the guitar in all situations where simple music making is required. Students will be requested to practice specific music repertoire outside of regular tutorial times to successfully complete the course. A body of work will be created throughout the course for students to use in the primary school environment or any vocation that may benefit. No prior musical knowledge is required.
learning_outcomes: Acquire ensemble skills through group performance.
Sight-read melodies in a range of keys.
Perform technical exercises and patterns.
Adapt music-making skills to a variety of classroom and extra curricula performance activities.
Develop aural skills with relation to pitch, rhythm, time signature and performing media.
Care and maintain the instrument including replacing strings.
Tuning the guitar including the use of a guitar tuner.
Perform simple chord progressions to a range of popular songs.
Develop the ability to select and sequence appropriate repertoire.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Assessment 3 - Performance Exam Solo and Ensemble

title: Introduction to Keyboard
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci

Demonstrate an understanding of the concepts and skills involved in performing including the concepts of time, beat, rhythm, chords and elementary music notation.
Develop aural skills with relation to pitch, rhythm, time signature and performing media.
Develop a basic understanding and practical working knowledge of elementary keyboard techniques.

faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
