learning_outcomes: Take actions to continually improve OSH performances
Monitor and measure processes and report the results
Establish an OSH policy and procedures, objectives and processes to deliver results
Implement the processes

assessment_tasks.task_name: A2 - Written Assignment - Worksite Visit Report

title: Occupational Health
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: Provides students with an understanding of the occupationally induced injuries and diseases affecting each body system. Through the study of occupational disease and the occupational effects on specific organ systems (such as respiratory disease, cancer, stress, back problems), students will gain an appreciation of the OHS problems of specific groups of workers. The course is only offered externally in Singapore.
learning_outcomes: Locate and assess the literature on occupational diseases and related conditions.
Write in an academic style, summarize, critique and synthesize relevant literature when writing scientific reports within Occupational Health and Safety
Demonstrate an understanding of the common and important occupational diseases of the major body systems, their nature, relationship to work exposures and prevention.

title: Hygiene and Toxicology I
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: The course is only offered externally in Singapore. Develops a conceptual framework for toxicology and knowledge and skills relevant to the practice of occupational and environmental hygiene in hazard identification, risk assessment and control of the environment. Topics include: toxicological terminology; toxico-kinetics and toxico-dynamics; toxicological testing methods; toxicity of specify groups of industrial chemicals; environmental and biological monitoring; setting and using hygiene standards; methods for monitoring environmental pollutants, including noise; strategies for the control of environmental pollutants; and reporting on hygiene surveys.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an awareness of factors influencing toxicity;
Demonstrate an awareness of the factors involved in determining hygiene standards and describe the types and applicability of hygiene standards used in Australia;
Explain key toxicological terms such as dose, effect, response, toxico-kinetics and toxico-dynamics;
Describe the principles of operation and methods of use of a range of instruments for monitoring environmental pollutants;
Discuss the role of the hygienist in the assessment and control of the work environment;
Compare and contrast the roles of environmental and biological monitoring in workplace assessment;
Outline methods of testing for toxicity;
Outline the toxicity of specific groups of industrial chemicals;
Outline strategies for the control of environmental pollutants.

title: Ergonomics for OHS
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: Introduces the student to the scope of ergonomics and the application of ergonomic principles to workplace design and work organization. It includes physiological, anatomical, psychological, environmental and management perspectives on work capacity, workplace design and work organization. The course is only offered externally in Singapore.
learning_outcomes: Assess the effect of physical environmental factors on comfort and performance;
Identify and evaluate the impact of various personal attributes (anatomical, physiological and psychological) on proper safe working practice;
Apply principles of good ergonomic design of work areas and equipment to a range of occupational settings;
Explain the influence of ergonomic principles on work organisation and culture.

title: Occupational Safety
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: Considers the fundamental principles and practice of chemical, fire and explosion, electrical, machinery and construction safety, with reference to Singapore OHS legislation. The course is only offered externally in Singapore.
learning_outcomes: Prepare clear instructions and reports;
Develop strategies to eliminate hazards or minimize risk;
Identify relevant sections of OHS legislation and assess if legal requirements are satisfied.
Evaluate the potential consequences of identified hazards;
Identify the physical, chemical, biological, mechanical and electrical hazards in a wide range of working environments;

title: Hygiene and Toxicology II
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: Enhances the knowledge and skills acquired in Hygiene & Toxicology I and relates them to the practice of occupational and environmental hygiene in the field, to the toxicological evaluation of chemicals and to hazardous substances risk assessment.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the scientific, social and ethical issues in risk assessment
Conduct and report on a dust and noise survey
Review scientific data used in setting hygiene standards
Describe the principles of operation and methods of use of a range of instruments for monitoring environmental pollutants
Conduct hazardous substances risk assessments
Discuss the classification of toxicity with reference to international harmonisation of labelling of hazardous substances
Explain the key factors involved in determining hygiene standards and describe the types and applicability of hygiene standards used in Australia
Work effectively as part of a team or group to achieve a shared goal

title: Epidemiology and Environmental Health
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: Introduces students to epidemiology as a way in which new knowledge in EOHS is gained, and provides the tools by which the EOHS literature can be critically evaluated. Explores the relationship between the environment and human disease and looks at specific environmental pollutants and health.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the relationship between the environment and human health;
Be familiar with causal reasoning and how to assess the strength of causality from study reports;
Understand the challenges of doing environmental epidemiologic studies and the basic types of study questions and matching study designs;
Understand the basic methods of analysing, reporting and interpreting quantitative data from environmental epidemiological studies;
Be familiar with the various special environmental exposure settings and associated health problems (eg, indoor and outdoor air, food, water, radiation.)
Understand the basic study design elements & their variations, their purpose and their strengths & weaknesses;
Apply knowledge of epidemiology and research principles to the appraisal of published environmental and occupational exposure and health outcome data;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Written Assignment 2: Critical Review & Interpretation of research results
Written Assignment 1: Basic comprehension of a research report

title: EOHS Management I
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: Considers the theories and ideas underlying management and organisational behaviour. Supporting tutorials provide exposure to the more practical aspects of work in organisations. The course is organised to give a general introduction to human behaviour and management, including an examination of individual behaviour followed by the study of groups and group processes, the organisation, management and management practices. The course is only offered externally in Singapore.
learning_outcomes: Able to critically discuss theoretical concepts and ideas from management and organisational behaviour;
Familiar with the theories and language of management and organisational behaviour;
Able to apply the theories and concepts to case studies;
Able to understand the basic elements of working in a group.
Able to develop and present a coherent case analysis, both oral and written; and
Able to write essays at an academically acceptable standard;

title: International Perspectives on EOHS
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: Considers international perspectives on environmental and occupational health and safety. In particular it provides an international context for examining the scope of EOHS, the impact of global economic and political climates on EOHS developments, and explores the functions and activities of international organisations, such as ILO, WHO and Greenpeace. The course is only offered externally in Singapore.
learning_outcomes: Provide an opportunity for self-directed learning of a specified international EOHS issue.
To explore the function of international organisations such as ILO and WHO;
To examine EOHS issues in a global context and the role of specified countries and/or global organisations in EOHS development;
Work effectively as part of a team or group to achieve a shared goal.
To provide an international context for examining the scope of occupational and environmental health and safety;

title: Research Methods in EOHS
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: Introduces students to the nature of research and how to start conducting research. Students work in small groups or individually to develop a research question and hypotheses in an organised and systematic format. The course is only offered Off Shore (externally) in Singapore.
learning_outcomes: Apply these skills and knowledge to case studies on the prevention and management of environmental health problems.
Defend choices made and processes used in research development.
Appraise critically the environmental and occupational health literature;
Apply a knowledge of epidemiology to the review of routine environmental and occupational health data relating exposures to health outcomes;
Discuss the basic steps in health risk assessment as it applies to the environment;
Demonstrate an understanding of the relationship between the environment and human health;
Describe the various environments that can influence human health (eg, indoor and outdoor air, food, water.)

title: EOHS Law
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: Provides the essential legal framework for students to understand how the law functions, both as a tool to improve the environment and health and safety, and as part of the background against which other techniques for improvements must operate. It provides a sound knowledge of the specific discipline of law as it relates to environmental and occupational health and safety; and outlines the major pieces of legislation governing environmental planning, environmental and public health, and occupational health and safety. It assists students in understanding the role of decision-making in EOHS and contributes to students' analytical, problem solving and written communication skills. The course is only offered externally in Singapore.
learning_outcomes: Discuss remedies available for breaches of legal standards;
Develop a critical understanding of occupational health and safety legislation;
Develop a critical understanding of environmental and public health, and environmental planning legislation;
Appreciate the ethical issues inherent in operating as a safety or environmental control professional.
Discuss the nature of law making and operation in Singapore;
Describe the legal system and how it relates to the operation of environmental and occupational health and safety;
Discuss the concepts of negligence and liability in relation to environmental and occupational health and safety laws;

title: Risk Assessment and Management
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: Develops knowledge and skills in risk assessment and management, as required for effective occupational health, safety & environment practice. It includes the application of adult learning principles to the development of EOHS training; accident theories in the analysis of accident causation; accident investigation techniques; inspections and audits; and practical approaches to risk assessment and risk management, including disaster and emergency planning. This course is only offered externally in Singapore.
learning_outcomes: Examine various approaches to safety auditing, to be able to make appropriate choices;
Recommend and implement risk controls;
Conduct job safety analysis and carry out risk assessment;
Utilise accident theory as an investigative tool in accident causation;
Examine features of risk/safety management systems;
Design and implement a disaster management plan.
Use a case study approach to accident investigation and reporting; and

title: Occupational Health
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the relationship between health and the work environment. It illustrates aspects of the structure and function of the human body and investigates the recognition of how hazards in the workplace can affect the body (diseases and injuries) . It also includes an introduction to health services required to address these problems.
learning_outcomes: Discuss in general terms the main occupational health problems associated with the major body systems, their nature, relationship to work exposures and prevention;
Discuss the provision, organisation and limitations of occupational health services; and
Locate and assess the literature on occupational diseases and related conditions.
Explain current topical occupational health issues and the their relationship to work exposures and preventions

title: Human Factors and Work Health and Safety
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: Introduces the student to the scope of ergonomics and the application of ergonomic principles to workplace design and work organisation. The course is organised around the following modules: Worker: -Work physiology, -Anatomy and biomechanics in ergonomics, -Anthropometry. Workstation: -Task analysis, workspace and workstation design and the workplace -Ergonomic assessment of the work environment, Organisation: -Work organisation and productivity.
learning_outcomes: Describe and apply the principles of good ergonomic design of work areas and equipment to a range of occupational settings.
Practice in an ethical and socially responsible manner.
Assess and manage workplace ergonomic issues using an appropriate assessment strategy, incorporating the principles of the 'hierarchy of controls' in a range of occupational settings.
Identify, explain and evaluate the impact of various personal attributes (anatomical, physiological, anthropometric and psychological) on proper safe working practice.
Access, interpret and apply evidence-based ergonomics and human factors literature to provide high-level advice.
Synthesise complex information, initiate improvements and disseminate knowledge and recommendations to key stakeholders.
Explain the influence of ergonomic principles on human factors, work organisation and culture.

title: Occupational Hygiene Fundamentals
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the field of occupational hygiene. While this is a specialist field of study and practice in its own right, Workplace health and safety practitioners and professionals rely on their expertise to address a wide range of workplace hazards and risks. Topics covered include key principles, concepts and scope of occupational hygiene and toxicology, occupational hygiene standards, environmental and biological monitoring; controlling airborne gases, vapours and particulate, exhaust ventilation, noise assessment and control, personal protective equipment, and the occupational hygiene survey.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of how occupational hygiene standards are set and used in work health and safety.
Outline strategies for identifying, assessing and controlling risks associated with airborne gases, vapours and particulates
Compare and contrast the roles of environmental and biological monitoring in work health and safety
Provide high-level advice on managing and controlling noise and noise-related hazards
Discuss how personal protective equipment can be used to reduce risks associated with workplace exposures
Explain how occupational hygiene surveys are used to inform work health and safety practice
Apply cognitive, technical and creative skills to investigate, evaluate and synthesize occupational hygiene and toxicology concepts and principles

title: Contemporary Work Health and Safety
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with advanced knowledge and skills in Contemporary work health and safety for improving practice. Students are exposed to the theoretical and conceptual foundations and evidence-based approaches as applied in the field. They gain an insight into leading-edge theories and models of causation, prevention and management of work-related incidents and events, investigate safe systems of work, human error and behavioural control strategies. They also learn about fire safety and emergency management
learning_outcomes: Critically analyze and evaluate safe systems work, human error and behavioural control in contemporary WHS practice
Apply evidence-based approaches in contemporary WHS practice
Provide advice on fire safety and emergency management in contemporary WHS practice
Compare and contrast theories and models of causation and prevention of work-related incidents and events
Apply advanced knowledge of contemporary work health and Safety (WHS) in known and unknown contexts

assessment_tasks.task_name: Presentation on Contemporary work health and safety

title: Workplace Hazard Management
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: Achieving and maintaining high standards of safety in any workplace by managing workplace safety hazards is the heart of a safety practitioners day-to-day functions. This course provides students with advanced knowledge and skills to identify, assess, and effectively control a range of workplace hazards through an evidence-based approach.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge and skills in applying an evidence-based approach to Workplace hazard management methods and processes
Adapt and apply an evidence-based Workplace hazard management processes and methods to manage safety risks in known and unknown contexts
Provide high-level advice on effective methods for managing Workplace hazards and risks to a range of audiences
Engage and collaborate with key stakeholders to inform, evaluate and improve Workplace hazard management practice

title: Workplace Health and Safety Management
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: Effective management of workplace health and safety risks is an important in driving organisational performance This course equips students with advanced knowledge and skills to do this effectively in a changing context of work through an evidence-based approach. They also learn to evaluate workplace health and safety management
learning_outcomes: Provide advice on how organisational climate and culture initiatives can be integrated with high reliability and resilience engineering strategies to improve an organisation's safety culture
Integrate conceptual and theoretical knowledge and principles of organisations and human motivation to plan workplace health and safety management interventions
Assess and evaluate workplace health and safety management interventions and strategies
Apply evidence-based workplace health and safety management solutions to evaluate and improve performance
Analyse and evaluate organisational safety behaviour and leadership for improving workplace health and safety

assessment_tasks.task_name: Presentation on Workplace Health and Safety Management
Review on Workplace Health and Safety Management

title: Research Methods in Workplace Health and Safety
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course is designed for students to develop advanced research knowledge and skills in health-related research methods and concepts. The course will explore epidemiology, human research ethics, and qualitative and quantitative research methodologies. Students will develop both knowledge and skills in qualitative and quantitative research and learn how to critique both methodologies.
learning_outcomes: Analyse and evaluate the appropriateness of qualitative and quantitative research methodologies and research design ideas.
Apply knowledge of research ethics principles.
Identify and compare the differences between qualitative and quantitative research methodologies.
Explain and describe commonly used terms in epidemiology.
Critically appraise qualitative and/or quantitative research in an area of occupational health and safety practice.
Define epidemiology in the context of occupational health and safety research.
Identify and describe effective methods of presenting and communicating research through a variety of platforms.

title: Applied Project in Environmental Health and Safety Part B
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: Planning and executing a substantial research-based project and/or scholarship is an important part of operating as a professional. This course enables students to complete a research-based project and/or scholarship in Environmental Health and Safety under academic supervision. The project and/or scholarship may entail an in-depth review of the published literature, an analysis of an existing data set, or a work-based project. This course is Part B of a multi-term sequence. Part A must also be completed to meet the requirements of the sequence. In Part A students initiate and progress their project in consultation with their supervisors, and complete their project in Research Project B. Students must complete the sequence within a twelve month period. If students complete Part A but are unable to complete Part B within the time frame, they must re-enrol in Part A. The main output from this sequence includes a Final Report that is suitable for presentation and/or submission for external peer review. Students enrolling in this course will have successfully completed Research Project A.
learning_outcomes: Develop a research question (or set of questions) targeting an significant Environmental Health and Safety issue, suitable for a Master's-level research-based project and/or scholarship.

Select an appropriate research design to collect, analyse, and interpret data required to answer the research question(s) in accordance with the accepted standards of scholarly conduct, and within the boundaries of any ethics approval.
Plan and execute a substantial research-based project and/or scholarship in Environmental Health and Safety.
Synthesise critical arguments and generate defensible conclusions regarding their research-based project and/or scholarship.
Use discipline-specific language and genres to demonstrate scholarly understanding for a specified audience.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Oral Presentation (Research Questions, Findings and Discussions)

title: Oral Health Sciences I
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: ORHL1101 introduces students to the development, structure and function of the dental hard and soft tissues. The aetiology, pathology, clinical presentation and principles of management of the plaque related dental diseases (dental caries and periodontal disease) will be described. This course is a compulsory program component and students must pass in order to progress in the Bachelor of Oral Health Therapy program. Students are unable to enrol in Year 1 Semester 2 and Year 2 and 3 clinical courses until they have passed this course.
learning_outcomes: Interpret how dental caries and periodontal disease can present and identify such disease;
Describe the aetiology and pathology of dental caries and periodontal disease;
Develop an understanding of the development of the teeth, periodontal tissues, mucous membrane and alveolar bone;
Describe the macroscopic and microscopic appearance of the teeth, periodontal tissues and alveolar bone and relate these to composition and function;
Understand the underlying principles of the management of dental caries and periodontal disease;
Recognise abnormalities of appearance and structure of the teeth, periodontal tissues, mucous membrane and alveolar bone;

title: Applied Project in Environmental Health and Safety Part A
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: Planning and executing a substantial research-based project and/or scholarship is an important part of operating as a professional. This course enables students to complete a research-based project and/or scholarship in Environmental Health and Safety under academic supervision. The project and/or scholarship may entail an in-depth review of the published literature, an analysis of an existing data set, or a work-based project. This course is Part A of a multi-term sequence. Part B must also be completed to meet the requirements of the sequence. In Part A students initiate and progress their project in consultation with their supervisors, and complete their project in Research Project B. Students must complete the sequence within a twelve month period. If students complete Part A but are unable to complete Part B within the time frame, they must re-enrol in Part A. The specific proposal associated with the project and/or scholarship proposal and any ethics approval that is required for data collection needs to be obtained either as part of their Research Methods Course, or well before any data is collected. The course coordinator will make the final decision regarding allocation of supervisors. Alternatively, students who are considering enrolling in this course and who do not have a research question/idea should contact the course coordinator at least one month prior to the beginning of Semester 1.
learning_outcomes: Plan and execute a substantial research-based project and/or scholarship in Environmental Health and Safety.

Select an appropriate research design to collect, analyse, and interpret data required to answer the research question(s) in accordance with the accepted standards of scholarly conduct, and within the boundaries of any ethics approval.
Synthesise critical arguments and generate defensible conclusions regarding their research-based project and/or scholarship.
Develop a research question (or set of questions) targeting a significant Environmental Health and Safety issue, suitable for a Master's-level research-based project and/or scholarship.
Use discipline-specific language and genres to demonstrate scholarly understanding for a specified audience.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Oral Presentation (Research Questions, Findings and Discussions)

title: Oral Health Therapy Clinical Skills I - Introduction to the Clinical Environment
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: ORHL1102 introduces students to clinical environment, with a focus on the importance of infection prevention & control, development of clinical skills including extra and Intra-oral examination. Students will also be introduced to the oral health of individuals and communities. Students will be exposed to the common risk factor approach to assessment and introduced to the relationship between oral and general health. Students will commence preclinical and simulation activities with a focus on infection control, history taking and along with intraoral and extraoral examination skills. Small group sessions will relate theory to practice, and introduce infection control and oral health prevention skills useful in the clinical environment. This course is a compulsory program component and students must pass in order to progress in the Bachelor of Oral Health Therapy program. Students are unable to enrol in Year 1 Semester 2 and Year 2 and 3 clinical courses until they have passed this course.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate skills in clinical communication and self-reflective practice
Identify and interpret the social, cultural and environmental factors that contribute to health or ill health;
Describe and demonstrate skills in Infection Control and Occupational Health and Safety procedures in the clinical environment
Describe and demonstrate the elements and purpose of recording detailed clinical histories and risk management
Understand and implement the medico-legal, ethical and moral responsibilities of members of the oral health team, including scope of practice
Describe and demonstrate skills in completing a clinical assessment, including history taking and examination

title: Oral Health Promotion I
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: ORHL1103 introduces the fundamentals of public health and health promotion. The work in this course will enable you to understand the current theories, frameworks and models of public health and health promotion and relate them to both individuals and populations with a focus on oral health. In addition you will be introduced to health data and statistics, health education, models of communication and health promotion planning, enabling you to develop simple health promotion material for use in a pre-determined setting. This course is a compulsory program component and students must pass in order to progress in the Bachelor of Oral Health Therapy. Students are unable to enrol in Year 2 and 3 courses until they have passed this course.
learning_outcomes: Apply the principles of health promotion to analyse and evaluate current oral health promotion activities
Apply models of communication to health promotion materials
Demonstrate and understanding of oral health in the public sector and the policies that support oral health promotion
Develop an oral health promotion resource
Evaluate the benefits and limitations of teamwork in oral health
Explain the components of health behaviour models, social determinants of health, the common risk factor approach and epidemiology
Analyse and reflect on the effectiveness of various individual and group communication strategies
Describe the differences between health promotion and health education at both individual and population health levels
Demonstrate an understanding of the strategies for a successful smoking cessation program
Demonstrate an understanding of a target audience and develop an age appropriate lesson plan.

title: Oral Health Therapy Clinical Skills II
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: ORHL1104 integrates knowledge of dental morphology with cavity preparation for simple therapeutic procedures including restorative techniques, use of hand and rotary instruments, knowledge of carious lesions, pulpal physiology and protection, selection of dental materials and infection control. Clinical skills laboratory sessions provide opportunities for students to develop the necessary clinical skills in relation to cavity design, preparation, placement of restorations and extraction of primary teeth. This course is a compulsory program component and students must pass in order to demonstrate clinical safety and to progress in the Bachelor of Oral Health Therapy program. Students are unable to enrol in Year 2 and 3 clinical courses until they have passed this course.
learning_outcomes: Recognise the factors influencing the selection of materials in management of active caries or preventive care
Explain the influence of tooth morphology on cavity preparation and restorative techniques
Demonstrate competent extraction of primary teeth, including the establishment of haemostasis

Describe the design, function and mode of action of hand and rotary instruments and understand the principles of hard tissue and dental caries removal using slow and high speed rotary and hand instrumentation
Explain the principles and techniques for assessing pulp vitality, and the pulpal response to the deep carious lesion.
Explain the principles and management of the different types of carious lesions in conjunction with a thorough understanding of cavity design, classification, and pulpal protection
Demonstrate methods and clinical skills in cavity preparations and restorations, including pulpal management and competent infection control

title: Oral Health Therapy Clinical Skills III - Dental Hygiene
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: ORHL1105 introduces students to the disease processes that are relevant to the periodontal complex. The course will integrate the aetiology, pathology, progression and presentation of various periodontal diseases with assessment and management. Clinical skills laboratory sessions provide opportunities for students to develop the necessary clinical skills in relation to recording periodontal diseases, reaching a clinical diagnosis, formulating a treatment plan and provision of periodontal treatment. This course is a compulsory program component and students must pass in order to demonstrate clinical safety and to progress in the Bachelor of Oral Health Therapy program. Students are unable to enrol in Year 2 and 3 clinical courses until they have passed this course.
learning_outcomes: Describe techniques for implant maintenance
Describe the etiopathogenesis of periodontal disease, including local and systemic factors
Describe and demonstrate techniques for removal of supragingival and subgingival deposits (plaque and calculus)
Describe and interpret the use of clinical records including indices and radiographs in diagnosis of periodontal diseases
Explain the role of periodontal risk assessment in prevention, diagnosis and treatment of periodontal disease

title: Oral Health Sciences III
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: ORHL2102 introduces students to the basic principles of pathology and bacteriology. The course integrates knowledge of oral structures and function to the recognition, diagnosis, assessment and management of common mucosal and salivary gland lesions, in both children and adults. It will also reinforce radiation safety and the principles and practice of dental radiography and radiology. This course is a compulsory program component and students must pass in order to demonstrate clinical safety and to progress in the Bachelor of Oral Health Therapy program. Students are unable to enrol in Year 2 Semester 2 and Year 3 clinical courses until they have passed this course.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the provision of appropriate advice, referral or treatment for common minor oral pathologies within the scope of oral health therapists.
Identify and describe and pathologies that occur commonly in the oral environment;
Demonstrate an understanding of and clinical competence in intra-oral and extra-oral radiography and radiology
Explain how pathologies can affects development, structure and function of oral and peri-oral tissues;
Analyse and describe the need for modification of an individual treatment plan or referrals for oral pathologies
Analyse and describe the potential impact of oral ill health on systemic health and vice versa;

title: Introduction to Oral Health and Therapeutics
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: ORHL1106 will build on the material delivered in HUBS1401, ORHL1101 and HUBS1106 to help establish evidence-based clinical practice through highlighting aspects of the medical and dental sciences that directly influence oral health practice. The course will provide an introduction to pharmacology, with a focus therapeutic agents that are commonly used in the dental clinic, as well as an introduction to pain management. Common systemic conditions, and their medications, particularly those that affect oral health and patient management, will be introduced. This will provide the foundation for medical history taking, and the management of patients with special medical needs. Genetic and developmental influences on health and disease will be examined, along with an introduction to orofacial developmental disorders. By the end of the course students will have an understanding of the therapeutic management of oral and systemic disease, and the requirement to address the special medical needs of patients. This course is a compulsory program component and students must pass in order to progress in the Bachelor of Oral Health Therapy. Students are unable to enroll in Year 2 clinical courses until they have passed this course.
learning_outcomes: Develop an understanding of the main therapeutic agents used in the dental clinic
Demonstrate a knowledge and understanding of the basic concepts of pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics
Develop an understanding of the common mechanisms underlying human oral and systemic diseases
Demonstrate a knowledge and understanding of the common approaches to pain management in the dental clinic
Identify developmental abnormalities of the dental hard and soft tissues

title: Oral Health Therapy Clinical Skills IV - Dental Therapy
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: ORHL2103 integrates clinical skills and knowledge of intra and extra-oral radiography, cavity preparation for permanent and primary teeth, including pulpotomy procedures, stainless steel crown application, emergency restorative procedures for dental trauma and extraction of deciduous teeth. This course builds on existing clinical skills to enable students to provide clinical treatment. This course is a compulsory program component and students must pass in order to demonstrate clinical safety and to progress in the Bachelor of Oral Health Therapy program. Students are unable to enrol in Year 2 Semester 2 and Year 3 clinical courses until they have passed this course.
learning_outcomes: Apply diagnostic methods, including intra- and extra-oral radiography, to identify hard and soft tissue pathology.
Apply the skills and knowledge necessary to employ an evidence based approach to decision making in the clinical setting.
Demonstrate competency in the clinical care of patients, including appropriate infection control.
Recognise active caries and understand the factors involved in provision of clinical restorative care.
Reflect, evaluate and critique personal performance during clinical sessions.
Recognise and explain the management of common dental emergencies and trauma in the primary and permanent dentition.
Demonstrate an understanding of the principles and techniques for the management of deep carious lesions and pulp therapy, including stainless steel crowns.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Diagnosis and Teatment Planning, Clinical Communication.

title: Oral Health and Community
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: ORHL2106 relates to understanding and providing specialised oral health care to individuals and populations within the community who have additional or complex needs. The course emphasises inclusive, patient-centred care and the importance of adapting professional practice to meet diverse health and social circumstances. This course is a compulsory component of the Bachelor of Oral Health Therapy program. Students are required to successfully complete the course to demonstrate clinical competence, ensure safe practice, and progress within the program.
learning_outcomes: Identify and apply appropriate and effective communication with social and cultural sensitivity, with patients, carers and team members;
Apply social and cultural understanding to deliver evidence-based information and care within community settings.
Apply professional, ethical, and legal principles in oral health therapy practice with reflective awareness of personal values
Demonstrate an understanding of the impact of racism and discrimination on oral health, health, and wellbeing, and apply anti-discriminatory principles to deliver culturally safe and inclusive care
Explain and apply knowledge of the general and oral health needs of priority populations.
Demonstrate and apply oral health education strategies for individuals, groups, and priority populations using a person-centred approach

assessment_tasks.task_name: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health and oral health essay
Develop an information sheet for a Special Needs Group

title: Oral Health Promotion II
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: ORHL2105 builds on the knowledge gained in ORHL1103 and introduces the theories and approaches used in evaluating Oral Health Promotion projects. You will work with other students to plan and evaluate an oral health promotion project idea to present to your tutors and peers. In addition you will be introduced to research in population health which includes fundamental epidemiology and health statistics. You will complete a literature review and critical appraisal to support your evidence based practice and understanding of the literature. This course is a compulsory program component and students must pass in order to progress in the Bachelor of Oral Health Therapy. Students are unable to enrol in Year 3 clinical courses until they have passed this course.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate data obtained from oral health indices and other research methods
Present a project proposal
Access and critically evaluate scientific literature
Analyse and evaluate existing oral health promotion material in the context of ability to implement change
Apply the principles of health promotion to plan and evaluate an oral health promotion project for a select target group
Explain the components required to complete a project plan
Analyse and reflect on the effectiveness of various individual and group communication strategies
Demonstrate an understanding of health statistics and research design
Reflect on the benefits and limitations of groupwork

title: Oral Health Therapy Clinical Skills V - Dental Hygiene
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: ORHL2104 introduces students to the management of oral health therapy patients including Local Anaesthetics, dental occlusion and orthodontic patients. Clinical skills laboratory activities introduce new skills such as impression taking, pouring models, construction of mouthguards, clinical photography and placement and removal of orthodontic components and consolidation of previously learned skills. This course is a compulsory program component and students must pass in order to demonstrate clinical safety and to progress in the Bachelor of Oral Health Therapy program. Students are unable to enrol in Year 2 Semester 2 and Year 3 clinical courses until they have passed this course.
learning_outcomes: Understand the role of clinical photography and its relevance
Implement effective communication, clinical skills and patient management
Describe and practice appropriate Infection Prevention and Control in dental laboratory and clinical environments
Recognise and manage Medical Emergencies
Understand and demonstrate competency in the safe administration of Local Anaestheics
Understand and demonstrate the methods and materials used to take impressions and construct fixed/removeable prostheses including mouthguards
Describe dental occlusion and malocclusion as it relates to contemporary orthodontics
Understand the process of placement and removal of orthodontic components

title: Oral Health Therapy Clinical Skills VI - Clinical Practice
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: ORHL2107 builds on the knowledge and skills developed in first year and Semester 1 of second year, focusing on the assessment, diagnosis, and patient-centred clinical management of dental hygiene and therapy patients. This course supports the development of safe, effective, and patient-centred care through supervised clinical practice at the University of Newcastle Oral Health Clinic. As a compulsory component of the program, successful completion is required to demonstrate clinical safety and to progress into 3rd-year clinical courses within the Bachelor of Oral Health Therapy
learning_outcomes: Apply person-centred communication strategies, using appropriate verbal and non-verbal techniques, to effectively interact with patients, carers, and the oral health team in ways that are culturally safe, socially aware, and age-appropriate.
Demonstrate knowledge of oral disease aetiology and effects to inform clinical judgement and guide preventive, restorative, and patient management strategies for individuals and communities.
Develop and implement evidence-based treatment plans, including preventive and restorative care, pain management, and appropriate referral pathways within the Oral Health Therapist scope of practice
Conduct comprehensive assessments of oral health needs, including risk factors and overall health status, to support safe and effective clinical decision-making.
Demonstrate safe and effective clinical practice, including the application of infection prevention and control principles to ensure patient safety and maintain clinical standards.
Select and appropriately use medicaments, medications, and antimicrobial therapies in the management of oral disease.
Reflect on and evaluate personal clinical performance to support continuous professional development and improvement.

title: Introduction to Oral Health Promotion
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: ORHL2108 will build on the health promotion and preventative care themes established in PUBH1080, ORHL1102 and ORHL1105. The course will focus on aspects of health promotion and preventative care that are especially relevant to the oral health of Australian communities. In addition to examining the strategies used for oral health promotion in Australia, the Course will introduce the theories and approaches used in evaluating Oral Health Promotion projects. You will work with other students to plan and evaluate an oral health promotion project idea to present to your tutors and peers. In addition, you will be introduced to research in population health which includes fundamental epidemiology and health statistics. You will complete a literature review and critical appraisal to support your evidence-based practice and understanding of the literature. By the end of the course students will have gained experience in the design, development, implementation and evaluation. This course is a compulsory program component, and students must pass in order to progress in the Bachelor of Oral Health Therapy. Students are unable to enrol in Year 3 clinical courses until they have passed this course.
learning_outcomes: describe the differences between health promotion and health education at both individual and population health levels
analyse and evaluate existing oral health promotion material in the context of ability to implement change
apply the principles of health promotion to plan and evaluate an oral health promotion project for a select target group
demonstrate an understanding of health statistics and research design
access and critically evaluate scientific literature and data

assessment_tasks.task_name: Planning and developing a research project proposal

title: Oral Health Therapy Clinical Skills VII - Adult Clinical Practice
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: ORHL3101 is placement course that builds on the clinical application of knowledge and skills gained by students in Year 1 and Year 2. In this course, students will treat patients in the University of Newcastle Oral Health Clinic under supervision. Students will develop clinical judgment skills to be able to diagnose and manage patients requiring simple treatment procedures within the scope of an OHT along with those that require referral for complex treatment. This course will specifically include clinical management of oral health patients such as simple pediatric extractions, direct restorations and periodontal therapy. This course is a compulsory program component and students must pass in order to demonstrate clinical safety and to progress in the Bachelor of Oral Health Therapy program. Students are unable to enrol in Year 3 Semester 2 clinical courses until they have passed this course.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate critical thinking and clinical judgement in the holistic management of dental patient.
Explain the regulations relating to the clinical practice of oral health therapists and have a clear understanding of the limits of their scope of practice
Evaluate medical history and medications in provision of dental care.
Generate person-centred treatment plans, including appropriate referral pathways.
Describe age related changes in teeth and supporting tissues.
Demonstrate the comprehensive understanding of patients' treatment needs.

title: Oral Health Therapy Clinical Skills VIII - Clinical Practice
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: ORHL3102 is a placement course that provides an opportunity to apply the knowledge and skills gained by students in first and second year courses. This course and relates to the assessment, diagnosis and clinical management of oral health patients within the scope of oral health therapists. Students will be expected to treat patients at various external placements including residential aged care facilities, under supervision. This course is a compulsory program component and students must pass in order to demonstrate clinical safety and to progress in the Bachelor of Oral Health Therapy program. Students are unable to enrol in Year 3 Semester 2 clinical courses until they have passed this course.
learning_outcomes: Reflect, evaluate and critique personal performance during clinical sessions
Demonstrate professional behaviour and integrity
Demonstrate the knowledge of the aetiology and effects of oral diseases
Demonstrate the provision of evidence based preventive and restorative clinical patient care, within the Oral Health Therapists scope of practice
Demonstrate sound cultural, social and age appropriate communication skills with child, adolescent and adult patients, carers and team members

assessment_tasks.task_name: Clinical Logbook - Marks from external placements

title: Oral Health Promotion II
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: ORHL3103 builds on the knowledge and skills gained in PUBH1080 and ORHL2108 and provides an opportunity for you to gain an understanding of oral health needs of the specific population such as the elderly living in the community and in Residential Aged Care Facilities (RACF) through a project-based learning activity completed across the semester. This course is a compulsory program component and students must pass in order to complete to the Bachelor of Oral Health Therapy program.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate and address the oral health needs of priority populations
Access, analyse and collate evidence-based data and complete a literature review
Demostrate the benefits and analyse limitations of teamwork in research and clinical care
Analyse and utilise various communication strategies within a multidisciplinary model of care

assessment_tasks.task_name: Supporting priority population oral health needs

title: Oral Health Therapy Clinical Skills IX - Clinical Practice
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: ORHL3104 is the capstone course of the program, building on the knowledge and skills developed across the first two years and Semester 1 of third year. It focuses on the assessment, diagnosis, and person-centred clinical management of oral health therapy patients. The course prepares students for practice by strengthening their ability to deliver evidence-based, culturally safe, and patient-centred care, while practising within their scope and upholding professional and ethical responsibilities. Students will achieve required competencies through supervised clinical placements. As a compulsory component of the program, successful completion is required to demonstrate clinical safety and meet the requirements for the Bachelor of Oral Health.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate oral health status, risk factors, and systemic influences to support advanced clinical decision-making and prioritisation of care.
Critique and apply legal, ethical, and regulatory frameworks to guide professional conduct, decision-making, and interprofessional practice.
Analyse the aetiology and progression of oral diseases to inform clinical reasoning and optimise preventive, restorative and patient management strategies for individuals and diverse populations.
Integrate person-centred communication to manage complex interactions with patients, carers, and the oral health team

Design and justify comprehensive, evidence-based treatment plans, incorporating preventive, restorative, and therapeutic interventions, pain control, and referral pathways within the Oral Health Therapist scope of practice.
Critically apply infection prevention and control principles to ensure safe, high-quality clinical practice and uphold professional standards.
Critically reflect on clinical performance and feedback to identify areas for improvement and inform ongoing professional growth and lifelong learning.

title: Basic Science in Orthopaedics
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview: This course will give the student a comprehensive and critical understanding as well as latest advances in basic science in orthopaedics. This course is a core course in the Orthopaedic Specialisation of the Master of Traumatology.
learning_outcomes: analyse cutting edge research advances in orthopaedic related basic science questions in a critical manner.
define and analyse basic science related problems in orthopaedic disease;
demonstrate understanding of the treatment and management of joint disease in particular arthroplasty related problems as well as understand limitations of different modes of treatment; and

title: Paediatric Orthopaedics
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview: This course will give the student a comprehensive and critical understanding of the pathophysiology, aetiology, management, and advances in paediatric orthopaedic diseases. This course is a compulsory course in the Orthopaedic Specialisation in the Master of Traumatology.
learning_outcomes: critically analyse research advances in paediatric orthopaedic disease.
define and analyse specific paediatric orthopaedic disease;
demonstrate understanding of the management of paediatric orthopaedic disease during the preoperative, operative and postoperative period; and

title: Financial Accounting 1
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Fundamental principles underpin accrual accounting and financial reporting. Financial Accounting 1 critically examines these principles providing students with the technical skills of accounting, including the analysis, recording, preparation and interpretation of accounting information.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on learning behaviours and identify strategies to improve learning.
Resolve a financial accounting problem, and justify a solution using appropriate financial accounting concepts and principles.
Prepare and analyse financial statements in accordance with conventional rules of accounting.
Apply the double-entry system to a transaction data set, and proceed through the steps of the accounting cycle.

title: Corporate Finance
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: The course provides an introduction to corporate finance theories and how these theories can be applied to problems relevant to managers. Topics covered will include: corporate objectives, operations of capital markets, alternative sources of finance, dividend decision, financing decision, cost of capital, time value of money, evaluation of investment projects, and risk and return.
learning_outcomes: Explain the importance of finance and risk in personal/business decisions.
Exhibit an understanding of how risky assets are priced.
Demonstrate an understanding of the investment and financing decision processes of the firm.
Explain the concept of risk management and its importance to management.
Use basic financial mathematics.
Illustrate an understanding of the role cash flow estimates and analysis have in the decision processes.

title: Auditing and Assurance Services
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: The course introduces students to the major conceptual and technical aspects of auditing. Emphasis is placed on financial statement audits conducted under the Corporations Law. The course also provides insight into other types of audit and assurance activities and emphasises the risk-based approach to auditing.
learning_outcomes: Comprehend the conceptual underlying theory of auditing.
Demonstrate written and oral communication skills in explaining auditing concepts.
Apply professional auditing techniques.
Critically analyse financial information to facilitate the implementation of auditing techniques.
Work effectively as part of a team in exploring and resolving audit issues.
Identify and assess contemporary auditing and assurance issues.
Interpret the legal, ethical and societal role and responsibilities of the auditor.

title: Management Accounting
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Within organisations accounting practice and data directly influence everyday management decision making. The course introduces students to the concept of cost, cost behaviour, product costing systems, cost allocation and activity-based costing, budgeting, and standard costing control systems, relevant costing, pricing decisions and customer profitability analysis. Professional communication within management settings and contexts will be emphasised as an important attribute.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the preparation and use of management accounting information in an organisation
Evaluate the performance of an organisation
Explain cost concepts used in management decision making
Apply key costing methods and principles to generate information for decision making
Critically analyse costing information taking into account the needs of management

title: Financial Accounting 2
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: The course examines general purpose financial reporting from the perspective of a single incorporated entity. In doing so, the course emphasises the development of the knowledge, understanding and skills needed to interpret and apply accounting standards and procedures to solve accounting problems which companies encounter in practice.
learning_outcomes: Illustrate an awareness of the relevant accounting standards, statutory requirements and listing requirements that impact on corporate accounting and the preparation and presentation of financial reports.
Critically integrate and apply theoretical and technical accounting knowledge and skills to solve routine accounting problems.
Explain the issues surrounding contemporary accounting controversies and the corporate decision-making process.

Demonstrate an understanding of the nature of the corporate entity and be aware of the concepts, statutory requirements and other authoritative influences that underpin accounting and reporting in the Australian and international regulatory environment.
Evaluate solutions for routine accounting, corporate reporting and corporate governance problems in diverse contexts using social, ethical, economic regulatory and global perspectives.

title: Financial Accounting 3
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This courses focuses on company accounting. It provides students with an understanding of the regulatory framework for corporate financial reporting in Australia, and provides detailed coverage of the requirements for the preparation of financial statements for a group of companies operating under common control. Topics covered include accounting for corporate acquisitions; consolidation accounting; consolidated cash flow statements; accounting for company income tax; and accounting for foreign operations and corporate insolvency.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the technical skills, underlying concepts and issues in accounting for corporations.
Understand the theoretical and practical aspects involved in the preparation and interpretation of a set of consolidated financial reports.
Demonstrate an understanding of the theoretical constructs of contemporary financial accounting.
Interpret integrated reports, sustainability reports and extend external reporting.
Exhibit an awareness of selected accounting standards, including the ability to apply these standards in appropriate circumstances.

title: Taxation Law
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Taxation in Australia originates from a complex legal and constitutional foundation. This course analyses both the legal concepts of income and capital and the fiscal treatment of individual, corporate, and other taxpaying entities. Specific topics covered include GST, assessable income and exempt income, allowable deductions, special classes of taxpayers including trusts, partnerships and companies, calculation of individual income tax, capital gains tax, fringe benefits tax, depreciable assets, residency and retirement and termination payments. Course experience will assist students to define and articulate taxation issues as well as professionally communicate recommended solutions.
learning_outcomes: Identify specific Australian Income Tax Laws and their relevance to particular tax paying entities.
Communicate technical tax information effectively and professionally to client taxpayers employing formats to suit both context and audience.
Demonstrate an integrative awareness of tax planning issues as they relate to real life situations and environments.
Access provisions of the Income Tax Assessment Act and related legislation.
Identify taxation issues and apply critical analysis skills for effective solution.

title: Economics
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Economics addresses problems and issues at every level of business, government and community. This course investigates both microeconomic and macroeconomic principles. The microeconomic component explores supply and demand; elasticity; the operation of markets; costs and production; perfect competition & monopoly; monopolistic competition & oligopoly; wages, the distribution of income & inequality; market failure and government policy. The analysis of macroeconomics includes the determination of economic activity, money and the financial system; inflation and unemployment; the balance of payments and exchange rates; and macroeconomic policy. A problem oriented learning approach will be taken in lectures developing a mastery of concepts and associated economic analysis applied to real world issues.
learning_outcomes: Interpret, apply and analyse microeconomics and macroeconomics principles and define their relevance to current global issues and events.
Critically analyse and synthesise multiple sources of economic information in order to support conclusions and address issues.
Critically examine both social phenomena and public policy issues facing individuals and firms locally, nationally and globally.
Produce presentations using academic standard, style and structure appropriate to purpose and audience.

Investigate the predominant factors that determine overall levels of production and employment in the economy; inclusive of the influence of fiscal and monetary policy on international trade and balance of payments and financial markets.

title: Business Decision Making
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Quantitative techniques are frequently employed as essential research and analytical tools in accounting, financial and economic environments. This course provides an understanding of the quantitative techniques that are frequently used in accounting, financial and economic studies to aid business decision making. Statistical techniques such as data screening and descriptive techniques, inferential statistics, sampling, questionnaire and research design, hypothesis testing, analysis of variance and regression analysis are covered. Use is made of Microsoft Excel statistical package to analyse data sets and produce reports based on quantitative analyses. Participants will build increased competency in business communication skills and techniques.
learning_outcomes: Exhibit an awareness of the principles of hypothesis testing.
Design a quantitative study.
Demonstrate an understanding of appropriate analytical strategies to test specific hypothesis.
Report statistical findings in a clear and concise fashion.
Use Microsoft Excel to conduct statistical analysis.
Demonstrate an understanding of quantitative techniques that are frequently used in accounting and financial studies research.

title: Business Law
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Business Law provides the necessary legal framework to inform professional practice within accounting and related professions. This course encompasses both contract and commercial law introducing the participants to the Australian legal system, including sources of law, legal institutions and torts law. Topics developed under contract law include the law of offer and acceptance, consideration, breach of contract, remedies for breach of contract, and contract law with respect to the sale of goods. Commercial law topics comprise consumer law, the Competition and Consumer Act, principal and agent, property, trusts, consumer credit and law with respect to bankruptcy.
learning_outcomes: Understand the protection and privacy laws associated with the collection, storage, access, use and/or sharing of data and information.
Comprehend and apply the main principles of the law of contract to resolve problem situations arising in business environments.

Interpret the law of consumer protection, business competition, principals and agents, property, business organisations, consumer credit bankruptcy and implement these principles to critically analyse and evaluate relevant problem situations.
Investigate, formulate and apply a range of problem-solving approaches to resolve business law issues.
Identify and recount the sources of law in Australia.
Exhibit an integrative understanding of the law of torts, particularly the law of negligence as it relates to professional responsibility and the duty of care.
Recognise and be able to restate the principal features of the Australian legal system including selected laws relating to business which form part of that system.

title: Company Law
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: A company possesses its own legal identity. This course provides an in-depth analysis of features of companies and their classifications, the obligations and rights of parties to companies with emphasis on the main legislation. Directions for focus include consideration of the company as a legal person; the incorporation of companies; internal governance; director's duties and shareholder's rights; accounts and financial disclosure; transacting and external administration. As alternatives to companies, the course sources and interprets the different legal structures such as sole trader, partnership and trading trusts. Students will experience increased confidence in employing legal terminology, tools and communication in diverse situations.
learning_outcomes: Interpret and restate the legal rights and duties of parties to the corporation (governance).
Demonstrate an integrative understanding of the legal structure of a company.
Communicate your professional knowledge in an articulate style and structure.
Recognise, assess and resolve basic legal issues in an ethical and professional manner when interacting with corporations.
Demonstrate an evaluative understanding of corporate finance and failure.
Discuss how a company contracts with others.
Identify the principal legal forms of business organisations differentiating between strengths and weaknesses.
Explain the legal consequences of the main feature of a company, particularly separate legal personality.
Exhibit an awareness of the rights and duties of directors and shareholders of a company.

title: Accounting Information Systems
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Examines the theory and practice of Accounting Information Systems. Covers all aspects of the use of information technology to support the contemporary organisation, with particular emphasis on support for Accounting and Finance. Industry-focused case studies and detailed practical exercises are used to underpin the conceptual models used to describe the elements of modern accounting support systems.
learning_outcomes: Use technology-assisted tools for project control, audit, financial analysis, and reporting.
Appreciate the nature of the interactions between the traditional accounting applications and other transaction management systems.
Demonstrate a strong knowledge of the applications of a computer-based accounting system.

title: Introduction to Podiatry
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: The broad aim of this course is to introduce the work of podiatrists in health care and explain the important role of podiatric services in the community. Students will gain knowledge of professional and legislative requirements and develop basic skills in clinical and reflective practice. The focus will primarily be on areas designed to prepare students for incorporating the clinical standards for infection control and general clinical assessment skills in preparation for competent and culturally safe practice in clinical courses. Foundations of dermatology including the function and structure of the skin, assessment, differential diagnosis, aetiological factors and the management of disorders of the skin, with particular emphasis on common foot conditions and co-morbidities will be investigated.
learning_outcomes: Explain and perform basic biomechanical assessments of the lower extremity and interpret the results.
Describe the scope of practice of podiatry and the role of the profession within the health care setting.
Describe the presentation and treatment of common skin and nail disorders.
Describe the legal and professional standards associated with documentation and management of patient data in clinical settings.
Explain and perform basic vascular and neurological assessment of the lower extremity and interpret the results.
Describe one's own cultural worldview, values and perceptions of health and the implications of these for health care practice.
Demonstrate appropriate and safe professional behaviour consistent with that required in a clinical setting.
Discuss the relevance of clinical skills in assessment of foot problems and the role of footwear in treatment.
Discuss and apply the framework of infection control standards in the health care environment.

title: Musculoskeletal Disorders and Imaging
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: Becoming a podiatrist requires an understanding of the clinical and theoretical foundations of musculoskeletal conditions that impact on function of the lower extremity. This subject aims to expand your podiatric knowledge and skills needed to manage patients with musculoskeletal disorders. This subject further aims to develop your knowledge and clinical application of diagnostic techniques (i.e. x-ray, ultrasound, magnetic resonance imaging, computer tomography and bone scans).
learning_outcomes: Evaluate available treatment strategies (pharmacological, physical, mechanical, surgical, Traditional etc.) to provide effective culturally safe person-centred are for musculoskeletal disorders of the lower extremity
Describe the role of interprofessional practice in the management of musculoskeletal disorders of the lower extremity
Safely apply the examination techniques needed to diagnose and treat a range of musculoskeletal disorders affecting the lower extremity
Describe and safely apply the principles of musculoskeletal rehabilitation to the management of acute and chronic injuries of the lower extremity.
Effectively and safely integrate diagnostic imaging into clinical practice to diagnose musculoskeletal disorders of the lower extremity

assessment_tasks.task_name: Attendance and participation at all allocated practical sessions

title: Fundamentals of Podiatry Practice
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This is a pre-clinical course that provides an introduction to the clinical environment in Podiatry practice. Students will gain an understanding of the scope of practice of Podiatry and learn to apply evidence based practice to the clinical setting. Musculoskeletal anatomy of the foot and ankle and dermatology will be covered in detail. Students will also develop essential clinical skills including infection control and sterilization, learn to perform basic podiatric assessments and treatment, and undertake observational placement.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate safe and appropriate basic clinical podiatric skills including general treatment and neurovascular and biomechanical assessment techniques
Demonstrate a sound understanding of the functional anatomy of the foot and ankle
Describe the structure and function of skin and know common dermatological conditions affecting the foot
Demonstrate adherence to appropriate infection control and sterilisation procedures
Describe evidence based practice and how it is applied to the clinical setting in Podiatry practice
Demonstrate appropriate professional behaviour and communication in a clinical setting including clinical history taking and patient note writing and formatting

title: Pathomechanics and Podiatric Medicine
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course will introduce students to clinical/practical and theoretical foundations of human biomechanics of the foot and lower extremity, and the assessment, diagnosis and treatment of common foot and lower extremity pathologies. The course consists of co-ordinated lectures and practical components to cover the theory and application of foot and lower extremity biomechanics and gait analysis, relevant physical examinations (bones, joints, soft tissues), diagnosing common foot and lower extremity conditions and related treatment options.
learning_outcomes: Explain lower back, pelvic, leg and foot biomechanics in relation to normal and abnormal function in static & dynamic environments.
Employ am evidence-based approach to non-pharmacological and pharmacological management of common foot and lower extremity pathologies.
Safely apply relevant skills required for static and dynamic assessment of pelvic, lower extremity, and foot structures.
Describe and apply valid, reliable and appropriate health outcome measurement tools and technologies for diagnosis and management of lower extremity pathologies in different populations.
Identify and describe the aetiology, pathophysiology, and clinical presentation of common musculoskeletal pathologies of the foot and lower extremity.

title: Evidence in Podiatric Medicine
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course will introduce skills for finding and using the best available evidence in health. This begins with understanding thinking systems, biases and why we don't often accept, or respond, to facts, science and evidence. Students will learn the evidence-based practice process to formulate questions and find them appropriate and relevant evidence from the unending amount of information available. The course covers key concepts in how to read and understand a research paper. Students will develop skills for communicating evidence to strengthen arguments in academic writing and professional practice.
learning_outcomes: Recognise personal thinking styles and associated biases
Design a sensitive and specific PICO search strategy to find best available evidence
Describe the reasons for the 5 steps of evidence-based practice
Identify type, level and key research concepts in journal articles
Integrate strength and relevance of evidence findings into academic writing

title: Podiatry Pre-Clinical
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course will prepare students for working with patients in the Clinic and external placements through consolidation and application of podiatric theory and assessment skills. This subject will emphasize Clinic procedures, and equip students with basic management, communication and correspondence skills. The subject will also apply student knowledge of functional anatomy, dermatological, vascular, neurological and biomechanical assessment techniques and management into the context of common podiatric conditions.
learning_outcomes: Apply and interpret appropriate vascular, neurological, biomechanical and dermatological assessment skills for use in the context of common pathological conditions

Analyse the characteristics of effective strength-based communication that facilitates the building of respectful, inclusive, and culturally responsive relationships with patients and their families, carers, and other health professionals.
Apply the principles of professionalism, infection control and work health and safety (WH&S) in theoretical and clinical setting
Critique the role of culture and culturally safe practice on foot health outcomes across population groups including Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples.
Apply reflective clinical practice principles in health care provision.
Demonstrate safe instrument handling, manual skills application, and skills in manufacture of basic orthotic therapies for management of podiatric conditions.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Clinical Attendance (compulsory attendance at all clinical teaching activities)

title: Introduction to Podiatry Clinical Skills
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course provides an introduction to clinical skills commonly required in podiatry and the manufacture of foot orthoses. The clinical component includes sterilization and infection control, basic podiatric treatments, such as nail cutting and scalpel techniques. Students are introduced to common podiatric assessments including biomechanical assessment, clinical gait analysis and neurovascular assessments. The use of medical records including the legal obligations of podiatrists, making entries and writing referral letters is also covered. The orthoses component develops student understanding of orthotic therapy and the manufacture of basic orthotic devices.
learning_outcomes: Take accurate negative impression plaster casts
Apply padding and strapping to the foot and ankle.
Demonstrate adherence to appropriate infection control procedures.
Describe evidence based practice and how it can be applied to the clinical setting.
Describe and demonstrate appropriate professional behaviour and communication.
Describe the history of orthotic therapy.
Take a basic patient history and conduct a podiatric physical examination.
Demonstrate and adhere to the OH and S requirement of an orthoses lab.
