Demonstrate competency in ethical and legal clinical practice.
Discuss the practice of a pharmacist in healthcare and in the delivery of pharmaceutical care.
Explain the basic principles of workplace health and safety and explain the process of risk management potential or actual hazards in the work environment.
Demonstrate professionalism in the development, provision and management of pharmaceutical services across all areas of the pharmacy industry.

Apply therapeutic knowledge, skills and attributes to describe the quality use of medicines' issues surrounding therapeutic agents in the treatment of a range of conditions encountered in practice and develop clinical and communication skills in the therapeutic management of these conditions.
Apply the components and concepts of Public Health, holistic health and the core principles underpinning individual health-related behaviour.

Describe the pathophysiology and management of a range of conditions across the age spectrum including paediatric and geriatric clients and develop advanced skills in medication management with the aim of optimising health outcomes.
Describe the role of Health Promotion in maintaining and improving the status of health as well as minimising illness for individual and population groups.

title: Pharmacy Projects (Part A)
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course is Part A of a multi-term sequence. Part B must also be completed to meet the requirements of the sequence. Students will undertake group pharmacy projects with assistance from their course coordinator/supervisor incorporating self-directed learning. Projects will address a health sciences related research question. Students will use evidence-based techniques and published literature to study the question(s) and prepare a written report and oral presentation which discuss the issues being examined.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate advanced oral and written communication skills including the presentation of a written literature review and an oral presentation of methods.
Collect, analyse and interpret data as required to investigate the question/issue.
Apply research skills to study a pharmacy or health-related question/issue.
Critically appraise the literature related to the pharmacy question or issue.
Demonstrate the application of research skills and knowledge.

title: Pharmacy Projects (Part B)
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course is Part B of a multi-term sequence. Part A must also be completed to meet the requirements of the sequence. Students will continue the group projects that were initiated during semester 1 and will apply techniques to analyse their data and synthesise the findings coherently, culminating in a manuscript that is structured according to author guidelines.
learning_outcomes: Apply research skills to study a research question/issue.
Collect, analyse and interpret data as required to investigate the question/issue.
Demonstrate the application of research skills and knowledge.
Critically appraise the literature related to the professional pharmacy question/issue.
Demonstrate advanced oral and written communication skills.

title: Pharmacogenomics and Health Technology Assessment
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the emerging fields of pharmacogenomics and personalized `precision' medicine that are now transforming the face of modern health care. Powerful modern technologies revolutionizing genomics and molecular medicine are creating unprecedented opportunities for patient-specific treatments and health care. The course helps students build their knowledge and understanding of these new fields and develop professional evidence-based approaches to keep apace of these fast-moving areas into the future.
learning_outcomes: Perform balanced, evidence-based assessments of controversial issues and new information and concepts in these and other emerging fields.
Discuss how modern pharmacogenomics differs from traditional pharmacogenetics and why this is important for clinical utility.
Explain the new field of precision medicine and how recent technological advances in areas such as genomics, pharmacogenomics and bioinformatics are revolutionising modern health care.
Apply evidence-based, systematic approaches to understanding and implementing pharmacogenomics and personalized health care.
Discuss probable future trends in applications of these fields in clinical practice.
Discuss the advanced concepts of multifactorial drug-gene interactions and maternal-fetal pharmacogenomics.
Demonstrate fundamental knowledge of the molecular basis of responses to drugs and other therapeutics.

Describe potential impacts of personalized healthcare for consumers, health professionals, industry, government and society and demonstrate responsible professional attitudes in relation to ethical, legal and social issues (ELSI) in personalized health care.

Provide balanced, critical evaluations of the benefits and limitations of important current and emerging technologies in these fields, including modern genotyping technologies such as polymerase chain reaction (PCR), microarrays and next-generation sequencing.
Explain how genomics and other individual factors such as environment or lifestyle can influence drug pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics.

title: Clinical Leadership in Health Care
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: In this advanced course, students will build on the cognitive knowledge and technical skills learnt throughout the program by considering and applying the principles of good business practice and leadership to the delivery of related services across the health sector. This course provides an advanced examination of the foundations of management and leadership theory within a clinical / healthcare context. It defines and explores management theory and characteristics and styles of leadership, and introduces individual, group and organisational structures. The role of the clinician/health scientist in health promotion, and in disaster and crisis management within a global context, is also discussed in this clinical leadership course. Through practical learning, students will explore the fundamentals of managing an organisational unit (team) in developing and implementing health promotion services in regard to procurement of resources (including human resources and clientele) within a business and professional framework.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an integrative understanding of the concepts of management within health services and an ability to apply these in an effective, ethical, and socially responsible manner.
Demonstrate an understanding of health promotion and the clinician/ health scientist role within this.
Apply professionalism including legal, ethical and clinical principles, to leadership roles.

Describe the effectiveness of a marketing position; including the, design, ethically and socially responsible strategies, and demonstrate an understanding of the impact of these strategies on an organisation, its customers, the workforce and all other stakeholders.
Describe the qualities of effective leadership, critically assessing the leader's role in driving quality performance and effective, ethical change in organisations.

title: Foundations of Professional Prescribing and Patient-Centred Care
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: Foundations of Professional Prescribing and Patient-Centred Care is the first of two courses that provides pharmacists with the necessary skills to become safe, responsible and culturally appropriate prescribers and health professionals. Students will investigate and explore the relevant legislation and professional and ethical guidelines and frameworks that guide safe prescribing and gain an understanding of their responsibilities to the consumer, themselves and society. They will develop and learn to apply a systematic approach and biopsychosocial model of health to their patient-focused consultations. Skills developed will include motivational interviewing techniques, history-taking, clinical examination and patient assessment skills and the development of problem-focused, prioritised, management plans. Management plans will also include plans for patient monitoring and follow-up and there will be a strong emphasis placed on the need for appropriate documentation in all stages of the prescribing process, and collaboration with other healthcare providers to ensure continuity of care. Students will also build on their undergraduate knowledge and recognise the need to prescribe clinically appropriate medications that are supported by clinical evidence and prescribe in a manner that always ensures patient safety.
learning_outcomes: Develop evidence-based, problem-focused management plans that incorporate pharmacological and non-pharmacological strategies appropriate to the patient's needs and context.
Describe the legislative, professional, and ethical frameworks that underpin safe, culturally responsive, and accountable pharmacist prescribing in Australia.
Collaborate effectively with patients, carers, and other healthcare providers to ensure safe prescribing and continuity of care.
Document prescribing decisions clearly, accurately, and in accordance with legal, and professional requirements.
Reflect on prescribing practice to identify risks, manage patient safety, and engage in continuous quality improvement.

Enhance health outcomes by applying patient-centred consultation skills, including history-taking, motivational interviewing, clinical assessment, and communication strategies to support shared decision-making.

title: Advanced Clinical Management of Chronic and Complex Conditions
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course is designed to equip pharmacists with the advanced knowledge, skills, and professional behaviours necessary to prescribe safely and effectively for chronic and complex conditions within the scope of practice of a pharmacist. Building on prior pharmacotherapy and prescribing foundations, students will apply clinical reasoning and evidence-based practice to real-world prescribing scenarios across these therapeutic areas. The course emphasises competence in patient assessment, therapeutic decision-making, and the full prescribing process - including medical selection, monitoring, and review. A strong focus is placed on patient-centred care, interprofessional collaboration, and the ethical, legal, and regulatory frameworks that govern pharmacist prescribing practice in Australia. Through a blend of case-based learning, simulation, and applied assessment, students will develop and demonstrate advanced clinical management capability in alignment with contemporary pharmacist scopes of practice.
learning_outcomes: Apply clinical reasoning, evidence-based guidelines, and therapeutic knowledge to develop safe and effective prescribing plans for chronic and complex conditions.

Communicate prescribing decisions clearly and collaboratively with patients, carers, and other health professionals to ensure safe, coordinated, and integrated care for a range of chronic and complex conditions.
Conduct focussed clinical assessments of chronic and complex conditions within the pharmacist's prescribing scope and develop evidence-based management plans to optimise patient outcomes.

Evaluate treatment outcomes for chronic and complex conditions and adjust therapy as needed by monitoring effectiveness, identifying and managing adverse effects, safety concerns, and medicine interactions within the pharmacist's prescribing scope.
Reflect critically on prescribing practice, demonstrating accountability, commitment to quality improvement, and readiness for prescribing in the context of chronic and complex conditions.

Make prescribing decisions that uphold patient-centred care, addressing individual needs, preferences, health literacy, and supporting shared decision-making in the management of relevant chronic and complex conditions.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Chronic Condition Action Plan and Viva Voce

title: Advanced Clinical Decision Making and Professional Prescribing
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: Advanced Clinical Decision Making and Professional Prescribing is the second of two courses designed to prepare students for safe, effective, and collaborative prescribing practice. Building on the foundational knowledge and skills developed in Foundations of Professional Prescribing and Patient-Centred Care, this course provides students with opportunities to apply and demonstrate prescribing competence in a range of clinical scenarios. Students will undertake structured, patient-centred consultations, applying advanced clinical reasoning to develop and implement evidence-based management plans. The course emphasises safe and appropriate prescribing, accurate documentation, effective communication, and collaboration with patients, carers, and other healthcare providers to ensure continuity of care. Students will also develop and demonstrate skills in monitoring therapeutic outcomes, managing adverse effects, and adjusting treatment plans where necessary. Reflective practice, prescribing governance, and a commitment to ongoing quality improvement will be central to developing readiness for practice as a prescriber.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate prescribing practice, identify personal learning needs, and provide leadership to improve the safety and quality of prescribing.
Accurately document prescribing decisions, monitoring strategies, and interprofessional communications in line with legal and professional standards.
Integrate legal, ethical, clinical and cultural considerations into safe, accountable prescribing decisions across a range of real or simulated clinical settings.
Work collaboratively within interprofessional teams to support safe, coordinated, and person-centred prescribing and care.
Formulate and implement safe, evidence-informed prescribing decisions and management plans for patients with varying levels of complexity.

Achieve effective patient-centred care by undertaking comprehensive, structured patient consultations and demonstrating advanced communication, clinical assessment, and shared-decision making skills in authentic scenarios.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Prescribing Portfolio and Workplace Based Assessments
Reflection on the use of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Documentation

title: Advanced Clinical Management of Acute Conditions
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course is designed to develop the knowledge, skills, and professional behaviours required for pharmacists to prescribe safely and effectively for common acute conditions within the scope of practice of a pharmacist. Building on foundational pharmacotherapy knowledge, the course focuses on applying clinical reasoning and evidence-based practice to real-world prescribing scenarios within these therapeutic areas. Students will develop competence in patient assessment, clinical decision-making, and the prescribing process, including medicine selection, monitoring and review. Emphasis is placed on patient-centred care, collaboration with other health professionals, and the application of regulatory and ethical frameworks that govern pharmacist prescribing practice in Australia. Through case-based learning, simulated practice, placement, and applied assessments, students will develop and demonstrate advanced clinical management capability in alignment within contemporary pharmacist scopes of practice.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate treatment outcomes for acute conditions, and adjust therapy as needed by monitoring effectiveness, identifying and managing adverse effects, safety concerns, and medicine interactions within the pharmacist's prescribing scope.
Communicate prescribing decisions clearly and collaboratively with patients, carers and other health professionals to ensure safe, coordinated, and integrated care for a range of acute conditions.
Implement prescribing decisions that support patient-centred care, addressing individual needs, preferences, health literacy, and shared decision-making in the management of acute conditions.
Conduct focussed clinical assessments of acute conditions within the pharmacist's prescribing scope and develop evidence-based management plans to optimise patient outcomes.
Critically reflect on personal prescribing practice, demonstrating accountability, continuous quality improvement, and readiness to prescribe within the context of acute conditions.
Apply clinical reasoning, evidence-based guidelines, and therapeutic knowledge to develop safe and effective prescribing plans for acute conditions.

title: Introduction to Pharmacotherapeutics and Prescribing for Health Care Professionals
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course is designed to enable students to continue the accumulation of knowledge necessary to function safely and effectively as health care professionals within the Australian health service. The course will introduce students to the principles of pharmacotherapeutics, including clinical pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics and a revision of basic pharmacological principles. This course provides an overview of the principles of prescribing for health care professionals, including the Poisons and Therapeutic Goods Act and Regulation (NSW), the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS) and Quality Use of Medicines (QUM). The course will provide an overview of the role of non-prescription medications, including complementary and alternate medicines. This course incorporates principles of professional communications focused on performing comprehensive medicines assessment and collaboration with others in implementing a medication management plan. This course is a core course in the Master of Nurse Practitioner, Graduate Certificate in Medicines for Health Professionals, and the Graduate Certificate in Prescribing for Midwives. It is a compulsory course in the Midwifery Primary Care specialisation for Master of Midwifery Studies students working towards endorsement for scheduled medicines.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the Poisons and Therapeutic Goods Act and Regulation (NSW)
Demonstrate a sound knowledge of the legal and policy framework underpinning prescribing in Australia
Critically review the clinical pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of therapeutic agents in the context of clinical practice
Synthesise and apply the knowledge gained of the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme to application in clinical practice
Make informed, high-level judgements on the implementation of the principles of quality use of medicines
Justify the importance of obtaining a comprehensive medication history, including assessing use of non-prescription and complementary/alternate medicines

title: Integrated Pharmacotherapeutics for Clinical Practice
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course is designed to allow the students to continue the accumulation of additional knowledge necessary to function safely and effectively as an advanced practitioner. The course will provide students with advanced knowledge around pharmacotherapeutics as it applies to the pharmacological management of diseases within the context of advanced practice. The course uses targeted case-based scenarios to further develop students knowledge of the mechanisms of actions of drugs as well as the quality use of medicines and implications surrounding these therapeutic agents. Other courses in the program will allow students to use this knowledge in their practice.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of the mechanism of action of the drugs commonly used in the treatment of these diseases

Demonstrate the ability to make informed and autonomous decisions about therapeutic responses and interventions that are based on clinical judgment, scientific evidence and patient determined outcomes
Demonstrate a commitment to Evidenced Based Practice
Demonstrate knowledge of the pharmacotherapeutic management of various diseases in the context of advanced healthcare practice
Demonstrate knowledge of the quality use of medicines issues associated with the treatment of these diseases

assessment_tasks.task_name: Written, Presentation and Viva Assignment – Case Study

title: World Religions
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course provides an introduction to the principal features of the world's major religions through reference to key events, characters, beliefs and related phenomena. With regard to each tradition, there will be a focus on both historical and contemporary events relevant to the understanding of religion today.
learning_outcomes: Identify key events, characters and beliefs of the religions being studied;
Apply humanities methods relevant to the study of philosophy and religion;
Critically analyse historical developments within religious traditions in light of their relevance today;
Demonstrate writing, research and information technology skills appropriate to studies of philosophy, religion, and ethics.

title: Pharmacotherapeutics for Midwifery Primary Care
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course is designed to meet the educational requirements of registered midwives seeking endorsement for scheduled medicines. This course enables students to acquire the additional knowledge necessary to function safely and effectively as an autonomous prescriber within the Australian health care system. It will provide students with advanced knowledge in the area of clinical assessment and history taking, and pharmacotherapeutics as it applies to the pharmacological management of health conditions within the context of midwifery primary care. The course uses targeted case-based scenarios to further develop students' application of knowledge of drug action, understanding the pharmacological and non-pharmacological treatment options in generating a medication management plan using evidence-based approaches, as well as the quality use of medicines implications surrounding these therapeutic agents.
learning_outcomes: Critically review and apply advanced pharmacotherapeutic management principles in the context of midwifery primary care to clinical situations.

Make informed, high-level judgements and autonomous decisions about therapeutic responses and interventions that are based on clinical judgment, scientific evidence and safety of the childbearing woman and/or neonate within the context of the Prescribing Competencies Framework.
Synthesise and apply knowledge of the impact of quality use of medicines issues associated with midwifery practice, including prescribing to clinical situations.
Effectively use woman-centred communication skills about medication used across the midwifery continuum to ensure informed decision making by the childbearing woman.
Adapt a commitment to evidence based practice and the ability to consult and refer to other health professionals when required.
Critically reflect on the mechanism of action of the drugs commonly used by women during pregnancy, labour, birth and the postnatal period.
Synthesise and apply knowledge of the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic changes to women in pregnancy, labour, birth and the postnatal period.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Written, Presentation and Viva Assignment - Portfolio

title: Pharmacology of chronic conditions
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Biomedical Sciences and Pharmacy
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with knowledge of the pharmacological management of chronic conditions, and the effects of long term drug administration on an individual. The course will emphasise application of this knowledge to specific case examples relevant to students of allied health professions.
learning_outcomes: communicate information around medications to patients, including purpose, importance of compliance, lifestyle, and exercise-related considerations.
demonstrate and apply knowledge of the impact of various medications on clinical status, exercise management, and functional capacity.
apply the basic concepts of pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics to the safe use of drugs in individuals being treated for chronic diseases.
apply knowledge of the pharmacology of the drugs used to manage chronic diseases, including problems and risks arising due to long-term pharmacological management.

title: Religion, Science and Popular Beliefs
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: In several films, streamed media and video games religion, science and popular beliefs are often depicted. At times, science and religion conflict with each other, but in some contexts they are deeply intertwined. So too, technological change continues to impact scientific approaches to religion with new virtual reality technologies being employed to evoke religious experiences. The course will explore the interactions between religion, science and popular beliefs. Students critically reflect upon the historical, philosophical and ethical implications on those interactions.
learning_outcomes: Apply relevant academic methods to the study of religion, science and popular beliefs;
Implement writing, research and information technology skills appropriate to studies of philosophy, religion and ethics.
Analyse the historical and contextual factors that influence the relationship between religion and science;
Evaluate religion and science as represented in film, television, video games and other popular culture media;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Film, media, game or virtual reality review 1
Film, media, game or virtual reality review 2

title: Ethics of Emerging Technologies
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Emerging technologies hold both enormous potential to foster human flourishing as well as significant new challenges to democratic societies. This tension requires that we understand the technology as well as its ethical implications. In response, each week of the course will introduce how a mathematical, algorithmic, or design principle raises new ethical questions about an emerging technology. It provides both an insight into how a technology works as well as an outline of its unpredictable environmental, economic, political, and social consequences. In each case, a significant ethical approach will be brought to bear by noting its historical and philosophical relevance to today. The course enhances student capacities to evaluate technological dangers as well as direct its positive potentialities.
learning_outcomes: Apply ethical responses to AI dilemmas that arise in diverse democratic societies;
Reflect on the impact of human values when making design decisions in the creation of AI technologies;
Report on peer group discussions that analyse key AI ethical challenges.
Evaluate the ethical challenges arising from current AI practices;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Case Study Response to a Problem

title: Philosophy of Religion
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The course examines a number of issues in philosophy of religion which came to the fore in the ancient, medieval, early modern, enlightenment, and later periods. Topics to be discussed may include proofs for the existence of God, various conceptions of transcendence, the nature of the self, the concept of religion, and the relation between religious and scientific forms of inquiry. Diverse philosophical movements will be explored such as Platonism, Aristotelianism, phenomenology, existentialism, and hermeneutics.
learning_outcomes: Apply critical skills to interact with these issues in their historical forms and assess their relevance to contemporary philosophical discussion of these matters;
Demonstrate writing, research and information technology skills appropriate to studies of philosophy, religion, and the history of ideas.
Evaluate the main issues addressed and approaches taken by philosophers with respect to religion;
Analyse the historical contexts that help generate but not exhaust the ways in which an issue can appear and reappear in the history of philosophy;

title: Philosophy of Relationships
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Human relationships have provided one of the richest touchstones for philosophical reflection. For centuries people have sought to improve their experiences of other people, and this has resulted in significant ethical innovations in the history of ideas. Sometimes this includes analysis of painful experiences that defy meaningful description. The course investigates diverse recommendations to improve human relationships. It develops comparative methodologies in the academic study of philosophy, religion and ethics in order to help students evaluate a range complementary viewpoints on the topic.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate diverse reflections upon human and other forms of health relationships;
Critically analyse key categories for understanding how to improve relationships;
Apply comparative methodologies to different accounts of relationships;
Employ writing, research and information technology skills appropriate to studies of philosophy, religion, and ethics.

title: Ethics of Emerging Technologies
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Emerging technologies hold both enormous potential to foster human flourishing as well as significant new challenges to democratic societies. This tension requires that we understand the technology as well as its ethical implications. In response, each week of the course will introduce how a mathematical, algorithmic, or design principle raises new ethical questions about an emerging technology. It provides both an insight into how a technology works as well as an outline of its unpredictable environmental, economic, political, and social consequences. In each case, a significant ethical approach will be brought to bear by noting its historical and philosophical relevance to today. The course enhances student capacities to evaluate technological dangers as well as direct its positive potentialities.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse the impact of human values when making design decisions in the creation of AI technologies;
Formulate reports on peer group discussions that analyse AI ethical challenges.
Evaluate ethical challenges arising from current AI practices;
Construct independently researched ethical responses to AI dilemmas that arise in diverse democratic societies;

title: Critical Thinkers
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Critical thinking is considered a foundational skill in the study of philosophy, religion and ethics. The course provides a capstone overview of some of the most influential critical thinkers of the last century. As Isaac Newton wrote in a seventeenth-century letter, ‘If I have seen a little further it is by standing on the shoulders of giants'. By exploring major innovations in critical thinking students will learn to see a little further for themselves. They will be better prepared to respond to contemporary ethical, political and technological challenges.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate key developments and movements in the study of philosophy, religion and ethics debated today;
Critically reflect upon the implications of philosophical, ethical and religious claims;
Demonstrate advanced writing, research and information technology skills appropriate to studies of philosophy, religion and ethics.
Apply the insights from influential critical thinkers to contemporary challenges;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Case study application of a critical thinker's works to a set problem of contemporary challenge 2.
Critical discussions of thinkers' main works.
Case study application of a critical thinker's works to a set problem of contemporary challenge 1.

title: Democracy and Diversity
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The course examines the complex relationship between democracy and various forms of cultural and religious diversity. It analyses key concepts developed by political philosophers who impacted democratic theory with particular attention to social inclusion and enfranchisement. Topics covered include political theories of the State, secularisation theories, religion as a pacemaker for cultural rights, democratic enfranchisement movements, surveillance, the paradox of tolerance, and deliberative democratic responses to cultural strife.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate writing, research and information technology skills appropriate to studies of philosophy, religion and ethics.
Critically analyse key concepts developed by political philosophers concerning democratic enfranchisement;
Evaluate the changing relationship between democracy and diversity;

title: Introduction to Physiotherapy
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course will provide an introduction to the role of the physiotherapist and contexts of physiotherapy practice. The course will cover foundational physiotherapy skills and knowledge needed for general physiotherapy practice.
learning_outcomes: Discuss the roles, responsibilities and skills of a physiotherapist as a member of the health care team in a variety of contexts and health care settings
Demonstrate introductory skills in communication, professional behaviour and attitudes for physiotherapy practice including culturally sensitive, ethical and reflective practice

Apply basic biomedical and behavioural knowledge to the measurement and evaluation of various parameters of physical function and demonstrate an understanding of biomechanical and methodological issues related to basic measurement and evaluation skills used in physiotherapy practice.
Discuss ethical, lifespan, gender, cultural and legal considerations for physiotherapy practice

Appropriately select, and correctly demonstrate, basic measurement and evaluation procedures used for the physiotherapy assessment of physical function; appreciating age, gender, cultural and ethical considerations
Describe and demonstrate basic intervention techniques used by physiotherapists to improve patient function.

title: Physiotherapy II
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course provides basic assessment, treatment, clinical reasoning and health intervention skills and related knowledge needed for general physiotherapy practice and safe, ethical and culturally sensitive care of patients. This course will further develop students’ foundational skills for physiotherapy practice by building on the knowledge acquired in previous courses
learning_outcomes: Apply basic biomedical and behavioural knowledge to the evaluation and treatment of physical dysfunction in physiotherapy practice
Demonstrate an understanding of age, gender, cultural, legal and ethical considerations for basic assessment, treatment and health intervention procedures in physiotherapy practice
Describe the theory and concepts of clinical reasoning for physiotherapy practice
Discuss the biological basis and evidence for the physiotherapy assessment and treatment of people with physical dysfunction
Appropriately select and safely demonstrate basic assessment and treatment procedures commonly used in physiotherapy practice including outcome measurement

assessment_tasks.task_name: Safe application of heat and cold therapies

title: Musculoskeletal Physiotherapy I
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: Physiotherapy clinical skills and knowledge needed for the evaluation and management of common disorders of the musculoskeletal system across the lifespan. The course includes musculoskeletal and manual therapy and orthopaedic physiotherapy.
learning_outcomes: Apply introductory clinical reasoning skills and an evidence-based approach to decision making in musculoskeletal physiotherapy practice
Appropriately select, modify as necessary, and correctly and safely demonstrate basic active and passive treatment procedures used in the management of musculoskeletal dysfunction
Describe the aetiology, epidemiology, pathogenesis, clinical presentation, conservative and surgical management of common musculoskeletal disorders;

Conduct an appropriate, safe and effective examination of the musculoskeletal system, including history and physical examination and correctly select, modify as necessary, and demonstrate measurement and testing procedures commonly used in assessing musculoskeletal dysfunction
Apply biomedical and behavioural scientific knowledge to the physiotherapy evaluation and management of basic musculoskeletal disorders;
Demonstrate an understanding of relevant lifespan, gender, cultural, legal and ethical considerations in the management of people with musculoskeletal disorders
Apply basic treatment evaluation and intervention outcome processes appropriate for musculoskeletal physiotherapy practice

title: Neurological Physiotherapy I
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: An introduction to physiotherapy knowledge and clinical skills for the evaluation and management of selected basic neurological disorders across the lifespan. The course includes preliminary studies in symptomatology; assessment procedures to define impairments and limitations in activity and participation; relevant clinical reasoning processes; and management skills and techniques.
learning_outcomes: Integrate biomedical and behavioural sciences to evaluate and manage basic neurological disorders across the lifespan.
Evaluate treatment outcomes and consider lifespan, cultural, gender, legal, and ethical factors in neurological physiotherapy practice
Conduct and interpret basic Physiotherapy neurological assessments, including history-taking, physical examination, and the use of standard measurement tools
Apply clinical reasoning and evidence-based approaches to select, adapt, and implement Physiotherapy treatments for people with neurological dysfunction.
Demonstrate research literacy and professional communication through the development and presentation of critical discussions relevant to neurological Physiotherapy practice
Describe the pathophysiology, clinical presentation, and epidemiology of common neurological conditions, with emphasis on stroke-related motor and sensory impairments.

title: Cardiopulmonary Physiotherapy I
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: Physiotherapy clinical skills and knowledge needed for the evaluation and management of basic disorders of the cardiopulmonary system across the lifespan. The course involves introductory studies in physiotherapy practice related to the pulmonary, cardiac and vascular systems, including surgical care.
learning_outcomes: Conduct an appropriate basic examination of the cardiopulmonary system, including history and physical examination;
Effectively work with others in developing and giving an oral presentation.
Apply biomedical and behavioural scientific knowledge to the physiotherapy evaluation and management of people with basic pulmonary and cardiovascular disorders;
Apply basic treatment evaluation and intervention outcome processes appropriate for cardiopulmonary physiotherapy practice;
Describe the aetiology, epidemiology, pathogenesis and clinical presentation of common simple pulmonary and cardiovascular disorders;
Describe the conservative and surgical management of common simple pulmonary, cardiac and vascular disorders;
Appropriately select, modify as necessary, and correctly demonstrate basic physiotherapeutic treatment procedures commonly used in the management of people with cardiopulmonary dysfunction;
Appropriately select, modify as necessary, and correctly demonstrate basic measurement and testing procedures commonly used in assessing cardiopulmonary dysfunction;
Discuss relevant lifespan, gender, cultural, legal and ethical considerations in performing basic cardiopulmonary physiotherapy evaluation and management procedures;
Apply introductory clinical reasoning skills and an evidence-based approach to decision making in cardiopulmonary physiotherapy practice;
Demonstrate an awareness of the physiotherapist's role in promoting wellness as relevant to the pulmonary, cardiac and vascular systems;

title: Cardiopulmonary Physiotherapy II
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: Physiotherapy clinical skills and knowledge needed for the evaluation and management of complex disorders of the cardiopulmonary system across the lifespan. The course involves advanced studies in physiotherapy practice related to the pulmonary, cardiac and vascular systems, including surgical care. This course is only available to students enrolled in the Bachelor of Physiotherapy (Honours) program.
learning_outcomes: Plan and conduct an appropriate, safe and effective examination of people with complex cardiopulmonary dysfunction, including but not limited to, history and physical examination
Apply advanced clinical reasoning skills and an evidence based approach to decision making in cardiopulmonary physiotherapy practice.
Appropriately select, modify as necessary, and correctly demonstrate treatment procedures commonly used in the physiotherapy management of people with complex cardiopulmonary dysfunction.
Demonstrate an understanding of relevant lifespan, gender, cultural, legal and ethical considerations in delivering a physiotherapy service for people with complex cardiopulmonary disorders.
Apply biomedical and behavioural scientific knowledge to the physiotherapy evaluation and management of people with complex pulmonary and cardiovascular dysfunction.
Describe the aetiology, epidemiology, pathogenesis and clinical presentation of complex pulmonary and cardiovascular disorders.

title: Physiotherapy Clinical Practice I
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This is an introductory physiotherapy clinical practice course in which students participate in the delivery of a physiotherapy service under supervision. This full-time clinical placement course will provide students with the opportunity to integrate basic theory and practical skills in the physiotherapy management of patients in a health care setting. This course provides an introduction to full-time clinical practice. This course is a Compulsory Program Component and students must pass in order to progress in the Bachelor of Physiotherapy program.
learning_outcomes: Communicate at an introductory level verbally, non-verbally and in written and electronic forms with patients, care-givers, clients and other members of the multiprofessional health care team
Demonstrate introductory-level skills in reflective practice
Participate in the delivery of a physiotherapy service in a safe, collaborative, ethical, client-centred and culturally responsive manner.
Deliver safe, evidence-based physiotherapy management, intervention and manual skills at an introductory-level for patients with non-complex clinical problems
Demonstrate introductory-level skills in clinical reasoning and planning of client-centred goals and evidence-based management for people with non-complex clinical problems

Demonstrate appropriate introductory-level professional behaviour and attitudes including: patient rights and consent, ethical, legal and culturally sensitive practice, commitment to learning and teamwork
Demonstrate all of the standards expected of a student physiotherapist practicing at an introductory level
Identify, manage and minimise risk associated with physiotherapy assessment and intervention at an introductory level
Take a history and perform a physical examination at an introductory-level for patients with non-complex clinical problems
Demonstrate an evolving understanding of the role of the physiotherapist and the multiprofessional team within the context of healthcare service delivery at an introductory-level

title: Advanced Neurological Physiotherapy
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: Advanced clinical knowledge and skills are needed for physiotherapy evaluation and management of complex neurological disorders. The course includes advanced studies in symptomatology; assessment procedures to define impairments and limitations in activity and participation; relevant clinical reasoning processes; and management skills and techniques.
learning_outcomes: Apply advanced clinical reasoning skills and an evidence-based approach to decision making in neurological physiotherapy practice; including the role of the physiotherapist in advocacy, health promotion and secondary prevention of disability

Appropriately select, modify as necessary, and correctly demonstrate advanced physiotherapeutic assessment, outcome measurement and treatment procedures commonly used in the management of neurological dysfunction

Demonstrate advanced communication skills and teamwork working with clients, carers and other health care professionals in a manner that promotes participation and that is client-centred and holistic for people with neurological conditions

Discuss relevant gender, cultural, legal and ethical considerations in managing people with complex neurological disorders; This includes recognising the importance of providing neurological physiotherapy services in a culturally appropriate context, including cultural competence in the management of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples
Describe the aetiology, epidemiology, pathogenesis and clinical presentation of selected common complex neurological disorders
Apply biomedical and behavioural scientific knowledge to the physiotherapy assessment and management of more complex neurological disorders

title: Physiotherapy Clinical Practice III
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This is a physiotherapy clinical placement course in which students are required to integrate theory and practical skills to deliver a physiotherapy service under supervision. This physiotherapy clinical practice course will provide students with an opportunity to develop and demonstrate competence in safely delivering physiotherapy clinical services in a variety of practice environments, and with people across the lifespan. This course consists of one five-week, full time clinical placement. The placement in this course will occur in one of the following areas of practice: acute/cardiopulmonary, rehabilitation/neurology, musculoskeletal/ambulatory care, community practice and/or integrated general. This course is a Compulsory Program Component and students must pass in order to progress in the Bachelor of Physiotherapy program.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate effective clinical communication including, but not limited to verbal, non-verbal, written and electronic forms, with patients, care-givers, clients and other members of the multiprofessional health care team
Demonstrate all of the capabilities expected of an entry-level physiotherapy practitioner as determined by Physiotherapy Professional entry-level standards.
Demonstrate competence in analysis, clinical reasoning and decision making in order to plan and progress physiotherapy intervention and management
Demonstrate the ability to provide a safe and effective physiotherapy clinical service including identification, minimisation and management of risk and adverse event

Demonstrate competence in selecting and safely implementing physiotherapy intervention and management (including but not limited to physical treatment techniques, patient education, discharge planning)
Demonstrate competence in selecting and safely applying appropriate assessment methods and tools (including, but not limited to; patient history and physical examination)
Demonstrate appropriate professional behaviour for physiotherapy and interprofessional practice
Demonstrate competence in providing a evidence-based, patient centred, culturally sensitive physiotherapy service for people across the lifespan in a workplace setting

title: Physiotherapy Through Life Stages
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course provides the physiotherapy clinical skills and knowledge needed for the evaluation and management of issues specific to particular life stages, for example, childhood, adolescence, the childbearing years and older age. The course involves advanced studies in physiotherapy practice related to specific life stages.
learning_outcomes: Communicate effectively and professionally in physiotherapy practice, demonstrating research literacy and reflective practice
Conduct comprehensive physiotherapy assessments and apply advanced clinical reasoning and evidence-based decision-making across diverse life stages
Demonstrate an understanding of the roles of multidisciplinary teams, physiotherapists, carers, and community resources in holistic patient management
Incorporate financial, cultural, legal, and ethical considerations into physiotherapy practice across different life stages

Integrate biomedical, epidemiological, and behavioural sciences to assess and manage individuals and populations across key life stages, including childhood, adolescence, childbearing, and older adulthood
Select, implement, and evaluate physiotherapy interventions tailored to the needs of people across the lifespan including applied clinical exercise prescription

title: Advanced Musculoskeletal Physiotherapy
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: Physiotherapy clinical skills and knowledge needed for the evaluation and management of complex disorders of the musculoskeletal system with a focus on the spine. The course includes advanced studies in occupational health and manual therapy
learning_outcomes: Describe the aetiology, epidemiology, pathogenesis clinical presentation and conservative and surgical management of selected complex musculoskeletal disorders
Develop appropriate strategies of physiotherapy management to address functional requirements in the home and occupational environment
Appropriately select, modify as necessary, and correctly demonstrate advanced measurement and testing procedures commonly used in assessing musculoskeletal dysfunction
Apply biomedical and behavioural scientific knowledge to the evaluation and management of complex musculoskeletal disorders
Adapt the clinical examination for more complex disorders of the musculoskeletal system, integrating advanced physical examination procedures
Appropriately select, modify as necessary, and correctly demonstrate advanced active and passive treatment procedures commonly used in the management of musculoskeletal dysfunction
Demonstrate a well developed understanding of the physiotherapist's role in promoting wellness as relevant to the musculoskeletal system

title: Critical Thinking in Musculoskeletal Physiotherapy
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: Higher level analytical and clinical reasoning skills in the assessment and management of musculoskeletal disorders. This course emphasises the critical thinking process in examination, problem analysis and treatment prescription extensively using a case based approach.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of the role of diagnostic statistics in evaluation of musculoskeletal disorders
Demonstrate an understanding of relevant lifespan, gender, cultural, legal and ethical considerations in delivering a physiotherapy service for people with complex musculoskeletal disorders
Apply sophisticated treatment evaluation and intervention outcome processes appropriate for musculoskeletal physiotherapy practice
Appropriately select, modify as necessary, and correctly demonstrate advanced active and passive treatment procedures commonly used in the management of musculoskeletal dysfunction
Apply biomedical and behavioural scientific knowledge to the evaluation and management of complex musculoskeletal disorders
Demonstrate a well developed clinical reasoning and evidence based approach to decision-making in musculoskeletal physiotherapy clinical practice
Adapt the clinical examination for more complex disorders of the musculoskeletal system, integrating advanced physical examination procedures

title: Advanced Concepts in Physiotherapy Practice
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing

learning_outcomes: Apply knowledge of inter-professional collaborative practice to a complex case

Demonstrate an understanding of the ethical, legal, socioeconomic, and cultural influences for people across the lifespan, across populations and in a range of settings (including rural), when developing complex physiotherapy management plans

Select, adapt and apply safe, effective, culturally appropriate and evidence-based physiotherapy assessment, clinical reasoning and management, including the use of technology, self-management and discharge planning, for people and populations with complex conditions.

title: Advanced Concepts in Evidence-based Physiotherapy Practice
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course will develop skills in evidence-based physiotherapy practice and health communication. Students will develop skills in finding, appraising and synthesising research evidence as it applies to clinical physiotherapy practice contexts.

Written Assignment - Topic selection and Plan

title: Transition to Professional Practice
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course will prepare physiotherapy students for the transition from student to graduate physiotherapist across a variety of health care settings.
learning_outcomes: develop skills required to transition to work in private practice settings, including business skills, working with relevant external agencies and quality improvement activities
develop skills required to transition to work in public health care settings, including working with government and compensable agencies, and quality improvement activities
design strategies for delivering culturally safe health care to people from diverse backgrounds, including Indigenous Australians
demonstrate advanced interprofessional working skills including, principles of leadership, effective teamwork and conflict resolution
demonstrate an understanding of health professional registration and regulation, including relevant professional, ethical and medico-legal issues
demonstrate skills in career planning, including preparing job applications and interviews

title: Fundamentals of Engineering Physics
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: For engineers, knowledge of physics is essential to understand and transform the world around us. This course is designed for students in selected Engineering programs with no or little physics background. It focuses on illustrating and developing an understanding of the interplay between mathematics and physics in engineering. The course examines some of the core topics in physics essential for further studies in engineering such as Mechanics, Vibrations & Waves, Fluids and Optics.
learning_outcomes: Perform laboratory and computational experiments and interpret the significance of the results with regards to the principles and applications of physics.
Contribute to team and group work for scientific investigations and for the process of learning.
Communicate the results and significance of both theoretical and experimental work in written form.
Solve qualitative and quantitative problems using mathematics and the principles of physics.
Explain the basic principles of physics and mathematics and how they apply to practical situations and engineering problems.

title: Introductory Physics for the Life Sciences
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Physics underpins most aspects of modern technology including those with application to the life sciences and medicine. Two examples include the development of electromagnetic wave theory, which led to electric power, radio and television; and atomic physics, which resulted in electronics, microchips and computers, nuclear medicine and radiation treatment of cancers. This course provides an overview of topics in physics that are of particular importance to the life and medical sciences. The course is non-calculus based and covers mechanics (units, motion, biomechanics, energy), electricity and magnetism, heat, nuclear physics, fluids, and waves.
learning_outcomes: Explain the basic principles and concepts underlying a broad range of fundamental areas of physics;
Perform experiments using scientific equipment and interpret the results in terms of the basic concepts in physics;
Connect their knowledge of physics to everyday situations and to life sciences and medicine;
Solve qualitative and quantitative problems using basic mathematics and principles of physics;
Contribute to team and group work for scientific investigations and for the process of learning.

title: Advanced Physics I
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Physics underpins most aspects of modern engineering, technology, and medicine; developments in physics often drive social change. Knowledge of physics is therefore vital to understanding the world around us. Physics is needed to make new materials, monitor our environment, put satellites into orbit, harness energy, determine the strength of structures, take scans of the human body, develop faster computers, etc. The course is calculus based and covers topics from mechanics and kinematics, wave mechanics, electricity, particle physics, cosmology, and thermal physics.
learning_outcomes: Perform laboratory and computational experiments and interpret the significance of the results with regards to the principles and applications of physics.
Solve qualitative and quantitative problems using mathematics and the principles of physics.
Contribute to team and group work for scientific investigations and for the process of learning.
Explain the basic principles of mechanics, waves, electricity and thermodynamics, and their relevance to aspects of engineering, technology, physical phenomena and everyday situations.
Communicate the results and significance of both theoretical and experimental work in written form.

title: Advanced Physics II
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Physics underpins most aspects of modern engineering, technology, and medicine. For example, about 25% of the world's economy is tied to the quantum mechanics of silicon, and many of the most important practical advances in chemistry and biology can be traced to the precise understanding of the behaviour of atoms and molecules provided by quantum mechanics. Knowledge of physics is therefore vital to understanding the world around us. This calculus-based course continues on from PHYS1210 and covers the topics of mathematical tools, electromagnetism, optics and physics of matter.
learning_outcomes: Communicate the results and significance of both theoretical and experimental work in written reports.
Solve qualitative and quantitative problems using mathematics and the principles of physics.
Contribute to team and group work for scientific investigations and for the process of learning.
Perform laboratory and computational experiments and interpret the significance of the results with regards to the principles and applications of physics.
Explain the basic principles of electromagnetism, optics and quantum mechanics and their relevance to aspects of engineering, technology, physical phenomena, matter and everyday situations.

title: MRS Physics and Radiation Protection
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: This course develops a foundational knowledge of links between fundamental physics and the vocation-specific instrumentation, radiobiology & radiation protection associated with Medical Radiation Science (MRS). Issues discussed include the physical principles and instrumentation associated with diagnostic radiography, radiation therapy and nuclear medicine, including interaction of radiation with matter and the implications these processes have on image quality and optimised \ treatment planning in clinical practice. The interactions of radiation with matter are also extended to biological systems and their implications, with the concepts of radiation dose and its accurate measurement, radiobiology and radiation protection also discussed.
learning_outcomes: Analyse relevant clinical information to solve vocation-based imaging, treatment and radiation dose problems in real-time.
Demonstrate a practical understanding of working safely with radiation.
Describe the key steps in how clinical instruments produce ionizing radiation for imaging as well as for radiation therapy treatment.
Recall the key principles of radiation protection and connect these to various strategies utilized in practical settings.
Describe the key roles of associated equipment used for producing an image and evaluate their impact on image quality.
Classify the various different quantities used to describe radiation dose and explain the differences between them.
Describe the biological effect that occurs when radiation interacts with the body.
Define how an X-ray beam is characterized (quantity & quality), and explain the different ways these characteristics can be altered in a clinical instrument.
Describe the equipment used for the detection of radiation and identify the key advantages and disadvantages of each different type of equipment.

title: Introduction to Astronomy
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Astronomy is vital and exciting because it extends the frontiers of knowledge. As a science, astronomy has two important roles. It provides us with a clearer picture of our place in the universe, and it stimulates the development of new technology, much of which ultimately finds practical application. This course covers both aspects. Topics covered include astronomical coordinates and measurement, instrumental techniques, the solar system, the structure and life cycle of the sun and other stars, clusters, quasars, pulsars, and cosmology.
learning_outcomes: Communicate concepts in astronomy in the written form.
Perform laboratory and computational experiments in the field of astronomy.
Solve problems in Astronomy using analytical thinking and problem solving strategies.
Describe the principles, processes and techniques that form the basis of modern astronomy.
Apply their scientific knowledge to interpret astronomical phenomena.

title: Quantum Science
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: Quantum Science is necessary to understand the natural world around us and has been key to developing new technologies. Quantum technologies from the 20th century include energy-efficient lighting, computers, and MRI scanners to diagnose disease. This course teaches the foundations of quantum mechanics from 1905 with the discovery of wave-particle duality. The basics of the next quantum revolution are explored, with a focus on quantum computing and quantum communications. This is an important part of Australia’s future technology industry, which students will be part of.
learning_outcomes: Use the Schrödinger Equation to solve for a wide variety of problems in quantum mechanics
Solve quantitative and qualitative problems, using appropriate quantum mechanics principles and computing techniques
Collaborate with team members for scientific investigations of quantum phenomena.

Perform quantum experiments that involve making correct and appropriate use of a range of scientific equipment, following ethical and accurate record keeping, analysing results and reaching non-trivial conclusions from them.
Communicate the results of both theoretical and experimental quantum mechanics work in various forms including written reports and oral presentations.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Weekly continuous assessment of experimental, computational and problem-solving work in workshops

title: Advanced Mechanics
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: How objects move through space and time is important for launching communication satellites into space, for understanding celestial orbits, and for determining complicated weather and climate patterns on Earth. This course moves beyond basic first year classical mechanics to consider relativistic effects in fast-moving objects. It also looks at the complicated motions seen in chaotic systems around us. Several important techniques in classical mechanics will be developed through lectorials, experimental laboratories and computer workshops.
learning_outcomes: Communicate the results of theoretical and experimental work in classical mechanics through written reports.
Explain physical phenomena using the principles of advanced mechanics.

Perform mechanics experiments that involve making correct and appropriate use of a range of scientific equipment, following ethical and accurate record keeping, and analysing results to reach non-trivial conclusions.
Collaborate with team members for investigations of mechanics.
Solve quantitative and qualitative problems, using appropriate techniques of classical mechanics and/or the postulates of special relativity.

title: Particles and Space
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: Since the dawn of humanity, we have been looking at the skies for navigation and for inspiration. In this course, the origins of the Universe will be examined through the study of stars, planets, and galaxies. Intimately linked to the Universe’s largest objects is the study of our smallest constituent particles including quarks, neutrinos, and gravitons. This course is intended for science students with a first-year preparation in mathematics to examine particles and space physics. Innovative computer labs, workshops and some experiments will be used to demonstrate concepts.
learning_outcomes: Solve quantitative and qualitative problems, using appropriate mathematical and computing techniques.
Collaborate with team members for scientific investigation of astrophysics phenomena and for the process of learning.
Explain phenomena in particle physics and astrophysics using physical models, laws and theories.

Perform particle physics and astrophysics experiments that involve making correct and appropriate use of a range of scientific equipment, following ethical and accurate record keeping, analysing results and reaching non-trivial conclusions from them.
Communicate the results of both theoretical and experimental astrophysics work in various forms including written reports.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Weekly continuous assessment of experimental, computational and problem-solving work in workshops

title: Electromagnetism
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
syllabus_overview: Electricity and magnetism are part of the one physical theory that explains the behaviour of light in the Universe. From the behaviour of our Sun to the function of a single human cell, electromagnetism is key to our survival. It also underpins technologies such as laser scanning, cancer treatments, wifi, radio and fibre optic communications. Lectorials, computer workshops and technologically advanced experiments will be used to understand electromagnetism and its applications.
learning_outcomes: Solve quantitative and qualitative electromagnetism problems, using appropriate mathematical and computing techniques.
Explain the importance of electromagnetism in human endeavours based on an understanding of electric fields, magnetic fields, and light.
Collaborate with team members for scientific investigations of electromagnetism.
Perform electromagnetism experiments that involve correct use of scientific equipment, following ethical and accurate record keeping, analysing results and reaching non-trivial conclusions.
Communicate the results of both theoretical and experimental electromagnetism studies in various forms including written reports and oral presentations.

title: Climate and Energy
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: The global effects of climate change associated with the reliance on fossil fuels for our energy needs are among some of the most challenging problems facing the world today. In this course, students will develop an understanding of the physical principles behind the greenhouse effect and the observational evidence for its existence. They will investigate the scientific principles relevant to energy and energy resources, including aspects such as thermal, nuclear, solar, wind and hydroelectric power generation. The prospects and challenges for a transition away from fossil fuels will be evaluated. This course is suitable for any student interested knowing more about the science of climate change and the possible routes for a transition to an emissions free energy sector.
learning_outcomes: Apply scientific concepts to describe the greenhouse effect and its impacts on the climate system
Describe and perform simple calculations relevant to the generation of electricity, its transmission and storage
Critically assess and discuss the reporting of energy issues in the media
Qualitatively describe and quantitatively analyse energy, power and thermodynamics
Compare and contrast the different types of energy sources used for electricity, transport and storage

title: Statistical Mechanics
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: Thermodynamics is the only field of physics that studies systems at temperatures above absolute zero. This is important as most physical phenomena take place at finite temperatures! In this course, statistical methods of treating thermal systems will be developed through interactive lectorials and workshops. These methods will then be applied to studying diverse systems such as gases, solids, magnets, neutron stars, metals, blackbody radiation, and biological cells. Fundamental questions about how the universe works will be answered, such as why does time only run forward and never backward?
learning_outcomes: With minimal guidance, perform statistical mechanics experiments that involve correct use of scientific equipment, keeping an accurate record, analysing results and reaching non-trivial conclusions.
Collaborate with team members on high level tasks relating to statistical mechanics.
Solve quantitative problems, using appropriate statistical mechanics and computing techniques.
Explain and derive the origins of thermodynamic laws and relationships.
Communicate at an advanced level the results of both theoretical and experimental work in statistical mechanics via written reports and computer codes.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Weekly continuous assessment of experimental, computational and problem-solving work in workshops

title: Biophysics
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: Biophysics deals with the application of physics to biological systems, from the first picture of the structure of DNA, to the treatment of cancer, and the understanding of allergic reactions. The concepts and techniques of biophysics find applications in bioelectronics, medicine/health, and population dynamics and are closely related to statistical mechanics and transport processes. Interdisciplinary skills and knowledge have heralded novel scientific outcomes with benefits to society. As such, this course develops foundational thinking and methods that are fundamental to an effective interdisciplinary STEMM workforce. Specifically, this course provides an introduction to the physics of many body systems, transport phenomena and biological systems. Blended problem-based conceptual learning (lectorials) will be used to gain an understanding of key developments, ideas and theories covered in Biophysics. Blended problem-based, hands-on learning (computational and laboratory workshops) will be used to gain an understanding of key concepts.
learning_outcomes: Collaborate effectively with team members for scientific investigations and for the process of learning.

Perform experiments which involve making correct and appropriate use of a range of scientific equipment, keeping an accurate record of experimental work and analysing results and reaching non-trivial conclusions from them.
Explain models of biological systems and models dealing with statistical mechanics and transport phenomena.
Communicate at an advanced level the results of both theoretical and experimental work in various forms including written reports, oral presentations and poster presentations.
Solve qualitative and quantitative problems, using appropriate statistical mechanics and computing techniques.

title: Materials Physics
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: Everything we touch is a material. The thermal, electrical, magnetic and structural properties of materials need to be known to understand both nature and emerging technologies necessary to solve environmental and energy problems. In this course, the basic theories of solid state physics will be developed, supported by experimental and computer laboratories. Many areas of Physics -- including electromagnetism, quantum mechanics and statistical mechanics -- converge to explain the properties of materials around us.
learning_outcomes: Collaborate effectively with team members on high level tasks related to materials physics.
Solve quantitative problems relating to materials, using appropriate physics models, mathematical tools and computing techniques.
Communicate at an advanced level the results of both theoretical and experimental work on materials via written reports.
With minimal guidance, perform experiments on materials while keeping an accurate record of work, analysing results and reaching non-trivial conclusions.
Explain and derive the properties of materials.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Weekly continuous assessment of experimental, computational and problem-solving work in workshops

title: Photonics
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: Photonics deals with the applied concepts and constructs of electromagnetism across the boundaries of science and engineering. The time dynamics of electromagnetic fields, as solutions to Maxwell’s equations, underpin all of optics, communication signal and power propagation in transmission lines, waveguides and antennas. Specific instances of photon-induced amplification forming laser systems are of central focus in this holistic and balanced course. Lectorials and blended delivery of knowledge together with engaging laboratory and computational experiments will elucidate electromagnetism and laser technologies to allow advanced understanding of EM applications as learning outcomes.
learning_outcomes: Communicate the results of both theoretical and experimental work in various forms including written reports, oral presentations and poster presentations.
Contribute to team and group work for scientific investigations and for the process of learning.

Explain the importance of electromagnetism in human endeavour based on a profound understanding of light as an EM wave, its sources, including lasers sources, properties and behaviour, uses and guidance.

Perform experiments which involve making correct and appropriate use of a range of scientific equipment, keeping an accurate record of experimental work and analysing results and reaching non-trivial conclusions from them.
Solve qualitative and quantitative problems, using appropriate mathematical and computing techniques.

title: Atomic and Nuclear Physics
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: Atoms are the building blocks of all matter in the universe. In this course, the theory of quantum mechanics will be used to show why atoms behave as they do. This includes emitting certain colours of light, changing in response to applied magnetic and electric fields, and even transmutating into entirely different atoms via spontaneous nuclear decay while emitting huge amounts of energy. Important applications to computing, astronomy, nuclear medicine and new material discovery will be discussed. Laboratories will involve some of the key experiments in the 20th century discovery of atomic physics, together with computer simulations that show students the current state of nuclear physics.
learning_outcomes: Communicate at an advanced level the results of both theoretical and experimental work on atoms via written reports and oral presentations.
Apply their knowledge in the field of advanced quantum mechanics and nuclear physics to explain the behaviour of atoms, and applications in technology.
Collaborate professionally with team members for scientific investigations of atoms, molecules and their nuclei.
With minimal guidance, perform atomic and nuclear experiments at a high level with accurate and complete records, sophisticated analysis and conclusions.
Solve qualitative and quantitative problems, using appropriate quantum mechanics and computing techniques.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Weekly continuous assessment of experimental, computational and problem-solving work in workshops

title: Nanoscience
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: Nanoscience lies at the heart of all modern technology, from solar cells to sunscreen and drug delivery. There is a fundamental change to the physical properties of structures on nanometre length scales, where quantum confinement becomes important.
