For instance, topics that may be included in this course are techniques of the body; tattooed bodies or cosmetic surgery; political bodies, organisations and meanings of embodiment; as well as social and cultural understandings of working with body politics.
learning_outcomes: Provide a critical understanding of how approaches to the body from both social and cultural perspectives have been used and developed over time.
Assess the integration and application of anthropological perspectives of bodies in cultural perspective in the social sciences approaches.
Review knowledge of the way in which experiences are culturally constituted and socially controlled.

Demonstrate an understanding of different theoretical perspectives used to study social and cultural practices of living and experiencing the body, embodiment and human experiences, as well as bodies in cultural perspective.
Critically analyse cultural understandings, representations and social practices of bodies in cultural perspective.

title: Youth Culture and Risk
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Provides an understanding of contemporary youth cultures in relation to sociological theories. It moves between examination of theoretical and empirical accounts of contemporary youth cultures, concepts of risk, and broader sociological theories which can be used to understand youth culture phenomena. A primary focus will be on urban youth cultures, and class and gender in Australia and other countries.
learning_outcomes: Discuss general sociological theories in the light of the focused study of youth culture and risk.
Apply skills in the presentation of well-supported arguments and ideas in written and verbal form.
Communicate a critical understanding of the way modernity, youth culture and risk have been dealt in sociology.
Explain the significance of contemporary youth cultures in the global context.

title: Identity,  Culture and Place: Communities in Transition
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course explores how communities navigate economic, social, and environmental transitions, focusing on post-industrial and post-extractive futures. Using theories of identity, culture and place, as well as environmental justice, students will analyse case studies from rural, urban and regional contexts worldwide. They will explore how carbon is intertwined with modern democracy, identity and culture, interrogate how key issues in identity (including gender, race, age and social class) shape debates about transition, and how identity, culture and place inform experiences and responses to decarbonisation. At the end of the course, students will have a broad critical understanding of social scientific theories of decarbonisation and transition, and of how identity, culture and place inform politics shaping local, regional and global debates about and action for a fossil free future.
learning_outcomes: Assess relevant theoretical perspectives for understanding contemporary social and political debates about communities in transition.
Critically investigate social scientific approaches to identity, culture, and place, environmental justice and community transitioning.
Apply social scientific theories to case studies and evaluate the role of power, identity, culture and place in shaping transition outcomes.
Formulate professional and academic responses that address complex questions in the area of community transition.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Case Study: Community Transition Analysis Report

title: Health, 'Wellness' and Power: The Social Contexts of Expert Knowledge
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course examines contemporary and historical debates over knowledge in health and medicine. It will focus on the social construction of knowledge and examine contested claims to truth and expertise in the fields of health and health care. The course will draw on contemporary sociological and anthropological theories of knowledge related to medical professional power, health and body ideals in the digital world and the social construction of mental illness.
learning_outcomes: Apply sociological theories to explain aspects of health discourses.
Demonstrate high-level oral and written communication skills.
Identify and critically analyse the social, political and cultural conditions which give rise to health discourses.
Demonstrate an informed and critical understanding of key concepts employed across paradigms of medical knowledge.
Formulate arguments about the relationships between medicine, knowledge and power.

title: Leading Social Change: Applying Critical Theories in Critical Times
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Before we can change the world, we need to understand how it works. Social theories help us do that. This course examines how theory can be used to guide social change and solutions to today’s most pressing social problems. You will learn how to analyse the world around you by using cutting-edge research and theories from the social sciences, identify contemporary issues linked to the study of social inequalities and develop practical solutions to respond to and create change in the world. Students will explore strategies for thinking with and against ideas, writing about, using, and engaging theoretical texts. This course prepares students for complex problem-solving in their future careers, and helps them develop a multifaceted understanding of social change.
learning_outcomes: Analyse authors’ tactics and techniques to contend with theory through written reflections.
Identify key concepts and social theories underpinning social change and in contemporary research
Apply a relevant theoretical framework to evaluate and respond to contemporary social problems
Generate an emergent research agenda and propose crucial areas for future research.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Integrated analysis of real-world issues + Interactive Oral: Part 3

title: Gender, Religion and Power
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course is an introduction to, and examination of, sociological and feminist literature relating to expressions of gender and power relations in religious traditions. The treatment of gender in relation to religion will be the focus of empirical and theoretical investigation. The course will introduce students to the central theoretical concepts and empirical research in an effort to understand current expressions of religious activity.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse theoretical and empirical contributions to the operations of gender and power in religious traditions.
Demonstrate competence in scholarship, essay construction and academic argument appropriate to graduation at Bachelor level.
Effectively communicate relevant analytic models to contemporary issues.
Understand sociological theories of religion as an institutional and symbolic system.

title: Rage Against the Machine: Indigenous Activism, Ways of Life and the Future
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course explores the contemporary social, cultural, economic and political situations of Indigenous peoples across the world. Students are introduced to definitions and parameters of 'Indigenous' peoples and their overlap with 'ethnic minorities' and the concept of 'fourth world nations'. Throughout the course, students will engage with case studies that illustrate Indigenous peoples' struggles, including battles over land/marine rights, co-existence with settler/migrant communities, independence and nationhood, and reclamation of pre-colonial political boundaries and entities. The course offers an anthropological exploration of indigeneity and ethnicity, and students are introduced to post-colonial and de-colonial theory. By investigating examples of 21st century land use struggles (e.g. Standing Rock, Adani Carmichael Mine, the Brazilian ‘war of survival’), it places distinct emphasis on how contemporary challenges facing Indigenous peoples continue to relate to questions of land and land use.
learning_outcomes: Apply constructive feedback and review in peer contexts.
Recognise the various international organisations, institutions, and legal mechanisms to advance the position of Indigenous peoples in various countries.
Communicate research objectives and outcomes to a wide audience.
Articulate, in written and verbal forms, informed positions on different types of struggles that indigenous peoples are waging in the contemporary world.
Understand the different situations in which Indigenous peoples coexist with other, non-indigenous peoples in various states and societies.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Campaign: media release, newsletter and interactive strategy presentation

title: Religion and Politics in Contemporary Society
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course covers religion in contemporary societies, and in particular the impact of religion on the political arena. Topics include religion and social policy, the rise of religious fundamentalism, the rise of atheism, gender and religion issues and intersections between religion and the state. Case studies are drawn from various societies and cultural arenas. The aim is to enable students to reach a sympathetic yet critical understanding of the place of these developments in contemporary societies.
learning_outcomes: Describe the variety of religious expressions in the contemporary world.
Critically analyse the impact on the political process, local and global, of such expressions, in particular in regard to processes of identity formation at individual and group levels.
Effectively communicate the social, political and cultural conditions which give rise to such expressions.
Demonstrate an informed and critical understanding of key concepts employed in this field, including "globalisation," "secularisation" and "fundamentalism".
Make informed and intelligent judgments and appreciations of such expressions.
Demonstrate high-level oral and written communication skills.

title: International Health: Cross-Cultural and Critical Social Science Perspectives
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course explores how social and cultural dimensions of globalisation influence the making of international health. The uneven nature of many globalisation processes (such as the transnationalisation of: market/corporate capitalism, post-welfare policies, new technologies, population movements, consumerist cultural values and attitudes, financial crisis, food and environments insecurities, as well ethnic conflicts and violence) will be analysed in terms of their consequences for public health in different social contexts. The course helps students to develop a better understanding of the major challenges posed by the global worlds and culturally distinctive local practices to health and well-being in the 21st Century and the roles that different agents, organisational bodies and body politics play in dealing with health problems, both locally and globally.
learning_outcomes: Develop social science analytical skills through a cross-societal and critical study of international health issues.
Critically engage in assessing and analysing local, global and international health literature through employing a global justice perspective.
Demonstrate a critical understanding of the social, economic, political and cultural factors involved in the creation, reproduction and perpetuation of health problems at local and global levels.
Evaluate an understanding of social science approaches to international, local and global health.

title: Gender and Social Change
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The course offers social science perspectives on gender and social change. These include feminist perspectives, different agents and their social and cultural perspectives, as well as cross-cultural settings and contexts. The course begins with an introduction to contemporary theories which inform social change, then moves to consider a number of case studies of gender and social change in a variety of settings. Themes include: women and education, labour force restructuring, comparison of female and male engagements in the workforce, and changes to family structures.
learning_outcomes: Investigate different theoretical perspectives on the relationships between gender and social change.
Demonstrate advanced skills in writing academic essays.
Demonstrate an understanding of different social science approaches used to study gender and social change.
Critically analyse social practices and cultural representations of gender.

title: Project Design and Evaluation
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The course will introduce students to designing projects, social programs and their evaluation. This will include some of the research activities, techniques and applications necessary for designing, implementing and appraising social programs.
learning_outcomes: Critically examine the merits of existing programs in line with international standards and attempts to improve them.
Assess the utility of new programs and initiatives.
Evaluate the extent and severity of problems requiring social interventions.
Effectively manage and administer programs.
Design programs to ameliorate social problems.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Weekly contributions to online forum or in class discussion
Report 2: Designing Evaluation of a Project

title: Development and Social Change
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course aims to provide students with the concepts and analytical skills to understand the rapid changes that are taking place in developing countries. The course examines globalisation and economic development in relation to states and specific social and cultural groups, as well as forces of internal change including gender, ethnicity and social movements. The course will focus on governmental as well as non-governmental actors on local, national and international levels.
learning_outcomes: Employ development theories in analysis and evaluation of empirical case studies.
Analyse the role of the state in dealing with the basic needs of its citizens.

Investigate the role of international actors in the development arena, ranging from the World Bank and IMF, inter-governmental agencies, non-governmental organisations to international trade and business lobbies.
Appraise the role of social movements in raising the specific concerns of women, workers, impoverished farmers and other marginalized groups.
Explain different approaches to development adopted by post-colonial societies since the 1960s.

title: Key Issues in Institutional Equity and Inclusive Practice
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Equity, diversity and inclusion have become central priorities across institutional and professional spaces. This requires specialised expertise and knowledge to ensure these priorities are addressed in the context of the complexities they present. In both public and private sectors there is a need to continue to develop a workforce that reflects a philosophy of social justice, which underpins commitments to equity, diversity and inclusion and awareness of the need for change to meet the challenge of these commitments. Because of this, terms like equity, inclusion, belonging and diversity have become watch words. But these watch words lack a clear intent and may be taken at face value. They are ambiguous and are often understood in numerous different ways. This leads to divergent, even incoherent, goals, rationales, intentions and strategies within and across institutions and organisations. This course provides an overview of the key concepts, debates and strategies for equity, diversity and inclusion across institutional and professional spaces, as they relate to themes such as gender, race, Indigeneity, disability and more. It brings in examples of international and domestic best-practice, and introduces the students to case studies from industry. At the end of this course, students will be able to critically assess the impact of social and institutional inequalities for communities and individual lives, and to produce effective strategies for different professional and institutional contexts.
learning_outcomes: Construct the foundation for an equity initiative within an institution or organisation.
Evaluate EDI issues and design strategies and recommendations for institutional equity practices.
Apply diverse conceptual lenses and analytical skills to deepen understandings of EDI case studies.
Critique cross-societal equity problems in professional contexts.
Investigate issues that impact upon professional and institutional equity, diversity and inclusion strategies and initiatives.

title: Shaping Organisations and Communities: Advocacy and Change
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The role of advocacy and advocates is central in shaping inclusive, equitable and diverse communities, organisations and workplaces. Advocates work across global and local spheres, speaking up for injustice, drawing our attention to struggles, vulnerability and unfairness, and driving positive change that aims to increase the welfare of individuals, local communities and the world. But, what is advocacy? Why is advocacy important? Who advocates and who is advocated for? Do we advocate for people or for issues? And, what is good advocacy practice? This course takes on these questions and interrogates the phenomenon, concept and practice of advocacy across a diverse range of equity themes, including Indigeneity, race, ethnicity, class and gender. It builds students’ knowledge and insights into the role of advocacy in driving social and cultural change (both globally and locally), the pitfalls and dangers embedded in advocacy, and the potential for advocacy to be co-opted by other agendas. We will explore the distinction between advocacy within organisations and advocacy for groups, interrogate the line between advocacy and activism, and consider where and how advocacy can become counter to its mission and reproduce inequitable, colonial and hegemonic structures. The course has an embedded work-integrated element and, through the course, students will get the opportunity to build their own advocacy campaign and champion a cause they are passionate about, meet and learn from advocates who work in different sectors and for various causes.
learning_outcomes: Appraise the role of individual actors and organisations driving social change and working for collective rights and wellbeing.
Identify risks for advocacy and potential pitfalls.
Design an issue-centred advocacy campaign based on rigorous desktop research and interrogation of the policy field.
Assemble strategies that drive positive institutional, organisational, social and cultural change.
Identify and locate suitable practices of advocacy within institutions and communities.
Analyse the field of advocacy, champions and campaigns from a critical social theory perspective.

title: Environmental Justice
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Environmental Justice is predicated on the idea that environmental harm is borne by the most marginalised communities in society, while environmental profits are unequally shared. In this course students will explore the ways environmental injustice is experienced between and within societies, the fissures that exacerbate and overcome injustice, and the strategies and tactics different actors adopt to challenge environment injustice. We are interested in the complexities, contradictions and dilemmas of environmental justice and in developing tools to navigate through these. Course content has been designed around case studies from the Global South and Global North that encourage students to engage with existing issues and think of ways to approach similar scenarios.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate environmental justice as a mechanism for understanding relations between the environment and society;
Analyse the actors, institutions, conditions and approaches that enable and constrain environmental justice and identify these in weekly readings and the readings quizzes;
Research, extend and communicate in-depth case studies in written form and examine the implications of these for theory, policy and practice.
Identify and present environmental justice case studies in oral form and provide written comments on the case studies presented by peers;

assessment_tasks.task_name: Essay Based on EJ Case Study

title: Social Change and Development Research Project
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course is a core (compulsory) course within the Master of Social Change and Development (MSCD). The course counts for 20 units, twice as much as most of the other MSCD courses in the program. The course provides students with the opportunity to undertake a small research project of their own choosing, under the supervision of the course coordinator.
learning_outcomes: Appraise the role of key stakeholders participating in the specific concerns of women and men, workers, farmers or other marginalised groups.
Explore the foundations of an agreed area of research interest within the field of social change and development.
Identify the research skills required for the successful completion of a small research project.
Collate and critically analyse research materials collected from a diverse range of sources.
Apply development theories in the critical analysis and evaluation of concrete research projects within the social change and development arena.

title: Social Science Research Methods
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Provides students with a sound grounding in the range of research methods relevant to the wider teaching program in Social Change and Development. It also provides an awareness of some of the relevant debates in the area of methodology. Both quantitative and qualitative research methods will be covered. The course will be student-centred, problem-oriented and delivered in a multimedia format.
learning_outcomes: Design research frameworks appropriate to the research tasks arising from other parts of the course.
Analyse linkages between (a) theories of social change and development and (b) social research practice and methodology.
Demonstrate a critical understanding of the range of research techniques employed by social researchers, both qualitative and quantitative.
Discuss the ethical implications of research practices and the external environment within which social research is conducted.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Weekly contributions to, and participation in, online forum; and 2 day intensive
Applying qualitative research methods with specific population groups
Designing a mixed methods research project

title: Rural Food Security and Sustainable Agriculture for Community Development
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: In the rural areas of developing countries, food security is frequently a problem despite proximity to agricultural land. This course investigates this problem and considers useful solutions for community development in the social contexts of different parts of the developing world. Governments can operate to relieve food security by enacting policies at a national level, with impacts on urban and rural food security. What are the options and the advantages and disadvantages? Sustainable solutions through interventions in agriculture are also proposed and can be enacted at a local level by government agencies or initiated by local or international NGOs. What kinds of nutritional deficit are typical and what are the agricultural strategies that can address these in the context of rural poverty? How can we design an agricultural strategy for a particular situation? How does the local context of land ownership and culture impact on what can work in community development? A commonly proposed solution is to move farmers away from dependence on subsistence and into a greater involvement in the market. What are the pitfalls of this strategy and how can we decide when the local context makes it appropriate?
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an understanding of agricultural strategies used in food security interventions for sustainable rural development
Demonstrate an understanding of options for national policy on food security
Demonstrate the ability to design and present an effective intervention for a local context that takes into account agricultural options and their social context

title: Professional Skills and Key Debates in Social Sciences
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course comprises two streams. The first stream introduces students to the utility of the Social Sciences; to an understanding of the social world in which social scientists operate to develop and run social programs; and to social issues and debates which relate to the professional work of social scientists. The major assignment for the second stream is a focus group - run the group, transcribe the interview and analyse the interview data. Along with this a series of practical workshops which will provide students with the skills necessary to undertake this task and produce a professional research report. In addition to interview and analysis skills, the workshops will cover: computer literacy, effective use of the internet, and competency with word processing, spreadsheets, databases and presentation software as they apply in the Social Sciences. Other aspects of professional practice such as written, oral and interpersonal communication skills, and working in groups are also covered. Students are expected to reach a level of competence in these skills, starting from very different skill backgrounds.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a proficient understanding of foundational social science knowledge and debates in the areas of program management, policy analysis and social research.
Competently use a range of information and communication technologies in social sciences and humanities.
Demonstrate professional competency in written, oral, group work and interpersonal communication skills.
Critically appraise and discuss the relevant literature .

assessment_tasks.task_name: Executive Skill Set Exercises In class exercises

title: Organisational Management and Social Behaviour
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course draws on the field of organisational sociology for students to develop the managerial and administrative knowledge and values needed to effectively coordinate programs in government, private sector, non-government organisations (NGOs), and community organisations. The course also examines social behaviour in the workplace through the study of leadership styles, teamwork and group processes, work organisation and management practices.
learning_outcomes: Contribute to informed debate about organisational theories, leadership styles, teamwork and group processes.
Apply theories of organisational management and social behaviour to a case study of a particular industry or work situation.
Compare and contrast theories of organisational management and social behaviour.
Identify a range of competing theories of organisational management and social behaviour.

title: Social Analysis: Theorising Social Problems
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: In this course, students engage with major social theories to analyse contemporary (extra-human) social issues, social changes, and possibilities for future transformations. The course explores critical perspectives on power, inequality, and change, examining themes such as the evolution of social theory, class, race, and gender in social and institutional structures, the impact of digital and AI driven technological shifts on labor and identity, the ecological crises and their social dimensions, and the role of utopian thinking in imagining alternative futures. Students will apply these theoretical frameworks to real-world case studies, developing analytical and creative skills to critically assess and address pressing social challenges.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate effective communication of social theories at an intermediate level.
Compare and contrast social theories informed by the relevant literature.
Apply the insights of social theory to professional practice in the Social Sciences.
Identify and describe a range of social theories and research relevant to the Social Sciences.

title: Surveying the Social: Applied Quantitative Research
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: In this course students develop a comparative understanding of social science methods for the design of social inquiry. This course concentrates on the collection and analysis of quantitative data and the reporting of results. Students develop an understanding of the uses, strengths and limitations of various research strategies and approaches to conducting social inquiry, and develop skills necessary for designing social survey research tools, data processing and analysis, the interpretation of numerical data and report writing. The computer workshops will include an introduction to appropriate software packages such as SPSS. The course does not require previous statistical knowledge.
learning_outcomes: Correctly interpret social figures and the results of data analyses and write up academic report on the findings.
Develop appropriate research tools for conducting quantitative research and evaluating their validity and reliability.
Apply appropriate primary data processing and data analysis skills using a relevant computer program.

Demonstrate a proficient understanding of a range of social research approaches and strategies, their applicability, strengths and weakness, and the relationship between social research methods and social theory.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Project I, Devising A Survey Questionnaire and its Research Rationale
Project II, Secondary Data Analysis and Report

title: Ethics for the Social Sciences
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: In this course students are introduced to: (i) the nature of ethics and moral discourse in the social sciences; (ii) a range of ethical issues and moral debates that they may encounter in their professional lives; and (iii) methods for addressing these ethical issues.
learning_outcomes: Critically appraise and discuss the relevant literature in written and oral forms.
Participate in discussions concerning ethical issues as they arise in workplace contexts.
Demonstrate an understanding of a range of ethical issues, perspectives and debates as relevant to the social sciences.
Effectively communicate understanding of ethical issues in written and oral forms, by employing analytical skills.

title: Bachelor of Social Science Placement
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Through this course students will engage directly with organisations which require social science input into their policy, planning and evaluation practices. This direct experience will expose students to the discourses and practices of researchers and managers and will require that students consider the many complex factors which influence research and policy. Under supervision, students will locate and undertake an 80-hour work placement with appropriate organisations involved in social research, education or community service. This course may be taken in Australia or at an overseas organisation supported by an approved provider.
learning_outcomes: Set objectives and evaluate outcomes.
Demonstrate professional knowledge gained through experiential learning by providing written reports to the organisation and the convenor.
Design and carry out small scale projects as required by the organisation to a professional standard.
Critically reflect on the relevance of social science skills in the workplace.

title: Qualitative Social Inquiry: Applied Research Project
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course provides grounding in advanced social research methods. In this course you will practise your qualitative research skills. You will identify, workshop and apply social science research skills by developing a research proposal, writing a literature review, collecting and analysing data, and producing a research report based on the data collected. Your small research project will be conducted under a Human Research Ethics Committee (HREC) approved topic area.
learning_outcomes: Develop a research question appropriate for a small qualitative research project.
Assess the ethical issues involved in the project and identify appropriate ethical research decisions.
Plan, collect and critically analyse qualitative research data.
Justify the validity of a qualitative research method in addressing the selected question.
Communicate research results in written and oral forms, at a capstone level.

assessment_tasks.task_name: In Class or Online Oral Exam

title: Fluency Across the Lifespan
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: Focuses primarily on management of fluency disorders in preschool-age and school-age children, adolescents and adults. Key issues related to assessment and intervention practices are addressed. Clinical speech measures and specific intervention techniques are studied within the World Health Organisation's International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (WHO-ICF) conceptual framework, ethical and evidence-based practice (EBP).
learning_outcomes: Identify and develop relevant, comprehensive, and detailed plans for intervention related to fluency disorders.
Report on findings and make recommendations for future management.
Demonstrate and apply theoretical and etiological knowledge involved in disorders of fluency across the lifespan.
Identify further information and referral requirements.
Identify and administer relevant assessments for fluency disorders and report on analysis/interpretation of assessment findings.

title: Policy Development, Program Management and Evaluation
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course provides an understanding of how to formulate, implement, manage and evaluate social programs and social policies by developing skills in systematic reviews, policy briefs, social audit, social impact analysis, and needs analysis in relation to real-life case studies. Includes consideration of ethical issues and development of skills in dealing with clients and institutional stakeholders.
learning_outcomes: Identify and critically appraise a range of theoretical perspectives, research methods and debates on policy development, program management and evaluation.
Critically appraise and discuss the relevant literature.
Apply relevant theories to the analysis of a case study in policy development.
Apply principles of program management to develop a program management tool.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Develop Briefing Paper or Evaluation Critique

title: Introduction to Speech Pathology
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the speech pathology profession and its clinical processes and practice. It provides an overview of the general principles of working with individuals, families, and communities, and of conducting assessments and therapy.
learning_outcomes: Describe and report on speech pathology scope of practice in relation to health and allied health professions.
Demonstrate understanding and application of Speech Pathology Australia's professional standards (2020) to clinical practice scenarios and demonstrate effective teamwork skills.
Demonstrate an understanding of relevant aspects of the Workplace Health & Safety Act (2011).
Demonstrate an understanding of appropriate professional, legal, and ethical practice principles.
Engage in reflective learning
Describe and demonstrate application of principles of practice (e.g., cultural safety and responsiveness EBP) and the WHO-ICF

title: Language, Literacy and Hearing
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course addresses school-aged language and literacy (children and adolescents) at an advanced level, including typical development, assessment, analysis, diagnosis and intervention within the World Health Organization's International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) and evidence-based practice (EBP). Speech Pathology assessment, intervention and technology for hearing across the lifespan. Also considers the impact of hearing on Australian Indigenous peoples.
learning_outcomes: Identify gaps in comprehensive language, literacy and hearing assessments.
Report findings from comprehensive language, literacy and hearing assessments.
Identify and discuss hearing habilitation and rehabilitation issues and methods.
Develop comprehensive and detailed plans for language and literacy intervention.
Describe etiological factors involved in literacy and language disability in school-aged children, and in hearing loss.
Analyse and interpret comprehensive language, literacy and hearing assessments.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Language and literacy assessment and intervention

title: Complex Communication Needs
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to acquired and lifelong disability in relation to individuals with complex communication needs who need or use Alternative and Augmentative Communication (AAC). The course covers in detail; intentional communication, aided and unaided multi-modal communication systems, assessment and intervention for individuals with complex communication needs.
learning_outcomes: Describe etiological factors involved in populations of individuals with complex communication needs.
Identify further information and referral requirements for individuals with complex communication needs.
Develop comprehensive and detailed plans for intervention, incorporating multi-modal communication, AAC strategies and the use of other assistive technologies to enhance communication and inclusion.
Report on findings and make recommendations for future management for individuals with complex communication needs and those who use AAC.
Analyse and interpret findings from assessment of an individual with complex communication needs.

title: Complex Communication Needs 2
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: The course follows on from the coverage in SPTH2003 Complex Communication Needs 1 of multi-modal communication and AAC. Assessment and intervention methods for adult and children who use AAC will be considered, for example, AAC applications and acquired disabilities. The course will also cover the assessment and management of various genetic conditions including, cleft palate and other craniofacial anomalies.
learning_outcomes: Develop comprehensive and detailed plans for intervention for those with craniofacial anomaly and AAC users
Administer, analyse and interpret findings from comprehensive assessment of craniofacial anomaly and complex communication needs.
Report on findings and make recommendations for future management for a person with craniofacial anomaly and an AAC user.

Discuss aetiological factors involved in persons with AAC/complex communication needs such as those with craniofacial anomaly especially cleft lip & palate, acquired neurological conditions such as stroke, dysarthria, apraxia of speech and other complex conditions such as cerebral palsy, Childhood Apraxia of Speech (CAS) developmental disability, hospitalised populations, those with life-limiting illness/death & dying.
Identify further information and referral requirements for craniofacial anomaly and AAC users.

title: Writing the Field of Equity
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Within professional and institutional equity diversity and inclusion writing is a key tool for producing effective change. However, though clear and effective communication is expected, rarely is the construction of equity, produced through the dominant conventions of writing, called into question. Drawing on critical theory and Indigenous methodologies, the students will be introduced to notions of storywork and writing as a deeply political process that reveals and masks important dimensions of equity, diversity and inclusion. This course aims to enhance students’ understanding of the craft and social practices of researching, evaluating and writing across equity, diversity and inclusion contexts. It will provide students with a strong foundation for practicing the various forms of writing that are used in equity, diversity and inclusion strategies and implementation and to develop this foundation within a strong ethical framing, underpinned by social justice methodologies.
learning_outcomes: Analyse the ways that social hierarchies, differences and inequalities are represented in written form in institutional, organisational and professional contexts, and how these enable and constrain different approaches to equity policy and practice.
Identify and present equity case studies through a variety of formats, including posters, written and oral form.
Appraise the challenges of writing in equity strategies and implementation, advocacy and research.
Design equity strategies using different modes of understanding of in-depth case studies and examine the implications of these for theory, policy and practice.

title: Professional Practice
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: Students undertake supervised face-to-face clinical experience with child speech pathology caseloads. Clinical experience placements are usually in speech pathology student units in health, education, or on-campus outpatient settings and attendance for one day (8.00am - 5pm) each week will be required for the period allocated. (Note that placements typically include attendance outside the semester). One hour a week will be spent in tutorials on-campus during the semester period to assist with the preparation for clinical placement experiences and to facilitate transferability and integration of academic and clinical knowledge.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrates professional and ethical behaviour appropriate to the clinical placement setting.
Provision of clinical management to children with communication needs using evidence based, culturally responsive and ethical practice.
Demonstrates reflective practice and and critical thinking.
Demonstrate progress from beginning levels of clinical competence to between novice and intermediate levels of competence across all units of COMPASS®.
Uses professional verbal and written communication.

title: Voice across the lifespan
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course addresses voice disorders including perceptual and instrumental measurement and description of normal and abnormal voice. The course covers assessment and management of voice disorders in children, adolescents and adults. The course includes speech rehabilitation following laryngectomy.
learning_outcomes: Identify further information and referral requirements for voice disorders.
Discuss etiological factors involved in disorders of voice.
Select and administer appropriate assessments for voice disorders.
Develop comprehensive and detailed plans for intervention for voice disorders.
Analyse and interpret interprofessional collaborative practice that takes place for individuals with voice difficulties.
Analyse and interpret findings with regard to knowledge of voice.
Report on findings and make recommendations for future management for voice disorders.

title: Child Language
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course will focus on child language disorders including typical language development, assessment, analysis, diagnosis and intervention of children with language disorders within the World Health Organization's International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) conceptual framework and evidence-based practice (EBP).
learning_outcomes: Apply general and case specific interventions for children with language disorders, with particular emphasis on evidence based practice (EBP) and service delivery.
Apply the theory, aetiology and classification of child language disorders in children.
Conduct, analyse and interpret assessment procedures suitable for a child with a language disorder.
Identify and discuss language development in children from birth to school age.
Identify and implement management decisions in children with language disorders.
Apply the World Health Organization's International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) conceptual framework to facilitate a holistic understanding of child language disorders.

title: Adult Speech and Language
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course reviews speech and language development and change from young adults to the elderly. The course focuses on communication disorders typically seen in hospital settings or specialist service facilities. Acquired communication disorders of neurological origin are covered, i.e. aphasia and related disorders, apraxia of speech and dysarthria.
learning_outcomes: Select appropriate assessments for acquired neurological disorders of speech and language.
Describe the etiological factors involved in impairments of acquired neurological disorders of speech and language.
Demonstrate an understanding of typical ageing changes in relation to communication in adults.
Propose recommendations for future management for acquired speech and language disorders.
Identify further information and referral requirements for acquired neurological disorders of speech and language in adults.
Develop and provide justification for interventions plans for adults with acquired speech and language disorders.
Analyse, interpret and report on assessment findings.

title: Child Speech
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course will focus on speech sound disorders (SSD) in children, including typical speech development, assessment, analysis, diagnosis and intervention of children with speech sound disorders within the World Health Organization's International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) conceptual framework and evidence based practice (EBP).
learning_outcomes: Identify and discuss speech development in children.
Apply the theory, aetiology and classification of child speech sound disorders (SSD).
Identify and implement management decisions in children with SSD.
Apply the World Health Organization's International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) conceptual framework to facilitate a holistic understanding of SSD.
Conduct, analyse and interpret assessment procedures suitable for a child with a SSD.
Apply general and case specific interventions for children with SSD, with particular emphasis on evidence based practice (EBP) and service delivery.

title: Swallowing Across the Lifespan
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: Focuses on normal and disordered swallowing and mealtimes. This course involves assessment and management of feeding/swallowing disorders in infants and children, and adults. Key issues related to assessment and intervention practices are addressed. Clinical assessment and specific intervention techniques are studied in relation to specific dysphagic populations.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate and apply knowledge of normal swallowing across the lifespan and etiological factors involved in impairments of swallowing.
Report on assessment and intervention findings and make recommendations for future management.
Analyse and interpret assessment findings.
Identify and justify appropriate swallowing assessments for children and adults.
Determine further information needed and referral requirements.
Analyse and interpret interprofessional collaborative practice that takes place for individuals with swallowing difficulties.
Develop and provide justification for intervention plans for children and adults with swallowing disorders.

title: Adult Speech
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course will focus on the anatomy, physiology, speech characteristics, assessment and treatment of acquired motor speech disorders (dysarthrias and apraxia of speech) within the World Health Organization's International Classification of Functioning, Disability, and Health (WHO-ICF) conceptual framework, and evidence-based practice (EBP).
learning_outcomes: Analyse the major neurological health and medical conditions, aetiology, physiology, and symptoms associated with motor speech disorders.
Apply general and case specific interventions for adults with acquired motor speech disorders, with particular emphasis on evidence based practice (EBP).
Provide detailed perceptual, acoustic and physiologic descriptions of acquired motor speech disorders.
Analyse and interpret distinctive features of motor speech disorders for differential diagnosis.

Apply the World Health Organization's International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) conceptual framework to facilitate a holistic understanding of acquired motor speech disorders

title: Professional Practice
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: Students undertake supervised face-to-face clinical experience with adult speech pathology caseloads. Clinical experience placements are usually in speech pathology student units either in community/health or on-campus settings, and attendance for up to three days (8.00am - 5pm) each week may be required for the period allocated (and typically includes attendance outside the semester). Tutorials will be provided on-campus and online to facilitate transferability and integration of academic and clinical knowledge.
learning_outcomes: Use professional verbal and written communication.
Demonstrate progress to an intermediate level of across all units of COMPASS®.
Provision of clinical management to adults with communication and swallowing needs using evidence based, culturally responsive and ethical practice.
Demonstrate reflective practice and and critical thinking.
Demonstrate professional and ethical behaviour appropriate to the clinical placement setting.

title: Adult Language
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course will focus on the theoretical and clinical features of adult acquired language and cognitive communication disorders, within the World Health Organization's International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (WHO-ICF) conceptual framework and evidence based practice (EBP).
learning_outcomes: Describe acquired language and cognitive communication disorders in adults, including their aetiologies and prognosis.
Discuss the impact of acquired language and cognitive communication impairments on caregivers, communication partners and the community.
Conduct, analyse and interpret assessment procedures suitable for adults with acquired language and cognitive communication disorders

Apply the World Health Organization's International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) conceptual framework to adults with acquired language and cognitive-communication disorders.
Apply general and case specific interventions for adults with acquired language and cognitive-communication disorders, with particular emphasis on evidence based practice (EBP).
Identify and implement management decisions for adults with acquired language and cognitive communication disorders.

title: Holistic Practice Across the Lifespan
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: This course focuses on the complexity of clinical practice within speech pathology. Complexity may arise in various ways including multiple diagnoses, co-occurring health conditions, cultural diversity, disabilities, and access to services. This may involve multiple professionals working in interprofessional and collaborative, person or family centred-practice. Complexity also arises considering quality of life and equality for all, including disadvantaged and vulnerable communities. Complexity is also viewed in terms of clinical practice; caseload diversity, size, and service delivery models.
learning_outcomes: Explore previously investigated clinical domains and transfer knowledge and skills in greater depth through integrating impairment, compensatory, and functional components in the best available evidence (EBP)
Apply new knowledge and skills to case scenarios to advance clinical practice and reasoning when working in complex clinical situations.
Demonstrate application of relevant professional standards (Speech Pathology Australia Professional Standards, 2020) when managing complexity in clinical cases.

Apply the World Health Organization's International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health (ICF) conceptual framework and the social determinants of health to speech pathology practice for complex clients (including medical and social complexity, e.g. co-occurring diagnosis).

title: Professional Issues 1
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: In this course students will gain a deep understanding of their own professional identity as a speech pathologist ready to enter the profession, developing key job seeking and career planning skills. Guided by evidence and quality processes, students will demonstrate informed ethical judgement and an understanding of interprofessional collaborative practice to achieve respectful partnerships.
learning_outcomes: Apply principles and processes of professional conduct, including ethical judgment, to clinical scenarios in speech pathology

Demonstrate appropriate negotiation, communication, and organisation when working within a team to address shared healthcare challenges demonstrating understanding of roles and responsibilities across various disciplines
Develop a professional curriculum vitae that reflects speech pathology practice (including knowledge, skills, and attributes)
Demonstrate professional communication and presentation skills

assessment_tasks.task_name: Recorded mock Interview + curriculum vitae for speech pathology practice

title: Professional Issues 2
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: In this course, students gain and demonstrate their knowledge of contemporary workplace issues associated with speech pathology practice. Using their knowledge of communication and swallowing needs, students will demonstrate their understanding of culturally safe and responsive practice for individuals and communities they are supporting. Students will demonstrate knowledge and understanding of digital literacy across practice areas and tasks.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate the ethical use of artificial intelligence to support speech pathology practice that is culturally safe and responsive to the needs of individuals and communities they are part of
Recognise workplace issues which impact speech pathology service efficiency and quality
Collaborate and present on sustainable practices in speech pathology, demonstrating individual competence in negotiation, communication, and organisational skills

assessment_tasks.task_name: Written Assignment (use and reflection of AI in practice)
Group (live) presentation + individual response to examiner questions

title: Professional Practice 1
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: Students undertake supervised face-to-face clinical experience with a diverse range of speech pathology caseloads with child, adult, and disability populations. The clinical placements are on a block basis, involving full day attendance, Monday to Friday, for approximately 25 day child and 25 days adult placement. This extended block program supports placements with different models of service in order to provide experience with different models of service delivery appropriate to these settings.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate professional and ethical behaviour appropriate to the clinical placement setting.
Demonstrate near-entry and entry levels of clinical competence across all units of COMPASS®.
Provision of clinical management to individuals with communication and swallowing needs using evidence based, culturally responsive, and ethical practice.
Use professional verbal and written communication.
Demonstrate appropriate reflective practice and critical thinking.

title: International Speech Pathology
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: SPTH4420 involves the advanced study in the field of speech pathology internationally. The course explores cultural and linguistic diversity, cultural understandings, how health and illness are conceptualised and speech pathology practices across the world. The course allows for advanced level study in relevant areas with students undertaking an individualised learning program (ILP) arranged in consultation with the course coordinator.
learning_outcomes: Present information in a manner consistent with scientific and professional requirements.
Critically evaluate approaches to a specific area of speech-language pathology relevant to practice internationally.
Describe social, economic, political and cultural factors involved in health and illness at an international level.
Develop and implement a project, which is theoretically and methodologically sound to address a relevant issue or specific question, with supervision.
Critically evaluate the extent to which empirical research supports those approaches.

title: Research Methdologies
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: Research Methodologies forms part of the Honours Program in Sustainable Resource Management. This course covers advanced approaches to research methodology, with relevance to Honours projects undertaken by students at the 4000 level. Students enrolled in this course will explore contemporary perspectives in Sustainable Resource Management research and focus specifically on; developing research skills; formulating research proposals; framing research questions; reviewing existing research; and choosing appropriate methodologies for different types of study. Methodologies are examined in the context of their application to their project (and associated research grouping), such as Sustainability, Resource Management, Environmental Science and Climate Science.
learning_outcomes: Design and develop a structured research plan using cognitive skills and critical thinking.
Demonstrate skills in information searching, selection, retrieval, and interpretation.
Apply discipline specific theoretical and practical research skills.
Interpret, summarise, and synthesise the literature of academic and professional literature.
Identify appropriate methods of quantitative and/or qualitative data collection as relevant to the research project undertaken.

title: Research Review
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: Students' prior learning of research methodology is reviewed in the context of speech pathology clinical research. Students review the current theoretical and empirical research literature in order to argue for a specific research question or direction for further research.
learning_outcomes: Acquire, critique, interpret and integrate knowledge from different sources (including contemporary theory, empirical research evidence etc.) with regard to theoretical and clinical validity, and methodology (strengths and limitations).
Present and defend a logical argument in a professional manner.
Identify, select and describe an area of research relevant to speech pathology practice with potential for further research (i.e., research question/gap/direction).
Argue for a methodologically feasible research question, gap, or direction.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Oral Presentation and line of argument outline

title: Thesis Creation
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: Thesis Creation forms part of the Honours Program in Sustainable Resource Management. This course is part of the multi-sequence research component of Honours which requires the development of original research under the supervision of a member of academic staff from the School of Environmental and Life Sciences. It is a continuation from research undertaken in SRMT4002A with the students completing their final Thesis.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate scientific writing skills.
Use research skills to undertake higher-level and post-graduate research and writing.
Apply constructive feedback to improve thesis.
Communicate research findings that positions conclusions within the overall field of enquiry.
Critically analyse and evaluate published research material.
Present information in written and verbal formats in a logical and comprehensive manner.

title: Vegetation Classification and Ecological Restoration
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: The United Nations General assembly have declared 2021 – 2030 as the UN Decade on Ecosystem Restoration. Restoration practice that rebuilds ecosystem resilience is fundamental to sustainable development, mitigating and adapting to climate change and enhancing food security as well as water and biodiversity conservation. SRMT3060 explores the science of assisted recovery of degraded, damaged or destroyed ecosystems. Real-world degradation problems are investigated in the context of examining traditional evidence-based restoration as well as novel solutions, in order to equip students with the knowledge and skills for entry into careers involving ecological restoration policy and/or practice. Underpinning effective ecological restoration is accurate classification of vegetation communities, a process which requires skills in aerial image interpretation, field survey methods, analytical classification and desktop mapping. These are fundamental skills for any environmental scientist in government, consulting or research.
learning_outcomes: Describe and interpret environmental information obtained from the field and other scientific resources;
Demonstrate full floristic sampling, vegetation classification and analysis
Explain and apply the key principles underpinning ecological restoration and vegetation classification.
Design and explain appropriate restoration strategies and techniques to address specific problems eg. re-vegetation, weed control;
Identify and describe appropriate restoration goals and evaluation strategies;
Assess the condition of an ecosystem through fieldwork and desktop activities and understand threats to ecosystem health.

title: Professional Practice 2
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: Students undertake supervised clinical experiences with children and adults with communication and swallowing needs (e.g., voice, fluency and feeding and swallowing). Clinical experiences are usually in the University Speech Pathology clinic and involve full day attendance, as allocated for up to 25 days (and may include attendance outside the semester).
learning_outcomes: Use professional verbal and written communication.
Provision of clinical management to individuals and communities with communication and swallowing needs using evidence based, culturally responsive and ethical practice.
Demonstrate appropriate reflective practice and critical thinking.
Demonstrate professional and ethical behaviour appropriate to the workplace setting.

title: Thesis Preparation
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: Thesis Preparation forms part of the Honours Program for Sustainable Resource Management. This course provides students an opportunity to advance the skills and knowledge they acquired throughout their undergraduate studies through thesis formulation. It covers advanced topics in research methodologies and ethics relevant to the projects undertaken by the cohort of students at this level. This course is part of the multi-sequence research component of honours which requires the development of original research under the supervision of a member of academic staff from the School of Environmental and Life Sciences. In Part A, students will undertake preparation work for their thesis, completing this final body of work in Part B.
learning_outcomes: Select appropriate research principles (including ethics where applicable), procedures and capacity to obtain appropriate approval for a research project.
Demonstrate scientific writing skills.
Critically analyse and evaluate published research material.
Work safely in a variety of laboratory and/or field contexts.
Establish the aims, objectives and boundaries of the thesis, methodology and research plan, and an appropriate timetable for completion.
Present information in written and verbal formats in a logical and comprehensive manner.
Undertake scientific experimentation from the generation of a hypothesis through to the publishing of results including ethics and safety considerations.

title: Communicating Research
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: Communicating Research forms part of the Honours Program in Sustainable Resource Management. This course utilises students’ skills and knowledge in the development and communication of research and research findings. Students will conduct research relevant to the nature of their course and share their findings under the guidance of an academic supervisor. Students will communicate the results of both theoretical and experimental work to a scientific audience.
learning_outcomes: Communicate research findings that positions conclusions within a student's overall field of enquiry.
Apply learned procedures for undertaking a successful research project within the field of Sustainable Resource Management.
Display professional conduct and practice.
Demonstrate a range of communication strategies for presenting research in field of study to a wide variety of audiences.

title: Presenting Research
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: Presenting Research forms part of the Honours Program for Sustainable Resource Management. This course allows students to showcase their presentation and communication skills, and knowledge of research process and outcomes. Students will share their findings to a range of audiences, communicating the results of their theoretical and/or experimental work through a Final Seminar and Viva.
learning_outcomes: Effectively communicate research methods and results to an audience.
Structure and formulate responses to questions by written, graphic and oral means.
Demonstrate professionalism in presentation of thesis to an audience.

title: Sustainable Resource Management Honours 411
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course builds knowledge and understanding about research in the discipline of sustainable resource management. The course aims at enhancing skills and capacities in reading and reviewing literature, critical reasoning and argument, and verbal communication. Students will enhance their skills through discussions of theoretical and applied directions in sustainable resource management studies; student-based presentations of key issues; and training in computing skills, on-line bibliographic searches, risk assessment, oral presentation techniques.
learning_outcomes: Apply skills and methods needed to critically analyse scientific literature and communicate scientific issues in verbal form.
Demonstrate knowledge of research ethics and safety procedures associated with sustainable resource management research and a capacity to obtain the appropriate approvals for a research project.
Gain an advanced understanding of the use of the scientific method to examine problems.
Demonstrate an advanced understanding of the theory and practice of research in the discipline of sustainable resource management.
Comprehend contemporary issues in sustainable resource management.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Literature review outline and initial research plan outline

title: Sustainable Resource Management Honours 412
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course develops preliminary research skills in sustainable resource management studies. The course is conducted under the direct supervision of an academic staff member who is also the student's honours research supervisor. The course builds skills and competencies in research design including literature reviews, identification of research questions, methodological approaches, discussion and written communication skills.
learning_outcomes: Formulate appropriate boundaries to a research project and identify appropriate methods and processes to undertake critical analysis.
Comprehend the procedures for undertaking a successful research project within the field of sustainable research management.
Identify relevant texts and information gaps in the student's field of research and understand the methods of reviewing literature.
Identify research issues and frame research questions in the context of existing scholarship and available resources.

title: Sustainable Resource Management Honours 413
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course involves the direct application of research skills and competencies introduced in SRMT4120. The course is conducted under the direct supervision of an academic staff member who is the student's honours research supervisor. It concentrates on the data collection and analysis portion of the research process. By the start of this course, students will have completed a major literature review, identified a suitable research question and developed a robust research design. The course explores and implements appropriate data collection techniques and develops advanced skills in data analysis. The course develops chapter drafts for the student's research thesis, as well as a poster and oral presentation of research findings.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate their capacity to implement appropriate methods of quantitative and qualitative data collection and statistical analysis used in their individual research projects.
Demonstrate competency in the selection of various methods of quantitative and qualitative data collection and statistical analysis used in sustainable resource management studies.
Appreciate the methods used to distil and communicate specific findings in concise formats.

title: Statistical Reasoning and Literacy
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to statistical thinking, statistical methods and the interpretation of results from these methods. Examples from a range of science related disciplines are used to illustrate the key concepts. Interested in studying further statistics courses to develop your skills and improve your employability? Information about available statistics courses can be found here: https://www.newcastle.edu.au/school/mathematical-and-physical-sciences/study/statistics-courses
learning_outcomes: Identify appropriate methods of data collection (sampling and study designs) and analysis (e.g., for comparison of groups) for scientific studies
Critically appraise statistical techniques/elements/aspects/issues in the scientific literature
Identify and interpret appropriate graphs and summary statistics
Describe conceptually confidence intervals and hypothesis testing and interpret these in reports and articles
Describe conceptually statistical models and interpret corresponding results in reports and articles

title: Sustainable Resource Management Honours 414
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Environmental and Life Sciences
syllabus_overview: This course develops a student's skills and competencies in developing and communicating research findings in a written form. The course is conducted under the direct supervision of an academic staff member who is the student's honours research supervisor. The course operates in conjunction with SRMT4130 which is largely concerned with data collection and analysis and other forms of scientific communication. SRMT4140 involves discussion of research findings, their reconciliation with existing literatures and the development of written texts which form drafts of chapters for the student's honours research thesis. The course includes submission of a completed thesis.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate their capacity to communicate research findings that positions conclusions within a student's overall field of enquiry.
Demonstrate their capacity to communicate research findings involving very high analytical levels.
Demonstrate advanced competency in developing and communicating research findings in a 100 page thesis.
Demonstrate the research skills necessary to undertake higher-level and post-graduate research and writing.
Demonstrate advanced competency in developing and communicating research findings in a 100 page thesis.

title: Statistics for the Sciences
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: How do we use data to make informed scientific decisions? This course introduces students to statistical thinking, data collection, data presentation and statistical analysis. Examples from a range of science related disciplines are used to illustrate the key concepts. Although the emphasis is on applied data analysis rather than statistical theory, the course also provides an appropriate introduction for those students who intend to study statistics at a higher level. Interested in studying further statistics courses to develop your skills and improve your employability? Information about available statistics courses can be found here: https://www.newcastle.edu.au/school/mathematical-and-physical-sciences/study/statistics-courses
learning_outcomes: Explain how probability and sampling concepts relate to statistical analysis of data.
Apply basic principles of experimental design when collecting data.
Analyse data using common statistical software and interpret results to solve science related problems.
Describe the role of statistics in developing scientific knowledge.

title: Data Communication and Modelling
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Information and Physical Sciences
syllabus_overview: Extracting and presenting information from data lies at the heart of statistics and data science. In practice, data is not often in an immediately usable format, requiring management, manipulation and error-checking. Visualisation of data is an invaluable asset in discovering and presenting key information. This course provides a practical introduction to data wrangling and visualisation. Students will learn to tidy, validate, transform and summarise data, and design graphics that present insights from the data. Students will also develop coding skills using the Python language which is one of the most popular and preferred languages used in practice. No prior programming experience is necessary. Information about further statistics courses is available at the link: https://www.newcastle.edu.au/school/information-physical-sciences/study/statistics-courses
learning_outcomes: Design and create advanced data visualisations to present insights.
Implement data checking, wrangling and tidying methods.
Write and interpret code in the Python programming language to wrangle data and create visualisations.
Interpret and evaluate the effectiveness of data visualisations.
Identify key strategies for effective data presentation and reporting.
Apply exploratory techniques to identify and present underlying patterns in data.

title: Fundamentals of Statistics
faculty: College of Engineering Science and Environment
school: School of Computer and Information Sciences
syllabus_overview: Statistics provides us with a quantitative framework to utilise data for describing, summarising and modelling the world around us. This course provides students with fundamental concepts of probability, random variables and their distributions, and then applies them to provide the theoretical foundation for data analysis through statistical modelling, estimation and hypothesis testing. These concepts are motivated by real problems and illustrated with the leading statistical software platform R, a free, open-source, growing library of functions for object-oriented statistical programming. Both the theory and the introduction to R provide the foundation for subsequent 2000 and 3000 level statistics courses. The theory is also is of general interest to users of statistical methods, reaching beyond the application of these methods to address their underlying principles, formal description and rigorous justification.
