Self-assess personal values, assumptions and beliefs in response to practice scenarios, interprofessional practice and course content.
Analyse historical and contemporary conceptions of, and approaches to, providing grief and loss support and the care and protection of children.
Explain the various social work roles in providing grief and loss support and the care and protection of children, and how these roles relate to those of other professions.
Assess and apply national and state legislation relevant to the areas of care and protection of children.
Critique and apply a range of theories relevant to grief and loss and the care and protection of children.

title: Interpersonal Skills for Professional Practice
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course develops interpersonal skills for professional practice, including the ability to reflect on, analyse, and work with a supervisor, in order to enhance professional practice. This course is taught in classroom-based workshops complemented by online learning tasks. A compulsory attendance of 80% is a course requirement for SWRK2003 to fulfil Australian Association of Social Workers accreditation requirements for 12317 Bachelor of Social Work (Honours) students.
learning_outcomes: Reflect on their own professional practice, and give and receive feedback.
Describe and analyse the role of context, purpose and self in defining professional relationships.
Apply appropriate listening skills, including verbal and non verbal cues, empathy, and genuineness.
Develop rapport with another person within a professional context.
Name and explore the impact of their own values in professional relationships.

title: Violence, Abuse and Trauma : Theory and Practice
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course critically examines the intersecting dynamics of violence, abuse, and trauma across individual, family, community, and structural contexts. Drawing on interdisciplinary theory and contemporary research, students analyse the social, cultural, political, and historical conditions that produce and sustain violence, with particular attention to the impacts of colonialism, gender inequality, racism, and other forms of structural oppression in the Australian context. Students engage with key theoretical frameworks including trauma-informed practice, ecological and systems approaches, feminist and intersectional perspectives, and strengths-based and recovery-oriented models. The course develops advanced understanding of the impacts of violence and trauma across the lifespan, including neurobiological, psychological, and social dimensions, and considers diverse experiences of victim-survivors, perpetrators, families, and communities. Through applied learning, students critically evaluate evidence-informed intervention strategies and develop foundational practice skills in assessment, risk management, ethical decision-making, and interprofessional collaboration. Emphasis is placed on culturally responsive and trauma-informed practice, including working with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and communities. Students will reflect on their professional positioning, values, and responsibilities in responding to violence, abuse, and trauma in complex practice settings.
learning_outcomes: Recognize, define and identify types of violence and abuse across individual, family, community and societal contexts
Critically evaluate responses to violence and trauma drawing on a range of theories, perspectives and approaches as well as relevant legislative and policy frameworks
Demonstrate an understanding of the prevalence, nature and impacts of violence and abuse on individuals, groups and communities.
Articulate theories relating to the occurrence of violence and abuse, identifying the concepts of power and control as significant factors in victimisation.
Examine and articulate personal values, assumptions and beliefs in response to practice scenarios and develop strategies to deal with confronting material encountered in the professional context.
Demonstrate a commitment to values of respect, social justice and human rights.

title: Social Work Theory and Practice B
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Learning in this course addresses three domains of social work practice: 1. Health and wellbeing 2. Mental Health 3. Disability Students work through major social work methods of intervention: casework, group work, community work and social action; and develop competence in articulating the theoretical bases for assessments and decision-making for practice. Self-awareness, analysis of political contexts and commitment to social justice goals are fundamental themes.
learning_outcomes: Critique and apply a range of social work theories relevant to health and wellbeing, mental health, and disability.
Assess national and state legislation relevant to the areas of health and wellbeing, mental health, and disability.
Examine and articulate personal values, assumptions and beliefs in response to practice scenarios and course content.
Analyse historical and contemporary conceptions of health and wellbeing, mental health, and disability, in social work.
Identify the various social work roles in health and wellbeing, mental health, and disability contexts.
Display social work skills in assessment models, risk assessment procedures, and working in groups.

title: Social Work Ethics
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This online course focuses on high level ethical decision making relating to individual, group and community practice. It runs parallel to SWRK3300:Field Practicum. Students will be required to integrate and critique theoretical models and decision making tools relevant to their practicum field of practice.
learning_outcomes: Develop and apply knowledge from a range of ethical frameworks, models and approaches to assessment and intervention with clients, paying particular attention to work with people from culturally, linguistically and spiritually diverse backgrounds

Incorporate a critical understanding of the application of the AASW Code of ethics and knowledge of a range of perspectives and theoretical frameworks that influence ethical decision making in practice
Develop a capacity to search for, analyse and present relevant literature in relation to ethical social work practice and specific issues related to social work practice.

Formulate an advanced awareness of their personal and professional values and how these impact on ethical decision making, and a capacity to appraise these values with reference to the requirements of professional practice.
Demonstrate a high level of self-awareness and open transparent decision-making that integrates and is responsive to feedback from clients, peers, supervisors and teaching staff

assessment_tasks.task_name: Ethical Reflection on a Case Study

title: Social Work Theory and Practice C
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: In this course students examine social work practice with groups and in organisational environments. Students develop knowledge, skills and approaches in groupwork. These are applied to group program development and working in groups or teams in organisational settings. Students also gain knowledge of organisational processes and the management of organisational change. The focus of this course is on the broader organisational environment in which client interventions are informed and occur and explores the application of social work knowledge, skills and approaches within organisations.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate writing skills appropriate to audience, purpose and organisational context.
Describe changes to improve practice in an organisation that are linked to an organisational analysis and a change management process.
Demonstrate group participation, facilitation and presentation skills. Reflect critically on own role and that of others in groups.
Apply different approaches within groupwork in class, including assessment, planning, contracting, conflict management, problem solving, and closure.
Using a critical social work approach, analyse and explain elements of the organisational environment, organisational processes and dynamics using organisational and social work theories.

title: Field Placement 1
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Each student is placed in a human service organisation for a minimum of 500 hours to complete social work tasks with the support of supervision from an Agency Mentor. Academic staff locate and support the field practicum. Each student is allocated to a practicum organisation by the Social Work Field Education Coordinators, taking into account the learning needs of the student and the type of placements available. The practicum is assessed against learning objectives in line with the Australian Association of Social Workers (AASW) learning attributes. Students are well supported during the practicum with a Pre-Placement workshop prior to the commencement of the placement, a Mid-Placement workshop during the practicum, an End of Placement workshop, and a staff liaison person allocated to each student. Policies, procedures and expectations relating to field practicum courses in the Bachelor of Social Work (Hons) program are detailed in the BSW (Hons) Field Education Handbook, a copy of which is available on the Social Work Program Canvas site, and also on the Professional Experience Unit site. .
learning_outcomes: Show proficiency in social work practice, including assessment, intervention, collaboration, and critical reflection.
Use effective communication and teamwork when interacting with a diverse range of individuals, including professionals from other disciplines.
Apply ethical and legal standards to interactions with clients, service users, and communities in a respectful, inclusive and culturally responsive manner.
Demonstrate knowledge of social work practice, including systemic influences, theories, and concepts.
Employ effective written communication skills to record and report on practice, following ethical principles, legal requirements and organisational procedures.
Participate in supervision and self-reflect to enhance self-awareness, manage stress, and improve practice.

Practice professional social work values and ethics outlined in the AASW Code of Ethics and recognise the impact of following organisational policies, procedures and structures on the outcome of clients, groups and communities.

title: Social Work Theory and Practice
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: The final year of the social work degree builds on learning from the three previous years of study in the BSW program. This course focuses on advanced theory and practice issues with a focus on interpersonal intervention skills relating to individual, group and community practice. A compulsory attendance of 80% is a course requirement for SWRK4300 to fulfil Australian Association of Social Workers accreditation requirements for 12317 Bachelor of Social Work (Honours) students.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a high level of effective communication in a range of contexts, presenting information clearly, concisely and in a balanced and constructive way.
Generate a critical understanding of the application of the AASW Code of ethics.
Formulate an advanced awareness of their own values, interpersonal skills and ability to align these with professional practice.
Apply advanced knowledge from a range of theoretical frameworks, to work with communities and people.

title: Social Work Honours Project
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Each student undertakes independent research into a specialised area of social work policy practice and develops a body of work that incorporates a social work theory, practice, ethics, research and policy analysis. Course content includes: 1. Historical, social, cultural and political influences on social policies, policy practice and social services, and contemporary policy initiatives. 2. Social policy development processes, including analysing and debating social policy. 3. Links between economics, law, politics and social policy. 4. Ways in which policy and services address equality, social justice and human rights, including activism. 5. How social work skills, practice, research and intervention methods are applied to policy practice. 6. How to present written, oral and multimedia information to a target audience (including government submission, video, conference abstract, conference presentation, conference paper).
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate understanding of the historical, social and political impacts on contemporary social policy, theories that inform policy practice, and the policy making process.
Demonstrate an advanced and coherent theoretical and research knowledge of one issue or social problem pertinent to social work practice.
Demonstrate skills to prepare a body of work, including written and visual materials for commenting on, informing, and changing or promoting policy and or social change.
Critique the role of social workers in the policy process and social work skills related to policy practice.

title: Field Placement 2
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: Each student is placed in a human service organisation for a minimum of 500 hours to complete social work tasks with the support of supervision from an Agency Mentor. Academic staff locate and support the field practicum. Each student is allocated to a practicum organisation by the Social Work Field Education Coordinators, taking into account the learning needs of the student and the type of placements available. The practicum is assessed against learning objectives in line with the Australian Association of Social Workers (AASW) learning attributes. Students are well supported during the practicum with a Pre-Placement workshop prior to the commencement of the placement, a Mid-Placement workshop during the practicum, an End of Placement workshop, and a staff liaison person allocated to each student. Policies, procedures and expectations relating to field practicum courses in the Bachelor of Social Work (Hons) program are detailed in the BSW (Hons) Field Education Handbook, a copy of which is available on the Social Work Program Canvas site, and also on the Professional Experience Unit site.
learning_outcomes: Use effective communication and teamwork when interacting with a diverse range of individuals, including professionals from other disciplines.
Apply ethical and legal standards to interactions with clients, service users, and communities in a respectful, inclusive and culturally responsive manner.
Demonstrate knowledge of social work practice, including systemic influences, theories, and concepts.
Show proficiency in social work practice, including assessment, intervention, collaboration, and critical reflection.
Employ effective written communication skills to record and report on practice, following ethical principles, legal requirements and organisational procedures.
Participate in supervision and self-reflect to enhance self-awareness, manage stress, and improve practice.

Practice professional social work values and ethics outlined in the AASW Code of Ethics and recognise the impact of following organisational policies, procedures and structures on the outcome of clients, groups and communities.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Students must demonstrate competency in all listed assessment items below

title: Social Work Research
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This is the initial research course in the BSW (Hons). It provides advanced level research skills required for practice and progression to the 4th year Honours Project (SWRK4009). Students will develop a sophisticated understanding of the role that research plays in social work practice and competence in planning a practice-based research study that would inform social work intervention. Students will attain advanced knowledge and skills in qualitative and quantitative methods that may be used in practice-based social research. Ethical issues and critical debates in social work research will also be examined.
learning_outcomes: Develop knowledge in research methods and an understanding of when particular methods are most appropriate to answer different types of research questions encountered in social work practice.
Understand the role of research in social work practice
Develop competence in identifying and appropriately responding to ethical and cultural issues encountered in social work research.
Gain practical skills in gathering and analysing research data.
Understand and critique the use of evidence based practice in social work.
Engage in informed debate on social, political, ethical, technical and practical issues surrounding social work research, particularly in relation to diverse cultural groups.
Critically review the published research.

title: Social Work Identity, Values, and Ethics
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to what it means to be a social worker, examining the values, ethics and practice standards that govern the profession across different fields of practice. Students critically analyse the complex history of social work in Australia and internationally including First Nations’ perspectives. The competing theoretical frameworks that define the purpose and place of the profession are examined. Students interview social workers to discover how they apply theory in practice and how they make choices among various courses of action in complex situations. Active participation in these interviews stimulates critical thinking, ethical reasoning, and self-reflection to support students in beginning to develop and articulate their social work identity.
learning_outcomes: Apply ethical reasoning and decision-making skills to navigate complex situations in social work practice.
Recognise personal values and beliefs and evaluate how these align to a professional social work identity.
Apply social work values, ethics, and practice standards in real-world contexts.
Critically analyse the history and theoretical frameworks of social work, and their alignment with the lived experiences of diverse communities.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Journey to Social Work: Digital Story

title: Critical Practice for Child Protection
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course focuses on the integration of critical social work theory and practice and the development of professional competencies for thoughtful, critical, and effective child protection practice. Analytical skills are honed as students examine theories and power structures to understand how social, cultural, and political structures impact privilege, and the marginalisation of diverse cultures and communities. Students evaluate universal and specific risk factors related to child abuse and neglect, scrutinising attachment, and development theories from a critical perspective.Through the industry-engaged “Social Work Big Day In” simulation learning activity, students synthesise, apply, and evaluate legislative, policy and practical knowledge gaining hands-on experience of engagement and assessment techniques and multi-level interventions.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate attachment and developmental theories, risk factors, and protective factors related to child protection, synthesising traditional and alternative perspectives to inform critical practice.

Analyse the impact of intersectionality and power structures on child protection practice, critically examining how social, cultural, and political factors contribute to the marginalisation of diverse communities.
Produce clear, accurate, and ethical professional documentation in accordance with industry standards and legislative requirements in the context of child protection practice.

Demonstrate effective engagement, assessment, and intervention strategies in a simulated child protection setting, applying theoretical knowledge and reflective practice skills to navigate complex scenarios.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Professional Documentation: Social Work Big Day In
Reflection Report: The Social Work Big Day In

title: Skills for Professional Practice
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course uses a range of simulation learning activities to develop interpersonal skills for practice across professional contexts of help, care, service, and support with diverse communities. Students develop universal communication skills for practice including building rapport, active listening, summarising, using questions appropriately and with sensitivity. This course emphasises the application of these skills in a supportive, feedback rich environment, preparing students for the complex dynamics of contemporary practice.
learning_outcomes: Synthesise communication theories, emotional intelligence principles, and interpersonal skills to effectively address complex situations in simulated professional scenarios.
Apply emotional intelligence principles to enhance engagement and communication in simulated professional settings.
Apply advanced interpersonal skills, including rapport-building, active listening, and effective questioning, in simulated professional contexts of help, care, service, and support.
Critically analyse professional interactions using reflective practice methods, integrating feedback to develop strategies for continuous personal and professional growth.

title: Social Work Placement 1
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: SWRK6905 is a placement course designed for students to gain hands-on experience in a social or human service organisation. Over the course of 500 hours, students are placed in a professional setting where they work under the guidance of qualified, experienced social workers. Placement provides an invaluable opportunity to apply social work theories and concepts in real-world settings, develop professional skills, and embody the values and ethics central to social work practice. The course emphasises professionalism, integrity, cultural responsiveness, effective communication, teamwork, and the ability to critically reflect on practice.
learning_outcomes: Integrate social work theories, concepts, and systemic understanding into practical settings, utilizing assessment and intervention strategies.
Apply professional integrity, adhere to social work ethics, and engage with clients and communities in a culturally responsive and non-discriminatory manner.
Engage in supervision to develop self-awareness, manage stress, and foster professional growth, critically reflecting on experiences to promote continuous learning.
Communicate effectively and collaborate in a professional context, adapting both oral and written communication to meet the needs of social work practice.

assessment_tasks.task_name: End of Placement Interview and End of Placement Report

title: Social Work and the Law
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course is designed to bridge the gap between social work practices and the Australian legal system. It offers a deep dive into how legal frameworks impact social work, covering essential areas such as child protection, family law, disability rights, and refugee law. The course equips social workers with the knowledge and skills to navigate legal processes, advocate effectively for clients, and uphold ethical standards within legal contexts. Through a blend of theory and practical applications, students will learn to collaborate across disciplines, enhancing their ability to support individuals and communities within the legal system.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse the reciprocal influence between social work practices and legal outcomes.
Evaluate the complexities of legislation, ethical standards, and professional guidelines regulating social work practice.
Apply relevant legal rules and standards to real-world social work scenarios.
Identify legislative processes, judicial structures, statutory contexts affecting social work practice.

title: Violence, Abuse and Trauma
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with essential knowledge and skills for working with violence, abuse and trauma. It is designed to offer a comprehensive and critical exploration of theory and evidence informing social work practice with individuals experiencing or using violence. The course emphasises reflective self-awareness and self-regulation, and aims to cultivate a framework for trauma informed practice and trauma stewardship that is culturally responsive and ethically grounded.
learning_outcomes: Explain the dynamic and systemic factors that contribute to the experience, use and impacts of violence, abuse, and trauma.
Recognise the need to manage personal responses for ethical practice with individuals who use and experience violence.
Apply trauma-informed principles with cultural sensitivity in diverse contexts.
Critically analyse theoretical frameworks for addressing violence, abuse, and trauma.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Postcards on Violence, Abuse and Trauma: A Journey Through Learning and Reflection
Voices of change: Unpacking Trauma and Transformation

title: Critical Practice for Health and Wellbeing
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course uses a case study frame to examine critical practice for health and wellbeing. The course revisits the simulation activity The Social Work Big Day to explore human development, behaviour and needs across the lifecycle including: (a) Major life transitions (b) Gender identity and sexual orientation (c) Grief and loss (d) Addiction; and (e) Disability. It examines dominant discourses and constructions of mental and physical health and the medicalisation of personal and social problems. It applies theories of ethnicity, race and whiteness, diversity, intersectionality, sexuality and racism, alongside systems and strengths perspectives for understanding diverse cultural understandings of health, mental health and wellbeing. Students work with industry to create a health promotion campaign and learn skills to conduct a bio-psychosocial assessment.
learning_outcomes: Apply theories of ethnicity, race, whiteness, diversity, intersectionality, sexuality, and racism to practice scenarios.
Integrate systems and strengths perspectives in assessing and responding to life transitions, gender identity, sexual orientation, grief and loss, addiction, and disability.
Employ critical practice skills to address complex health and wellbeing issues through the collaborative development of a health promotion campaign.
Critically analyse dominant discourses in mental and physical health to understand how personal and social problems are framed within these paradigms.

title: Research and Evaluation for the Social Services
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course is designed to equip students with the knowledge and skills to conduct practice-based research and evaluation. Students gain knowledge and skills in qualitative and quantitative methods and learn to navigate the ethical landscape of social work research and evaluation. A key component of the course is the collaborative research project conducted with an industry partner, providing a real-world context for students to apply their learning. Students present their findings to fellow students, community members, and industry peers at the annual UON student social work conference.
learning_outcomes: Critically evaluate research literature pertinent to social work practice issues.
Conduct research on practical social work issues with consideration to associated ethical concerns.
Compile an academic research report using appropriate research methods and tools.
Recognise the importance and application of research and evaluation in social work practice.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Peer-Reviewed Journal Article Manuscript and Presentation

title: Advanced Skills for Clinical Practice
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course equips students with advanced clinical practice skills in social work through immersive simulation learning activities. Students will develop expertise in engagement, assessment, and practice responses in complex and crisis situations. The course emphasises the 'use of self' in social work and integrates theoretical knowledge with practical applications, fostering person-centered care and cultural competence.
learning_outcomes: Apply advanced communication skills, including listening, reframing, and questioning, to build safety and connection with clients.
Implement interventions for grief and loss, manage safety and risk, and facilitate client change using trauma-informed and anti-oppressive methods.
Use deep listening, validation techniques, and reciprocal communication to develop and maintain therapeutic relationships.
Critically analyse knowledge, theory, and practical perspectives in clinical practice.

title: Decolonising Social Work
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: In this course you will learn about the history of colonisation, dispossession and child removal leading to intergenerational trauma for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people in Australia. You will explore how this history is relevant to social work and your role as emerging practitioner. Furthermore, through and immersive and critically reflective curriculum including a cultural experience workshop this course will support your understanding of Indigenous ways of knowing, being and doing. The course intends to challenge conventional approaches and your own taken for granted assumptions about working with Aboriginal and Torres Strait people and communities. Decolonising knowledges and practices that promote culturally safe, sensitive practice aligned with the principles of self-determination and social justice will be explored.
learning_outcomes: Apply a decolonised approach to social work practice that respects Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultures, practices, and values.
Critically analyse the significance of country, language, and kinship in social work practice with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities.
Recognise the impact of colonisation on the health and wellbeing of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and its implications for social work practice.
Integrate Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander ways of knowing, being, and doing into readiness for social work practice.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Policy discussion paper on Truth Telling

title: Social Work Placement 2
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: SWRK6911 is a course designed for students to gain hands-on experience in a social or human service organisation. Over the course of 500 hours, students are placed in a professional setting where they work under the guidance of qualified, experienced social workers. Placement provides an invaluable opportunity to apply social work theories and concepts in real-world settings, develop professional skills, and embody the values and ethics central to social work practice. The course emphasises professionalism, integrity, cultural responsiveness, effective communication, teamwork, and the ability to critically reflect on practice.
learning_outcomes: Apply effective assessment and intervention strategies, social work theories, and systemic knowledge in practical settings.
Exhibit effective communication and teamwork skills in a professional context, including both oral and written communication tailored to social work practice.
Demonstrate professional integrity, adherence to social work ethics, and the ability to engage with clients and communities in a culturally responsive and non-discriminatory manner.
Utilise supervision for self-awareness, stress management, and professional development, critically reflecting on experiences to foster continuous learning.

assessment_tasks.task_name: End of Placement Interview and End of Placement Report
Mid-Placement Interview and Mid Placement Report

title: Critical Practice For Sustainable Systems
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course provides a critical examination of eco-social work with an emphasis on the impacts of climate change and natural disasters. Utilising a social justice lens, students will explore the interplay between social policies, sustainable development goals, and social work practice at mezzo and macro levels. The course will dissect historical, cultural, and political factors influencing policy initiatives, focusing on how social workers can effectively engage with communities, organisations, and institutions for systemic change.
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse eco-social work principles and assess the impacts of climate change on vulnerable communities.
Design and implement group work initiatives for disaster preparedness and response
Propose organisational change to enhance sustainability practices in social work institutions.
Develop an intervention plan to advocate for environmental justice in eco-social work.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Policy Submission and Organisational Change Proposal
Groupwork Intervention Design for Disaster Preparedness or Recovery

title: Foundations of Social Work and Human Services
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with a comprehensive introduction to the key concepts, theories, and frameworks that underpin social work and human services practice. Students will explore the historical development of the field, the role of social work and human services in Australian society, and the core values and ethics that guide professional practice. The course emphasises the importance of cultural competence, social justice, and human rights in working with diverse populations. By the end of the course, students will have a strong foundation in the key concepts and principles that shape social work and human services practice, preparing them for further study and professional practice in the field.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the role and purpose of social work and human services in contemporary society, and apply the knowledge and skills required for effective practice.
Apply critical thinking skills to evaluate diverse perspectives and experiences, and to identify and address ethical dilemmas in social work and human services contexts.
Identify social issues and challenges using relevant theoretical frameworks and ethical principles to inform social work and human services practice.
Reflect on personal values, skills, and professional development goals in relation to social work and human services practice, and identify strategies for ongoing learning and growth.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Job Advertisement Analysis and Personal Statement

title: Lifespan Development and Intervention Strategies
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course explores the physical, cognitive, social, and emotional development of individuals through the lens of psychology and behavioural and human sciences. Students will examine major theories and research findings related to human development, with an emphasis on understanding the psychological, social, and cultural factors that influence development at each stage of life. The course will draw on key concepts and principles from psychology, such as theories of cognitive development, social learning theory, and attachment theory, as well as research from behavioural and human sciences on topics such as brain development, social cognition, and family, community and kinship systems.
learning_outcomes: Distinguish between independent and intersecting aspects of physical, cognitive, social, and emotional development across the lifespan.
Analyse the impact of family, community, and kinship systems on psychological and social development throughout the lifespan.
Apply key theories and research findings to analyse psychological development throughout different stages of life.
Evaluate factors that influence social development and interpersonal relationships across the lifespan.

title: Professional Practice in Human and Social Services
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course is designed to provide graduate students with a foundational understanding of the principles and practices essential for professional work in human and social services. Students will explore key concepts such as effective communication strategies, case work and case management, alongside practical skills needed to support diverse populations. The course emphasizes hands-on practice and the development of competencies to effectively serve individuals, families, and communities in various human and social service settings.
learning_outcomes: Successfully integrate theoretical knowledge with practical skills, demonstrating competency in real-world scenarios.
Demonstrate ability to engage with clients using effective communication techniques.
Apply self-awareness and self-regulation skills for enhanced professional practice.
Identify and apply the core concepts of assessment, planning, and management of client cases.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Reflective Practice Journal and Professional Practice Plan

title: Fields of Practice in the Human and Social Services
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
school: School of Humanities Creative Industries SocialSci
syllabus_overview: This course explores the various fields within human and social services. Students gain insights into the specific roles, responsibilities, and challenges associated with different areas of practice, such as child protection, mental health, ageing and disability services, and community development. The course examines the types of issues that human and social service workers address, including disadvantage and discrimination, violence, abuse and neglect, health and wellbeing, and identity and belonging.
learning_outcomes: Identify diverse contexts and key issues in human and social services, including disadvantage, discrimination, violence, health, and identity.
Examine the roles, responsibilities, and challenges of human and social service professionals in different fields of practice, and the importance of interdisciplinary collaboration.
Recognise the nuances of various fields within human and social services, including child protection, mental health, aging, disability services, and community development.
Formulate an emerging professional identity in human and social services, informed by new learnings, practical insights, and self-reflection.

title: Sustainable Tourism Systems
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course examines the critical role of sustainability in shaping the future of tourism on a global scale. Through the lens of sustainability, students will examine the economic, environmental, social and cultural dimensions of tourism systems, gaining insight into governance mechanisms and policy frameworks influencing sustainable practices. Through analysis of global case studies and best practice initiatives, students will develop a holistic understanding of sustainability principles and emerging innovations.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the concepts of sustainability and ethics within international tourism systems.
Examine the impacts of tourism, hospitality and events on destinations and related sustainability initiatives.
Analyse the role of governance and policy in operationalising and managing sustainable tourism.

title: Event Management Principles
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This foundational course provides students with a comprehensive overview of the principles of event management. Through theoretical frameworks and practical case studies, students will explore the significance of events in the global tourism context. With a focus on project management, students will learn best practices for planning, implementing and evaluating impactful and sustainable festivals and events.
learning_outcomes: Analyse management challenges and propose solutions related to implementing sustainable practices in event management.
Articulate knowledge of event management through a reflective analysis of principles and practices.
Identify the characteristics of events and the fundamentals of event project management.
Examine the interests of key stakeholders in events and report on their roles in event planning processes.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Case Study Presentation and Live Q+A

title: Service Management in Tourism and Hospitality
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course examines service features from an experiential perspective, focusing on developing skills in value co-creation to ensure high-quality service experiences in the global tourism and hospitality sectors. Students will apply service management theory across diverse organisational contexts, synthesising insights from service operations management, talent management and marketing management in tourism and hospitality. As technologies are the lifeblood of tourism and hospitality services, the course will also develop student knowledge and capabilities in using technological advances and applications for designing and managing physical and virtual tourism and hospitality experiences.
learning_outcomes: Recommend technologies that increase the efficiency and effectiveness of service management processes in physical and virtual tourism and hospitality service experiences.
Apply Customer Relationship Management (CRM) tools and practices to facilitate and enhance customer experiences.
Appraise feedback mechanisms and talent management strategies for driving continuous service improvement.
Identify service quality standards tailored for tourism and hospitality settings, including the design of servicescapes.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Innovation Proposal and Strategic Impact Analysis

title: Experience Design and Management
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Designing memorable experiences is essential for success in tourism, hospitality, and events. This course examines the creation staging and management of experiences, emphasising the collaborative creation of value between consumers and businesses. Students will explore innovative strategies employed in international contexts that enhance the experience design process through integration of sustainable development principles.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate how the characteristics of tourism, hospitality and event consumers influence effective experience design.
Analyse the concept of experiences and the principles of experience design.
Critically examine the relationships between sustainable development principles and the design of tourism, hospitality and events experiences.
Apply design process tools and approaches to develop experience prototypes.

title: Introduction to Global Tourism
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course introduces students to the study of the global tourism, hospitality and events sectors, providing insight into their historical evolution and contemporary dynamics. Students will learn about the fundamental principles of tourism management within international systems, exploring societal trends and their impact on these sectors. Through the examination of key concepts and theories, students will gain an understanding of travel motivations, tourist behaviour and patterns of tourist flows, as well as trends in destination product development.
learning_outcomes: Analyse emerging travel trends and their impacts on destinations within the global tourism, hospitality and events sectors.
Explore the dynamics of global tourism and the tourism system.
Describe factors within the broader societal context that influence travel motivations and various forms of tourism.

title: Tourism and Intercultural Encounters
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Culture is intricately connected to the appeal of tourist destinations, from heritage tourism and urban tourism to creative tourism and Indigenous tourism. In this course, students learn about the dynamics of intercultural encounters in global tourism contexts, examining contemporary issues and case studies across various forms of cultural tourism in Australia and around the world. With an emphasis on sustainability, students investigate innovative approaches to maximise the benefits of cultural engagement in global tourism.
learning_outcomes: Assess the effectiveness of communication strategies employed in cultural attractions to engage visitors and facilitate cultural learning.
Analyse how culture influences tourist behaviour and decision-making.
Evaluate ethical and sustainability considerations in intercultural tourism encounters, focusing on Indigenous cultural tourism.
Examine global case studies to identify best practices in cultural tourism management.

title: Tourism, Hospitality and Event Economics
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course provides students with an in-depth understanding of the economic principles that underpin the tourism, hospitality and events sectors, underscoring their role in the broader economic landscape. Students will examine both the micro and macro factors influencing economic change in these industries. Through theoretical frameworks and global case studies, students will gain skills to analyse economic factors to make informed decisions for the visitor economy.
learning_outcomes: Identify the role of government and other stakeholder groups involved in the economic analysis tourism, hospitality and events.
Define core economic concepts and their application to tourism, hospitality and events.
Apply economic theories to formulate strategic decisions in tourism, hospitality and events sectors.

title: Tourism and Hospitality Marketing
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: The global context of tourism and hospitality marketing is evolving rapidly, influenced by several key trends and challenges. In this course, students will learn how tourism and hospitality marketing is being reshaped by digital transformation, a growing emphasis on sustainability and responsible tourism, personalised experiences tailored to tourist consumer behaviour, and shifting travel patterns. Through the examination of these trends and challenges, students will gain an understanding of the global context that shapes marketing strategies in these sectors.
learning_outcomes: Critique branding strategies to develop a brand story for a tourism or hospitality business.
Develop a digital marketing campaign for a tourism or hospitality business.
Examine how digital marketing tools shape tourism and hospitality marketing campaigns.
Construct a consumer persona through research on current trends in tourist behaviour and travel patterns.

title: Managing and Marketing Destinations
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course focuses on strategic management and marketing strategies for tourism destinations. Students gain specialised knowledge on the complexities of sustainable development of multi-dimensional global tourism destinations. Through problem-based learning, students gain a deep understanding of destination marketing concepts, including the destination marketing mix, destination and place branding, disaster and crisis recovery, and the roles of stakeholders in sustainable tourism implementation. The synthesis of marketing and communications approaches, provides students with the knowledge and skills to create destination marketing strategies in line with current global tourism practices.
learning_outcomes: Analyse current trends, challenges and opportunities in managing and marketing sustainable destinations.
Apply specialised marketing theories and concepts to create a destination marketing strategy.
Present strategic recommendations to enhance destination marketing, and effectively respond to feedback from destination stakeholders.
Evaluate strategic approaches to marketing tourism destinations.

title: Strategy for Tourism Futures and Innovation
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course examines contemporary challenges confronting the tourism industry, providing students with advanced knowledge and essential skills for professional roles in the tourism, hospitality and events sectors. Emphasising innovation for sustainable tourism futures, students engage in the comprehensive study of strategic management to plan and produce new products and solutions. Through applied projects across multiple tourism sectors, students will develop management skills in preparation for careers that will shape the future of tourism, hospitality and events in Australia and internationally.
learning_outcomes: Synthesise knowledge across diverse tourism sectors to address complex real-world management challenges.
Formulate innovative strategies to address contemporary issues in tourism management and research-informed approaches for sustainable futures.
Evaluate the role of innovation as a strategy for sustainable tourism futures.

title: Leadership for Tourism, Hospitality and Events
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course focuses on leadership in the tourism, hospitality and events sectors. Students will examine the complexities of leadership practice and how entrepreneurial initiatives influence these interconnected industries. Through a combination of theoretical insights and experiential learning, this course equips students with the skills and mindset required to lead and innovate in the ever-evolving global landscape of tourism, hospitality and events.
learning_outcomes: Align leadership strategies with local and global priorities in ethics, responsibility, inclusivity and sustainability.
Produce research-informed critical reflections that integrate leadership theories with personal experience.
Evaluate leadership theories and practices to advance professional development.
Utilise collaborative leadership skills to develop and pitch innovative and entrepreneurial projects.

title: Digital Transformation in Tourism, Hospitality and Events
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Explore the digital revolution transforming the global tourism, hospitality and event industries. This course offers analytical frameworks and global case studies to explore the catalysts of digital transformation. From the evolution of online platforms for travel bookings to immersive virtual travel experiences, students will examine the technologies driving rapid change, and the adaptive strategies employed by organisations to maintain competitiveness in these sectors.
learning_outcomes: Formulate digital strategies that prioritise ethical standards and sustainable development.
Recommend innovative digital solutions to improve business practices.
Evaluate emerging digital technologies and their transformative potential.
Analyse the effectiveness of digital platforms and mobile applications in enhancing customer experiences and operational efficiencies.

title: Hotel and Hospitality Simulation
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course places students in the driver’s seat of hotel management through an immersive simulation package. Tailored to emulate real-world scenarios, this course allows students to synthesise all aspects of hotel operations, such as revenue management, customer service, human resources and sustainability practices. Students will experience the complexities of running a hotel and make data-driven decisions to achieve business success in the ever-evolving hotel industry.
learning_outcomes: Design strategic and operational plans for a hotel business using integrated management principles.
Apply decision-making skills to manage operational challenges that improve hotel performance in a simulated environment.
Evaluate service delivery strategies and propose customer experience enhancements based on performance feedback.
Interpret and analyse financial data to optimise pricing and revenue management in a hotel simulation.

title: Tourism Experience Economies
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course offers an in-depth exploration of tourism experiences through contemporary case studies that reflect current and emerging global trends. Through engagement with destination management plans, the course focuses on the diverse experience economy, addressing topics driven by current industry and government priorities. These topics include, but are not limited to, events tourism, Indigenous tourism, sports tourism, wine region tourism, health and wellbeing tourism, adapting as new experience economy trends arise. This course equips students with expertise in the political economy of tourism experience development.
learning_outcomes: Propose enhancements to tourism experience offerings to respond to shifts in market demand, societal trends, and government plans.
Analyse opportunities and challenges in the visitor experience economy.
Evaluate factors that contribute to the development of unique tourism experiences.
Evaluate and propose strategies for implementing ethical and sustainable practices in different sectors of the tourism experience economy.

title: Destination Management and Marketing
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: The marketing of tourism is a planned and progressive strategic priority to ensure sustainability and enhance global competitiveness. Building upon theories and models unique to experiential tourism marketing, this course investigates a range of approaches and challenges associated with destination marketing. The course examines the challenges of contemporary tourism marketing in the context of the management and marketing of sustainable destinations. Key topics also include the role of destination management organisations and destination communities in experience creation and promotion, and the role of governments in destination recovery following crises. Working through experiential exercises you will undertake research and develop marketing strategies reflective of professional practice in tourism marketing. Work integrated learning is embedded in the curriculum with specialised insights further gained through industry engagement in course delivery.
learning_outcomes: Work independently and as a team member to collect and analyse information to guide your problem solving and decision making
Access, examine and assess the effectiveness of marketing strategies applied to tourism
Examine and discuss the key concepts and principles of marketing as applied to destinations and the tourism experience
Demonstrate an evaluative understanding of current issues associated with destination marketing
Demonstrate skills in oral and written communication as well as critical and analytical thinking in accordance with professional contexts
Engage in tourism and marketing research and inquiry to inform strategic decision making and problem solving

title: Strategic Management for Tourism
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course requires students to apply the knowledge and skills they have developed throughout the tourism major to a contemporary management challenge in specialised sectors of the tourism industry. Students will work in groups to focus on a project that explores the intersections of broad (e.g. events, hospitality, transport) and specialised (e.g. adventure tourism, indigenous tourism, volunteer tourism) sectors of tourism and the professional perspectives of their intended career paths (e.g. policy and planning, marketing, management). This course engages a problem-based approach to develop knowledge of management challenges and to critically explore pathways to formulating strategies in `real-world tourism management contexts. This course draws on career development and leadership theories, and the principles of personal and corporate social responsibility to enable students to defend and justify their decision-making in tourism management leadership contexts.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate critical thinking skills in analysing theoretical and applied perspectives of tourism management leadership and decision-making
Demonstrate an awareness of various stakeholders and varying managerial perspectives associated with contemporary tourism management
Communicate knowledge of tourism management in both written and verbal formats
Formulate appropriate plans and strategies for addressing tourism management issues
Analyse problems and develop managerial solutions to tourism management challenges within specialised sectors of the tourism industry at both national and international levels
Demonstrate a capacity to work effectively in a team

title: Tourism and Sustainability
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: This course introduces and contextualises the phenomenon of tourism within the broader social, cultural, economic and natural environments. It provides a historical overview of the development of tourism, describes the tourism industry and its constituent sectors, presents theories of tourism motivation and tourist behaviour, and outlines different types of tourism and their impacts on the various environments within which it operates. The course engages with the principles of sustainability as they apply to tourism management and planning, and critically examines issues relating to sustainable tourism development.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a critical understanding of the principles of sustainability as they apply to tourism at both a micro and macro level
Explain key concepts and terminology that underpin the phenomenon of tourism and the field of tourism studies
Demonstrate an understanding of the primary structures, functions and operations of industry and government bodies which comprise the tourism system nationally and internationally
Work autonomously and collaboratively to develop scholarly skills including effective research and the critical evaluation and presentation of information related to tourism in written and oral form
Demonstrate knowledge of the relationships between tourism and the environments in which it operates, and the connection this has to contemporary issues in sustainable tourism development

title: Tourism and Cultural Heritage
faculty: College of Human and Social Futures
syllabus_overview: Culture and heritage are intricately connected to the appeal of tourist destinations. In this course we examine the relationship between culture, heritage and contemporary tourism, exploring the phenomenon of cultural tourism from a demand and supply perspective. In examining the cultural dimensions of tourism we focus on two important and interrelated aspects. The first relates to the role that tourism plays in the production and transmission of cultural forms and practices; the second concerns the impacts of tourism on Western and Indigenous cultures. The course is underpinned by a multidisciplinary perspective and explores key theoretical concepts such as power, globalisation, authenticity, commodification, interpretation and representation. Students are introduced to various case studies of culturally informed special interest tourism to examine these concepts. Drawing on a range of examples from Australia and around the world, this course provides a critical examination of contemporary issues in cultural and heritage tourism management, focusing in particular on culturally sustainable principles and practices. Through the assessment tasks, you will apply critical thinking to current practices in cultural and heritage tourism management, and gain experience in researching and documenting cultural tourism experiences and cultural tourism sites.
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the positive and negative impacts of tourism on cultures and communities;
Identify and apply a range of theories which describe and explain tourism as a cultural phenomenon;
Effectively communicate a critical understanding of the relationships between culture, heritage and tourism and sustainability;
Analyse the role that tourism plays in the production and consumption of culture through global case studies;
Demonstrate professional skills in cultural and heritage tourism management through the analysis, evaluation and synthesis of academic research with field observations.
Identify and analyse current issues in the development and management of cultural and heritage tourism products;

title: Introduction to Trauma Care
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview: This course will provide the comprehensive foundation for the Master of Traumatology program by defining the discipline and defining the effects of injury on society. The course also serves as a background for the body region specific modules of the program by covering patients' journeys through the trauma system, including outcomes.
learning_outcomes: understand the outcomes of major trauma including extremes of age; and
analyse trauma systems and optimal prehospital, emergency and ward care;
be familiar with principles of quality assurance process and organisation of disaster response.

title: Torso Trauma
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview: The Torso Trauma course will discuss contemporary management of thoracic, abdominal and pelvic injuries. The emphasis will be on prompt diagnosis and surgical treatment.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate understanding of management of the vast variety of torso injuries and combinations of these
Identify and analyse guidelines, controversies and evidence based strategies related to torso trauma management
Identify an approach to diagnosis and treatment which will allow a smooth transition of trauma patients from the resuscitation bay to the radiology department to the operative theatre
Demonstrate awareness of a more holistic and contemporary approach to the torso trauma patient

title: Post-Injury Critical Care
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview: The course discusses the current intensive care management of trauma-related critically ill patients. It will bring up-to-date information and evidence-based practice in the field of shock resuscitation, fluid replacement targets and management, organ dysfunction and other miscellaneous topics. The lectures are prepared by a group of experienced intensive care specialists. In our field, information from properly conducted RCTs that changes practice is not frequent. Hence our content is based on the physiology and more recently updated therapeutic management and assessment.
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate understanding of the management of the patient at the end of life, prognostication, death and organ donation.
Define and analyse current strategies for cardiovascular, respiratory, neurological and renal support in the area of critical care illness;
Identify supportive measures in the post trauma patient including transfusional therapies, deep venous thrombosis prophylaxis, infection prevention and early physiotherapy; and

assessment_tasks.task_name: Invigilated Online Multiple-Choice Quiz - Part E
Invigilated Online Multiple-Choice Quiz - Part A
Invigilated Online Multiple-Choice Quiz - Part D
Invigilated Online Multiple-Choice Quiz - Part C
Invigilated Online Multiple-Choice Quiz - Part B

title: Musculoskeletal Trauma
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview: The Musculoskeletal Trauma Course will discuss both low-energy and high-energy injuries of the extremities. This course will cover all diaphyseal, metaphyseal and articular fracture management of both the upper and lower limb.
learning_outcomes: Describe typical injury mechanisms of upper and lower limb fractures
Discuss optimal timing, complications and priorities
Recognise limb threatening injuries

title: Neurotrauma
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview: The Neurotrauma Course covers brain and spinal injuries including pathophysiological, diagnostic, management and outcome aspects of both. This course includes a mandatory three day on campus workshop. All costs associated with this compulsory element of the Program are to be met by the student.
learning_outcomes: Describe the pathophysiology and patterns of neurotrauma
Define the principles and outcomes of spine and brain injury

title: Trauma in Austere Environments
faculty: College of Health Medicine and Wellbeing
school: School of Medicine and Public Health
syllabus_overview: This course covers the management of trauma in low-resource environments and extreme environments. It will be of interest to students who will practice clinically in rural and remote Australia. It also covers topics usually described in wilderness or expedition medicine, and includes battlefield trauma, maritime trauma and retrieval and trauma in extreme climates.
learning_outcomes: Apply the latest knowledge of trauma management as used in the battlefield
Understand the organisation of trauma services in rural and remote Australia
Apply specialised knowledge about alpine trauma, challenges in hot temperature environments and principles of expedition medicine
